Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Ānanda, if you wish for a brief instruction from me, then let go of what is unwholesome and cultivate what is wholesome; abandon what is blameworthy and undertake what is blameless; relinquish all unwholesome states and enter and dwell in the final Nibbāna in this very life. “But, venerable sir, how does one know and see so that while abandoning what is unwholesome, one cultivates what is wholesome; while abandoning what is blameworthy, one undertakes what is blameless; and while relinquishing all unwholesome states, one enters and dwells in the final Nibbāna in this very life? “Ānanda, when a noble disciple knows and sees the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the eye, he—abandoning what is unwholesome, cultivating what is wholesome; abandoning what is blameworthy, undertaking what is blameless; relinquishing all unwholesome states—enters and dwells in the final Nibbāna in this very life. When he knows and sees the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the ear... the nose... the tongue... the body... the mind in the same way, he enters and dwells in the final Nibbāna in this very life. “Venerable sir, how does one know and see the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the eye? “The gratification in the case of the eye, Ānanda, is its pleasure and joy. The danger in the case of the eye is its impermanence, suffering, and subject to change. The escape from the eye is the complete dispassion toward it, its fading away, and its cessation. When he knows and sees the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the eye in this way, he—abandoning what is unwholesome, cultivating what is wholesome; abandoning what is blameworthy, undertaking what is blameless; relinquishing all unwholesome states—enters and dwells in the final Nibbāna in this very life. When he knows and sees the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the ear... the nose... the tongue... the body... the mind in the same way, he enters and dwells in the final Nibbāna in this very life. “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! [And] by Nahuṣa...

The employment of Agastya and other Brahmins to carry the palanquin; then, the granting of a curse by the enraged Agastya that Nahuṣa would become a python; thereafter, after Nahuṣa’s fall from heaven due to his transformation into a python, Yayāti was established in Indra’s place; and upon the exhaustion of his own merit through the recounting of it, his descent back down; and then, the onset of anxiety among all the gods.

For the purpose of bringing Indra, Śacī issued commands to Bṛhaspati and others; Bṛhaspati, however, gave them a curse because they had offended him. Fearing Śacī’s curse, the terrified Bṛhaspati went to the shore of a lake to bring Indra back. While Indra was being summoned, Hāritī, who resided on the shore of that lake, made a request to the gods for her own dwelling place. In response, he cast four portions of her into the earth, trees, mountains, and women, respectively, after granting her boons.

The sinless Indra was brought from Amarāvatī to the city of Anaka-saka-da-sa-va-vka-na-kabra for his consecration in the office of Indra. Then, having propitiated Tvaṣṭṛ—who had become enraged by the slaying of Viśvarūpa—through ascetic penance, he requested many sons out of fear of the gods. Then, by virtue of a boon from Brahmā, he obtained a son named Vṛtra. Thereupon, the Asura Vṛtra, having slain the Ṛṣis who were shining with splendor, returned to Pātāla. Because of that deed, the gods were seized with fear and consulted one another.

The composition of mantras; by the command of Brahmā, the gods went to the hermitage of Dadhīci and requested his bones for the sake of the sacrifice; Dadhīci, being entreated by the gods for the sacrificial bones, relinquished his own body through yoga; Surabhī, the wish-fulfilling cow, fashioned a body from the marrow of Dadhīci’s bones using her own tongue; the gods fashioned weapons such as the thunderbolt from those bones; and by means of the *svadhā* known as Dadhīci-palanyā, the gods were granted freedom from childlessness.

Savitrī, having instructed her son Pippala while he was staying near the Aśvattha tree, followed her husband in death through meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Then follows the commencement of the battle between the gods and the asuras, and the commencement of the conflict with the asura Vṛtra. For the sake of slaying the asura Vṛtra, Indra, by the command of Bṛhaspati, performed the Śanipradoṣavrata and propitiated Śiva; [this includes] the ritual procedure for the Śanipradoṣavrata. [The text also recounts] the story of the asura Vṛtra in his previous birth as the Gandharva Citraratha.

The description of Śani’s attainment of the state of an Asura and the concluding rites (*udāpana*) for the Śanipradoṣavrata; the attainment of valor by Indra through the power of the Śanipradoṣavrata and his subsequent engagement in battle with the gods; Vṛtrāsura’s exposition of the code of war to the Daityas who had fled from the field; the depiction of the tumultuous battle between the Devas and Dānavas; the fall of Indra in combat due to a blow dealt by Vṛtra; and thereafter, Indra, whose consciousness was lost, [being restored] by the command of Brahmā.

Indra performed austerities in the form of worshipping Śiva for the sake of slaying Vṛtra; considering Vṛtra invincible by the word of Śiva, he refrained from killing him and, having made friends with Vṛtra for a thousand years, stationed himself near Vṛtra to slay him. Vṛtra was filled with pride. On the banks of the Narmadā, Indra, holding the thunderbolt in his hand, worshipped Umāmaheśvara with the Pradīpa-vrata. However, at the time of Pradīpa, Vṛtra forgot the worship of the Liṅga and fell asleep; due to this loss of his ascetic merit (*tapas*), he became bereft of his splendor.

The frustration of his desires; then, by means of the *vrata* of the three nights (*tri-rātra*), Indra attained his wish. Satisfied by Brahmā’s prayer, the Blessed One spoke to Brahmā through a voice from the sky (*ākāśavāṇī*) regarding the ritual of the Pradoṣa-vrata, explaining how it removes the calamities caused by Daityas and Asuras. In connection with that, the procedure for the worship of Kālī is described. Then, by the command of Śiva, the gods performed the worship of the quarters (*digpūjā*) according to the scriptures. By the power of that, the mountain [was moved] to the northern side.

The piercing [of Vṛtra] and his exit from the body, the description of the falling of Vṛtra’s head, the falling of the body between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers in Antarvedī, and the falling of the head at Mākhva; the subsequent chapters concerning the regions [of heaven] with the gods; the cutting off of Vṛtra’s head after six months of effort; Indra’s attainment of victory; then, despite the report of Vṛtra’s slaughter brought by the Daityas, the recovery of the chariot while the sacrifice was being performed by Śukra’s command; and having mounted that chariot—

The departure of Bali, accompanied by the enemy of the Daityas (Viṣṇu), toward his own abode after the victory over the gods; Indra’s grief upon hearing of his arrival; the departure of Indra and all the other gods, at the urging of Bṛhaspati, from heaven after assuming the forms of birds such as peacocks; their arrival at the hermitage of Kaśyapa and the reporting of their own suffering to his mother Aditi; and the instruction given to Aditi by Kaśyapa, who was entreated by the gods to protect them, regarding the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī.

The description of Aditi’s worship of Viṣṇu; the manifestation of Viṣṇu through Aditi’s performance of that vow; and, after Aditi had offered praise for the sake of Bali’s subjugation, the Lord commanded his own discus and mace—which were present at Bali’s abode—to subdue him, whereupon they declared their own inferiority to him and withdrew.

The narration of how Bali, who had been consecrated to the throne of the lord of the gods (Indra) by Śukra, bestowed the wealth of Indra equally upon the Brāhmaṇas; and in connection with that, the description of how any Indra whatsoever, while seated on the throne of Indra, failed to give gifts, and consequently, upon the exhaustion of his merit, was deprived of the status of Indra; and the account of a certain merchant who, seeing a handful of flowers and other offerings brought for a courtesan fall to the ground through his own negligence, thought, "May this be an offering to Śiva!"

Through his intellect, he attained certainty, whereby all his sins were destroyed; consequently, after death, according to the words of Yama, he reached the station of Indra (Śatakratu) within three and a half ghaṭikās. At that moment, he recounted to the great sages such as Agastya the gift of Airāvata and other [treasures]. After three and a half ghaṭikās had passed, Indra, remaining in his own abode, rebuked Rātri; thereafter, having first rebuked her, he praised Candra, who had been made by Rātri to perform that rebuke. Thus, Indra regained his former splendor.

Having observed his own wealth consisting of elephants, horses, and other riches bestowed upon gamblers, Galendra rebuked the gambler in the presence of Yama. Then, Citragupta, commanded by Yama, described the greatness of that gift and how the gambler became exempt from hell. Upon hearing this, Śakra was delighted and returned to his own abode. That gambler entered the womb of Suruci, the wife of Virocana—the son of Prahlāda. Then Indra, in the guise of a brahmin, [approached] Virocana...

The description of Virocana approaching Bali and begging for his head; the account of how Śakra, having assumed the deceptive guise of a Brahmin, cut off and gave him his own head; the birth of Baka from Suruci after the death of his father named Virocana; and the sequence of Suruci’s subsequent births.

The chapters on the topics of the *Hiraṇyakaśipu* [section]: thereafter, the departure for the world of the husband; the consecration of Bali’s father Virocana upon the royal throne by Bhārgava; then, after the gods led by Indra had been defeated by Bali, Bali’s establishment in heaven and his issuing of commands to all; following that, Bali’s deliberation on whether he should remain in heaven, as expressed in the words of Śukra.

The description of how [Pṛthu], together with all the Daityas and Śukra, returned to the holy ford of Guruṅa on the banks of the Namadā on the surface of the earth and performed many sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha; then, during that very sacrifice of Baṭu, the descent of the Blessed One in the form of Baṭu, who was pleased by the vow performed by Aditi; thereafter, following the rites of his initiation (upanayana) and so forth, his journey toward the cow-pen of Bali; and the description of the hospitality shown to the dwarf-brahmin (Vāmana-baṭu) by Bali, as well as the Blessed One’s acceptance of the earth at that king's persistent request.

The request for three paces of land; when Bali had made his promise to grant him the land, his preceptor Śukra forbade that gift to the youth after first describing Viṣṇu’s true nature. [Seeing Bali’s persistence in giving the land to the youth, Śukra gave the earth to Bali as a reward for his resolve. When Bali had granted the land according to his vow, the Lord described the greatness of the illusory youth, who by two steps pervaded the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings.

Vāmana’s request for three paces of land measured by his third step; then, after Bali’s downfall, the return of the goddess Earth along with Bali to the presence of Lord Vāmana; then, her petition that she, her son, and her own foot—these three—be the places where the three steps of Vāmana might be set; and finally, the command of the gratified Lord for Bali to go to Sutala at the request of Bali himself.

The dwelling near Viṣṇu’s footstep in the presence of Baṅi; herein is the description of the power of the majesty of divine devotion, exemplified by the attainment of sovereignty by a gambler in a previous birth.

In the description of the lineage of Rāmbhogirūpa and the account of the battle between the gods and the asura Tāraka, it is told how the gods, having suffered defeat, went to the presence of Brahmā. There, following a celestial voice that described the necessity of a son born of Śiva himself for the slaying of the asura Tāraka, they were commanded to make efforts to provide a wife for Śiva, who was separated from his consort. Upon hearing that celestial voice, they went to Himālaya to bring about the birth of a daughter.

The contents of the chapters are as follows: the making of the request by Himavat to his wife Menā for the birth of a daughter; Menā’s description of the suffering of parents at the birth of a daughter; then, Himavat’s awakening to the fact that he was acting out of a desire to benefit others; the bearing of the Mother of the World (Jagadambā) within her womb by Menā at the request of Himavat; and the description of the manifestation of the Mother of the World.

...the arrival of the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) with Pārvatī from the Himalayas for the purpose of bestowing [him] upon Śiva; Śiva’s delight in Gaurī’s self-service; Gaurī’s performance of service to Śiva; in the meantime, Madana, instigated by Devendra, discharged his arrows at Śaṅkara; the description of Śaṅkara, pierced by Madana’s arrows, becoming afflicted by passion upon seeing Pārvatī; then, through discernment, reflecting on the cause of the mind’s delusion, [Śiva] himself—

Seeing Madana with his bow strung and desiring to pierce [Śiva], Śiva, under the influence of anger, reduced Madana to ashes with the fire of his third eye. Then, for the sake of restoring Madana to life, all the gods offered prayers to Śiva; subsequently, the day vanished from sight. Seeing Madana burnt, Madana’s wife Rati began to lament. Girijā, following Rati’s request, sat down in a vow preceded by a promise to restore Madana to life. Thereafter, at the very site where Madana had been consumed by fire, Rati— [The text continues with the narrative of Rati’s asceticism and the eventual restoration of Madana.]

The commencement of the practice of austerity: meanwhile, Nārada approached Rati and engaged in conversation; Rati’s deception of Nārada; Nārada going to the demon Śambara to command him to abduct Rati; the demon Śambara forcibly taking Rati back to his own home and appointing her as the superintendent of the kitchen; then, Pārvatī performing austerities with the desire to attain Śiva; and Viṣṇu [dealing] with Brahmā and the other chief demons regarding that austerity.

The performance of the marriage rites with Diti; the return of Brahmā and the other gods to Śaṅkara, who was established in meditative absorption on the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha) on the far shore of the ocean; the hymn of praise offered to Mahādeva by Brahmā and the others; the description of the burning of Madana, who was about to be wedded to Pārvatī, by Śaṅkara—who was pleased by the gods' hymn of praise—and his instruction to the gods regarding the renunciation of desire; and thereafter, while Śiva remained in meditative absorption, Nandin’s dismissal of all the gods, including Indra.

The state of absorption in the bliss of one’s own essential nature (*svarūpānanda-samādhi*); thereafter, due to the power of the penance performed by Girijā, Śiva’s entry into meditative absorption; Śiva’s arrival at the site of Girijā’s penance in the form of a young brahmin (*baṭu*); the performance of a censure of Śiva by the one in the form of a brahmin for the purpose of testing Girijā’s mind; when Girijā, unable to tolerate that, addressed her friends regarding the brahmin, Śiva vanished and manifested his own true form; the conversation with Śiva on the bank of the river; and [the request] for marriage by Pārvatī.

The fulfillment of Pārvatī’s request, followed by the granting of boons to Pārvatī and the departure of Śiva for his own abode; the withdrawal of the senses from the world, and then the bringing of Pārvatī back to his own home with great ceremony by Brahmā and the other gods, following her successful completion of penance at the place called Himavat.

... [the account of] Śiva’s dispatching the Seven Sages to the Himālayas to act as intermediaries for the giving of his daughter Pārvatī; the dialogue between Śiva and the Sages; after the Sages had made the decision regarding the marriage, their return to Śiva and the reporting of that decision; Mahādeva’s dispatching of Nārada to invite Viṣṇu and the other gods; and the arrival of Viṣṇu and the others at Śiva’s presence, preceded by Śiva’s grand preparations.

After first performing the rites of worship and other ceremonies, the departure of all the hosts of gods together with Śakra toward the city of the Mountain King for the sake of the marriage; the description of Himavat’s commissioning of Viśvakarman, preceded by the preceptor of the Ganges (Bṛhaspati), to construct an unprecedented pavilion for his daughter's wedding; and how, upon hearing from Nārada of the skillful arrangement of portraits of all the deities within the wedding pavilion built by Viśvakarman, a suspicion arose among all the gods; and thereafter, by Himavat [to Śiva]...

The return to his own city; the residence of all the gods, beginning with Indra, in their various respective abodes; after the residence of all the gods in their individual celestial realms, the satisfaction of seeing the splendor of the city of Manasā; then, Pārvatī, having donned her bridal garments and placed a necklace in her hand for the purpose of choosing the groom, meditated upon the Supreme Lord and remained there awaiting His arrival for the sake of the marriage ceremony.

The bringing of Śiva with great ceremony to the wedding pavilion at the auspicious moment prescribed by Garga; the marriage ceremony of Śiva and Pārvatī; the lustration (*nīrājana*) of Śiva and Pārvatī performed by Lakṣmī, Sāvitrī, Arundhatī, and other virtuous matrons; then, during the formal rite of giving away the daughter by Himavat, the father, in the context of Manu’s inquiry regarding the desire to know Śiva’s name and lineage, the description of Śiva as the Supreme Lord (*Parameśvara*) by Nārada. ... sa.

The giving away of the daughter by Himavat; the account of the emergence of sixty thousand Vāṇīkṣis from the Brahmarandhra marked by the nail of Pārvatī’s foot during the occasion of the domestic fire-sacrifice performed by Śiva and Pārvatī; and thereafter, the description of the marriage festival preceded by the hospitable reception of the bridegroom’s party by Himavat.

Then, Viṣṇu, belonging to the groom’s party, performed appropriate honors for the various members of the bride’s party, such as Sadya, Caru, Vindhya, Caṇḍa, and others; thereafter, the commencement of the bridal procession took place. During the bridal procession, Śiva and Pārvatī were seated upon a palanquin. Then, all the gods departed for their respective abodes. Following that, Śiva and Pārvatī enjoyed themselves on Mount Gandhamādana. Then, in a secluded spot, Śiva and Pārvatī...

The commencement of the sexual union; the sending of the gods to his side in private after they were overcome with fear and agitation born from that exceedingly wonderful coitus; the arrival of Agni at the time of the sexual union under the pretext of being a messenger, and his consuming Śiva’s semen along with Pārvatī; the description of how all the gods became pregnant by means of the semen emerging from Agni’s mouth; and then, the seeking of refuge by all the gods in Viṣṇu.

At the instigation of Viṣṇu, that [seed] was swallowed by the gods; then, by the command of Śiva who was pleased, the seed was vomited out by all the gods. [This is] the description of how the seed vomited by all the gods became a golden lotus. Then, Śiva gave the command to Agni to deposit the seed in the womb. Thereafter, as the seed-particles entered the bodies of the six Kṛttikās—known as the six star-clusters—who had approached for the sake of receiving it from Agni, who had collected it together, [the seed was deposited].

While immersed in meditation, [Śiva] first attained a state of repose; then, fearing that those drops might cause a lapse in his vow, he released that semen simultaneously into the Gaṅgā upon the summit of Mount Himavat. At the very moment that semen was emitted, the six-faced child was born. At the time of that child's birth, the breasts of Pārvatī suddenly began to flow with milk. At that very instant, Nārada returned to Śiva and related the news of the Kumāra’s birth.

For the sake of seeing that Kumāra, all the gods, together with Śiva and Pārvatī, returned to the presence of the Kumāra; the commencement of the festival for Kumāra’s exaltation took place, and there was the joyful embrace of Śiva and Pārvatī. Then, at the command of Śiva, all the gods set out with Kumāra at their head for the purpose of conquering the demon Tāraka. At that moment, a voice from the sky proclaimed the victory of the gods. In this very interval, the maiden named Senā, the daughter of Mṛtyu, arrived.

The choosing [of Kumāra] by the word of Brahmā; then the description of Kumāra’s attainment of the office of generalissimo; at that very time, Gaṅgā, Gaurī, and Kṛttikā arrived and requested Skanda to become their son, and he established them as his group of Mothers (mātṛgaṇa); thereafter, Kumāra’s expedition against the demon Tāraka together with all the gods; and then the mobilization of the armies of the gods and the Daityas.

In the battle between the gods and the asuras, when the gods had been defeated by Viṣṇu’s lifting of the earth, Kumāra engaged in combat with Tārakāsura in the sky; then, as they stood before him, Tārakāsura discharged his own mass of arrows. [The rest of the subject matter follows.]

[The command that the messengers of Śiva shall lead those [devotees] to the world of Yama; the description of King Śveta’s union with Śiva; and the introduction of the story of the Kirāta regarding the Śivadharma—once, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, the great Śivarātri, while a certain Kirāta named Caṇḍa was wandering in the forest seeking deer and other animals to kill as food, he stood at night near a banyan tree and, without knowing and without effort, cut a leaf from the banyan tree.]

The worship of Śiva situated below; the bathing of Śiva with mouthfuls of water; fasting without effort due to the absence of food; and the fasting of his wife as well, who, because of his lack of food, waits for him; then, on another day, when his wife had brought and placed food on the bank of the river, the subjects [were as follows]:

[The description of the battle between the gods and the demons, including the defeat of the gods; the description of the fierce battle between Kārttikeya and Tārakāsura; the battle of Kumāra; the consolation by Kumāra of Himavat and others who had gathered there, distressed by the sight of the war; then, the severing of Tāraka’s head by Kumāra; and thereafter, [the state] of Kumāra by the body of Tāraka.]

The description of the festival celebrating the victory over the demon Tāraka performed by all the gods, including the single worship of Jayadratha; ... the description of the majesty of Kumārasvāmin; therein, perceiving that even sinners become purified merely by the sight of Kumāra, Yama—considering his own realm to be devoid of inhabitants—approached Śiva after placing Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods before him, and having praised Śiva, he reported that due to the majesty of the sight of Kumāra, all sinful people would attain heaven, thereby rendering his own office redundant. Then...

Śaṅkara’s imparting of instruction on the nature of pure Dharma for the sake of Yama’s liberation from saṃsāra and the attainment of contrary realization; the description of Yama’s attainment of a purified self through Śaṅkara’s instruction; then the offering of praise by all the mountains to Kumāra; Kumāra’s granting of the boon of having the form of Śiva’s vehicle to the mountains; and the great joy arising from the thought that, when a certain deer had been killed and eaten by someone who came from somewhere, it turned out to have been the gift of food from a Kirāta.

Therefore, due to the power of the Śivarātri vow performed even by ignorance, the arrival of Śiva’s attendants (*śivagaṇas*) in a celestial chariot to lead the Kirāta to the world of Śiva; the Kirāta’s journey toward the world of Śiva together with the Śiva-attendants; a description of the origin of the Śivarātri vow; and, in connection with the greatness of the Śivarātri vow, a description of the account of how the son of a widow and a Nāraṇī born from a Caṇḍāla attained birth in another life as one named Vīramadra through the influence of the Śivarātri vow—[all] by means of the Śivarātri vow.

The narration of the attainment of perfection by the kings beginning with Bharata... "Then once, while Śiva and Pārvatī were seated comfortably in their own palace on Mount Kailāsa, engaged in a game of dice, Śiva lost all his possessions and, having been defeated, departed from Kailāsa to go to a forest of penance."

Chapter Nine: Then, after Pārvatī had become distressed by separation following her departure for Śiva’s abode, Nandin assumed the form of a forest fire while she was absorbed in meditation in a secluded place; when he caused an error regarding the worship of the directions of Śiva, Kumāra spoke of the greatness of worshipping the various forms of the Lord of Mountains (the Lingas) amidst various obstacles. Chapter Ten.

In this context, following the glorification of the greatness of worship during the day, there is the narration of the life of the king named Śveta. While King Śveta, who had been devoted to the worship of Śiva from birth, was absorbed in meditation at the time of his death, Yama and the other guardians of the quarters, though possessing the power of destruction, saw Kāla making an effort to slay him with his sword. Then, for the sake of protecting his own devotee, Lord Śiva, with the fire from his third eye, reduced him to ashes. Thereafter, King Śveta arose from his meditative absorption and [beheld] before him—

Not so—[the story continues]: while the wood was burning, Kāla, having become a bee, offered praise to Rudra; Rudra, wishing to strike him, said, "The wood has been burnt by me"—thus explaining the cause of the wood's burning; thereafter, at the request of King Śveta, Maheśvara restored the wood to life.

The praise of the Blessed One by Kālī; then, Kāṭa’s failure to grant a gift to King Śveta, who was devoted to the welfare of others; thereafter, Kāṭa, having bowed to heaven along with Yama and the other deities and having praised King Śveta, returned to his own abode and departed toward the presence of Śiva, preceded by a description of the greatness of the Śiva-dharma consisting of the application of the *tripuṇḍra*, matted hair, the wearing of the *rudrākṣa* beads, and so forth; upon merely being seen by Śiva, [Kāṭa] was roused from his meditative absorption (*samādhi*) by the Lord.

Upon merely seeing Pārvatī, the Sun became invisible due to his state of separation from her; then Śiva’s request for her hand to Śabari; thereafter, Śiva’s dispatch of Kāmavaroga to the sage Ṛṣi to bring him to his father’s presence on Mount Gandhamādana in order to request her hand; Śiva’s formal proposal to Himālaya for the maiden’s hand; and in the meantime, Nārada’s arrival there and his reporting of these events to Śiva.

Now, regarding the chapters of the Śiva-skānda-purāṇa: Chapter 106 describes how, upon seeing Pārvatī’s words regarding her own marriage, Śiva desired to depart once again for another forest out of anger; then, when the Mothers and others, placing Girijā at their head, offered prayers, his anger subsided. Following this, there is a description of the consecration of the divine lion-throne on Mount Gandhamādana by the goddesses. Thus, in the context of the majesty of Kedāranātha, there is a description of the praise of all the Śiva-dharma.
Thus ends the first section, the Kedārakhaṇḍa, within the Māheśvarakhaṇḍa.
Now begins the second section, the Kāmarikākhaṇḍa, within the Māheśvarakhaṇḍa.

In the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka, at the commencement of the description of the majesty of the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) situated on the shore of the Southern Ocean, there is the narration of the account concerning the majesty of the Pañcāpsaras-tīrtha. Within that, is the account of Arjuna’s pilgrimage; therein, when Arjuna had set out to bathe in the sacred fords located on the shore of the southern sea, he was prevented from bathing by the ascetics dwelling there due to the presence of crocodiles in those five fords. Then, having seen Arjuna’s righteous disposition, the ascetics granted him a boon of long life.

Then, having arrived at the Saubhadra-tīrtha, Arjuna descended to bathe; while he was engaged in his bath, he was seized by Rāhu. While Arjuna was forcibly extracting Rāhu, Rāhu assumed the form of a woman. The narrative of how that woman attained the state of being Rāhu through the curse of a Brāhmaṇa—who had been solicited for sexual pleasure along with her four thousand female companions—is described. Furthermore, by the words of Nārada, the dwelling of Rāhu in five sacred bathing places (tīrthas) is described, and subsequently, in the other four.

Having bathed at the sacred fords (tīrthas) and performed the ritual extraction of the local spirits (brahmahatyā), [Nārada] described the deliverance of all the Apsarases. Then, suspecting that Aja was the cause of the obstruction of the sacred fords, he informed the Apsarases that they should question Nārada regarding this matter when he arrived; having said this, he departed for his own abode.

The meeting of Aja with Nārada; following the hearing from the mouth of Nārada of the account of the Lavaṇa-Kuśa war, Aja’s request to Nārada out of a desire to know the greatness of sacred fords (tīrtha-māhātmya); then, by Nārada, after recounting the events of the world of Brahmā, the narration—preceded by praise—of the dialogue between Suśravas Śrauta and Kātyāyana Sārasvata; therein, the Great Sage Sārasvata’s exposition of the essence of Dharma to the Great Sage Kātyāyana; and thereafter, the narration of the greatness of giving (dāna-māhātmya).

The narrative concerning Nārada’s journey across various lands for the purpose of acquiring wealth to fulfill his own desire to practice charity—following his hearing of the preeminence of giving—and his subsequent arrival at the hermitage of Śrīśvara on the banks of the Narmadā while wandering the earth; and, following Nārada’s recounting of his own history to Śrīśvara, Śrīśvara’s description to Nārada of the sanctifying holy sites, specifically the glorification of Stambhatīrtha situated at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean.

Therein: the account of a certain Brāhmaṇa named Śama residing at the bank of the Tīrtha; his giving of the merit of his own Caturthī-vow to the Brāhmaṇa named Subhadra who was staying at the bank of that same Tīrtha, after having offered Śrāddha to the ancestors at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; and Nārada’s reflection on establishing a residence at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean upon hearing the greatness of Stambhatīrtha situated there, as described by his brother.

Nārada, having understood through inference that the establishment of a sacred site at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean required funds, and finding that the means for obtaining such wealth were not apparent, went before King Dharmavarman and spoke words that revealed his purpose. Having satisfied the king by explaining the meaning of a certain verse concerning the six bases [of sovereignty], he provided assistance for the king to accomplish the religious gift (*dāna-dharma*) he had prescribed for himself. ... .

Then, for the sake of obtaining Brahmins purified by the fruit of their charity, Nārada traveled everywhere, thoroughly investigating them, and subsequently proceeded toward Kaṅkāprāma in the guise of a Brahmin. Having arrived there, he assumed the form of a leper in order to test those Brahmins; and among those Brahmins, even as a mere boy of eight years, he gave the correct answers to the extremely profound questions posed by Nārada.

Then, after Nārada manifested his true form, the description of how he installed [the deity] at the great holy site of Mahīsāgarasaṅgama by first providing for the livelihood of the Brāhmaṇas; the description of how, in connection with that, he arrived at the village of Kaḍāpa; and the account of how, when Nārada was washing the feet of the Brāhmaṇas, a guest arrived, and at that guest's request, eight thousand Brāhmaṇas were selected from among those brought there and offered to him.

At the time of the *madhuparka* offering, when the Brahmin Hārīta first placed his left foot forward upon the washing stone, Nārada pronounced a curse upon all the Brahmins, saying, "You shall become fools. The Brahmins likewise pronounced a similar curse upon Nārada. The reason for placing the left foot forward is described; thereafter follows the story of Nārada’s son.

Table of Contents (Mahiśvarakhaṇḍa): Chapters and Subjects. Chapter [X]: Subjects. Therein, the recollection of the account of the Brahmin Cirakārin out of remorse; therein, [the story] of Medhātithi Gautama’s son, Cirakārin.

Due to his knowledge that his own wind had been pierced by the *Prākārakarṇa* mountain, Nāḍījaṅgha, acting on the command of Indra—the lord of the gods—set out to kill his mother, who was an adulteress, for the sake of the indifferent Śakra; however, under the influence of reflection, he desisted from the act. To demonstrate the necessity of this very knowledge, Prākārakarṇa himself, having attained long life, encountered Śakra, who had arrived in the form of a Brahmin within Mount Gandhamādana; through Śakra’s instruction, Gautama felt remorse regarding his mother, who was standing there for the purpose of being killed.

The bringing of Bhartṛiṣeṇa, Indradamana, Ākaṇḍeya, Nāḍījaṅgha, and Vakas into the presence of the vulture; the departure of Gautama behind Cirakārin as he was going near that vulture; and upon seeing his father, Cirakārin’s recounting of the circumstances regarding the breaking of his own long staff, preceded by a statement of his lack of recognition of Indra’s command, and his making a request to his father after setting down the broken branch.

Gautama’s father, Cirakārin—due to his habit of acting slowly—was shown the corpse of his wife and son by a vulture dwelling on Mount Gandhamādana; because the vulture was unaware that it was his own wind (breath), he offered praise and brought them home. Then, at the request of Nārada, who desired to test his patience, the vulture led him to the presence of a long-lived crane (*krauñca*) residing in Lake Mānasa, and there he caused the death of Akāṇḍeya, Nāḍījaṅgha, and Pāka.

[He said: "The eye; there, upon the bank of the lake, as the tax (*dāpa*) paid by the assembled brahmins will result in a rise on the mat (*kaṭā*), so says the author of the prophecy. Then, having seen King Indradyumna, all of them—after making a sign to the tortoise with their eyes—entered into the midst of the water. Thereafter, the brahmins reached the great ocean, and after giving gifts of gold, cows, land, and other riches, they themselves had the city of Mahīnagara constructed by Viśvakarman.

Description of the Installation... To him, indeed, by him, not so; "Of Indra-datta, what kind of sight on the shore? By the gods, having brought a celestial chariot showering flowers—" [Then follows: With extensive detail, Arjuna’s request to Nārada out of a desire to hear the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; Nārada’s departure as a messenger to the abode of Brahmā; the making of Indra’s throne; and the commencement for the purpose of describing the majesty of the Mahī and the ocean in full detail.

In this regard, the following is the commencement of the narrative concerning the events: having expressed his reluctance to go toward Brahmā, he posed a question to Kūrma out of a desire to know the cause of that very [reluctance].

After Indradyumna had remained there for a long time, Brahmā, having descended to the earth after a long interval, related the account of his own previous birth; then, following the performance of hospitality for Indradyumna and the others, and for the purpose of making their identities manifest once more, he offered a wager regarding the location of the earth. Having returned to the earthly realm, Indradyumna approached the vicinity of the small and large mountains situated at the source of the rivers and streams of the earth—all six of them.

Among those who were long-lived, Indra and others went into the presence of Mārkaṇḍeya—who was himself short-lived—to inquire regarding the scope of his own speech and knowledge, asking, "Who is even longer-lived than you, so that we may receive instruction from him? (This section concerns the inquiry into ignorance by Indra and others, which resulted in their distress; thereafter, following the meeting of Indra and the others with the great sage Lomaśa, they learned that although Lomaśa was exceedingly long-lived, he too had become weary of life, and thus they went to Nāḍījaṃgha, who was longer-lived than even he.)

In its vicinity is Tannayana; there, when Indradyumna asked about the cause for the absence of old age and death, Lomaśa described the state of worldly existence and spoke of his own divine knowledge. Then, Nāḍījaṅgha, son of Indradyumna, related the cause of his own long life in order to describe the reason for it—namely, the greatness of worshipping Śivapurī.

Immediately after hearing Somaśarman’s words, [the sages], with intense devotion solely toward Śiva, requested Śiva-initiation from him. Then, for the sake of attaining knowledge of the wind (the vital breath), they also requested initiation from Prākārakarṇa, who was long-lived and possessed the power of moving through the channels (nāḍīs). Having granted Śiva-initiation to them all, Lomarāma led Prākārakarṇa and the others to the presence of an owl named Śivaliṅgadharaṇa. By him, Prākārakarṇa—

The instruction on *sūjā* (the practice of breath control): Then follows the performance of austerities by Mākaṇḍeya and the others as a preliminary to the commencement of *kriyāyoga*; the narration of the story of Indradyumna by Raikva, including the account of his lack of knowledge and his subsequent explanation of the cause of his own long life; the arrival of Nārada before those performing penance; the hearing of the path from him; and the description of the greatness of Viṣṇu through the meeting with Nāḍījaṅgha and others, [all occurring] out of a desire to know the means for one's own liberation.
The introduction: Nārada [related] to them the great [account] of Saṃvarta residing in Vārāṇasī. (Skanda Purāṇa, Māheśvarakhaṇḍa) || 5 ||

Chapter [ddha-d-vada-vaya-ka-da-oṃ]: The instruction that Dīnāra must go; the description of the means for determining the *saṃvarta* [cloud] at Vārāṇasī; having gone to Vārāṇasī with Nāḍījaṅgha and others, the determination of the *saṃvarta* by the means taught by Nārada and the subsequent reunion with him; the granting of permission by Saṃvarta—having been liberated from the curse by Nāḍījaṅgha and the others—to depart for the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; and, in connection therewith...

It contains an account of the origin of the Mahī river; a description of the incident involving Naṅgula, who was humiliated because Yājñavalkya remained at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; and a detailed exposition of the majesty of the Mahīsāgara-saṃgama tīrtha.

From Saṃvarta, [Sūta] heard the majesty of the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; then follows the description of how even birds such as cranes, water-fowls, vultures, and hawks, having approached the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, attained liberation from the cycle of rebirth by establishing divine *liṅgas*. Next is the description of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) according to the Mākaṇḍeya [section], and therein the description of the majesty of the *Indradarśana* horse-headed *liṅga* established by Indra.

[The section] beginning with the *Mahīsāgarasaṃgama*, the *Śatarudriya*, and the *Ādikhaṇḍa*; then the description of the majesty of Kumāranātha; and in connection with that, the introduction to the narrative of Māra’s conduct. Therein, the birth of the son named Vajrāṅga to Diti, who was known as Daśakanyā; then Vajrāṅga’s departure for heaven at his mother’s command, his seizing Indra by the foot, and bringing him back to his mother’s presence; thereafter, the liberation of Vāsava by Vajrāṅga through the mediation of Brahmā and Kaśyapa; and finally, by the command of Brahmā, Vajrāṅga’s engagement in ascetic penance.

The manifestation [of his power]: while he was engaged in asceticism, Śakra subjected Varāṅgī, the wife of Vajrāṅga—who was devoted solely to the purpose of that penance—to various terrifying apparitions and mockery; then, having desisted from his austerity because he had not obtained [his boon] from Brahmā, Vajrāṅga, out of a desire to know the cause of his wife’s terror, caused her to be abducted by Varāṅgī.

Having witnessed the mockery of Vajrāṅga—who, despite having turned away from demonic tendencies through the power of his asceticism—Indra, desiring to do what was pleasing to Vajrāṅga’s beloved wife, once again caused him to perform penance for the sake of obtaining a son. Then, by virtue of that penance, Brahmā granted Vajrāṅga a boon consisting of a son capable of crushing the pride of the gods and brought him to an end of his austerities. Subsequently, Tārakāsura was born from Vajrāṅga out of his passion for his wife, and [the narrative continues] with the hostilities involving that Tārakāsura.

He was one who coveted the kingdom of his father; thereafter, having gone to a cave in the Pāriyātra mountain range with the desire to conquer the gods, he performed austerities. While performing those austerities, the objects of the senses did not disturb him. Brahmā granted him the boon of invincibility against all beings except for a six-day-old child. Consequently, when Tārakāsura had been subdued, his own kingdom came to an end.

After deliberating with his ministers, Tārakāsura prepared his army for mobilization and launched an attack against heaven for the purpose of conquering all the gods. Thereupon, with the approval of Bṛhaspati, Indra, the lord of the gods, organized the entire celestial host for battle. Then follows the commencement of the war between the demon Tāraka and the gods; in the midst of the armies of Tāraka and the gods, the description of the hand-to-hand combat between Yama and Prahlāda is given, including the account of Yama’s defeat in that battle. [...]

In the battle between the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) and Jambha, when the Lord of Wealth had slain Jambha, there was a battle with Ujjambha; in that battle with the Lord of Wealth, the Lord of Wealth was defeated. Then, in the battle between Kujambha and Niketa, Niketa was defeated by Varuna, who bound the two arms of Ujjambha with a noose. Thereafter, when Mahishasura was intent on devouring the flesh of Varuna, [he was countered] by Chandra.

The description of how the spreading radiance of the cool-rayed moon caused extreme distress to all the Daityas; then, observing that the cessation of the cold had been brought about by Kālanemi through the discharge of fire-arrows, the Sun, under the guise of Śambara, took up his bow and, by means of the *Indrajāla* illusion, effected a transformation of the forms of both gods and Dānavas; and thereupon, having fallen into delusion, Kālanemi slew only those Daityas whom he perceived as gods.

Then, having heard the words of Nigina, Kālanemi summoned Mūya and commanded him to wake [the serpent]. Upon being awakened by Kālanemi, Mūya released his coils to ward off all obstacles. Bhāskara, mounting the great pillar of Mahendra and assuming a terrifying form, dispersed the army of the Daityas with the spreading rays of his intense heat. Kālanemi, assuming the form of a dark cloud, produced a rain of weapons; however, through the downpour of arrows and other missiles, all the gods—beginning with Indra—[were protected].

The defeat of Kālanemi: thereafter, having heard the prayers of all the gods, the Blessed Lord Mahāviṣṇu rose from the depths of the Milk Ocean, mounted Garuḍa, and returned to the battlefield; there, after engaging in battle with Kālanemi, he brought about Kālanemi’s defeat. Furthermore, when Viṣṇu, desiring to slay him, fought with Jambhāsuras for the destruction of countless Daityas, [Kālanemi] suffered defeat at the hands of Jambhāsuras and fled from the field of battle, turning his back in retreat.

Then, the stabilization of Viṣṇu after he had drunk [the poison], through a hymn of praise composed by Indra; the description of Indra’s preparation for battle and his fierce combat with the demon Jambha at the command of Viṣṇu for the purpose of slaying him; the killing of the demon Jambha in that battle; and following the slaughter of Jambha, the return of all the Daityas—the Kandirīkas who were terrified by the divine army—to the presence of the demon Tāraka, and then the arrival of Tāraka with his entire host of Daityas at the battlefield.

Having encountered [the enemy] with great prowess, he brought about the total destruction of the entire army of the gods; beholding that [destruction], Viṣṇu informed all the gods and, having commanded their protector, himself vanished. Following the victory over the Asura Tāraka, [the deity] ascended the royal throne with great ceremony at Stambhapura on the shore of the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean (in the city of Khambāyatana). Upon his mounting the throne, the Fortune of the Three Worlds approached him.

The entry [of Viṣṇu], preceded by the bringing back of Indra and the other gods in the form of a boar from Tārakāsura by means of Nārāyaṇa, and the granting of safety to Indra and the others from Tārakāsura; thereafter, having incurred fear from him, the departure of Indra and the other gods toward Brahmā at the command of Viṣṇu; and the establishment of his own Daityas in the positions of Indra and the other gods by Tārakāsura...

Śiva, having gone before Indra and the other gods, made a representation of his own suffering preceded by hymns of praise; Brahmā informed the gods that the Mother of the Universe would descend into the house of Himavat; then the gods, led by Śiva, offered a hymn of praise to the Goddess and made a prayer for the entry of the Great Goddess, the Mother of the Universe, into the wife of Himavat named Menā; at the request of Brahmā, the Great Goddess entered the eyes of Menā; and from Menā, the Mother of the Universe [was born].

The manifestation [of Śiva]; the description of the festival at the time of the Mother of the World’s birth; the arrival of Nandin to Mount Himavat at the command of Śakra (Indra) and his speech regarding Pārvatī’s extraordinary beauty; the seating [of the gods] to generate further satisfaction by recounting the attainment of the boon of Umā from Mahādeva to these two, Himavat and Menā, who were distressed with anxiety; the description of how Pārvatī, with her hands always held aloft, grants protection and fearlessness to all living beings; and [her resolve] for the sake of serving Śiva.

Himavat’s instruction of Pārvatī regarding her marriage; then, Nārada, having arrived from the presence of Himavat, informs Indra of the entire situation and issues a command for Śiva to be united with the Goddess through marriage; Śakra commands Madana to delude Śaṅkara; while Pārvatī was engaged in her service, Madana discharged his arrow at Hara; then, seeing Madana, Hara, who was already afflicted by love, [acted].

The burning of Madana by the fire from Śiva’s third eye; then, at Rati’s request, the restoration of Madana to life by Śaṅkara in the form of Ananga. Furthermore, the description of Pārvatī’s engagement in ascetic penance for the sake of attaining Śiva, following the instruction of Nārada upon his return to the Himālaya mountains. Then, Śiva’s arrival in the guise of a Brahmin near Pārvatī while she was established in her penance to test her steadfastness, and subsequently, the consolation of Pārvatī by Śiva, who, being highly pleased, revealed his own true form.

Then follows the invitation of all the gods by Pārvatī, accompanied by Śiva; there, Śrīdaka arrives having assumed the form of a young boy (*bāṭarūpa*). Upon his arrival, the Daityas such as Tāraka and others who had gathered there are driven away to their respective abodes by the mere sound of the syllable *haṃ* uttered by him. Then all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, return to the wedding grounds. Thereafter, in the presence of all the gods, Pārvatī...

The offering of the Vairiṇa-Māḍa to the feet of Śrī Daṅkara; thereafter, preceded by the unanimous approval of Brahmā and the other gods, a description of the festival for the marriage ceremony of the Rākṣasa and the Vaitāla, performed according to the ritual procedure prescribed in the scriptures.

After the wedding, while Śiva was enjoying amorous dalliance with Pārvatī in a magnificent and beautiful palace during a journey to Mount Mandara, the gods, terrified by the demon Tāraka, offered prayers; thereupon, Pārvatī, having placed Gaṇapati upon her own body, granted him to the gods for their assistance. Gaṇapati then incessantly waged war against the Daityas for the sake of the gods' welfare. Following that, the account of how Pārvatī adopted the Gaṇa named Vīraka as her son is described.

Then, when Śiva called Pārvatī by the name "Kātī" in a joking manner during their mutual conversation, she became angry and rebuked Śiva with words that struck at his most sensitive points. Thereupon, as Pārvatī was departing from her palace, she issued an order to the attendant named Vīraka to prevent any other woman from entering Śiva’s presence. Taking Gaṇapati with her, she then [proceeded] toward Himavat along with her own childhood friends.

The command given by Śiva to another woman, Kṛtamañjarī, who was going to her own husband’s house, to announce her entry; then the creation of a diversion by her; and while this was occurring, the arrival of the Daitya named Andhaka in the form of Pārvatī near Śiva, and his being questioned by Śiva regarding her.
Thus it is said.

The elder Vṛddha-Vākaṭya, having recognized the illusion, placed a *raudrākṣa* bead upon his own penis in the midst of his retinue and killed him through sexual intercourse; then, at that very moment, Pārvatī whispered into Śiva’s ear, near her ear, a cry of distress; hearing that, Pārvatī bestowed a curse upon the host of Vīrakas.

The departure of Śiva from the root of the mountain in the form of a lion; the arrival of Brahmā near Pārvatī as she was performing austerities; the granting of a boon to the Goddess by Brahmā; thereafter, the emergence of a goddess of golden complexion from the body of Goddess Pārvatī; her naming as Kārttikī; then Pārvatī’s recovery of her former whiteness; and then Pārvatī’s journey toward the presence of Śiva, where she was sung about by the Vīrakas stationed at the gate.

Then follows his entry inside and the delivery of the message; having heard Vīraka’s words, Pārvatī feels remorse, thinking, "In vain did I bestow the curse upon him"; thereafter, Pārvatī grants a boon to Vīraka—consisting of the attainment of the status of a son of Śilāda and joy for Nandin—after first recounting her own story.

The goddess, having approached Śiva, engaged in dalliance with him; thereafter, the commencement of the amorous union between Śiva and Pārvatī took place. Therein, at the request of the gods, Mahādeva—having arrived in the form of a pigeon (pārāvata)—was urged by Agni to consume his semen. By that command, Agni consumed the semen in the womb of Aṅgirās. Then, seeing her husband desiring the wives of the sages, Svāhā, assuming the forms of the six wives of the sages—the six Kṛttikās—engaged in the act of love with Agni from his side.

Having taken the semen according to the sequence of the six spokes, its deposition into the *Ṛarartamba* [fire]; the consolation by a voice from the sky of Agni, who was tormented by grief due to exhaustion from union with the wives of the sages; then, by Agni, the casting of the eyes of the goddesses' sons into the sacrificial pit situated within the *Śarastamba* on Mount Cetaparvata—the account of the six wives of the six sages; then, Viśvāmitra’s arrival near Kumāra and the performance of praise for Kumāra with one hundred and eight names; [the account] of Skanda-Kumāra by the great sage Viśvāmitra.

Following the performance of the birth rites (*jātaka*) and other preliminary ceremonies, the rite of naming (*nāmakaraṇa*) was performed; then, after the boy was presented for the king’s inspection and the bestowal of gifts according to his capacity, the prince was beheld by Indra and the other gods. Subsequently, Śiva and Pārvatī returned to the prince and displayed parental affection toward him, after which the prince brought joy to all by fulfilling their every desire.

This is the description of the consecration of Kumāra as the commander-in-chief of the army of the gods at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, with Tārakāsura as the primary foe. Kumārasvāmin makes a vow to slay Tārakāsura; then, having gone toward the city of Tārakāsura with all the divine hosts, Kumāra prepares for battle and dispatches Nārada to Tārakāsura. At that moment, the sound of Kumāra’s victorious war-drum is heard from Mount Kṛmijaya, as he ascends his chariot drawn by peacocks.

**Hearing** (Chapters, Subjects, Verses): Having heard the hymn of praise to Kumāra being sung by the Kinnaras, Tārakāsura, having resolved upon the slaughter of the Rākṣasas who had approached him, consulted with his ministers; then, following the mobilization of the entire Daitya army, he marched out from his own city for the purpose of battle with the gods. Thereafter began the encounter between the gods and the Daityas. In that terrible battle, [the account of] Kumārasvāmin’s defeat of the Daitya host led by Tārakāsura in the presence of Tārakāsura.

The positioning for the sake of battle; the lack of inclination on the part of Kumārasvāmin to act upon Viṣṇu’s advice even though Tārakāsura was a devotee of Śiva; at that moment, Viṣṇu’s instigation of the gods, beginning with Rudra, by Tārakāsura; the arising of Kumārasvāmin’s desire to slay Tārakāsura through a voice from the sky as he advanced against Śaṅkara; and then, for the purpose of killing Tāraka, Kumāra’s departure from Mount Śveta after taking leave of Viṣṇu, [and his engagement] with the head of Tāraka.

Having observed that the Śakti had departed, he discharged his own Śakti upon the powerless Tārakāsura, thereby effecting the slaying of Tārakāsura. Then, at the request of Kera, he reduced to ashes Mount Krauñca, which was filled with Bāṇa and other Daityas along with their weapons, by means of his own Śakti. Following this, there is a description of the joy of victory celebrated by the gods, Gandharvas, and others over Kumārasvāmin.

The description of Kumārasvāmin’s grief arising from the fear of sin incurred by killing a devotee of Rudra through the slaying of the demon Tāraka; thereafter, the account of how Kumārasvāmin, having built three divine liṅgas through Viśvakarman at the command of Mahāviṣṇu, installed within them the Pratiṣṭheśvara and Chidreśvara liṅgas; and finally, the installation of the liṅga brought by Brahmā under the name Umāriśvara by Kumārasvāmin.

After Kumāra’s crossing over, he hears the procedure for the worship of Śiva from Roka; Kumāra performs a hymn of praise to Kumāreśvara Mahādeva; Kumāreśvara grants a boon to Kumārasvāmin; following a description of the eternal presence of Jagadambā in the vicinity of Kumāreśvara, she grants a boon to Kumārasvāmin; thereafter, Kapardin Gaṇeśvara grants a boon; and Kumārasvāmin remains established as a deity in the presence of Kumāreśvara.

Description of the Greatness of Kumāreśvara Mahādeva Situated at the Confluence of the Mahī and the Ocean. Now, following the prayer of the gods, [the Lord] established a pillar of victory (*jayastambha*) at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; on top of that, he installed a third *liṅga* fashioned by Viśvakarman and named Stambheśvara, and constructed the Kūpa Tīrtha. The installation of crores of *liṅgas* by deities such as Jadyendra and Radrāpamukha, and their majesty; then, the description of the life-story of the Siddha named Mahākāṭha; therein, the account of the five *liṅgas* beginning with Māṇṭi, who resided in Vārāṇasī, along with the narrative of the majesty of Siddhāmbikā, Siddhakūpa, Siddheśvara, and others.

While the fetus remained in the womb of the great sage’s wife Caṭikārī for four years, on account of the occasion of the majesty of Barbarīta, the life-story of the maiden Kumārikā—the daughter of a deceased man who had become a *kāraṇī*—was narrated; and observing that the sage had no intention of coming out, Māṇḍitā gave him the command to depart.

Having observed the fetus's lack of desire to emerge from the womb due to the fear of birth and worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), Māṇḍūkī offered propitiation to Śiva; [the text then contains] a description of the origin of the world through the connection with *tamas*, as well as the dimensions of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and the manner of its stability within the *Mūrdha-loka*. ...

Then, O Lord, for the sake of consoling that child within the womb, Śiva—by means of his own manifestations (vibhūtis) who had assumed the size of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) through their power of contraction, and who were stationed in the sky above all the upper worlds—issued a command to his own manifestations. When the consolation of the child in the womb was performed by those manifestations of Śiva, beginning with Dhara and the others, the birth of the boy occurred from the interior of the womb. After some time, that boy, having traversed the distance to the edge of the cosmic egg, descended into the netherworld (pātāla).

A description of the various hells situated below the surface of the earth; a description of the torments experienced by those who commit specific sins in their respective hells; likewise, a description of the entire universe, including its inhabitants such as the gods and the Vasus; furthermore, a narration of the supreme majesty of Maheśvara, who possesses the vast splendor of infinite crores of Brahmāṇḍas; then, a discourse on the measurement of time; and thus, [a description] of the entire creation consisting of the Vedhas and the rest.

The description of the established order; then, in the context of explaining the cause for the pig-like face of a certain maiden born among the nine children of Ratnaśṛṅga—the son-in-law of Araṭa, the son of Ṛṣabha—there follows the narration of how she immediately attained a beautiful countenance by casting her own birth into the waters at the confluence of the Mahī and Sāgara rivers after remembering her past life; and how that maiden established the Vakra-erā (crooked-ear) festival.

The description of the granting of boons by Vaka-reśāna to his daughter named Kumārī; the narration of how that region of Bharata-khaṇḍa, divided into nine parts, became famous by her name as the *Kaumāra-khaṇḍa* due to the gift of one such division to her; the enumeration of the number of cities of the gods located within Bharata-khaṇḍa; and the account of how that Kumārī, having divided her own portions among her brothers and sons according to their respective numbers, established pillars [of authority].

Having returned to the sacred ford (tīrtha), [the narrative describes] the attainment of the boon from Bhavānī—who was highly pleased by the performance of the Kumāraśadharakumāreśvara rite—by that lady through the instruction of Raśadro; the description of the great Siddha named Mahākārṇa residing on the bank of the Sarasvatī; the description of the power of her penance through which she attained the status of the Apsaras Citralekhā; and the description of the majesty of the Liṅga of Vṛṣeśvara.

While Kālabhīti was performing penance beneath a bilva tree at Kāmapanna, Śaṅkara approached him in human form and, having filled up a hollow with the big toe of his foot, created a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) and revealed his own true form. Then, at the request of Kālabhīti, the Lord remained there in the form of a great liṅga. Because Kālabhīti was liberated through the grace of that Mahākāla, and following the prayer for the bestowal of the title "Mahākāla," the Lord Mahākāla, by his grace, appeared in the form of Nandikeśvara.

The description of the account of the Pratihāra dynasty’s rise to power during the day; then, the description by Mahākāla of the instruction on the nature of Dharma, the divisions of the four ages (*caturyuganyavasthā*), and other religious duties for King Karandhama.

Then follows the removal of the doubts of the devotees of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Revā as requested by Karandhama; a detailed exposition of various types of karmas and their fruits; a concise description of the rules for Śiva-worship according to the scriptures; a description of the eternal conduct and daily observances; and thereafter, an account of how the Siddha Mahākāra attained the world of Śiva.

Now follows the description of the account of the greatness of Vāsudeva as brought forth by Nārada; and in that context, the description of the movement of the Aitareya and other *aṇas*. There was a Brāhmaṇa named Māṇḍuka, born of the Hārotā lineage, residing on the bank of the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean. To him, by his wife named Itarā, was born the Brāhmaṇa Aitareya. Although he possessed the perfections (*siddhis*) of a previous birth, in this present life he assumed a state of muteness and remained constantly intent upon the chanting of the Lord’s mantra within the temple of Hāremaṇḍira.
