The granting of boons by the Lord Tārāyaṇa, who was pleased by the exceedingly sweet hymns of praise; the marriage of the Brāhmaṇa Agavalrasapadiniteryan; the description of the gift of land provided after the enjoyment of all the pleasures of the earth for as long as the moon and sun endure; ... [the account of the story of the Sun-god Mādhvāditya established by Nārada at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean].

A description of the ritual worship of the Sun according to the rules through contact with his feet; a narration of the eightfold divine methods, such as the ordeal by heated axe, which produce immediate conviction for one standing before the Lord Āditya; the performance of the *cakrāṅka* (branding with the discus) upon the merchant Nandabhadra by the deity established on Mount Kapi; and a description of the merchant Nandabhadra’s excellent conduct and pure lifestyle, preceded by a reflection on the worthlessness of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). [The text continues with] the True Dharma...

While Nandabhadra, who was devoted to the practice of the *caraṇas*, was suffering due to the absence of his son Dhāyāputra, a certain nihilist named Satyavrata, living nearby, offered long-standing instruction with the intent of causing a split in his understanding. In response, Nandabhadra refuted that opposing doctrine and established the true nature of the deity; subsequently, for the sake of practicing the true Dharma, he returned to Bhadraṭārakasthaṭha, where there were many ascetics of the Bahūdaka order.

Having worshipped the Lord residing on the banks of the Bahūdaka-kunda, Nandabhadra prepared to renounce his own body; however, as he was about to leap from the riverbank, a certain Brahmin boy afflicted by a severe disease approached him and bestowed the instruction of knowledge upon Nandabhadra. Then, when questioned by Nandabhadra, the Brahmin boy recounted the history of his own life and conduct. Upon hearing that instruction from the Brahmin boy, Nandabhadra became exceedingly joyful, and following the teacher’s advice, he [prepared to give] the preceptor’s fee (gurudakṣiṇā).

A description of the account of the installation of Bālāditya by Gurunandin; a description of the installation of the fourteen great goddesses (Mahārākīs), such as Siddhāvikā, along with their retinues, by Nārada for the protection of the Bahūdaka Tīrtha; a description of the majesty of all those Mahārākīs; a description of the majesty of Somanātha; therein, a description of the account of the Brahmin named Ayetapraṣṭeya of Cauḍaderī; and [an account] of the two who, desiring to behold Somanātha, were on the road intent on journeying to the Prabhāsa-kṣetra due to extreme devotion.

The greatness of Somanātha as revealed by the two wandering mendicants on the way; a description of the greatness of the Somakuṇḍa bath at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, and the cave of Somanātha; and a description of the greatness of the pilgrimage to Dāṭakeśvara...

Chapter [X], Section on the Subjects: Pa. In the context of describing the majesty of the various holy places situated in Mahīnagara established by Nārada, there is an account of the majesty of Jayāditya. Therein, when Nārada—having gone toward the Sūryatāḍaka lake for the purpose of beholding the Sun—offered praise to the Brāhmaṇas residing in Mahīnagara which he had established, Sūryanārāyaṇa arrived there in the guise of a guest to bestow gifts upon those Brāhmaṇas present there, desiring them as supreme vessels for the discussion of knowledge.

The narration of the account of how Bhāskara attained extreme satisfaction through the Lord Sūrya by providing very clear answers to the questions regarding the motion of the soul (*jīva*) as established in the Vaiśākhrīya-siddhānta by Kamaṭha, the eight-year-old son of Harīta. Next, the thorough answering of Bhāskara’s question concerning the definition of the ten bodies (*daśa-śarīra-lakṣaṇa*) by means of Kamaṭha’s statement of the definition of the bodies as established by the authority of his own branch [of scripture]; and, in connection with that, the description of the soul’s movement according to the Pāratantrika school.

Then, following the description of the ripening of the karma of the merchant Sarākhagrāmaṇī by Kamaṭha—who was eager for the various fruits of the rites performed by Bhāskara—there is the granting of the correct answer; the incitement to the practice of Dharma through that connection; and the proclamation of his own name by the Blessed One Bhāskara, who was satisfied by hearing the correct answer given by Kamaṭha, preceded by the bestowing of favor upon his son Praśasti, Hārīta, and other leading men residing in that city. Then...

Because of the preeminence of the Brāhmaṇas, the Lord Bhāskara, known by the name Jayāditya, established his permanent residence in that city of Mahīnagara; the praise of Jayāditya through the hymn of eight verses composed by Kamaṭha; the granting of a necklace to Kamaṭha by the Lord Bhāskara as a boon for his protection of the Brāhmaṇas; and the description of the great majesty of Jayāditya.

Next, the description of the account of the greatness of Koṭitīrtha established by Brahmā at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; the greatness of Īśvara, Bharadvājeśvara, Gautameśvara, and the Ahalyā-saras situated near Koṭitīrtha; and, in the context of describing the Ahalyā-saras, the narration of the account of Indra’s flight, his humiliation, and other related events.

Then follows the majesty of Rākṣā, preceded by the account of the establishment of the branch of the Niṣpurusha [temple] for the protection of the site where Nārada had established the *madahīsakhāgara* [liquor]; then the majesty of the Nāradīya-sarovara and Nāgeśvara; and further, the description of the majesty of Dvārakottara-hārakā.

[The contents of the chapters: Chapter 1: The arrival of the Nāgas; Chapter 2: The arrival of the Nāgas; Chapter 3: The account of the establishment of the venerable Nārada Muni at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; in connection with that, the meeting of Vābhravya and Arjuna; Chapter 4: The excellence of Ghaṭotkaca’s palace in Kāmakarṭaṅkaṭā; Chapter 5: [The encounter] of Ghaṭotkaca with Kāmakarṭaṅkaṭā.

Through Bābhravya, by means of the occasion of installing the image of Nārada made of *arjuna* wood, and preceded by the narration of the dialogue between Ugrasena and Śrī Kṛṣṇa, [the king] was rendered speechless by the Lord via the narration of unprecedented stories while remembering Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Then, for the sake of removing the distress of Ugrasena through the means of war, preceded by the narration of the praise of Nārada, the performance of the hymn of the eight verses to Nārada (*nāradāṣṭaka*) is described; [and finally], having defeated that Kāmakaṭakaṭā and having mounted upon her back...

The narration of the arrival of Nārada and his discourse on the worship of Viṣṇu-Kṛṣṇa in the presence of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍavas; the description of the majesty of Nārada; the arrival of [Nārada]; then the marriage of Ghaṭotkaca and Kāmakaṭaṅkaṭā; thereafter, in the forest of Hiḍimba, Ghaṭotkaca hears from the mouth of Vābhravya about the birth [of himself] and the majesty of Nārada, and after performing a great sacrifice, he establishes his sovereignty over the kingdom of the Rākṣasas in the sacred field of Rāpta; [the account of] Ghaṭotkaca [residing] with Kāmakaṭaṅkaṭā.

The bending of the eyebrows out of a desire to hear the account of the daughter named Barbarīkā; the narration by Nārada to Arjuna of the greatness of the goat that was the vehicle of the sage Gautama while he resided at Guptakṣetra; and, in the course of that narration, a detailed description of the nature and characteristics of the principles of Yoga. ... ... |

Then follows Ghaṭotkaca’s departure for the city of Dvārakā to see Śrī Kṛṣṇa, taking his son Bāṇa with him; then the description of the greatness of the Lord of Brahmāsaras at Mahīnagara-kāpyūta, established by Nārada; thereafter, Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s brief exposition of the fourfold duties (*cāturvarṇya-dharma*) to Bāṇa, followed by the description of the greatness of Mokṣeśvara—a name for Vyakropanagaśvara—attained through the practice of the warrior code (*kṣatra-dharma*), victory, and other means.

The bestowing of the name Sudṛḍhaya upon Kavaṭaprāpta after instructing him in the worship of the Goddess; then, by the instruction of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, [the account of] Kedāra wandering and the majesty of Nīṭakaṇṭha.

Having come to the burnt *sthaṭī* at the *gapa-kṣetra* with his compassionate wife, he performed the propitiation of the goddesses; then, by the permission of the well-pleased goddesses, the description of the reason for which that confluence of the Mahī and the ocean came to be established under the name *gapa-kṣetra* is told. While staying right there out of compassion for the world, during the spring season (*madhupaka-samaya*) in the context of describing the greatness of sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha-kṣetra*), he [the sage] spoke before Siddhāmbikā at the hermitage named Vijaya.

Upon arriving at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, as he set out to accomplish the Great Vidyā, Suhaṭadaya rendered assistance for the sake of warding off obstacles. While his own face was being applied to his own navel by Dharma—the eldest son of Brahmā—for the purpose of remaining unmanifest, [the narrative describes] how, at the outset, the Brahmin Vijayan performed the worship of Gaṇeśvara for the sake of accomplishing the Great Vidyā.

The granting of the gift; then, following the hearing of that curse, Guha’s arrival there and his recounting of the dream as told by him; then the description of the origin of Gaṅgeśvara Kṣetrapāla; the description of the procedure for the worship of Kṣetrapāla and others; then the departure [of the deity]; then Dharmagupta’s seeking forgiveness for his transgression before Guha with hymns of praise; the accomplishment of the Vaṭayakṣiṇī-vidyā by the Brahmin Vijaya at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean;
and thereafter, the accomplishment of the Aparājitā-mahāvidyā...

[The narrative] concerning the origin of the place known as Stambhatīrtha, preceded by a description of its fame and the story of Kaṣatra’s cow-shaped [form], which was suppressed by Mava through the name of Stambhatīrtha— Now, at the end of the first watch of the night, after the destruction of obstacles, there is the narration of the greatness of the confluence of the Mahī and the Sāgara (the ocean), which is a synonym for Ghaṭotkaca; the account of Arjuna’s completion of his pilgrimage to the holy ford (tīrthayātrā); the subduing of him by the son of Damana; and then, at the time of midnight, [the arrival] of one who had come to cause obstacles.

The description of Ghaṭotkaca, the son of Bhīma; his subduing by Aśvatthāman, the son of Droṇa; then, at the end of the third watch, the arrival of the one named Duḥśalā for the purpose of performing the marriage ceremony; then the majesty of Siddhāmbikā at Siddheśvara; in connection with that, the meeting of Ghaṭotkaca, the son of Bhīma, with the Pāṇḍavas during their pilgrimage to the Pāṇḍava-tīrtha; then the consultation regarding the marriage arrangements of the Pāṇḍavas with Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

Then, having heard the account of the one named Kāmakaṭaṅkaṭā from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Ghaṭotkaca’s marriage to her was arranged following his victory; with the permission of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the others, Ghaṭotkaca set out for the city of Prāgjyotiṣa. When she was killed along with her army, the fame of the demon named Duḥsaha, who resided there, was described. Then, in the fourth watch of the night, [the encounter] of him who had arrived to cause obstacles...

[The killing of the Daitya] who was wearing the guise of a Kṣapaṇaka, who subsisted on cloth, and who was accompanied by a Daitya army of ninety million, by the son of Bhīma (Bhīmasena) who followed him into the secret cave of Pātāla with a compassionate heart; and furthermore, the gratification of the gods by that slaying of the Daitya as heard [by them].

The granting of a boon for the sake of the welfare of the world; then, by way of the path prepared by the Naga maidens who worship the jewel-tipped mountain situated at the bottom of the netherworld (Pātāla), the arrival of Suḍṛḍhadayā on the surface of the earth before the city of Siddhāmbikā; her return to the presence of the Brahmin named Vijaya; thereafter, the bestowing of blessings upon Suḍṛḍhadayā by the highly pleased Brahmin Vijaya, who was endowed with the perfection of all great Vidyās; and then, for the purpose of protecting the Pāṇḍavas in the forthcoming battle...

[This is] the first chapter on the naming of Siddhasena as "Sudṛḍhadaya" (of firm heart) by the Goddess herself, following the acceptance of the vermilion, the tuft of hair, and the sacrificial ashes bestowed by Vijaya Brāhmaṇa, with the permission of both the gods and the goddesses. Now, while Siddhasena remained in the presence of the Goddess Siddhāmbikā, intent upon her worship, Bhīma—extremely distressed by the circumstances of his exile in the forest—stood before the Goddess among the Pāṇḍavas and entered the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*); thereupon, Siddhasena became exceedingly enraged.

Having fought with Bhīma, he caused Bhīmasena to be worn out; then, as Siddhasena was about to cast Bhīmasena into the ocean after seizing him, the Lord Rudradeva approached him in the sky and described to Siddhasena that Bhīmasena was his own grandfather. Upon hearing those words of Rudra, Siddhasena, filled with joy, begged for forgiveness for the offense committed against Bhīmasena. Then Bhīmasena embraced his grandson. Now...

Siddhasena, despondent due to the fault of his offense against his grandfather, set out toward the ocean with the intent of sacrificing his own life; Bhīmasena also followed after him in order to dissuade him. Then, by the goddesses Siddhāmbikā and others, who were accompanied by Rudra, Siddhasena was consoled and given the name Caṇḍiṣeṇa. Bhīma, together with Caṇḍiṣeṇa, went into the presence of Yudhiṣṭhira and the other Pāṇḍavas and reported the entire account of what had occurred.

Description of the Greatness of the Excellent Rudra-liṅga Established by Bhīma as Bhīmeśvara; then, having heard the hymn composed by Yudhiṣṭhira to Siddhāmbikā, Bhīmasena, perceiving that Yudhiṣṭhira was intent on praising his own self, rebuked him; subsequently, due to the insult caused by that dejection, Bhīmasena suffered a physical deformity, whereupon Bhīma offered a hymn to Siddhāmbikā, the Mother of the World, to seek forgiveness for his transgression; thereafter, the Mother of the World granted him a boon; then, by that dejected [Bhīma]... [his own]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the narrative flow up to the point of interruption.)

Through various manifestations (*nibhittāntara*), by means of different names and locations—such as Lohāṇāsthaka, Keṭeśvarī, Durgāvatteśvarī, Gayatā, and so forth—the text describes his dwelling in that region, followed by the granting of fearlessness to all the Pāṇḍavas; and after establishing Veṣerīka there at that very spot for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas alone, he undertakes a pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*). Om Om Om Kai Kai.

Which chapters and what subjects? Now, after thirteen years, when the Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas had arrived at the field of battle with their armies for the purpose of regaining their respective kingdoms following the forest exile—among them...

When the counting of heroes capable of slaying their own brothers-in-law’s armies had reached its conclusion, Caṇḍaṭa—the son of Ghaṭotkaca—having previously made a vow before the Goddess to display his own extraordinary prowess, discharged an arrow that joined together all the arrows in the sky, resembling a mass of clouds, thereby causing the destruction of the entire army. This was accomplished by means of a magical weapon called Vijaya, bestowed upon him by a Siddha named Nābhāga. Now, for all [the warriors], this was...

While a great cry of "Well done! was breaking forth from Yudhiṣṭhira and the others, preceded by a surge of grief, Kṛṣṇa suddenly severed the head of Ghaṭotkaca’s son with his own discus. Then, as Kṛṣṇa cut off that head, the Siddhas in that assembly praised him for having thus relieved the Pāṇḍavas and others who were overwhelmed with sorrow, as well as Ghaṭotkaca himself.

The arrival of the fourteen goddesses, beginning with Ambikā; their consolation of all present by recounting the history of the yakṣa named Suvarcās, who had been born as Caṇḍīḍasa through his own past deeds; then, the account of how Śrī Kṛṣṇa severed his head; and finally, the immortalization of that head by the Goddess through the sprinkling of nectar.

Then, Śrī Kṛṣṇa granted a boon to Caṇḍikarṣi, who was in the form of a head; then, by the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Barbarīka climbed a mountain peak near the battlefield and observed the battle between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas; then, the conclusion of the great Bhārata war.

Immediately thereafter, after Śrī Kṛṣṇa—having manifested as a certain Supreme Person whose form is non-different from Hari—to confirm that the entire army had been destroyed by another Supreme Person through the mouth of Barbaroka, he related the account of how Bhīma’s pride was removed by the respectful handling of the skull-bowl of Baka, who had remained hidden in the sky. Then, having arrived at the field of battle, Śrī Kṛṣṇa granted a boon to Ghaṭotkaca’s son, Varabairika. Then...

The Praise of Barbarīka; the Greatness of the Worship of Barbarīka; then the Greatness of Kedreśvara situated in Mahīnagara; the Greatness of Atraiśvara; the Greatness of Nīṭakaṣḍeśvara; the Greatness of Jayāditya; and thus the declaration of the fruits of hearing, reciting, and so forth, regarding the Greatness of the Milk-Ocean at the confluence of the Madī and the Sea—known by the synonym Guptakṣetra, consisting of seven hundred *krośas*. Thus ends the second section, the Kaumārikākhaṇḍa, within the Madaśavarakhaṇḍa.

Speak, O Vaṭaka! Here, in the third section concerning the greatness of Aruṇācala within the Mahiṣa-khaṇṭa, the subjects are: the conclusion of the chapter; the meditation upon the Lord in the form of Aruṇācala; and the description of the identity between the Lord and the mountain. Thus ends the first part.

The narration of the dialogue between Brahmā and Sanaka, occurring at the commencement of the Sūta’s discourse on the *Aruṇācala-māhātmya* when he was questioned by the forest-dwelling sages out of a desire to hear the greatness of Aruṇācala; the description of the commencement of the exposition of the *Aruṇācaleśvara-māhātmya* by the Lord Brahmā—preceded by meditation upon the Tejasa-Śivaliṅga—at the request of Sanaka, who had inquired about the majesty of the Tejasa-Śivaliṅga; and therein, the purification of Viṣṇu and Brahmā.

While the two were fighting against one another, preceded by the desire for self-glorification, there appeared between them the Lord in the form of a pillar of fire; and through His speech, they were diverted from their combat. Then, having gone in the form of a boar to the bottom of that infinite Lord who was a pillar of fire in order to determine its lower limit, and having reached despair because He could not find the end of the Infinite One, he returned to his former place. [Likewise,] he went to determine the upper limit.

After Brahmā, having assumed the form of a swan, became despondent because he was unable to find the end of Ananta—that is, to determine his limit—he learned of Ananta’s true infinity from the words of the Siddhas dwelling in the upper world; then, returning to his rear, he stood before the Blessed One and described the situation.

Oṃ Bha. Now follows the hymn to the Lord consisting of the Pillar of Fire (Vahni-stambha) by Brahmā and Viṣṇu; then the granting of boons to Brahmā and Viṣṇu by the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) who consists of the Pillar of Fire; the description of His own form by the Supreme Lord as the Pillar of Fire at the request of Brahmā and Viṣṇu; and therein, the description of the conduct of the Lord of Aruṇādri, wherein the Goddess, the Mother of the World, once closed the three eyes of Śiva in the course of their secret play.

When the three eyes of Pārvatī—which possess the forms of the moon, the sun, and fire—were closed by her husband, there occurred an untimely destruction of the entire world. At that time, the Siddhas, who were non-dualists whose vision was awakened by asceticism and whose eyes of wisdom were fixed upon the root of the tree of penance, perceived that this was the dissolution of the world caused by the Lord Sāmbasadāśiva. Having heard the hymn of praise offered by the Siddhas with folded hands, and perceiving through his own power that the period of ten million days had elapsed, [the Lord brought about] the dissolution of the world.

When it was said to Pārvatī, "O Daughter of the Mountain, you have committed this improper act," Pārvatī performed penance to remove the sin born of her intention to destroy the world; having thus dispelled her distress, the Blessed One instructed her through the teachings of the ninth chapter of the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* and granted her permission to perform austerities. Then, by the command of Śrī Śaṅkara, Pārvatī went to the Icāmrataṅa forest on the banks of the Kampaṇadī river in Kāñcīpurī for the purpose of performing penance.

Then, having installed a sand Śivaliṅga at the foot of an *ekāmra* tree situated on the bank of the Kampā river, Pārvatī performed austerities while following her own religious duties; then Śaṅkara [appeared].

In order to test her firm devotion, Śiva caused the entire region to be flooded by the surge of a river in flood. Fearing that the current might sweep away the earthen *liṅga* of Śiva, Pārvatī firmly grasped it; yet, even as she was being surrounded by the torrential flow, she did not abandon the *liṅga* to go elsewhere. Due to Pārvatī’s firm embrace, the earthen *liṅga* became marked with the imprint of the nipples from Pārvatī’s breasts. Then, a voice from the sky comforted Pārvatī and granted her a boon for the worship of that earthen *liṅga*.

Having bestowed [the boon], she went toward Aruṇācala and, by the instruction of Gautama, granted permission for the performance of penance. Then, to the sages and gods who had arrived there at the bank of the Kāverī river for the purpose of seeing her and for service, Pārvatī gave the command to worship the sand-Śivaliṅga. Thereafter, Pārvatī, together with all the gods, proceeded to the hermitage of the great sage Gautama on Mount Aruṇādri.

Then follows the reception and hospitable honoring of Pārvatī by the great sage Gotama; at the request of Pārvatī, the great sage Gautama’s description of the majesty of Aruṇācala; and, in connection with that, a description of the account of the majesty of Bahāpuṣkara. [Thereafter] follows a detailed description, preceded by their respective accounts, of the various sacred sites (tīrthas) established at Aruṇācala by the hosts of gods beginning with Śrī Mahāviṣṇu, as well as by the multitudes of great sages and royal sages.

Then, when the reason for the presence of the name Pārvatī on the linga made of cloud was asked, the Great Lord sang this hymn, which describes the different names of the Lord according to the four ages.

Therein is the description of the account of the Lord Śītaṭāṭārāma, performed by the gods through hymns of praise; then, the narrative concerning the eight sacred bathing places (tīrthas) situated in the eight directions established by the eight world-protectors (lokapālas) at Aruṇācala; then, the description of the unification of all those sacred bathing places by Maheśvara at the request of Mārkaṇḍeya; and finally, after Pārvatī, being highly pleased upon hearing the majesty of the sacred bathing places, inquires about the worship of the venerable Supreme Lord (Śrī Parameśvara) and addresses Gautama with a request for instruction.

Then, by the great sage Gautama, the venerable Śaṅkara revealed to Pārvatī his own account beginning with the descent of the Lord as a child out of divine grace; this is followed by a description of the greatness of worshipping the goddess Aruṇācalēśvarī, as taught in the *Śrīśaṅkarabhārātāgama*.

The description of the various names of Śoṇādri by Śrīṅkara; then, the narration of the greatness of the circumambulation of Śoṇādri; in connection with the greatness of the circumambulation of Śoṇādri, the account of King Dharmaketu; the description of the greatness of offering various services to the Lord; and [the account of] Gautama approaching the Lord and the Goddess named Pārvatī, known as Apītakucā, for the purpose of undertaking ascetic initiation.

The narration of the future events beginning with the return [of the gods], the instigation of the goddess Pārvatī; then, the description of Pārvatī performing penance according to the prescribed rules while residing for some time at Gautama’s hermitage, having been encouraged by Gautama in the midst of the sages; then, the arrival of all the gods, headed by Indra, who were terrified of Mahiṣāsura, before the Goddess as she was practicing austerities there; and the dialogue between Indra and the Goddess.

Perceiving that the gods were terrified by the oppression of the demon Mahiṣāsura, the Goddess, having observed the dejection of the gods, made a vow for the slaying of Mahiṣāsura and brought comfort to the gods. Having received consolation from the Goddess, when the gods had departed, the Goddess established four Caṇḍeśvaras on the mountains in the four directions surrounding herself in order to protect her own person. Furthermore, she issued a command for her four personal attendants to go as quickly as possible toward Aruṇādri. Thus it is said.

Having established the arrangement, [the narrative describes] Pārvatī’s performance of penance in the vicinity of Gautama’s hermitage; then, due to the power of Pārvatī’s penance, the description of universal tranquility in that hermitage; and then, once upon a time, [the arrival] of Mahiṣāsura as a deer.

The meaning is as follows: First, the sporting in the vicinity of the ocean; then, Mahiṣāsura, obstructed by the young students at the abode of the Goddess, approached her in the guise of a guest seeking food and, after offering praise, announced his intention to choose her as his bride to his master. Next, the Goddess expressed her own inclination to Mahiṣāsura for the sake of battle. Upon seeing Mahiṣāsura ready for combat, that Jagadambā (Mother of the World), who had assumed the form of a maiden, displayed her terrifying and beautiful form.

Her manifestation in physical form; the summoning of his own army by the demon Mahiṣāsura; the Goddess’s display of various weapons against the enemy; seeing the Goddess’s true form, Mahiṣāsura fled in fear, whereupon the Goddess dispatched the monkey-faced Bṛhaspati to forbid his retreat; hearing the Goddess’s command as spoken by the monkey-faced one, the extremely enraged Mahiṣāsura fought with the Goddess on Mount Aruṇācala and was slain along with his entire Daitya host.

Upon seeing the army of the Daityas approaching, the Goddess, by means of her own splendor, caused the host of various beings—the Ṭaṅkaṇas, Mātaṅgas, Yoginīs, and others—to assume their forms. A description of the fierce battle between the Daitya army and the Goddess’s army follows; therein, in that battle, the commencement of the fight with Mahiṣāsura and the Goddess is described. The subjects of the Goddess’s victory include the slaying of the Asura Mahiṣa by the Goddess in their battle. Then, Durgā, the crusher of Mahiṣa, was praised by Indra and the other gods. And then—

The description of the Goddess’s hand being placed upon the head of the bird (Garuḍa) as she stood before Mahiṣāsura; then, the Goddess, the Mother of the World, thinking that the slaying of a devotee of Śiva had occurred by her own hand, makes a formal resolve for a pilgrimage to sacred sites and announces it before Gautama; thereafter, Gautama, after first pacifying the Goddess’s mental agitation, recounts the slaying of Mahiṣāsura and describes the means for removing the fault [of killing a devotee] through the performance of a pilgrimage to the sacred site at the peak of Aruṇācala.

Then, having fashioned Khaḍgatīrtha with his own sword while chanting the *ākāḍavāṇī* mantra, he performed an immersion there for the duration of the month of Kārtika. On the bank of Khaḍgatīrtha, he installed the Liṅga situated upon the head of the demon Mahiṣāsura, which had fallen from his own hand. Then, in the month of Kārtika under the constellation Kṛttikā, he offered a hundred thousand arrows to the Lord Aruṇādrīśvara. Thereupon, the gracious Lord Aruṇādrīśvara manifested in the form of light and, appearing as the golden Puruṣa within that light, bestowed a boon upon Jagadambā.

Then, the performance of circumambulation by the Mother of the World (Jagadambā) around the Lord of Aruṇādri; thereafter, the description of the meeting of the Mother of the World with the blessed Lord Śoṇādrīśvara, who was pleased and accompanied by Saṅkara; then, the application of musk-paste upon Pārvatī’s body by Śiva, out of a desire to sport with her after having first granted boons to Pārvatī; the narration of the origin of the musk and the account of the life of the Daitya named Puṭaka; and [the story] of the tortoise that arose from the hand of the Goddess.

The narrative; the prayer addressed to Śiva by Pārvatī for the sake of increasing the majesty of the Aruṇācala mountain—whose greatness had been proclaimed through her attachment to it; the granting of boons to Pārvatī by Śiva; and the description of the supreme majesty of the Lord of Aruṇādri. Thus ends the first half of the third section, the *Aruṇācalamāhātmya*, within the *Māheśvarakhaṇḍa*.
Now, in the third section of the Māhervara-khaṇḍa, [this is] the latter part of the *Āruṇācala-māhātmya*.

(—) In the dialogue between Sūta and Loma-harpaṇa, the commencement of the conversation between Mārkaṇḍeya and Nandīśvara; therein, the description of the introduction to the majesty of the sacred site (*sthānamāhātmya*) in the form of a prayer offered by Mārkaṇḍeya, accompanied by various eminent sages, to Nandikeśvara with the desire to hear the details of the divine sports (*līlā*). Herein [are contained] the subjects of the chapters. (End of Chapter 1).

Then follows the description by Nandikeśvara of the various sacred fields (*kṣetra*) and shrines (*tīrtha*) situated within the Araha maṇḍala, which has become the abode of Śrī Śiva; his departure for the heavenly realm (*svarga*); and the purification of the lower part of the *liṅga*, after which he returned from there. Then Mārkaṇḍeya, desiring to know all the locations that grant the fruit of sacrificial sessions (*satra*), returns once again to the eastern region and approaches Nandikeśvara.

This treatise provides the means for those groups of great sages who are eager to hear [the truth] that purifies all sins. Now, in order to determine the extent of the limits of his effulgent form, Brahmā assumed the form of a swan and ascended upwards. Then, having praised Mārkaṇḍeya together with his disciples, Nandikeśvara departed from the Draviḍa country in the southern direction toward Śoṇa. There, he beheld Brahmā, who had gone a very great distance ahead of him.

[The description of] the extensive and great majesty and *māhātmya* of the sacred site of the glorious Aruṇācala, ending with the arrival of the sages. Then, by Nandikeśvara, for the sake of strengthening devotion to Śiva, in the context of describing the *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* dispositions of persons—having approached the abode of Brahmā together with the wind-god Māthita and the Ketaka flower—the description of the ripening of various karmas [is told]. ...oṃ... [End]... [Beginning].

The offering of *ketakī* leaves mixed with water to Viṣṇu at the conclusion of the *liṅga* rite; the swearing of an oath for the purpose of averting false testimony; the selection of various penances (*prāyaścitta*) such as bathing in the waters of the Kaḍamaṅā river for the removal of sin; and, in connection with this, the description of the splendor of the Lord residing on the glorious Guṇācala mountain, who is to be worshipped through various duties—now, by Viṣṇu, having determined that [the matter] was false, the description of his own splendor for the sake of bathing and the cessation of the [false] Brahmin’s [deceit], and the offering of praise to the Blessed One whose nature is the form of Mayaṅiga.

...Now, regarding the specific times—such as the days of the week beginning with Sunday, the lunar dates beginning with the first day (pratipad), the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī, and the zodiac signs beginning with Aries—the Lord Maheśvara, out of compassion for Brahmā, revealed the method for the attainment of desired fruits through the greatness of special offerings and worship, which depend upon the particular distinctions of time such as the day, the forenoon, the afternoon, and the solstices and months; and he established the sequence by which the *ketaka* leaf serves as the means for his own worship.

[Ha, , & ca] And the bestowal of the curse of form. Then the hymn of praise by Brahmādeva. Then, in detail, the commencement of the narration of the majesty of the life of the illustrious Aruṇācala Śaṅkara; therein, the offering of a hymn of praise by Brahmādeva to Śrī Śaṅkara. Then, through the medium of the hymns of praise by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, from the Lord Śaṅkara’s own right and left limbs, the birth of Brahmā and Viṣṇu [occurs], [respectively] from the qualities of Rajas and Sattva.

After [the Lord] had first granted boons to Brahmā and Viṣṇu, He again issued His command, which was like the splitting of His own authority; then He joined the bones of the thigh and the calf. Thereafter, by the command of the Blessed One, He assigned the state of maintenance to Brahmā and the state of sustenance to Mahāviṣṇu, and they both carried out that command accordingly. Following that, under the direction of the Blessed One, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, due to their preoccupation with their respective offices and the resulting forgetfulness of the Blessed One who had bestowed them, [neglected] their own respective bodies of qualities.

[The narrative concerning] the attainment of the cows; then, the entry into the abode of the Lord of Aruṇācala, preceded by the construction of the city of Aruṇapura; [the description of] the sporting of Śiva and Pārvatī; the description of the events of the performed penance; and therein, the description of the great dispute between Virañci and Acyuta regarding their respective superiority, born of delusion, amidst the context of their own offices.

The description of the account of the four-faced Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa [seeking] Hara, like the story of the six-faced one. Now, as Brahmā and Viṣṇu were disputing with envy, Śaṅkara, consisting of light, emerged from between them for the sake of their peace. Then, having departed from the ear of Pārvatī who was enraged by a lover’s quarrel, the account of the manifestation of the Lord’s own body from within her own form is described; thereafter, the account of Brahmā and Viṣṇu reaching the upper and lower limits of that *liṅga*.

The return to the hermitage of Gautama with her friends for the purpose of performing penance; then, following the instruction of Gautama, making a firm resolve to purify the sky, the casting away of internal impurities... [and] the performance of penance in the form of the worship of Aruṇācala-Īśvara every day near that hermitage, preceded by the observance of extremely rigorous restraints; and then, for the sake of cutting through the path to the end beneath that mass of splendor, [the arrival of] Viṣṇu assuming the form of a boar... [end of fragment].

The naming of the daughter of Dhāravṛkala as Apītakucā; then the regions of Durgā, the slayer of Mahiṣāsura; then, for the sake of the Goddess who had been sought through penance, the dispatching of a messenger by Mahiṣāsura to bring the Goddess to his own palace; the expulsion of the messenger of Mahiṣāsura by a friend of the Goddess from that place; then the return of Mahiṣāsura with a vast army toward the Goddess; and finally, the Goddess hearing the clamor of Mahiṣāsura’s army.

The execution of the Goddess’s command for the purpose of destroying the divine [demon] host; the creation by the Goddess Durgā from her own limbs of various circles of Yoginīs and the army led by Kāli and others; then, a description of the tumultuous and fierce battle between the army of the Goddess and the army of the Daityas; then, seeing that Mahiṣāsura was invincible, the offering of hymns of praise to the Goddess Durgā by Mātṛkā and the others; and then, [the slaying] of Mahiṣāsura by the Goddess Durgā.

The narration of the account of the slaying of the demon Mahiṣāsura by Durgā, who was accompanied by Surāṇa; then, at the instruction of the Goddess, Durgā, having severed the head of the demon Mahiṣāsura with her sword, plunged it into the Khaḍgatīrtha after first tearing through his crest-lock (śikhā); at the moment of that immersion, the *liṅga* situated in the throat of the demon Mahiṣāsura fell; that *liṅga* was then established on the bank of the Khaḍgatīrtha by the command of Pārvatī; thereafter, by Durgādevī...

At that time, while emerging from the sacred ford (tīrtha) in his hand, Mahiṣāsura’s head fell. Then, after Pārvatī had granted her own permission to Durgādevī for the purpose of slaying the great demon Mahiṣāsura, Gautama, following the removal of the sin of contact with the mire of evil, requested instruction on penance for the expiation of that sin. Thereupon, Gautama gave instructions for performing penance at the Caṇḍeśvara Jyotirdhāma until the full moon of the month of Kārttika. Then, by the instruction of Gautama, Pārvatī—

The performance of penance; then, on the full moon day of Kārttika, at the peak of Mount Śoṇācaṅga, the bathing of the Lord of the Śoṇādri mountain with the waters of the Jyotirdarī river; thereafter, by the Blessed One, who was pleased by the hymn of praise offered there, the immediate manifestation of His own true form followed by the description of Pārvatī, the Mother of the Universe, together with her son.

Then, Śrīdarāṅkaraṇa [describes] the placement of the noose that proclaims the praise of the Mother of the World (Jagadambā), and how Skanda, for the sake of milk, performed penance through knowledge in the presence of Pārvatī; then, due to the command of Śrī Śaṅkara, the Mother of the World remained near Śrī Jagadīśvara. Furthermore, Śrī Śaṅkara granted boons to Khaṅgatīrtha, Gautama, the Maruts, and others, including the Pramātṛkas. That indeed is the power of the Cow (Ajacyā) [and] the primordial source of the Khaṅga forest.

Regarding the description of King Vajrāṅgada of Pāṇḍya-deśa: while Vajrāṅgada was pursuing a deer on horseback toward Śroṇācaṭa, he fell from his mount due to confusion. Both the horse and the female deer (kastarī) fell from the mountain peak; because both died instantly upon their bodies falling, they immediately attained the state of celestial beings (*khecaratva*). Then, between those two celestial beings who had descended, the king [recognized] the one of radiant beauty...

The narration by the *vidyādhara* Vajrāṅgada of his own misfortune caused by the offense of Durvāsas, and the description of the greatness of the Lord of Śrīśaila; therein, the account of how the Lord of Śrīśaila, having first granted a boon to Heramba who had performed circumambulation of him, subsequently began his own circumambulation of Śrīśaila; then, the report by the *vidyādhara* named Kaṭādhara to King Vajrāṅgada concerning the history of his own curse. And then—

With a mind intent on the elevation of the lowly and the subduing of pride, King Vajrāṅgada—who was like nectar to the eyes of the virtuous—established a firm resolve regarding the final goal in the matter of the Śramaṇas. Then, by means of the wealth he had acquired through his own exertion, he bestowed upon the Brāhmaṇas various agrahāras and other gifts as a purificatory rite. Having established a forest hermitage near the holy site of Gomatīśrama for the practice of penance, the Blessed One, pleased by his constant pilgrimage and asceticism, granted Vajrāṅgada the gift of his own supreme instruction.

Through the grace of the boon granted by the Blessed One, the attainment of all enjoyments for Vajrāṅgada; the description of the greatness of the Lord of Aṇahilapāṭaka (Aṇahillapura) as he dwells with his wife on the banks of the Śatruñjaya; and the description of the greatness of the Aṅga-mountain—thus ends the third section, the latter half of the "Greatness of Aṅga," in the *Māheśvaralīlā*.
Thus ends the first section, the Mahēśvara-khaṇḍa, in the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. || 1 ||
What is this? [It is] the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa, the second Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa within the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. 2.

The first section of the Viṣṇu-khaṇḍa: the greatness of Veṅkaṭācala; the residence of Śrīnivāsa as announced by Bakulamālikā to Dharaṇīdevī; the performance of penance by Haihayānuja at Svāmitīrtha according to the words of Śrīnivāsa; and the determination of the marriage by Dharaṇī and others according to the words of Bakulamālikā.

The sequence beginning with the sounds of tinkling ornaments produced by Karama; the journey of Vakṛkhā together with Śuka to the presence of Śrīnivāsa; Nārada’s description of the Yajñavarāha at the peak of Mount Sumeru as he was returning from the Dardura mountain; thereafter, the account of the marriage of Padmāvatī to Śrīnivāsa at Svāmipuṣkariṇī; the description of how Padmāvatī surpassed the holy places given by Śuka to Śrīnivāsa; the majesty of Kumāradhārā; the majesty of Tuṃbatīrtha; and the arrival at Pāṇḍusamādhi.

The majesty of Catā, the greatness of Pāpanāśana and Devatīrtha, the hymn to Dharaṇīkara Varāha, and the joy of Śrīnivāsa’s marriage to Lakṣmī following the defeat of Khakṣya, as described by Brahmā and the others.

The return of Śrīnivāsa and Oṃkāra along with Dharaṇī from the mountain of anger; the occasion for hearing the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Vaṅṭācala; the journey to the city of Viyadrāja; the granting of boons such as invincibility (*prāśratādi*) by Viyadrāja to the bridegroom and the bride; the acquisition of the knowledge of the Vedas through the grace of Śrīnivāsa; the attainment of the boon of supreme devotion by Viyadrāja; the departure of Brahmā and the other gods, who had come to witness the wedding, to their own abodes; and the ritual for the offering of the boar’s meat. ... ... yu ... [end of fragment]

Now follows the account of the Niṣāda named Vasu; the Lord’s speech addressed to Vasu regarding the killing of his son; [the account] of Raṅgadāsa. Then, by the prayer of Agastya, the description of the Lord becoming visible to all people; thereafter, the arrival of Śrī at Śrīparvata from the sky via Mitravarmā; the description of the divine garden-mansion named Rājā, built by Raṅgadāsa for the sake of Śrīnivāsa; the manner of Padmāvatī’s emergence from the surface of the earth; and the [account] of Ākāśarāja.
The various arts of the lute, and the Lord’s forgetfulness of his own true nature due to the Gandharva’s performance of musical entertainment at Raṅgarāpata.

The birth of the son named Vasudāna to the queen named Dharaṇī; the account of King Toṇḍamān, including the deceptive stratagem of the sage Saṃghānana, the arrival of Nārada at the hermitage of Śrī Śeṣācala, the story of Padmāvatī residing in the garden, the arrival of Nārada near Padmāvatī, the departure of Śrīnivāsa for the hunt as described by Nārada, and the account of Pañcavaṇeḍuka situated near Śrīnivāsa.

The moments [described include]: Padmāvatī’s journey to the flower forest with her female companions; the arrival of Śrīnivāsa near the hunter Reṇuka while he was in the flower forest for the sake of hunting; the arrival of Śrīnivāsa before King Toṇḍamān; and the mutual conversation between the Lord and the maidens.

[The king] having seen [the queen], out of affection for his father, attained the kingdom by striking down the enemy; then, having reported the wealth to King Toṇḍabhānu, he was filled with great joy upon seeing Padmāvatī. While wandering through the city of Trāṇaka, he was struck by a sudden longing for her; then, due to the sound of her voice and the scent of her body, he proceeded toward the path of the rogue, and there— (Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment of a Sanskrit narrative involving a king, his father, the acquisition of a kingdom, the reporting of wealth to a sovereign, and the protagonist's longing for a woman named Padmāvatī while traveling through the city of Trāṇaka. Nārada gave a detailed explanation of the auspicious nature of that dream. Then, having seen a certain tree that had suddenly appeared on the shore of the ocean near Viśveśvara, the king was filled with wonder; his guards reported the account of seeing the tree to him. Subsequently, the sacrifice was completed with a ceremonial bath (avabhṛthasnāna). Nārada described the majesty of that tree, saying it had been fashioned from the hairs of the Lord, and [described] its establishment as the Vakṣa-liṅga.

Then, at a certain time, while Indradyumna was standing there to perform worship, he spoke thus to Nārada regarding the image of Viṣṇu: "Who indeed will fashion such a form? He was anxious because that king had never before seen the true form of the Lord. Having said, "I shall fashion that image," Viṣṇu vanished right there on that altar covered with cloth, assuming the form of a boar. Indradyumna [searched] with the two forms of the boar and the man-lion.

The command regarding the commencement of worship, beginning with the installation preceded by the consecration (*samskāra*) of the perfected forms; then, after fifteen days, the untying of the enclosures around the great altar (*mahāvedi*); the offering of oblations to Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Subhadrā, Vāsudeva, and Sāmba seated upon their thrones; and the description by Nārada of the extraordinary rise in fortune of the couple who were overwhelmed by the great bliss born from that offering.

The king, enlightened by Nārada, performed a hymn of praise to Viṣṇu; Nārada, moreover, offered a prose eulogy to Sthāṇu, who assumes the form of the Blessed One; and others as well, such as Atri and Kaśyapa, described the Blessed One. Then Indrayuj worshipped the Blessed One along with his retinue using numerous mantras, sūktas, and other texts. Subsequently, the king bestowed ten million cows upon the brahmins there. Finally, Candrasuśruta began the construction of a temple for the Blessed One.

The arrival of the gods there by the command of Brahmā for the purpose of installing the temple constructed by Indradyumna; and the desire of Nārada to go to his own world, Brahmaloka, in order to invite Brahmā at the time of the installation—after having heard from a certain Brāhmaṇa reciter of the Ṛgveda, who had described the greatness of the wooden image [of the Lord], that the eating of the Lord's food cannot occur without the means prescribed in the Śruti and other scriptures, and after having first given instruction on the worship of the Lord as known through the Vedas to King Indradyumna.

The manifestation [of his intent]: even the King’s desire to invite Brahmā toward the world of Brahmā (Brahmaloka) through Nārada was made manifest. Then, Indra’s departure for the world of Brahmā together with Nārada by means of a flower-chariot celestial vehicle (puṣparatha-vimāna); on the way, Nārada’s inquiry regarding the cause of the King’s sorrow to the monarch whose mind was agitated by anxieties concerning his kingdom; and having heard the cause of the King’s anxiety, Nārada’s providing of consolation to the King.

The removal of their anxiety [is described], followed by the account of how Indra and Nārada, having traversed all the worlds, reached the world of Brahmā (Brahmaloka) and were received with hospitality by the gatekeepers and others; then Indra performed a prostration before Lord Brahmā. When Brahmā asked, "For what purpose have you come?", Indra replied, "In the temple being constructed by me, you must certainly come to install the deity."

Then Brahmā, having perceived the future state of the world, approached the Goddess along with the Lord of Wealth (Padmanidhi) and Indradyumna. Having arrived there, he performed the consecration of the Blessed One’s image for the sake of Indradyumna.

After Mūta had related the account of Bahukākhasya, Padmanidhi, together with the gods, was commanded to descend to the earth. He was granted reassurance that he would return once the rite of installation (pratiṣṭhā) was complete; thereafter, by the command of King Indradyumna, Padmanidhi returned to the earth along with the gods, the Ṛṣis, and Indra.
Having taken him [the image], they performed a hymn of praise to the Lord with the Puruṣasūkta. Then, a voice from the sky directed the Lord to establish the form of the Goddess through Padmanidhi.

The collection of materials for the construction of the chariot as recorded by Nārada; the casting of the golden image of Śrī-Indrayumna by Padmanidhi at the command of [the king]; the construction of the three chariots by Viśvakarman at the command of Nārada; the installation of that chariot by the hand of Nārada; in that context, a description of the procedure and method for the installation of the chariot; and the description of the consecration of the Lord’s form within the chariot after fashioning the form of Garuḍa upon the chariot-banner with mantras and performing prayers to Garuḍa.

The description of the defects such as the unevenness of the wheels—by which part of the chariot was the worship of the Lord performed, by what [part] were the spokes lost, and so forth; the description of the manner of establishing the deities of the directions after the chariot has been set in motion; the description of the true nature of the Lord; and the granting of boons to the worlds by the Lord.

[The story of] the arrival there of King Gāla together with his army; how that lord of the earth was struck with wonder upon seeing the mountain of Durabhasa produced by Indrayudha; how he then related the entire account of his journey to the battle against Indra after becoming a cloud, and so forth; and then, following the conversation between Gaṇendra and Indrayudha, King Gāla recognized Indrayudha as a person of supreme purity and self-restraint.

Having first established [the deity] upon the throne of the chariot, Indra accepted its command. Then follows the description of how Indra, accompanied by Brahmā and others, came from the world of Brahmā to the earth out of devotion to the Lord who had entered the temple built for him; thereafter, Indra, satisfied by the arrival of Brahmā, offered prayers to the god Brahmā, and having accepted the gift of the chariot, palace, and other items from Brahmā, he performed a hymn of praise to the Blessed One. Following that, [the description of] Subhadrā’s chariot.

The subjects of this chapter are: Indra’s performance of worship for the Blessed One installed in the temple; the account of the arrival of King Svarṇabhuja; the description of the praise offered by Brahmada and Varatāsumadra upon their arrival; the composition of a hymn by Babhadra; and the narration of the fruit resulting from the worship of the three chariots.

Then, the sudden appearance of the terrifying Narasiṃha in his fearsome form, causing the gods led by Viṣṇu and Indra to be struck with terror; the description of their state of fear; the narration by Brahmā, at the word of Nārada, of the manifestation of Narasiṃha; the composition of a hymn by Brahmā to Narasiṃha; the direct perception of the respective deities as they were invoked by the mantras recited at the time of the installation of the icons, and their remaining in their respective places; the arrival of the Vedas and others also in personified forms; and [the account] of the sacrifice performed by Brahmādeva.

The imparting of the mantra-instruction; then, the performance of pacification rites for Lakṣmī and Nṛhari; a description of the greatness of worshipping the wooden deity; the propitiation of Indra’s charioteer Mātali by Bṛhadbhadra with the twelve-syllable mantra, of Nārāyaṇa with the Puruṣasūkta, and of the Goddess with the Devīsūkta; then, the composition of a hymn by the god Badraka for the purpose of breaking Indra’s chariot; [the verse] "dāraṃ pacha pṛṇa."

Chapters: Description of the procedure for the great festival of Mahādevī, including the worship of Madhānadeka, the offering of food, and the distribution of gifts; description of the procession after preparing the chariot and installing the image of the Lord, including its circumambulation of the city limits; description of the attainment of great fortune through the chanting of the names of Viṣṇu while seated upon the chariot; description of the fruits of the Mahādevī-vow, the Puruṣottama-vow, the Balarāma-vow, and the Sumadrā-vow; and the fruit of beholding the wooden body [of the deity] on the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha.

The greatness of the illumination of the lamp of the assembly of the virtuous; a description of the greatness of the lake-tīrtha that is an ancillary of the Aśvamedha sacrifice; the greatness of Jindutīrtha; a description of the fruit of the ancestral rites (pitṛ-karma) performed at Mahāvedi; and a description of the greatness of bathing, giving gifts, and other acts at the tīrthas such as Indradayamna, Siṃhakṣetra, Banajāgaraṇa, Vīthahaṣīka, and others.

The description of the chariot protectors and the *kapardika*; therein, the praise of Puruṣottama, Balarāma, Subhadrā, and Anaphara; the description of the methods of their worship; the description of the ritual for the festival of the lying down (*śayanotsava-vrata*); the granting of a boon by the Blessed One from his wooden body to King Indradyumna during the four-month holy period (*cāturmāsya*) beginning from the full moon of Āṣāḍha until the full moon of Kārttika; the description by the Blessed One himself, from his own mouth, of the greatness of the site (*sthānamādātmya*) regarding the wooden body; and [the account] according to the conjunction of months, lunar days, and so forth.

A description of the fruits of recitation, giving, and other such acts; a description of the greatness of bathing, giving, and other rites performed during the eighth month; and, preceded by a description of the greatness of the sacred sites (tīrthas) located at Mārkaṇḍeya, Avaṭapa, Vāruṇa, Nyagrodha, Nārāyaṇa, Sīradhvaja, Syandana, Trayasthadrudra, Dehaviṣṇu, Bala, Madra, Subhadra, and others, as well as Svargadvāra, Catur-svastika, Koṇaka, Sidhurāja, and so forth—a narration of the results of various ritual procedures such as hymns of praise and worship.

Then follows the description of the greatness of bathing at the Anaradrayunasa lake, followed by the narration of how one attains great fruit through the recitation of the Nṛsiṃha mantra; the greatness of beholding Puruṣottama situated there; the greatness of bathing at Puruṣottama in the month of Āṣāḍha; a description of the city; the washing away of various kinds of sins during the Cāturmāsya; the fruit of bathing at sacred fords (tīrthas) and beholding Puruṣottama and other deities; the discourse on what items should or should not be accepted during the Cāturmāsya; the enumeration of the observances to be maintained during the Cāturmāsya; and the fruit of hearing the greatness of these vows arising from the Cāturmāsya.

...the description of the sequence of observances during the meritorious period marking the commencement of the southern transit at the time of the Karka-saṃkrānti; the fruit of worshipping Puruṣottama during the southern transit; the enumeration of the names of the deities stationed in the ten directions of Puruṣottama and the description of the fruits of their worship; the offering of a hundred cows by Indradyumna; the praise and worship of Puruṣottama and Narasiṃha by Śvetarāja; and the granting of boons to the king by the Blessed One.

The granting of boons to Śvatarāja and the disappearance of the Blessed One; the description of the fruit of consuming the remnants of the Blessed One’s meal; the description of the sequence of hymns for the supreme Lord Vaṭa-Puruṣottama; the description of the fruit of seeing Puruṣottama and the attainment of all desired fruits; the description of the greatness and fruit of beholding Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the description of the Jyeṣṭha-pañcaka vow; the description of the greatness and fruit of the Puruṣottama tree born on the day of Mahājyaiṣṭhī; and [the instruction] to kindle five lamps.

A description of the greatness [of the text] beginning with the injunction that the worship of Nṛsiṃha must be performed; a statement of the fruits of fasting on the full moon and new moon days, as well as the drinking of the water from the Kṛṣṇavaṭa-tīrtha and the wearing of the *nimāla*; a determination of the nature of the Kali age; a description of how one attains fruit through meditation on the Lord in the Kali age; a description of the Lord’s inherent nature of compassion, kindness, and so forth; the arrival of a certain twice-born man at the sacred field of Puruṣottama; and [the account of] that twice-born man, who was possessed by a spirit, regarding the food-remnants of the Lord...

The narration of how the food offered by Janivēdita was not eaten and how that resulted in bodily affliction for him; furthermore, O Blessed One, the description of another matter concerning the fruit of worshipping a certain auspicious *druma* (tree) by the twice-born... (Ma)
The account of how a twice-born man attained divinity by eating what he desired, and how another who had abandoned the offering (naivedya) attained the state of the Lord. || 14 ||

The second section, the *Puruṣottama-kṣetra-māhātmya* (the Greatness of the Sacred Site of Puruṣottama/Jagannātha), within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, consists of: [the description of] how, after making a prayer, by the grace of the Man-Lion manifested thereby, he immediately attained [his goal]; the account of the origin of the fragrant *damanaka* flower at the time of the battle with the demon Damanaka; and the exposition of the ritual for worshipping the gods, preceded by the worship of the Lord’s devotees.
(-) dhai ||

The contents of the chapters are as follows: first, the description of the fruits resulting from the consumption of food offered to the Lion [Viṣṇu] along with his beloved; then, the narration of the attainment of the fruits of all pilgrimages through the performance of the festival of the gift-giving (dāyana), the observance of vows, and the circumambulation of the southern-facing cave; next, the description of the section concerning the times for the Lord’s sleeping and waking; and finally, the description of the section concerning the ritual for the great festival of awakening known as Kausudī, and within that section, the description of the materials required for the worship of the Blessed One.

The description of the fruit of worship; the statement that by this very worship the practitioner attains the fruit of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the path taught in the Trika; the description of the festival of the *prāvaraṇa* (garment) on the sixth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, and the description of the procedure for the rules of the *prāvaraṇa* festival; the description of the rules for the day of the festival of the *puṣya-snāna* (auspicious bath), and the narration of the ritual worship and other details of the *puṣya-snāna* festival; and the description of the fruit of bathing in the holy waters at the time of the northern transit (*udagayana*), preceded by the rite of the sun’s entry into Capricorn (*makara-saṃkramaṇa*).

The description of the piercing of the sprouting pulse-beans (*dālyarohaṇāvedha*) in the month of Phālguna; the prescription for the *Sāṃvatsaravrata* on the full moon day of Phālguna; the description of the consecration of the image of Viṣṇu; the description of the *Jyeṣṭhapañcaka-vrata*; (the description of the spring festival of the *Damanabhañjikā-yātrā*; the description of the *Akṣayamokṣa-yātrā*; the description of hymns to the Lord during that pilgrimage—including the description of the Lord’s wooden body as it lies upon the *Nīḍaḍā* [bedstead], and the description of the *Drōṇakha* [funeral pyre]).

— Following the consecration of the temple, what did Indradyumna do? In response to the great sages’ inquiry, this [section] contains a description of the Lord’s true nature as performed by Indradyumna, the granting of a boon by the Lord, and the conclusion of the *Purāṇa-māhātmya* through the hearing of its fruit. Chapters: Subjects. Now, in the *Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa*, the third is the *Badarikāśrama-māhātmya*.
