In the context of the dialogue between Sūta and Lomaśa, regarding the question of by whom liberation might be attained, begins the dialogue with Śivaskanda. Therein, after first describing many sacred fords (*tīrtha*) such as the Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Yamunā, and Narmadā, there follows a description of the greatness of the city of Ayodhyā; then the greatness of the sacred field (*kṣetra*) of Ayodhyā, a description of the ritual procedure for bathing at the Gomatī Tīrtha, the fruit of the pilgrimage to Pañcakrośī Tīrtha, and the fruit of bathing at Viśrānti Tīrtha.

The greatness of the gift of a cow at Rāmatīrtha; the greatness of bathing in the Mākaṇḍaya lake preceded by the fulfillment of desires and the greatness of the Jagannātha lake; the greatness of the knowledge of the Indradyumna lake; the description of how all fruits are obtained through the forest named Badarī; the description of the origin and greatness of the sacred field (kṣetra) called Badarī; and the narration of how the head of Brahmā was severed from his fifth [body] by Śiva when he caused the daughter’s union [with him], and how that skull subsequently became his hand.

Having accepted [the gift], Śiva went to all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) for the purpose of removing the fault of the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). Then he went to Badarikāśrama, the hermitage of the Lord of Girijā; by going to Badarikāśrama, the sin of killing a Brahmin was dispelled from Śiva. Next follows the description of the Daśāśvamedha Tīrtha. By the command of Vyāsa, [Śiva] proceeded toward Badarikāśrama. There is a description of the hymn of praise (*stuti*) offered to the Blessed One, a description of the greatness (*māhātmya*) of Abhitīrtha, and a description of the greatness of Nāradaśilā and Mārkaṇḍeyaśikhā.

The description of the majesty of the Śainateya stone; the majesty of the Vārādī stone and the offering of praise there by the Lord, Devadyūti, and others; the majesty of the Nārasida hill-peak and the description of the Lord’s southern face; the sight of the Lord in the form of a child by the gods beginning with Rahasa; the offering of praise to the Lord by them in the Ocean of Milk; the manifestation of the Lord; and the Lord’s disappearance after declaring, "I have withdrawn myself out of fear that the pride of the learned might increase."

The establishment of the Lord by Śiva; the attainment of the fruit of gifting the entire universe (*brahmāṇḍadāna*) through the mention of the name "Badarī" and the sight of Badarī; a description of the greatness of giving gifts such as feeding Brāhmaṇas at the Badarī-forest; a description of the origin and history of Pitr-tīrtha, Kapālamocana-tīrtha, and other holy sites; the performance of penance there by Brahmā; the propitiation of the Lord who was pleased upon seeing Brahmā; and the manifestation of the Vaiṣṇava community through the grace of the Lord.

—The *Gurukalpa* of Śatakaṇṭha. **Chapters and Subjects:** 1. The qualification of Brahmā for the creation of the universe; the attainment by Brahmā of the qualification to know the meaning of all the Vedas; the bath in the Sarasvatī, the characteristics of the superior, middling, and inferior types of people, and praise of the husband (Bhartṛ). 2. The fruit of bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*); the characteristics of human beings; the attainment by Vyāsa, through the power of his bath, of the qualification to compose the *Saṃhitās* of the Purāṇas and other texts.

The greatness of Kāmyatīrtha; the protection of the fourfold bath; the greatness of Vasudhārātīrtha; the description of Samyavarṇana; the determination of daily duties beginning from dawn; therein, the rules for the evacuation of urine and feces, the cleaning of teeth and so forth; the greatness of the five Tīrthas such as Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, Gayā, Naimiṣa, and Kurukṣetra; the ritual for the construction of monasteries at the five Tīrthas; the performance of bathing and other rites; the definition of sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) and forbidden food; and the determination of the directions for facing while eating.

Oṃ. [This section contains] the departure of those [sages] to the hermitage of Badarikā for the sake of removing the aforementioned [faults]; the description of the origin of Somakuṇḍa; its majesty (māhātmya); the greatness of the four tīrthas on the plateau along with their attendants; the determination of what is to be done and what is not to be done during the month of Kārttika; and the departure of Indra and the other gods toward Virāṭa after leaving Mera, due to their satisfaction with the Lord’s dwelling in Viśākhā. At that time...

The greatness of offering lamps in the temple of Viṣṇu, including the narrative of Kṛtsadrijaka; in connection with the greatness of rekindling another’s lamp—the installation of a wooden image of the Lord in Viśākhā for the sake of the happiness of Indra and others; the performance of hymns of praise to the Lord; the narration of the history of Indumatī; the greatness of offering lamps through their forms and other qualities; the narrative of the crow and the cat; the residence of the gods in that very place by the command of the Lord; and the establishment of the world-guardians at Badarikāśrama. Badarikāśrama.

In that very section, through the dialogue between Candraśama and Sunanda, there is a description of the performance of the Kārttika vow; the majesty of the lamp; how all fruits are obtained through giving, including the liberation of a wife from the curse of her husband; the description of the Daṇḍapuṣkariṇī Tīrtha; the procedure for offering lamps in the sky and so forth; and the account of liberation from the state of a Piśāca by offering a lamp in the sky. Thus ends the third [chapter], the *Badarikāśrama-māhātmya*, in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.

[Chapter on] Charity, the locations for establishing lamps, the ancient account of Harikara regarding the offering of lamps, and the *kapṛradīpa*; now begins the fourth [chapter], the Greatness of the Month of Kārtika, in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.

—The introduction of the six gifts, the auspicious invocation, and Raunaka’s inquiry to Sūta regarding the glory of the month of Kārtika; following the answer, the narration of the greatness of Kurukṣetra, in the course of which Harimedha, Sumedhas, Vṛddhaśarman, and Brahmadatta were mentioned.

And there is the *Sutākti*; in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, preceded by an introduction, the inquiry regarding the Kārttika vow; the [discussion of] the desire for prosperity in times of distress; the prescription for the Vatsadvādaśī vow; the observation of omens in the five lamps (*pañcadīpa*); and the determination that by means of the Vatsadvādaśī vow, one may perform other vows such as the Ekāṅga-gopāla-vrata.

Ha Ma: A description of the body, wealth, grain, happiness, and their origins; the ritual for the three days of Yama; the account of Hemanaka; Brahmā’s instruction to Nārada regarding the Kārttika vow and its duties; therein, within the context of service to the guru, the laughter of Medhas upon hearing the song of the sages; the ritual for the Caturdaśī of Naraka; the ritual for the Dīpāvalī festival; therein, the etymological meaning of the word *kaumudī*; the historical accounts and religious duties of Pārvatī, Raṅga, Trika, Pilu, and Sumati; and [this section] in connection with the gift of food.

The narrative of Syaketu and the twice-born; the performance of *śrāddha* and other rites; the evening worship of Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī, and Mahāsarasvatī; the festival of Lakṣmī’s awakening (Lakṣmī-prabodhotsava); the legend of the Brahmin Sumati in connection with the gift of a cow; the recounting of the legend of Puṣkara in connection with the remembrance of names (*nāmasmaraṇa*); the section on the *dīpotsava* (festival of lights) and *nīrājana*; and the observation of auspicious and inauspicious omens during the game of ball-play (*vaccirājyavārkrīḍā*).

And [the text contains] the narration of the history of the dull-witted Brāhmaṇa in connection with the greatness of reciting the *Gītā*; the expulsion of all the inhabitants outside at midnight in connection with the gift of a cow; the description of the *Sukharātri* vow; the narration of the story of Raṇoka; the description of the acceptance of a messenger; the determination of the lunar day for the acceptance [of the guest]; the decision regarding the lunar date; and the description of the commencement and conclusion of the vow involving the application of cow-dung on the courtyard in the form of a bull, preceded by the investigation of the time.
The worship of Tipu, the worship of Govardhana, the viewing of the combats and sports of buffaloes and bulls at Barīvadā, and Māgapāḍī-ru.

The determination of the time for bathing; the procedure for bathing that bestows progressively greater merit at wells, holy fords (*tīrtha*), and other sites; the ritual for the worship of Varuṇa at night; the description of the sport of the cows; the observation of the *yaṣṭi* omen... [the determination of the time for bathing; the determination of the fruit of bathing in the Tuṅgabhadrā and Kāverī; the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the Pañcanadī-tīrtha; the procedure for the Yamadvitīyā vow; etc.]

The chapters and their subjects: the majesty of the *dhātrī* tree; therein, the ritual procedure for the worship of the *dhātrī*; the narrative account of the origin of the *dhātrī* tree; the description of the deities residing within the *dhātrī*; the majesty of the *dhātrī*’s shade; therein, the ancient history (*itihāsa*) of Vaikya; the liberation of a mouse by listening to this story; the majesty of eating under the *dhātrī*’s shade; the description of how eating under the *dhātrī*’s shade removes defects; the wearing of *dhātrī* fruit; the offering of a garland of lamps under the *dhātrī*’s shade; [the majesty of] the *dhātrī*’s shade—...

The fruit of eating *dhātrī* [myrobalan] with one's husband; the greatness of the *dhātrī* fruit; the merit of bathing in *āmalka* [myrobalan] water and wearing a garland of it; the fruit of offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) in the shade of a *dhātrī* tree; a description of the specific parts of the body for wearing the *dhātrī* fruit; the fruit of worshipping Brahmā in the shade of a *dhātrī* tree; the lunar days (*tithi*) for the worship of *dhātrī*; the rules for eating in a forest; the greatness of touching a *dhātrī* tree; and the greatness of a *dhātrī* tree standing within one’s house. ... ;

In this dialogue between Satyabhāmā and [Kṛṣṇa], there is a description of how Satyabhāmā attained the status of Kṛṣṇa’s wife through the merit of the Kārttika vow in her previous birth; and when asked why the month of Kārttika is the most excellent among all months, Kṛṣṇa explains to Satyabhāmā the reason for its preeminence by recounting the slaying of the demon Raṅka.

The greatness of the sacred site of Prayāga; how Tulasī arose and how Irigriyā was born; the account of the origin of Jaḍandhaya when Śiva was struck by Indra’s thunderbolt and consumed by the fire of his wrath; the description of Jaladhara’s world conquest and his attainment of victory; the description of the cause for Bṛhaspati losing his life-force; and the manifestation of Viṣṇu, who appeared before the gods defeated in battle and engaged them in combat at their request.

In the assembly of Jaṭādhara, by the instruction of Nārada, there was the seizing of Pārvatī by Khīralana and the swallowing of Rāhu; the description of the emergence of the Kīṭamukha Gaṇas from the middle of the eyebrows of Śiva, who was enraged by that; then the description of Rudra’s defeat by Deva in the battle between the gods and the asuras, and the falling of Vīrabhadra; and then the battle between Jaṅgudhara and Divyabhadra.

The contents of the tenth chapter are as follows: Reflecting that the slaying of the Cloud-King (Jaladhara) would result from the violation of Vṛndā’s vow of chastity, Viṣṇu bestowed a *māyā* upon Vṛndā; thereafter, the description of the events occurring between those two, Vṛndā and Viṣṇu; when Vṛndā performed the renunciation of her body (*dehavisarjana*), Viṣṇu’s play with her bodily ashes; then, having slain Jalandhara in battle, by the command of Śiva—who remained bowed down in devotion—the gods [prepared] to subdue Viṣṇu.

The hymn of praise by the Rādiśṣaktis; then, the goddesses, being pleased, bestow the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) upon the gods for the purpose of awakening Viṣṇu. Haḥ... [From the seed-syllables] the daughter of Dhātṛ, Māḍhatītulasī, is born. Through the gift of the merit of the month of Kārtika by Dharmadanta, there is the liberation of Kaṭadahā from her birth as a *rākṣasī*. ...

In the month of Kārttika, during a dispute over the distribution of alms, there is the narration of the great gift; then, together with the celestial chariot brought by the messengers of Viṣṇu, there is the binding of her neck with a garland of *kadamba* flowers. Furthermore, the granting of a boon to Dharmadatta by the messenger of Viṣṇu, who said: "In another birth, you shall become a king renowned by the name Daśaratha in the solar dynasty, and the Lord Viṣṇu himself shall descend as your son."

Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ. [The narration of the greatness of devotion to Viṣṇu; and, in connection with that, the telling of the history of the twice-born Viṣṇudāsa, king of Aṭarāja. The twice-born named Viṣṇudāsa’s pursuit of a Caṇḍāla who had stolen his coarse food, for the sake of giving him alms out of faith. Then, seeing the Caṇḍāla fallen and unconscious, that Viṣṇudāsa, out of compassion, performed hospitable rites for that Caṇḍāla. Thereafter, by the Blessed One assuming the form of a Caṇḍāla, [the testing] of Viṣṇudāsa...]

The bestowing of grace; the arrival of a celestial chariot from heaven for the Brahmin Viṣṇudāsa through the Lord’s favor; while Viṣṇudāsa was departing after ascending that [chariot], the Cola king’s entry into the ocean; thereafter, the manifestation of the Lord’s true form to him; the dialogue between the Cola king and the Brahmin Viṣṇudāsa; and the attainment of the supreme state of Viṣṇu by Jaya and Vijaya through bathing in the Gaṇḍakī river.

...the description of how the son of Dhaneśvara attained birth through the merit of his wandering as a *kāika-nartaka*; the description of the attainment of merit and sin by those who have not [previously] given; the narrative of the vow for the fallen (*patita-vrata*); the procedure for the month-long fast (*māsopavāsa-vrata*); the ritual for the Kūṣmāṇḍa-navamī; the narration of the marriage rite of Tuṭasī; the procedure for the Bhīṣma-pañcaka-vrata; the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Śravaṇa-dvādaśī; the procedure for the Dvādaśī vow; and the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) for the Kārttika-vrata.

Chapter 1: The Greatness of Paravaikuṇṭhacatardaśī; Chapter 2: The Greatness of the Śrīpurotsava. [Forbidden items: Cow’s milk, black gram (rājamāṣa), drinking or eating from a bell-metal vessel, twice-baked bread (dvidakhāna), eggplant (vṛntāka), the greatness of the three final lotus-pools (puṣkariṇī) on the lunar days, the description of the fruits of the rules for hearing the Purāṇas. [Additional forbidden items: Radish (mūlaka), *tekhama*, defiled food, citron (jambīra), and sexual intercourse during the day.

Now, in connection with the eternal greatness of the month of Kārttika, the rules that must be observed and those that must not be observed by those undertaking the Kārttika vow are first described. || 1 ||

In this regard, the rules for what must be performed are as follows: constant remembrance of the Name; the worship of Rādhā and Dāmodara; the recollection of the names of Viṣṇu, Hari, and Śiva; mastery over the senses; restraint of the mind; compassion toward all living beings; meditation on the Lord; worship of the Lord; truthful speech; eating sacrificial food (haviṣya); the vow of eating only at night (naktavrata); the vow of observing the fast until the completion of the meditative concentration (dhāraṇāpāraṇāvrata); the vow of silence (maunavrata); the vow of celibacy (brahmacaryavrata); association with the virtuous; worship of the *dhātrī* tree; and the worship of Viṣṇu in the shade of the *dhātrī* tree.

Listening to discourses on the eternal [Dharma]. The gift of land. Service to one's mother and father. Service to one's teacher. Constant worship of the deity. Singing in the temple of the deity. Offering a perpetual lamp at a place called after the deity. Offering a lamp at a crossroads. Offering a lamp to a Brāhmaṇa. Offering a lamp at a cow-pen. Worship of turuṣī. Worship of the aśvattha tree. Worship of the deity, the Brāhmaṇa, and the cow. Performing circumambulation of the deity. Performing circumambulation of a hundred thousand turuṣī plants. Circumambulation of the aśvattha tree. Feeding Brāhmaṇas.

The giving of food; the giving of cows, bulls, buffaloes, and elephants; the giving of gold, minerals, and gems; and the feeding of the destitute—one should certainly observe these observances during the month of Kārttika. Now, the prohibitions to be avoided: desire for another’s property; performing actions for others; slandering others; coveting another’s wealth; eating another’s food; stale food; yellowish food; association with sinners; consorting with other men; sexual intercourse with another’s wife; deceit toward others; intolerance of others’ excellence; proclaiming the faults of others; and contemplating what is undesirable for others.

False rumors; sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached; food that ought not to be eaten; that which is not declared by the Śāstra; articles of meat; false scriptures; lack of faith in the Śāstra; doubt; speaking falsehood; association with the wicked; evil speech; meat; the milk of a cow whose calf has died; food seen by a woman in her menses; water drawn by a low-born person; the fruitlessness of bathing after eating molasses-mixed food; the fruitlessness of bathing after eating *dakhāḍaka*; indulgence in intoxicants; and the sale of liquids—one should avoid these during the *kālika* month. The determination of what must be performed during the *kālika* month is as follows: [The text continues with a list of permitted activities: ...the study of the Vedas; the performance of *agnihotra*; the offering of oblations; the recitation of mantras; the study of the *Upaniṣads*; the performance of *svādhyāya*; the performance of *tarpaṇa*; the performance of *śrāddha*; the performance of *pūjā*; the performance of *homa*; the performance of *japa*; the performance of *dāna*; the performance of *vrata*; the performance of *niyama*; the performance of *yoga*; the performance of *dhyāna*; the performance of *samādhi*; the performance of *tīrtha-yātrā*; the performance of *deva-darśana*; the performance of *guru-sevā*; the performance of *ātma-cintana*; the performance of *brahmacarya*; the performance of *satya-vacana*; the performance of *ahiṃsā*; the performance of *asteya*; the performance of *śauca*; the performance of *saṃtoṣa*; the performance of *tapas*; the performance of *svādhyāya*; the performance of *īśvara-praṇidhāna*.
These are the duties to be performed during the *kālika* month. This is the definitive conclusion.
Thus ends the fourth [chapter], the Greatness of the Kārttika Vow, in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the fifth [chapter], the Māgha-māhātmya, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.

In the context of the dialogue between Sūta and Nakasavāda, the Blessed One describes to Brahmadeva the attainment of the supreme state by all the Manus through hearing the majesty of Mārgaśīrṣa; he describes the morning bath performed by the Gopīs at the confluence of the Mārga river; and following the description of the merit of that morning bath and how the Gopīs attained Kṛṣṇa through it—preceded by the knowledge of the rules for bathing, applying unguents, and other rituals—he describes the majesty of wearing the *ūrddhvapuṇḍra* after the bath.

The procedure for wearing the *tripuṇḍra* made from clay originating from Dvāravatī, from the *vastika* (tirtha), or from the *tuchasīma* (tirtha); the description of the procedure for wearing *gopīcandana* and *sudarśana*; the fruit of wearing the marks of the incarnations of the Lord upon one's own body; the statement regarding the attainment of the fruit of merit for one whose body is marked with the weapons of the Lord; the description of the eligibility for all rites for one whose body is consecrated by the eight-syllabled name of the Lord; and [the rules] for wearing the *sudarśana* marked with the *sudarśana-cakra* and for wearing the *padmaka* and *caturthī-mālā*.

Description of the *phaḍa* [mark]; the greatness of wearing the *dhātrī* fruit; the greatness of wearing *tulasī* wood; description of the methods for installing, meditating upon, and worshipping the image of the Lord; description of the sequence of worship of the *raṅkha* [deity] and others accompanied by mantras; and the description of the fruits of the worship of the *raṅkha*.

[Contents: Description of the greatness of the *vaṭa* tree and the *ānanda*; worship of the form of the Blessed One; description of the offering of sandalwood paste and other substances; the greatness of the twelve-night vigil (*dvādaśī-jāgaraṇa*); description of the greatness of *jāti* flowers and fruits offered for the sake of the Blessed One; description of flowers dear to the Blessed One; the greatness of the *jāti* flower as the most excellent among all flowers; the fruit of placing a garland adorned with ten thousand *jāti* flowers upon the neck of Viṣṇu.

The description of greatness: the description of the greatness of *tulasī*; the attainment of the merit of giving all things by the gift of a *tulasī* leaf; the description of the fruit of worshipping the Blessed One with *tulasī*; the greatness of the fruit of offering incense and lamps; the greatness of a lamp equipped with a thousand wicks; and the exposition of the rules for the proper preparation and offering of vessels, food, and other articles.

The narration of the greatness of the power of the Lord situated to the north of Vaidyanātha; the description of the fruits of circumambulation and other rites; the fruit of reciting the *Viṣṇusahasranāma*; the explanation of the reason for the Lord’s acquisition of the name Dāmodara; the greatness of partaking in the holy water and sacred offerings (*prasāda*); the conclusion of the procedure for worship, its ritual completion (*udyāpana*), and the description of its fruits; the story of King Vīrabāhu; the greatness of the Ekādaśī beginning with the *Indrīna-pūrva*; and the manifestation of great compassion toward King Vīrabāhu by Bharadvāja. By Bharadvāja...

In the narration of Vīrabāhu’s account of his previous birth, there is a description of how he attained the status of a king in this life due to the merit arising from his respectful reception of a Śūdra in a former existence. When questioned by Devaśarmā as to the cause of his own attainment of Śūdra-hood in a previous birth, Vīrabāhu recounts the story of how that Śūdra attained his low status through the fault of observing the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) conjoined with the tenth (daśamī). Following this, he explains the prohibition against observing the dvādaśī when it is joined with the daśamī.

The description of the procedure for the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) of the Ekādaśī vow by King Bharatarāja, including the account of how he attained a noble mind even while in the womb due to his virtuous deeds such as hospitality toward Brahmins in a previous birth, and the narration of the unbroken Ekādaśī vow.

A description of the sequence of rites such as giving gifts during the vigil; a description of the qualifications for eligibility; on the twelfth day, a narration of the greatness of the Matsya festival followed by an exposition of the rules for bathing, giving, worship, and so forth; the prescription for the recitation of mantras during the Matsya festival; the statement of the mantra for praying to the river at the time of bathing; the description of the offering of fruits, flowers, and water to the Blessed One; a description of the greatness of the gift of an image in the form of a fish; and a description of the manner of honoring the deity at the conclusion of the festival.

The greatness of the gift of cows, land, gold, garments, beds, ornaments, and food; the greatness of offering fruits and flowers at the time of worshiping the Blessed One; the greatness of providing Brahmins with excellent requisites such as sandals and other items during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa; and the greatness of the fast on the twelfth day (Dvādaśī).
