The majesty of remembering the names of the Blessed One (1); meditation on the Blessed One and its majesty; a description of the section concerning the instruction of hymns to the Blessed One; the characteristics of the teacher and the disciple; a description of the majesty of the *Bhāgavata*; the hearing of the fruit of the *Bhāgavata*; a description of the fruits of worshipping and reciting the *Bhāgavata* text first; and a description of the majesty of Mathurā—thus ends the fifth [chapter], the majesty of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the sixth section, the *Bhāgavatamāhātmya*, within the *Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa*.

In the context of the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka, there is a description of how, after consecrating Vajra as the successor to the royal throne of Mathurā and Hastināpura, Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍavas departed for their own abode; following the conversation between Vajra and Parīkṣit, Śāṇḍilya Ṛṣi arrived; Śāṇḍilya then explained the meaning of the word *traja* and described the pastimes performed by Kṛṣṇa at Trajāvatī; and finally, the account of Govardhana’s protection and the establishment of the kingdom of Mathurā and elsewhere, concluding with the statement that Uddhava attained the vision [of the Lord] through this means. (Having spoken thus, Śāṇḍilya...)

The return to his own hermitage; the arrival there of King Parīkṣit at Mathurā-maṇḍala; the establishment of the sites of Govinda’s and Gopī’s pastimes by Kings Vajra and Parīkṣit; the establishment of many sacred shrines all around Jāṭhura; the installation of a Śiva-liṅga with the performance of purificatory rites such as the consecration of wells and ponds in Mathurā; the description of the beauty of the forest created by Kṛṣṇa’s consorts due to their separation from Śrī Kṛṣṇa; the description of the battle of the Lord [Balarāma] against the serpent Kāliya; and [the events] near Mount Govardhana.

The description of the meeting between Uddhava and Parīkṣit and so forth; then, the dialogue between Uddhava and Parīkṣit, the narration of the greatness of the Blessed One by Uddhava, the description of Kṛṣṇa’s childhood sports and pastimes, the statement that by reading the Bhāgavata text one attains the fruit of all desires, the description that where the Bhāgavata is found there is the abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the description of the attainment of liberation through hearing the Bhāgavata, and [the account of] that which was performed by the illustrious Blessed One.

A description of the instruction on the maintenance, origination, and dissolution of the effects of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva, who consist of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas; and [the account of] the sage’s purification through the reception of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, which destroys the accumulation of the quality of tamas.

Ka, Ke, Ka-kha: *Kākaḥ* (The Crow). Chapters and subjects: The power of a serpent gained through hearing the greatness (*māhātmya*) of the month of Vaiśākha; the narration of that very serpent’s account of his previous birth; the dialogue between Śaṅkha and the hunter (*vyādha*), including the narration of how the hunter attained the state of a *Vālmīki* in another birth; ... [and so on] ... the description of the greatness of the lunar days (*tithi*) occurring in the month of Vaiśākha; the definition of the duties of the *kaṭi* (waist/region); ... [and so on] ... the greatness of the *Akṣayyatṛtīyā*.

(The majesty of the goddess Uddharadākṣī; the story of the god and the brahmin residing in the land of Kāmarūpa; a description of the majesty of the thirteenth, fourteenth, and full-moon days of the month of Vaiśākha; and a description of the fruit of hearing the majesty of Vaiśākha. Thus ends the seventh [chapter], concerning the majesty of the month of Vaiśākha, in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.)
Now begins the eighth [section], the Greatness of Ayodhyā, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.

The *Sūta-kratu*, followed by the hymns of praise (*stuti*) offered by Vyāsa and others; then, in the context of the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka, a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Ayodhyā, adorned with various trees and creepers; the arrival of the sage Agastya at Ayodhyā; a description of Agastya’s joy upon witnessing the power of Ayodhyā; a description of Ayodhyā as abiding in the nature of the three qualities (*tri-guṇa*), along with an etymological explanation of the word "Ayodhyā"; and, preceded by the dialogue between Agastya and Vyāsa concerning Ayodhyā, [the account of] that which was performed by Viṣṇu...

The description of the means of recognition; Viṣṇudāman’s composition of a hymn of praise to the Blessed One; Viṣṇuśarman’s arrival at the Blessed One; the granting of a boon by the Blessed One to Viṣṇuśarman; the bringing of a torrential flood of water by the Blessed One with his own discus at that very spot; the description of the renown of that sacred ford under the name Cakratīrtha; the installation of the image of Viṣṇuharitī preceded by the name of Viṣṇu; and the description of the greatness of Viṣṇuharitī.

The arrival of Brahmā in Ayodhyā; the performance of a pilgrimage and the conduct of a sacrifice; the establishment of the Brahmakuṇḍa in his own name; the description of the majesty of the Brahmakuṇḍa by the god Brahmā; the description of the majesty of the Pāpamocana-tīrtha by Agastya through the power of the Ṛṇamocana-tīrtha situated on the bank of the Sarayū; the description of the majesty of the Sahasradhārā by Agastya; the chapters [concerning] the subject matter; and the narration by Agastya of the majesty of the Svargadvāra-tīrtha.

The greatness of the Suktidrāra Tīrtha; the description of the procedure for the concluding rite (*udāpana*) of the Candrahārī Vrata; the description of the greatness of the concluding rite of the Candra-sahasra-vrata; the greatness of Dharmahari; therein, the arrival of the Blessed One upon seeing the bowing performed by King Dharma; the offering of praise to the Blessed One by Dharma; the granting of boons to King Dharma by the Blessed One; and [the account of] the sacrifice named *Sarvasvadakṣiṇā* performed by the king named Raghu after he had completed his conquest of the quarters, by the command of the Sun.

After the completion of the sacrifice, the sage Kautsa arrived; seeing the provisions brought for his own honor, the astonished sage Kautsa expressed his desire to go elsewhere due to a lack of wealth. Raghu set out with the intent to conquer Kubera in order to obtain the northern wealth to give to Kautsa. Out of fear of Raghu, Kubera caused a shower of wealth to fall. The description of Raghu’s gift of wealth along with the Veda to Kautsa, and [the account] by Kautsa...

The description of the destruction of the enemies of Rādhāghūrāja; the return of Kautsa to his own hermitage; the description of the greatness of the gold mine; the narration of the account of Kautsa; there, hearing of Viśvāmitra’s performance of penance, the arrival of Durvāsas who was hungry for it; the description of the food, such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*), offered by Viśvāmitra upon hearing of Durvāsas’s request for a meal; and the issuing of the command to give Kautsa a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of fourteen crores of gold pieces. Tilos... [text ends]

Description of the greatness of Dakītīrtha, Chapter 55; description of the greatness of Sītākuṇḍa; when the gods were defeated by the Asuras in the battle between the gods and the Asuras, the gods offered praise to the Blessed One; upon hearing the praise of the gods, the manifestation of the Blessed One; the arrival of the gods in Ayodhyā according to the instructions of the Blessed One; description of the fame of that holy place through the name Supraharīti; the greatness of Suprahāra; the greatness of giving gifts at Cakrahariṣīṭha; [and the confluence] of the Sarayū and the Dharā rivers.

The majesty of bathing; the majesty of the Gomatī-tīrtha; the description of the granting of boons to the monkeys at the time of Rāmacandra’s departure for his own abode; Rāmacandra’s vision of Māma-Sarayū; the arrival of all the gods there; the composition of hymns by the gods in praise of Rāmacandra; the departure of the gods with Rāmacandra to heaven; and the majesty of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at the Svargadvāra-govāra-tīrtha.

[The chapters] beginning with "Na ajana ta na nava" and ending with "talamojaka," and the subsequent chapters, describe the subject matter concerning the identity of Kṣodaikadhama; therein is the description of the *Putrakāmeṣṭi* sacrifice performed by Daśaratha for the sake of obtaining a son, the greatness of Dhanayaśas-tīrtha, and the account of how Yakṣa, having become foul-smelling due to bathing at Dhanayaśas-tīrtha contrary to Viśvāmitra’s word, attained a fragrant body through that very bath; and the treasure [revealed] which was spoken to Yakṣa by Viśvāmitra.

The description of the ritual procedure for the worship of Ṣmī; the majesty of Vasiṣṭhakuṇḍa; the majesty of the worship of the sixty-four Yoginīs; the majesty of the bath at Yoginīkuṇḍa; the majesty of Uvaṃśīkuṇḍa; King Ghoṣa’s performance of a hymn of praise to Āditya; the majesty of Ghoṣākakuṇḍa; and the majesties of Rukmiṇīkuṇḍa, Vṛhaspatikuṇḍa, and Sāgara-kuṇḍa.

The majesty of Ratiṅkaṇḍa; the majesty of Kusumāyudhakuṇḍa; the description of the ritual for the worship of Ratikaṇḍapa; the majesty of Mataṅgāśvara-kṣetra; the majesty of Mahāranta-tīrtha; the majesty of the tīrtha named Durbhara; the majesty of Mahābhara-tīrtha; the majesty of Mahāvidyā-tīrtha; the majesty of Siddhapīṭha-tīrtha; the majesty of Dugdheśvara; the majesty of Hanumatkuṇḍa; and, in the context of the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Rāma, the description of the majesty of Ayodhyā.

The majesty of Kṣīreśvara; the majesty of Sītākuṇḍa; the majesty of Samrīvatīrtha; the majesty of Vibhīṣaṇasara; a description of the sequence of holy sites in Ayodhyā; the majesty of Gayākūpa; the majesty of Piśācamocanatīrtha; the majesty of Māṇḍavyatīrtha; the majesty of Bharatakuṇḍa; the majesty of Mānasatīrtha; a description of the hermitages of Gautama and others; the majesty of Sītākuṇḍa-Dugdheśvara; the majesty of Mairavakuṇḍa; and the majesty of Jaṭākuṇḍa.

The description of the majesty of the site of Mattagajendra; the description of the sequence of the journey to Ayodhyā; the description of the Sarayū river; the majesty of the site of Viśveśvara; the majesty of the birthplace of Rāma; and the fruit of hearing the majesty of Ayodhyā. Thus ends the eighth [section], the Majestic Glory of Ayodhyā, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.
Thus ends the second section, the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, in the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. 2.
Ka Ka Ka Da Vda. Now, in the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, the third section, the Jāhnavī-khaṇḍa. 3.
Now, regarding the external swelling, the greatness of the Seṭha is the remedy for fear.

The auspicious invocation; the arrival of the Puranic sage Sūta at the assembly of the great seers, such as Śaunaka and others, who dwell in the Naibhiṣāraṇya forest; after the great seers, headed by Śaunaka, had offered him hospitality, their inquiry regarding the majesty of sacred sites and holy fords (tīrthas); Sūta’s commencement of the description of the majesty of the sacred field of Śrī Rāmeśvara; and therein, first, the pilgrimage to the Setubandha constructed by Śrī Rāma on the southern ocean, and the [glory of] the Rāmasetu.

The Majesty of Narāmeśvara and Khiṅgada... (Now, in connection with the narrative of Setubandhana, the description of the events of the Rāmāyaṇa beginning with Śrī Rāmacandra’s departure for the Daṇḍaka forest by his father’s command, the abduction of Sītā, his alliance with Sugrīva, his journey to the shore of the ocean, and his meeting with Vibhīṣaṇa; then, following the consecration of Vibhīṣaṇa as king over the kingdom of the Rākṣasas, while staying at Cakratīrtha with Sugrīva and the others, reflecting on the means for crossing the ocean and remaining there in a state of fasting...)

The composition of mantras; then, while contemplating the means of crossing the ocean for three nights, Śrī Rāma’s waiting for the fulfillment of the ocean’s propitiation; then, seeing the ocean’s disregard in the form of its failure to return to him, Śrī Rāma made a vow to dry up the ocean; thereafter, the ocean, terrified by fear, sought refuge with Śrī Rāma and offered praise to him; then, pleased by that praise, Śrī Rāma [prepared] for the arrival of the bridge.

The request made by the Ocean to Śrī Rāma for the construction of a bridge over him for the purpose of crossing; thereafter, the building of the bridge across the ocean by Śrī Rāma with the assistance of all the monkeys, through the monkey Nala, the son of Viśvakarman; the description of the bed of Dūrvā grass as the foundation of the bridge; and [the description] of the bridge.

Then follows the description of the twenty-four sacred sites (*tīrthas*), beginning with Cakratīrtha; next, the account of the origin of the fame of the Cakratīrtha known as Setumādhava. Therein is the narration of how the Lord, pleased by the great penance of Gālava on the banks of the Dharmapuṣkariṇī, granted a boon to Gālava, and how, through the grace of Hara—who was propitiated by Dharma’s worship—the bull that serves as Hara’s vehicle attained its preeminence. Then, [the account of] the great sage Gālava, who was devoted to the service of his preceptor, being [attacked] by a certain Rākṣasa...
O Blessed One, he who was seized for consumption has been released by the Sudarśana discus. || 18 ||

What? There are eight chapters: the slaying of Rākṣasa; then the praise by Śvāphalka of the Sudarśana discus, which stands before him blazing brilliantly after he has slain Rākṣasa; then, after granting a boon to Gālava, the establishment of the perpetual presence of the Sudarśana discus at Dharmapuṣkariṇī; and from that very fact, the renown of Dharmapuṣkariṇī as Cakratīrtha, [located] at Cakratīrtha, which is synonymous with Dharmatīrtha.

The description of the praise of his own majesty, and the narration of the events that caused intense and great terror; therein, having observed the state of intoxication resulting from sporting with beautiful women by Duradama—the son of the Gandharva Viśvāvasu—who was rendered helpless upon the banks of the Śatitā river, the great sage Vasiṣṭha, who had arrived there seeking a straightforward refuge for the sake of performing the midday rites, pronounced a curse. Due to Vasiṣṭha’s curse, Duradama attained the state of a Rākṣasa; and at the request of his wives, Vasiṣṭha— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the content available.)

The limit of Durda’s curse; thereafter, Durda’s divine body [is restored] immediately after his head is severed by the Sudarśana discus; Durda’s offering of the Sudarśana discus; and a description of the event concerning the clipping of the wings of mountains performed by Indra—despite the stated length and breadth of the Cakratīrtha extending from Darbhaśayana to Devīpattana, according to the accounts explaining the causes for its various interruptions along the way. ...

Now follows the description of the account of the sage Alambuṣa, son of Vasu, in connection with the preeminence of the greatness of Cakratīrtha: there, in the world of Brahmā, while Brahmā was seated in his own assembly hall together with Sāvitrī, Sanaka, and all the gods, sages, Siddhas, Vasus, and Gandharvas, at the commencement of the successive dances of the celestial nymphs (Apsaras), as the nymph named Alambuṣā was dancing, her garment was suddenly blown away by the wind into the interior of her private parts.

Upon seeing Vidhūma—who was tormented by the arrows of Kāma due to the sight of the beautiful thighs, hips, and breasts of the woman—Brahmā granted him the boon of attaining human form; meanwhile, he pronounced a curse upon Aṭavusā that she would become a human woman. At the request of Vidhūma, Brahmā established the limit for the end of that curse. Then, on the surface of the earth, Vidhūmavasu was born as the son of King Sahanīka through his queen, named Sahasrānīka, along with three companions. And [the account] of those three followers...

His birth in the house of his minister’s army commander and friend; his status as the daughter of Kṛtavarman, the lord of Ayodhyā, whose wife was named Alaṃkuśā; then, when King Rātānīka had died in battle against a Daitya in heaven, the coronation of Sahasrānīka; thereafter, during the great festival of the spring season, at the conclusion of the invitation to Indra, for the sake of turning away from worldly objects, by means of the wives Sragavatī, Vasantaka, Karabhaka, and Daugandharāyaṇa—[these are the subjects of] six chapters.

Now follows the account of the events at Devīpattana, situated on the site of the new stone. Having gone to the abode of Indra with Sahasrānīka, and having learned the news regarding his own old age from the words of Śakra, he returned and married Mṛgāvatī. After the marriage to Mṛgāvatī, as Sahasrānīka was setting out toward the city of Kauśāmbī, he recalled the word of Śakra while on the way; then, by means of an invisible Apsaras named Tirottamā, he was joined for fourteen years with that wife.

Thinking that a separation would occur, he offered his own flesh as a gift. Then, while a pit was being dug in a low-lying area near a pond filled with safflower blossoms for the sake of the pregnant Mṛgāvatī—who was like a doe—she was carried away by a monstrous bird born from a *suparṇa* egg; she was led to the peak of Mount Udaya. There, Jamadagni consoled Mṛgāvatī, who was weeping in grief, and settled her in his hermitage. Subsequently, when Mṛgāvatī gave birth there, [he performed the rites] for her son.

The naming of Udayana as Jamadagnya; Udayana’s journey to Pātāla with the Kinnara named Manuṣyarūpadhṛt, who had been released from the Rākṣasa by him after he gave his own marriage bracelet [to the Rākṣasa]; his marriage there with Chitrā, the daughter of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and sister of the Kinnara Nāga; the birth of a son to him by Chitrā; then Chitrā’s release from her curse; and Udayana’s receipt of a casket of betel leaves from Chitrā.

Taking the lute Ghoṣavatī, he returned to his mother at the hermitage of Jamadagni. Having seen the ring marked with his own name that had been left near the hunter Śabara, and having heard from him how it was recovered by Sahasrānīka, he went toward the hermitage of Jamadagni along with his ministers. There, Queen Mṛgāvatī, from Jamadagni, received her son Udayana and her grandson; they then returned to their own city. Subsequently, regarding his son named Udayana...

Having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to his own ministers and sons, including Vasantaka, Marubhūti, and Yaugandharāyaṇa, he went to Cakratīrtha situated on the shore of the southern ocean; there, by the mere act of bathing, he attained his original form preceded by the removal of the curse, followed by the description of how all four of them likewise regained their former states. Furthermore, at Cakratīrtha, Aditi, the mother of the gods, commanded her daughter to perform penance there.

By the command of Diti, her daughter assumed the form of Aditi and went to the penance grove; there she performed severe austerities, such as the *pañcāgni-sādhana* (the practice of sitting amidst five fires). Enraged by that penance, the sage Supārśva spoke to her in harsh words. The subjects of this chapter include her receiving a son who would defeat the gods and have the face of a buffalo with a human body, her taking him and returning to her own abode, and subsequently, the birth of the demon Mahiṣāsura from that daughter of Diti.

After Mahiṣāsura attained sovereignty over the entire kingdom of the Daityas, he waged war against the gods and brought about their defeat; then, taking the defeated gods with him, he proceeded toward Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and Śiva at the abode of Brahmā.

Having heard this account of the affliction caused by the demons Diti, Aditi, and Asura from the mouths of the Lord of Lakṣmī and Maheśvara, there emerged a great mass of splendor; thereafter, splendor issued forth from the bodies of all the gods, and from the union of all those splendors, there was the birth of a maiden named Subhadrā, who was exceedingly radiant and possessed of beautiful limbs. Then, all the gods presented her with weapons produced from their own respective weapons, and she was praised by all the gods.

The Goddess mounts her lion and lets out a most terrifying loud laugh for the purpose of slaying the demon Mahiṣāsura; then follows the exceedingly fearsome battle between the gods and the armies of Mahiṣāsura; and therein, a description of how the Goddess effects the slaughter of Mahiṣāsura’s forces in that battle.

And *oṃ*. Now, after the Goddess had slain the asuras known as Caṇḍa and Kopa who had been dispatched by Mahiṣāsura, Mahiṣāsura himself arrived for the sake of battle; [this section describes] her engaging in a hand-to-hand combat with him, followed by the Goddess’s slaying of Mahiṣāsura, and the gods’ offering of praise to the Goddess, being satisfied by the killing of Mahiṣāsura. Then, when the gods had returned to their respective positions of authority, the Goddess, the Mother of the World, [remained] on the shore of the southern ocean.

The granting of boons preceded by the offering of jewels at the two holy sites of Dharmapuṣkariṇī and Devopattana; the construction of the bridge by Śrī Rāmacandra, preceded by the installation of nine stones representing the forms of the nine planets; a description of the boundary site where the construction of the bridge began; the majesty of Setunātha Hari; the praise of Cakratīrtha; the account of the commencement of the pilgrimage to the bridge starting from the site of Darbhadāyana; then, the narrative concerning the Vetālavarada Tīrtha, wherein [the story] of the daughter of the great sage Gāṅga...

The secret union of Kāntimatī with the Vidyādhara youth named Sudaśana in the groves of Madanavihāra; the granting by Gāskha to the Vidyādhara named Sudarśana of the attainment of human status followed by the attainment of the state of a Kevalin; and the granting of the boon of attaining merely human status to his younger brother, named Sukaṇaka, who had consented to that—subsequently, [the birth] of those two, Sudarśana and Sukaṇaka, in the house of Govindasvāmin, a resident of the banks of the Yamunā.

The contents of the next chapter: the attainment of the status of being the son named Vijayadatta; then, Govindasvāmin, having gone toward Vārāṇasī due to the famine in his own country, hearing from the mouth of the ascetic named Kapālakaṅkābharaṇa about the future separation from his son named Vijayadatta; the hearing of the account of Vijayadatta’s sudden transformation into a Vetāla named Kapālasphoṭana; and then, Govindasvāmin, distressed by grief for his son, returning to his own home.

The slaying of the sorcerer named Adoka-datta by his second son, Gaurivita, with the permission of King Pratāpamukuṭa; then the residence of Adoka-datta under the patronage of King Pratāpamukuṭa; and then, once while wandering in a forest with the king, Adoka-datta, accompanied by his wife, went to the hermitage of a certain Rākṣasī named Vidyunmālā who possessed illusory powers.

Having seized the foot-ornament and taken the jeweled anklet, he went into the presence of the king and presented the jeweled anklet to the king for his satisfaction. Then, being pleased by that, the king named Pratāpamukuṭa gave his own daughter, named Madanalekhā, to Aśokadatta according to the marriage rites. Subsequently, having learned of this, Aśokadatta went to the cremation ground to obtain a second anklet, taking with him human flesh; there, as he was summoning the spirits through mantras...

The arrival of the Rākṣasī named Vidyutkeśī, surrounded by Rākṣasa maidens, to his side with the desire to devour him for her meal; then, the Rākṣasī Vidyutkeśī, satisfied by his fortitude, giving her own daughter named Vidyutprabhā to the son of a twice-born man named Añjokadatta, preceded by the gift of the second jeweled anklet resting upon her foot; and furthermore, the gift of a golden tortoise to that very son-in-law as a reward for the merit of giving his daughter—all this.

Having taken Aśokadatta, he went into the presence of the king named Pratāpamukuṭa; there, Pratāpamukuṭa caused Aśokadatta’s beard to be shaved. Then, once upon a time, when Vidyaśvarī was asked in private about the origin of the golden lotus-mark given by her mother, she related the account of the divine lake belonging to the lord of the Vetālas named Kapālīsphoṭaka. Subsequently, together with Vidyaśvarī, Aśokadatta [went] to Kapālīsphoṭaka...

The journey toward the Vetāṭaṭa-rakṣita Cāṇakya-maṭha lake; there, having slain the Vetālas who were causing obstacles, Aśokadatta, desiring to kill the Vetāla named Kapāṭāvisphoṭaka, was blinded by the Vidyādhara named Vimānārūḍhavijñaptikautuka. Immediately upon that [act of killing], Aśokadatta was released from the curse of becoming a human being given by the great Ṛṣi Gāṅgava and attained his own true form as the one named Sukaṇa. Then, by the word of the Vidyādhara Vimānārūḍhavijñaptikautuka, [he regained] his state as a Vetāla.

In order to rescue his own son who had fallen ill, Prāpta went with him to Cakratīrtha situated on the shore of the southern ocean and performed a ritual bath; by the mere touch of a drop of water from that holy site, Vetāla’s state as a vampire was removed, and he regained the status of being the son of the twice-born man named Vijayadatta. Then, when that Vijayadatta again made a formal resolve to bathe there, Vetāla attained the form of a human being, and upon the cessation of his demonic nature, he achieved the status of a Vidyādhara named Sudarśana.

The description of the fame of that holy ford (tīrtha) by the name Vetāḍadhavara-dana due to its power to liberate from the state of being a Vetāla; then, the description of the majesty of the Gandhamādana mountain situated on the southern ocean; the majesty of the Pāpavināśana-tīrtha located on the Gandhamādana mountain; therein, the narration of the account of the sage named Dṛḍhamati; in connection with that, the description of the duties of the virtuous; and the performance of penance by the sage named Dṛḍhamati, preceded by the construction of a temple for the Lord and other religious acts, while desiring to perform a sacrifice.

While he was living according to the conduct of a sage, the Brahmin named Sumati performed the instruction of Vedic rituals for him; however, due to the fault of causing his son to become a non-sacrificer (*ayājya*), Sumati fell into hell and other states, and the description of his various miserable births, such as those of poisoners and rogues, is given. Then, after several births, upon his attainment of birth as a Brahmin, because he was seized by the planet Brahmārāsa, he became averse to Vedic rituals. Thereupon, his father took him and went to [the Lord] Prati...

Then, following the instruction of Agastya, he went to the shore of the southern ocean. At the holy ford named Pāpavināśa, by the mere act of bathing preceded by the proper resolve (*saṃkalpa*), his father—who had been led there—attained liberation from the host of Rākṣasas and the attainment of all enjoyments followed by final liberation (*mokṣa*). Furthermore, for the Brahmin named Dṛḍhamati, who was intent on performing the Vedic rites taught by him, there occurred the exhaustion of many births in the wombs of animals preceded by a stay in hell; thereafter, he gradually attained birth as a vulture.

The attainment of heaven through drinking the water of the holy ford (*tīrtha*) named Pāpavināśana, located on Mount Gandhamādana by the Southern Ocean; a description of the power of the Pāpavināśana Tīrtha; then, a description of the majesty of the Sītāsaras Tīrtha; and in connection with that lake, a narration of the account of Indra’s release from the sin of Brahman-slaughter. Therein, the battle of the Rākṣasa named Kapālābharaṇa, together with his army, against the gods headed by Rāma [Rudra]; and in that battle, by Śakra...

The slaying of the Rākṣasa Kapālābharaṇa; the affliction of Śakra by the sin of Brahman-slaughter resulting from that killing; the account of how the Rākṣasa named Kapālābharaṇa attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa as a narrative digression; and the story of how the wife of the Rākṣasa Śivakara, Suśīlā by name, produced a son through the Nāga named Nyuci at her husband's command—thus detailing how the son-in-law Kapālābharaṇa attained the state of a Brāhmaṇa; and finally, the instruction of Brahmā to Śakra, who was afflicted by the sin of Brahman-slaughter.

The description of liberation from the sin of killing a Brahmin through knowledge, sacrifices, and the propitiation of Sadāśiva at the Sītā-kuṇḍa located on the Gandhamādana mountain range bordering the Southern Ocean; then, a description of the Sītā-saras and the Māṣā-saras; and finally, a description of the majesty of the sacred ford known as Maṅgala.

In connection with that, follows the narration of the royal history of the one named Manojava. Due to the sin arising from seizing the sacrificial rice (*kūrca*) from Brahmins, King Gokharba first seized the kingdom of Manojava—who was possessed of ego—and then exiled him from his realm. Subsequently, Manojava departed for the forest together with his wife and son. There, seeing his son afflicted by hunger, Manojava, overcome with grief and intense remorse, fell into a swoon; [and so did] his wife.

The mockery of the one named Sumitrā; the weeping of her son as well; then, at that moment, the arrival of the great sage Parāśara near them; by Parāśara, through the sprinkling of water purified by mantras upon his matted locks, the removal of the king's fainting spell; thereafter, at the king’s request, the sage Parāśara imparted the instruction of the six-syllable Rāma-mantra to the king, preceded by an exposition of the means for the pilgrimage to the holy site known as Magara on the Śrīrāma-setu; [all this] by the command of Maṅgu.

Having gone with his wife and son to the Maṅgala-tīrtha, Manojavānu performed the observance of the *mātṛ-upāsana* for forty days; before him [appeared] the bow named Maṅgala, along with a quiver, a sword, a shield, a mace, a club, and a trident.

There appeared a chariot equipped with a driver, banners, and golden armor; then, with the speed of thought, he presented all those objects to the sage Parāśara. Next, the sage Parāśara performed the consecration of King Manojava with mantras, followed by the granting of weapons such as the Brahmāstra and the bestowing of boons. Then, having returned to his own city, King Manojava destroyed the king Gorabha with the Brahmāstra and established himself in his own kingdom.

Having reached this [place] through righteousness, one attains Maṅkaṭatīrtha; it is described how, immediately after casting off the body there, one obtains the speed of thought and reaches the world of Śiva. Next follows the description of the sacred site (kṣetra) named Ekāntarāmanātha, wherein lies the greatness of the Āsṛtavāpikā Tīrtha. In connection with that, the account of the younger brother of Agastya is told: how he performed penance on the Himalayas, and upon the manifestation of Śaṅkara, who was pleased by that penance, the younger brother of Agastya offered hymns of praise to Śiva. Then, [Śiva], being satisfied—

By the command of Śiva, [this work was composed] at the holy site (tīrtha) situated upon the Gandhamādana mountain range on the southern ocean, inhabited by the younger brother of Agastya, concerning the sacred field (kṣetra) of Ekāntarāmanātha. Herein are the chapters and their subjects: First, a description of how that holy site attained the fame of the name "Aghṛtavāpī" because one attains liberation through the yoga of meditative absorption (samādhiyoga) after bathing there and becoming immortal; then, in the context of explaining the cause for the fame of the sacred field of Ekāntarāmanātha, [the account] of Śrī Rāmacandra with Lakṣmaṇa...

A description of the account of contemplating the means for crossing [the ocean] preceded by staying in solitude; the majesty of Rādhava in solitude; then, a description of the majesty of Brahmaṇḍakuṇḍa situated on Mount Gandhamādana by the southern ocean; in connection with that, the majesty of wearing the *tripuṇḍra* mark with the ashes from Nahayakuṇḍa; the account of the origin of Brahmaṇḍakuṇḍa; and therein, when a dispute arose between Brahmā and Viṣṇu regarding the matter of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) in their midst...

The manifestation of the two [deities] from the Bhadra-liṅga of the Blessed One occurred for the purpose of purifying the limits of its upper and lower extremities. Brahmā and Viṣṇu proceeded while assuming the forms of a swan and a boar; however, having returned to their respective abodes without seeing the lower limit of the Liṅga, Viṣṇu spoke the truth regarding the extent of the Liṅga's base. Then, although Brahmā had also returned without seeing the upper limit, he deceitfully spoke a falsehood regarding the extent of the Liṅga's summit. Now...

Enraged by that false speech, Śaṅkara manifested as a *khiṅga* (prostitute) and bestowed upon Brahmā the punishment of being rendered unworthy of worship. Then, at the request of the distressed Brahmā, Śaṅkara commanded him to perform a sacrifice for the purpose of removing the falsely imputed fault on Mount Gandhamādana, situated in the southern ocean. By the Lord’s command, Brahmā performed a sacrifice dedicated to Śiva on Mount Gandhamādana; there, having manifested as a *mātaṅga* (outcaste), Śaṅkara [bestowed] upon Brahmā...

The granting of boons preceded by the bestowal of the status of being worshipful for all rites upon Śrī Tasmā; the granting of boons at the holy site named Brahmakuṇḍa; the majesty of Brahmakuṇḍa; then the description of the majesty of Hanumānchaṇḍa; in connection with that, the description of the life of the king named Dharmasakha; the account of the scorpion sting of Ukha-candra, the son of King Dharmasakha; then, by King Dharmasakha, who was desiring many sons, [the procurement of] sacrificial materials through his own words—

Having performed the rites with his wives and all his attendants, together with the officiating priests, he set out toward the Hanumadmaṇḍapa on Mount Gandhamādana situated on the shore of the western ocean. Having bathed there and performed the *putrīyeṣṭi* sacrifice, he reached Hatocadaṣṭa; having bestowed villages and agrahāras upon the Brahmins, he performed an ablution with his wife Bhāgyarāti and returned to his own city. There, by the power of Hanumadmaṇḍapa, among the hundred wives of that Dharmasakha—

The attainment of a hundred sons by Bhavyā; then, at the time of death, King Danuma approaching the Hanumat-kuṇḍa and performing penance with his friend; thereafter, his attainment of the realm of Vaiṅuṇṭha; the performance of the funeral rites for his father by his son Sucandra; the description of the brotherly affection of all the sons beginning with Sucandra and their enjoyment of royal pleasures; the majesty of Hanumat-kuṇḍa; then the description of the majesty of Agastitīrtha; and in connection with that majesty—

The narration of the deeds of Kakṣīvat, the son of the sage Dīrghatamas. Therein, after Kakṣīvat had completed his study of the sixty-four branches of knowledge at the house of his teacher named Udaṅka, the teacher’s brother-in-law prevented him from returning home. Subsequently, the teacher explained a stratagem for his marriage; then, by the teacher’s command, Kakṣīvat went to the Agastya-tīrtha, mounted a bright, four-tusked lordly elephant that had emerged from that sacred bathing place, and while on the way, by a mere sign, [he was joined] by one named Svanaya.

The king’s journey toward his city with him; then, at the request of King Svanaya, Kakṣīvata was invited through the mediation of the family priest named Sudarśana to receive the gift of the king’s daughter, and having been welcomed with honors, he was escorted back to the capital; thereupon, Kakṣīvata offered salutations to his father Dīrghatamas and reported the account of his own studies in the sciences; then, at that sacred site of Agasti, by King Svanaya—

The honoring of the sage Dīrghatamas. In the meantime, at that very spot, the great seer Udaṅka arrived at the Agasti-tīrtha accompanied by his assembly of disciples; there occurred a meeting between Udaṅka and Dīrghatamas. Then, King Svanaya approached for the sake of Droṇa and announced his own purpose. Subsequently, with the consent of Udaṅka, King Svanaya agreed to bestow his daughter upon Kakṣīvat. Thereafter, King Svanaya had the maiden brought from the city of Madhurā by his attendants and [performed] the marriage ceremony according to the prescribed rites.

The giving of a maiden in marriage to Kakṣīvat; thereafter, the bestowing of gold, cows, female slaves, villages, and other riches upon the bridegroom; then, the sage Dīrghatamas taking his son and daughter-in-law and returning to his own hermitage situated in the Vedāraṇya forest; King Svanaya bathing with the ladies of the inner court at the Agastitīrtha and departing for his own city; the majesty of the Agastitīrtha; and finally, the description of the majesty of the holy site known as Rāmakuṇḍa.

In connection with that, there is a description of the sage Sutīkṣṇa, the disciple of Agastya; the performance of penance by Sutīkṣṇa at the holy ford of Rāmacandra-saras; the offering of praise to Śrī Rāmacandra by Sutīkṣṇa while performing penance; and, in the context of describing the perfection of Sutīkṣṇa’s eightfold penance as he thus practiced austerities, a description of the greatness of Rāmakaṇḍa. 20.

In the *Kāyī-yiti-rākā*, there is a description of the majesty of the Śrī Śiva-liṅga installed by Rāma on the banks of the Rāmakuṇḍa; in connection with that, there is an account of how Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, was freed from the fault of speaking untruth. In that regard, during the Bhārata war, in order to defeat Droṇa, Kṛṣṇa spread a false report that Aśvatthāman had been killed in battle by Bhīma’s wife. Having heard that report—and having heard it likewise from Yudhiṣṭhira—Droṇa believed it to be true and [resorted] to yoga.

The act of not sacrificing his own flesh; the acquisition of the sin arising from speaking a falsehood by Yudhiṣṭhira, who had always been a speaker of truth, during that time; and the declaration by a celestial voice at the time of his consecration to the kingdom after the conclusion of the war—that he was unfit for the royal consecration due to the sin born of speaking untruth under a pretext; Yudhiṣṭhira’s subsequent feeling of remorse; and at that moment, the arrival of the great sage Vyāsa before Yudhiṣṭhira.

At Rāmatīrtha, situated on the shore of the southern ocean, the performance of the *śrāddha* rites was undertaken. Then, Yudhiṣṭhira, having installed his younger brother Sahadeva upon the throne, set out toward Rāmasetu together with his preceptor Dhaumya and his own brothers, Bhīma and the others. Without ascending a boat, he reached Rāmatīrtha by means of the *yātrā* ritual and performed his ablutions according to the path prescribed by the family priest. By the power of that bathing, giving, *śrāddha*, and month-long fasting at Rāmatīrtha, [he attained] divine speech.

The description of Yudhiṣṭhira’s fitness for ascending the throne, preceded by the removal of the sin born from his speaking untruth; then the majesty of the Rāmakuṇḍa holy site; next, the description of the majesty of the Lakṣmaṇatīrtha; and in connection with that, the account of Balabhadra’s liberation from the sin of Brahman-slaughter. Therein, Balabhadra—unwilling to witness the slaughter of the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas—goes to a great assembly of ascetics in the forest under the pretext of a pilgrimage to holy sites; and there, by Balabhadra...

While Sūta was seated upon the Brahmāsana to narrate the Purāṇas, he unintentionally struck him with the tip of a blade of grass held in his own hand, resulting in the sin of killing a Brahmin. Then, at the word of the sages and desiring to perform an expiation for the sake of the world’s welfare, he made a request to the sages. The sages instructed him to perform an expiation in the form of a pilgrimage after slaying a Rākṣasa named Bāṣkala; subsequently, Balabhadra killed the Rākṣasa named Bāṣkala.

Then, for the duration of a year, there is the description of performing a pilgrimage to all the sacred bathing sites (tīrthas) situated on the surface of the earth, preceded by ritual ablutions; and even after such a pilgrimage to the holy sites has been completed, the description of liberation from the sin of killing a Brahmin through merely bathing at the Rakṣmaṇatīrtha located on Mount Gandhamādana in the southern ocean, and through the sight of the Liṅga of Rakṣbhaṇeśvara, despite the fact that the objects of the senses have ceased to exist or are like poison, as stated in the words of Jahnu.

The greatness of the Rāmaṇatīrtha: when Śuka asked Vyāsa for a means to purify his mind, Vyāsa, after recounting the ancient history of Śrī Śuka and Varuṇa, described the majesty of Jaṭātīrtha located at Rāmasetu. Then, having heard Vyāsa’s instruction, Śuka went to Jaṭātīrtha, where it is described how his mind was purified by mere bathing; this is the greatness of Jaṭātīrtha.

Then follows the description of the greatness of Lakṣmītīrtha; in connection with that, the account of Yudhiṣṭhira’s history is told. While Yudhiṣṭhira was staying on Mount Indrabhaṭṭa, he posed a question to Śrī Kṛṣṇa regarding the dharma that bestows great sovereignty; in response, Śrī Kṛṣṇa recounted to Yudhiṣṭhira the greatness of Lakṣmītīrtha at the site of Gandhamādana, preceded by numerous ancient legends. Thereafter, Yudhiṣṭhira went to Lakṣmītīrtha and performed ritual bathing for a full month according to the prescribed rules.

Having performed these rites and returned to his own city, he then, by virtue of the unsurpassed wealth and sovereignty attained through that very disposition, undertook with great effort and the assistance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa the performance of the Rājasūya sacrifice.

The majesty of Lakṣmī-tīrtha; then the description of the majesty of Abhra-tīrtha; and in connection with that, the account of Sītā’s purification. There, after Rāmacandra had slain Rāvaṇa at Laṅkā, he returned toward Gandhamādana by way of the bridge along with Indra and the other gods. Having stayed on the bank of Lakṣmī-tīrtha, he summoned the fire for the sake of purifying Jānakī. Then Abhra arrived there and, in the presence of Rāma, declared Sītā’s purity. Following Abhra’s words, by Rāmacandra—

The acceptance of Jānakī; the renown of the place where Anasūyā emerged as the sacred ford named Abhitīrtha; and, in connection with the majesty of Abhitīrtha, the narration of the life of a preeminent merchant named Paśuman, who, among his six sons including Paḍumanta, was the sixth son named Duṣpaṇya—a man of extreme wickedness who committed the murder of the city’s gardeners—and whose head the king saw while on a hunt, leading to the merchant's banishment from the country; thereafter, even though he had fled to the forest...

When Tenograśravas, the son of a sage, was killed after being submerged in the *jaṭā* (matted-hair) [pool], Satyubhraśravas, the sage, seeing him, pronounced a curse: "Because you have caused [him] to be submerged in the *jaṭā*, you shall become a crocodile. Then, during a great deluge at Vaṣaukāṭha, Duṣpaṇya entered the interior of the carcass of a dead elephant that had fallen; when that elephant's body was carried away by a vast flood of water into the ocean, there follows a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Jaṭātīrtha, and in connection with that, a description of the life-story of Dukācārya.

There, when the six syllables *oṃ ka ka ka ka* entered the sphere of Bhavyā, Duṣpaṇya, who was situated within it, met his death. Immediately thereafter, he attained the state of a Piśāca. Then, having returned to the vicinity of Agastya’s hermitage in the form of a Piśāca, he made a fervent appeal to the great sages for his own liberation. Subsequently, for the sake of his release, the great sage Agastya directed him toward the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) known as Suvīkṣṇa.

The performance of the bath according to the command; upon performing the bath at the Abhitīrtha—the place designated for the liberation of the Piśāca by the son of Tīkṣṇa—the Piśāca, having been freed from his state as a Piśāca, ascends a divine celestial chariot (*vimāna*), pays homage to the great sages (*maharṣi*), and departs for the divine realm. Then follows the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the Abhratīrtha, and subsequently the description of the majesty of the Cakratīrtha. In connection with that, there is the narration of the worship of the Sudarśana [mantra] performed by a Brāhmaṇa named Ahivudhnya, and how that Brāhmaṇa was [liberated] by the sight of the Sudarśana-cakra.

The destruction of the Rākṣasas who cause obstacles to ascetic penance; the fame of the sacred ford as Cakratīrtha due to the presence of the discus of the Lord of the Good Discus (Viṣṇu); the performance of a sacrifice to Maheśvara by all the gods, terrified by the Rākṣasas, at the command of Brahmā in the vicinity of Cakratīrtha; the narration of the account of how the hand of the Sun-god was restored—having been severed by the mere touch of the sacrificial ladle (*prāśitra-pātra*)—through the power of bathing in Cakratīrtha upon the word of the sage Aṣṭāvakra;
and the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Cakratīrtha. ... ||

32. Now follows the description of the greatness of Śivatīrtha, and in that context, the narration of the events concerning Kāṅkābharava. When a dispute arose between Gaṅgā and Viṣṇu regarding their mutual superiority, and although Śiva’s superiority was proclaimed by means of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), Gaṅgā and Viṣṇu, due to their stubbornness, did not acknowledge Śiva’s supremacy; thereupon, Śiva manifested his true form as the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*). Upon seeing Maheśvara, Jahnu nevertheless treated him with disrespect.

The conversation between Gava and Uttanka; then, Maheśvara’s dispatching of the personage named Kārbherava to Brahmā; the severing of the fifth head of Brahmā by Kārbherava during the battle with Brahmā; thereafter, the propitiation of Brahmā by the Blessed Maheśvara; the offering of praise to the Blessed Śaṅkara by the god Brahmā; the granting of fearlessness to Brahmā by Śaṅkara; and then, by the command of Śiva, [the action] of Kālabhairava.

For the purification of the sin of killing a Brahmin, one should sever one's own head and hold it in the hand, then wander for a year visiting all the sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrthas*). By performing a bath at the Śiva-tīrtha located on Mount Gandhamādana in the Southern Ocean, the sin of Brahmin-slaughter is removed. It is there that Kālabhairava established the *kapāṭa* (the skull); thus, that Śiva-tīrtha is designated as the Kapāṭa-tīrtha. [The following is] the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the Diva-tīrtha. [End of] the *jā*, *jā*, *ja*, *pa*. [End of] the chapters (*adhyāyas*). [End of] the subjects (*viṣayas*). Now...

Description of the Greatness of Śaṅkha-tīrtha: This sacred ford (tīrtha) became renowned as Śaṅkha-tīrtha because it was established by the sage Śaṅkha after he had performed austerities there. In connection with the greatness of that tīrtha, the narrative of the person named Vatsanābha is recounted. While the twice-born man named Vatsanābha remained there performing austerities, an anthill grew over him; then, when Indra caused a disturbance by raining down a torrent of rain to obstruct his penance, the Lord Dharmadeva [manifested] as a great buffalo...

Assuming the form of a bull and standing upon a mountain slope, he caught the torrents of rain on his own back and protected the sage. Then, having withdrawn from his meditative absorption (samādhi), Vatsanābha—realizing that he had failed to worship Dharmanātha, his protector who was nearby in the form of a buffalo, and resolving to rekindle his mind in meditation—made an effort to cast himself down from Mount Arbuda to end his life in order to atone for the fault of his transgression. At that moment, by the god Dharma...

Having abandoned his buffalo form and manifested in his true nature, [Viṣṇu] prevented the death of the Brahmin Varasānābha; he then performed the purification of the fault of ingratitude and, for the sake of the Brahmin's mental purification, caused him to bathe at the holy site (tīrtha) known as Śaṅkhatīrtha located on the shore of the southern ocean. Through this instruction in Dharma, it is described how, immediately after the Brahmin Varasānābha’s purification from the fault of ingratitude by the mere act of bathing at Śaṅkhatīrtha, he attained the state of Brahman preceded by mental purification. This is the glorification of the greatness of Śaṅkhatīrtha.

Now follows the description of the triad of sacred fords known as Yamunā, Gaṅgā, and Gayā; in connection with that, the account of King Jānaśruti is narrated. Therein is described the birth of one who was lame from birth—also known by the name Sayugvā—who, while performing austerities for many years on Mount Gandhamādana situated in the eastern ocean, was afflicted by a skin disease. Then, desiring to bathe in the triad of sacred fords called Yamunā, Gaṅgā, and Gayā, he invoked those three fords through meditation preceded by the recitation of mantras; and at the mere utterance [of the mantra], Yamunā—

The presence of the three holy sites—Gaṅgā, Gayā, and Prayāga—in his vicinity; the eternal proximity of those three *tīrthas* there by virtue of the words of the great seers (*maharṣis*); and on one occasion at that time, while King Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa was situated at the window of his palace, the arrival of the great seers in the form of swans at midnight for the sake of a discussion regarding the soul; and among those seers, by one great seer in the form of a swan, [the teaching] to Jānaśruti on the supreme reality through the instruction of the *Udgītha*.

Having offered praise to the great seers, they departed together with their own followers toward the world of Brahmā; then, after those great seers had gone, Jānaśruti sought refuge with the great seer Raikva, who was accompanied by his chariot-horse, in order to obtain the knowledge of the Self. || 21 ||

Then, at the command of King Reka, Viṣaya and Sayugvana performed ablutions at the triad of holy fords—Yamunā, Gaṅgā, and Gayāli—and thereafter, through the instruction on the knowledge of the One given by King Janaśruta, their attainment of the state of Brahman is described.

Now begins the description of the greatness of Koṭitīrtha, and in connection with that, the narrative of the life of Śrī Rāmacandra. Therein is described the account of how Śrī Rāma, having installed the divine Liṅga named Rāmanātha on Mount Gandhamādana in the southern ocean to dispel the sin incurred by the slaughter of Rāvaṇa, pierced the earth with the tip of his bow and brought the Gaṅgā from the netherworld (Rasātala) for the purpose of bathing it; and thereafter, [the description] of that sacred site.

The renown of Koṭitīrtha as a sacred site, an account of the greatness of Koṭitīrtha, and a description of the deeds of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; therein, after Vasudeva’s marriage, as he was setting out for his own city by chariot, Kaṃsa—the charioteer of that vehicle—having been summoned by Akrūra, prepared to kill the future slayer of Keśin, Devakī’s son, whom Vasudeva had promised to deliver; [the account of] how Vasudeva, through conciliation, turned him away from the act of killing on the condition of providing the child. Then...

After the transfer of the embryo from Devakī, the wife of Vasudeva—who was then pregnant with her seventh child—to Rohiṇī by means of Yogamāyā, the birth of the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa occurred. Vasudeva offered prayers of praise to the Blessed One; then, by the command of the Blessed One, Vasudeva carried Śrī Kṛṣṇa to Gokula and brought back the daughter of Yaśodā to Mathurā. Subsequently, while Kaṃsa was about to strike the infant on a stone slab out of fear of his enemy, that Primordial Māyā emerged from his hand and ascended to the sky.

The departure in the form of the auspicious and the inauspicious; the Goddess telling Kaṃsa, "Your death shall come from someone anywhere"; the attainment of worship at various places where [the Lord] was hidden; the description of the sporting of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma while staying in Gokula; then, having gone toward Mathurā, the killing of Kaṃsa and the performance of the royal consecration of Ugrasena; and then, on one occasion, regarding Nārada and others who had arrived to see him, Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s [action] for the sake of expiating the fault incurred by the killing of his maternal uncle.

The commencement of the expiation; then, according to the words of Nārada and others, Rāmaseta arrived and, by the mere act of bathing at Koṭitīrtha, [was freed from] the defect arising from the killing of his maternal uncle, Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s maternal uncle; this is not a subject for the Madhyamā [branch]. Now follows the description of the majesty of Sādhyākhṛta-tīrtha, and in connection with that, the narration of the history of King Purūravas, including his union there with the Apsaras Urvaśī, and subsequently, due to the failure of his promise regarding the appointed time—

Following the separation from that son of Atidhṛti, there is an account of his meeting with the two Bhṛṅgis in the field of Kuru, preceded by the narration of the recovery of his son; then, after some time, the king’s reunion with Padmāvatī at the lotus-lake in Kurukṣetra; the handing over of her son Āyuṣmat, born to her through her own power, to the king by Urvaśī; and subsequently, during the course of a single night, the implanting of the seed of Pañcacūḍa within that very womb of Urvaśī.

Then, at her suggestion, Purūravas made a request to the Gandharvas for the sake of attaining uninterrupted union with Urvaśī. At his request, the Gandharvas, being pleased, gave the sacrificial fire-vessel (*agni-sthālī*) to Purūravas and instructed him on how to perform sacrifices. Due to his failure to attain Urvaśī, the dissatisfied Purūravas threw that very fire-vessel into the middle of a forest and returned to his own city. From the place where the fire-vessel was deposited, a *śamī* tree and an *aśvattha* tree grew forth; then, from that *aśvattha* tree...

Having kindled the fire by rubbing together the two fire-sticks of the twenty-four syllables, and having performed many sacrifices, Urvaśī attained the world of the Gandharvas and sported with King Purūravas. Then, once, while the sacrifice was being commenced in the presence of Śakra, Tumburu—the preceptor of the gods—seeing Urvaśī and Purūravas looking at one another with intent laughter, pronounced a curse that their separation would occur. Thereafter, Purūravas made a plea to Indra.

Desiring to employ the means prescribed by him, he went to the surface of the earth; having reached the Sādhyāmṛta tīrtha located at Gandhamādana on the shore of the Southern Ocean, he was liberated from the curse merely by bathing there. Returning once more to the world of Urvaśī, he engaged in dalliance with her. [This section concludes with] the majesty of the Sādhyāmṛta tīrtha, followed by the description of the majesty of the Sāvitṛ tīrtha.

The narration of the extraordinary life of the Brahmin named Sucarita due to his attachment to worldly existence; therein, the Brahmin Sucarita, afflicted by old age and devoid of all desire, having arrived at Mount Gandhamādana in the Daṇḍaka forest with the longing for the knowledge of all sacred sites (*tīrtha*), took up the initiation of Śiva and performed penance; when Śaṅkara appeared before him through that penance, the Brahmin Sucarita offered a hymn of praise to the illustrious Śiva; and the illustrious Śiva, in order to fulfill the wish of Sucarita, [appeared] near the friend of Sucarita.

Having invoked all the holy fords (*tīrthas*) into one place and thereby effecting a confluence of all holy fords, [the sages] bathed in the *Sarvatīrthābhipaika* and issued a command to Sucarita for the purpose of bathing. By means of this, through the agency of the sage Sucarita, at the head of the Śibi [region], [all the holy fords were established]. Now, following the context of the majesty of the Dhanuṣkoṭi holy ford, there is the narration of the life of Aśvatthāman. In that regard, there are chapters concerning the Aśvatthāman [episode]; the subjects therein include: the performance of a bath in the holy ford; the attainment of freedom from old age, youth, beauty, and other qualities by the Brahmin named Sucarita as a result of performing a bath in the holy ford; and the majesty of the holy ford known as Sarvatīrtha.

Oṃ. (Now begins the description of the majesty of Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha; the description of Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha as the means for destroying various kinds of sins; in connection with the majesty of Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha, the description of how Śrī Rāmacandra, at the request of Vibhīṣaṇa, drew a line with the tip of his own bow so that other worlds would not enter the Saṅkāra [the confluence], thereby describing the breaking of his own bridge; the description of the presence of all deities at Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha; and [the description of the merit] in Māgha and other months at Dhanuṣkoṭi...)

The description of the greatness of bathing at the Ṣkoṭi-tīrtha: Having made a vow to slay all the brave warriors stationed in the camp, he approached the gate of the camp at nightfall with Kṛtavarman and Śatānīka; having propitiated Mahādeva and received from him, who was pleased, a sword of victory, he first gave it to his father’s slayer, the preceptor Droṇa, and then proceeded to the camp of the five Pāṇḍavas, where he slaughtered the entire army, including Draupadī’s sons and others, beginning with Dhṛṣṭadyumna, from the gate of the camp.

The slaughter of the Senānya troops led by Barhin, who had been equipped with armor and weapons by their preceptors; thereafter, the flight of Aśvatthāman and the others from the camp to various different regions; then, when Aśvatthāman had entered among the great sages on the banks of the Narmadā and was declared fallen from his status as a Brahmin by the other Brahmins, he departed from there and undertook a pilgrimage to sacred fords at Aśvatthāman’s command; then, having heard of Vyāsa residing at Badarikāśrama, he sought refuge with him; and thereafter, by the instruction of Vyāsa, Aśvatthāman—

For the pacification of the fault of excessive killing, [the sage] reached Rāmasetu and performed service to Lord Rāmanātha Śiva at Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha preceded by ritual ablution; thereafter, having arrived at Śrīraṅgam, he offered praise to Śiva. Then, the Great God, being pleased, granted a boon at Aśvatthāna. [The text continues with] the majesty of Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha; and then, in the course of describing the majesty of Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha once more, [the account concerns] Dharmarāja, the son of King Nandana, who was born in the Lunar Dynasty.

Description of Conduct: In that regard, after Nanda had departed for the forest to perform austerities, Dharmagupta was consecrated as king. Once, having entered the forest for the sake of hunting, he mounted a bull out of fear of lions and other wild beasts during the night. There, a certain wicked sage, desiring to save his own life from someone pursuing him, approached the king who was situated in the tree. Following this, there ensued a mutual conversation between them.

Having inspired confidence, he established a system of alternating sleep and wakefulness between the king and the tiger during the night by dividing it into two watches. Then, while the king was asleep and the tiger had been told by the king to guard him under the constellation Siṃha, the tiger—instead of guarding the king—declared his transformation into a fire of treachery and enmity toward the king. Thereupon, when the king woke up and found himself under that very same constellation, the tiger [seized] the monarch.

While the king was sprinkling water around the sacrificial fire with the grass-bands (*nīva*), the sage cried out, "I am here! and caused the king's eyes to fall. At that moment, the sage, having seized the king’s feet with his own nails, climbed back onto the pedestal; then, after first describing his own state as a sage named Dhyānakācha, he declared that he had assumed the form of a seer out of desire. He then bestowed a curse upon the lord of Bharata, saying, "Become insane," and departed for his hermitage. There, he related the previous account of how he had attained the status of a sage through the power of the curse he had previously given to Gīta.

Just as the lion immediately ascended a celestial chariot (*vimāna*)—which was the very embodiment of his form and nature—upon hearing the words of the sage Dhyānakāṣṭha and departed for the realm of the *yakṣas*, so too did the sage Dhyānakāṣṭha, having assumed the form of a bear at his own will, proceed at his pleasure into the depths of the forest. After the sage Dhyānakāṣṭha had restored Dharmagupta from his state of madness, he returned to his own city; thereafter, [he dealt with] that Dharmagupta who had been rendered insane by the *tārā*...

The bringing of Dharmagupta to the presence of his father, King Nanda—who resided on the banks of the river Nairamada—by the ministers; then, thereupon, Nanda’s making of a request to the great sage Jaimini for the sake of subduing the fault of his son’s excessive pride; thereafter, by the command of the great sage Jaimini, King Nanda took his son Dharmagupta and, having arrived at the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha located on the Rāmasetu, performed an ablution; [the result of] merely bathing in the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha.
