The granting of boons; the description of King Śaṅkara attaining union with Śiva through the grace of Śrī Rāmanātha. ... Then, the performance of hymns of praise to the Lord Śrī Rāmeśvara by Śrī Rāmacandra, Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā, Hanumān, and all the monkeys, as well as all the sages, gods, and others. Thereafter, the description of the granting of boons to Śrī Rāmacandra and the others by the gracious Śrī Rāmeśvara. At one time, having bathed at Rāmadhanuṣkoṭi in Puṇyanivāsa, the jewel of Madhurāpurī...

Regarding the gifts such as the *tulāpuruṣa* and others: when [the King] was about to set out for his own city, he was protected by a maiden who had assumed a female form. That maiden spoke her intention daily to King Puṇyanidhi, saying, "I shall become your daughter and dwell in your house without fear. Thereupon, Puṇyanidhi brought that deceitful maiden back to his own home and raised her like a son near his wife, named Vindhyāvasī, after paying a fee. Then, regarding her...

The search for Lakṣmī; Viṣṇu’s arrival there disguised as a Brahmin; the forceful seizing of the hand by Lakṣmī, who had assumed the form of a maiden while the other girls were gathering flowers in that garden; then, hearing the weeping of the girls, Puṇyanidhi led that Viṣṇu in the guise of a Brahmin to the temple of Śrī Rāmanātha through his own gatekeeper and placed him in shackles; thereafter, at night, in a dream, Puṇyanidhi [saw] that Brahmin in the form of the Lord Viṣṇu.

And the manifestation of his own daughter in the form of Lakṣmī; then, at dawn, taking his daughter and going to the one named Rāmanātha, seeing that Brahmin who possessed the form of the Lord as he had been shown to him, recognizing him as Viṣṇu, and seeking forgiveness for his offense while offering praise; and the offering of praise to that Lakṣmī who was in the form of his own daughter; and by means of that prayer, the granting of boons to the devotee by the gracious Lord accompanied by Lakṣmī in the city of Puṇyaniketa. Of that devotee...

For the sake of the uninterrupted praise of King Puṇyanidhi, the Blessed One, known by the name Setumādhava, remained stationed there specifically for the purpose of wearing the image upon his head while bound in fetters; King Puṇyanidhi performed service to the Blessed One Setumādhava; at the end of King Puṇyanidhi’s life, he attained liberation; and [there follows] a description of the majesty of Setumādhava. (Now, the description of the sequence of the procedure for the pilgrimage to Setu: having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) in one’s own home preceded by bathing, with the intent of going on pilgrimage...)

First, a detailed description of the ritual procedures for the pilgrimage preceded by the observance of constant daily vows; then, a description of the greatness of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha, following an account of the Setubandha; a narration of the episode concerning the granting of boons by Śrī Rāmacandra at the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha; and, in the context of giving gifts, a praise of worthy recipients as presented in the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Dilīpa at the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha on Rāma’s Setu.

The first section of the Brahmakhaṇḍa begins with the Setumāhātmya, comprising: the description of the performance of rites such as bathing preceded by the removal of gadflies and other insects; the exposition of virtuous deeds such as worship, vows, and fasts; the greatness of reading, hearing, and giving gifts related to the Setumāhātmya; and finally, the conclusion and completion of the Setumāhātmya.
Chapters and Subjects, Paṭala; Chapters and Subjects. Now begins the second section, the Dharmāraṇya-khaṇḍa, within the Bālakhaṇḍa.

The wandering of Yama; the gathering of the great ṛṣis, such as Śaunaka and others, at the Naimiṣa forest to honor Sūta with due ceremony out of a desire to hear stories concerning the Dharma-raṇya; then, the commencement by the great ṛṣi Sūta to describe the majesty of Dharma-raṇya; therein, the journey of Yama-dharmadeva to the assembly of Brahmā; and there, having heard the divine narrative of Dharma-raṇya being recited by the great ṛṣi Vyāsa in that assembly of Brahmā, Yama-dharma—

The departure of the Lord toward his own city; the arrival of Nārada there before Yama, the King of Dharma; the narration by Yama, the King of Dharma—having been questioned by Nārada regarding the cause of his satisfaction—of the *Dharmāraṇya-kathā* heard from the mouth of Cyavana in the world of Brahmā; and the return of Nārada to the earth to see Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, after having heard [the account] from the King of Dharma. By Nārada, who had heard it from the King of Dharma...

To Dharmarāja, who desired to hear the *Camariṇya-kathā*, [Nārada] said: "In the month of Māgha, go to bathe in the Gaṅgā; before you do so, the great sage Vyāsa will arrive, and from his mouth you shall hear the *Camariṇya-kathā*. Having spoken thus, Nārada vanished. Then the arrival of the venerable great sage Vyāsa before Dharmarāja occurred. Thereupon, Yudhiṣṭhira, having seated Vyāsa upon the throne and honored him, inquired after his health. Then, by Vyāsa, to Yudhiṣṭhira...

The commencement of the discourse on the *Dharma-āraṇyaka*; a description of the various holy places (*tīrtha*), forests, and other sites of merit; Yudhiṣṭhira’s inquiry to Vyāsa out of a desire to know its greatness; Vyāsa’s undertaking of the narrative of the *Dharma-āraṇyaka*; therein, the description of Dharmadeva’s performance of penance after going into the middle of the forest with the intent to behold the true nature of the Blessed Lord and meditating upon Mahādeva; and the splendor of the mountain peak produced by that penance.

Having gone to Kailāsa along with Śiva, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and other deities, they offered praise to Śrī Mahādeva. Then, at the word of Rudra, Dharma realized that there was no cause for fear and all the gods departed for their own abodes. Indra, however, became suspicious despite the absence of any cause; with the consent of Bṛhaspati, he sent the Apsaras named Urvaśī at the request of the latter to perform a test of Dharma’s ascetic power. She approached Dharma and, through singing accompanied by dancing—

Next, the description of the greatness of the forest-dwelling (*dhamāraṇya*), which is another name for *nehiraka*; therein, the objects of that forest-dwelling, the causing of the King of Dharma’s mind to lose its momentary composure, and, as a digression from the description of the apsarases of Vardhanī, the recounting of the faults inherent in the nature of women. (Then follows the encounter of the King of Dharma with the apsarases of Vardhanī; the granting of a boon to the apsarases of Vardhanī by the King of Dharma; and subsequently, the report of the Dharma’s resolve to Śakra, preceded by [the intervention] of Vardhanī.)

Having descended from Śakra’s abode, he returned to his own place; then, immediately after the departure of the Apsarases, Dharmadeva performed severe penance through the practice of meditation. When the gods and others became anxious in mind due to that fierce asceticism, they went toward Kailāsa and offered praise to Śiva. Then, together with the gods, they returned to the forest where Dharmadeva was performing penance. Dharmadeva offered praise to the Blessed One, and Śaṅkara, pleased by that hymn of praise—

In the context of granting boons, following the establishment of the fame of the *Dharma-araṇya* within the Tapovana forest extending for two *yojanas*, there was the granting of a boon to the god Yamadharma; thereafter, the installation of the *Dharma-araṇya-piṭha*. Therein, first, by Yamadharma, the self-manifested image of the Lord Viśveśvara was installed under the name Dharmeśvara, followed by the construction of the Dharmavāpī tank. The identity between Dharmavāpī and Dharmeśvara is recounted in connection with that [episode].

The description of the majesty of the eighteen *khaṇḍas* of Yama-dharma; then, the granting of boons and the preeminence of the sacred field established by Yama, the King of Dharma, following his own description of the glory of Dharmāraṇya; then, the description of the majesty of the eighteen thousand Brahmins created by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa in the forests of Dharmāraṇya; and, as an incidental topic, the description of the general daily duties beginning with morning remembrance (*prātaḥ-smaraṇa*), preceded by the description of the proper conduct for the various stages of life (*varṇāśrama-sadācāra*).

A description of the conduct and occasional observances (*naimittika-karma*) pertaining to the householder, including therein the honoring of guests; then, a description of the eight forms of marriage; a description of the duties such as the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) to be performed by the householder; then, a description of the actions to be avoided by the householder; and finally, a description of the excellence of serving the elderly, giving gifts, and so forth.

The description of the greatness of offering *tapaṇapiṇḍas* and other rites at the Dharmavāpī in Ghamoraṇya; then, in response to the inquiry of Śaunaka and others, the narration by Sūta of the conduct of unchaste women and those of evil character; the demonstration of the miserable consequences for women of wicked conduct as an occasion for praising the duties of chaste wives; the description of the rules and duties for widows; the description of the greatness of the *śrāddha* ceremony preceded by the narration of the merit of giving gifts such as sesame and cows at the Dharmavāpī; and then, in the form of a dialogue between Diva and Skanda—

The section concerning the destruction of Dharma-araṇya: there, Śiva, having heard from the mouth of Skanda that the gods beginning with Indra had arrived, suddenly rose from his seat; desiring to depart, he did not mount his bull, whereupon Skanda, wishing to know the reason for Śiva’s haste to go, questioned him. Then, Śiva, after first describing the conduct of Khaṣṭratha and others, narrated a Puranic story; therein [is the account of] Marīci, the son of Brahmā...

Following the description of the entry of Cyādi and Mahārvi, there is an account of the greatness of Dhamāraṇya established by Yama, the son of Sūrya. Then, Śiva—eager to go to Vaikuṇṭha in order to bring the illustrious Mahāviṣṇu to Dhamāraṇya—set out for Vaikuṇṭha along with Skanda and other deities such as Brahmā. Having arrived there, Brahmā and the others offered praise to Viṣṇu. Upon hearing the hymn of praise from Brahmā and the rest, Viṣṇu arose; thereafter, Viṣṇu [addressed] the gods, beginning with Brahmā...

When asked the reason for his arrival, Viṣṇu, after first reporting on the state of Dharma, requested permission to go there; Viṣṇu then replied, "So be it," mounted Garuḍa, and arrived at Dharmāraṇya along with Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the other gods. There, Yama, the King of Dharma, offered them hospitality and composed hymns of praise. Then, Viṣṇu made a request to Yama, the King of Dharma, for a boon. Thereafter—

When Yamadharma made a request to establish great hermitages in his own Forest of Dharma (Dharmāraṇya), Viṣṇu and the other gods brought from various regions Brahmins endowed with virtuous conduct, together with their disciples and retinues; having settled them in that Forest of Dharma, they established well-provided hermitages for those sages.

Then, among the Ārāḍyaṇas dwelling there in the Dhamāraṇya together with their sons, grandsons, and others, there is a description preceded by the detailed expansion of the lineages, ancestral clans (*gotra*), and *pravara* of the four and twenty principal great sages (*maharṣi*), as well as a description of the character of the Bāhyaṇas born of those respective clans; and then, in connection with the majesty of Dhamāraṇya, a description of the account of the yakṣa named Jasbhaka.

There, at the request of all the Brahmins who had been terrified by the Yakṣa Jumbhaka, all the gods established the venerable Vṛddhaśruti Yoginīs—appearing in the forms of the deities of the various lineages (*gotra*) and ancestral clans (*pravara*)—within that Dharmāraṇya for the protection of those Brahmins; consequently, the Brahmins protected by the Yoginīs attained well-being. Then, once, when Rudra and the other gods had arrived there in the Dharmāraṇya, Viṣṇu, desiring to perform service for the sages, [approached] Brahmā... [na].

The objects of the senses are the cause of attachment; therefore, by Brahmā, for the sake of destroying the lineage of the twice-born, when the Kāmadhenu was summoned to the Ghamāraṇya forest, the cow came into the presence of Brahmā at his command. Then, after Brahmā had granted the boon of granting all desires to the merchants, and when the earth was covered with the streams of her own milk by the Kāmadhenu, there arose from that place sixty thousand sons of merchants wearing tufts of hair and sacred threads. Thereafter—

By Brahmā, who was instructed by all the gods, there was established for each of those Brāhmaṇas a follower, and for each of those followers, a gift of a cow; furthermore, according to their respective speech, a system of lineage (*gotra*), clan (*pravara*), and so forth was established for those various Brāhmaṇa-followers and merchants. Immediately thereafter, all the gods offered praise to the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*). Then, at the request of those cow-protecting merchants, Rudra brought the Gandharva maidens from Viśvāvasu and Gandharvavata, and with them—

The taking of wives by the Gobhujas together; thereafter, the detailed account of their marriage rites and domestic life; the description of how those thirty-six thousand Gobhuja merchants, along with their countless multitudes of sons and grandsons, took up residence in Dharmāraṇya and performed service and attendance upon the Brāhmaṇas; and then, at one time during the Tretā Yuga, when a Rākṣasa named Rauhineya arrived at Dharmāraṇya and began to cause disturbances, [the place was protected] by the clan-deities (gotradevīs) such as Omā and others against that Rākṣasa.

The account of the battle; on that occasion, Viṣṇu, having arrived and being implored, slew the Rākṣasa Khoṭajihva with his own discus (*cakra*); thereafter, at the command of Viṣṇu, the gods took leave of the Brāhmaṇas and others dwelling in the Dhamā forest who were fleeing out of fear of the Rākṣasa, and re-established them in the Dhamā forest; [the description] of the city established for the welfare of the Brāhmaṇas by the Blessed One after he had come from Satyaloka, slain the Rākṣasa, and settled them there.

The description of the fame of the name Satyamandira; then, following the account of the establishment of [the deity] Tyandi, a description of the splendor of the city of Satyapura, preceded by a description of the abodes of all the deities beginning with Gaṇeśa and the Sun throughout all its parts; therein, in connection with the installation of Gaṇeśa, the narration of the history of the birth of Gaṇeśa from Pārvatī and others; and the offering of prayers by the inhabitants of Dharmāraṇya for protection, preceded by the praise of Gaṇeśa.

The leader of the community (Gaṇādhyakṣa), having accepted the request of the gods made by the inhabitants of Dharmāraṇya, [discussed] with all the people there matters concerning auspicious occasions such as marriages. Then, in Dharmāraṇya, to the west of Śambhu, follows a detailed narrative of the origin of the two Nāsatyas (the Aśvins) from the seed of the Sun; therein, after Saṃjñā—the wife of the Sun—having placed Chāyā near the Sun due to her inability to endure the Sun’s brilliance, she departed for the sake of performing penance. By Chāyā...

Due to the imbalance caused by his excessive affection for his son, Yama struck him with his foot, intending to kill him; consequently, Yama pronounced a curse. Then, having heard the account of his mother’s death as reported by Yama, Sūrya perceived through meditation that his wife Saṃjñā was performing penance in the form of a mare. Assuming the form of a horse, he went near her. Thereupon, after Sūrya had united with the mare by inserting his sword into her nostril, the two Aśvins were born. [He remained] assuming the form of a horse.

The origin of the two *tapaḥkuṇḍas* on the ground where the eastern and western hooves of the Sun fell; a description of the majesty of that *taparavikuṇḍa*; then, the installation of the Sun there by Brahmā and the other gods under the name Bakulāditya, as well as the installation of Saṃjñā and the two Aśvins, the sons of Karmāra; a description of the majesty of the *bakulāka* of the *ravikuṇḍa*, and the reason for its fame by the name Bakulāka; then, the account of Viṣṇu’s performance of penance in the Dharmāraṇya forest after having subdued the horse-headed Hayagrīva, accompanied by Śiva and Skanda.

The narration of events: therein, when the other gods had begun their deliberations on the surface of the earth regarding the invocation of Viṣṇu, Rudra and the others departed for Veṅkaṭha. At that time, the Lord, while in a secluded place, performed penance through the yoga of meditative absorption with a bow in his hand. Then, for the sake of awakening him, he employed the means described by Bṛhaspati; and by promising the gift of a portion of the sacrifice, he caused the string of the bow held in the Lord’s hand to be bitten by an ant.

The gods issued a command; then, as soon as it was consumed by Daśagrīva while he was bearing it, Viṣṇu severed his head with a blow of his discus. That head, characterized by the sound "cakāra" and possessing the power of movement, remained suspended in the sky. Then, when that head had been cut off and remained unextinguished despite repeated efforts at purification, Brahmā and the other gods spoke these words.

The command for the purpose of rejoining Viṣṇu’s head; then, the promise by Viśvakarman to the gods regarding the granting of a share in the sacrifice; thereafter, when the horse of the chariot drawn by *suyai* had reached the middle of the sky at midday and was brought by the gods, Viśvakarman joined the head of the horse to the trunk of Viṣṇu; then, the gods performed the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of Viṣṇu with the horse-head and other rites; and then, by Hayagrīva, who was gratified by that hymn of praise.

Brahmā caused the gods to be born; then Rākā granted a boon to Savitṛ. Thereafter, Brahmā and the other gods performed the sacrificial rite. During that sacrificial procedure, they bestowed upon the wives and Viśvakarman the sacrificial portions previously promised to them. Having completed the sacrificial rite, Brahmā and the others departed for their own respective worlds.

Then, in the context of explaining the cause of Viṣṇu’s transformation into a horse-headed being, there is a description of the incident in Brahmā’s assembly where, due to a dispute with Viṣṇu, his head fell off as a consequence of a curse; then, Viṣṇu, having assumed the form of a horse-necked one (Aśvaśīrṣa), established the Devasaras-tīrtha in Dharmāraṇya and performed penance there, while Brahmā also stood before him and performed penance; thereafter, the account of how Viṣṇu’s horse-head was restored to its original state and natural appearance through the power of that sacred site (tīrtha); and then—

The description of how that fifth mouth of Brahmā—which, out of pleasure, had cast a curse upon Viṣṇu—became like a crow’s face; the narrative of how that fifth mouth of Brahmā was cut off by Hara at Dharmāraṇya; the description of Brahmā’s establishment of Mokṣeśvara preceded by the creation of the Mokṣatīrtha; the description of the attainment of a son and the cessation of barrenness resulting from bathing at the Devasaras Tīrtha; and the majesty of Mokṣeśvara.

Description of the Power of the Devakhāta Lake. Next, the description of the establishment of the Śrīmātā and other gocara goddesses in various excellent locations within Dharmāraṇya for the destruction of the fear of Rākṣasas and others among the people residing in that forest of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; followed by a description of the specific forms, names, and modes of worship of those goddesses who manifest in the form of their respective sites; and therein, on the eastern side, a description of the majesty of the goddesses beginning with Śrīmātā and ending with Ānandā.

Now, following the description of the majesty of the goddesses beginning with Śāṃtānī situated in the southern direction, comes the majesty of the venerable goddess Mātā. In the context of describing the majesty of the venerable goddess Mātā, there is a narration of the account of the goddess Mātangī’s manifestation and other events for the sake of slaying the demon named Gīṭaka—who had abducted the wife of a twice-born man residing in Dharmāraṇya after disputing with him—and a description of the battle between Mātangī and the demon Kaṇauṭaka; in that battle, Kaṇauṭaka, having caused Mātangī to be bewildered by means of illusion...

Śrīmātādevī returned and made a request for her own marriage; thereafter, Śrīmātā sent Śyāmalā, saying that her own marriage would be difficult, and dispatched her toward the Karṇāṭaka Daitya. Then, following the account of the battle between Śyāmalādevī and the Karṇāṭaka Daitya, there is a description of the circumstances of Śrīkaṇṭharāja’s rebirth through the power of the greatness of Śivā. Subsequently, [the marriage] was performed for Pārvatī by Saṃtuñja and others.

A section concerning the Śrīmātā, Mātaṅgī, and Śyāmalā Devīs, including: a discourse addressed to the goddess Śrīmātā by those desiring to know the specific ritual procedures for their worship; the description of the method of worship for them as taught by the goddess Śrīmātā; a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the goddesses Śrīmātā, Mātaṅgī, and Śyāmalā; an account of the penance performed by Śatakratu at Setubandha in connection with the descriptions of the majesties of Indrarata and Puṣkaranadra; and the majesty of Indraratīya-nadra.

In that very vicinity, there is the description of the greatness of Jayantīśvara as told to Jayanta; the description by Śiva of the seed-syllables (*bīja-varṇa*) of the mantra; the Goddess’s attainment of a wicked state of mind due to the recitation of such a mantra; then Śiva’s sudden fall after going toward Dharmāraṇya; the birth of the Kūṭagaṇas from the sweat of his limbs; and when those Gaṇas, standing upon the peak of Mount Kāṭha, performed the accomplishment of the Kūṭamantra, they declared themselves to be Śiva himself because of their success.

Having heard of Pārvatī’s state of being possessed by a spirit, she then performed penance at the command of Śiva and gratified Śiva; the description of the fame of that place of penance as known by the name Dharā-kṣetra, and the glorification of the majesty of that Dharā-kṣetra. Then follows a detailed description of the deities Bhaṭṭārakā, Viṅu, and others situated in Dharmāraṇya, as well as the lineage-originating deities of the Brahmins residing in Dharmāraṇya, such as Vaṭeka and others.

Now, in Dharmāraṇya, there were yoginīs established by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, who pervaded the quarters beginning with the East. Then, once, having been defeated by the Dānavas in battle, the gods went toward the Lord of the Gods (Śiva). Thereafter, by the command of Brahmā, they returned to Dharmāraṇya and commenced a sacrificial session (*satra*) lasting for a thousand years. In that sacrifice, the Brahmins were gratified by the offering of various kinds of cooked foods. Thus, in Dharmāraṇya—

The description of the departure for heaven after the destruction of those suffering from the cold, having attained the excellence resulting from the power of their generosity; then, on one occasion, an asura named Hāsuraka returned to Dharmāraṇya and caused extreme harassment to the brahmins and merchants residing there; terrified by him, the brahmins and merchants fled in all directions, wandering aimlessly here and there. The establishment of a residence in the village of Imbhu, not far from Dhamauraṇya; and, in connection with the greatness of the holy site (tīrtha) situated at Dhamauraṇya, the account of the Blessed Śrī Rāmacandra’s residence in Sītāpura beginning from his childhood, including the description of the cause for the naming of those merchants—namely, his marriage, forest exile, battle with the rākṣasas, the slaying of Rāvaṇa, the recovery of Sītā, his return to Ayodhyā, and his coronation—and for that very reason, [the account] of the merchants residing there.

The description of the division among the kinsmen; likewise, a detailed account of the life of Ekapātṛṇa.
