The description of the conversation; therein, the account of Mārkaṇḍeya himself bringing the Sarasvatī from Satyaloka; then, the account of the sage [Kavi] abandoning his palanquin along with the merchants at the word of Vasiṣṭha and entering the waters of the Sarasvatī, followed by the description of the fruits of bestowing knowledge and performing *śrāddha* there; then, having personally performed the ritual of pilgrimage according to the scriptures on foot together with all his soldiers and attendants; and finally, the description of the majesty of the Dvārakā-kṣetra situated in the Dharmāraṇya forest.

[Having established the liṅgas known as Śrīrāmeśvara, Kāmeśvara, and Varāha, and having performed his duties with a composed mind,] there follows the description of the greatness of the Govatsaliṅga situated in Dharmāraṇya, which was formerly worshipped by the cowherd [Govaṇi]. Then follows the description of Govaṇi residing at Caṇḍāra. When Śrīrāma, who had arrived here himself at the Gaṅgā situated near the Govatsaliṅga, spoke, saying, "I shall relate my own history," [the narrative proceeds].

Then, having arrived at the cremation ground by means of messengers, he related the words of that woman; thereafter, Śrī Rāma himself went near that woman—who was lying on an iron bedstead called Sarasvatī—and when asked the reason for her weeping, she spoke. [Note: The provided text contains several scribal errors and archaic orthographic features (such as *nāyā* for *nāryāḥ*, *paṣṭa* for *pṛṣṭe*, *lohayaṣaṭikāyāṃ* for *loha-yaṣṭikāyām*). The translation reflects the intended meaning based on standard Sanskrit conventions.]

Then, Śrīmātā Devī [related] how, in former times, Rohāsura had caused suffering to the inhabitants of Dharmāraṇya by assuming his own form; and how, in that place on the banks of the Sarasvatī, Lohāsura performed penance to propitiate Śiva, preceded by the experience of such suffering, and subsequently established the conduct of all people in Dharmāraṇya, beginning with Urmimān and others; and how, while he was performing that penance, he was struck with a fist-blow by Indra for the sake of obstructing his ascetic power; and thereafter, how the gods [acted].

The offering of prayers to Śrī Rāma by Sada Bhavṛta with the intent of victory; upon hearing the words of Śrīmātā, Śrī Rāma’s engagement in battle against the demon Dhamokhodahāsu, who had fallen prostrate; the placing of Śaṅkara on his chest, Brahmā on his neck, and Viṣṇu at his feet; and finally, the description of the vow made before the Mother of the World to establish the city of Satyamandira once again as it was before.

Then, at the word of Brahmā, the Asura, having placed Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara within his own body and dispatched them, sent them forth to satisfy all the Brāhmaṇas residing here and there through praise, prayer, and service; he remained in that Dharmāraṇya in a state of prostration. Thereafter, having brought those [Brāhmaṇas] with great honor and performed worship and hospitality for them, [the Asura gave] to them wealth, garments, and riches, along with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.

And the description of the granting of boons: "O people, protect me! Ka... ka... na... ti... Oṃ! Having performed various kinds of offerings and gifts, and having provided for the drinking water for men, [the Lord] gave [the land]. Then, Śrī Rāma, having made arrangements for the restoration of the dilapidated Dharmāraṇya region for the welfare of those Brāhmaṇas residing in that holy field (tatakaṣetra), made a formal request for the purpose of bestowing gifts preceded by a sacrifice; thereafter, by them..."

Having gone everywhere and consulted together, [the gods] described their own duty as being intent on turning away from accepting gifts from Śrī Rāma, and recounted how they had been commanded by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. Then, Śrī Rāma remembered all the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu; by the mere act of remembering them, all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, arrived. Śrī Rāma then honored all those gods with worship and other marks of respect. Thereafter, by all the gods...

Having heard of Śrī Rāmacandra’s desire to restore the dilapidated Dhamoraṇya-kṣetra, they offered him praise; thereafter, Śrī Rāmacandra, having obtained the permission of those gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the others—began the restoration of the venerable Dhamoraṇya-kṣetra, and having constructed various outer branches, intermediate branches, and primary branches, he filled all of them with an abundance of diverse wealth, grain, gold, jewels, and other articles.

The bestowal of one hundred and forty-four women upon the Brāhmaṇas; the issuance of commands for the Brāhmaṇas to perform service by granting thirty-six thousand cows, white horses, chowries, and swords to the merchants of Bhuja; the issuance of commands at the time of marriage and other occasions for the wearing of royal insignia such as chowries, and for the worship of Goddess Gurāṅkukh; and [the granting] of chowries, swords, and so forth to the merchants of Sāpādaṣṭakṣamāṇḍaṭīka and Maṇḍaṭeśvara.

Having performed service to the twice-born and carried out their commands, and having thereafter established the shrines of his own ancestors and lords, he first installed the deities such as the River Goddess Śrīmātā, Culyasvāmin, and Harigaṇādhyakṣa; then, having constructed structures beneficial to the city—including forts, ramparts, gateways, religious tanks, and wells—and having inscribed an unbroken edict upon a copper plate, he bestowed it upon learned Brāhmaṇas. Furthermore, for that *dharmāraṇya-kṣetra* and for the Brāhmaṇas, merchants, and others residing therein—

The protection provided by Māruti, who was none other than [Hanumān], and his carrying out of orders; likewise, having performed the installation of the image, Śrī Rāma, as was his duty, worshipped and prostrated before the venerable Mother (Śrīmātā), and received the acceptance of the offering from the gods and the twice-born. Then follows the description of the treaty. Thereafter, the Brahmins performed service day after day to the copper-plate edict (*tāmrapaṭa-śāsana*) granted by Śrī Rāmacandra. Following that, Śrī Rāmacandra sent blessings toward Bharata for the Brahmins and merchants residing there.

Now, having received the command of the Brahmins—who had been granted a copper-plate edict inscribed with their own request by Śrī Rāmacandra, promising that he would always carry out their work and granting them words of assurance of safety—the king returned joyfully to the city of Ayodhyā; this is the description of his governance there. Then, on one occasion during a conversation in Ayodhyā, Śrī Rāma heard from the mouth of Śrī Vasiṣṭha the account of the forest-dwelling of the Kṣatriyas.

Having heard of Prayāga, Nīveṇī, Tīrtha, Siddhakṣetra, Kāśī, Gaṅgādhama, Araṇya, Vaṇau, Harikṣetra, and other such places, he went with his attendants to Dharmāraṇya in order to perform a pilgrimage there once more. Staying in Moherakapura, he completed the sacrificial rites together with Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and other great sages such as Ūrṛika. Upon concluding the sacrifice, he performed the final ritual bath. There, at the end of the sacrifice, having been requested by Sītā, he founded the city named Sītāpura in front of Moherakapura for the sake of a learned man.

The entrustment [of the land] to the Brāhmaṇas; then, having gone toward Dhamaukha, the narration of the account of Śrī Rāmacandra’s gift of fifty-five villages beginning from Sītāpura and ending at Satyamandira, preceded by the performance of the great sixteen-fold gift (*ṣoḍaśamahādāna*) to the Brāhmaṇas according to the words of Sītā and the command of his preceptor; and for the sake of serving the eighteen thousand great sages (*maharṣi*) of the Vātsyāyana lineage residing in those fifty-five villages, the establishment of sixteen thousand courtesans and their four attendants...

The granting of gifts to the Brāhmaṇas; then, at the request of the Brāhmaṇas, Rāma’s command to the prostitutes and Śūdras to perform service for those Brāhmaṇas; thereafter, the return of Śrī Rāmacandra to his own city; thus, the description of the account of Śrī Rāmacandra’s restoration of the dilapidated holy sites and shrines located in the Dharmāraṇya region; and finally, the description of the well-being of Dharmāraṇya due to the power of the protection established by Hanumān, as related by Brahmā to Nārada.

In the *Yudhiṣṭhiravijaya*, Yudhiṣṭhira inquires of Vyāsa whether the Dharma-forest has ever been destroyed; thereupon, the great seer Vyāsa recounts the events of the previous Kali age, including the account of King Śālivāhana Āma, the sovereign of Kānyakubja. Having heard a certain secret from his own preceptor, that king, through the power of that secret, with a heart embittered by [hostility], uprooted the Vaiṣṇava dharma.

King Āmabhūpa, having embraced Buddhism, then begot a daughter named Ratnagaṅgā upon his queen named Āmā. A description is given of how that girl, Ratnagaṅgā, became devoted to the Jaina religion after being deluded by the Kṣapaṇakas. Subsequently, she was given in marriage to King Kambhīpa, the ruler of Brahmāvarta; at her wedding, her father, King Āmabhūpa, bestowed the city of Moherakālī, situated in Dharmāraṇya, upon her husband. Thereafter, by the king...

Having arrived at Dhamāraṇya, he made the city of Modiraka his own capital; there, he caused the Jaina Dharma to spread in every direction throughout his kingdom. At that time, all castes took refuge in the Jaina Dharma. When the *randharāsana* edicts issued by Śrī Rāmacandra were lost, those same Brāhmaṇas went to King Sāvabhauma in the Kānyakubja region and reported to him the matter concerning the *Rāmadatta-kṣātra-napatra*.

The report of the news concerning the conduct of his own son-in-law, brought about by the nature of the messenger; the sending of an order by King Āma through that same messenger to his son-in-law Rāma to destroy the forest of Dharma; and the statement made by Kumārapāla—known as Kābhīpāḍāparanyāya—to the Brahmins, who, despite the command of their father-in-law, had shown disregard for Rāma’s edict and were preparing to seize the livelihoods of the Brahmins, saying: "Let proof be given by summoning Māruti through the doctrine of Nāstika (atheism)."

Then, all those Brāhmaṇas, having gathered together at that place of justice (dharmasthāna) to bring back Māruti who was staying in Sedabandha, formed a collective agreement by drawing up a document with their signatures. Having made a firm resolve to go as a group toward Rāmeśvara to bring back Māruti, they drew up the hand-written signatures. [This was done] for the purpose of preventing the eighteen thousand Brāhmaṇas from proceeding toward the Rāmeśvara shrine. To all the Gōbhuja [chiefs],...

When King Kumārapāla issued his command, thirty-six thousand Jaina *dharma-bhāṇakas*—merchants, artisans, and Brahmins—adopted a vow of silence out of fear of the king’s curse and the violation of their livelihoods. Subsequently, the king dispatched several Śūdras from among those devoted to the Jaina faith who resided in the place called Aḍā to restrain the Brahmins; by royal decree, some of those Śūdras, whose hearts were hardened by the intense impressions of the Jaina Dharma, [acted accordingly].

Having approached those three thousand brāhmaṇas, he engaged them in conversation through reasoned discourse for the purpose of turning them back from their resolve. Upon hearing the words of those śūdras presented with logical arguments, fifteen hundred brāhmaṇas among the eighteen thousand brāhmaṇas—having loosened the firm knots of their resolve and having previously offered their consent without regard for Rama’s command—departed toward the sacred field of Rāmeśvara, while the remaining three thousand twice-born ones stayed behind.

With firm resolve, they set out toward the sacred site of Śrī Rāmeśvara to experience the delights of Māra; however, becoming exhausted by the great fatigue of the journey, they were urged on by Śrī Rāma to approach him. Yet, due to their desire to see the region of the Jālandhara mountain and their preoccupation with that, they were unable to behold Rāma. Then, through the power of the Brahmins who had been blessed by the wind-god (Māruti), they offered hymns of praise. Satisfied by their eulogy, the wind-god and the [deity] bestowed many boons upon those Brahmins.

Then Hanumān, having tested them, revealed his own true form to them and brought those Ādyaṇas back to Rāmeśvara on the Setubandha; after causing them to perform the vision of the Great Lord Rāmeśvara and other rites, he expressed his own blessedness through that vision and offered his prostrations.

He gave fruit to the beggars for them to eat; then, as a token of recognition for those brahmins, he gave each of them two small pouches made from the hair found on his own armpits and elsewhere, and instructed them to present them to the king in due order.

And for the sake of reviving the dog once more, he gave orders to throw [the dog] at the king’s gate; then, taking those two earthen pots, the highly delighted and contented Brahmins stayed for three nights near Śrīmāruti on the bank of the Śrīrāma [river], performing the Brahma-yajña and other rites. Then, on the night of the third day, Hayumanta, having stationed those twice-born ones upon a bed of darbha grass extending ten yojanas in width, made a request for them to lie down. When those twice-born ones had fallen asleep, Māravidā [heard] the voice of his father.

The transport of that stone to Dhamoraṇya; then, when they had arrived at Dhamoraṇya along with Viśākhā Śikhā, those Brahmins, accompanied by their sons and grandsons, returned to her presence through the power of their ascetic energy. After a festival of meeting and conversation with all three thousand Brahmins and their families, they returned to their respective homes with great ceremony. Then, on the following morning...

Having thus spent five days, immediately thereafter, on the sixth day, he entered the royal assembly hall and delivered his master Mārutī’s message to the king. Upon hearing Mārutī’s message as related by that Brahmin, while King Kumārapāla was preparing for battle against him, [Mārutī] threw from the midst of the hair-pores on one of his left armpits—out of the mass of hair-pores on his body—a single hair-pore located at the royal gate. By that mere throwing of the hair, at that very moment, his...

The burning of the entire wealth of King Kumārapāla—including his sons, elephants, horses, and so forth; the description of the extreme misery of the Jaina mendicants (Namanakṣapaṇakas) and King Kumārapāla due to the king's great wrath; then the immediate departure of those Brahmins from the presence of King Kumārapāla; then their presentation of a small pouch of hair from the right side of Bhīmaratha’s head to the compassionate Mūṣaka; and immediately upon that being thrown at the palace gate, [the restoration] of the king once again.

There was the attainment of all peace, preceded by the restoration to life of all cows, sons, elephants, horses, and buffaloes. Then, having gained conviction through the power of Śrī Rāma and Hanumān, that king prepared and granted to those Brahmins a new charter of land tenure as before. Furthermore, there was the expulsion from his kingdom of heretics such as Jains and Buddhists who were outside the Vedic fold. Subsequently, there was the restoration, as previously, of the thirty-six thousand merchants of good conduct, cowherds, and grain-dealers.

An investigation for the purpose of serving the learned; then, a description of the authority of the three thousand Brāhmaṇas residing at Setubandha regarding the grant of a livelihood-land-deed issued by the King; a determination that the three thousand Brāhmaṇas known as Jayīvidyas—who had made a vow to travel to Setubandha and were assisting with their own funds—had no entitlement to the land-grants (bhūmivṛtti) associated with those who had gone there; [and the account] of those three thousand Brāhmaṇas named Jayīvidyas while they were fulfilling their vow of truthfulness within the city of Mehiraka.

The establishment of a residence; the settlement outside the village of Meheraka of all the Brāhmaṇas known as Cāturvidyas—numbering fifteen thousand—who were breaking their own vows, in a place for their comfortable dwelling; the description of the performance of the worship of the family deity by those very Māṇḍavya-beśaja Śaiva Cāturvidya Brāhmaṇas every year on the thirteenth day of the month of Pauṣa; and the performance of honors such as worship for them by the merchants known as Gobhijas.

Then, after Taitaba and the other non-gods had assigned the various divisions of livelihood to those Brahmins dwelling in the Dharma-forest, they returned to their own abodes. Thereafter, there is the description of the settlement of fifteen thousand Brahmins—both those learned in the four Vedas (*cāturvidya*) and those ignorant of them (*avidya*)—in the five groups of villages (*pañcapañcaka-grāma*). This includes the names of the fifteen lineages (*gotra*) of the *cāturvidyas*, the description of the names of the fifty-five villages beginning with Sītāpura, and so forth. Now...

A detailed description of the lineage, origins, and nature of the *Cāturvidya* Brāhmaṇas residing in the fifty-five villages on the left side, beginning with Sītāpura; then, a description of the seventeen villages, such as Rīṭakhāyā, inhabited by the *Traividyas* who arrived from the vicinity of Hanumān; a description of how a conflict arose for some period of time between the twenty-four *Cāturvidyas* and the *Traividyas*; and finally, a description of the distinctions among certain castes based on their adherence to the eightfold conduct (*aṣṭācāra*). Then...

When the Kṛta Yuga had arrived, among certain merchants residing there, due to the influence of the eightfold conduct and the practice of separate conduct, there is a description of the emission of the syllable *kham* and so forth; now, [regarding] the ancients...

Then, at one time, when the gods beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra returned to the Dharmāraṇya forest, the inhabitants of that place—out of fear of the Śabaras, Trairas, and Chamarapārutajas—had abandoned Sītāpura and gone to dwell on the banks of the Sakhāñjabatī river. Upon their return, there is a description of how they established pleasant dwelling places and sustained themselves by means of tending herds of cows. Among them were those who maintained the livelihoods of *cāturvidya*, *trāyaṇa*, widows, maidens, and cowherds, and it is described how offspring were produced through the *vrīḍyaṇa* rite.

The description of the fame of the Kātībhagokhaka-ghenujanas among the Kumāras; then, regarding the three thousand Brahmins who had arrived from the presence of Hanumān and held the office of village priests (*grāmadūtya*), [it concerns] those Brahmins born of illicit unions (*bhiśrasabhūta*) through the marriage of certain very foolish, deaf, one-eyed, lame, and mute men with Cāturvidya girls for the sake of obtaining brides for their own marriages and for the purpose of progeny.

Description of the perception of the three banners (*tri-daṇḍa-khaṅga-saṃjñā*) and the classification of their knowledge preceded by a division into three; then, following the aforementioned manner, after the emergence of the division among kinsmen in the city of Moheraka, a description of the drafting of a formal agreement (*vyavasthā-patra*)—by the consensus of all Brāhmaṇas and others in the Kali age, out of fear of sinful conduct—to establish the worship of the Mother, the lineages (*gotra*), the ancestral sages (*pravara*), the ritual procedures, family customs, local customs, and the preeminence of the established traditions; and a description of the lineages, ancestral sages, sub-lineages (*avaṭaṅka*), and Vedic branches (*śākhā*) of all the Moḍha Brāhmaṇas.

In the Brāhma-khaṇḍa, the second [section] is the "Māhātmya of Dharmāraṇya," which concludes with the summary of the greatness of Dharmāraṇya—preceded by a description of the fruits of hearing the majesty of Dharmāraṇya—and how merchants and Śūdras dwelling in Dharmāraṇya attained the state of being devoted solely to the twice-born and the gods.
Now, in the outer section, the third sub-section of the outer part.

Now, in the Naimiṣa forest, the great Ṛṣis headed by Śaunaka inquire of the great Ṛṣi Sūta regarding the greatness of Śrī Śaṅkara and the means of attaining Him; there, the great Ṛṣi Sūta first describes to the great Ṛṣis headed by Śaunaka the greatness of the five-syllabled mantra of Śrī Śaṅkara, followed by a description of the rules for its reception from a qualified Guru, and in that context, the narrative of King Daśārha, the lord of Mathurā, who, having married the daughter of the king of Karīra, [proceeded] from there...

Then, out of haste and a desire for pleasure, the king forcibly drew her toward him; as soon as he touched her body, it became exceedingly hot like a mass of glowing embers. At that very moment, she rose up in fear, and when asked by the king the cause of her burning body, she described to him the power of the five-syllabled Śiva mantra she had practiced. Thereupon, the king, along with his ministers, made a great effort to receive the five-syllabled Śiva mantra from her.

Then, having heard those words, when the king had received from his preceptor Garga the instruction on the Śrīśiva-mudrā at the root of a most meritorious tree on the banks of the Kāverī, the sins [of that king]—numbering as many as a hundred crores—emerged from the apertures of his body in the form of crows and were reduced to ashes. Thereafter, by the command of his preceptor, the son of Vyāsa, the body of that King Dāśaratha was smeared with sandalwood paste.

The governance of the kingdom preceded by the enjoyment of pleasures together with his own wife who had returned to her home; the majesty of the six-syllabled mantra of Śiva; then, a description of the majesty of the Great Śivarātri on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha; therein, the majesty of fasting, the worship of the Śiva-liṅga, and the offering of *viśva* leaves; in connection with that, a description of the accounts of the kings named Ikṣvāku, Vedāja, and Amitasaha; and therein, when King Amitasaha, having gone out for a hunt, slew a certain Rākṣasa.

The Rākṣasa’s brother-in-law, assuming the guise of a servant, approached the king in a humble manner to wait for an opportunity to search for his brother; the king then appointed him as the superintendent of his own kitchen. Subsequently, when the king once invited his family preceptor Vasiṣṭha for a meal, the Rākṣasa, still wearing his disguised attire, placed human flesh into the preceptor’s food vessel; that impure meal—

Having observed [the king], the great seer Vasiṣṭha, filled with anger, bestowed upon the king the curse of assuming the form of a Rākṣasa for a period of twelve years. Then, having heard that the curse was without cause, the enraged king took water in his hand to bestow a counter-curse upon his own guru, Vasiṣṭha. Thereupon, Queen Madayantī, having made a plea to the king who was intent on pronouncing a curse upon his guru, caused him to desist. Then, by that king, the water held in his hand for the purpose of cursing his guru—

He threw [the sage] at his own feet; because of that act of making the sage's feet marked with black spots (*kalmāṣa*), the king became famous by the name Kalmāṣapāda. Then, after attaining the state of a *rākṣasa*, while King Kalmāṣapāda was wandering in the forest and had seized a certain hermit’s son to devour him, the wife of that hermit’s son, who was accompanying him, pronounced a curse upon the *rākṣasa*-state King Kalmāṣapāda: "When you have sexual intercourse, you shall become a man. Thus [it was said].

Having bestowed [the kingdom], there was the performance of the *agnīdhra* sacrifice; then, after the period of the curse had passed, having cast off the curse and regained his own true nature, he returned to his own home. Thereupon, Madayantī, the wife of that king, having heard of the curse upon the wives of the brahmins, prevented her husband—who, fearing his own wife’s barrenness, was entreating for sexual union—from doing so. Then, when the king, having renounced the enjoyment of sovereignty, had departed for the forest, the sage Vasiṣṭha, for the sake of establishing the Solar dynasty (*sūryavaṃśa*), [approached] the queen Madayantī.

The birth of Suta; then the pursuit of King Kalmāṣapāda, who had gone to the forest, by the terrible personification of the sin of Brahman-slaughter; the departure of the king, afflicted by that Brahman-slaughter, toward Gautama Mahārṣi at Mithilā-Udāna; then the instruction given by the great seer Gautama to the king for the removal of the fault of Brahman-slaughter, regarding the vision of the Śiva-liṅga at Gokarṇa-kṣetra and the journey there; and, in connection with that, the description of the majesty of Gokarṇeśvara. Now...

In this section, following the description of the great majesty of Gokarṇeśvara, Gautama recounts his conversation with the messengers of Śiva who had arrived there to lead a certain prosperous Caṇḍālī woman to the world of Śiva; therein, Gautama [describes] the Caṇḍālī woman [being led] by the messengers of Śiva to the world of Śiva.

When the messengers of Śiva were questioned regarding the cause of her being led back, they related the account of that outcaste woman’s previous birth. In that former life, she was the widow of a Brahmin who, through the power of a boon from Kāmadeva, attained the status of a superior caste; however, having become attached to a Śūdra, she unintentionally killed a calf at night with her hand. Upon seeing it in the light and realizing it was a cow's offspring, she cried out "Śiva, Śiva! in remorse. Then, she met her death by means of a wooden stake.

A description of the transformation of Devadudhi into the state of an Aṇḍālī upon her attainment [of that status]; and the account of her journey through the forest of Gokarṇa for the purpose of begging alms such as food from this Aṇḍālī.

The description of how Śiva, through the power of the recitation of His auspicious names performed by that Kṣatriya, remembered her; how He drew out her life-breath which had been seized by Śiva, and having enlivened her with divine splendor, led her toward the realm of Śiva (Śivaloka). Then, in connection with that, when the King asked Gautama about the nature of Śivaloka, Gautama—also known as Kaṇva-māṣapāda—described the nature of Śivaloka to the King, who was devoted to Śiva. And so it continues. Now... [the text ends].

A description of the greatness of the worship of Śrī Śiva; in that context, the account of the king named Vimardana residing in the country of Kirāta, followed by a description of the greatness of devotion to Śiva; and in that connection, the account of King Candrasena of Ujjayinī, describing how he attained the world of Śiva after being purified from the sins such as the slaughter of a Brahmin.

The description [of the king]: although that king was constantly devoted to the lowest [vices], he remained intent upon devotion to Śiva. Then, once in private, his wife Kusumatī questioned the king, desiring to know the reason why he was so devoted to Śiva despite being utterly addicted to wicked conduct. Thereupon, King Vimardana described the events of his own previous birth: how, in a former life, while he was a dog in the city of Pāpa, he had performed a great worship of the Lord Śiva in the temple of Śiva during the Great Festival of Śiva (Mahāśivarātri).

The circumambulation of the temple of Śrī Śiva while the queen was pregnant; the description of how, when certain people there attempted to kill that dog with sticks and stones, he attained birth as a king through the power of the presence of Śrī Śiva; the description of his wicked conduct, such as his desire to eat dogs and his habit of devouring all things due to the terror [he felt] in the womb of a dog; and then, by the king, the narration of the history of that queen's previous birth, wherein, in her former life—

The account of how a female dove, having taken a lump of meat and ascended to the peak of a mountain, met her death when struck down by a vulture with a sharp beak desiring to seize that lump of meat; how, through the power of dying in the presence of the venerable Śaṅkara, she attained the status of a queen; then, at the king’s request, the narration of the future history of both the king and the queen throughout seven births, concluding with the description of how, through the power of worshipping Lord Śiva at Mahābalipuram, they will attain the state of Śiva. Om Om.

Oṃ ca oṃ ni kai. There, having observed the king Candrasena’s devotion to Śiva, a Śiva-gaṇa named Maṇibhaṭṭāraka caused a breach [in his service] and bestowed upon that king the Cintāmaṇi jewel. Wearing that Cintāmaṇi around his neck, King Candrasena ruled his kingdom. Unable to endure the power of that lord of the earth, other kings, seeking to seize that Cintāmaṇi jewel, marched against him; they laid siege to the city of Avantī.

Having returned and besieged the city of Avantī on all sides, at that juncture, King Candrasena sought refuge with the illustrious Mahākāla Maheśvara and performed a great worship of him. At that same time, Queen Riddhimaṇḍarī, having arrived at the temple of the Illustrious One (Śrī-Ribha) upon the advice of Gautama, went with the king to the sacred field of Gokarṇa.

The contents of the sixth chapter concerning the power of beholding and worshipping the great lord Śrī-Gokarṇeśvara: Having witnessed the festival of worship performed by the king for a certain young cowherd woman accompanied by her own son, and after she had departed toward her own home, her five-year-old son established a stone Śiva-liṅga in a secluded spot near the temple of Śiva, and having gathered flowers as they were available...

Having prepared the offerings of perfumes and other requisites for the worship of Śiva with an undistracted mind, she was then approached by that cowherd girl, who in her anger destroyed the Śiva-pūjā he had performed with his own hands. Seeing the destruction of the worship of Śambhu, the boy fell into a swoon due to the excessive grief and lamentation caused by it. Then, after some time, having regained consciousness, that boy [beheld] right there in that place a divine, golden temple of Śiva made of jewels.

If it was a vision, then by that gracious boy, there was a request for forgiveness before Śrī Śaṅkara for the offense caused by interrupting his mother’s worship of Śiva; then, at the arrival of evening, having seen the entire camp of the cowherds transformed into divine gold through the grace of Śrī Śiva, he approached his own mother who was sleeping there in a divine form, awakened her, and told her that the entire camp had become golden; then, by that cowherd woman—

Having seen that wonder, he approached the king and reported the entire account to him. Then the king, accompanied by his ministers and others, came to that camp and embraced the five-year-old cowherd boy Gopāla, who was made of gold and jewels. Thus, with great joy, as that night passed away and at dawn, all those stationed nearby heard the words of the scouts.

Having heard this conduct of the cowherd’s son, the king of another kingdom was struck with wonder; abandoning his state of enmity toward the king and establishing supreme friendship, he entered that city. Having received the honors bestowed by the king and having beheld Śrī Mahākāla, they went to Gopadivira. There, with hearts filled with joy upon seeing the celestial temple manifested through the grace of the cowherd’s son, they all presented garments, gold, jewels, and other gifts to that son of the cowherd.

At that very moment, while the cowherds remained there with their heads bowed in humility, the goddess Durgā appeared on the battlefield. Having accepted the worship and honors from all the kings, she singled out that cowherd boy from among them all and spoke to all the monarchs.

Having described the greatness of the evening twilight (divasa-niśā-pradoṣa), he bestowed the name Śrīkara upon that cowherd boy Gopāṅkura, instructed him in the conduct of Śiva (śivācāra), and departed; this concludes the account of how King Candrasena and the cowherd boy Gopāṅkura, named Śrīkara, attained the world of Śiva through the power of their worship of Śiva.

And then follows the description of the greatness of the Pradoṣa-pūjā; in connection with that, the account of the king named Satyaratha residing in the region of Vidarbha is told. Therein is described the death of the king named Satyaratha in battle along with the Śālva kings. Subsequently, his pregnant wife, having exerted herself to depart from the city and travel to a remote forest, gave birth to a son there at the foot of a certain tree. At that time, while she was overcome by extreme thirst, near her—

Then, while Bharata was wandering in that region, he heard the sound of crying from a newborn boy who had been abandoned by Bharata due to his fear of old age. At that moment, a certain Brahmin woman named Ahilyā, accompanied by a one-year-old child, was wandering there; seeing that helpless infant with an uncut umbilical cord, her heart was overcome with compassion. With the intent of taking him to her own home to nourish him, she approached those who were disguised as physicians.

Having gained confidence from the words of Śaṅkara, the female elephant took charge of nourishing that boy and brought him back to her own home. Then, while living in the city of Ekacakrā, that Brahmin woman named Umā, out of non-dual affection for the child, provided him with food and nurtured him together with her own son. Later, when that Brahmin lady went somewhere to visit a deity named Deva along with those two boys, [the boy] was in that place called Deva.

While the great sage Śāṇḍilya was staying there, he recounted the wondrous nature of destiny by relating the story of those two boys and the prince among them; having heard his words, when that Brahmin woman questioned him out of a desire to know the lineage and other details of the boy she had brought, the venerable Śāṇḍilya related in detail the account of that boy’s birth and deeds, including his previous life as the Pāṇḍya king.

Due to the fault of interrupting the worship of Śiva during Pradoṣa, there is death at the hands of an enemy in a future birth. Due to the fault of neglecting the worship of Śiva during Pradoṣa, even for Tatapatra, there is the attainment of poverty in a future birth. And due to the fault of having killed his own wife under a pretext in a previous birth, both he and his mother suffer a painful death from dysentery in a future birth.

Having recounted the greatness of both of those youths, there follows the instruction for the worship of Śiva during the *pradoṣa* hour. Then, at the request of that Brahmin woman named Mā, the great seer Śāṇḍilya, in the context of the excellence of the *pradoṣa* vow, described in detail the performance of the complete and constituent rites of the worship of Śrī Śiva and so forth. Subsequently, among those two—the Brahmin youth and the prince—the great seer Śāṇḍilya gave the name Śucivrata to the Brahmin youth and Dharma-rāja to the prince.

Having performed the naming ceremony for the two of them, he gave the instruction on the Śiva-mantra for the purpose of performing daily worship; then, having bowed to the sage Śāṇḍilya and taken his leave, that brahmin woman departed along with the two boys. Subsequently, at the king of brahmins' residence, during the evening twilight, they established themselves under their mother’s command, preceded by the performance of Śiva-worship. Then, one day, while wandering on the riverbank, the brahmin boy discovered a treasure consisting of a golden vessel. This was reported to his mother.

Having divided those two bags equally, he gave the command to take them; then, the prince gave his own satisfaction by means of the wealth obtained through his own merit, which was acquired solely through his good fortune. Then one day, while wandering in the forest, the prince and the son of the brahmin saw the daughters of the Gandharvas playing. Although the son of the brahmin forbade him from going into their presence, that prince [proceeded] toward those Gandharva maidens.

Approaching that handsome-limbed youth, the prince, the Gandharva princess named Draviṇa—also known as Aṇḍumatī—arrived alone in his presence. As both were tormented by the arrows of love upon beholding one another, they conversed; then, having made a vow to the prince that she would give him her pearl necklace from her own neck and perform the marriage ceremony with him the day after tomorrow, she bestowed it upon him.

He went with his own female companions into the presence of his father; then, having gone to his own residence together with the prince Dharmaśāta, who was the son of a Brahmin named Ujjvalatā, he reported the events occurring in the forest to his mother, Viprabhā. Then, when the challenge arrived, that prince named Dharmaśāta went into that forest together with the son of a Brahmin. Upon their arrival, they were honored by the Gandharva Kṣemāmara.

Having bestowed his own daughter upon Dharmagraprāya, the king of Kasama, after performing the rites of taking her hand in marriage, and having provided him with the splendor of various jewels, elephants, horses, chariots, weapons, beautiful armor, swords, female slaves, and other riches, he himself departed by celestial chariot for the world of the Gandharvas; and together with that Gandharva maiden, Umāvatī, he lived in wedlock with that king named Dharmagraprāya.

Having been given a dowry by her father-in-law, she arrived at Vidarbhanagara, the capital of her own paternal kingdom, together with the army of the Śūrasena Gandharvas; and after performing the royal consecration upon the ancestral throne of her father, she honored that young Brahmin as her brother-in-law amidst the festivities for her husband’s victory, and remained there with her Gandharva son, her own husband, that prince named Dharmapra[khya].

A description of the governance of the kingdom with great happiness through the power of the Pradoṣavrata and the supreme grace of Śrī Śaṅkara in the city of Vidūrba; and a description of the majesty of the Pradoṣavrata and the worship of Śiva.

Now follows the description of the greatness of the Somapradoṣa vow; in connection with that, the narrative of Sīmantinī, the daughter of King Citravarmā of Āryāvarta. Therein, having heard from two astrologically skilled Brahmins who had come into the presence of her father about her own future great fortune and future misfortune respectively, she—out of fear of attaining widowhood—took refuge with the wife of the great sage Yājñavalkya, named Maitreyī.

Taking refuge for the sake of hearing the means to attain fortune, wealth, and beauty; then, on that Monday, the narration of the ritual procedure for the worship of Śiva and Gaurī; then, by that princess Sīmantinī, the commencement of the Monday vow with all its constituent parts according to the path instructed by Maitreyī; the marriage of Sīmantinī with Citrāṅgada, the son of Indrasena; and then, while Citrāṅgada was residing in the city named Śvethura, at one time, [his intention] to cross the Yamunā river.

The sudden sinking of the boat in mid-stream as it had set out; the death of all those who had boarded that boat; the grieving of Citravarmā and the others upon learning of the death of Prince Citrāṅgada caused by the sinking of the vessel; likewise, Sīmantinī’s failure to obtain the desired boon; and even when such a misfortune occurred, Sīmantinī’s performance of the Monday vow (somavāra-vrata) until she reached the hermitage of the bestower of boons; and then, [the events] below the sacrificial ground.

While Citrāṅgada was sinking, Sīmantinī, with her arms clasping his chest, led him down to the abode of Takṣaka, the king of serpents. Takṣaka, having heard the account of that Citrāṅgada, personally approached Sīmantinī and, after honoring her, engaged her in conversation regarding the deities she worshipped; meanwhile, Citrāṅgada— (Note: The provided source text appears to be a corrupted or fragmentary manuscript. The translation above reconstructs the narrative flow based on the legible portions: the drowning of Citrāṅgada, Sīmantinī’s rescue of him by leading him to Takṣaka, and Takṣaka’s subsequent meeting with Sīmantinī.)

The narration of the devotion of Śarabhaṅga, who was devoted to the Lord Śiva whom he himself worshipped; upon hearing his words, Takṣaka, being pleased, bestowed great honors upon Citrāṅgada; then, having heard Citrāṅgada’s request to return to his own home, Takṣaka nourished him with food consisting of the juice of the *kalpavṛkṣa* tree, gave him much wealth, and likewise provided a *rākṣasa* and a serpent for assistance, as well as a chariot that travels at will and moves unhindered.

Having bestowed the horses upon him and bound him with various blessings, he gave the command for Citrāṅgada to depart for his own abode. Then Citrāṅgada, having bowed to the king of the Takṣakas, took the horse, mounted it, and having taken the wealth along with those two—the Rākṣasa and the Pannaga—who had been granted as assistants, he descended from the netherworld (Pātāla) into the waters of the Yamunā. Emerging on the bank of the Yamunā, he mounted the steed and began to sport. Now, at that very moment, by his female companions...

Upon arriving at the Yamunā to bathe together with Sīmantinī, he witnessed her cremation; then, hearing from the mouth of a friend that he would soon return, she comforted Citrāṅgada by saying, "Be composed in mind and do not grieve; these are the Siddhas who move at will, gods," and [sent him] toward his father's city.

Regarding the departure: there, having heard that his father Indrasena had been deprived of his royal status by his non-heirs, Citrāṅgada sent a message through the son of a Nāga to those non-heirs, urging them to relinquish the throne; upon hearing Citrāṅgada’s message as spoken by the Nāga’s son, all the non-heirs restored the royal status to Indrasena, informed him of the news of his son’s arrival, and after making a plea for forgiveness for their own offenses, they propitiated him.

Then Citravarmā, having gone to his own palace and paid homage to his parents, received a letter from them which brought him a flood of supreme joy. Subsequently, King Indrasena dispatched a messenger to Citravarmā to inform him of the auspicious news of his son’s safe arrival from Pātāla. Upon hearing the news of his son-in-law’s arrival through the mouth of the messenger, King Citravarmā experienced an outpouring of intense joy and auspiciousness. Thereafter, the king [prepared] for his daughter Sīmantinī... [the marriage ceremony].

She also announced the arrival of Citrāṅgada; then, having summoned Citrāṅgada by means of Citravarmā and Gajendra, and having again performed the elaborate rites of hospitality for him, she [bestowed] her own daughter, Avyayā, upon that Citrāṅgada.

In the context of describing the power of the vow of observing Monday (Somavāra) on the part of a woman (*sīmantinī*), there is the account of Sumedhas and Sāmava, concerning which the two [latter] gave their daughter to the Brahmin with great effort; then, after Śatrughna had brought articles such as ornaments from the netherworld (*pātāla*) and satisfied the outcaste woman, he took her and returned to his own city, where he enjoyed the pleasures of sovereignty with great joy; thus, regarding the worship of Śiva and Gaurī on Monday—

A description of the attainment of their desired happiness by Ratnaprabhā, Aśokāṅgada, and Sīmantinī; and a narration of the story of the two sons of the Brāhmaṇa named Mitrāsārvasvata. Therein, after the three sons of the Brāhmaṇa Sumedhas had completed their study of the Sāmaveda along with its auxiliary branches, they went to the presence of the King of Vidarbha at their father’s command to acquire wealth for the purpose of their marriage. Then, the King of Vidarbha beheld those two sons of the twice-born as they were making their request.

Regarding the task: when the two [sons of the Brahmin] were told, “Clothe one of you in the middle in female attire, become a Brahmin couple, and after enjoying the hospitality of Queen Mālinī, come to me; then I shall give you much wealth,” those two Brahmin youths, considering the king’s command to be inviolable, dressed their master in the guise of a female attendant and, appearing as a Brahmin couple, set out for the city of Niṣadha. And then...

On Monday, between those two, the man was worshipped by Sīmantinī with the thought that he was Mahādeva, and the woman was worshipped with the thought that she was Pārvatī. At that very moment, the Brahmin’s son named Sāmavat, who had been worshipped by Sīmantinī with the thought that he was Pārvatī while wearing the guise of a female companion, truly attained womanhood. Then, having taken the jeweled earrings, ornaments, and other gifts given by Sīmantinī, as the two young Brahmins departed, Sāmavat attained womanhood.

The arising of a transformation of desire; then, because Sāmavatī had been born, Sumedha’s making a request to her for the sake of amorous dalliance; then, having observed his own friend’s female form, her lack of aversion to sexual union, and her nature in private, and seeing her requesting sexual pleasure, [Sumedha] somehow consoled her with words of discernment, took that Sāmavatī away, brought her to his own home, and reported the entire account to his father and the others; then, by those two parents who were overwhelmed with grief—

Taking his two sons with him, he went toward the abode of Chyavana and related to him how he had obtained the kingdom through your grace. Then, at the instruction of that sage Bharadvāja—who was intent on the welfare of the twice-born boy and devoted to the practice of friendship—the king, together with those two brahmin youths, went to the hermitage of Ambikā and performed the worship of the venerable Jamadagnyāmbā. Thus it happened.

The Mother of the World, appearing with a gracious countenance, declared that she could not allow the state of her devotee’s distress to remain as it was; she then commanded Sāmavatī to enjoy the pleasures of desire with Sumedhas as his wife. Furthermore, she granted a boon to Sāmavatī’s father, the Brāhmaṇa Sārasvata, stating that he would have a son of superior virtue compared to his previous children. Subsequently, by that Brāhmaṇa Sārasvata, his own daughter named Sāmavatī was given to that Sumedhas according to the rites of marriage.

The act of giving; the description of the enjoyment of sensual pleasures preceded by the performance of the Samedhas, Sāmavati, Gīdvaiṣya, and Dhamekha sacrifices for those two; and thus, the description of the devotion and identity with the form of the Sīmantinī. ... |

That Brahmin named Mandra, being devoted to attachment to sensual objects, made his permanent residence in the house of a courtesan named Piṅgalā. Now, while that twice-born man was dwelling in the abode of that courtesan, a divine yogi named Ṛṣabha, whose soul was righteous, arrived there. By Mandara, the Brahmin, and Piṅgalā, the courtesan, that yogi Ṛṣabha was served with perfect devotion, beginning from the washing of his feet and ending with the massaging of them.

The production of extreme contentment lasting for a day and night; then, on the second day, the departure of that Kramayogin who had arrived in connection with a pilgrimage; thereafter, after some time, following the death of the dull-witted Brahmin, the birth of [the child] in the wife of King Javāha, the lord of Daśārṇa; and therein, first of all, her death while still in the womb by the co-wives, and although poison was administered by them, she did not die due to the turn of fate, yet there was nevertheless a [condition] born of the poison.

Hādtyanta was a resident of Īśāvāsa; when Bāraka, born of that Ṛṣabha’s wife, suffered from a fever arising from poison, there was no one capable of curing him. Observing that both mother and son were afflicted by a terrible and fierce disease, the king, despite having applied medicine through compassionate means, saw that they were not recovering. Concluding through his own intelligence that "surely these two have come from hell," he had them abandoned in a desolate forest by means of his charioteer and his chariot. Then, by that disciple Bāraka—

While wandering in the forest, that queen, by the turn of fate, entered the city of Ceyhan via a merchant’s path she had never traveled before; then follows the account of her being taken as a slave, and in the course of describing the taking of Śiva, the narrative of the events at the place called Mandarāhi situated in the region of Avanti; there, having recognized that noble woman, she was led into the presence of her own master, the merchant Padmākara; and then, by Padmākara... [the account] of that queen.

Having offered consolation and established him in his own home with due honor, while that merchant’s wife was living there, at one point, by the power of destiny, her husband died from a disease such as a wound; then, while that queen-consort was performing the funeral rites, by a stroke of fate, on that very same day, the aforementioned sage Śivabhadra arrived at the house of that very merchant on the occasion of a pilgrimage.

Then the yogi Aṣeṣaśiva, having accepted the worship and hospitality offered by the merchant, went into the presence of the queen who was grieving over the death of her son. After instructing her in the supreme realization of the Truth and commanding her to practice devotion to Śiva, he went to the side of her deceased son and restored his life with ashes consecrated by the mantra of Śiva. Then, when the boy’s life had been restored, [he brought joy] to the queen and her kinsmen.

Upon attaining great joy, the yogi Ṛṣabhaśiva then touched that mother and son with consecrated ashes; by the mere touch of those ashes, both the mother and son attained divine bodies. Then, after bestowing the name Bhadrāyu upon that boy and describing the future destiny of both of them, the yogi Ṛṣabhaśiva led him to the house of Padākaravaidyaka for his residence until he reached the age of sixteen for the purpose of receiving sacred knowledge.

The departure for another place; then, through the power of worshipping and honoring the Śiva-yogi named Śivabhaktasabha by Piṅgarāviveśayā, the description of her birth in a future life as Sīmantinī, the wife of King Citrāṅgada; then, the growth of Bhadrāyus from childhood alongside Sunaya, the son of Padyākara, in the house of that Padyākara Vaiśya, accompanied by their friendship.

And [there was] their playing together and so forth; then, for those two—the prince Vaśaja and the royal prince Bhadrāyu—following the performance of the purificatory rites such as the initiation (*upanayana*) through the gate of a Brahmin, there was the accomplishment of their proficiency in the study of the Vedas. Then, when the sixteenth year had arrived for the royal prince Bhadrāyu, the aforementioned master of the Ṣaḍbhaya-yoga came into his presence. That master of the Ṣaḍbhaya-yoga performed a salutation with the mother of Bhadrāyu along with her son, for the purpose of instructing Bhadrāyu in the true path.

And [there was] the performance of service for others; then, by the yogi Ṛṣabhaśiva, the imparting of instruction on dharma appropriate to the hermitage of the eternal Varma to Prince Bhadrāyus, who was well-versed in the Purāṇas and Śrutis; then, for the sake of liberating his own people from distress, the imparting of instruction to Śrīśivaseva; and having given to Prince Yuvanāśva—who was seeking victory—the bow Vijaya, the sword Nārāca, and the mace Kaṅka, along with the Śiva-mantra as an inner companion, and having smeared his body with ashes, he gave him two thousand chariots, horses, and elephants.

Having taken up a sword that brings victory by its mere sight and having performed the ritual instructions for its use, and having instructed them with auspicious words, he received worship and hospitality from the two of them and departed for his desired destination. Then, the King of Magadha, an enemy of the King of Daśārṇa named Vajrabāhu, arrived with a great army to wage war; subsequently, having fought a battle with the King of Magadha, the ruler of Daśārṇa, he defeated him in that conflict.

Having destroyed the entire army and brought the kingdom of Daśārṇa under his control, he bound [the king] in his chariot and set out for his own country. Thus, while residing in the city of Vaiśyānagara, Prince Bhadrāyu heard from the mouths of people the news regarding his father’s kingdom. Accompanied by his friend Sunaya, the son of a merchant from Padmākara, he mounted a horse and with great speed reached his father’s ruined realm of Daśārṇa, which he saw devastated by the forces of the enemy king named Magadheśvara. From there...

Overcome by fury, he swiftly shattered the enemy army, blew the conch shell of victory granted by Śiva, and raised his sword of triumph. Having bewildered all the hosts of Asuras with his illusory power (*māyā*), he slew many enemies. He liberated his father, who was bound to the chariot, and released the wives of his own father and the lords of the city, as well as the women and daughters of the citizens, along with their cattle and wealth. Then, having cheered his father and all the others, he returned to his own city.

The dispatch [of the messenger]; then, having entered the enemy army, having seized their entire wealth—including women, elephants, horses, chariots, male and female servants—and having defeated the Lord of Magadha, he bound him along with his ministers and retinue and returned to his own city. Then, by that Bhadrāyu, whose name was clearly revealed, while acting as the charioteer, after first stating in general that he was the son of a Kṣatriya, he performed the salutation of his father's feet. Immediately following his arrival at his father’s presence, by that one named Sunaya—
Accompanied by Bhadrāyu, the son of Vadya, he went to the city of Vedaya. Then, after some time had passed, while Bhadrāyu was practicing devotion to Śiva, [the following occurred].

Then, after the illustrious Śivayogin Varṣabha had imparted the instruction on the *Sarvarakṣākara-bhīśiva-kavaca-stotra* to him, Bhadrā related to her own mother, that lady named Padyākarā, the account of his own battle and other events; then, on the second day, regarding Citrāṅgada—who was also known as Candrāgada—the arrival of that aforementioned Śivayogin named Ṣaḍbhuja at the camp, and the bestowing of his daughter upon the prince Bhadrāyuṣ.

First, the Lord performed the preliminary instructions and the formal invitation; then, following the words of the yogi Ṛṣabha, King Citrāṅgada summoned Bhadrāyus and, having bestowed his own daughter named Kauravī upon him, he initiated the commencement of the marriage rites. Thereafter, having dispatched a messenger to Vajrabāhu, the father-in-law, he extended an invitation according to proper custom for the sake of his son’s wedding. Subsequently, Vajrabāhu arrived there at the royal capital of Niṣadha along with his retinue.

Upon his arrival, Vajravāhu received a salutation from his son Bhadrāyu; however, because Vajravāhu did not recognize him, Bhadrāyu, desiring to test him, caused a fall to be made. When the Lord of Niṣadha related the account of his past conduct to Vajravāhu—stating that "this one named Bhadrāyu was abandoned by you along with your mother in the forest, and he is indeed your own son"—it followed immediately after Vajravāhu’s realization of his own deed of abandoning both son and wife.

Having attained ultimate bliss through her son Bharata, who had destroyed all enemies, she then took the honor and hospitality offered by King Citrāṅgada; and taking her daughter-in-law Bhadrā along with her own son Bhadrāyuḥ, she departed together with Vajravāhana and his entire retinue.

With great joy, he returned to Khapura; then, having previously performed the duties of crown prince by his father’s command, after his father had gone to heaven, Bhadrāyu assumed the sovereignty over the entire circle of the earth. Following his accession to the throne, Bhadrāyu entered into an alliance with the minister named Hemaratha, the ruler of Magadha who was imprisoned by his enemy, and secured his release from bondage. Thereafter, Bhadrāyu ruled the kingdom while enjoying pleasures together with his wife Kīrtimālinī. Thus...

A description of the power resulting from the worship and hospitality offered to Śiva-yogins in a previous birth. Then, once Bhadrāyu had attained the throne of sovereignty, he went one day to the forest with his wife and wandered there at will. At that very time, while a certain tiger was pursuing and harassing a pair of brahmins in that forest, they made a fervent plea to the king for their protection. At that moment, the tiger arrived...

The abduction of the Brahmin’s wife; the subsequent pursuit of those two by Bhadrāyu through the regions of the Śaikhara mountain range; the constant distress of all living beings in the lake; and when the Brahmin’s wife had been carried off by the tiger, the Brahmin’s lamentation and his making a formal complaint against the king.

Then King Bhadrāyu made various kinds of supplications for the sake of consoling that brahmin whose wife had been devoured by a tiger. Thereupon, the brahmin made a request to the king to send him to the royal village for the sake of quelling his own desire for sensual enjoyment. Then, Bhadrāyu, having given his own wife to that brahmin, kindled the sacrificial fires, meditated upon Śiva, and prepared himself to leap into the fire. At that very moment, for the purpose of testing his devotion, [the Lord] assumed the form of a brahmin...

The manifestation of Śrī Śaṅkara in his own true form; the offering of praise to that Śrī Śaṅkara by Bhadrāyu; the granting of boons to Bhadrāyu and his wife by the Blessed Lord Śrī Śaṅkara, who was pleased by that praise; the description of Bhadrāyu’s attainment of the enjoyment of happiness through the grace of Śiva; and finally, after entrusting the kingdom to his sons, Bhadrāyu’s attainment of union with Śiva, and [the account] of Bhadrāyuścadurya and Vicāṅgada along with their own wives.

The description of [the king] attaining the state of Śambhu together with Sīmantinī; then, the description of the majesty of devotion to Śiva; next, the description of the majesty of sacred ash (*bhasma*). In connection with that, the account of the life of the Śiva-yogin named Vāmadeva is told. Once, while that Śiva-yogin Vāmadeva was wandering in the Krauñca forest, a Brahmarākṣasa approached to devour him and squeezed him firmly with his two arms; yet, by the mere touch of his body, he was instantly liberated.

The attainment of the state of a *brahmarākṣasa*; then, by that *brahmarākṣasa*, whose mind was filled with despondency upon remembering his own previously committed evil deeds, a description was given to the yogi Vāmadeva Śiva regarding his own past life, the evil karma performed therein, the ripening of that karma, the tortures of Yama, and the subsequent attainment of the state of a *brahmarākṣasa*. Then, [he said] to Vāmadeva: "By the mere sight of your body, the memory of my previous thousands of births has arisen; my mind is also exceedingly serene; therefore, such [is the case]."

When asked by the yogi Vāmadeva, "How was this power obtained?", [the sage] described the efficacy of the ashes by stating, "This is the power of the ashes residing in my own body. In connection with that, he narrated the account of how a certain Brahmin of wicked conduct from the Draviḍa country—whose feet were struck by a dog—attained the world of Śiva merely by the touch of those ashes. Then, having witnessed the direct manifestation of Śāradā and her son—who had been delighted by the dream and born from his own body—the Brahmin’s mind was overcome with wonder. Kukkuṭa and Makaṭa, who had attained mastery in the art of dancing performed daily before that courtesan—wearing Rudrākṣa beads, sacred ash, earrings, armlets, and crest-jewels—used to dance every day at the conclusion of her ritual worship before Śiva. Having granted the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*) to that king, the king then honored all the brahmins with various offerings. The arrival of the great sage Śrī Nārada; then, by King Bhadrasena—who performed the worship of Truth with true devotion—and by Nārada, [the following was related] to the king: "When Yama arrived here to take away your son, Vīrabhadra, sent by Śaṅkara, carried out the punishment of Yama. Through the power of hearing that *Bindumāhātmya*, when the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas* were gradually subdued within her heart, there arose an auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*). Then follows the commencement of the narrative of the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa* by Vyāsa, the arrival of Nārada, and the praise of Lord Śiva. Thereafter, she daily practiced the meditation on the syllable *Oṃ* before the image of Lord Śaṅkara, situated upon the Vindhya mountain range, according to the path instructed by her guru; and in the course of this, [the description of] the Vindhya mountain.

The description of Meru; the words of the sage Nārada stating that Meru seemed to hold him in contempt; the description of the obstruction of the path of the sun due to the killing of Vindhya; on one side, the description of the lack of connection with the rays [of the sun], and on the other, the description of the inability to remain in the sky due to the fierce heat of the sun's rays; the praise of Brahmā by the gods; the description of the virtuous conduct of the men who have come to Satyaloka preceded by the demonstration of the absence of fear in Satyaloka; and the pacification of the gods performed by Brahmā.

In order to dispel the fear of the gods and to prevent the destruction of the world, she became eager to go to the presence of the sage Agastya at Śrīkāñcī on Mount Kārttikeya; there, through the power of her devotion to Śiva, she completely severed the entire bond of karma and departed for the celestial realm. Having arrived there in the world of Śiva in the presence of the illustrious Pārvatī, the Mother of the Universe, she was honored by Pārvatī. Then, having heard from Pārvatī’s own mouth the account of her former birth as a jackal, [she attained liberation].

For the sake of her husband’s liberation from his birth as a *piśāca*, she made a request to the Gandharva named Tumburu, asking him to reside within the body of Vidhyādhari and narrate the *Purāṇas* to her husband. At the request of Tumburu, he went to Vidhyādhari; when he had caused the story of Śrī Gaurīpati to be heard by that *piśāca*, the latter was liberated from his state as a *piśāca*. [This concludes] a brief description of Kāśī.

The description of the husband’s ascent of a radiant celestial chariot from the womb of a Piśāca and his journey toward the world of Śiva; the performance of the primary pilgrimage at Maṇikarṇikā in the sacred field of Kāśī by the Lord of Viśveśvara after bathing there; the granting of the name Agastya to the sage by the gods; the description of how liberation and Kaivalya were attained by that couple through the singing of the praises of the glorious Lord Śiva; the departure of the glorious Śiva; and the bestowing of the form of the sage Agastya upon the gods who were worshipping him in his hermitage.

Following the description of the Vaimava narrative concerning the merit of the *Varāhottarakhaṇḍa* which elucidates the [preceding] section, and in connection with the conclusion of that *Brāhmottarakhaṇḍa*, there is a description of the praise offered by the sage Agastya composed by Bṛhaspati, along with a description of the means for the destruction of sins; in connection with this, there is an exposition on the conduct of devoted wives (*pativratā*). Then follows the prayer of the Lord of the Gods (Indra) to prevent the growth of the Vindhya mountain which was obstructing the path of the Sun. Thus ends the third section, the *Varāhottarakhaṇḍa*, within the *Brāhmakhaṇḍa*.

The consolation of the gods by Agastya according to their words, the departure of the gods to the heavenly world, and the acceptance of the gods' request; then, for the purpose of removing the obstruction of the Vindhya mountain, the sage Agastya’s journey with his wife outside Kāśī-kṣīra-drahi; and the deities such as Viśvanātha and Kālabhairava [appearing] to the sage who was grieving at the separation from Kāśī—thus ends the third section, the Brahmakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. 2.

The utterance of lamentation preceded by the recognition [of his own state]; the refusal of the Vindhya mountain to accept its dwarfed condition until Agastya’s arrival; and the sage’s command to the mountain: "Until my return, you shall remain other than a donkey."

The narration of the arrival of Kaddha; the honoring of the sage Agastya by Madākadamodaśa; the granting of boons to Agastya by the sage Chakshmya; and the departure of Agastya for Prayāga. [This section] describes the benefit of helping others, the merit of visiting holy sites such as Śrīśreṣṭha and Rikharādi, and the realization that one has truly reached Kāśī through the grace of the Lord. In the context of describing the majesty of sacred fords (*tīrtha*), the greatness of the Kāśī-kṣetra is recounted, establishing that all other holy sites lead one toward the field of Kāśī.

And [this work] illuminates the sixfold duties of the *kāraka*. It describes how the twice-born man named Śivaśarman, residing in the city of Mathurā, became filled with anxiety upon seeing old age come upon his own body; his departure from home for the purpose of visiting the seven sacred cities; his arrival at Prayāga after completing his pilgrimage to Ayodhyā; an incidental description of the greatness (*māhātmya*) of Prayāga; the account of the twice-born man’s pilgrimage to Kāśī; his journey to Mahākālavana; and, through that association, a description of the majesty of Mahākāla.

The narration of the pilgrimage to the holy site (tīrtha) of Māyāpurī; the death of the twice-born (dvija) in Māyāpurī; and his ascent to the celestial realm (nabhovartman) by means of a golden aerial chariot (svarṇavimāna) attended by a group of Vaiṣṇavas named Puṇyaśīla and Suśīla. Furthermore, regarding the twice-born Śivarāma who died in the city of liberation called Māyā, there is an account of how he failed to attain release due to the lapse of the chaste Lopāmudrā; and the commencement of the dialogue between Śivarāma and the Viṣṇu-gaṇas to demonstrate that direct union (sāyujya) with the Divine does not exist in the six cities, beginning with Māyā.

The description of the world of Yama by the Brahmin Śivaśarman, who had arrived there, through the narration of the virtuous conduct performed by men dwelling in the realms of the twice-born, the radiant ones, the Sāraṇas, the cuckoos, the Guhyakas, and the Gandharvas; the arrival of Dharmarāja with honors and worship for the Brahmin who had come to the realm of Yama; and the Brahmin’s question, "How is this? upon hearing the gentle words of the gentle-formed Dharmarāja, followed by a brief description of the realm of Yama in connection with the examination of Yama’s form and appearance. ...

A description of the world of the Apsarases; a description of the world of the Sun; an exposition on the greatness of the Gāyatrī mantra in connection with the description of the worship of the Sun; and an exposition on the rule for the offering of the half-verse.

The description of the city of Taikṛta; the rescue of a caravan of merchants—who were about to set out for the city of Viśvanātha from the Pahlava lord Piṅgākṣa in the Vindhya forest—by means of the protection of his life, and the attainment of the joy of his own life; the description of the city of Varuṇa; the abduction of Śuciṣmat, the son of the patriarch Kardama, by Śiśumāra while he was sporting in a lake; and the arrival of the celestial host before the sage, who, despite hearing that his son had perished in the lake, remained excessively intent on his worship.

The description of the city of Gāndhavatī belonging to Jagaṭpāṇa, the Wind-god; the performance of penance by the pure-souled Kaḍayapayaputra after installing the image of Śrīkārttikeya; his attainment of the status of a guardian of the quarters (dikpāla) from Śiva; and the description of the city of Alakāvatī belonging to the Lord of the Guhyakas. In the city of Kāmpilya, there was a Brahmin named Yajñadatta who had a son named Guṇanidhi, who, though a treasury of virtues, was addicted to vice and became a drunkard; and the long period during which his mother [concealed] the secret misconduct of that [son].

The father’s expulsion of Suta from his own home for his misconduct; then, the description of how he, having offered lamps at Śiva’s temple and performed many fasts, was born as the son of the King of Kaliṅga on the night of Śivarātri due to the theft of food; and there, through the offering of lamps at the temples of Śiva, his attainment of being the son of Viśravas in another kalpa, followed by the description of his acquisition of friendship with Śiva and the power to create and destroy through his practice of unbearable austerities.

Description of the city of Īśāna as pleased by Radara-makata; description of the greatness of the mountain established by the host of Rudras, beginning with Jajaikapād; description of the penance of Dhruva while staying in Madhuvana on the bank of the Yamunā; description of the various obstacles to his penance sent by Indra; description of the world of the Moon (Candraloka); the establishment of a *liṅga* by Soma, who was born from the mind of Brahmā, after he had settled in Vārāṇasī; and the direct vision of the Supreme Lord (Śrī-Bhagavat) by Dhruva.

Furthermore, there is the narration of his liberation through the grace of Śiva. [The text] describes the determination of the Lord’s descent brought about by Dhruva: "I shall grant you the foundational station of the celestial sphere (*jyotiścakra*); nevertheless, go with me to Kāśī, which is the common husband of twenty-seven maidens beginning with Rohiṇī. Having performed the worship of the Liṅga there, fulfill your duty. Having thus instructed Dhruva and established him in marriage, [the Lord] performed penance at Vārāṇasī, and by the power of Śiva’s boon— [Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on a Purāṇic narrative concerning Dhruva, the Pole Star, and his attainment of a place in the celestial sphere.]

Having reached Soma as her husband, the blessed Kārīṣugandhī set out on her journey; having attained fulfillment through the installation of the *dhruva* star, there follows a brief description of the world of the constellations she had achieved, and the departure of Soma, the son of Atri, to the house of his preceptor’s wife. [Then follows] the abduction [of Rohiṇī], the account of the non-battle between Rudra and Candra, and the prevention of the battle by the words of Brahmā, whereby Candra was established in the world of the people by Bṛhaspati.

Discourses on the praise of the twice-born; the birth of Budha in that [lineage]; the propitiation of Śiva performed by Budha; the dialogue between Budha and Śiva regarding the boon granted by Śiva; the conversations with Brahmā of those who had assembled; the description of the origin of the dog, and so forth... [and] the restoration to life by Bhārgava Śukra, through the *saṃjīvanī* mantra, of the hosts of the Dānava lord Andhaka and his soldiers who had been slain in battle by the gods.

The restoration of the preceptor [Śukra] to life; through the prayer of the gods, Śiva, by means of Nandikeśvara, summoned Śukra and placed him within his own mouth; the description of the battle between Andhaka and his army along with the demons; the departure of Śukra, that twice-born one, from Māyāpurī, and upon his death, his attainment of various enjoyments for a year in the world of Viṣṇu and the presence of Brahmā; his exit from there; and the granting of boons such as lordship over the worlds to Śukra due to his performance of penance at Vārāṇasī and his grace by Śiva.

Having attained sovereignty over the two Kakunva regions, which were adorned with the prescribed prosperity, he reached Kāśī; there follows the description of the greatness of Śiva. Upon hearing of that [greatness], joy arose within him, and out of fear for Kāśī, he constructed a temple of Śiva. There, by the grace of Śiva, a linga named Keśava was established; the origin of this is told as follows: while performing penance before that Śivalinga installed by Śiva’s grace, his body became covered with drops of perspiration which fell upon the ground. The description of how Śiva, having arrived for the purpose of testing him, bestowed upon him the sovereignty over the world and other boons; the account of Aṅgiras performing penance in Vārāṇasī for the sake of Śiva’s grace, followed by Viṣṇu’s intervention stating that the king shall become his companion and remain ever devoted to him; the attainment of the status of Lord of the World and divine power through the granting of boons by Śiva; and the description of the manifestation of the form born from Mātaṇḍa and the establishment of the Śiva-dharma as proclaimed by the Gaṇas.

The account of the birth of Śanaiścara (Saturn) from Chāyā; his performance of penance at Vārāṇasī and the attainment of the status of a world-guardian (*lokapāla*); the subjugation of Skanda by Agastya, the chief of sages, together with his wife, after circumambulating Śrīgiri to the south; and the description of how he attained the name Agastya. ... ; Śa Va.

The *Chṛtaskandastotra*; the discourse of the great sage [Brahmā] to Skanda regarding the majesty of the *Kādī* [mantra]; the description of the worlds obtained by the sons of Brahmā’s mind-born sons, such as Marīci, as appointed by Skanda; and the description of the location of the Arundhatī constellation, the sight thereof, and the fruit of residing in the *Kādī* [place]. (Bha.)

...the description of the penance of Avimukta; the description of Viṣṇu’s penance on the bank of the Cakroṣṇī; and the account of the birth of Śravaḥ—who, while residing on his father’s lap at Maṇikaṇikā, was insulted by his stepmother—and his subsequent departure to the forest for penance at the command of his mother, as well as the exposition of the ritual procedure for Maṇikaṇikā.
