The meeting with the sages there; the instruction of the twelve-syllable mantra to him and the disappearance of the sages; the description of the taking up of the Gaṅgā; the recitation of the Daśaharā hymn—[which describes] how, due to the weight of Śiva’s presence, the Gaṅgā at Kāśī pacifies great and minor sins; and the killing in the forest by a tiger of a certain Vṛṣīpati named Vāhīka, who was a Brahmin in name only, along with his bones and flesh.

The vulture’s battle with another bird; the great merit resulting from the falling of that vulture onto the thigh of Devavrata (Bhīṣma) and its contact with the waters of the Gaṅgā; the astonishment of all upon seeing that even that Vāhīka, who was being dragged through hells such as Raurava and Kumbhīpāka for the sake of digging up various kinds of corpses, attained happiness; finally, the Vāhīka’s departure for the heavenly realm after ascending a celestial chariot (*vimāna*); and the narration of the majesty of the Gaṅgā, which grants the attainment of fruits equal to those of knowledge to those who are incapable [of higher practice].

The *Mahāghaughanivāraka-Śrī-Gaṅgā-Sahasranāma-Stotra*; the narration of the superiority of the greatness of the sacred field (*kṣetra*) at the confluence of the Gaṅgā brought by King Bhaṃīratha to Maṇikarṇikā; the description of the location of the southern and northern gateways; the appointment of Kiknora to prevent those who enter within Deharī Vināyaka without the command of Śiva; the narration of the history of the merchant Dhanañjaya; and the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the name Vārāṇasī.

The severing of Brahmā’s head by Śiva; the birth of Kālarāja from that severed head of Brahmā; the departure of Kālarāja to the earth in the form of a skull-bearer (*kāpālika*) after cutting off Brahmā’s head, which caused day and night; the arrival of the sin of Brahmin-slaughter (*brahmahatyā*), which followed him like a shadow, as he went there; and the description of Kālabhairava’s dwelling at the Kapālamocana Tīrtha for the sake of purifying all sins.

) The narration of the birth of the son named Harikeśa to the wife named Chanakakuṇḍalā from the Yakṣa named Pṛṇabhadra, following his propitiation of Śiva; the departure of Harikeśa—who, from childhood, was devoted to Śiva—into the forest out of fear of being beaten by his father; the description of the Forest of Bliss (Ānandakānana) as assigned to Harikeśa by Śiva regarding Pārvatī; and the account of how Maheśvara, pleased by Harikeśa’s penance in the Forest of Bliss, granted him the status of Daṇḍapāṇi, along with the *Daṇḍapāṇyaṣṭaka*.

And... [the description of the origin of the holy site named Jñānavāpī, followed by the description of its greatness; the abduction of the daughter of Harisvāmin, a resident of Kārī, while she was worshipping at Jñānavāpī by a Vidyādhara infatuated with her beauty; the description of the battle between that Vidyādhara and a Rākṣasa; and because both the Rākṣasa and the Vidyādhara died simultaneously in the battle, the daughter of Harisvāmin’s resentment toward the Vidyādhara.]

The account of the renunciation of their bodies; how both, having attained the king’s body, were married there immediately after beholding the portrait-scroll; the journey of Mālyaketu and Kalāvatī to Kāñcī; how, having performed the Kārīrī sacrifice there, they ascended a celestial chariot near the Jñānavāpī pond due to the instruction of Śiva, and the description of their departure for the realm of Śiva; the narration of the majesty of the Jñānavāpī; and, in connection with the description of the virtuous conduct of the Brāhmaṇas who recite the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, the definition of the duties that must be performed daily.

[The section on] the description of good conduct and the determination of the duties of studentship (*brahmacarya*) for the twice-born; [the section on] the description of the characteristics of women, as the householder’s stage of life cannot exist without a woman possessing auspicious marks; the description of the eight types of marriage; the detailed narration of the virtuous conduct that leads the twice-born and others to attain Kāśī; ...; and, in the context of the account of King Divodāsa, the narration of the origin of the *Avimukteśvara* Liṅga at Avimukta.

—A description of the nature of prohibited conduct for Brahmins and others regarding the journey to the sacred field of Kāśī; a delineation of the prescribed conduct for those in the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*); a detailed exposition of the duties of forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and ascetics (*yati*), including the teaching on Yoga; a narration of the means for attaining liberation for one whose death is imminent, interspersed with the majesty of the sacred field of Kāśī; and [an account of] when Divodāsa, having conquered Kāśī, was ruling the kingdom of the earth, all the gods, beginning with Viśveśvara, abandoned it.

The journey to Mount Mandara; a description of the happiness of the subjects during King Divodāsa’s reign; Agni’s departure for heaven after abandoning his own domain; the description of the king’s grief at the separation from Kāśī upon seeing Viśvanātha and Bhavānī stationed on the peak of Mount Mandara as he spoke of his own power; and the description of Śiva sending a host of Yoginīs to cause King Divodāsa to abandon the sacred field of Kāśī.
55. By the command of Śiva, the sixty-four Yoginīs enter the city of Kāśī for the purpose of creating obstacles for King Divodāsa; this is followed by the description of their names.

And hereafter, the account of the arrival of Śiva as directed by the gods for the purpose of expelling Kādyā from Divodāsa’s kingdom; the description of how Rataṅgada, who was intent on seeking out vulnerabilities in King Divodāsa’s realm through various efforts, divided himself and took up residence in Kādyā herself; the description of the location of Roṭārka; and the narration of the procedure and the greatness of that pilgrimage site.

The description of the Uttarāka-kuṇḍa; the performance of penance by a Brahmin girl residing there near Uttarāka after the death of her parents; the granting of a boon in the form of Gaurī’s own status as a friend to her; and the description of the majesty of the Uttarāka-kuṇḍa. ...

An account of how Kṛṣṇa’s son Sāmba contracted the disease of leprosy due to the insult inflicted by Nārada; his recovery from the disease through performing penance after having fashioned a *kuṇḍa* (sacred pool) at Kāśī in his own name; a description of the greatness of that *kuṇḍa* along with the majesty of Sabāditya; and, in connection with the Pāṇḍavas’ forest exile, their journey to Kāśī, where Draupadī propitiated the Sun, who granted her a boon, and the attainment of a son by her through the grace of the Sun propitiated by Draupadī.

The description of the location, the account of how the Sun was brought there by Maya, the description of Uccaiḥśravas, the narration of the dispute between Kaṭu and Vinatā, the infliction of a curse upon Vinatā by Kaṭu out of malice, the description of Garuḍa’s fetching of the nectar (*sudhā*) to remove his mother’s suffering, the performance of penance by Vinatā and Garuḍa after installing the Linga of Śiva at Kāyāvarohaṇa, and the narration of the greatness of the station of Khoklāditya following the granting of boons to them.
Thus ends the first half of the glorious *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*.
Now follows the second half extracted from the Kāśī-khaṇḍa.

The description of the majesty of Aruṇāditya; the narration of the cause of Vinatā’s servitude; the description of the majesty of Vṛddhāditya worshipped by Vṛddhahārīta; the performance of penance by Sūrya after installing a Śiva-liṅga at Kāyāvarohaṇa according to the word of Viṣṇu; the description of the majesty of that [place] preceded by the attainment of the name Kedārāditya; and the [description of the majesty] of the Vimānagaṅgā and the Ādityas.

[The account of] the naming of the Tīrtha as Daśāśvamedha due to its being the site where ten Aśvamedha sacrifices were performed by the four-faced Brahmā, who was sent by Śiva for the purpose of excavating the Niṣka of Divodāsa’s lordship; and a description of the majesty of that Tīrtha.

Furthermore, [the description of] the expedition of Śaṅkukarṇa and others, at the command of Śiva, to Kāśī in order to ascertain the situation of the Yoginīs and Bhairavas sent by the Lord—who had established their respective stations there—and to expel Divodāsa; and [the account of] the siege of Kāśī...

In the context of describing the destruction of the demon Aghasamyu, established by the host of Kapardin’s attendants who were exceedingly devoted to Śambhu, there is the narration of the history of the twice-born man named Vārmīki; the description of the liberation of the Piśāca performed by him; and the exposition of the greatness of the pilgrimage to the holy site of Pidhyācamocana.

An exposition on the majesty of the *śivaliṅga* installed by the host of Gaṇas headed by Piṅgala; and how, having observed that those Gaṇas and others who had been sent by Śiva to investigate the situation in Kāñcī would not return, [Śiva], by his command, caused the entry of the leader of the Gaṇas into the city through a tunnel.

[The description of Gaṇeśa assuming the guise of an astrologer and traveling to Kāśī; how, through his own illusory power, he deluded the many people residing in the city and conversed with Raṇekaca in the king’s inner apartments along with the queen; and at the meeting with King Divodāsa, how Gaṇeśa, preceded by the king's inquiry, told him a prophetic account concerning the arrival of a Brahmin and the subsequent instruction regarding the practice of Brahman.]

Now follows a description of the hymn to Gaṇeśa composed by Śiva, an incidental account of Gaṇeśa’s name as Duṇḍirāja, and a description of the locations of Gaṇeśas such as Agastya and Hariścandra. Then, while Śiva was thus speaking and was overcome with anxiety, he appointed Viṣṇu for the purpose of driving King Divodāsa out of Kāśī; this includes a description of the various locations of Viṣṇu in Kāśī, as well as those of Viṣṇu, Lakṣmī, and Garuḍa.

A description of the manner in which the female ascetic Ariṣṭā established the Buddha-dharma; how she caused the subjects to take pleasure in that dharma and, according to the word of Gaṇeśa, instructed King Divodāsa on the installation of Viṣṇu in the form of a twice-born brahmin; and the description of King Divodāsa’s departure for Kāśīpurī after worshipping the divine sign and ascending his celestial chariot. Furthermore, [the account of] the birth of a daughter from the seed of the sage Ṛcīka, who was pure and whose mind was tranquil, through the agency of a radiant Apsaras. Of her—

The performance of penance by the maiden named Dhūtapāpā at her father’s command; the account of how she attained a special state of purity through the granting of a boon by Śiva; the description of how, upon seeing them, Dharma and Kāma were overcome with passion and, through their mutual union, attained the state of being the lords of the senses; the account of the confluence of the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, and Kaphiṇā with the Dhūtapāpā as the single sacred ford (tīrtha) of the Pañcanada; the narration of its majesty; and therein, the description of the hymn of praise offered to Viṣṇu by Agni, Indra, and the Sun.

A description of the locations of Vidumādhava; a description of the majesty of Bindumādhava; a concise description of Vaiṣṇava sites such as Ādikeśava and Tāpyakeśava; a delineation of the various places and their respective lords as established by Vidumādhava; and a description of how the sage Bindu obtained the splendor of the Sudarśana discus through the discourse on Vidumādhava. Then, following the discourse of Viṣṇu, when [the gods] had entered Kaiṭāsapura, the assembly of Viṣṇu and the others was held in the presence of Hara.

The journey for the purpose of bringing Śivā; the description of the Kapiratīrtha and the account of the manifestation of the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva) at Kapiratīrtha; the description of the penance performed by Jyeṣṭhā and Ṣaṣṭhī; the account of how Śivā attained her husband there, and the narration of the greatness of Umeṣeśa; the vision of Śiva accompanied by his attendants and Ambā by the twice-born who had come from various holy places upon the arrival of Mandra and others, and the description of the excellence of the Kṣetra established by Śiva.

The description of the emergence of Śakti from the body of the Goddess; the narration of the battle between the goddess Durgā and the asura Durga, along with the identification of the names of the powers born from the body of the goddess; the account of the battle between the Daityas and the goddess; the description of the hymn of praise offered by the gods, gratified by the slaying of the Daitya Durga, to goddess Durgā; and the exposition of the fruits of worshipping Durgā and Bhairava.

The counting of the fourteen syllables beginning with *ka* as described by Śiva to Pārvatī; the narration of the origin of Oṃkāreśa, including the account of the hymn of praise to the syllable *ka* composed by Brahmā; the description of the greatness of the Linga of Oṃkāreśa; and the story of the Kṣatriya named Garga—who, having studied the sciences under Bharadvāja and Suvadana during the Pādma-kalpa, became detached from the world and went to the bank of the Revā at Amarakaṇṭaka—where the sage Garga described the majesty of Oṃkāra, which serves as the sole means for warding off the sins accumulated over many births.

And [therein is] the exposition of the division [of the sacred sites], as well as the determination of their majesty. [Therein is] the narration of the greatness of the Śiva-liṅga named Trilocana, which follows the description of the Pārvatī temple situated within the palace adorned with jewels and rubies. [Furthermore,] in the context of describing the majesty of Kedāra, there is the narration of the history of the Ujjainīrītha and the determination of the greatness of the Śiva-liṅga named Dharmeśvara, established by King Udayana.

In this [work], there is a detailed description of the *Tṛtīyā-vrata* known as *Viśvabhujā*, dedicated to the deities Gaurī and Vināyaka, which was ordained by Śiva for the sake of Puṣkaramālā—the daughter of Viṣṇu and wife of Dharmarāja—beginning from the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra and ending on the third day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika; [a description] witnessed by Dharma, Tapas, and Sākṣin, and [performed by] young parrots and śikhaṇḍins.

Upon hearing the words of the Preceptor of the Gods (Bṛhaspati), Indra, tormented by the fear of the sin of Brahman-slaughter, performed penance in the vicinity of the sage Dharmeśa at Kāśī, where the goddess speaks with a northern voice; following the account of the expiation for that Brahman-slaughter, there follows the description of the lineage of King Mitrajit, including the manifestation of the majesty of Lord Vīreśvara, and how King Mitrajit, a great devotee of Viṣṇu, slew the demon Kaṅkāṭa, and [rescued] the daughter of a Vidyādhara named Gandhinī, who had been killed by the demon Kaṅkāṭa.

The marriage by the Gāndharva rite and the arrival [of the prince] with her in Kāśī; regarding the desired Tṛtīyā-vrata, Queen Bhāratī and King Prabhānuśāsana, in accordance with the king’s command, describe the Tṛtīyā-vrata dedicated to the deity Gaurī as prescribed for the queen on the third day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa; through the performance of the vow, the queen’s desire for a son was fulfilled; and when he was born under the Mūla asterism and placed before the goddess Vikaṭādevī by his mother, he was sent near the Māheśvarī and other Mothers by the permission of Riddhidevī. The manifestation of the Śivaliṅga resulting from Bāṣkula’s performance of penance near the goddess Pañcamudrā in Ānandakānana after he was cast away; the attainment of the name Vīreśvara for this very Liṅga and the narration of its majesty; how the Lord Vīreśvara granted various boons to him and described the sequence of holy sites situated at the confluence of the Asi and Gaṅgā, which were established by King Bhṛṅgin’s son, the one named Vīreśvara, beginning with Rīmadādi, Keśava, and ending with the Bhagiratha-tīrtha.

Having established his residence in the Bhānandakānana forest and performed extensive austerities, Durvāsas, due to the absence of fruit, cursed Kāḍī; [this section contains] the description of the manifestation of Śiva’s Liṅga and so forth. Because he fulfilled the desires of Durvāsas, the name Kāmeśvara was given to that Śaivite deity, along with an account of its majesty. Following the description of the name Viśvakarmeśvara for the celestial Liṅga fashioned by Viśvakarman at Kāśī, there is a description of its majesty, preceded by an account of the origin of Dakṣeśvara.

Due to some external circumstance, Dakṣa Prajāpati, an enemy of Śiva, commenced a sacrifice without the two Śivas (Śiva and Pārvatī). Having heard the account of the sacrifice from Nārada, Satī disregarded the words of Śiva and proceeded toward Dakṣa’s sacrifice. There, having heard the censure of Śiva from her father’s mouth, she, being extremely enraged, cast off her body. For the sake of [Śiva’s] welfare, Vīrabhadra, a hero among Śiva’s attendants, performed the destruction of Dakṣa’s head by first causing the ruin of the sacrifice. Then, by Vīrabhadra...

The auspicious liberation of Dakṣa by Śiva after transforming him into the form of a ram; the establishment of a Linga of Śiva at Kāśī and the performance of penance there; the narration of the origin of Dakṣeśvara; the installation of a Linga of Śiva by Pārvatī and the description of its greatness; and the description of the greatness of Gaṅgeśvara, which was installed by Bhagīratha upon his arrival at Viśvanātha Śivalinga.

The granting of a boon by Brahmā, who assumed a form equal to that of Raṅgā, to perform penance at Kāśī after installing a Śiva-liṅga; the description of the greatness of that place following the narration of the boon granted by Nabhodeśvara to Dattātreya; the description of the greatness of the Satīśvara-liṅga established by Satī in Kāśī when she departed for heaven; and the description of the greatness of the Śiva-liṅgas known as Amūrteśvara, Karuṇeśvara, and Jyotīrūpeśvara.

In Kāśī as well, having heard in the forest of Vakākhava that "Mujamūradhavī is to be served by Hari" and "Hāra is to be served by Senya," there is a description of the paralysis of Vyāsa’s tongue caused by Śiva and others. Then, at the instruction of Viṣṇu, Vyāsa desists from the paralysis resulting from the contact with Viṣṇu’s throat and performs a hymn of praise to Śiva. ... [This includes] the account of Vyāsa’s release from the curse, the description of the true nature of Icchārāma and the others, and the narration of the episode of Vyāsa’s expulsion from Kāñcī. ...

The description of all the holy fords (tīrthas) situated within the sacred field that dispels all sins; a detailed account of the great festival of the arrival of Śrī Viśveśvara at Muktimaṇḍapa in Kāśī; the description of the sequence of the final liberation granted by Śrī Viśveśvara—the supreme deity of the Kāśī field—to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and other gods as told by Śrī Agastya; the description of pilgrimages to various holy sites; and the description of the merits of hearing and reciting the Kāśī-khaṇḍa—this is the latter portion of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa.
Thus ends the fourth section, the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. 2.
[The syllables] vi, sa, ka, ni, jā, ki, ka, ra, ka, ca, ka, i, ṭha, ta. [This is] the description of the fruits for men who wear the *vidhivarman* on their bodies.
In the *Bhāgavataskānda Mahāpurāṇa*, the first part, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa.

[Chapter 10]—Oṃ. In the context of the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Vyāsa, the description of the greatness of giving in the Mahākālavana forest, at the feet of Śiva and Gaurī.
Now, in the section on Avanti, first is the majesty of the Avantikṣetra.

The description of the birth of Kalakaṇṭheśvara; the description of the origin of Dānaṅguṇḍa; the description of the greatness of the gift at Hanārānaṅkaṇḍa; the description of the origin and greatness of Apsarastīrtha. First, the hymn to the illustrious Mahākāla deity by the most auspicious Vyāsa; the greatness of Mahākālavana; the description of the greatness of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at that holy site; the description of the greatness of the Apsarakhaṇḍa.
The arrival of Śaunaka near Sanatkumāra; the commencement of the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Vyāsa; therein—

The description of the battle between Śiva and Sanatkumāra at Madākālavana; the account of the defeat of the Rākṣasa named Hāṭāhaṭa, who had assumed the form of a buffalo, by Śiva; the installation of the Liṅga there after Śiva’s victory over the Rākṣasa; the description of the manifestation of Khaṣṭaśuti at the beginning of the Mahiṣakuṇḍa Kalpa; and the account of the origin of the lords Nahnā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, as well as the destruction of the demons by the gods.

The praise of Nambhaṇa; his head was severed into five pieces, and because he bore those skull-bowls (*kapāla*), he is known by the name Kapārī. The description of the majesty of Kauṭumbakeśvara by the gods. ... The installation of the Śiva-liṅga. [Text fragment]. The departure of Vidāḥ, Patavāsava, and Verama. Oṃ. Gamana-bhi.

Taking a garland of *pārijāta* flowers, [Indra] approached the lord of the Vidyādharas, the enemy of Vāsava (Indra). There, at the command of Brahmā, Menakā was sent to Śiva; she adorned herself with earrings made of the blood from the head of Brahmā. By the order of Brahmā, she went to Śiva’s hermitage and offered that garland to him. Seeing Menakā adorned with that garland, Śiva went to the dance-hall. Then Śiva went to the abode of Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu, with his right hand, [bestowed] it upon Śiva.

The granting of the *vidyā* (knowledge) to the *vidyādhara*; the arrival of the lord of the *vidyādharas* in Avantī by the command of Śakra; the battle between the two; the combat between the man born from the sweat of Brahmā and the man born from the mouth of Viṣṇu; the departure of the lord of the *vidyādharas* to his own abode after bathing at that sacred site (*tīrtha*); the description of the majesty of the Vidyādhara-tīrtha; and the description of the prescription of expiatory rites for Brahmā, who had incurred the fault of creating Rākṣasas for the purpose of destroying the sacrifice.

Oṃ. The description of the majesty of Maṇidvīpa; the description of the Rītaka-tīrtha and its sacred power; the account of Sanatkumāra and his discourse on the *Kakāradvāra*; and the description of the Khagadāra-mālya-vana.

The departure of Nara and Nārāyaṇa toward the hermitage of Badarī; their performance of penance for the sake of the welfare of the world; the majesty of that forest situated within the central region between the four oceans; and there, Śaṅkara, being pleased upon seeing King Sumanas, bestowing boons upon Pāda and the others.

Nara and Nārāyaṇa, having arrived there with their wife Sacīcandrāṇī and the sons of Dṛbhya and Marut, attained the fruit of their desired goal through the word of Śiva’s son; Śiva himself resided right there, and at his command, Brahmā and the other gods came to that place.

The narration [of the following]: at the word of Dāruka, Sudurjaya’s departure for Gandhamādana to worship Śiva; his undertaking of austerities on that mountain, beginning with one thousand years and continuing until ten thousand years; at the conclusion of his penance, his departure for Vandyā according to the words of Śiva; the sight of the four oceans in their mortal form through the circumambulation of the four seas; the gods’ performance of praise to Śiva; Śiva’s granting of boons to the gods; and the departure [of the gods] at the word of Śiva.

The granting of boons to the king by the four *Avṛddhis*; the establishment of a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) at that very spot; the establishment of the four oceans; a description of the greatness of the *Kapālamokṣaṇa* Tīrtha; the account of the *Śaṅkara-vāpī* Tīrtha; the worship of the Sun by Divākara and a description of the majesty of Kaṅkārāditya; a description of the power and greatness of Nīḍagandhavī; and a statement regarding the fruits of merit.

In the context of the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Āḍhyā, it is described how ten *aśvamedha* sacrifices were accomplished; furthermore, there is an illustration regarding the attainment of knowledge through the goddess Ekānaṃśā, including Brahmā’s explanation of the means for the destruction of Tāraka, a description of the sacred pilgrimage site (*tīrtha*) of the goddess Ekānaṃśā, and the subduing of the two Daityas, Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, at that location during the time of the divine sports of Śiva and Pārvatī. Also included is the establishment of his own *liṅga* by Śaṅkara under the name Harasiddhi after he had assumed the form of Pārvatī.

In that regard, there is a description of the greatness of Sāna-dānādi (bathing, giving, and so forth) through the performance of *śrāddha* and other rites; a description of [the river] by Manu and others through bathing; the establishment of her by Brahmā when he was afflicted by hunger and despondency; the arrival of the two [sages]; the naming of those two by Pārvatī; the description of the greatness of Vaṭayakṣiṇī resulting from the attainment of their desires; the description of the greatness of Agastyeśvara; and the description of the greatness of Anādikalpeśvara.

Description of the majesty of Śrārati-tīrtha; description of the majesty of Mahāmāyā; description of the majesty of Sakharmadārīthaiyārāma. In the description of the majesty [of that place], following the slaying of Rāvaṇa, the departure of Rāma and the others for Ayodhyā; having gone there, by the command of Vibhīṣaṇa, the installation of the Liṅga on the bank of the lake and the performance of the knowledge-rite (jñānakaraṇa) by Halumat; [description of] the establishment of that very Liṅga there by his command and the description of its majesty; description of the majesty of Kapāṭeśvara at Svaṇajāṭa.

The description of the final consecration of the kingdom by Danu-makki; the arrival in Avanti after taking hold [of the kingdom]; the description of the greatness of the Śivotkaṭa-tīrtha upon seeing the immovability of the Liṅga of the companions; the description of the greatness of Yaneśvara; the description of the greatness of Rudrasakha-śoma; the description of the great pilgrimage of Mahākālī as Khaṃkaṃ went to Lumatā to request the Liṅga; and the description of the greatness of that pilgrimage.

The description of Prince Aniruddha, born to the Kairika queen of the Brahmin named Saṃmati, regarding his abandonment of practice; the description of his repeated encounters with the eight [women]; how, because he was devoid of life-breath and his body was like a corpse, the seven sages arrived and, out of compassion, devised a means for his restoration; how, at their word, he went to the city and asked his retinue about his share in the sin; and then, how his father and others remaining in the house did not accept the experience of the fruit of that sin.

Śrutavān, having felt remorse for his transgression, sought refuge with the great sage and offered prayers; thereafter, through the practice of the mantra bestowed by the great sage, the description of his liberation from sin is given. Then, because she was born from a clump of grass (*valmīka*), the sages gave her the name Vālmīki. Having gone to Kuśasthalī, that Vālmīki propitiated Śiva and established a city in his own name; this is the description of the origin of Vālmīki and the city.

The description of the beauty and greatness of Kāḍabaṇa; the description of the majesty of the deities such as Piṅgala who reside on all sides of Kāḍabaṇa; the description of the great glory of Kṛpāsāgara; the greatness of the pilgrimage to Pañcaśānī; the greatness of Akrūreśvara; the description of the greatness of Brahmakuṇḍa; and the description of the greatness of the Mandākinī Tīrtha.

The description of the place called Aṅkapāda; therein, the narration of the birth of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa; the departure of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, who were intent on giving the teacher’s fee to Sāndīpani; their journey to the Yamaloka after killing the demon Śaṅkha residing in the ocean; their defeat of Yama there and the recovery of Sāndīpani’s son; and the description of the pilgrimage beginning from Mūlasthāna up to the temple of the Lord known as Aṅkapāda in Avantī.

The majesty of Candrādityabhāsa, the majesty of Karabheśvara, the majesty of Gajeśvara, the description of the majesties of Kusumeśvara and Jayeśvara, the description of the majesty of Śivadvāra, the description of the majesty of Mākṣaṇḍayeśvara, the majesty of Bahyeśvara, and the majesty of Bhṛṅgīkuṇḍa.

The majesty of Yajñavāṣī; the description of the majesties of the holy sites (tīrthas) such as Pañcūpatirudrapura, Rūpakuṇḍa, Kedāra, Chaṇḍakarīkuṇḍa, and Ājagaṃpacakra; the description of the majesty of Semavatīśi, Someśvara, and Ṛṅgi; [Chapter] 1–5; [Page] 1–5; [Chapters] 6–9; [Pages] 6–9; [Chapters] 10–12; [Pages] 10–12; [Chapters] 13–15; [Pages] 13–15; [Chapters] 16–18; [Pages] 16–18; [Chapters] 19–21; [Pages] 19–21; [Chapters] 22–24; [Pages] 22–24; [Chapters] 25–27; [Pages] 25–27; [Chapters] 28–30; [Pages] 28–30; [Chapters] 31–33; [Pages] 31–33; [Chapters] 34–36; [Pages] 34–36; [Chapters] 37–39; [Pages] 37–39; [Chapters] 40–42; [Pages] 40–42; [Chapters] 43–45; [Pages] 43–45; [Chapters] 46–48; [Pages] 46–48; [Chapters] 49–51; [Pages] 49–51; [Chapters] 52–54; [Pages] 52–54; [Chapters] 55–57; [Pages] 55–57; [Chapters] 58–60; [Pages] 58–60; [Chapters] 61–63; [Pages] 61–63; [Chapters] 64–66; [Pages] 64–66; [Chapters] 67–69; [Pages] 67–69; [Chapters] 70–72; [Pages] 70–72; [Chapters] 73–75; [Pages] 73–75; [Chapters] 76–78; [Pages] 76–78; [Chapters] 79–81; [Pages] 79–81; [Chapters] 82–84; [Pages] 82–84; [Chapters] 85–87; [Pages] 85–87; [Chapters] 88–90; [Pages] 88–90; [Chapters] 91–93; [Pages] 91–93; [Chapters] 94–96; [Pages] 94–96; [Chapters] 97–99; [Pages] 97–99; [Chapters] 100–102; [Pages] 100–102; [Chapters] 103–105; [Pages] 103–105; [Chapters] 106–108; [Pages] 106–108; [Chapters] 109–111; [Pages] 109–111; [Chapters] 112–114; [Pages] 112–114; [Chapters] 115–117; [Pages] 115–117; [Chapters] 118–120; [Pages] 118–120; [Chapters] 121–123; [Pages] 121–123; [Chapters] 124–126; [Pages] 124–126; [Chapters] 127–129; [Pages] 127–

The description of the Mahākāṅa forest and its great wonders; the narration of the non-attainment of hell by those who have heard [this]; and, within the dialogue between Śiva and Brahmā, the preliminary description of the city named Kaṅkaṅā. 1–6. ||

The greatness of the Anaraka-tīrtha; the description of the offering of lamps and the procedure for placing the vessels for worship therein; the description of the greatness of the Vīta-yata-kuśa-sthalī through the offering of lamps; the description of the attainment of growth in cattle and other blessings; and the description of the greatness of the city named Avanti.

Description of the Greatness of Kedāreśvara Tīrtha: The Jaṭātīrtha, Gaṅgātīrtha, Indratīrtha, and the Kuṇḍa of Kedāreśvara; the Gopītīrtha at Vārāṇasī; and the penance performed by the Asura Tripura upon Brahmā at Ujjayinī, and the granting of boons to him by Brahmā. Description of the greatness of Paṭātīrtha, Jaṭeśvara, and Rāmeśvara; therein, Rāma’s journey with his father Daśaratha and Indra and the other gods, who were oppressed by the Asura Tripura, before Śiva, and the granting of fearlessness to them by Śiva.

The section on the performance of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*); the worship of Cāmuṇḍā at Avantī by Śakra and others during the conjunction of the Saubhāgya-tīrtha, Gharṛta-tīrtha, Yogeśvara-devī, Raṅkhāvata, Sudhodaka, and Sudheśvara; and a description of the great majesty of Panatopattaneśvara, Dūpasthavira-vināyaka, Kāmodaka, and others, following the words of Cāmuṇḍā.

The causes of defeat; therein, because the Dānava Vṛṣaparvan was elevated [to power], the establishment of Kedāraka by Arjuna at the city named Ujjayinī according to the word of Rāma; the paralyzing of the sun by Arjuna at the word of Kṛṣṇa—these are descriptions of well-known events; and the description of the majesty (māhātmya) of Ujjayinī. Va.

The granting of boons by Sūrya to him; the offering of praise by Jañjana; and likewise, by the command of Suyājña, the churning of the ocean to produce the jewel of men (Narasimha), and for the sake of obtaining the nectar (*amṛta*), the establishment of two suns for two days, as well as the description of the majesty of Narāditya; and furthermore, when the gods and demons were dividing the nectar, [Sūrya], assuming the form of Mohinī, appeared before the divine sage (*devarṣi*) while the division was being made.

The composition of the *Suyasta-vastavana*, the description of the majesty of Keśavāditya, and the severing of the head of Rāhu who remained there in disguise; therein, [it describes] the removal of the affliction caused by Rāhu and Ketu.

The description of the birth of Skanda; therein, the emission of semen by Raukara, the prayer for Shiva’s seed by Agni, and the arrival at the sacred ford (tīrtha); the description of the greatness of Rāhutīrtha; the arrival at Ratnakuṇḍa; the casting of the seed into the Gaṅgā; the account of how that seed entered the wombs of the six Kṛttikās who had come there after bathing, and the subsequent narrative of the city named Padyāvatī; then the birth of Skanda, and the description of the majesty of Raktibhada-tīrtha.

And [there is] a description of the splendor of the city of Kumudvatī; a description of the majesty of the nature of Kumudvatī; a description of the majesty of Agastyeśvara... in the description of Mahākālavana, a description of the Nandana forest; a description of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu); the account of the city named Amarāvatī; a description of the sacred fords (tīrtha) preceded by the citation of the names of various liṅgas situated in each Kalpa; and a description of the time of the battle with the demon Andhaka. ... ||
Dhara.
The description of the majesty of Naradīp Tīrtha established by Śiva; the description of the majesty of the city named Viśālā. —... (Ra)

— A description of the majesty of Oṃkāreśvara; the majesty of Abhayeśvara and Ākhaṅga; and a description of the rules regarding the duration of time, beginning from the commencement of the Aṅgārakī-caturthī vow up until the end of eighty-four kalpas.

The description of the true nature [of Śiva]; the journey of Śiva, who wears the crescent moon on his head, to Vaikuṇṭha for the purpose of begging alms; at the time of giving the alms, the description of the Andhaka Asura—who could not endure the humiliation caused by the Goddess Caṇḍī—performing a hymn of praise to Śiva; when Śiva struck him there with the tip of his trident, the emergence of the entire host of weapons from Viṣṇu’s finger; and the establishment of Cāmuṇḍā and the other Mothers within that very stream [of weapons].

Description of the ritual for worshipping Mātṛkā; the account of how Andhaka was transformed into the form of a river and became famous by the name Śiprā; the description of the battle between Bāṇa and Kṛṣṇa, including the narrative of his attainment of the status of a Gaṇa; the dispatching of messengers by Śiva and Viṣṇu to one another during their mutual combat; the defeat of Raivata in the conflict between the devotees of Śiva and the devotees of Viṣṇu; and the description of that place becoming famous by the name Varanīti.

Description of the Greatness of Jvaraghna Tīrtha: In the context of describing Pāpanāśinī Tīrtha, King Damanaka, a practitioner of unrighteousness, goes into the forest for the sake of hunting; having tied his horse to a banyan tree, he leaves the king right there, whereupon a serpent falls upon the king's head, and while the king is tormented by the serpent, the messengers of Yama arrive at that spot.

Then, at the time of his torment by Yama, when the king had gone to the realm of Yama, the flesh of that [king's] body, smeared with soot, fell into the Śiprā; by that merit, Damanaka went to the world of Śiva. In the assembly of Yama and Yama’s attendants, the majesty of the Śiprā was described. Bhikṣāṭana went to the world of the Nāgas; because of the absence of alms-food there, he consumed the water from the twenty-one ponds situated there which had been brought by the terrified serpents, and all the serpents went to the Śiprā.

The performance of the hymn of praise to Śiva; then, by him being pleased, the establishment of the Amṛtoda (Nectar-Ocean) tank there; the description of the greatness of Bhāratī; Indra and the other gods, oppressed by Hiraṇyākṣa, going to the celestial realm and relating the entire account to Brahmā; Brahmā’s narration to the gods of the cause of the curse upon Jaya and Vijaya; the description of the birth and deeds of Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu; the description of the descent as a Boar for the slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa; [and] from the body of the Boar...

The description of the origin of the Dīprā; the description of the beauty of the river Riprā; the description of the majesty of the Riprā; the description of the majesty of the Sundara-tīrtha within Mahākālavana; and therein, the narration of the story of Devaladdhija.

Description of the majesty of the Nīkhagaṅgā; the performance of penance by Agastya on the Vindhya mountains for the purpose of uplifting the land submerged in the waters of the Revā; the departure of Vindhyavāsinī, who was pleased by that penance, to Ujjayinī; description of the majesty of the [river] flowing from the Vindhya-dweller’s displeasure; description of the majesty of the Māndhātṛkṣetra-sadrasa-roma; and within the description of the Kṣātā-saṅgama-tīrtha, the account of the birth of Yama and Yamunā following the dispute between Sūrya and Anasūyā.

The Greatness of the Kṣātasaṅgama Tīrtha (Chapter 1). The Description of the Greatness of the Pitṛca-mocana Tīrtha (Chapters 2–6). The Description of the Greatness of the Gayā Tīrtha: therein, within the praise of the Gayā Tīrtha, the departure of the gods, who were oppressed by the Rākṣasa Tuṇḍa, to the abode of Brahmā; the journey of Brahmā and the others to the world of Viṣṇu and the performance of a hymn of praise to Viṣṇu; and, with the permission of Viṣṇu, the departure of them all to the Gayā Tīrtha. The Gayā Tīrtha.

The description of the greatness of the Gayā-kṣetra river, including the *Sāmānyavidhāna-pūta-vraka-śrāddha-krama-māhātmya*; the greatness of the fruits of bathing and giving gifts at the various holy sites (*tīrthas*) such as Ādi-gayā, Buddhagayā, Svapnupada-gayā, Kāṣṭhagadādharavedikā, Aśvayavara-pratimukti-karīri, and Ācchoda; therein, within the dialogue between the sage Pañcacūḍā and Nārada, the description of the greatness of the Pañcamī-vrata by Nārada; and the description of the greatness of Puruṣottama, occurring in the context of the dialogue between Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.

The description of the taking up of the *malamāsa* (intercalary month); the exposition of the rules and ordinances for the *vrata* and other rites during the intercalary month; the description of the greatness of bathing and giving gifts during the *māṅgalya-māsa* (auspicious month); the procedure for the worship of Puruṣottama and its greatness, beginning with the residence at Mahākālavana during the intercalary month; the greatness of the Jaṭeśvara-Maheśvara Tīrtha; the greatness of the Bhāgīrathī Tīrtha; the greatness of the Kārikī River; the description of the greatness of bathing, giving gifts, and so forth during the intercalary month; the greatness of Gomatīkuṇḍa; and the greatness of Kāṭā.

A description of the attainment of the fruits of merit through bathing and other rites at Gomatīkuṇḍa; a description of Kanthaḍeśvara, Lagartā-saṅgama, Vīreśvara, Vāmanatīrtha, and Māhalya; therein, the distress of Bali [upon being cast into the netherworld] and his departure to the world of the gods to report the account of his own situation; the statement by Brahmā regarding the means for the propitiation of Viṣṇu; and within that context, during the course of a dialogue between Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods, the narration of the thousand names of Viṣṇu.

Along with the narration of the account of hearing the fruits of one's name, the description of the greatness of the events concerning the establishment of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) such as the Vāmana incarnation, the description of the holy sites of Kāverīśvara and Airāvata, and therein the recitation of the eight verses of Bharadvāja; — in the section on the Nāgākhyatīrtha, the narrative of Janamejaya the believer, preceded by the description of the greatness of the sight of the nine sacrificial pits (navakuṇḍa), and the greatness of the Ramāsaras Tīrtha. . . sa.
Following the description of the account of his birth as a householder, [in] the first section of Avantī within the Avanti-khaṇḍa, [is] the highly meritorious sacred field of Avantī.

Now begins the introduction to the greatness of the eighty-four *gamās*, starting with the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara; therein is the description of the greatness of the Pradhāna-Pranrāsya *caraṅaga*, followed by an account of ancient history in connection with that. Therein, for the sake of attaining happiness, Kaṃbhayoni killed the Daityas; subsequently, fearing the sin of slaughter due to his remorse, he performed worship of Īśvara, and by Śiva’s command, established a *liṅga* of Śiva under his own name. Now follows the description of the greatness of that Agastyeśvara *liṅga*.

A description of the greatness of the Guheśvara Liṅga: there, after Maṅkaṇaka had performed austerities as a student (brahmacārī), at a certain time, having attained a miracle by swallowing a ladleful of vegetable juice (śākarasa) from his hand, he caused all beings to dance; seeing this dancing of all things, both mobile and immobile, the gods departed for the heavenly world; then, by divine grace, the pride of that Maṅkaṇaka was removed; by the command of Śiva, the installation of the liṅga at Mahākālavana was performed; and a description of how Maṅkaṇaka attained liberation.

The description of the majesty of Gudeśvara; then the description of the majesty of Duṇḍhi. In that regard, the journey of the Gaṇa named Duṇḍhi to the assembly of Indra; there, the granting of a boon by Indra to Duṇḍhi, who was filled with lust upon seeing Rambhā being teased; then his birth as a human. Now, in the Avanti-khaṇḍa, the second [section]: the majesty of the eighty-four Liṅgas situated in Avanti.
(-) || [End of section] ||

Chapters and Subjects: Description of the greatness of Kaḍaṭumbi; description of the penance and worship of the ten great gods and others; description of the greatness of Devaprabhāga Tīrtha; the greatness of Ānandabhairava Tīrtha; in the description of Akhaṇḍeśvara Tīrtha, the account of how even the great sinner Jahmadatta attained the world of Śiva upon dying there; and, in the context of the dialogue between Nārada and Brahmā, the description of the greatness of Akhaṇḍasara Tīrtha.

The majesty of the Karkarāja-tīrtha; the description of the Vidhūmrārcis-tīrtha; the description of the Cāturmāsya-vrata; the majesty of the Bindusaras and Ramyasaras-tīrthas; the sequential enumeration of names preceded by a calculation of the number of tīrthas; the mention of the sequence of the pilgrimage (tīrthayātrā) beginning with the Devayātrā; the description of the majesty of the Avarantī-kṣetra and the hearing of its sacred verses (śruti); and the conclusion of the work.
Bha: The sixth chapter: The establishment of the Liṅga by King Jada Kaki through the propitiation of Mahākālavana; and the description of the greatness of the Duṇḍeśvara Tīrtha.

Now follows the description of the majesty of Ḍamarukeśvara: therein, the defeat in battle of Indra and the other gods led by Rāghava at the hands of the Daitya Vajra, the son of Ruru; the departure to the world of Brahmā of those gods; the description of the battle between Vajra and the maiden Sakandhakā, who emerged from the body of Brahmā; the description of the humiliation of Vajra after his purpose had been thwarted; the performance of worship to Īśvara by Śruti and others; the description of the battle between Īśvara and Vajra; and the destruction of Vajra by means of the *ḍamaru* drum wielded by Īśvara.

Then, there is the establishment of the shrine of Ḍamarukeśvara and a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Umāruka. Next, a description of the majesty of Anādikalpeśvara; then, a description of the majesty of Svarṇajaḍeśvara. Therein is the account of how Śaṅkara, while sporting with Pārvatī, was pursued by the fire of his own seed, and for the sake of quelling that fire, he caused it to be cast into the Gaṅgā. Subsequently, by the sight of the first offspring named Kāñcana, everywhere...

The trembling of the earth; seeing that, Vahni’s presentation of Kāñcana’s son to Śaṅkara; by the command of Śaṅkara, Kāñcana’s departure to the Mahākāra forest; Kāñcana performing austerities and, at the word of Īśvara, the establishment of the Svana mountain; and the description of the greatness of Svarṇajākhaścaraṅiga.

[1.1] Now, the description of the greatness of Triviṣṭapeśvara-Ṛṣiga; therein, the establishment of Triviṣṭapeśvara-Ṛṣiga at Mahākāvana according to the words of Nārada; the description of the greatness of Triviṣṭapeśvara-Ṛṣiga; then, the description of the greatness of Kapāleśvara-Ṛṣiga; therein, at the Great Horse Sacrifice (Aśvamedha) in Mahākāvana, Śaṅkara’s arrival while holding a skull in his hand; the Brahmins’ showing of contempt upon seeing Śaṅkara’s appearance with a skull; and thereafter, by Śiva, in that sacrificial pavilion—

Having placed the door-panel [there], he departed; then, having thrown the door-panel from outside the maṇḍapa of the Nīlakaṇṭha [shrine], he gave a gift of more than a thousand cows. Having seen that miracle, the Nīlakaṇṭhas performed a hymn of praise with joy. He installed a liṅga under the name Kapāṭeśvara. By the greatness of the Kapāṭeśvara-liṅga, there is described the destruction of great sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and the avoidance of hell. Thus ends the section.

a. Oṃ. Dha. Da Ṣka Kā Jana -----na----- ---: Ja Ka Aiḥ Bha Kke Va Ka Dda Ka Nā Jo Ma Ka Ka Ka Vada Ka Kaka Ka Vdkaḥ. The objects of the senses. Now follows the description of the Svargadvāra-liṅga-maṣṭha-samyavarṇana (the detailed description of the Svargadvāra-liṅga). Therein is the description of the battle between the divine hosts led by Vīrabhadra and others, on the one hand, and Viṣṇu and the other gods, on the other, following Śiva’s command after he had been insulted by Dakṣa during the sacrifice of Dakṣa. In that [battle], there is the defeat of Viṣṇu and the other gods, and the [triumph of the] Rudra-host.

The establishment of the Svargadvāra [gate]; the gods, having observed the absence of the lord of heaven (Indra), going to the Mahākālavana forest for the worship of Śiva by the command of Viṣṇu; the installation there of the *daṇḍī* named Svargadvāra; the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Svargadvāra; then the description of the majesty of Karkoṭakeśvara; and therein, the performance of penance by the Nāga Karkoṭaka in the Mahākālavana forest for the sake of destroying the sin incurred from killing his mother; and [the granting of boons] to him by Śiva, who was pleased by that penance.

The granting of boons; the installation of the *digambara* [ascetic] named Śiva under his own name; the description of the majesty of Karkoṭakeśvara; then the description of the origin and majesty of Siddheśvara-liṅga; therein, the departure for the Mahākāṭavana forest after hearing a divine voice from the Devadāruvana while performing austerities for the sake of attaining perfection (*siddhi*); having performed penance there, the attainment of perfection and the installation of the liṅga; the description of the majesty of Siddheśvara-digambara; then the description of the majesty of the Chokapāṭara-vara-liṅga; therein—

From the presence of Hiraṇyakaśipu, he (Viṣṇu), having become subject to fear due to the world-guardians (*lokapālas*), went to the Mahākālavana forest for the performance of penance by the command of Viṣṇu; by the power of his penance, having destroyed the Daityas, he returned to his own abode. He established the quarters in the Mahākālavana forest under the name Lokapāleśvara. Then follows the description of the majesty of the deity Lokapāleśvara, and therein the narration of the greatness of Kāmeśvara; there, Brahmā, for the sake of obtaining a wife, produced Kāma and [established] his twelve locations.

The dispatching of Kāma to ignite passion in heaven; the reduction of Kāma to ashes by Śiva for his interference with his own asceticism; Rati’s making her home there upon learning that her husband had been consumed; then, at the command of Śiva, Kāma’s departure to the Mahākālavana forest having become bodiless (anaṅga); his performing penance there and the installation of a Liṅga; and the description of the majesty of Kāmeśvarī...

Now begins the description of the great and beautiful holy site of Ṅuṭambakeśvara. There, when the Kālakūṭa poison emerged from the churning of the Ocean of Milk, Śaṅkara, unable to endure the burning heat arising from it, gave that Kālakūṭa to the Śiprā. Having received it, the Śiprā went to the Mahākāvana forest; and by the Śiprā, on the bank of the river near Kāmeśvara, [the shrine was established]. Chapter 50. Section 3. Dha.

Next, the description of the greatness of the Kaṭhkaṭeda Varaliṅga: therein, during the occasion of the dispute between Umā and Maheśvara, when the three worlds were shaken, the depositing of that Kālakūṭa poison; the description of the imminent death of the Brāhmaṇas who had come to the Lord of the Eye (Śiva) due to the discharge of the Kālakūṭa poison; the reviving of the Brāhmaṇas by Śiva after he arrived there; the naming of the Liṅga as Kuṭumbakeśvara by Śiva; and the description of the greatness of the Kuṭumbakeśvara Liṅga.

Now follows the description of the greatness of Indreśvara Tīrtha. Therein is the account of how Indra, due to the loss of his merit, fell from heaven; and how, out of remorse, he performed penance on the Himavat mountain, where Mārkaṇḍeya took him and, by his command, went to Mahākālavana to perform the worship of the Liṅga of Śiva. Having established undecaying fame there, he installed a Liṅga in his own name. This is the description of the greatness of Indreśvara Tīrtha. Now follows the description of the greatness of Īśāneśvara Tīrtha. Therein—

By the command of Śiva, Tuhuṇḍa, the son of Muṇḍa, conquered the gods; having gone to Mahākākha forest, he performed the worship of Śiva. Being pleased, Īśvara bestowed upon that Liṅga the name Īśāneśvara. The gods composed a hymn of praise for Īśāneśvara, and the majesty of Īśāneśvara is described.

Now follows the description of the greatness of the Apsarases' Liṅga. There, having seen Rambhā dancing before Śakra while she was being watched by the other [gods], Śakra, out of anger, pronounced a curse upon Rambhā. To counteract the effect of that curse, at the word of Nārada, she installed a Liṅga under her own name in Mahākālavana; by pleasing Śiva through its constant worship, she obtained a boon from him and returned to her own world. This concludes the description of the greatness of the Apsarases' Liṅga.

Because the sound "kalakaṭa" arose there from a broken potsherd (*sarāvaita*), the manifestation of the *liṅga* occurred; thus, that *liṅga* was given the name Kalakaṇṭha. [This is] the description of the identity of the Karkaṭeśvara *liṅga*. Next, the description of the identity of the Nāgacaṇḍeśvara *liṅga*: regarding the arrival of the gods to the *liṅga* established there by Nāgacaṇḍa, when the fault of excessive attachment (*niḥsaṃsya-raṃghana*) and so forth arose during the worship of that *liṅga*, [the story concerns] that Nāgacaṇḍeśvara *liṅga*.

The installation of the Liṅga in the vicinity; by that, the description of the greatness of Nāgacaṇḍeśvara, which removes the defects of the inhabitants such as poverty and oppression; [End of Chapter] 109.
