[Fragmentary Text] ...the objects [of the senses], then the description of the majesty of Pratihāreśvara Liṅga. Therein, while Umā and Maheśvara were sporting, Nandin, the gatekeeper, remained standing at the door; being unrecognized, he allowed the fire [of Śiva's wrath] to enter the inner apartments. Enraged by this, Śiva pronounced a curse upon Nandin. Having been cursed, Nandin went to the Mahākālavana forest and established a divine image under the name Pratihāreśvara. By his grace...

The departure of Nandin once again for the world of Śiva; the description of the greatness of the excellent *liṅga* at Bhṛtihāra; then the description of the greatness of the *liṅga* at Kukkuṭeśvara. Therein, due to his constant consumption of cocks in a previous birth, King Kaurika experienced the delusion of being a cock every night by virtue of a curse pronounced by Tāmracūḍa. For the sake of destroying that curse, he worshipped the *liṅga* named Pakṣiyonivimocana in the Mahākāṭa forest, whereby his attainment of the state of a cock was brought to an end.

The installation of the Kukkuṭeśvara Liṅga; a description of the majesty of the Kukkuṭeśvara Liṅga; then, a description of the majesty of the Kakaṇṭeśvara [Liṅga]. In that regard, while King Dharmamūrti was desiring to know the cause for the attainment of sovereignty, he questioned Vasiṣṭha, who—upon being asked—[explained] that his attainment of the state of a crow was due to a sin committed by him in a previous birth.

The narration of the account wherein a certain Rāyasena, having seized a female crab, threw it at Śiva; thereafter, at the time of death, by the power of Śivadāsa, he attained sovereignty in this very [world]—this is the description of the greatness of the Karkaṭīśvara Liṅga. Next is the description of the greatness of the Meṣanāda Liṅga, wherein a king named Madāndha performed sacrifices out of wickedness and other such [vices].

Due to the absence of rain caused by the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the gods departed for the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). Then, by the command of Brahmā, the gods went to the Mahākālavana forest. There, they offered praise to the *liṅga* installed by the gods themselves. By worshipping that *liṅga*, the cessation of the drought is described. Consequently, that *liṅga* installed by the clouds was named Meghanādeśvara. Next follows the narration of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the Meghanādeśvara-liṅga; then the narration of the majesty of the Mahālayeśvara-liṅga; and then [the account of] Suktīśa.

The description of the greatness of Raliga: there, at Muktiriga near Mahākāra, while a brahmin named Mukti was meditating upon Nārāyaṇa in the form of Jayodreśvara, a certain hunter suddenly arrived at his hermitage. Upon seeing the brahmin and the holy site (ṭiga), the hunter’s wickedness vanished and he attained a state of auspiciousness; having remained in that place, the hunter performed penance, and through the recitation of the eight-syllable mantra, he attained liberation at that very spot.

The description of the liberation of a certain tiger who had attained [this state] through hearing that mantra; the tiger’s narration of his own previous birth story and the explanation of the cause of his own slaughter; the departure of both the tiger and the liberated Brahmin to the Bhṛgukaccha region; the installation of a linga there; the description of the majesty of Yuktīśvara; then the description of the majesty of Someśvara; and therein, seeing that the Moon had no affection for any of his wives except Rohiṇī, Dakṣa’s bestowal [of a curse] out of anger.

The departure of Soma to the world of truth (Satyaloka) for the sake of removing the curse; his journey with Brahmā to Vaikuṇṭha and the offering of praise to Viṣṇu; by the command of Viṣṇu, Soma’s departure to Mahākāvana and the installation of a linga there; the description of the cessation of Soma’s disease of consumption (yakṣmaroga); the description of the greatness of Someśvara-liṅga.

Next, the description of the greatness of Anarakeśvara, wherein, following a description of the sequence of torments in hell, Nimi goes to the abode of Yama despite his great store of merit due to a slight sin.

Furthermore, upon seeing Anarakeśvara, all his sins were destroyed, and he ascended a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) to travel to the world of Indra. [The text describes] the consolation offered by Nimi to those living beings who were suffering from the pain of undergoing Yama’s tortures; then follows the description of the greatness of the pilgrimage to Anarakeśvara, followed by the description of the greatness of Jaṭeśvara. Therein, preceded by the narration of the story of King Vīradhanvan, the greatness of Jaṭeśvara is described, including the description of the installation of the directions for Jaṭeśvara and so forth. Now...

Description of the greatness of Rāmeśvara-Nigama; therein, having ruled the earth twenty-one times as a Kṣatriya, Paraśurāma, for the sake of removing the sin of Brahmin-slaughter, visited various holy places (*tīrthas*) but finding no cessation of his fault, went at the instruction of Nārada to the presence of Jaṭeśvara in the great forest of Rāma; having performed penance there, he attained the destruction of his sin and established a Liṅga in his own name—this is the description of the greatness of Rāmeśvara-Nigama. Now, Cyavaneśvara.

Description of the greatness of the pilgrimage site (ṅigama-māhātmya); therein, the sage named Cyavana, having chosen the daughter of King Śyāti, performed penance in the Mahākālavana forest and established a Liṅga bearing his own name; description of the greatness of the Cyavaneda-vakhaṭaṇa [site]. Sakāma || 0 ||

The objects [of the senses]. Now, the description of the greatness of the Khaṇḍavara region: therein, the departure of Bhadrādavarāja, son of Bhrīyavrata, for Mahākālavana due to the words of a person of base birth; there, the installation of a linga by Khaṇḍitavrata for the sake of purification; and the description of the great festival of Khaṇḍaśavaraṅiga. Bhi.

Now begins the description of the majesty of the *Pattaneśvara-liṅga*. Then follows the description of the majesty of the *Ānandeśvara-liṅga*: therein, a certain son of Anamitra named Ānana, having gone to the great forest of Kāṭavana for some reason, established a *liṅga* in his own name; this is the description of the majesty of the *Ānandeśvara-liṅga*. Next is the description of the majesty of the *Kaṃthaḍeśvara-liṅga*: therein, a Brahmin named Pāṇḍava performed penance on account of a rag (*kaṃthā*), and established a *liṅga* named Kaṃthā.

Description of the greatness of Caradigama at Kanthaḍa; description of the greatness of Śvarar̤ga; there, due to the fall of his own banner, Kuradhvaja, the son of Brahmā, was struck by an angry Brahmā, who caused him to fall to the ground with his matted locks; from that arose the birth of the demon Vṛtra; then the battle between Vṛtra and Indra, and the defeat of Indra; at the command of Bṛhaspati, Śakra went to Mahākālavana to conquer Vṛtra; having slain Vṛtra through the power of his penance, he went there to remove the sin of that slaughter.

The description of the greatness of the Liṅga-installation at Idara; then the description of the greatness of Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara, including the account of the birth of Mārkaṇḍeya and the installation of a Liṅga by Mārkaṇḍeya under his own name in Mahākālavana, followed by the description of the greatness of the Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara Liṅga. Next, the description of the greatness of the Śiveśvara Liṅga.

Therein is the narration of the story of Ripukshaya; then the excellent description of Śiveśvara; then the description of the greatness of the pilgrimage site of Kusumeśvara, wherein the name "Kusumeśvara" was given because he delighted in playing with flowers; then the description of the greatness of the pilgrimage site of Kusumeśvara; and then the description of the greatness of the pilgrimage site of Ākarūra, wherein Śaṅkara, having established the deity Mahākāla in the forest to destroy his own cruel disposition, performed worship of him; by that, his cruelty—

The cessation of worldly existence; the renown of that hill by the name Akrūreśvara; the description of the majesty of Akrūreśvara-hill; then the description of the majesty of Kuṇḍeśvara-hill; therein, the disappearance during the day of Śiva and Pārvatī while mounted upon their bull due to some cause, and the internal reason for Pārvatī’s sudden vanishing while longing for Śiva; the chapters and topics concerning the bestowing of a curse upon Kagaṇa; and the [narrative] of Kuṇḍa going to Mahākālavana with his companions for the sake of removing that curse.

The installation [of the deity], and the description of the greatness of the *Champeśvara* Liṅga. Now follows the description of the greatness of the *Champeśvara* Liṅga: therein, due to the slaughter of a Sāmaga Brahmin, King Caṇḍarāja was cursed by that man; following the instruction of Nārada, he went to Mahākālavana. There, for the sake of curing his leprosy, he installed the *Champeśvara* Liṅga. Then follows the description of the greatness of the *Saikeśvara* Liṅga, and the description of the greatness of the *Raṅgeśvara* Liṅga. In that regard—

The greatness of the *liṅga* established by Bhagīratha on the bank of the R̥pā at the place called Gaṅkeśvara, where the Gaṅgā descends from the matted locks of Śiva onto the earth; and a description of the greatness of the procedure for worshipping Gaṅkādeva and other rites.

Now follows the description of the greatness of Aṅgārakeśvara; the account of the birth of Aṅgāraka’s son from the body of Śibi; and the description of the greatness of Aṅgārakeśvara. Next follows the description of the greatness of Uttareśvara: therein, the journey of Indra and the other gods, who were afflicted by the planet Rāhu, to the north at the command of Śiva; the installation of the Śivaliṅga performed by Uttara Medha; and the description of the greatness of Uttareśvara.

Now follows the description of the greatness of the Trilocaneśvara-liṅga; then the description of the greatness of the Vīreśvara-liṅga; then the description of the greatness of the Nṛpureśvara-liṅga; then the description of the greatness of the Abhayeśvara-liṅga; then the description of the greatness of the Prathakeśvara-liṅga; then the description of the greatness of the Sthāvareśvara-liṅga; then the description of the greatness of the Śūleśvara-liṅga, wherein there was the destruction of the demon Aghakāñjura by the Lord.

Having established the *śūla-liṅga*, there is a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Śeṣvariga. [Then follows] the description of the majesty of the *Athokāreśvara-liṅga*. Therein is the description of the majesty of the *Athokāreśvara-liṅga* installed by the sage Athokāra at the bidding of Śiva, who had manifested in a human form. [Then follows] the description of the majesty of the *Viśveśvara-liṅga*. Therein, King Vidūratha, having taken twelve births due to the sin born of killing a Brahmin, assumes the state of a *caṇḍāla* in his thirteenth birth.

Having reached the presence of Śiva and received various instructions, there is a description of his subsequent birth as a king; remembering [his past] in a great forest, he established a *liṅga*, followed by a description of the greatness of the Viśveśvara-liṅga (then follows a description of the greatness of the Kaṇṭheśvara-liṅga, wherein a certain king, defeated by his enemies, [sought refuge with] Vasiṣṭha).

The journey to the hermitage; at his word, the king went to Mahākārvaṇa and performed worship after establishing the *Ṛgveda*; through that, he attained a kingdom free of thorns, from which the fame of that *Śaṅkha* as Kaṇṭeśvara arose; a description of the greatness of the pilgrimage site of Kaṇṭeśvara; then, a description of the greatness of the pilgrimage site of Siṃheśvara; there, while Mauryā was performing penance for the sake of attaining Śiva, Brahmā arrived; by the word of Brahmā, from the mouth of the goddess Karandhā—

The birth of the lion and its nourishment, the description of the two lions emerging from the breasts of the Goddess; by the command of Pārvatī, the lion’s departure for the Mahākālavana forest and the account of his attainment of the status of Śiva’s vehicle; the establishment of a Liṅga by that lion with his own name, namely Siṃheśvara-liṅga; then the description of the majesty of Revanteśvara-liṅga; there, having installed a deity, Revata—the son of Sūrya—went to Kāśī; and by the word of Śiva, having arrived at Mahākālavana, [he established it] there under his own name.

The destruction of Nārada’s ignorance through the grace of Sāvitrī; Sāvitrī’s narration of her own life story when questioned by him out of wonder at that miracle; Nārada’s attainment of steadfastness in proceeding to Prayāga upon Sāvitrī’s words; Priyavrata’s description of the greatness of the pilgrimage to the Lord of Mātagā; the installation of the Liṅga by Mataṅga, the son of the Brahmin Sugati; and Nārada’s journey to Prayāga in Avantī along with Mataṅga, where he established the Liṅga and performed its worship.

A description of the greatness of Prayāgeśvara-Ṛṅgi... [and] a description of the greatness of Siddheśvara-Ṛṅgi; therein, the appearance of the great sages Jaigīṣavya and Kapila before King Aśvaśiras; the king’s taking refuge in wonder at the true nature of the Lord as revealed by the illusory power (*māyā*) displayed by those two; and, by their command, that king’s going to the Mahākāṭa forest to perform the worship of the *liṅga* after attaining perfection—a description of the greatness of Siddheśvara-liṅga.

The worship [of the Liṅga], and the description of the greatness of the Matageśvara Liṅga. Now follows the description of the greatness of Saubhāgyeśvara: therein, the wife of King Aśvavāhana, being deeply distressed by separation from her husband, worships the Lord of the Mountain (Himavat) according to the instructions of Samatī with the desire to recover her husband; through the success of that [worship], her husband returns, and she attains good fortune; this is the description of the greatness of the Saubhāgyeśvara Liṅga.

Now follows the description of the majesty of Rūpeśvara. In that regard, there is the account of King Padma’s journey to the hermitage of Kaṇva; there, being infatuated by desire, he gave his daughter to the sage Kaṇva and committed adultery with her. When Kaṇva perceived this with his eye of knowledge, he inflicted upon them both the punishment of having their thighs transformed into those of animals. Subsequently, at the command of Kaṇva, they went to the Mahākālavana forest. There, through the worship of the *liṅga*, the description of the restoration of their own original forms is given. This concludes the description of the origin and majesty of the Rūpeśvara *liṅga*.

Now follows the description of the majesty of the Dhanuḥsāhasreśvara Liṅga: therein, the abduction of King Vidūratha’s daughter by the demon Kumbha; thereafter, his battle with the two sons of Vidūratha; and when King Vidūratha, having learned of the defeat and captivity of his two sons, went to Mahākālavana at the request of the sages to perform the worship of the quarters for the sake of their victory; and through the power of that worship, his [Dhanuḥsāhasra-].

The attainment of the bow by Tuṣita; the defeat of the Daitya by means of that prowess in archery; the description of the king—along with his sons, daughters, and others—attaining liberation at the end after reaching Śukla; the description of the greatness of the Dhanuḥsāhasreśvara Liṅga and its worship; the description of the greatness of the Paḍupati Liṅga; then the description of the greatness of the Braddhavarkhi Liṅga; and therein, the departure of the Daitya Pukhoma to Śīrāśca with his own army in order to conquer Viṣṇu.

Then follows the departure of Brahmā to the Mahākālavana forest for the purpose of conquering the Daityas; there, the description of his penance and how Śiva, being pleased, brought about the defeat of the Daityas; the establishment of a *liṅga* by Brahmā under his own name and the description of the majesty of that *Brahmahṛdaya-liṅga*. Next is the description of the majesty of Jvālēśvara, where King Jalpa, having established his five sons in the kingdom, departed for the forest, and thereafter [the account of] the mutual discord among his kinsmen.

Having learned that his five sons were dead, King Jaṣpa, distressed by their separation, went to the Mahyaka forest at the command of Vasiṣṭha; there he established a *liṅga* in his own name, and the majesty of that excellent *liṅga* of Jaṣpa is described. Next, the majesty of Kedāreśvara is described: the gods, including Brahmā, went to Kedāra while afflicted by cold; having meditated upon Śiva, they proceeded to Kedāreśvara in that direction, and the cessation of the affliction from the cold through the power of that merit is described, as well as the majesty of the pilgrimage site of Kedāreśvara.

Then follows the description of the greatness of the *piśāceśvara-liṅga*; the description of the wicked conduct and extreme cruelty of the deity named Soma; therein, the narration of the dialogue between the *piśāca* Rākaṭāyana and a Brāhmaṇa; the departure for the Madākāṭa forest by one who had attained liberation from the state of a *piśāca* through the words of Śākayāyana; there, having worshipped the goat, the Lord of the Earth brought about the liberation of that *piśāca*; the description of the greatness of the *piśāceśvara-liṅga*; and then, the description of the greatness of the *saṅgameśvara-liṅga*.

Therein is the narration of the story of the previous births of Pannī, Subāhu, and Vacanā; then follows the description of the attainment of liberation by Saṅgameśvara at the conclusion of his reign; the glorification of the greatness of the Saṅgameśvara-varamaṇḍapa; and then the description of the greatness of the Eraṭaga mountain, which is difficult to behold.

The departure of King Duḥṣanta to the forest for hunting; there, having given his daughter to the sage named Kaśyapa, he performed sacrifices together with her in that place. Then follows the description of the greatness of the Paśupatīśvara Liṅga, wherein King Paṇḍu established [the deity]; through the worship of Śiva in the Mahākāla forest, he attained sovereignty, and after the enjoyment of all pleasures, he attained liberation at the end.

The description of the eighth day of the lunar fortnight dedicated to Udakśavaraliṅga. Next, the description of the greatness of the eighth day of the lunar fortnight dedicated to Prayāgeśvara. Therein, the attainment of liberation from human birth by Śotanu through penance, his journey to Prayāgeśvara upon hearing the words of Nārada, the removal of sins through the worship of Śiva, and the description of the greatness of the eighth day of the lunar fortnight dedicated to Prayāgeśvara.

Now follows the description of the greatness of Candrādityeśvara; the journey of the two [Candra and Āditya] to Yoruṭha; by the command of Viṣṇu, their arrival at Mahākārvaṇa, and the account of how they brought about the defeat of Śambara by means of that light; there, having seen the gods defeated by Śambara, Candra and Sūrya went and performed worship of Śiva; the departure of Candrādityeśvara from Śivigata; and the death of the camel belonging to King Vīraketu in the great forest while he had gone out on a hunt.

Then, by the command of someone, there is a description of how Mahākāla attained the state of Dailāsa; next, a description of the greatness of the Karabheśvara limb. Then follows a description of the greatness of the Daivara-linga at Rājasthala, where King Puñjaya, having performed a sacrifice for his son and having dispelled the curse of a woman, went to the Mahākāra forest, worshipped Śiva, and through His grace, [attained his goal]. Then, for the sake of victory, the king gave a gift to the Karabheśvara-pañcaga-sāhasra.

[This section contains] a description of the means for bringing happiness to the people who were terrified by droughts, floods, and other calamities; a description of the lineage of the lords of the royal lineages... Then follows the glorification of the greatness of Vaḍaṭeśvara: therein, [the account of] Maṇibhadra, known as Vaḍaṭa, going with his wife to play; there, the battle of Vaḍaṭa with the Rākṣasas who were guardians of Kror̤avana; therein, the defeat of the Rākṣasas; and then, [the account of] [Maṇibhadra] being enraged by the actions of his own son.

The Yakṣa Maṇibhadra’s bestowing of a curse upon Vaḍala; Vaḍala’s journey to the Mahākālavana forest for the sake of removing that curse; the description of his attainment of liberation there; and the description of the greatness of the Vaḍaleśvara Liṅga and the necessity of visiting it.

The contents [of this section] are as follows: a detailed description of Aruṇa, the son of Vinatā born from the egg, who, having gone to Mahākālavana upon the instruction of Nārada, attained the greatness of Aruṇeśvara through the worship of Śiva; then, a description of the greatness of the deity Puṣpadanta, wherein it is told how a twice-born man named Śini, desiring to obtain a son, performed the propitiation of Lord Īśvara, and by His grace, a son named Puṣpadanta was born to him; and [finally], [the account of] Puṣpadanta in Mahākālavana.

The installation of the Śivāṅga; the description of the greatness of the Puṣpadanta-liṅga. Then, at the request of King Citrasena’s daughter, Kanyakā, his arrival at Avimukta; the description of his attainment of liberation through the worship of the Śivaliṅga there, and the description of the majesty of the Avimukteśvara-liṅga. Next, the description of the majesty of the Hanumatkedāra-liṅga; therein, preceded by a description of the Hanumat-rākhī festival, the account of Hanumān’s attainment of boons through the worship of the directions (dig-pūjana).

After the slaying of Rāvaṇa and following the consecration of Rāma’s kingdom, when a certain brahmin insulted Hanumān during a description of Hanumān’s glories, Hanumān went to the Mahākālavana forest and gathered his disciples. Then follows the description of the majesty of Hanumān Kedāra; then the description of the majesty of Skandaraṅga; therein, preceded by the narrative of Kalmāṣapāda, the description of the account of the Śvetaśvara who destroys bad dreams; and then the description of the majesty of Svataṭeśvara. Now...

The description of the majesty of Pigaṭheśvara; therein, the description of the four Liṅgas situated in the four directions; therein, the account of how a daughter of Piṅga named Piṅgā, distressed for her father and mother, having recalled the evil deeds committed in a previous birth, went with the permission of her husband to the Mahākāṭa forest; and having gone there, the installation of a Liṅga by her own name, followed by the description of the majesty of Pigaḷeśvara.

And *ṣaḥ*. Now begins the description of the greatness of Kāyāvarohaṇeśvara. Therein, at the time of the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, Dakṣa and the others, having been defeated by Vīramadra, Bhadrakālī, and others, went to the Mahākālavana forest. By worshipping Śiva there, they were released from their bodily confinement; thus the name Kāyāvarohaṇeśvara was established for him. [This concludes] the description of the greatness of Kāyāvarohaṇeśvara. ... .

(Va Śada Atha: Description of the Greatness of the Liṅga of Viśveśvara; therein, the attainment of invincibility by Kapila through the propitiation of Śiva, and likewise the attainment of invincibility by the Naga Cilva through the propitiation of Viṣṇu. Furthermore, the making of a request for boons by Cilva, saying: "Act in such a way that when I speak to Kapila, 'I am afraid of you,' he might say, 'I do not fear you,' and so forth. Then, having said "So be it," Viṣṇu granted the boon. And in order to make his own gift of the boon true, Viṣṇu [addressed] Kapila... [requesting a boon].)

Chapter 10: Description of the greatness of the Caturaṅgī River situated in Avanti, as told by the maiden who had returned after being remembered during her act of remembrance; [this concludes] the Āvantya-khaṇḍa. Now begins the third section, the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the Āvantya-khaṇḍa.

In the context of the dialogue between Uñchavṛtti and Mārkaṇḍeya, during the time of the forest exile when the Pāṇḍavas had gone forth on their journey, there is the description of their arrival in the territory of King Vindhya; the description of the battle of Kṛṣṇa with Kapila, who was disregarding his own words; the defeat of Kṛṣṇa therein; then, by the command of Śakra, King Vilva propitiated Viśveśvara and made a verbal agreement with Kapila through the latter’s mouth, saying, "I am afraid of you"; and finally, the description of the majesty of Vilveśvara.

Now follows the description of the majesty of the Liṅga of Ujjayinī. Therein is the journey of Parīkṣit, the ruler of Ayodhyā, to the forest of Gayā; there, he engages in conversation with a certain maiden through a series of questions and answers. While the king is sporting with her after taking her [with him], she enters a pond and goes to the netherworld (*pātāla*). Parīkṣit falls into grief. By the command of Parīkṣit, the chief ministers and others carry out the killing of the frogs. Then, by means of one old frog...

The description of the attainment of the Dadhīra-tīrtha, preceded by the narration of the story of his own previous birth; the handing over of Dadhīra to Parīkṣit from afar; the cessation of Dadhīra’s suffering through the worship of Uttaresvara; the description of the majesty of the pilgrimage to Uttaresvara; and the concluding description of the majesty of the pilgrimage to Sthitacaturmukha. Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter on the majesty [of the Liṅgas] in the Āvantya-khaṇḍa.

The auspicious invocation; the description of the Revā river; the introduction of the dialogue between Sūta and the Ṛṣis, including a description of the preeminence of those who know the Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstras, and the Ātman; the enumeration and naming of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas and Upapurāṇas; the description of the fruits of hearing the Purāṇas; the journey toward Prabhāsa; therein, the arrival at the hermitage of Mārkaṇḍeya situated in the Vindhya forest; and the discourse by Dharmarāja (Yama) regarding the majesty of sacred fords, holy sites, and other matters to Mārkaṇḍeya, who was performing his meditations.

Description of Bandhiprabhra; by Mārkaṇḍeya, description of the majesty of holy places (tīrthas) such as the Gaṅgā; description of the majesty of the Revā, which is even greater than that. [End of] Chapter 6. Subjects of Chapter 7: By Mārkaṇḍeya, in describing his own life story, description of the state of existence at the time of universal dissolution (pralaya); while wandering in the forest, the fruit of studying and reciting the Vedas on the bank of the Narmadā; regarding the Narmadā—
The fruit of giving food, charity, recitation, burnt offerings, oblations, and so forth; the arrival of a certain woman in a boat upon the sky; and the meeting of Mārkaṇḍeya with Manu.

The fruit of the merit of giving; the description of the attainment of all perfections (*siddhis*) and other desires through residing on the banks of the Narmadā; the boarding of the boat; the description by Mārkaṇḍeya of the hymn of praise to the Blessed One; the description of the fruits of daily rites such as the application of holy ash (*bhasma*) on the banks of the Narmadā; the statement that the Narmadā is superior even to all [other rivers]; Mārkaṇḍeya’s vision of Mahādeva situated on the peak of Trikuṭa; and the account of the origin of the Narmadā within the narration of Abhakṣa’s history.

The narration [of the story]; the description of the inconceivability of the Narmadā due to the grace of Śaṅkara; the offering of the fifteen names of the Narmadā and the composition of a hymn to the Narmadā on her banks by Sūtapañcaka;

the description of the twenty-one Kalpas according to their respective names; within those Kalpas, the description of the seven Kalpas in the context of the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Mārkaṇḍeya; and the description of the locations and stations of the Narmadā throughout the extent of all the Kalpas.

Then, Yudhiṣṭhira’s description of the Narmadā-māhātmya to Mārkaṇḍeya with the intent of seeking its greatness; the narration of the destruction of the Kālarātri created by Kaṅka; the discourse by Mārkaṇḍeya on the majesty of the Narmadā, wherein first the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of the name "Narmadā" is described.

The description of the gathering of the gods who had been scorched by the heat of the wind at the time of the *saṃvarta* (universal dissolution); the account of the conversation between Mahādeva in the form of a peacock and the river Narmadā; the offering of the inexhaustible *kālarātri* (the night of destruction) by Śiva to the gods led by Brahmā, who were terrified; the arrival of the gods led by Viṣṇu; and the description of the origin of the rivers Narmadā and Gaṅgā from the crevice in the peak of Mount Śikhara.

The description of the burning of Carikūṭa by Brahmā; the description of Badarāyaṇa performing a hymn of praise to Śiva; the description of the origin of the mountains along with their peaks from the third summit of Mount Bhṛgutuṅga; the description of the name of the Narmadā river together with its cause; the description of the scorching heat of the Sun at the time of the dissolution (saṃvarta); the description of the agitation of the five great elements; the destruction of the world; and the description of the emergence of the Nandīśvara mountain and others at the end of one kalpa.

The drying up of the four oceans; the description of the earth being scorched by the falling of torrents of rain measured by the trunk of the elephant Airāvata; the burning of a certain crane by Mārkaṇḍeya out of anger; the description of how, among the various birds questioned by Mārkaṇḍeya as to what was to be done, one bird offered praise to the Blessed Lord out of fear of Mārkaṇḍeya; and the description of the granting of boons, beginning with the preservation of the world's stability, requested by Mārkaṇḍeya. Of Mārkaṇḍeya... [text fragment].

The granting of a boon by Narmadā, who had assumed the form of a Ruru deer, to Mārkaṇḍeya while he was praising the Blessed One; the hearing of the sound [of her voice]; the sighting of the maiden standing nearby; then the hymn of praise to Narmadā composed by Mārkaṇḍeya upon his arrival at Mahāśiva-tīrtha; the description of the events of the Śrī-Vārāha-kalpa; the sighting [of the deity]; the giving away of the maiden who was performing the service of serving the great sages; and by her [the maiden], the declaration of her own name as Narmadā.

A description of the signs and characteristics of the destruction of living beings; an account by Mārkaṇḍeya of the Lord reclining on Śeṣa alone at the end of the aeon; and thus, a description of the emergence of the Bakakalpa.

The composition of the hymn; then, the vision of a certain goddess; thereafter, at the time of the *kalpa*, having seen the Blessed Lord reclining and likewise having seen a certain maiden, and then beholding Śaṅkara, the performance of the hymn to the *Nṛsiṃha* [mantra] while another goddess remained hidden; the description of the dialogue between Śaṅkara and Narmadā; the description of the origin of Narmadā and the fruits of her bathing; and, at the commencement of the description of the majesty of the holy sites (*tīrtha*) situated on the banks of the Narmadā, first of all, the description of the origin of the river Kapilā.

—The description of the directions; the performance of penance directed toward Lord Agni for the sake of attaining the status of a river like the Gaṅgā and the other sixteen rivers; the description of the residence of the Narmadā among all fruitful [rivers] by virtue of that penance; the granting of a boon to Kaṅka by the gratified Agni; and the description of the origin of Vidārī.

This is the sixth chapter, concerning the description of the greatness of the fruits of knowledge and charity regarding the two [sages] Paṇaka and Kapikhāviśalya, the prohibition [of the sacrifice], and then, when King Durjaya, desiring to perform a sacrifice, saw the absence of fire in the sacrificial pit despite his efforts, he was filled with wonder; having learned the cause of that, he performed the marriage of Agni with his own daughter, the celestial Gaṅgā.

When the gods, headed by Indra, were oppressed by the demon Bāṇāsura and others, they performed the worship of the Sun with a certain mantra before Brahmā; this is followed by a description of the installation of the divine image on the banks of the Narmadā. Then, at Ravitīrtha, [the gods] sought refuge in Viṣṇu, after which Brahmā, together with Viṣṇu and all the deities, [described] the greatness of bathing and giving gifts at Kaiṭabhasthāna.

The arrival [of Nārada]; there, the praise of Maheśvara by all the gods and sages; at the command of Śiva, the description of Nārada’s playful excursions by celestial chariot with Bāṇāsura, preceded by an account of the marriages of Mandodarī and Rāvaṇa; the approach of Rāvaṇa’s son to his presence; at the word of Bāṇāsura, Nārada’s desire to see the wives of Bāṇa in the inner apartments of Bāṇa; Meghanāda’s performance of penance to Śiva and the installation of a Liṅga of Śiva under his own name; the entry into the Meṣatīrtha at Meghanāda; and [the account] of Bāṇa’s wife.

When questioned by Nārada regarding her, [the text] describes the greatness of the merit derived from the Madhūka-ṛtīyā vow, ritual bathing, giving of gifts, and so forth; it recounts the installation of a Liṅga by the friend of Śiva named Dāruka through the grace of Śiva; and, as an incidental narrative within the dialogue between the King and Nārada, it describes the splendor of the Dāru-tīrtha, the greatness of bathing and other rites there, and the manifestation of the city of Tripura. Furthermore, it describes the arrival of Nārada at that place where Śiva was sporting with Umā on the banks of the Narmadā, and the description of the greatness of Devatīrtha for Nārada, whose purpose had been accomplished.

The performance of hospitality by Śiva; the launching of arrows preceded by mantras by Śiva for the sake of slaying Tripura; the arrival of Śaṅkara with Pārvatī in a celestial chariot at the Forest of Wood (Dāruvana) as dispatched by Śaṅkara; the reduction of all enemies to ashes by the wooden arrow following the dialogue between Śaṅkara and Pārvatī; the description of the great glory of the bowing of Śiva upon his head after being struck by the arrow; and the description of the majesty of the Namadeśvara Tīrtha.

The granting of boons by Īśvara to Bāṇāsura; the praise of Kapilā, who arose from the *kuṇḍa* of the deity named Uvākhā at Jvāleśvara-tīrtha, and the description of the origin and majesty of Kapilā by the command of Brahmā; and the description of the majesty of Amareśvara-tīrtha. ...

The return from heaven to the mortal world by means of a bird; the description of the installation of various deities upon each limb of Kapilā; the account of the conversation between Yudhiṣṭhira and Mārkaṇḍeya occurring in that context; and the description of the greatness of the pilgrimage and other rites at Kapilātīrtha.

At the confluence of the Verī, Kala—the son of Kubera—having observed the Cāndrāyaṇa and other desired vows and restraints of austerity, performed the propitiation of the Lord under the name Karaja. By His grace, he established a temple in his own name; the arrival [of the deity]; the hymn of praise to the Lord by Kubera; the description of the greatness of bathing in that sacred ford (tīrtha) by the gratified Lord; the greatness of knowledge at the Karajeśvara-tīrtha; and then, the greatness of the Dāru-tīrtha. 2.

A description of the majesty of Kuṇḍaleśvara Tīrtha established by Kuṇḍala, the son of Viśravas; the majesty of Brahmāvarata Tīrtha; the arrival there of Yājñavalkya’s sister while she was searching for her husband; the majesty of Patraśvara; and the majesty of Śakareśvara.

The emission of semen by Yājñavalkya during his own recitation; the greatness of Abhitīrtha for one who, in the morning, was searching here and there for his garment; the arrival of the king’s sister before Yājñavalkya at the instance of King Duryodhana—who, having assumed the form of a Brahmin, had come there to ask for the hand of the king’s daughter named Sudarśanā—and the narration of the entire account by her upon the urging of her sister.

When Yājñavalkya’s sister, whose husband had died, conceived a child through contact with a dream-encounter with his semen, she went to the root of an *aśvattha* tree and described her abandonment of that [child]; [the child] was raised at the root of a *pippala* tree.

After slaying the demon Andhakāsura, Śiva went to Mount Kailāsa with Umā. Upon arriving at Kailāsa, he was praised by the gods. Then, having observed the suffering caused to him by the planet Saturn (Śanaiścara), Nārada—the son of the sage Parvata—requested his intervention. Consequently, Śiva established the Śūlabheda Tīrtha at the site of the battle with Andhakāsura. By the mere casting of his glance upon Saturn as he was traveling along the Vārāṇasī path, Śiva caused him to fall downward; such is the majesty of the Śūlabheda Tīrtha.

The narration of Bāṅaka’s persistent declaration that no pain from the serpent Śeṣanāga shall occur; the description of the rules regarding the examination of worthy and unworthy recipients, giving, and so forth, through the practice of the Āgneyī-dhāraṇā; the construction of a shrine for Pippalāda after he had been established there; the offering of a sacrifice by Yājñavalkya’s father; and the description of the greatness of the gift of the *Śalabheda* [manuscript].

The departure of Yājñavalkya to the realms of Brahmaloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and others for the sake of his own protection; the description of the penance performed by Śaṅkara; the naming of that hermitage Yogīśvarī by him; the description of the asceticism of Pippalāda; and, through the grace of Śiva, the installation of the *liṅga* named Pippalādeśvara after his own name by Pippalāda; and the description of its greatness and the account of the ascent of Duṣpaṃtapa to heaven.

The destruction of the demon Śālva by Viṣṇu; the supreme dialogue between Uttānapāda and his son; the praise and description of Śūlabheda, including the account of how the Gaṅgā was brought to the earth by the gods through the worship of Śiva on the Vindhya mountain... [the arrival of the Gaṅgā], the description of the greatness of the forest on the bank of the Gaṅgā, the description of the origin of the Śūlabheda Tīrtha, and the narrative of the granting of boons to the chief of the Asuras.

[In the description of the origin of the Śalabhedatīrtha: The Asura Andhaka, having defeated the gods, carried off Śacī; [the gods] went to the abode of Brahmā, and after offering praise to the Lord, they explained the reason for their arrival. Brahmā, together with his wife, went into the forest for the sake of hunting a tiger; having killed the deer, at the word of Māyā, the gods went to the world of Viṣṇu, and Brahmā and the other gods offered praise to Viṣṇu.

Viṣṇu’s journey to the Śabara on the shore of the lake to seize his abode and the taking of the lotus; the dispatching of Śūlabheda and others as messengers to the gods and the delivery of the message; the performance of Śiva-worship by the Śabara with lotuses; the dialogue between Bhānumatī and the Śabara wife; the description of the battle between Andhaka and Viṣṇu regarding the dispute over Uttānapāda and Śaṅkara; the offering of oblations (śrāddha) at sacred sites by those hurling weapons at one another; and the description of the greatness of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at those holy places.

Namely: the pacification by the Blessed One of Andhaka, who was incapable of being subdued in battle; Andhaka’s performance of bathing and other rites after going to the Mākaṇḍeya lake on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada; the departure of the hunter to heaven; Andhaka’s battle with Śaṅkara when he had gone to the Kekāsa mountain at the command of Viṣṇu; and the great battle of Andhaka with the enraged Ribi, as well as the [account] of Durgā, who had come for the sake of Śaṅkara’s destruction.

The account of the dialogue between Uttānapāda and Śiva; the performance of penance by Bhānumatī at Śūlabheda; the arrival of Bhānumatī in heaven; the defeat of Andhaka by Durgāsāhasrabhuja; the offering of praise to Śiva by Andhaka; the description of the events of his departure; the description of the majesty of Śūlabheda. ... [the description of] Śaṅkara making Añjana equal to himself... the description of the majesty of the Puṣkariṇī Tīrtha; the majesty of Ādityatīrtha. Chapter Six: The Glory of Malukakaṣṭha.
Bowed down. || 9 ||

Other subjects [of this chapter] are: the performance of a hymn of praise by Reṇukā to remove the curse; the greatness of the divine Lord residing on the banks of the Reṇū; the people’s prayer for the removal of that curse after the curse was pronounced upon them; and the establishment of a Śiva-liṅga after performing penance.

The description of the greatness of bathing, giving gifts, and other meritorious acts at Avaratīrtha by those who have committed sins such as the killing of a cow or the insulting of Brahmins; the narration of the story of Nibācipuṣkara and Mekṣaprāpin; the description of the greatness of the Gopāreśvara Tīrtha, which emerged from the earth during the ritual service of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu); and the description of the greatness of the Śakareḍavara Tīrtha, preceded by the account of Indra’s journey to heaven.

“Description of the greatness of the Gautameśvara Liṅga established by Gautama; description of the greatness of the Avaratīrtha established by Indra; description of the greatness of the Śaṃlacūḍa Tīrtha; description of the greatness of the Camāricāvara Tīrtha; in the description of the greatness of the Parīśvara Tīrtha, the account of the penance performed by the sage Parāśara for the sake of obtaining a son; and the description of the greatness of the Agastyeśvara Tīrtha resulting from that penance.”

The description of the greatness of Ākandevaram Tīrtha; the description of the greatness of Māvṛtti Tīrtha...; in connection with the description of the greatness of Śaradaśvara Tīrtha, the description of the performance of penance by the Dānava Kālṛṣṭha, the granting of a boon to him by Śiva, the bull among Dānavas being destined for defeat by the Bull (Vṛṣabha) through its own tail, and upon seeing the Dānava approaching, the Lord’s departure for Kaiḍāsa together with Umā, mounted upon the Bull, along with Śalareṇa.

Having seen the Danava pursuing him closely, Indra’s flight from the worlds of Brahma and the other gods; the granting of a boon by the Sun to Parashara; the installation of the Linga by Parashara there; and the description of the greatness of the Bhimesvara-Virya at the Paresvara Tirtha.

On the northern bank of the Revā, Nārada’s offering [of his body]; Nārada’s performance of penance at the command of Raiveśvara; the granting of a boon to Nārada by Śiva, who was pleased by that penance, and the establishment of the Śivagaṅgā; and a description of the majesty and fruits of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at the Nāradeśvara Tīrtha.

[The description of the offering of curd and honey at the Dadhiskanda and Madhuskanda tīrthas; the narration by Nārada to Viṣṇu of the entire account of the oppression by the Dānavas and other events; Viṣṇu’s assumption of the form of a maiden near the Nyagrodha tree through his illusory power (māyā) for the purpose of deluding the Dānava; and [the account of] Kālaghaṣṭha, who, having seen the maiden and being infatuated, came after visiting various holy sites in order to bestow the excellence of the Dadhiskanda and Madhuskanda tīrthas.]

Nandin, placing his hand upon his own head, [attained] the abode of ashes; then Viṣṇu, having performed penance at his own place, established a Liṅga there by his own name. [This is followed by] a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the Nandikeśvara Tīrtha, the departure [of the deity], the establishment of Chakeśvara, and a description of the majesty of bathing at the Ṭaṭakeśvara Tīrtha. ... [Then follows] a description of the majesty of the Varuṇeśvara Tīrtha. ... [And finally] a description of the majesty of the Śanada Tīrtha. ...

The description of the greatness of the five holy sites beginning with Dadhiskanda, preceded by the praise of the excellent Vahitīrtha; the description of the greatness of Maṅgaladevī, preceded by the account of her birth and manifestation established at Saṅkaṭa; and the description of the greatness of Hanumatkeśvara, wherein, after Rāma had brought about the destruction of Rāvaṇa and the others, the greatness of the Ravitīrtha manifested from the sight of Śiva by Hanumān is described.

The departure of Nandi; the description of the greatness of Kāmeśvara-tīrtha by Nandi, because he had warded off the sin of Brahmin-slaughter upon the destruction of the Rākṣasas; the subduing of Hanumān on the [appointed] day; the arrival of Hanumān at the Narmadā for the purpose of removing the Brahmin-slaughter; the manifestation of the Lord (Īśvara) at Maṇināga-deva-tīrtha through the power of those two; the satisfaction of the Lord by that penance; the speech of Hanumān to the Lord; and by the command of the Lord, the mutual [meeting] of Hanumān and the Liṅga.

The *Pravijmakaraṇa* (The Determination of the Truth): the effort of both parties to establish their respective claims. Therein, the establishment of the case: the meeting of King Suparvan’s son, named Hātabāhu, who had come to the mountain of Hanumat while wandering, with a Brahmin named Piṅgalaka who had arrived there for the purpose of casting bones [into the sea]. [The Brahmin said: "O Prince, [I am] Śikhaṇḍin the Brahmin. [He spoke] to the prince, who was asking the cause of the bone-casting.

The account preceded by the story of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the description of the greatness of Hanumānveśvara, the greatness of Kaparditīrtha, and the description of the supreme merit of bathing, giving gifts, and so forth at the Rāmeśvara, Ḍhuṇḍheśvara, and Kumbheśvara tīrthas; [and] how Dakṣa, having observed that the Moon was indifferent toward all his daughters except Rohiṇī, out of compassion for his own daughters, cast a curse upon the Moon in the form of leprosy, and thereafter by the Moon—

The performance of the praise of Mīdava for the sake of removing the curse; thereafter, the installation of the Liṅga named Somanābha by Īśānu; the description of the narrative concerning the gift of a Kaṇva Ṛṣi’s daughter accompanied by a hundred thousand cows for the purpose of purifying the sin of killing a Brahmin through the power of the Somanātheśvara Liṅga; the description of the greatness of the Somanātheśvara Liṅga; the description of the greatness of the Piṅgaleśvara Tīrtha; and the description of the greatness of the Ṛṇatrayamocana Tīrtha.

...the description of the greatness of Kapiṅgeśvara-vīrtha; the description of the greatness of Pūtikeśvara-vīrtha; ...in the description of the greatness of Cakratīrtha, which was manifested by the Discus-wielder [Viṣṇu]: having seen the gods defeated by the Dānava Tālamegha, Brahmā went into the presence of Viṣṇu; upon hearing the self-praise offered by the gods, the Blessed One granted a promise of fearlessness to the gods; then, in the battle between Viṣṇu and Tālamegha, they hurled weapons at one another; thereafter, by the Blessed One’s own discus, Tālamegha—

The description of the cutting of the thigh; the sight of that [thigh-bone] floating in the waters of the Narmadā and the establishment of a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) there; the renown of that *tīrtha* by the name Cakratīrtha, also known as Jarāśāyin; the enumeration of its greatness through the prescription of rites such as bathing and giving of gifts; ... the description of the greatness of Caṇḍāditya-tīrtha; ... the description of the greatness of Yamahāsya-tīrtha; ... (the description of the greatness of Kaldāḍī-tīrtha; ...)
The greatness of Na-na-viṣaya; the description of the greatness of the Nārāyaṇa-tīrtha established by Nara and Nārāyaṇa; the description of the greatness of Koṭīśvara-tīrtha.

In the context of describing the birth of Vyāsatīrtha, there is an account of the sage Parāśara’s performance of penance; at the conclusion of his asceticism, the sage Parāśara’s union with a certain fisherman’s daughter, a celestial nymph; his addressing her as "you are a princess" and recounting her past life; then, upon his union with that woman who possessed the scent of a fish, the description of the birth of Vyāsa through the power of the sage Parāśara’s spiritual energy; and [finally], by Vyāsa, on the banks of the Narmadā.

The performance of penance; the granting of boons to Vyāsa by that supreme Lord through the satisfaction of that penance; the composition of the Narmadā-stotra by Vyāsa; and the installation of a Liṅga of Śiva on the bank of the Narmadā by Vyāsa.

The description of the greatness of the confluence of the Eraṇḍī at Vyāsatīrtha, including the fruits of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites there; the grieving caused by Anaṣūyā due to her childlessness; the arrival of the gods, beginning with Brahmā; the granting of a boon to Anaṣūyā by the gods for the sake of obtaining sons; then the narration of the account of the three sons of Anaṣūyā named Durbāsas, Datta, and Soma; and subsequently, in connection with the description of the greatness of that holy site, [the story] of the sage named Govinda who was tormented by grief for his son.

The description of the narrative; therein, the description of his lying upon that very ground and attaining a state of radiance; then, his wife’s journey to the confluence of the Eraṇḍī for the purpose of bathing; their liberation from suffering there through the giving of cows, land, gold, and other gifts; the description of Anasūyā’s asceticism and her hearing [the teachings] from Govinda; and the description of the majesty of the Eraṇḍī confluence. Oṃ. The departure of Anasūyā to perform penance at the Eraṇḍī confluence on the bank of the Narmadā; and at the conclusion of her penance, the description of the greatness of the three [confluences].

The description of the majesty of Prabhāsa-tīrtha; the description of the majesty of Nāgeśvara-tīrtha; the description of the majesty of Mārkaṇḍeyeśa established by Mārkaṇḍeya; the description of the majesty of Saṃkarṣaṇa-tīrtha; and the description of the majesty of Manmadeśvara.

The battle between the gods and the demons; Indra’s journey to the banks of the Narmadā to perform penance after being overcome by the sin of Brahman-slaughter following the slaying of Vṛtra; the arrival of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara there at the conclusion of his penance; the establishment of the three worlds by Indra according to their command; and a description of the greatness of Indratīrtha.
The description of the greatness of the Kahoḍītīrtha.

The journey of the Dānava named Kaṃlu to the bank of the Narmadā for the sake of penance; the granting of a boon to him by Karṇikāra, who was pleased by the power of that penance; the establishment of a Śivaliṅga by Kaṃlu; and the description of the greatness of the Kevalakṣetra-tīrtha, the Suvarṇaśikhā-tīrtha, the Karañja-tīrtha, and the Kāmarada-tīrtha.

The description of the greatness of Bhaṇḍārī-tīrtha; the description of the greatness of Rohiṇī-tīrtha preceded by the account of Rohiṇī’s performance of penance; the description of the greatness of Cakra-tīrtha; the description of the greatness of Dhautapāpa-tīrtha; in connection with Skanda-tīrtha, the narration of the birth story of Skanda; the installation of Skanda as the commander-in-chief (senāpati); the installation of Śiva’s emblem (liṅga) by Skanda; and the description of the greatness of Skanda-tīrtha.

The description of the Trilecana Tīrtha; the installation of Śiva by Bharadvāja after performing penance with Soma; the greatness of Somatīrtha and Candrahāsa Tīrtha; the description of the creation of Jahnu; the description of the establishment of the four castes; the terrifying sight of Yama mounted upon a buffalo, produced by fear when a Brahmin well-versed in righteous conduct heard the words "Kill!"; the granting of a boon by the Lord through the praise of the Śatarudriya hymn; [the section on] Yama.

A description of Mavavarṇana; a description of the establishment of Kohanasvin; a description of the majesty of the Kohanasvatīrtha; a description of the majesty of the Karmadeśvara-tīrtha; a description of the majesty of the Dammadeśvara-tīrtha; an account of the causes for the acquisition of the two names of Ravi—Āditya and Bhāskara; a description of the penance of Raviṅkata; the establishment of Śivari by Ravi; a description of the majesty of Ravitīrtha; and a description of the majesty of the Ayoniprabhava-tīrtha.

(1) Description of the majesty of Annitīrtha; (2) Description of the majesty of Śarakuṭeśvaratīrtha; (3) Description of the majesty of Brahmatīrtha; (4) Description of the majesty of Devatīrtha; (5) In the narration of the origin of Nāgatīrtha, the account of the conflict between Vinatā and Kadrū and their subsequent union; (6) Description of the majesty of Naṇedavara Tīrtha; (7) Description of the majesty of Ādivārāhatīrtha.

The description of the propitiation of Īśvara by Cakrapāṇi with four [offerings], followed by the narration of the attainment of the desired boon; the installation of the Śivaliṅga by the four world-protectors (Lokapālas); the description of the majesty of the four Liṅgas beginning with Kavera; the description of the majesty of the Rāmeśvara Tīrtha; the description of the majesty of Siddheśvara; and the pronouncement of a curse upon Indra by Gautama for his illicit union with Aditi.

The liberation from the curse of Aditī, who had been struck by Rāma with his foot; the removal of the sin of Divodāsa by Ahalyā through her own name; a description of the greatness of the Ahalyeśvara Tīrtha; a description of the majesty of Karakakeṭeśvara;

Śakra performing penance for the sake of removing the curse given by Gautama and establishing a Śiva-liṅga; a description of the greatness of Rakrekavara Tīrtha; a description of the greatness of Soma Tīrtha; and a description of the greatness of Laṃtāpiśvara Tīrtha.

In the context of describing the greatness of Rukmiṇī-tīrtha, there is an account of the marriage of Rukmiṇī by Śrī Kṛṣṇa; therein, a description of the battle involving Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Caidya, Māgadha, and others; a description of the defeat of Rukmin brought about by Śrī Kṛṣṇa; a description of the marriage ceremony between Rukmiṇī and Kṛṣṇa; a description of the greatness of Rukmiṇī-tīrtha established by Rukmiṇī; and a description of the greatness of Yojanagandhā-tīrtha.

(1) Description of the greatness of Dvādaśī; (2) Description of the greatness of Sītīrtha; (3) Detailed description of the greatness of Asmadakātīrtha, including the performance of various rites such as bathing, giving gifts, recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), and the *ṛṣotsarga*; (4) Description of the greatness of Sibdeśvaratīrtha; (5) Description of the greatness of Maṅgalēśvaratīrtha; (6) Description of the greatness of Īśagavārāhatīrtha; (7) When Kāma was reduced to ashes by Śaṅkara, the gods offered prayers for his restoration, and [the account of] the reconstitution of Anaṅga’s limbs.

The instrument; the performance of penance by Kāmadeva and the installation of Śiva; the description of the majesty of the Liṅga of Ṛṣabheśvara, Paṭala, page, chapters, subjects, Paṭala; the description of the majesty of the Oṃkāra-Vārāha Tīrtha; the description of the majesty of the Bhārgaveśvara Tīrtha... Description of the greatness of Ādityeśvara Tīrtha; description of the greatness of Kalkaleśvara Tīrtha; the narrative of Cāṇakya, who was abandoned by two crows, during the account of the origin of Śuklatīrtha; Cāṇakya’s abandonment of crookedness (kauṭilya); description of the account of Cāṇakya’s attainment of perfection; description of the greatness of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at Śuklatīrtha; description of the greatness of Hakārasvāmī Tīrtha; description of the greatness of Saṅgameśvara Tīrtha; and description of the greatness of Anarakeda Tīrtha.

A description of the ripening of karma (*karmavipāka*); a description of the stages of the womb (*garbhāvasthā*); a description of the greatness of the fruits of great gifts such as the *trivaraṇa* and others; the greatness of offering lamps and other oblations to Yama on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina; a description of the greatness of the Anarakedvara Tīrtha; a description of the greatness of Mokṣatīrtha; a description of the greatness of Sapetīrtha; ... a description of the greatness of Gopeśvaratīrtha; a description of the greatness of Nāgatīrtha; ... a description of the greatness of Sāvaireśvaratīrtha.

The description of that oil-presser; O King, having heard of this from him, the king’s dispatching of his ministers and others for its investigation; the discovery of the royal lady’s ornaments in the hermitage of Māṇḍavya and the subsequent reporting of that incident to the king; and then, by the king’s command, the description of Māṇḍavya’s impalement upon a stake.
