... [Description of the greatness of] Ekaśāra-Ḍiṇḍima-deva-tīrtha. ... ka. [Description of the greatness of] Āmala-deva-tīrtha. ... [Description of the greatness of] Śrīkapāla-tīrtha. ... [Description of the greatness of] Śṛṅgī-tīrtha. 216. [Description of the greatness of] Āṣāḍhī-tīrtha. ... [Description of the greatness of] Eraṇḍī-tīrtha. ...

When his father, Jamadagni, who had committed an offense, was slain by Paraśurāma, and when twenty-one times all the Kṣatriyas had been killed, Paraśurāma established Jāmadagnyeśvara and created the Jāmadagnya-tīrtha in order to suppress that sin; [this section contains] a description of the majesty of the Jāmadagnya-tīrtha and a description of the ritual procedure for the worship of Jāmadagnyeśvara... [followed by] a description of the majesty of Koṭitīrtha.

Description of the majesty of Loṭaṇeśvara Tīrtha... Description of the majesty of Haseśvara preceded by the dialogue between Vyāsa and Khasa... Description of the majesty of Tiradeśvara Tīrtha... Contents: Chapter 6, Subject matter; Chapter 9, Subject matter: Description of the majesty of Koṭīśvara Tīrtha...

The falling of the *liṅga*, the performance of hymns of praise to Śiva by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others; the installation of a Śiva-liṅga by Indra, who was pleased by that [praise], using his own name along with a Gandharva maiden named Alikā; the description of the ritual procedure beginning with the Acikīścara-tīrtha; then, the account of going to the sacred field of Devalokeśvara and the installation of that very same liṅga there; and finally, the description of the greatness (*māhātmya*) of worshipping the *liṅga*.

Trishanku, desiring to ascend to heaven in his own physical body, made a request to Vashistha; the description of this [is as follows]: Trishanku, having performed penance together with his wife Shanta for the sake of dispelling his throat disease by means of the sun-god Bhānu—who had become a dwarf—caused the earth to be uprooted and brought down the Ganges from the netherworld (pātāla). Furthermore, it describes how Trishanku attained the state of a Chandala by the command of Shiva, the installation of a Shivalinga under the name Vimaleshvara, the greatness of the Vimaleshvara-tirtha, and the narrative account of how Trishanku requested Vashistha to take him to heaven in his own body.
When Vasiṣṭha stated that this was impossible, he resolved in his mind with stubborn persistence to question another teacher.

A description of the pilgrimage rites for those residing on the banks [of the river], detailing the procedure for visiting all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) in their proper sequence; specifically, regarding the sage Vasiṣṭha’s son Śrīrīku, who, disregarding Vasiṣṭha’s words, was intent on acting according to his own will at the Durāma forest, there is a description of his greatness. Furthermore, the bestowal of the curse "Become a Caṇḍāla," by which he immediately attained the state of a Caṇḍāla; and subsequently, through remorse, the performance of a pilgrimage to other sacred fords and the narration of its greatness, merit, and so forth. Na. Ā. (End of chapter).

The description of the gift of the Revākhaṇḍa, including its hearing, recitation, and so forth, as told by the ministers to the distressed King Triśaṅku at his command; the departure of Triśaṅku on foot into the great forest; the description of the various holy fords (*tīrtha*) and their confluences; and the description of the sacred sites (*tīrtha*).

The departure of Triśaṅku, whose face was fierce, to the forest; the journey of Viśvāmitra with him; then, while enumerating the number of sacred fords (tīrthas), the description of the sequence of the pilgrimage preceded by an account of the arrangement of all the sacred sites; having heard that account, the making of the vow by the sage, "I shall lead you to heaven in this very body"; the description of the fruit of giving the manuscript of the Revākhaṇḍa, preceded by the conclusion of the Revākhaṇḍa. ... [End].
And as those two were wandering together with that Caṇḍāla to various holy bathing places for the sake of dispelling his sin, this was the third section, the Revākhaṇḍa, within the Āvantyakhaṇḍa.

(—) The dialogue with Kaṇḍeya; the journey to Hāṭakeśvara at the word of Mārkaṇḍeya; the liberation of Triśaṅku from his state as a Caṇḍāla through the worship of the Hāṭakeśvara-liṅga; thereafter, the acceptance of the invitation for him to perform a sacrifice that would secure the attainment of heaven. ... Thus ends the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, in the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. 9.

Even though Brahmā had not granted permission for such an act to be performed, Viśvāmitra, through the power of his own asceticism, completed the twelve-year sacrifice—which had been interrupted by Indra—by means of a Brāhmaṇa; then, at the conclusion, he performed the ritual ablutions and other rites to bring the sacrifice to completion.
Now, in the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, the sixth section, the Nāgara-khaṇḍa.

The departure for heaven by Vidurāmiśra after praising the Creator and receiving a boon from Him; the commencement of the dialogue between Sūta and Dvaipāyana; therein, having heard the question of Dvaipāyana and composed the *Naraka-svarga* (Heaven of Naraka) to provide an answer to it, his departure for heaven with his physical body.

In the context of Sūta’s description of the origin of the *Ṛgveda*, there is an account of Śiva, separated from his consort, going to the hermitage of the Ṛṣis. Having seen the mutual dispute between Brahmā and Viṣṇu, who had been created by Viḍvāmitra, the gods approached Brahmā; thereafter, seeing the sky-clad [Śiva] in the heavens, they bestowed a curse upon him. Due to that curse, Śiva departed from that very place. Then, for the sake of the stability of the world, Brahmā and the others went into the presence of Viḍvāmitra. [Viḍvāmitra...]

The objects of the *Caraka* school: the departure of Triśaṅku from his own realm due to the word [of Viśvāmitra] and having no other recourse; the voluntary return of Vidavāmitra from his newly acquired kingdom; and the conclusion of the narrative of Triśaṅku.

Having heard of the splendor of Hāṭakeśvara, all people went there; even Vidāmitra abandoned his own home and took up residence right there. Thinking that this Kṣatriya lineage was intent on liberation even without performing sacrifices and other rites, he established [the deity] at the foot of the Hāṭakeśvara mountain by the command of the God. Because of that, even the Nāgas traveled everywhere with him. In the description of the majesty of Hāṭakeśvara, it is told how the daughter of Hiraṇyakaśipu, named Ramā, for the sake of obtaining her husband, directed her prayers toward Viṣṇu.

The performance of penance; thereafter, the birth of the demon Vṛtra through the grace of Viṣṇu; the departure of Dadhīci before Indra and the other gods, at their request to Viṣṇu for the purpose of slaying Vṛtra and for the sake of producing the thunderbolt from his bones; the defeat of Vṛtra by the thunderbolt fashioned from Dadhīci’s bones; Śakra’s journey to Hāṭakeśvara for the purpose of purifying himself from the great sin arising therefrom; and the dispatching of Saṃvartaniras by Indra after he had filled the serpent-hole, followed by Saṃvartaniras’s journey to the serpent-hole at the command of Śakra.

The return of Saṃvarta, who had been terrified by the curse of Chyavana, to the city of Śakra; then, at the command of Bṛhaspati, Śakra’s departure to the presence of Himākhya in order to dispatch [his sons] for the purpose of making Viśvakarman build [the city]; and seeing that his three sons—named Bhema, Kanakavardhana, and Raktaśṛṅga—who had been commanded by Himākhya to perform Śakra’s task, did not accept the command and refused to comply, Śakra’s pronouncement of a curse upon them.

Out of fear of a curse, he went there for the purpose of making the mountain named Raktaśṛṅga foul-smelling with serpents; thereafter, Devendra established numerous holy bathing places (tīrthas) that produce happiness on this mountain named Raktaśṛṅga, followed by a description of Indra’s encouragement of the peak of Raktaśṛṅga.

(The description of the greatness of Śaṅkhatīrtha: Camatkāradarpa’s hunting; the killing of the deer by the astonishment of the doe who was giving her teat to its young; the king Camatkāradarpa’s attainment of leprosy due to the curse given by the doe; the journey to Śaṅkhatīrtha for the sake of removing that suffering and the curse; the description of the eradication of the leprosy of Camatkāradarpa through bathing at Śaṅkhatīrtha; and the description of the majesty of Śaṅkhatīrtha.)

The cessation of faults through the worship of Hāṭakeśvara, returning to one's own place, and the description of the majesty of Hāṭakeśvara; these are the topics [discussed] in the account of the origin of Śaṅkhatīrtha within the dialogue between King Camatkāra and the sage.

Having perceived that the breaking of the conch was an act of theft, Śikhin (Skanda) inflicted the punishment of cutting off the hand of Śaṅkha. Thereafter, Śaṅkha performed penance at Hāṭakeśvara; pleased by his penance, Śiva granted a boon to Śaṅkha. He then related how he had previously lost his hand due to a curse. There, he established a Liṅga in his own name. Following a description of the origin of Śaṅkhatīrtha, there is a description of the majesty of Śaṅkhatīrtha.

King Camatkāra, having caused a city to be built for the Brahmins, established the foundations of the city at the command of the Brahmins and gave instructions regarding his sons. Receiving the blessing of Brahmadatta, he entrusted his kingdom to his sons and went to the temple of Oṭakeśvara to perform penance. There, having propitiated Śiva, by the grace of Śiva he installed a linga named Acadeśvara.

Regarding the majesty of Acaṅeśvara: in the city of Camatkārapura, one cow from a certain cowherd's herd wandered into the forest out of greed for grass; the cowherd went into the forest to search for her. After some time, both attained the state of being a *paśu* (a bound soul). Then, the description of the cowherd’s birth in the household of a village headman (*daṇḍādhipati*), as well as the cow’s birth into a family of excellent intellect; thereafter, having recollected the events of their previous births, [they attained liberation].

The attainment of liberation via the path of the *tairthika* through the performance of the southern circumambulation (*dakṣiṇā-karaṇa*) of Camatkārapura; a description of the greatness of the southern circumambulation of Camatkārapura; a unique description of the excellence of the greatness of the southern circumambulation of Camatkārapura, preceded by a description of the power of Raktāṅga; a description of the fruits of serving Raktāṅga while standing upon the crest of the red mountain; a description of the fourteen sacred sites (*tīrtha*) situated there in Camatkārapura; and therein, first, the greatness of Gayāśiras.

In the course of the description, there was Vidūratha’s journey into the forest for the sake of hunting. While Vidūratha was pursuing deer there, his horse, exhausted from galloping through the woods, fell to the ground. Then, leaving the horse right there, Vidūratha proceeded on foot, following the tracks of the deer. [Note: The final fragment "ka ga śane na" appears to be a scribal or typographical error.]

Then, after crossing the Kakkara, Kaka, Daka, and Rra-ra rivers and traveling further along the path, there occurs the sighting of the three Piśācas beginning with Māṃsāda. Following the account of Māṃsāda and the others, there is the conversation between King Vidūratha—who had reached the hermitage—and the sages, as well as the performance of the evening rites and the offering of the Śrāddha to Māṃsāda and the rest. Subsequently, there is the departure of Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā from the Piṭrkūpikā Tīrtha toward the Piṭrkūpikā Tīrtha, where they perform the Śrāddha ceremony.

The description of how Rāma and others traveled to the hermitage of Vidūratha, the son of Khaṇḍika, despite the presence of others; the account of Vidūratha’s own liberation as told by him in a dream at the well of the Gayā-tīrtha; the detailed narration of Khara’s treachery and deceit as he set his mind upon killing Rāma and Sītā; and, following the extensive description of the Jāṭhayaṅgī-tīrtha, the account of Mārkaṇḍeya’s birth and the long discourse by Mārkaṇḍeya on the majesty of the twelve sacred fords (dvādaśatīrtha-māhātmya).

Having reached Hāṭakeśvara and performed austerities, there is a description of the installation of the Liṅga. Then follows the account of Vāḍha-maṇḍana-tīrtha: how the hundred sons of Diti were born from her womb by Śakra (Indra) at the instigation of Vena; how she went to Vāḍha-maṇḍana-tīrtha and how her sin was removed by bathing in that sacred site; and how, thereafter, she set out toward the southern direction following Rāma, entered his belly at Vāḍha-maṇḍana-tīrtha, and how Śakra cut the fetus into pieces, causing her great lamentation.

For the removal of those faults, Śakra performed a rite for the acquisition of knowledge at the Bāṇamaṇḍana Tīrtha; through this pilgrimage to the Tīrtha, Śakra’s faults were eliminated. This is the description of the majesty of Maṇḍanatīrtha. In the description of Sṛgatīrtha: hunters arrived there while seeing birds perched in the shade of a certain tree; then, upon being discovered by the hunters, the birds fled from that place, and the hunters pursued them. By the birds’ crossing over to the other side of the lake, [the hunters] were immediately...

The transgression against the human state; the bathing in that lake by hunters under the pretext of deer-faced women due to the power of that lake; the description of the greatness of the Sṛgatīrtha, which brings about the attainment of even the blind; the description of the attainment of liberation for all; and at the time of the secret union of the sages, Vāmana, having covered the worlds with two steps, [covered them] with his third step.

In the section on the divisions of the universe (*brahmāṇḍa*), when the skull of a certain Brāhmaṇa was split by the messengers of Yama who had arrived from the abode of Yama, there follows the description of the descent of Gaṅgā’s matted locks; then the greatness of the Viṣṇupada-tīrtha, including its origin and the story of the flood; and the description of the greatness of the Gaṅgā at Viṣṇupada, including the account of how the sin of drinking liquor was removed for a certain Brāhmaṇa who was performing the recitation of the *Madyapāra* [text] while describing the majesty of the Gaṅgā at Viṣṇupada through bathing therein. Finally, there is the description of the greatness of the Gaṅgā at Viṣṇupada.

The description of the journey to the realm of Yama with the negligent; therein, the inquiry by Yama regarding the desire for Gokarṇa, and the account of which specific sin leads to which hell; the departure of Gokarṇa for Camatkārapura by the permission of Yama; the description of liberation through bathing at the holy ford (tīrtha) there; the enumeration of the four ages beginning with Gokarṇa; the demonstration of the nature and magnitude of the four ages; the definition of the fourfold duties (cāturyyakarma); and specifically, the description of the origin of the Caṇḍālas, including washermen and others.

Description of the majesty of Kaḍikāra. In the dialogue between Bṛhaspati and Indra, a description of the resorting to all sacred fords (*tīrthas*). Upon the success [of his penance], at the command of his father, the great sage Vatsa performed the *śukrābhimantraṇa* (consecration of the seed). Therein, the great sage Vatsa narrates the account of his own previous birth: Devarāta, desiring to bathe in the Sanerāmra, beheld a certain woman in distress; he discharged his semen into the water. From that semen, a fetus was conceived; at the end of ten months, a daughter was born from the water.

Devarāta gave his daughter in marriage to Vatsa; after a long time had passed, the death of a friend occurred due to the bite of a serpent, and Vatsa set out for the forest. Although the sages offered him consolation in many ways, he persisted in his grief over the snake-bite and began to perform a snake-sacrifice. While he was performing that snake-sacrifice, one serpent assumed a human form and described their conversation. As he, assuming a human form, told Vatsa the cause of the former’s curse, [he said]: "In my previous birth, by me..."

Bha-nana-ki-da—ka----- --- -- -- - - -- Jyāḥ-na-a-savyaḥ. In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, [it describes] the renunciation of worldly duties by Īśāna through association; then, the resolve in the mind of Vatsa, the sage, to perform the worship of Maheśvara due to his remorse for having killed a cow; the description of Vatsa’s attainment of perfection through the worship of Siddheśvara; the account of the origin of Siddheśvara; and the worship performed after Bṛhaspati, at the command of the Lord of Siddhas, established the image of his son Parāśarya-Cchiga.

Upon the completion of that [account], follows the description of the majesty of Siddheśvara... then, in the context of describing the majesty of the Nāgahrada, the arrival of the nine Nāgas at the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara by the command of Brahmā; the installation of a linga there under their own names; the description of King Indrasena’s death from the bite of a serpent; thereafter, Indrasena’s arrival at his father's funeral pyre in a dream and his narration of how he attained the state of a ghost; and the son’s journey to the Nāga-tīrtha at his father’s command, where—

The description of the father’s liberation through the performance of the *pitṛśrāddha* and the worship of the *liṅga*; the description of the Nāgatīrtha and the Saptarṣitīrtha along with the method for worshipping the Saptarṣis; the description of the origin of the Saptarṣitīrtha, including how the seven seers (*saptarṣi*) wandered everywhere during a twelve-year drought while suffering from hunger; their arrival in the kingdom of King Ṛṣabha; and the exertion made by the seven seers to find food there upon seeing a newborn infant, until at that moment Ṛṣabha appeared.

Having arrived there, he engaged in discussion with them; then, without even consuming the food offered by the Ṛṣikulyās, he went to Camatkārapura, where they performed austerities and established the holy sites (tīrthas).

In the description of Agastya’s hermitage, it is told how the Vindhya mountain, out of mutual rivalry, grew so high as to obstruct the path of the sun; consequently, the sun went to Agastya’s hermitage. At the sun’s request, Agastya turned the mountain face downwards and proceeded toward Hāṭakeśvara in the southern direction. Having gone there with his wife Lopāmudrā, he established a linga. Regarding the greatness of Agastya’s hermitage (and the account of the reason for Agastya’s drinking of the ocean), it is first described how, during the battle between the gods and the Daityas, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the other deities [were overcome].

The description of the defeat of the Daityas by Śaṅkara with his trident, and the determination that the defeat of the gods must indeed result from the destruction of Dharma; furthermore, the subjugation of the Brāhmaṇas—who perform sacrifices, recitations, and other rites through the power of knowledge—by the Daityas, and the command issued by the Goddess for the purpose of slaying those Daityas who dwell within their bodies.

The account of Agastya’s departure for the western ocean; the drinking of the ocean by Agastya for the sake of the gods' mission; the slaying of the Daityas by the gods; the description of the greatness of Citravarapīṭha—the name given to the seat established by Agastya because the gods made it their own—along with the description of the origin of the temple known as Duḥśīla; the description of the greatness of Dhundhumāreśvara Liṅga; ... and the description of the greatness of Yayātīśvara Liṅga.

The installation of the stone slab by Brahmā on the vast [ground]; then, by the command of Brahmā, the arrival of Sarasvatī at that place for the purpose of bathing; then, after performing austerities there, the installation of the *liṅga* by the great seer Maṅkaṇaka; and the description of the greatness of Citraśikhaṇḍa, Maṅkaṇaka, Kedāra, and the river. ...;

The Daitya Bāṣkala, having oppressed the gods led by Indra, performed penance at Hāṭakeśvara under the command of Viṣṇu. Thereafter, at the instruction of Bṛhaspati, on the day of Aśanyaśayana-tithi, the Lord was pleased by his worship; then, by the Lord’s command, he engaged in battle with Bāṣkali. Having defeated the Daitya Bāṣkala, the Lord sent Śakra back to his own abode and took up residence there himself, establishing the Rigveda. This is the description of the origin of Jalaśāyin.

The narration of the account of the origin of Viśvāmitra’s sacrificial pit; therein, in the description of the meeting between Viśvāmitra and Menakā, the teaching of the dharma of knowledge by Viśvāmitra to Menakā.

Having disregarded the laws of chastity proclaimed by Viśvāmitra, when Menakā became deceitful—asking "From where have you come? and "Where are you going? and so forth—Viśvāmitra uttered a curse of reproach against their union. When their meeting was thus rejected by Viśvāmitra, Menakā, tormented by great sorrow, and Viśvāmitra mutually bestowed upon each other a curse consisting of the attainment of old age; thereafter, [the story continues] with their transformation into a pair of earrings.

The curse of Śakti, the establishment of a sacrificial post there by Viśvāmitra, and the account of Viśvāmitra’s [encounter with] the sage Kaṇva; [the text continues with] the [narrative of] the Nāgarakhaṇḍa... [fragmentary].

In this description of the majesty of the Sarasvatī-tīrtha: the arrival of Ambuvīci—born from the bite of Balabhadra, possessed of a mute son, and seeking the removal of his son’s muteness—at the Sarasvatī-tīrtha; the curing of the son’s muteness there through the worship of Jāneśvara; Ambuvīci’s hymn of praise to Sarasvatī; and the description of the majesty of the Sarasvatī-tīrtha.

In the description of the greatness of Mahākālavana: King Radrāsena, accompanied by his wife, travels to Hāṭakeśvara; having worshipped the Lord there and given many gifts to the Brahmins, the king relates the account of his own previous birth to the assembly of Brahmins. There, because he was born into the merchant caste and lacked sufficient food, he fasted and went with his wife to Mahākālavana; there, with skillful efforts, he performed the worship of the Lord. By that—

Birth in a royal family through the power of merit; the greatness of the *liṅga* at the great *kṛta* and excellent *tīrthas*; in the *Umāmaheśvara-liṅgamāhātmya*, the worship of Umāmaheśvara by Hariścandra for the sake of obtaining a son; the granting of a boon that bestows a son by Umāmaheśvara, who were pleased by his asceticism; taking that boon and Hariścandra’s departure to his own palace; thereafter, the installation of a *liṅga* in the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara for the propitiation of Umāmaheśvara; Umā—

The description of the greatness of Maheśvara’s *Ṛigama* [penance]; the description of the greatness of Kaṭaśreṣṭha; the arrival of Dūrvāsas at the house of Kaṭadāpa; the offering of food and other provisions by the sage to Dūrvāsas—who had come to perform the breaking of his *Cāturmāsya* vow—preceded by the rites of hospitality; and there, upon seeing meat well-prepared with salt and other seasonings in the vessel of food, [the sage cursed him], "Become a tiger!"

Thus ends the section on the granting of the curse. This is the description of how the bull attained liberation from the tiger through an oath, in the dialogue between Nandinī and Vyāsa. In this account, Nandinī makes an oath in the presence of the tiger; at the tiger’s word, Nandinī returns to her own place and causes the bull to swear an oath. Then all the cattle go before the tiger with Nandinī, and by that means, her truthfulness is established. Subsequently, out of remorse, he questions her for the sake of attaining liberation. [This concerns] the bull who had attained the state of a tiger due to the curse.

The description of the greatness of the Tripuṣkara Tīrtha through the worship of the Liṅga installed by Nandin with an arrow; the restoration of his former kingship after being released from the curse that had caused him to become a tiger; the installation of a Liṅga in his own name after performing the propitiation of Hara; his departure to the world of Śiva; the description of the greatness of the Kaṭarodaka Liṅga; and the description of the greatness of Rudrakoṭi.

The description of the account of King Mitrasaha, who had fallen into the state of a *bhrūṇahan* (feticide), regarding his transformation into a *rākṣasa* due to the curse of Vasiṣṭha; how that king, while following the conduct of a *rākṣasa*, even killed Brahmins and others; how, by that very act, he undertook a pilgrimage to sacred fords (*tīrthayātrā*) at the command of Vasiṣṭha after being released from the curse in order to remove the sin of *brahmahatyā*; how, upon bathing in the sacred fords visited by those who kill embryos, he was liberated from the sin of *brahmahatyā* and resumed his former kingdom; and finally, after his reign, his departure to the world of Śiva.

And [there is] a description of the greatness of Śraṇama; and [there is] a description of the greatness of Muṇḍā, preceded by a narrative concerning Nala and his nails; and a description of the greatness of Neibara, established by him under his own name, which wards off undesirable defects such as disease; and in the Sāvāditya-māhātmya, the attainment of a boon through the grace of Āditya by Gākhva, and the obtaining of a son through the worship of Sāṃbāditya due to the absence of offspring, followed by a description of the greatness of Sāṃbāditya. ...

Description of the narrative of Gāṅgeya’s pilgrimage; description of the establishment of the four *chigas* by Gāṅgeya; description of the greatness (*māhātmya*) of Hivagāma... [and] the establishment of a *liṅga* named after himself by Vidura after he had performed penance for the sake of obtaining a son; description of the greatness of Vidureśvara; description of the account of the divine vision experienced by Vidura; [and] the establishment of a deity named Māhittha by the son of Mitra and Varuṇa; description of the greatness of Narādīveśvara.

In the *Śarbhiṣṭhātīrthamāhātmya*, there is a description of the origin of the Poison-Maiden (*viṣakanyā*), and an account of how the sage met his death for failing to abandon her. Having heard the censure of his own world, the Poison-Maiden departed for the forest to perform penance. On the way, Pārvatī, having assumed the form of Indrāṇī, approached her after seeing the severe penance she was performing, including the practice of standing on her heels. Although Indrāṇī offered her a boon, she refused it and continued her asceticism once more.

While [the sacrifice] was being performed, the chapters concerning the future subjects, which are the very essence of the story, follow; then the praise of Pārvatī by Niṣakanya; the departure for Kailāsa with the six companions; and the description of the Śarmiṣṭhā-tīrtha and other sacred sites. Dha.

The description of the greatness of Somanāthavarāha; the worship of the Lord by Roga through the sacrifice of his own hair, following the curse of Soma; the establishment of Roga by means of that very essence; the description of the greatness of Somanāthavarāha; the description of the greatness of Goddess Durgā, who causes wonder to the inhabitants of Camatkārapura; and the description of the greatness of Ānaikeśvara and Dareśvara, along with the narration of their origins.

In the context of describing the Rāmahrada forest, there is the account of Jamadagni’s slaughter and the departure of the king with his army. There, when King Sahasrārjuna requested the power of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) and Jamadagni refused to give it away, the king became enraged and killed Jamadagni.

Hearing of his father’s death, Paraśurāma performed the funeral rites for his father and made a vow to rid the earth of the Kṣatriyas. Subsequently, Rāma slew Sahasrārjuna upon learning of his intent.

After the slaughter of the thousand kings, Paraśurāma went to Hāṭakeśvara and performed the ancestral *śrāddha* rites with the blood flowing from the bodies of those thousand kings. Having thus secured the entire earth for the Brāhmaṇas, he caused the ocean to recede to provide space for his own dwelling. Furthermore, having forcibly seized the earth given back to the Brāhmaṇas by the Kṣatriyas, Rāma slaughtered them; in this manner, twenty-one times he rendered the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas and gave it to the Brāhmaṇas.

The establishment of the holy site named Rāmahradā, which was reached by Ādivodhya through the recitation of the *Jrāda* hymn; the description of the special fruit obtained through the *śrāddha* for those killed by Rākṣasas; the general narration of the history of Kārttikeya’s birth and deeds within the context of the slaying of the demon Tāraka; and the description of the majesty of the spear (*śakti*) established by Kārttikeya (Skanda).

Then follows the description of the installation of the deities Hāṭakeśvara and others by Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the Pāṇḍavas; subsequently, the account of Duryodhana’s marriage to Bhānumatī in Dvāravatī; then the journey of the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas together with Vidura to Hāṭakeśvara; the narration of the events concerning the construction of palaces and other matters undertaken by Dhṛtarāṣṭra; and therein, at Hāṭakeśvara, the establishment of one hundred and one Liṅgas by Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the others.

The establishment of the Liṅgas by the Pāṇḍavas, such as Savyadroṇa and others, and by the Yādavas and others, each according to their own individual names; the description of the installation of the Kaurava, Pāṇḍava, and Yādava deities; the description of the majesty of the sacrificial ground (yajñabhūmi); and the description of the three Tīrthas—Muṇḍāraka, Aṅghriyamūla, and Itibhāskara—at which the story is told of a certain leper who, at the word of a Brāhmaṇa, was cured of his leprosy by bathing in those three Tīrthas. [The text continues with] Muṇḍīrakāṅghriyamūla...

Description of the greatness of the sacred site; at the time of the marriage of Hara and Pārvatī, the spilling of Brahmā’s semen due to a glance from Pārvatī; how Brahmā, through that sin, propitiated Rudraśiras to bring about the removal of his fault; description of the greatness of the Harāśrayavedikā and the greatness of Rudraśīrṣa; the account of how a certain Brāhmaṇa woman who was unchaste was freed from her sin by worshipping Rudraśīrṣa; and the description of how the wife of King Vidūratha likewise attained liberation through the grace of Rudraśīrṣa.

The description of the greatness of Śudraśīrṣa (Jāgeśvara); the description of the greatness of the Vāṅkhilya hermitage; the account of the manifestation of anger by the Vāṅkhiyas toward Śakra; the greatness of the Vāṅkhilya hermitage; the description of the greatness of the Suparṇa [hermitage]; the account of Kaśyapa giving the vessel of *amṛta* to his wife for the sake of obtaining offspring, after it had been consecrated with Atharvanic and Maitra mantras by the Vāṅkhiyas; and the birth of Garuḍa from Kaśyapa through the consumption of that vessel of *amṛta*.

The departure of Garuḍa with the two Nāga maidens for the purpose of choosing a bridegroom for Mitrā, the daughter of the Brāhmaṇa; the meeting with Nārada on the way; the journey of them all to Hāṭakeśvara together with Nārada for the sake of seeing Viṣṇu; having gone there, the obtaining of an audience with Viṣṇu by Nārada and Garuḍa; and after receiving the audience of Viṣṇu, Garuḍa’s making a formal request to Viṣṇu for the hand of the daughter of Dhiṣaṇa as a bridegroom.

The battle; indeed, the emergence from a single pit of deities such as Rajavakra and Ashvamukhi; seeing that, Garuda’s desire to consume the sacrificial oblation and his bringing of a Brahmin together with his daughter to Vishnu’s presence; the arrangement made by the two of them—Vishnu and the Brahmin—for the sake of preventing the Brahmin’s daughter from sitting on Vishnu’s lap and for the consumption of the various objects of enjoyment; and having seen that they had attained happiness, the story is indicated [by the text]: "Become horse-faced," thus the pronouncing of a curse upon that girl.

Then, by his own command, the establishment of the image of Hāṭakeśvara; a description of the majesty of Ambābaddhā; likewise, the granting of a curse by the Brahmin to Bhājavakrā, saying, "Become a female jackal"; then, at the command of Viṣṇu, for the sake of severing the influence of those deities who had caused harm, the making of a *khāṅkhanaka* (a protective mark) on the daughter of King Camatkāra and the granting of a boon; and, by the order of Viṣṇu, the sending of the Brahmin along with his son to his own home by the goddess Ambābaddhā.

The placing of his own sandals; the removal of the suffering of people by the gift of sandals; when Garuḍa laughed at Śāṇḍilī, who was standing before Viṣṇu and was either bound or had her nose cut off, [Viṣṇu] entered [her] as if to protect her; the description of the Ganges water that touched the feet of the one who gave the sandals; the reduction of Garuḍa to ashes by the mental bestowal of a curse from Saṃkarṣaṇa upon him while he was performing meditation;—from the second chapter onwards, the birth of a girl, and the restoration of the state [of the world] through the worship of the sandals according to the word of Śaṃkara.

The attainment of all perfections by his own disciple; the vision of Garuḍa and Viṣṇu and the hymn of praise to Śāṇḍilī; thereafter, the narration of the primary discourse according to the words of Śāṇḍilī; the description of the greatness of the Pādukā-māhātmya; Garuḍa’s journey to the excellent Hāṭakeśvara [Kṣetra], where, having bowed to Sadāśiva, Kālabhairava, Nīlarudra, and others, he performed the worship of Śiva; the description of the greatness of the Bahiṣtīrtha; the younger brother Śantanu’s performance of the funeral rites for his elder brother; and the description of Garuḍa’s golden-feathered body once again.

In the narration of the greatness of Suparṇa’s sacrifice, King Veṇu, due to his lack of devotion toward the gods, was afflicted by the impurity resulting from the ripening of his evil conduct. To dispel that impurity, King Veṇu set out toward the god Suparṇa; however, perceiving him to be a mere bird, Śakra caused a drought as a means of disregarding him. Consequently, Vidurāmitra, wandering in the forest, went to the house of a Caṇḍāla and performed the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) there with dog meat obtained through theft, cooking it over a fire.

By that [incident], the description of his removal of the curse is given. Because he was enraged by the fire, he performed a complete concealment of himself through his own power. When the supreme name "Sumadrā" had been proclaimed by the elephants and others during the Kṛṣṇa incarnation—after the daughter of the sage Ṛcīka, who had been offered as a bride by Viṣṇu’s curse, had been seen by the gods desiring her for themselves—the elephant and the rest, being angry toward him, were cursed by him. Following the release from the curse previously granted, there is the description of Viṣṇu’s sisterhood and other matters; [and finally] the giving [of the gift].

Having seen that Indra’s head had been severed by Brahmā for the purpose of protecting himself, Śiva performed austerities directed toward Brahmā in order to remove the curse. When it was said, "By means of the offering of the hindquarters of the sacrificial animal (*vājajaghanī*) prepared by Viśvakarman, after the curse was lifted by Brahmā, my own self has been protected," Śiva granted him a boon. Brahmā bestowed upon him the name Gajavaktramahālakṣmī, and by his own command, Śakra [was restored].

The bringing of rain; then the granting of a boon by Brahmā at Abhratīrtha; the greatness of that lake as Abhratīrtha, and the *Nahālakṣmīmāhātmya*... [the ceremony of] naming; therein, the majesty of the continuous stream of clarified butter (*vasodhārā*) poured into the fire; the greatness of Abhratīrtha; for the sake of increasing the joy of the Moon-god, who was afflicted by twenty-seven daughters, through the propitiation of Caṇḍī at Hāṭakeśvara; the making of the Moon the lord of the quarters; and the establishment of the sage [Bṛhaspati] under the name Saptaviṃśati.

The consolation of the elephants and other creatures who had been driven outside by the heat of the sun’s rays, following the granting of protection by the gods beginning with Brahmā; then the description of the emergence of the [divine] energy (*devatā*). ... Bhūḥ (Bha, Dha, Da, Da); the departure of each to their respective abodes, and the description of the manifestation of the *Abhayavīrya* (Fearless Heroism). ...

Description of the majesty of the Somapāda temple; description of the majesty of the Garahakuṇḍa established by me, Āṇḍeya; therein, the account of how a certain person performing a sacrifice caused the deity residing at Kādīrāja—known by the names Ambāvṛddha and Pināśkecara—to be installed for the protection of the city, surrounded by a multitude of attendants. ... Description of the origin of the power of Gomukha, preceded by a description of the greatness of the Gomukha-tīrtha; therein, the performance of penance by King Ambarīṣa for the sake of removing the leprosy that had afflicted his own son; the narration by the Lord, being pleased with him, of the faults committed by that son in a previous birth; the description of how, by the command of the Lord, the son’s disease was removed through bathing at the Gomukha-tīrtha; and the description of the great majesty of the Gomukha-tīrtha. ... |||

—After the words of Vasiṣṭha, Paraśurāma broke his axe and, by releasing the iron staff, established the *ḍoda* staff in its place; this is the description of taking up the *rohayaṣṭi*. (In the description of the origin of the Goddess, which includes the breaking of the sacrificial post and the performance of rites, there is the departure of Ajāpāla for the excellent forest of Dāṭaka at the word of Vasiṣṭha; having propitiated the Goddess there, the Goddess, being pleased with him, granted him boons; by accepting the boons, [he saw] the people who were suffering in hell while remaining in the kingdom of Ajāśṛṅga.)

Seeing that there were no sinners left and observing his state of refuge, Mṛtyu departed for the world of Brahmā. While staying there, Śiva heard of this; assuming the form of a tiger, he went into the presence of the king. After the tiger had devoured the goat, the king dispatched Caṇḍidatta and others [to kill it], but they were themselves eaten by Śaṅkara in the form of the tiger. Subsequently, due to the lack of food, the tiger engaged the king in a hand-to-hand struggle. Then, casting off the tiger's form, Śiva [revealed himself] to him.

The granting of a direct vision; the description of Śiva by Ajāpāla; the king’s departure for Pātāṭha at the word of Śiva and the installation of a linga under his own name; the installation of Caṇḍī by the daughter of Ajāpāla named Devī; the description of the majesty of Ajāpāla-devī; King Duṣṭharatha, having heard from the astrologer Bhūdhara about future events such as the siege of Rodinī and the piercing of the moon, goes to the vicinity of Śāṇḍilya to wage war in order to avert them; and [the account of] him being pleased upon seeing his prowess.

Śanaiścara made a vow, saying, "I shall not pierce this army," and granted him the gift of fearlessness; he recounted the fruit of the dialogue between Śanaiścara and Daśaratha, preceded by a description of Daśaratha’s heroism and the counting of his innumerable armies; then, having learned from the mouth of Kakutstha that he was childless, he undertook preparations for performing austerities for the sake of obtaining a son; [Pañcama Parvan] Śanaiścara, having first made the vow, "I shall not pierce the army of Rāma," subsequently bestowed a blessing upon him after Indra had likewise done so.

Regarding the section beginning with "Sadṛati": Daśaratha went to the kingdom of Haṭakeśvara and performed penance; Viṣṇu, pleased by that penance, granted a boon to Daśaratha, saying, "I shall incarnate as one possessing four forms. Viṣṇu, who had been worshipped by him at the site of Daśaratha’s penance, took his own name for that place—calling it Rājasvāmī—and named the pond he had constructed "Rājavāpī. This is followed by a description of the greatness of Rājasvāmī and Rājavāpī.

On the occasion of the installation of Rāmeśvara, after Rāma had abandoned Sītā and begun a sacrifice having fashioned a golden image of her, Durvāsas arrived there. A description of the dialogue between Durvāsas and Rāma follows, including how Lakṣmaṇa disobeyed Rāma’s command and departed from the city by Rāma’s order; the description of the removal of Lakṣmaṇa’s fault through bathing in the Sarayū; and subsequently, the departure of Lakṣmaṇa’s life-force through the practice of yoga. Seeing Lakṣmaṇa ascended to heaven, Rāma...

The making of the Śaka era; the consoling of Rāma by his ministers; the utterance of a voice from the sky forbidding Rāma—who had seen Lakṣmaṇa’s body and was about to perform the funeral rites—as he was about to abandon the consecration, saying "the funeral rites have already been performed"; thereafter, following the performance of Lakṣmaṇa’s post-mortem rites, Rāma’s journey to Kiṣkindhā by means of the Puṣpaka chariot; there, the description of the hospitality and honors offered by Sugrīva; then, having mounted the Puṣpaka, Rāma’s journey with the monkeys to Laṅkā; and there, [the meeting] with Vibhīṣaṇa.

The honoring of Rāmacandra; then, Śrī Rāma’s arrival at the holy site of Hāṭakeśvara together with all of them, the installation there of the image of Rāmeśvara, the description of the majesty of Rāmeśvara, and the description of the consecration of the five palaces of Lakṣmaṇa.

The arrival of Rāma at Ānarvabarada Lake along with the Rākṣasas; therein, during the conversation between Rāma and the Brahmin, the description of the majesty of the lake following the account of the previous birth of a blind Brahmin who, while seated in a celestial chariot surrounded by Apsarases on his way back to heaven, beheld it; and the description of the greatness of the Ānarta-tīrthaṅkapikā.

Now, after Śrī Rāmacandra had departed for his own realm, the Rākṣasas arrived at the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara to worship Śiva; there, they terrified the Brāhmaṇas by devouring those who had been brought there. Upon seeing this, Śrī Rāma, through the agency of the monkey Nala, brought about the defeat of the Rākṣasas. Furthermore, many Liṅgas were installed by the Rākṣasas in the lake situated there. Then, having sent a message to Vibhīṣaṇa, [Rāma] caused the destruction of the Rākṣasas through him.

The construction of the Nirodha temple; the description of the installation of Chareśvara and Khveśvara; when Tughlaq arrived, Marīcimākhin was struck by the curse of Vibhīṣaṇa, and at dawn, the Rākṣasa-hā [the destroyer of demons] filled the earth with four-faced lingas established by the Rākṣasas at the shrine of Ṭakeśvara; there, in the region of Prākhādraḍita, King Bṛhadaśva went; and there, upon the site of Prākhāda, the king had a palace constructed. Then, at the time of digging the ground...

—The description of the four gates; the account of the two kings digging the earth covered by the *chiga* (mound); the narration of the event concerning the covering of the *rākṣasa-chiga*; the description of the greatness of the sixty-four holy sites (*tīrtha*). ...

A description of the account of establishing the sixty-eight *liṅgas*. ... In the description of the sixty-eight sacred sites (*tīrtha*) within the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī, Nārada, Vyāsa, and others, beginning with the performance of rites at the *Camatkāra-kṣetra*, worship the *Śivaliṅga* and offer hymns of praise to the sacred sites and *liṅgas*; this is the description of the sixty-eight sacred sites of Vārāṇasī. Following this is the description of the nature of the sixty-eight sacred sites, preceded by the mention of the names of the distinct and non-distinct *liṅgas* located upon the banks of the rivers. Finally, there is the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the sixty-eight sacred sites.

At one time, Damayantī, the wife of King Nala, went to the sacred site of Hāṭakeśvara. On the day of Hari-bodha (the full moon of Vaiśākha), having learned that it was a holy ford (*tīrtha*), she was seen meditating upon the Lord; another Brahmin woman friend then approached her and described Damayantī’s beauty. After Damayantī finished her meditation, she gave away all her ornaments to the other women, with the exception of four female ascetics.

The refusal to accept ornaments from all the wives of the ministers; likewise, the daily giving of ornaments to them by the queen; on the fifth day, when the four wives of the ministers did not accept the ornaments, she took the ornaments from them and went away, saying, "These are impermanent objects"; their showing contempt for the acceptance of those ornaments; and as for those by whom the contempt was shown for the ornaments brought from Videha, who were they?

The wives returned to their own hermitage by way of the sky through the power of their own merit; however, because they had cast away the ornaments given to them by Damayantī out of shame, those husbands—due to the sin resulting from the curse uttered by that woman when she was seized by grief—fell right there as soon as their desire for life had ended. When Nala arrived by way of the sky-path, he saw the cause of this and pronounced a curse upon Damayantī, saying, "Become a stone," whereupon Damayantī turned into a stone at that spot.

Having reached that downfall and heard its account, the king of the Ānarta country came there to propitiate the twice-born; he caused his wife, who had become like a stone, to be released from her grief.

The description of how that land became barren because, when the Brahmins who had taken up water to cast a curse upon the king were pacified by the entreaties of another Brahmin, they instead poured the water onto the ground; furthermore, the account of the origin and sacred power (*māhātmya*) of that saline site, and how the lord of Ānarta went every month to Hāṭakeśvara, propitiated the Brahmins, performed rites for peace and so forth, and returned to his own city, [and] how, at the word of Vahni, someone [performs] the future *dhautaka* rite month after month.

Because that most base Brāhmaṇa did not accept the gift of wealth and other offerings under the pretext of performing the planetary rites (*graha-uddeśa*), it was understood that he was causing excessive suffering to the Brāhmaṇas. When a request was made by everyone, it was declared that all would attain purification by bathing at that sacred site (*tīrtha*), with the exception of one Brāhmaṇa. That impure Brāhmaṇa, having been excluded, then made a request to all the Brāhmaṇas, and the installation of the sacred fire (*agni*) was performed at that sacred site.

After the *trijātaka* [episode], a twice-born man named Abhiṇḍa, having gone to the forest with his wife, performed austerities. Śiva, pleased by those austerities, granted him a boon. While residing in Camatkārapura, Devarāta’s son, named Kratha, went to the Nāga-tīrtha. There, Kratha saw the son of the lord of the Nāgas named Śadramākha and struck him with a stone pestle. Seeing the killing of his son, Vasipiṅgala, Mākṛti, and others were filled with grief. Then—

When the rākṣasas first began the devouring of the people standing before them with cries of "ruṣaṭ," they commenced by eating the son of Devarāta along with his family; thereafter, those standing on Mount Bhara, terrified by fear, [cried out] "ṇa cla ka sa sa-va ra śa ta."
ṇṣa-na-stasya oṃ vi-kya-tha-ya-pa-ma-na-na-amuka.
The topics of the chapters [beginning with] *ṭha*, *cha*, and *ka*: what are they? ... the topics of the subsequent chapters; [this is] from the *Sko.ma.pa* [commentary], verse 51.

The narration of the birth of Ra-bava; the removal of the suffering of his son by means of his own [power]; the arrival of all the people near the Trijāta Brāhmaṇa; hearing of that suffering, the Trijāta performed propitiatory rites for Śiva and received a boon from the Lord to dispel the fear of the disease; and for those residing there who were afflicted by the poison, he gave them the great mantra, "Not poison, not poison," which acts as an antidote to the poison.

By the victory of that great mantra, he caused the serpents to become city-dwellers; thus the city itself was given the name of that [serpent] city. He gave the name "Nāgara" to the Brahmins residing there, and thereafter the venomous serpents became devoid of poison and began to roam about. This is the description of the account of the origin of the city.

[The description of] the lineage and other details of the Ātreya clan through the narration of his birth; the account of those ending in *sadyanta* and *uktanta* from the Ātreyas; the performance of sacrifices by Bharadvāja and the exposition on the system of the sage-lineages (*munigotra*); the seeing of the Brahmin’s sister named Bhaṭṭikā by Revatī-sarpiṇī out of curiosity after eating a *ṭuṃba* fruit; and the rebirth of Revatī-sarpiṇī in human form upon remembering her previous life as Bhaṭṭikā; and the propitiation of the Goddess performed by Revatī.

The establishment of a holy ford (tīrtha) by her own name at the command of the Goddess; the Goddess’s extensive praise of her as Ambā, Durgā, and so forth; and the narration of the greatness [of the place] preceded by the origin of the Ambārevatī Tīrtha.

Oṃ. When Takṣaka was about to bite Bhadrikā’s foot, she gave him a curse, saying, "Then you shall become a mortal. She then uttered a curse accompanied by a wailing cry of lamentation. Takṣaka set out for Bhadrikā’s wooden hut; there, Bhadrikā provided proof of her own purity by asking the fire, and when that fire was kindled, she made it cold by performing a miracle, and a shower of fragrant flowers fell from the sky.

The composition of the hymn to Derabṛkatidikā; Bhaddikā’s return to her own home after learning of her impending death from the words of a divine messenger; the establishment of a sacred site (tīrtha) by her at that very place under her own name; and the narration of the origin and greatness of Bhaddikātīrtha.

The description of the account of Kṣemaka’s birth on earth through the curse of Raivata, following his attainment of malice toward Bhaddikā; his departure for the Rākṣasa forest; and subsequently, their journey to the holy field (kṣetra) of Hāṭakeśvara and the installation of a Śiva-liṅga; and the description of the origin and greatness of Kṣemakarīraivateśvara.

[The description of the battle of King Taścañjana; the entrustment of his son to the kingdom and his departure with Kṣemaṅkarā to the mountain Raivata for the slaying of the Daityas, beginning with Madadhiṣu; the description of the birth of Kātyāyanī; the granting of a curse by Durvāsas to King Dīrghabāhu, saying "Become a buffalo," followed by his transformation into a buffalo; the propitiation of Śiva at Hāṭakeśvara by the command of Śukra; then, after Śiva had said, "Your death shall not occur without [your wife] Śrī," he granted him the boon of being invulnerable to others.]

A description of the visit to Mahiṣatīrtha; a description of the battle between the gods and the Daityas at Mahiṣapura; the defeat of the Daitya army by the gods; the gods, having united with Bṛhaspati, holding a council for the sake of increasing their own splendor; Kātyāyanī mounting a lion and going to the Vindhya mountains to perform penance; seeing her in the form of radiant energy, Mahiṣāsura, emaciated by passion, arrives there with his army and makes a request to her to become his wife.

The description of the great battle between the Goddess and the demon Mahiṣāsura, who became exceedingly enraged when his words were rejected by the Goddess; then, as Kātyāyanī began to seize the head of the Daitya Mahiṣa with her hand in order to perform the rite of *rātrivijñāna*, Gaṇeśa offered a hymn of praise to the Goddess; thereafter, out of compassion, the Goddess granted life to Mahiṣāsura, and thus, following the defeat of Mahiṣa, Kātyāyanī stood having trampled upon Mahiṣāsura.

The description of the majesty of Kātyāyanī; the naming of the stone situated there as Kedāra due to that context; and the description of the majesty of Kedāra. Regarding the description of the majesty of Śuṅatīrtha: because of the ignorance of the washermen named Śuddhaka, they threw fine garments into the middle of the river. Upon hearing this, the daughter of the washerman informed her friend, the daughter of the fisherman, of her father's conduct. Having learned of that, the fisherman’s daughter remembered the water-rite (*jalārāya*) that brings whiteness to black clothes, and [informed] the washerman...

The presentation of that [garment] to the maiden; then, the washerman’s daughter also reporting to her father, Śuddhakāya, the method described by her friend; therein, the washerman’s delusion regarding the extreme impurity of those garments even after washing them with alkaline salt; the washerman’s report of the incident concerning the garments and so forth to the Brāhmaṇas; then, the manifestation of the supernatural power (*siddhi*) of that bathing-place at every holy ford (*tīrtha*); and the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Śarutīrtha.

The Lord, gratified by the hymns of Hiraṇyākṣa and Gaḍitirada, assumed the form of a buffalo and uttered "Oṃ Dārayāmi" (I split). [End of chapter]. **Contents of Chapter 13:** The description of the origin of the Mukhāra-tīrtha; the narration of the life story of Vāsmīki, also known as Khohajaṅgha; and the description of the greatness of the sacred ford (tīrtha-māhātmya), wherein Yājñavalkya, having observed the extraordinary affection of Maitreyī for her husband, perceives a similar love from him toward himself.

The departure of Kātyāyanī, his second wife, to the presence of Śāṇḍilī in order to fulfill her purpose; the description of the Karṇotpala Tīrtha at Śāṇḍilī; the account of the birth of another daughter from King Satyasandha at the Karṇotpala Tīrtha; the narration by Kātyāyanī of her own circumstances to Śāṇḍilī; Kātyāyanī’s inquiry, following Śāṇḍilī’s words, as to which of the suitors this Karṇotpala girl should be given; the departure of King Satyasandha, accompanied by his daughter, for the world of Brahmā; and the performance of the worship of Gaurī until that point.

The description of the greatness of the five-piṇḍikā Gaurī; ... the daughter’s petition to her father, who was intent on remaining in the world of Brahmā at his word; the account of the origin of Īśāna, the greatness of the five-piṇḍikā Gaurī, and the greatness of Gaṇapati installed by Varavarcas;

... the king’s departure for his own country at the daughter’s request, his amazement upon seeing the transformation of the land, and the description of the origin and greatness of the Vāstupada-tīrtha established there by Kātyāyana.

The mutual conversation between them and the recounting of their respective life stories; the description of the greatness of the birth of Ajāgṛha, fashioned from goat-skin by Satyasaṃdha who was accompanied by his daughter; the description of his performing penance in that very vicinity; the departure of Dāritapalanyā to fetch water for bathing; the arrival of Kāmadeva at that same spot due to the impulse of passion; the performance of penance by King Satyasaṃdha and the consecration of the Linga; and the description of the greatness of Satyasaṃdha’s boon.

Having understood the truth regarding Kāma and his wife, Hārīta pronounced a curse upon them. Therein, the daughter of Satyasandha, known as Karṇotpalā, performed penance to the goddess Udīkya for the sake of recovering her husband. While she was engaged in that penance, it is described how she attained the state of being a parrot due to the curse of her husband. When Kāma had returned to his own nature by the word of the Brahmin, Karṇotpalā bathed at the Gītī-tīrtha by the command of the goddess; through that worship, she regained her youth.

The description of the cessation of the *chṭha* [festival]; the description of the origin and greatness of the *kūpikā* (small well) of Khaṇḍaśiḍhā-Saubhāgya; the description of the river Rāptī; upon seeing its beauty, when Kāmadeva made a prayer with the desire to possess it, there is the description of the origin of the *dīrghikā* (long pond). Then, by the Brahmin Vīraśarman, for the sake of warding off the evil influence from his daughter, the performance of the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow; by Satyasaṃdha, having learned the intention of his daughter, the making of a daily vow for that Kāma and for his daughter; and likewise by the daughter.

The performance of the *trataka* rite; the giving away of the Kulin Brahmin according to the ritual of taking the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) at the word of Rāka; the establishment of the deity Karṇotpala under his own name; her journey to sixty-eight sacred fords (*tīrtha*) following the husband’s command; and the description of the greatness of the Karṇaparvata Tīrtha on the way.

The bestowing of curses upon those two by Māṇḍavya; the obstruction of the sun’s course by her; the raising of the sun through the words of the King of Ānarta, who was true to his promise, saying, "We shall restore our lord to life, for we have seen this land without a king," and that she would provide milk from her breasts for the child; the death of the wicked Brāhmaṇa; the account of the birth of his sons known as Ṣaṭha and the others; and the description of the greatness of Aṣṭāvakra. ...

The restoration of Saṃjñī; the granting of boons by the gods to that devoted wife for her steadfastness; the curse pronounced upon Yama by Māṇḍavya—who was being held in his hand by Yājñavalkya out of anger at the obstruction of his own command—to the effect that he would enter a Śūdra womb; the description of the origin of Dīkṣāgara; the offering of knowledge to that sage and the performance of sun-worship for the sake of acquiring that knowledge; and then, by the Sun...

The narration of the cause for Māṇḍavya’s arrival at the tip of a spike... the bestowing of the knowledge of *khādhima* upon Yājñavalkya; [how] having become a goat through that [knowledge], he resorted to Sūrya-cakra and performed penance to destroy the curse of Māṇḍavya by Dharmarāja; and the description of the origin of Dharmarājeśvara.

The recitation of the Vedas by Yājñavalkya, who had gone forth from the lineage of Sūrya; the description of his grief following the death of his five-year-old son, the Brahmin named Upādhyāya, born of the Kadaca family, after he had completed the acquisition of all branches of knowledge; the composition by Yājñavalkya of these Upaniṣads, which are the essence of the Vedas; and then, out of anger, the Brahmin’s bestowing of a curse upon Yama at Hāṭakeśvara in his own name; and the arrival of the cursed Yama before Brahmā.

The description of the greatness of the Yājñavalkyāśrama-tīrtha; the departure of Yama to Hāṭakeśvara for the purpose of avoiding a curse due to the word of Brahmā; then, after Yama had assumed the form of a twice-born and described the greatness of the Ṭiga-tīrtha which bestows sweet food, the story of King Vasusena who, having gone to heaven by making many gifts, fell from it due to his greed; when Vasusena, afflicted by that [fall], questioned Indra, Nārada arrived there at that very moment.

Having seen him, [Vasusena] related the entire account to him; he then delivered his father’s command and message to Satyasena, the son of Vasusena, instructing him to perform the daily offering of food and other rites for his father’s *śrāddha* and so forth. Upon hearing his father’s message through Nārada, Satyasena offered food to his father. Due to the lack of food caused by the drought, Satyasena performed the worship of Śiva. Śiva, being pleased by that worship, granted him whatever food and desired things he wished for. Then—

Satyasena, under the guise of the name Miṣānnadeśvara, arrived there at Jābāli’s command in order to create an obstacle to his penance; there, Rambhā agitated Jābāli’s mind and sported with him in the three worlds created by her power.

(Jāvāli’s seeing his own daughter born of Raṃbhā and his raising of her; when Kumāravatī, Jāvāli’s daughter, had reached youth, she went to the Gandharva Citrasena. Taking that daughter of Jāvāli, the Gandharva went to Devaloka. Then, while searching for her, Jāvāli found his daughter in Devaloka and struck the Gandharva with his staff. And [he struck] the Gandharva.

The pronouncement of the curse; the performance of penance by the Gandharva to remove the curse and the establishment of a *liṅga* upon the cessation of the curse; the performance of penance by the Jābālinī named Phalāvatī for the sake of neutralizing the curse; when a dialogue arose with that maiden—who had attained a divine state through that penance—in the form of a response to Jābāli’s questions, the maiden rendered her father Jābāli speechless; [the account of] the wonderful gift from Jābāliśvara. (aḥ bha ka sa da va pi ya)

Who is not established in the directions? The narration of the greatness of Miṣṭānnadeveśvara; the description of the majesty of the triad of Gaṇapatis. [The subjects of the Bhavyā: the subjects of the Bhavyā, chapter...]: arriving at the house of a Brāhmaṇa and giving [the child] to the Brāhmaṇa as his son; the installation of a Śiva-liṅga by Dharmarāja; in the description of the majesty of Amarareśvara, the defeat of the gods caused by the Daityas and the performance of worship to Ādityeśvara; the description of the narrative of the majesty of Rajeśvara.

...—the description of the defeat of the Daityas in the battle between the gods and the Daityas through such grace of the Lord; the description of the narrative of the son of Dharmarāja because it bestows immortality; the naming of Śiva as Amareśvara; the description of the majesty of the Amareśvara shrine; the description of the manifestation of Amareśvara; the description of the names of Āditya, Vasu, Rudra, and others; the *Māhātmya* (glory) of the Amareśvara Kuṇḍa; the description of the birth of Vyāsa; and the description of the dialogue between Vyāsa and Luksa.

In the description of the origin of Keliśvaśra: the birth of the Asura Andhaka from Hiraṇyakaśipu; the account of his attainment of the kingdom; then, after performing penance for sixty thousand years, Andhaka’s acceptance of a boon from Brahmā; and by means of that boon granted by Brahmā, the intoxicated Andhaka, having conquered the gods including Indra and even Śambhu, engaged in battle with the Goddess—who had emerged from the sacrificial fire-pit fashioned by Śaṃyu—along with her retinue.

—The description of the defeat of his own Daitya army; the invocation of the goddess Kelīśvarī by Śukra when requested by Andhaka, who was distressed by that defeat, using mantras similar to those used by Śambhu to invoke Vahni; thereafter, Andhaka’s obtaining of a boon from that Goddess and his performance of a hymn of praise to Kelīśvarī; and the description of the greatness of Kelīśvarī... —.

Regarding the account of Andhaka and Śiva: it describes how Śiva brought about the defeat of Andhaka during their combat; how, being highly pleased by the hymn of praise offered by Andhaka, the Blessed Lord granted him the name Śṛṅgiriṭi and made him a member of his own retinue of attendants (gaṇas).

Then, following the words of Vasiṣṭha, Suratha—who had been deprived of his kingdom—went to Hāṭakeśvara and established Bhairava; through the worship of that deity, his recovery of the kingdom is described. There follows a description of the majesty of Bhairavaktra. In the description of the majesty of Cakrapāṇi, Arjuna, by the command of Yudhiṣṭhira, goes into the forest for the purpose of protecting the Brahmins and the cows. Having then liberated the cows and completed his pilgrimage, Pārtha (Arjuna) proceeds to Hāṭakeśvara.

The installation of Cakrapāṇi; the description of the majesty of Cakrapāṇi; in the description of the majesty of Rūpatīrtha, the account of the birth of Tilottamā; the departure of Tilottamā for Kāśī by the command of Brahmā; while Tilottamā was performing circumambulation after bowing to Śiva, Śiva’s mind became agitated upon seeing her; Pārvatī, observing this, pronounced a curse upon Tilottamā, saying, "Become many-formed"; then Tilottamā was led by Nandin to the Rūpatīrtha at Hāṭakeśvara.

The journey; by means of that, the granting of boons by Pārvatī to Viṣṇu, who had previously arrived there; the origin and majesty of the Apsaraḥkuṇḍa; and the description of the greatness of Citreśvara-ṛṣi-tīrtha. || 1 ||

After the dispute with Maṇibhadra, Maṇibhadra subjected the Brahmin named Puṣpa to mockery; then the city-dwellers, having first offered him consolation, invited that Brahmin for a meal. Thereupon, even while partaking of the meal, Puṣpaka departed for Camatkārapura to propitiate the Sun-god, accompanied by mantras.

Having performed the fire sacrifice with all its constituent parts using his own flesh, including the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and so forth, he observed the Sun’s return to his presence; the Sun then granted Puṣpa the power to assume the form of Maṇibhadra and to change his own appearance, as well as knowledge of mantras and other such things. Puṣpa, the Brāhmaṇa, established the deity Puṣpāditya under his own name. A description of the majesty of Puṣpāditya follows: by the power of the pill given by the Sun, Puṣpa assumed a form equal to that of Maṇibhadra and went to the house of Maṇibhadra. Of him—

Having gone to the house of Satyamāṇibhadra, he gratified the eunuch standing at the door with money and other goods, and having gratified his wife with money, ornaments, and the like, he enjoyed sexual union with her at his pleasure. Then, at the word of Chatrimamāṇibhadra, Satyamāṇibhadra was reviled by the eunuch standing at the door. A dispute between Chatrimamāṇibhadra and Attrimamāṇibhadra is described in the royal palace; thereafter, by the king’s command, [the matter of] Attrimamāṇibhadra’s wife...

When he refused to accept [the boy] as his own son, the King’s decree ordered that this artificial Maṇibhadra be executed by the King’s messenger at Śākhāvaṭa. Then, having summoned his circle of trusted associates, that artificial Puṣparūpamaṇibhadra described the distribution of food, clothing, and other gifts; there follows a description of the abundance of flowers. By means of Māhikā, the Puṣpa-brāhmaṇa assumed his former flower-body and instructed Māhikā in the science of spells (*sīkhyakara*). Thereafter, by means of that Puṣpa—

Having given wealth to his sons, he went to the Hāṭakeśvara Tīrtha to atone for the sin he had committed; there, he performed preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*) and invited Brāhmaṇas. [In the temple] of Puṣpāditya, there is a description of the greatness of the origin of the serpent Puṣpāditya-māhikā. In the account of the *Puraścaraṇa-saptamī-vrata*, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Roditāśva, the ritual procedure is described. Therein, the specific distinctions of worship for each month are detailed, and how Puṣpāditya was worshipped by a certain Brāhmaṇa named Caṇḍarāma.

The description of the ritual procedure for the *Puraścaraṇa-saptamī-vrata*; the public humiliation of Caṇḍaśarman when Puṣpa’s sins were destroyed through the rite of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed by him after he had thoroughly examined the scriptures; thereafter, the performance of austerities (*tapas*) by that Brāhmaṇa Caṇḍaśarman; while Caṇḍaśarman was circumambulating Puṣpa and his wife and performing a fire-oblation (*homa*) with his own flesh, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Bhairavas, offered his own head; [the account] by Sūryadāsa.

The account of Puṣpacanda and Śāmeṇa attaining a beautiful form preceded by the removal of their sins; the description of the origin and history of the Brahmanagara [community]; then again, the journey of Puṣpacanda and Śāmeṇa to the bank of the Sarasvatī; there, having performed worship including the construction of a linga by Dama, Caṇḍaśāmeṇa established a linga under the name Nāgareśvara; Śākaṃbhārī, the wife of Caṇḍaśāmeṇa, also established the goddess Śākambharī; and by Caṇḍaśāmeṇa, the installation of Nāgarāditya on the bank of the Sarasvatī.

The description of the greatness of Nāgareśvara, Varanāgara, Āditya, Śākambharī, and Tapatī; ... the narration of the birth of Viśvāmitra; the departure of Ṛcīka to request a maiden from Gādhi; thereafter, after the request, King Gādhi’s vow that he would give a daughter provided she bore a son with a thousand black teeth; for the sake of obtaining such a girl with black teeth, Ṛcīka performed austerities on the banks of the Sarasvatī; then, through the power of his mantras, Ṛcīka went into the presence of Gādhi accompanied by a girl with black teeth.

Description of the Aśvatīrtha pilgrimage site. Contents: [The topic of] giving; description of the greatness of the worship of the Śaṅku-movement; description of the removal of the curse of Oḍḍāṃbarī; the arrival of the local deities there along with the Lord (Īśvara); when the group of Mothers (Mātṛgaṇa) departed from her presence to return to their respective abodes, Sāvitrī’s narration of the account of the granting of boons to the Mātṛgaṇa; ... the description of the previous birth of Oḍḍāṃbarī preceded by her attainment of liberation; ... |

“Having summoned all the city-dwellers, Brahmā performed a sacrifice for them; he recounted to them the entire account of the sacrifice and the origin of the sacred ford (*tīrtha*). Then, having completed the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), Brahmā went to the foremost Puṣkara. He granted boons to Brahmā and the others [the gods], and at that time, Brahmā also granted a boon to Yakṣman who had arrived there. This is the description of the origin and greatness of the Yakṣma-tīrtha.”

A description of the emergence of ill omens and portents occurring at the time when Sāvitrī was about to enter the sacrificial pavilion; the arrival there of the Apsarases, Dhṛtācī and others; and a description of their singing, instrumental music, laughter, and so forth.

Nārada recounts to Sāvitrī the account of Gāyatrī’s marriage and other events; having heard this narrative told by Nārada, Sāvitrī is filled with grief. At the word of Gaurī, she disregards Nārada’s speech and proceeds to the sacrificial pavilion of Brahmā. There, Sāvitrī brings about a state of sleep in Brahmā and bestows a curse upon him. Then Sāvitrī pronounces curses upon Śakra, Agni, the Nāgaras, the Brāhmaṇas, the officiating priests (ṛtvij), and others. Thereafter, Sāvitrī departs from that place, traveling on foot.

The journey after ascending a mountain; the description of the greatness of Sāvitrī’s speech. After Sāvitrī had departed, Gāyatrī, remaining there, first brought about the cessation of all the curses given by Sāvitrī and then bestowed boons. ... [naḥ] ...

The description of Svadā’s performance of the *gāyatrī* hymn; the narration of the equal lifespans of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśāna; the enumeration of the durations of time from a *nimeṣa* up to the end of a *kalpa*; and the description of the greatness of the sandals of the Kṣatriya who went to the two Umārikā Tīrthas for the sake of attaining the knowledge of Brahman. In the description of the two Umārikā Tīrthas, there is the narration of the mutual friendship between the daughter of the Brāhmaṇa named Nāga, a student of the *Chāndogya*, and the daughter of the King of Ānarta named Rājñāvatī.

Chapters and Subjects: The return of Dāśārṇādhipati Avadharavarṇa, the lord of Ānarta, to his city. At that time, a certain son of Viśvāvasu named Parāvasu—a Brahmin learned in the Vedas—having gone to the house of a courtesan, was overcome by sleep at night; due to the affliction of lust, he unknowingly committed an act of sexual intercourse. Thereafter, filled with remorse, he went in the morning to Śaṅkhatīrtha, performed rites such as shaving, and stayed at a distance from the house of an outcaste woman.

"Those who are his fellow-students"—this refers to the group of five. By means of a joking remark to those hundred fellow-students, through the seizing of Rājñavatī’s breast and the tasting of her lower lip, there would be liberation from that sin; such was the statement regarding the penance. Then, by the command of the Guru, Viśvāvasu related the entire account. Now, seeing Viśvāvasu prepared to undergo the penance consisting of the consumption of clarified butter as prescribed for one who has tasted [forbidden things] in the *Dharmaśāstra* by a Brahmin, his mother and father spoke harsh words to him. Thus ends the section.

Thinking that the drinking of wine might be remedied by the act of embracing the breasts and tasting the lips of Ratnāvatī, the Brahmin students, out of delusion, prescribed a penance. Upon hearing this, they returned with all their followers to the king and made a plea for the life of the Brahmin. When the king asked his daughter, "Please grant favor so that the Brahmin may perform his penance," she, out of love for her son, granted that Brahmin the permission to perform his penance.

When that Brahmin had been commanded by me for the purpose of drinking from his own lips after having his own breast milked, and he had acted accordingly, milk flowed forth from the mouth of the Brahmin and from both breasts of Ratnāvatī. Then, the Brahmin was filled with great wonder. The description of the gods' peak named Śāligrāma on the Gaṇḍakī river and the account of its attainment; the description of the greatness of Śāligrāma; the description of the greatness of offering gifts during the Cāturmāsya; the installation of deities during the four months; the installation of deities such as Śakra, Varuṇa, Yama, and Kubera, in their respective order, upon various other trees; the description of the greatness of the trees; the description of the conversation between Pārvatī and Śaṅkara; and [the account of] the gods at Mandarācala during the Cāturmāsya.

While the Lord was intent upon the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the gods arrived at his presence; then, having been told by Hara, "You must come to assist me for the sake of pleasing Pārvatī," they accepted his words and departed for their respective abodes. Subsequently, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, Hara performed a dance to please Bhavānī. On that occasion of the dance, Brahmā and the other gods, as well as the great sages such as Nārada, Devala, and Vyāsa, arrived at Mount Mandara. At that time—

The arrival there of the Śrīrāga and other musical modes conceived by Hara; while the dance of Hara was proceeding, the gods such as Nārada and others providing assistance; Pārvatī offering a hymn of praise to Hara, being pleased by the dance of Hara; a description of the intensity of Hara’s tāṇḍava dance; a description of the greatness of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa; and the Nāgara-saṃhitā. 59.

The subject matter [of this chapter] is the description of the greatness of the recitation of the ten-syllable mantra of Viṣṇu (*oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya*) and the two-syllable mantra *rāma*, as related in the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī during the Cāturmāsya.

In the dialogue between Īśvara and Pārvatī, there is a description of the greatness of the twelve-syllable mantra by Śiva; then, upon the word of Śiva, when Pārvatī had departed for penance, Śiva, afflicted by desire, went to the Yamunā to bathe. Seeing that the water of the Yamunā had turned black from contact with the body of Hara after he had bathed there, the distressed Yamunā caused a drought. Due to the Yamunā’s distress, Hara established the Haratīrtha. [This occurred] due to a certain other cause.

Śiva, having incurred a curse from the Brahmins, goes to Kailāsa and composes a hymn to the Goddess. The gods, distressed by the curse bestowed upon Hara by the Brahmins, go into the presence of Hara. Thereupon, the establishment of the Amarakantaka Vīrtha is described, along with its majesty; and therein, the installation of the bull Nīlakaṇṭha by the gods, as well as the narrative of the Nīlakaṇṭha Cāturmāsya and the description of the various rites.

—The narration of the birth of Kārsikasvāmin; [the account of] Ṣaḍānana bowing to the syllable *ṅa*, crossing the lords of rivers and streams, and ascending to the stainless celestial chariot (*vimāna*); thereafter, Śiva’s vision of Viṣṇu; then, having crossed the islands of the sun and moon, the mountain Meru, and the oceans, the sight of Viṣṇu and the hymn of praise to Viṣṇu; and, in connection with that, a description of the yoga of meditation (*dhyānayoga*). ... ( ) ;

Having attained the yoga of meditation (*dhyānayoga*) through Śāvatī, and having attained the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), when a prayer was offered to Śiva, the attainment of the yoga of knowledge was described by Him through that twelve-syllable mantra. [The text contains] a description of the seed-syllables (*bīja-varṇa*) of the twelve-syllable mantra; a description of the nature of Viṣṇu; a description of the nature of the Lord as the Virāṭ; and an exposition on the yoga of knowledge.

Śiva’s imparting of the mantra to Pārvatī; the description of the primary essential reality for yogic practitioners; Śiva’s bestowing of the name Malleśvaranātha upon the son born of the fish-lineage who resided on the peak of Mount Malaya; and the description of the birth of Malleśvaranātha.

The description of the consecration of Kārtikeya as the commander-in-chief of the celestial army at the request of the gods oppressed by the demon Tāraka, followed by the account of his battle with Tāraka and the slaying of that demon, and the composition of hymns to Kārtikeya by the gods. Chapter [number], page [number].

Contents: A description of the greatness of the Bhīṣmapañcaka; a description of the ritual procedure for the worship of the Bhīṣmapañcaka; therein, a description of the greatness of Maṅkaṇeśvara at Bhagavatmāthana; a description of the greatness of Siddheśvara, concerning a certain thief who arrived at Devāṭya on Śivarātri for the purpose of keeping a vigil; the determination of the materials for the Tulāpuruṣa gift; a description of the procedure for the Tulāpuruṣa gift; an exposition of the means for attaining the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin); therein, [the description] of the gift of land made of gold.
