The description of the ritual procedure for the skull-cup (kapāla) established by Indra, including the account of the birth of Vṛtrāsura; his attainment of sovereignty and subsequent travels to sixty-eight sacred sites (tīrtha); the falling of the skull from Indra’s hand into the Amitrahada lake; and the arrival of the Jīva-puruṣas there to seize the wealth, whereupon they climbed and took their stand upon a Karṇikāra tree standing near that place—[and the account of] the Dharma [residing] beneath that Karṇikāra forest.

Out of ignorance, that thief plucked and threw *kāṇakāra* leaves over the image of Śiva; during that night, while intending to steal from another's house, he remained awake without effort; through that worship of Śiva which occurred even without his knowledge, that thief was liberated from his state of being a thief and attained a pure, *sāttvika* nature; thereafter, with that purified mind, he listened to the worship of Śiva, and through that association—

The description of the ritual for the worship of Śiva; the narration of the greatness of the worship, vigil, and other rites of Śivarātri; then, the birth of the deceased thief, the lord of Daśārṇa, through the power of his merit; the description of his attainment of the kingdom; the arrival of the great sages Śāṇḍilya, Puṣṭya, and others at the house of the lord of Daśārṇa; the bestowing of auspicious gifts such as cows and others by the sages upon the king; the description of the greatness of Śivarātri; and the description of the greatness of the gift of the four-faced Puruṣa.

The description of the greatness of the fruit of the gift of land; the description of the greatness of Gotameśvara;—[the account of] Śakra, who was distressed by the sin of killing a Brahmin due to the slaying of Vṛtra, and how, at the word of Brahmā, he was freed from the fault of that Brahmin-slaughter; the installation of a Liṅga in that very place; the description of its greatness; and the description of the greatness of Vātakeśvara, preceded by its origin, installed there by the Brāhmaṇa Vātakapana.—The topics of the chapters.

The people asked Aṅgiras, "What is the expiation for this, and how is there liberation from sin? He replied: [This is] the description of the fruit of offering the *pāpapiṇḍa* (sin-ball) through the Indra-yajña; therein, the description of constructing the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and so forth, the installation of the deities beginning with Earth (*Pṛthivī*) on all sides, the description of the procedure for worship accompanied by mantras, the description of the water for the offering of the *pāpapiṇḍa*, and the description of the greatness of the Indra-yajña, followed by the account of how Indra attained the grace of Viṣṇu through the Indra-yajña.

—The description of the account of Indradyumna’s journey to his own body while still alive; after Indradyumna had resided for a long time in the world of Brahmā, the Brahman sent him back toward the earthly realm so that his fame might be manifested on earth again after a long interval; having returned to the earthly realm, Indradyumna questioned Mārkaṇḍeya, who was living a long life there; and by Indradyumna, for the sake of fully recognizing his own fame...

Having seen people who were unable to describe the events connected with Rocaka-pura, [Indradyumna] went to the vicinity of Nāḍījaṅgha at the word of the inhabitants of Kāmpilyapura, together with Mārkaṇḍeya. There, after Indradyumna and Mārkaṇḍeya had explained the reason for their arrival to the distressed Nāḍījaṅgha, Nāḍījaṅgha related his own history, beginning with how he had attained the state of a Rākṣasa due to a curse in a previous birth. [He spoke of this] at the time of the transit of the sun into Capricorn (makara-saṃkramaṇa) on the bank of the river.

The description of the granting of boons by Divodāsa, who was pleased with the offering of clarified butter as a covering; then, after Indradyumna had lost his kingdom, the leading of Mākaṇḍeya and Indradyumna to the presence of Uddālaka Āruṇi, who possessed long life even compared to himself due to the power of his vital channels (*nāḍī-jīvana*).

After Baka Prākārakarṇa had failed to recognize Indradyumna, Indradyumnaprabha explained the cause of his own long life; then, to the indifferent Indradyumna who still did not know his own history, he demonstrated the fault of Baka Prākārakarṇa’s lack of knowledge regarding the identity of Indradyumna and Vātāpi. Consequently, Baka Prākārakarṇa himself took Indradyumna to the presence of a vulture named Gandhamādana, who resided on Mount Gandhamādana and possessed great longevity, and brought Nāḍījaṅgha and Baka along with him. By means of that [vulture]...

The vulture’s narration of his own long life-span and the circumstances of his birth; Indra’s attempt to enter the fire out of indifference due to his lack of recognition of the vulture; the vulture’s bringing of Indradyumna, Mākaṇḍeya, Nāḍījaṅgha, and Prākārakarṇa to the presence of Kama, who dwells in Lake Mānasa despite being himself long-lived, through his request for the earthen clod (prākārakaṇa); and [the events] among those who had gathered there on the shore of the lake.

Having seen Indrayumna with his army, Kūmai entered into the midst of the waters by means of a wooden raft (*tānasaka*). This is the fifth chapter. In connection with the story of Durvāsas, there was a certain head of a monastery named Nivaśuca; while he stood before him, [Indrayumna] beheld a great abundance of sensual objects. Then, when the vulture asked Jaṭambira about the cause of that, the latter related the entire previous account of Indrayumna. When Indrayumna’s stake-fight was won, the gods showered flowers upon Indrayumna.

The bringing about of rain; then, at that very moment, Devadatta brought a celestial chariot and made a request to Indradyumna to go toward the world of Brahmā; Indradyumna, expressing his own lack of desire to go to the world of Brahmā, questioned Kūma regarding the cause of his own long life.

Kūrma first related his own previous history and then performed hospitality for Indradyumna and the others. Thereafter, having met with the great sage Chāgaleya, they learned from him the cause of his long life; then all seven of them established Liṅgas under their respective names. Following that was the description of the origin of the Saptagaṅgā, and within the description of the measure of lifespans, the measurement of time beginning from a *nimeṣa* up to the four ages starting with Kṛta, as well as [the description of] the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices.

The description of attaining the world of the gods, the world of Brahmā, and so forth through various actions; the description of the conditions, duties, and other matters of the celestial realms throughout the four ages (*yugas*); specifically, the determination of the nature of the *kali-yuga* following that; the description of the measure of the lifespans of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others; the description of the measures of the lunar, solar, and civil months; the statement of the measure of the sidereal month; and the description of the measure of the *yugas*.

Do not hide the bundle with any deceptive intent for the sake of gaining trust, thinking you will live as a recluse; for after a long time has passed, at a certain point, you will go with a disciple to the river Muruñjana. There, having placed your own cloak in the hand of your disciple and having gone a great distance to perform the evacuation of urine and excrement, you will return and seize that cloak to wear it as a garment, [thinking] "by one named Nivāśucya."

The head of the monastery, having realized this, was overcome with grief. Then, Duḥśīla, having acquired wealth through that assistance, entered into business; after taking a wife, he claimed her to be his own daughter and went to Camatkārapura together with his wife for the sake of obtaining a son. There, having met with Durvāsas and reported to him the deceptive acts and wicked deeds he had committed against his brother, at the word of Durvāsas, Duḥśīla performed the giving of alms and other rites for the sake of a future son.

The establishment of a *liṅga* by his own name; the narration of the account concerning the cause for bestowing the designation "Duḥśīleśvara" upon that *liṅga*; and the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Duḥśīleśvara and Dvādaśeśvara.

Duḥśīla established a temple named Niveśvara under the pretext of building a cow-pen for his own cattle. Then, Duḥśīla’s wife, named Śākaṃbharī, established a cow-pen for vegetables. When Duḥśīla passed away, his wife Śākaṃbharī caused that Duḥśīla to be cremated along with him in the fire. [The text describes] the establishment of the shrine of Duḥśīleśvara-Niveśvara and the origin of Śākaṃbharyā; and how Śiva assumed eleven forms simultaneously in order to consume all of them at once.

The sages offered hymns of praise upon seeing that elevenfold form; therein is the installation of the eleven Rudras, the description of the origin and majesty of the eleven Rudras, and the enumeration of the names of the eleven Rudras. Following the description of the majesty of giving in the presence of the eleven Carandras, and in the context of the description of the twelve Ādityas, during the occasion of a sacrifice performed by Badhya, Śakra brought the daughter of Govaka as the wife of Brahmā, who was carried away by Govaka from the Ganges.

After the marriage of Gāyatrī and Brahmā, Sāvitrī arrived; however, due to a curse pronounced by Pitāmaha, she took birth in the house of Cārāyaṇa—the great-grandson of Nyuṅgaśepa—under the name Yājñavalkya. Seeing his excessive passion for the wives of others, Yājñavalkya’s father, Cārāyaṇa, expelled him from his own hermitage. Thereupon, having become a disciple of Śākalya, he resided in his house. Then...

Once, while Yājñavalkya was traveling to the royal palace in succession to his disciples for the purpose of bestowing blessings and peace, the king treated him with contempt. Thereafter, when the repentant king made a request on another day for Yājñavalkya to be sent back to the royal residence, the teacher gave Yājñavalkya permission to go to the king's house. However, Yājñavalkya disregarded that command of his teacher and refused to go to the king's palace.

Then, because his preceptor was enraged by Yājñavalkya and pressed him excessively, he vomited up the knowledge he had studied from him and presented that learning back to his guru. Thereafter, for the sake of obtaining knowledge, he performed the propitiation of Sūrya; having then received the knowledge from Sūrya and honored him, he set out alone on an expedition and arrived at the holy site of Hāṭakeśvara amidst a great scramble of eleven thousand [sages] who came there with intense joy. At that time, the students, having pledged to recite the subjects of the *Sūryajñāna*, [proceeded].

The arrival of Yājñavalkya to the presence of his teacher Śākalya in order to give the preceptor’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*); thereafter, having recounted the *Sūryapañca-vidyā* to Śākalya as the preceptor’s fee, Yājñavalkya’s departure with his disciples to the vicinity of the twelve suns (*dvādaśāditya*) together with Śākalya; the description of the origin of the twelve suns, preceded by the narration of the majesty of the birth of Aruṇāditya, followed by the account of the history of Yājñavalkya, and the proclamation of the supreme authority of the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa and its traditional scriptures (*āgama*). In that regard:

The description of the destruction of the Gāgara-khaṇḍa; the description of the majesty of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa; the narration of the hearing of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa; the description of the authority of the teacher and the disciple; and the description of the authority of Vyāsa, the narrator of the Purāṇas.
Thus ends the sixth section, the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. || 6 ||
Now, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, the seventh section, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa. 7.
Now, in the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, first is the majesty of the Prabhāsa constellation.

(—) The opening benediction; a description of the occasion for the inquiry of Sūta by Śaunaka and others; a description of those who are qualified and unqualified to hear the narrative; the posing of questions to Sūta by Śaunaka and the rest; the definition of a narrative (*kathā*); the exposition of the merits and defects of a narrative; a description of the examination of the characteristics of Vedic and human-authored texts; a description of the names and sequence of the eighteen Purāṇas; a description of the names and sequence of the Upapurāṇas; and a description of the number of verses contained in the Mahāpurāṇas.

Description of the procedure and majesty of the gift of the books of the eighteen Great Purāṇas; description of Mount Kailāsa; therein, the description of Śiva’s assembly hall preceded by the description of Śiva’s lion-throne; then the hymn of praise to Śiva by the Goddess; the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī; thereafter, the description by Śrī Śiva to Pārvatī of the Yoga of Vibhūti (the power of manifestation); then the description of the majesty of that [Yoga]; therein, specifically, the description of the majesty of Prabhāsa-kṣetra, out of a desire to hear the majesty of the sacred fords situated within Prabhāsa-kṣetra.

Pārvatī’s inquiry regarding Śaṅkara; [the dialogue] between Pārvatī and Śaṅkara, the best of the Pāśupatas, concerning the measurement of the land at the boundary of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra and the extent of the Jālandhara-kṣetra.

A description of the sequence of pilgrimages to the sacred site of Prabhāsa; a description of the three types of pilgrimage categorized as Maheśvara, Vaiṣṇava, and Bāhya; therein, a description of the various deities [of those categories] as well; a description of the fruits of reciting mantras such as the Mūrtiyoga; a description of how even great sinners residing at the sacred site of Prabhāsa attain liberation; and a description of the majesty of the divine attendants (Dauvārika-gaṇas) who protect the sacred site of Prabhāsa.

[This section contains] a description of the great sages such as Marīci and others, of the gods, of the celestial rishis, and of the holy rivers such as the Gaṅgā residing in the sacred precinct of Prabhāsa; a brief description of the efficacy of offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) in the field of Prabhāsa; a description of the greatness of various kinds of gifts in the field of Prabhāsa; and a description of the hosts of deities residing there.

In this [chapter], there is a description of the greatness of Śivā and the description of the manifested forms of Someśa, such as Pañcavaktra and others; a hymn to Someśa; a description of the true nature [of the deity] through the distinct states of servitude (*dāsya*) and so forth during the eight-fold divisions of the day; a description of the majesty of Somanātha; and, within the description of the origin of Somanātha, when the seventh Brahmā was presiding, the emergence of the *liṅga* which was named Somanātha—[the account of] how, upon the words of Pārvatī, Śaṅkara [established it] for all people of that time.

A description of the Brahmas and Prajāpatis in sequential order by name; likewise, in that same context, a description of Someśa under a different name; and a narration by Śaṅkara to Pārvatī concerning his future incarnations, preceded by the mention of the names of Pārvatī as they will be in each respective birth. Then, in the seventh Brahmā named Rātānanda, Candra propitiated Śiva and, having obtained a boon from Śiva, established the shrine of Someśvara after his own name.

An extensive account of the location of Prabhāsasthala; therein, a description of the Devikā, Yamunā, Vīkaṣatrapīṭha, Bhagṛha, Goyulāśvamedhaka, and other divine abodes; followed by a description of the greatness of all the holy fords (tīrthas) situated around Somanātha; a narrative of the manifestation of Somanātha; and further, in the narration of the majesty of Someśa, a description of the origin of the eight supernatural powers (siddhis), such as Ṛddhi, as well as the Garuḍa-mantras and other vidyās attained through the grace of Someśa, and the power gained by worshipping this Someśa.

The description of Gaṇḍa, Suṇḍa, and others who have departed, in their proper sequence; the description of Semeśvara and Īśvara; the explanation of the reason why he himself wears a garland of *suṇḍas*; the account of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others being intoxicated with passion and their subsequent conversation; the statement by Śiva that "birth" refers to the objects of the senses; the making of his permanent residence in the holy field named Bhramāsa during the passing of the *koṭi-kalpa*; and the reaction of the Goddess, who was struck with wonder upon hearing those words of Śiva.

The performance of the hymn of praise to Śiva; then, by the boon granted to Pārvatī by Śiva, who was pleased by that hymn, stating, "I shall describe the majesty of the Liṅgas situated in Prabhāsa-kṣetra"; Pārvatī’s posing of questions regarding the incarnations of Viṣṇu, such as the Matsya and others; then, by Śaṅkara, the description of the dwellings of Brahmā and the other gods in Prabhāsa, and the description of the abode of Hari.

A description of the locations and colors of the five deities within the five great elements; a sequential description of the various holy bathing places (tīrthas) situated in the sacred field (kṣetra), beginning with Chāgaraṇḍa and others, including those belonging to Lord Viṣṇu; a description of the greatness of the many Liṅga-tīrthas located in the site of Prabhāsa; and a description of how the sacred field of Prabhāsa is the most excellent among all sacred fields.

Then follows the description of the eight principal mountain ranges surrounding Jambūdvīpa; the description of the nine divisions constituting the boundaries of the extent of Jambūdvīpa; therein, the excellent description of Bhārata-varṣa as a land of merit and virtue; the description of the arrangement of the lunar mansions and planets above Bhārata situated in its proper form; the description of Śivālaya, located at a distance of one hundred yojanas in the ninth direction of Bhārata known as Parāmaśikā; and the description of the Bhrabhāsakṣatra and the Cidvāns.

The description of the origin of Prabhāsakṣetra and the establishment of the supreme meaning of the name Īśvara; the statement of the reason for naming that place "Pramāta"; the description of its origin from the burning of Brahmā by the splendor of the Blessed Sun while he was dwelling on Mount Manu at dawn; the description of the origin of the Sūryabhūmi-saṅgama; the emergence of the celestial regions (kha-sthāna) therefrom; the subsequent origin of humans and other beings; and the production of the deities of *svāhā* and *svadhā*, as well as the medicinal herbs.

(An account of the origin of the Marīcis and other sages, as well as the Daityas such as Hiraṇyakaśipu and others; the birth of Prahlāda from Hiraṇyakaśipu; the birth of Virocana, who was sonless, from Prahlāda; and the account of the birth of the daughter named Śarmiṣṭhā from Viśvakarman; the departure of Saṃjñā, unable to endure the brilliance of the Sun, to perform penance after leaving her shadow in the presence of the Sun; and when the shadow assumed the form of a woman by the Sun’s glance, the Sun became enraged.)

The granting of a curse by Kharaṇa-nāga and the departure of Sureṇu to his father; thereafter, after explaining the reason for his own arrival, Sureṇu’s return to the presence of Sūrya at his father’s command; then the description of the origin of the Śrāddhadevas in the realms of Yama, Yamunā, and Śanaiścara; and finally, due to a certain other cause, Sūrya’s arrival at the house of Viśvakarman to curse his mother-in-law, and Viśvakarman’s joyful reception and hospitality toward Sūrya.

The instrument [was forged]; then Viśvakarman began the process of tempering his [the Sun’s] excessive brilliance. While this was being done, the Seven Sages offered hymns of praise to the Sun; Viśvakarman composed a hymn for the Sun; Hāhā, Hūhū, Nārada, Tumburu, and others began to sing; Menakā and other celestial nymphs (Apsarases) commenced singing in the form of hymns to the Sun; various musical instruments were played; and when Saṃjñā, who had gone to perform penance, assumed the form of a mare (Vaḍavā), [the Sun took the form of] a horse—

The description of the birth of Sūrya, Daśavakra, Aśvinī, and Dhanvantari; the description of the origin of Rājanabhaṭa and Rārika; the description of the birth of Yama; the journey of Yama—who, having been cursed by his mother, had become lame—to the holy site of Prabhāsa; his worship of Śiva there and the removal of his lameness through the grace of Śiva; his installation of a Liṅga there by the command of Śiva; the description of the greatness of Yameśvara; and [the account of] the carving of the image of Īśvara while he was wandering in Piśāka-dvīpa.

Immediately following the [chapter on] Truth (Satya), there is the descent of the Sun (Vibhāvasu) onto the earth by means of Diraṇyagarbha; his renown under the names Sūrya, Savitṛ, Bhāskara, and Arkastha during the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages; the description of the greatness of Arka accompanied by a discourse on the prohibition against eating leafy vegetables; the description of the greatness of the gift of a buffalo and other items at the Arka-arka-stha-tīrtha; and the narration of the origin of the place known as Prabhāsa-pavitra. ... Śīdha.

The description of the worship of Akaisthala, preceded by the recitation of mantras; the narration of the majesty of Siddheśvara and Jaigīṣavyeśvara, including Jaigīṣavya’s performance of penance at Prabhāsa; the granting of a boon that bestows the yoga of knowledge to Jaigīṣavya by Sthāṇu, who was pleased by his long austerity as he performed the Nirāhāra, Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other vows; and the installation of the two deities Jaigīṣavyeśvara and Siddheśvara by Jaigīṣavya.

The description of the greatness of Jaigīṣavyeśvara-siddha; the description of the origin and greatness of Pāpanāśana; the chapters concerning the topics of how Prabhākara, seeing the triple world eclipsed by the splendor of the Rākṣasas stationed in Pātāla, meditated upon the Blessed One; the falling of those Rākṣasas from the sky to the earth as they were gazed upon by him with eyes blazing with wrath; then the departure of those Rākṣasas to Pātāla; and finally, the installation of the Linga at the confluence of that [river] and the Khadira-dvāra.

A description of the greatness of the fruit of giving *sakhu* nuts; the establishment of its fame by the name "Śrīmukhadvāra"; a description of the origin of the host of Mātṛs, such as Sunandā, from the openings of Pātāla; and the statement of the procedure for worship and the greatness of Sunandā and the others.

Now follows the description of the ritual for the worship of Arka (the Sun). In that regard, there is a description of Āditya as being composed of the three Vedas (*trayīmaya*). First, regarding the cleansing of the teeth, there is the determination of the appropriate wood for the morning and afternoon sessions, followed by the description of the method for cleaning the teeth. There is a description of how one becomes afflicted with leprosy and other diseases by touching the sun before washing the face. There is a description of the performance of rites such as the acquisition of knowledge while standing upon an *arka* plant. Following the recitation of the great mantra of the Sun, there is the description of the *japa* (muttering) of the *ṛc*. There is the description of the ritual of worship (*upasthāna*) with the hymn "ud u tyam," and [the description of] the *ṛk* beginning with "agnir dūtaḥ."

The description of the ritual procedure for Āditya through the sixteen services beginning with *kaṣṇena*; the description of the worship of the deities of the *ṛṅga-pīṭha* and others on all sides; the description of the offering of various kinds of maṇḍalas and other gifts; the description of the majesty preceded by the hymn of praise to Akaiṣṭha; and, in the context of describing the account of the moon’s origin as an ornament upon Śiva’s head, the description of the account of Vārāhaka.

In that [section], there is a description of the origin of the moon when the ocean was being churned for the sake of producing the fourteen jewels; the bearing of that moon on his head by Śiva; the description of the sixteen digits (*kalā*) of the moon according to the sequence of the lunar days (*tithi*), resulting from its bearing upon the head as "Moon-adorned" (*Śaśibhūṣaṇa*); the description of the wheel of time (*kālacakra*) beginning from the *cuṭu* and ending with the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*); and a brief account of the deeds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśāna during the first *parārdha* of Brahmā’s life. Then—

In the second [section], following the account of the birth and other details of Dakṣa and others, there is a description of the birth of the seven sages (Saptarṣis) and so forth; a narration of the incarnations of Candra, Dattātreya, and others; a description of the various divine incarnations of Viṣṇu occurring simultaneously throughout the ages (yugas); a description of the commencement of the Kṛtayuga and the reigns of Cakṣuṣa Manu and others; and a description of the incarnations of Vyāsa and others.

In the account of the succession of the Daityas and Ādityas, it is described how Hiraṇyakaśipu went to the worlds of Śakra and others to perform austerities; his attainment of sovereignty over the three worlds through those penances is told; then follows the narration of Balarāma’s birth and other details, a description of Bali’s power, and a description of Prahlāda’s birth and life story. Next is the description of Kārttikeya’s birth, the origin of Viśravas, and the account of the births of Kumbhakarṇa, Rāvaṇa, and the others.

The narration of Śrī Rāma’s destruction of Rāvaṇa; the account of Śiñjāpāṭha’s birth; the description of the names of the nine wives of Atri; the description of the lineage of Puṣkara, Harṣa, Māgadhi, and others; herein, the mention of the wives of Atri, namely the Apsarases Bhadrāśvā, Dhṛtācī, and Tārajā, as well as Bhadrā and the others who were the wives of Bhāskara; the description of how Soma-rasa was produced by Pramāka through his wife Bhadrā; and then, while Atri was performing penance after drinking that Soma-rasa, [it issued] from his two eyes.

The description of the origin of the *soma* plant from the flow of the *prāita-soma-rasa*; how the various quarters took that *soma* and brought about coolness everywhere; the description of the origin of medicinal herbs; the statement regarding the production of grains such as *kuṭattha*, *kaśyāmāka*, and others; the description of the origin of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) along with the seasons; the conclusion of the narrative concerning the granting of sovereignty over the lunar mansions, herbs, and so forth to the Moon; and how the Moon, having commenced the *rājasūya* sacrifice, approached Brahmā seated upon a lotus.

Having installed Viṣṇu, Sanatkumāra, and others in their respective positions, and having commenced the sacrifice, he satisfied the sacrificial priests and sages with fees and other offerings upon its completion. Then follows the narration of the origin of the Ṛkṣas; by the command of Brahmā, Daśa begot sixty daughters, and among them, from Dharma and the others, [the birth of] those daughters...

The gift of Pṛśni; the giving of twenty-seven daughters to Soma; the enumeration of the names of the ten wives of Dharma; the description of the lineage of Kaśyapa’s twenty-seven wives who were the daughters of Atri; the description of the lineages of the two wives of Ārāputra, the two wives of Īśāśva, and the two wives of Agni, preceded by the mention of their names; and how Candra, having neglected Rohiṇī, caused discord with the other wives of Candra.

The narration of the entire account: then, having heard [the report] from Dakṣa and observing the Moon’s partiality toward other maidens, Dakṣa related the story of how the Moon had been granted the disease of consumption as a punishment for his improper conduct. Subsequently, at the word of Dakṣa, the Moon went to the vicinity of the Southern Ocean in order to perform the propitiation of Śiva for the sake of curing himself of the disease of consumption and leprosy.

Having reached the Prabhāsakṣetra with Candra, he saw a footprint named Kṛtasmara; likewise, on that mountain, having taken up the staff of the sages such as Marīci who were performing various fasts and other austerities, and having performed ablutions and circumambulations toward them, he then offered praise to Śiva, who had appeared through his propitiation during the day. Having heard the praise of Śiva uttered by Candra, Śiva, with a gracious mind, [bestowed] upon Candra... [the remainder of the passage concerns the contents of the *Vatsyāyana-śāsana*]. **Subjects of the *Vatsyāyana-śāsana*: Joy in the Self.** Upon hearing this, Śiva, with a delighted heart, [granted] to Candra—

The granting of boons preceded by the establishment of the curse of Dakṣa; the description of the power of Śiva, the gods, and the twice-born; the narration of extraordinary matters; and the description of the qualities of Brāhmaṇas.

"Oṃ! Having taken the command from Candra to Viśvakarman for the installation of the *liṅga*, and having considered his own world, [Candra] commanded Hemagarbha and Manti through Candra to bring the sacrificial materials to Prabhāsa. At Candra’s word, Hemagarbha and Manti procured the sacrificial materials and went to the region of Prabhāsa. Then Viśvakarman fashioned the sacrificial hall, the wives of the gods, the *śālā*, and so forth. Thereafter, Candra, together with Brahmā and the others, emerged from the sacrificial ground."

Having caused the gods and the Vasus and others to enter their respective places, and having ensured that no material was lacking when the sacrificial ritual was commenced, he brought satisfaction to everyone. Having established the *ṛtvij* priests and others, and having made the moon together with Rohiṇī the *adhvaryu*, he performed the selection of all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) along with Brahmā accompanied by Sāvitrī. Having assigned the office of *hotṛ* to Bṛhaspati, the office of *adhvaryu* to Vasiṣṭha, the office of *udgātṛ* to Marīci, and the office of *brahman* to Nārada, he appointed Sanatkumāra to the positions of the *sadasyas*.

Having directed all [the priests] to perform the worship, having given the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and the *vaṣaṭ*-utterances, the commencement of the sacrifice was made; having completed the sacrifice with the *avaśratha* and other rites, the installation of the image of Someśvara was performed. Then, on the following day, in the Dvāpara age, having propitiated Śaṅkara through the Rodinī-nāyaka and having brought him face to face, a hymn of praise was offered; thereupon, being pleased, Śiva granted the bestowal of the *sānnidhya* (divine presence) upon the earth.

The description of how Śiva made the Moon his attendant; the narration of the procedure for worshipping Somanātheśvara; the account of the fruits of the pilgrimage to Somanātha; the description of the Moon’s release from his affliction; the mention of the flowers dear to Somanātheśvara; the departure of Candrabhāgā and the others to their respective abodes by the command of Vibhu (Śiva); and when Pārvatī questioned Śaṅkara regarding the reason for granting boons to wicked people, [Śaṅkara replied].

A description of devotees characterized by the qualities of goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), and darkness (tāmasa); an exposition on the non-duality of Hara and Iḍarā; a description of the incarnations of the Lord as Narasiṃha and others; a description of the discourse on liberation through forms such as *sārūpya*; a description of the rules for the Somavāra-vrata, fasting, and other observances. Regarding the greatness of the Somavāra-vrata: while the Gandharva named Ghana was residing at Svayaṃprabhā-nagara together with his wife Sudīlā, after a long time had passed, he begot a daughter named Gandharvasenā. [The text continues with] the account of Gandharvasenā...

The contents of the chapters concerning the procedure for the hand-holding ceremony (pāṇigraha-vidhi) [in the section] named Ghana: Chapter 1: Description of the procedure for the gift at Somanātha; description of the ritual for the pilgrimage to Somanātha; determination of the eligibility for the fruit of the pilgrimage; explanation of what should and should not be avoided by a person desiring to undertake a pilgrimage to a sacred site (tīrthayātrā), including matters such as what must be averted; description of the merit gained from performing great gifts (mahādāna); [the location of] the sacred site of Prabhāsa-kṣetra.

The description of the fear arising from the threat of enemies; the statement regarding the rules for the deceased and their kinsmen; the description of the fruits of giving sixteen specific items by Bhinnasena on each of the sixteen lunar days (tithis); the description of the fruits of dying in the sacred precinct of Prabhāsa; the statement concerning the qualification for going to the world of Śiva; the recitation of mantras during bathing at a holy ford (tīrtha); the procedure for a pilgrimage to a holy site; and the Gandharva’s bestowing of wealth through his servant while Rikhaṇḍika, the leader of the Gaṇas, was traveling through the sky.

Having heard the words of the Gandharva maiden named Gandharvasenā, beginning with "No one at all possesses such a beautiful form as mine," Śikhaṇḍi Gaṇa beheld the Gandharva maiden who was proud of her beauty and bestowed upon her a curse that brought leprosy. Upon hearing the plea of Śikhaṇḍi Gaṇa, Gandharvasenā accepted the curse. Then, at the word of Śikhaṇḍi, she went to the hermitage of the sage Godāvarī-tanaya on Mount Himavat to dispel her leprosy.

The narration by the demon named Ghana to Geraṅgasunu of his daughter along with the full account of events; the description of the means employed by Gokhagaṇa to repel the demons upon hearing that news; and the description of the demon named Ghana and the army of the Gandharvas.

The journey to Someśvara at Gośṛṅga; there, having performed the worship of Śiva through vows such as the *khoma* fast, and in the introduction to the description of the greatness of Sannitīrtha, first performing the shaving of the head and other rites at Padyakatīrtha, and then again taking up the *śivadhūpa*, he obtained a boon from Śiva that resulted in the complete eradication of his leprosy. It is stated that by performing the bathing and other rites for Śiva, one obtains double the fruit even compared to bathing at the Someśvara Tīrtha. [The text continues with: "For women, [the rite of] *kṣuraka*... [fragmentary].

The departure of the Gandharva army to their own homes; a description of the prohibition against shaving on Mondays; a description of women plucking out two hairs from each side of their heads with their thumbs; a description of the various procedures for shaving and related rites; and a description of the prohibition against touching the great ocean without having undergone a shave.

The Gandharva named Vana requested the sage Gośṛṅga for instruction on the complete knowledge of the procedure for the Monday vow (somavāravratavidhi). Thereafter, it is told how, by performing that vow and other rites, he was cured of leprosy through the grace of Śiva. Then, when that same sage began to instruct the Gandharva Vana on the performance of the Monday vow—beginning with the rules for cleansing the face and purity, and ending with the ritual bath—the [Gandharva], fearing the loss of his own splendor, sought refuge there, considering the ocean to be his protector, and entered it.

The procedure for the concealment [of the ritual], the method of libations (*tarpaṇa*) and other rites following the mantra-calculation, the observance of the Monday vow (*somavāra-vrata*), and the description of the subsequent rite performed by Soma—who had attained a state of emaciation through the exhaustion of his merit after the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice; therein, the description of the greatness and fruit of the gift of bulls and other offerings, the preparation of materials for the worship of the Lord of the Mountain (*Śarveśvara*), and the description of the procedure for the worship of Śiva with mantras; and the account of how, by giving food including meat and other items to the Brahmins on the ninth lunar day (*navamī*) during the month of Soma, their...

The description of the procedure for performing the *udyāpana* (concluding rite) and other rituals upon the cessation of the obstacle caused by the fault of eating meat; the narration of how the ocean gave a curse to the Brāhmaṇas, saying "May you become [unfit] even though you are Brāhmaṇas," so that they might satisfy the ancestors, gods, and others such as the *bhaurāṇikas*; the description of the rules regarding food, gifts, and other matters ending with the meal; and finally, after the Monday vow (*somavāravrata*) was completed according to the method described by Gośṛṅga, the ocean’s making of a petition to the Brāhmaṇas.

The narration of the account of the establishment of the holy ford (tīrtha) known as Vaḍavānala; the curing of leprosy for Gandharvasenā by the gracious Śiva; the description of the procedure for the performance of the Abhītīrtha pilgrimage; and thereafter, having performed the bath and other rites there, the offering of the vow (vratapūjana) as an ancillary to the bath.

To the north of Someśvara, the Gandharva named Ghanadāha, known by the name Gandharveśavara, established the quarters. Having worshipped Gaṇapati for a day in Gandharva, he proceeded to Someśvara; there, the worship of Someśvara with the sixteen-fold offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) and a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the Lord [are recounted]. ...

— and likewise the description of the ritual injunctions; the description of the majesty of the worship of Someśvara; the establishment of Gaṃdhaveśeśvara by Gandharvasenā, the daughter of the Gandharva Ghanavāha; the departure toward the hermitage when the war between the gods and the asuras had commenced due to the cause of the Gandharva Soma and the Daityas were defeated; then, the description of the majesty of Seneśa-vigama; and the description of the offering of their respective musical instruments by all the gods to the great sage Ṛddhivin.

Viṣṇu’s command to the maiden Sarasvatī to prevent the submarine mare from reaching the ocean; then, having drunk the essence of the *allāṇa* [soma] established by the gods along with the water, Dadhīci departed for the northern direction with his own wife named Subhadrā; thereafter, while Dadhīci was staying there in that hermitage, Subhadrā, whose mouth was filled with his semen, went to bathe in a river; and there, in that river, the semen entered the womb of Bhadrā as she was bathing.

Through the emission of semen, conception occurred; then, having stayed at the foot of an *aśvattha* tree, she cast off the fetus and uttered a curse: "May that wicked one by whom—whether through knowledge or ignorance—the placing of a fetus was performed in my womb, who am devoted to my husband, die. Then, after she had departed from there, the gods arrived, seeking her bones; knowing that Dadhīci had been reduced to ashes, the gods made preparations to seize his bones. For the purpose of fashioning the thunderbolt and other weapons, Dadhīci [was requested].

The act of abandoning the body; then, the gods such as Indra taking the bones of Dadhīci and fashioning their respective vajras, staffs, nooses, and so forth; and then, Subhadrā, who was overwhelmed with grief due to the death of Dadhīci.

The gods brought about a reconciliation; having heard that a son had been born from Dadhīci by Subhadrā, they were filled with joy; Subhadrā performed the rites for her son, beginning with the *auṣvedika* ceremony; there is a description of the birth of beings from a womb, an egg, sweat, and a sprout; Subhadrā gave her son the name Pippalāda and performed the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) prescribed in the Vedas; thereafter, Pippalāda made a vow to the gods, the enemies of the Daityas, and went to the mountain named Himavat to perform worship.

The departure; for the purpose of creating a mare, Pippalāda churned his own thigh and produced a *vaḍavā* (mare) joined with a *vaḍava* (horse); then follows the description of the birth of the *vaḍavānala* (submarine fire) from that *vaḍava* and *vaḍavā*; at the word of Pippalāda, the *vaḍavānala* went to the ocean to devour the gods; then the description of the account of how Mahāviṣṇu, praised by the gods, assumed the form of the *vaḍavānala*; and Sarasvatī, having been pacified by Brahmā, took the *vaḍavānala* and went to the ocean.

The submergence of the Sarasvatī by the mare’s mouth (*vaḍavāmukha*); the praise of the Sarasvatī and the Mare’s Mouth Ocean; the aquatic creatures seeking refuge with Kṛṣṇa when the water of the ocean was about to be consumed by the Mare’s Mouth; Kṛṣṇa granting them a promise of safety; then, seeing the ocean filled with inexhaustible water, the performance of the worship of Viṣṇu by the gods; and the description of the greatness of the descent of the Sarasvatī at the Bhābhasa-kṣetra. Chapter [X], Section [Y]: Subjects.

The departure of the Sarasvatī from the root of the Pippala tree toward the eastern direction; then her turning eastward as far as Siddheśvara, followed by her turning north and then facing west; thereafter, a description of the various holy bathing places (tīrthas) situated along the banks of the Sarasvatī; a description of the five streams beginning with Hariṇī; and finally, the confluence of the Sarasvatī with the ocean.

In the description of the majesty of Prācīsarasvatī: after the destruction of the Kauravas, the Pāṇḍavas travel with Kṛṣṇa to Hastināpura; then, at the time of Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, Arjuna, and Sahadeva’s departure for Gajapura, Yudhiṣṭhira tells the gatekeepers, "Nara and Nārāyaṇa must be barred. When the ignorant gatekeepers, desiring to know the truth about Niṣadha, raise an objection, [the narrative continues with] the binding of those two by Bhīṣma and other virtuous people such as Duryodhana.

The prohibition against being a vessel for faults by means of carrying [the burden]; then, having been thus exhorted, the ignorant man’s inquiry of Śrī Kṛṣṇa regarding the means for the removal of sin and the performance of expiation; thereafter, Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s description of the removal of sin through bathing at the Prācīsarasvatī Tīrtha; following that, his journey with Kṛṣṇa toward the Prācīsarasvatī; there, his effecting the removal of his own sins through observances such as fasting for three nights and bathing for three nights; [and finally,] the power of the Prācīsarasvatī.

Having learned that Bhīma, Nakula, Sahadeva, and the others had also arrived there, their sins were removed through the smelling of [the flowers] and other such acts as if they were not human beings; this is followed by a description of the majesty of the Prācī Sarasvatī. . . .

When Śiva was asked by Pārvatī, "Why was a bracelet thrown into the water on this auspicious day?", he related the story of Indumatī. In that account, the great sage Kaṇva arrived at the court of King Bṛhadratha; having performed the rites of hospitality for Kaṇva, the two engaged in a conversation concerning dharma. Subsequently, out of a desire to know the cause of her own misfortune, Indumatī offered herself to Kaṇva. By Kaṇva, [she was accepted]... Indumatī’s...

The narration of the events of her previous birth; therein, the description of the life of that Mahāśūdrathā in her former existence; the falling of the bracelet from her hand at the time of her bathing at the Someśvara Tīrtha; the account of her being born as a princess in another life due to the power of that bracelet’s fall at the holy site; and upon hearing Kaṇva’s words, Indumatī turning her face away and remaining silent, followed by Kaṇva’s departure for his own abode.

Then, having gone with Nandumatī to the banks of the Sarasvatī in the region of Vahadratha, they performed the casting of the marriage bracelets (*kaṅkaṇa*). Therein is described how, by that act, Vahadratha and Indumatī attained divinity; a description of the greatness of the ritual of casting the bracelets; and, in the description of the greatness of the Lord Kapardin, the distress of the gods caused by the Daityas and their subsequent offering of hymns of praise to Pārvatī. Then, placing their trust in the words of the Blessed Lady, the gods went to the holy site of Someśvara and other shrines, where, having performed their ablutions and other rites, [they worshipped] the Lord Kapardin.

Furthermore, through worship, the governance of the kingdom [is secured]; there is a description of the majesty of Kapardin-Vināyaka; in the account of the Prabhāsa pilgrimage, there is the journey to the Kedāreśvara Tīrtha north of the Kedāreśvara fire; then, the worship of the Vṛddhaliṅga situated near Bhīmeśvara; in the description of the majesty of Kedāreśvara, King Śaśaviḍu, together with his wife, undertakes a pilgrimage and goes to Kedāreśvara; there, upon seeing the groups of sages such as Rebhya, the king performs the vigil (jāgara) and other rites; then, by Rebhya and the others...

Śakbida’s departure for Someśvara to learn of his past-life history, and his journey to Kedāreśvara to discover the reason for [Someśvara’s] arrival; then, upon the King’s narration of his own previous birth, the account of his birth as Candra, a base servant distinguished by his devotion to the worshipper of Brahmins; thereafter, the description of himself and his co-wife traveling to Prabhāsakṣetra during a time of drought, afflicted by hunger and thirst. Therein...

Having bathed in all the sacred waters (tīrthas) and performed various rites of worship and so forth, he then went to Rāmasaras. Every day, he would gather the lotuses found in Rāmasaras, sell them, and sustain himself with that very income. Then, at one time, while staying with his wife in a certain part of the forest near Kāśī, he heard the sudden sound of a cry from a Śūdra. Realizing that a vigil was being held in a certain place there, he went with his wife to sell lotus stalks (*kamaṭas*) at that spot.

The journey; there, the sight of Vṛddhakeśava, whose other name is Kedāreśvara; there, one *droṇa* of the water of Anaṅgavatī; by that pure [water], when questioned by another man regarding the cause of his vigil, the description of the fruit of keeping a vigil on Śivarātri to him; then, the description of how a Śūdra, together with his wife, by performing the vigil, fasting, and other rites on Śivarātri, obtained birth in a royal family in another life; and the description of the majesty of Kedāreśvara (Rudreśvara).

The establishment of the Linga named Śvetaketvīśvara by Śvetaketu after performing penance at Prabhāsa; then, during the Dvāpara age, Bhīmasena, filled with devotion, performed a pilgrimage and, through his worship, gave it the name Bhīmeśvara; the description of the majesty of Bhīmeśvara; the description of the majesty of the Liṅga Śānaiścareśvara, wherein Dānaiśvara propitiated Śiva on Saturdays to attain lordship; and the description of the majesty of Devamātā-Bhairaveśvara. Caṇḍaṭhā.

Following the description of the ritual procedure for the worship of Caṇḍīśa, who was propitiated by the established host of Caṇḍas, there is a description of the majesty of Māda-Ādityeśvara. [Then] follows the description of the majesty of Someśvara. [Next] is the narration of the account of the origin of Aṅgāraka from the falling of a tear upon the earth from the eye of Śiva, who desired to burn Tripura, as well as the description of the majesty of Aṅgāreśvara.

Description of the greatness of Budheśvara established by Budha; description of the greatness of Bṛhaspatīśvara established by Guru; Śukra’s propitiation of Rudra, his acquisition of the *sajjīvanī* mantra with the assistance of Rudra, his attainment of the status of a *prahasta*, and the establishment of a *liṅga* in his own name—description of the greatness of Śukreśvara; thereafter, the establishment of a *liṅga* by Rāneśvara with the permission of Śiva; and the description of the results, such as the removal of the affliction of stinginess, through the worship of Saurīśvara.

At one time, having heard from the mouth of Vasiṣṭha that "when Śani pierces Rohiṇī, there will be a two-year period of famine," Daśaratha mounted his chariot and went toward the Lord of Raśanā by way of the Akāra road in order to dispel that calamity; there he engaged in battle. Having witnessed Daśaratha’s prowess and having seen the destruction of all his [the Lord's] weapons brought about by a mere glance, the Lord spoke out of fear, saying, "Choose a boon. Then—

The account of Daśaratha’s propitiation of Raudreśvara by means of a water-chariot (dakaratha) to ward off the affliction caused by the planet Saturn (Rāhu); then, the composition of a hymn to Śanaiścara by Daśaratha; the declaration by Śanaiścara that he would not cause further suffering due to the recitation of his own hymn; and the description of the majesty of Śanaiśvareśvara. The description of the majesty of Rāhaveśvara, who was installed by Rāhu. For the sake of attaining lordship over the planets, Ketu propitiated Śiva, and by his command, established Ketavīśvara on the northern bank of the Rāhu river; the description of the majesty of Ketavīśvara. 112. 113. 114. 115. 116. 117. 118. 119. 120. 121. 122. 123. 124. 125. 126. 127. 128. 129. 130. 131. 132. 133. 134. 135. 136. 137. 138. 139. 140. 141. 142. 143. 144. 145. 146. 147. 148. 149. 150. 151. 152. 153. 154. 155. 156. 157. 158. 159. 160. 161. 162. 163. 164. 165. 166. 167. 168. 169. 170. 171. 172. 173. 174. 175. 176. 177. 178. 179. 180. 181. 182. 183. 184. 185. 186. 187. 188. 189. 190. 191. 192. 193. 194. 195. 196. 197. 198. 199. 200. 201. 202. 203. 204. 205. 206. 207. 208. 209. 210. 211. 212. 213. 214. 215. 216. 217. 218. 219. 220. 221. 222. 223. 224. 225. 226. 227. 228. 229. 230. 231. 232. 233. 234. 235. 236. 237. 238. 239. 240. 241. 242. 243. 244. 245. 246. 247. 248. 249. 250. 251. 252. 253. 254. 255. 256. 257. 258. 259. 260. 261. 262. 263. 264. 265. 266. 267. 268. 269. 270. 271. 272. 273. 274. 275. 276. 277. 278. 279

Ka. Ma: A description of the majesty of the five Siddhādi-liṅgas; first, a description of the majesty of the Kapiñjeśvara Liṅga established by King Kapila after he had performed austerities and attained the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) beginning with *aṇimā*; [then] the propitiation of Soma by twenty-seven *somas* at Prabhāsa for the sake of his own favor, and the installation of a liṅga named Varāroheśvara in the vicinity of Someśvara; [and finally] the Varāroheśvara Liṅga.

Pārvatī said to Śaṅkara: "Since you lack a sixth face, how can the six-faced [Skanda] receive the Ajā [goat] as his portion? O Lord, describe the majesty of the Goddess. Thus, through the three powers of Rudra, there is the offering of fear, passion, and the rest—beginning with Sadoja and ending with Picu—to the ten directions. Then follows the description of the majesty of the Goddess Ajā; the description of the majesty of the Goddess Rudrīca-svarā; the description of the majesty of the Goddess Aja-dha; the description of the majesty of Lakṣmī-īśvara.

...7. Description of the Bāḍaveśvara Liṅga. ... (Description of the greatness of the Bāḍaveśvara Liṅga, concerning how the goddess Sarasvatī, who bears the form of a mare, having come to the Prabhāsa region and performed rites such as the acquisition of knowledge in the ocean, established the two liṅgas; description of the greatness of the Ārṣyeśvara Liṅga. ...;

The description of Pārvatī performing austerities in the Mahākrodha forest out of anger toward Śiva; then, the granting of boons to Pārvatī by the gratified Śiva; the statement that the sight of that penance grove grants the fruit of the accomplishment of all goals; the installation of a *liṅga* there; and the description of the majesty of Gaurī’s penance grove and the majesty of the Gaurīśvara *kṣetra*.

[The description of the greatness of the mobile *liṅga* of Varuṇeśvara installed by Varuṇa; the description of the greatness of Īśiśvara installed by the wife who was tormented by grief for her husband; ... the description of the greatness of Jaḍhavāsa Gaṇapati.]

[And so forth: A description of the greatness of Kumāreśvarī established by the six-faced one; the installation of the liṅga by Śākalya after propitiating Śiva at the request of King Rāja; the naming of that liṅga as Īśvara, Khavaśvara, and Śākalyeśvara during the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages; and a description of the greatness of Śākalyeśvara-liṅga.

The mention of names such as Kalakaleśvara, Catuyugeśvara, Bhinnatvena, Kamiśraṇueśavaranārodaśavara, and Kalakaleśvara; the account of how Nārada once established the *liṅga* known as Āṣanākara at Prabhāsa in Veṅkaṭa during the junction (*sandhi*) between the Dvāpara and Kali ages; and thereafter, having descended to the earth, Nārada’s performance of the great sacrifice named Pauṇḍarīka—these are the subjects of the chapters.

Chapter 10: Imperishable Subjects. Description of the great assembly at Ṭhakurīrāma near Karakaṭheśvara; description of the majesty of the Uttakeśvara Liṅga established there by Viṣṇu after he had cast the Daitya Medhavāhana into his own belly with a kick of his foot, and the account of how he remained stationed right there under the name Ādinārāyaṇa.

The description of the greatness of Ādinārāyaṇa; the account of a certain bird who, together with his wife, built a nest on a single branch; then the description of the incident involving the food offered by a nearby hunter; there, Viṣṇu and his retinue took up residence; thereafter, for the protection of the nest, the bird, accompanied by his wife, abandoned Mathurā and went to Prabhāsa; then, at the time of their capture by Viṣṇu and the others—

On the shore of the ocean, by the power of performing a circumambulation of Vaiśvānareśvara without effort, Kṛṣṇa brought Saṃnihitā there in a previous birth merely by means of meditation; the description of the fruit of merit obtained by performing ablutions there is given. Then follows the description of the succession of births of Agastya, and the description of the power of making gifts and other acts performed there by Agastya, who remembered his former birth; finally, the description of the majesty of Saṃnihitā.

(The description of the exhaustion of the fruits of their actions; the description of the majesty of Vaiśvānareśvara; during the period of living incognito, the establishment of directions by the Pāṇḍavas upon reaching Prabhāsa with five [objects] each according to their respective names; the description of the majesty of Chakulīśvara; the description of the majesty of the sacred ford (tīrtha); the description of the majesty of the Gautameśvara-tīrtha; the enumeration of the names of the eleven Rudras; therein, first, the description of the majesty of Bhūteśvara-Rudra.)

In the first section, titled "The Description of Daityasūdana," there is a description of the names beginning with Vāmana and ending with Daityasūdana; then follows the description of the greatness of Nīrasadra. Therein, during the hymn of Viṣṇu by Daityajita, the various incarnations of Viṣṇu are recounted; thereafter, the description of the greatness of Cakrapālīśvara Rudra by Viṣṇu.

[The account of] how, with the assistance of the Daityas, the gods were slain; the command of the gods to slay the Daityas; and the installation of the Blessed One (Bhagavat). A description of the names occurring in the Bhṛtikalpa of Vṛṣabheśvara, the slayer of Daityas. A description of the greatness of the Liṅga named Vṛṣabheśvara installed by Vṛṣabha, including the narrative of the fruits of worship such as fasting and other rites performed at Bālāva.

A description of the origin of Cakratīrtha and its great majesty; a detailed account of Ayaṃbakeśvara, including the mention of its various names in different ages; the performance of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at Ayaṃbakeśvara; the slaying of Mahiṣāsura—who had become intoxicated by the boon granted by Brahmā—after he was struck down by the gods acting in unison; the description of the *phaṭha* (the sacred site); and a description of the majesty of Ayaṃbakeśvara.

Nārada accepted that woman as his wife; Mahiṣāsura’s obedience to his command; Nārada’s speech; the description of the majesty of Aghoreśvara; having heard [it], Mahiṣāsura went with his army to the presence of that woman; Mahiṣāsura’s description of Mahākāleśvara; the description of its fame by the name Citrāṅgadeśvara in that age; and the Goddess, having observed the opinion of Citrāṅgada, [emerged] from her own body...

The slaying of the demon Rātaśca; thereafter, the establishment of that Goddess by the Lord under the name Mahākāleśvara, followed by a description of the majesty of the Mahākāleśvara Liṅga; the destruction of the demon Mahiṣāsura; the offering of praise to that Goddess by the gods; and subsequently, a description by the gods of the majesty of that Goddess known as Bhairaveśvara.

In that very place, there is the description of the establishment [of the deity], the exposition of the ritual for the worship of the Goddess, the recitation of the sword-mantra (*khaḍgamantra*), and the glorification of the greatness of the three types of Dugodevī-stotras; the description of the greatness of the lineage of the Yogīśvaras, and the description of the greatness of the Kāmeśvara-liṅga.

— Chapter 6: The sages, oppressed by the Daityas known as Meṣavāhana, perform a hymn of praise to Viṣṇu; having heard that hymn, [Viṣṇu], out of compassion, describes the majesty of the Yogeśvara-liṅga; [the topics include] Daṇḍapāṇi for the sake of the fortunate, and the journey of the Earth, oppressed by the burden of the Daityas, to Prabhāsa.

Therein, after establishing the Earth upon her own splendor and propitiating Rudra, there is a description of obtaining Rudra’s grace; a description of the majesty of Prithvishvara (Chandreshvara); and in the description of the majesty of Khandara, an account of how Pauṇḍraka, while residing in Vārāṇasī, assumed the emblems of Vāsudeva and engaged in battle with Vāsudeva, wherein Pauṇḍraka was slain by Vāsudeva.

The son of Pūṇḍraka caused Vāsudeva to create a magical phantom (kṛtyā) of a maiden; Vāsudeva, by means of his Sudarśana [discus], brought about the defeat of that phantom. Having been vanquished, that phantom sought refuge in heaven. Then, for the sake of protecting the phantom, Śaṅkara struck with his own arrows the Sudarśana sent forth by Viṣṇu. Seeing the Sudarśana approaching to carry out its duty as entrusted to it, the Blessed Lord placed the discus in his hand together with Śiva’s arrow.

Having assumed the form of a *kṛtyā* (magical phantom) created by Kālabhairava for the purpose of destruction, [Śiva] departed for Kāśī. There, at the request of the hosts of Daṇḍapāṇis who were stationed in that city for its protection, Kṛṣṇa remained under the name Cakradhara. A description of the majesty of Daṇḍapāṇi and Cakradhara follows, including the humiliation of Durvāsas. Subsequently, out of anger, Durvāsas bestowed the curse "Become a leper! upon Sāmba. Then, Nārada arrived at Dvārakā to take Kṛṣṇa with him.

Sāmba, arrogant because of his physical beauty, showed them contempt. Having settled that enmity, at a certain time when Śrī Kṛṣṇa had begun playing in the water with his gopīs, Sāmba suddenly went there upon hearing the words of Nārada. When they saw that Sāmba had arrived at the door, the gopīs were overcome with mental distress. Śrī Kṛṣṇa then gave them a curse, saying, "You shall fall into the hands of a thief," and he also bestowed upon Sāmba a curse that would bring him misfortune. Thereafter, by Sāmba... [the text continues].

Having remembered that the curse bestowed by the sage Durvāsas was difficult to endure, Sāmba, being greatly distressed, went to the sacred field of Prabhāsa and performed the propitiation of the Sun-god. There he offered a hymn of praise to the Sun; at the conclusion of the hymn, the Sun-god, being pleased, granted the desired boon to Sāmba and brought about the removal of his leprosy. He then related the name of that place as Ādityatīrtha. In that very spot, Sāmba installed the deity named Sāṃbādityeśvara. [The text then proceeds with] the description of the greatness of Sāṃbādityeśvara. In that regard:

The description of the Goddess Kaṇṭakañjashodhinī, who dwells near the Lord Sāmbāditya; how she was approached by Sāmba—who was born of Kṛṣṇa and Jāmbavatī and was proud of his beauty—and committed an act of injustice; the arrival of Śaṅkara in the guise of a rogue, holding a skull-cup during a sacrifice and casting that skull into the middle of the sacrificial pavilion; the display of grief by everyone upon seeing the skull there; and finally, through the praise of the great sages, the establishment of a Liṅga in the Vayunā-pramāsa-kṣetra under her own name.

The description of the installation of the *liṅga* by Prasyuṣeśvara; the description of the greatness of Anirasthāpiteśvara; the installation of a *liṅga* by the Vasu named Prabhāsa; the description of the greatness of Prabhāseśvara; the manifestation of his own form by Maheśvara; the installation of a *liṅga* there under the name Kapāṭeśvara; the description of the greatness of Kapāṭeśvara; and how it became renowned by the name Koṭīśvara because ten million Brahmins performed austerities at Kapāṭeśvara and installed a *liṅga*.

The instrument [of creation], the description of the greatness of Koṭīśvaraṅga, and within the description of the greatness of Brahmā, the description of the greatness of the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) in his forms as Bādarūpin and Dadhirūpin; then, the calculation of the duration of Brahmā’s lifespan up to the end of the Kalpa; the separate enumeration of the names of twenty-seven Kalpas, fourteen Indras, and four Manus; and, having explained the reason for Brahmā’s performance of penance and the installation of a Liṅga at Prabhāsa, the description of the installation of the Brahmaśvara Liṅga.

In the *Madhyayātrā*, there is a description of the majesty of the Lord; a description of how Yama meted out punishment to the lords of the fourteen realms who reviled Brahmins; a statement regarding the fruits of protecting the twice-born; a description of the various divisions of the Brāhmaṇas, such as the Prājāpatyas and others; a description of the rules for the performance of vows such as the Cāndrāyaṇa according to the duties of the four castes; a description of the praise of Brahmins; a description of the ritual procedure for worship with the sixteen offerings accompanied by mantras; a description of the pilgrimage to Brahmā; and [the description] of Brahmā...

The description of the place of residence; the glorification of the greatness of Brahmā in his various forms; the description of the majesty of each of the lords (Īśvaras); the birth of a son named Pradyumna, who was counted among the eight Vasus, from the maiden Viśvā—the youngest among the sixty daughters given by Dakṣa to Dharma; and, in the context of describing the ritual procedure for the worship of Brahmā by that [son] named Pradyumna, the description of the honor accorded to Nārāyaṇa as being worthy of worship due to his preeminence.

In the description of the worship of Brahmā, there is a detailed account of various forms of devotion; the exposition of the ritual for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); the departure of Rāma, accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, into the forest during the narration of the Gāyatrī-nyāsa and the pilgrimage to Rameśvara-tīrtha; then, after performing the journey, Rāma’s arrival at Prabhāsa; there, at night, while Rāma was sleeping soundly, he beheld his father in a dream driving a chariot; thereafter, Rāma related the events of the dream to the Brahmins; and then, according to the words of the Brahmins, by Rāma—

The performance of a *śrāddha* ceremony by taking large, sweet fruits such as jujubes (*badara*); the establishment of the shrine named Rāmeśvara; a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the Rāmeśvara field; [the description of the majesty of Maṇeśvara established by Lakṣmaṇa]; the description of the majesty of Jānakīdeva established by Sītā; and within the description of the majesty of Vāmanasvāmī, the carrying away of Bali to the netherworld (*pātāla*) by Viṣṇu through his request for land measuring three strides.

In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, the description of the origin of the Viṣṇupadī Gaṅgā through the establishment of the second foot [of Viṣṇu]; the majesty of Vāmanasvāmī; the majesty of the Viṣṇupadī Gaṅgā; the description of the majesty of Puṣkara due to the Viṣṇupadī Gaṅgā’s journey to Puṣkara; the description of the majesty of Puṣkareśvara; the description of the majesty of Śaṅkhodakakuṇḍeśvara and Gaurī; and the description of the majesty of Bhūtanātheśvara.

In the *Gopyādityavīryamāhātmya*, [the following is described]: the departure of Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by his sons and the gopīs, to Prabhāsa; there, having approached Mount Raivataka with the Yādavas, the construction everywhere of temple grounds marked by banners and discs; likewise, the gift of land filled with funeral pyres (*śivikā*); then, having set aside plots of land measuring one cubit at intervals, the construction of temples and other structures throughout those spaces; and the mention of the names of the sixteen gopīs who became the wives of Kṛṣṇa.

In that very place, the construction of sixteen thousand beautiful houses by the gopīs; the installation of the Sun-god there; his naming as Gopyāditya; the return of all those men and all those women toward Dvārakā; and the description of the great festival upon the attainment of the boon from Gopyāditya.

The description of the majesty of the origin of the goddess Balātibala-Daityayanī; the narration of the birth of the Daityas Balā and Atibala; how those two Daityas, Balā and Atibala, together with their armies, defeated the gods and established their sovereignty over the three worlds; the enumeration of the names of the sixty-four Yoginīs; the description of the majesty of the goddess Balātibala-Daityayanī; and the description of the majesty of Gopīśvara installed by Gopī at Prabhāsa.

The son of Jamadagni, Rāma, established a *liṅga* at Prabhāsa after killing Mārica; and the Gandharva lord Citrāṅgada, having propitiated the Lord, performed the installation of a *liṅga* there. [Furthermore,] while Citrāṅgada was traveling by means of the Puṣpaka chariot on his world-conquest, he saw that Rāvaṇa’s chariot had become stuck at Prabhāsa. Having performed penance there for the sake of increasing her own good fortune, Arundhatī became endowed with great beauty through Tāra.

A description of the greatness of the Śāṇḍilyeśvara-mahālaya established by Śāṇḍilya Ārva, after Tāṭakā’s daughter had performed penance for the destruction of Tāraka; and a description of the greatness of the Kṣemaṅkareśvara-mahālaya.

Then follows the description of the majesty of Sāgarāditya; the performance of praise by Naṭakaṇa; upon hearing that hymn composed by him, the Goddess assumed a form with many heads and held water-pots in many hands, and engaged in battle with the two Daityas, Bala and Atibala. Therein is the description of the Goddess’s destruction of the Daityas Bala and Atibala; and the description of the majesty of the sixty-four Yoginīs, ending with the words, "What is this? Come here!"

[The account of] his own wound in the Prabhāsa-kṣetra, the swift execution of the command by the messenger with joined palms, and how, having arrived at the Prabhāsa-kṣetra, he reported the matter of the wound to Rāvaṇa; then, the descent of Vibhāṇa at that Prabhāsa-kṣetra by that Rāvaṇa, the establishment of a shrine there under his own name at the word of Sarvanāgara, and the description of the greatness of the Rāvaṇeśvara [shrine].

Then, having attained *siddhi*, the installation of the Goddess and the naming of her as Saubhāgyeśvarī; the description of the taking up of the title Saubhāgyeśvarī; the consecration of the linga; the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Paureśvara; the description of the majesty of Akṣamālādevī and Maraseneśvara; [and] the subjects concerning Bhavānī. (Skanda Purāṇa, Māheśvarakhaṇḍa)

The sale of Bhavānī by the four attendants, Pāṇḍu and others; the propitiation of the God and the installation of the image of Pāṇḍupati by the boon-granting Pāṇḍu; the description of the great beauty of the Citrapatha river; Yama’s act of painting his own eyes with the wonderful picture; and the description of the majesty of the boon of Pāṇḍupati. ...

The sister named Citrā remaining in the form of a river to search for her brother; the description of the origin of the great Dhruveśvara on the Citrapathā river; Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda, propitiating the Lord at Prabhāsa and performing a hymn of praise to Śiva; the installation of the Liṅga by the name Dhruveśvara; the description of the majesty of the Dhruveśvara Liṅga; and the description of the majesty of the Kapericintāmaṇi [Liṅga].

Description of various sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and locations within the Prabhāsa pilgrimage site in the *Siddhalakṣmī-māhātmya*, a Vaiṣṇava work; therein, a description of the majesty of Citreśvara, a description of the majesty of the Siddhalakṣmī-pīṭha situated in the Prabhāsa-kṣetra, a description of the majesty of Vicitreśvara, a description of the majesty of Mahākālī-pīṭha, and a description of the majesty of Puṣkara-kuṇḍa.

The journey of Brahmā to Prabhāsa together with the gods when the sacrifice of Soma was being heard; the description of the greatness of Gajakumbhodra for the purpose of establishing Somanātha; the invitation of Brahmā by Candra; and then, when the time for the establishment of the Linga arrived, the curse of Pitāmaha.

The establishment of the quarters by Dharmarāja after performing penance at Prabhāsa; the mental recollection of Puṣkara during the festival of Yameśvara on the banks of the Nigamā; the arrival of the Puṣkaras there due to that recollection; the naming of that holy site Puṣkarāvarta because of the formation of whirlpools right there; and the description of the greatness of the Puṣkarāvarta river and the Brahmakuṇḍa created by Brahmā. In the section on the greatness of Kuṇḍaleśvara: King Sudarśana, having married Sunandā, the daughter of the King of Gāndhāra, [the narrative continues with] Queen Sunandā...

The description of the greatness of Śītalā Gaurī, who brings an end to suffering; the performance of vows such as the Śivarātri fast together with her after receiving joy; therein, the description of the greatness of the Lord Romaśeśvara installed by Māṭhoma at that site; and in the description of that greatness, the performance of the Śivarātri fast by a merchant named Dhana through his son, and the description of the greatness of her Śivarātri vow, which was fulfilled by the grace of the Lord of Kāñcī.

While Kuṇḍalī, the merchant, was searching for the wife of the merchant named Dhana—who had gone away—Tṛṇabindu appeared to him. He said, "Month after month, having drunk water from the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass, you have performed penance for a thousand years; therefore, at night, you must cut off the ear of the merchant named Dhana’s wife and weave it into a cloth. At that time, protect her!

Having established the guardians of the directions (*digpāla*) and described the majesty of Lord Binduśvara, and having heard the account of Karṇatroyana, Koṭāhaṅga performed the severing of the skull of Kṛṇḍalina. When his father had passed away, the son named Citra of the scribe (kāyastha) named Sarpamitra went to Prabhāsa and, having performed the propitiation of the Sun (*āditya*), Anīka Sudarśana went there to see that skull. Then Sudarśana and Sunanda went to that Prabhāsa and praised the Sun in many ways.

The granting of his own desired boon; then, seeing Kuṇḍarīnipāla immersing himself in lakes for the purpose of bathing, the act of showing him the Kuṇḍakūpa; a description of the majesty of the Kuṇḍakūpa; the leading of Citra to the world of Yama by the servants of Yama at the command of Yama; and therein, the description of the supreme majesty of Bhaireśvara as told by Yama.

The establishment of Vittrarūpa by Pretināga during the work of carving the lines for the temple; the description of the majesty of Naradeśvara installed by Brahmā at Citramāsa; the installation of Siga; the description of the majesty of Citrāditya and Agni; and the description of the majesty of Sāvitrīśvara and Mairava installed by Sāvitrī—thus [ends] the section on *na* and *nañ*.

Ka. Ma. At one time, when a musical instrument fell to the ground while being played, Nārada was questioned by the god Brahmā as to what had occurred. By the command of Brahmā, Nārada performed penance at Pramāsa-kṣetra to purify himself from the sin incurred by destroying the seven Brāhmaṇas; having propitiated Śiva, he established Bhairava by his command. This is the description of the majesty of Nāradeśvara and Bhairava. 6. (: [End]

When the sacrifice was commenced by Brahmā, he realized that it could not be completed due to the absence of sacrificial materials; thus, at dawn, he performed worship with whatever materials were available. Then, by the command of Śiva, Sarasvatī brought forth a stream of water in the form of material wealth. From that Sarasvatī, a golden lotus-stalk emerged, which Brahmā bound together as abundant wealth and thereby completed the sacrifice. There, he installed the Liṅga known by the name Hiraṇyeśvara, and the majesty of Hiraṇyeśvara is described.

The description of the greatness of Gāyatrīdevī established by Gāyatrī; the description of the greatness of Viṣṇu, who performed penance and established the Ralaneśvara-archa-kuṇḍa; the description of the greatness of Ranedavaraṭiga; the description of the greatness of Satyabhāmeśvara; the description of the greatness of Anaṅgadevavara established by Anaṅga; the description of the greatness of Ranakuṇḍa; the description of the greatness of Śaivatakara-bhaṭāraka; and the description of the greatness of Aṣṭakuṇḍeśvara.

The description of the greatness of the Nāsavyeśvara Liṅga; ... the description of the greatness of the Aśvineśvara Liṅga; ... the description of the greatness of Sāvitrī, including the account of the origin of the Vedas and the creation of the Ṛṣis by Śaṃkara in his chariot; then, the performance of preparations for the sacrificial rite by Bṛhaspati; then, Bṛhaspati’s arrival at the Puṣkara Tīrtha and the clearing of the sacrificial ground; and although the Adhvaryu priest extended an invitation to Sāvitrī for the sacrifice, Sāvitrī [remained behind]... [due to the presence of another woman].

Then follows the description of the greatness of the Vaṭasāvitri-vrata. In that context, regarding the king Aśvapati’s concern over his childlessness, Sāvitrī spoke to him, saying, "You must not go alone," and then she became attached to the task of fetching water for his household. Thereafter, the Adhvaryu priest informed Brahmā, "Sāvitrī has not come."

Then, overcome with anger, Brahmā issued the command for Rukmī to bring another bride; subsequently, Rukmī took a certain cowherd girl and brought her into the presence of Brahmā; thereafter, Brahmā married that cowherd girl and commenced the sacrifice.

Then, after the goddesses had escorted Sāvitrī to that sacrifice, she saw the sacrifice commenced by Jājali with another woman as his wife; filled with anger, Sāvitrī reviled Brahmā. When Brahmā explained the reason for choosing another wife upon hearing Sāvitrī’s words, Sāvitrī bestowed a curse upon Brahmā in the form of unworthiness. Then, Śakra, having appointed an Ābhīrī woman for the sake of Jājali’s marriage, [confronted] Rāvaṇa in battle along with the gods.

The pronouncement of a curse that brings about defeat; likewise, the giving of a curse by Sāvitrī to Viṣṇu for causing her separation from her husband; the giving of a similar curse by Sāvitrī to other gods as well; the praise of Sāvitrī by Viṣṇu; the granting of boons to all by Gāyatrī in order to nullify the curse given by Sāvitrī; the description of the ritual for the recitation (*japa*) of the Gāyatrī; the departure of Sāvitrī to Prabhāsa; and the description of the greatness of the Sāvitrī-mādahrata situated at Prabhāsakhetra. ...

The performance of worship and propitiation of Sāvitrī; the granting of a boon by the goddess, pleased with him, resulting in the birth of a daughter named Sāvitrī to King Aśvapati; the firm resolve made by that daughter Sāvitrī to marry none other than Satyavān as her husband; the narration of the entire account of Satyavān to Aśvapati by Nārada; the description of the marriage between Sāvitrī and Satyavān; and then, at a certain time, [her departure] for the purpose of gathering sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, and other items.

Satyavat’s departure for the forest with Sāvitrī; when a headache arose while splitting wood, Satyavat abandoned the logs and approached Sāvitrī, falling asleep on her lap. Meanwhile, Yama arrived; the description of the dialogue between Yama and Sāvitrī; Yama extracting the life-force (*jīva*) from Satyavat’s body and departing; Sāvitrī following after Yama; and although Yama made many attempts to dissuade Sāvitrī from following him, she remained steadfast.

The granting of a boon to her was witnessed; by the grace of Yama, she revived her husband, and after completing the *Jvālāsāvitrī-vrata* for three nights, Sāvitrī returned to her own hermitage with her husband. This section describes the greatness of the *Sāvitrī-vrata*, its rules, worship, gifts, and so forth, as well as the concluding rites (*udyāpana*) for the *Sāvitrī-vrata*.

In the description of the greatness of the Bhūtamātṛkās, following the account of Pārvatī’s birth on Mount Pāriyātra due to the curse of Dakṣa during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara, there is a description of the birth of one Nāyikā from the menstrual blood (rajas) of Pārvatī while she and Śiva were sporting for a period exceeding a thousand divine years after their marriage. This includes a description of that Nāyikā’s own form, a description of the names of her other companions, and likewise a description of the birth of one Puruṣa from the seed of Śiva.

The command given by Kāreṇu for the two sons of Śiva to go to Prabhāsa; the granting of a place upon their shoulders; a description of the festival of the goddess Pratipatpraśṛti; a description of the birth of fifty million Kapi-dās from the body of that Bhūtamātṛ; a description of the majesty of Bhūtamātṛkā; a description of the greatness of Śālkaṭaṅkaṭā; and a description of the majesty of Śaravasvateśvarī.
