The establishment of Bharateśvara by King Bharata after he had performed austerities on Mount Dṛśaratha; the description of the greatness of Bharateśvara, including how Bharata—the son of Āgnīdhra—divided the continents into nine parts and established his nine sons as their sovereigns, specifically the establishment of Bharateśvara at Prabhāsa on the ninth continent, Dvīpārikā, and the description of the greatness of Bharateśvara.
[Followed by] the description of the greatness of Kuśeśvara, Garageśvara, Puṣkareśvara, and Maitrayeśvara.

The description of the greatness of Kuntīśvara established by Kuntī at the time of the arrival of the Pāṇḍavas, endowed with splendor, at Prabhāsa; the description of the greatness of Arakasthala; ... the description of the greatness of Siddheśvara. (End of section).

ka) ... Description of the greatness of Dharmaka; description of the greatness of Bhavyāyāḥ Viṣaya; description of the greatness of Māṇḍavyeśvara; ... description of the greatness of Puṣpadanteśvara; ... description of the greatness of Śakreśvara; ... description of the greatness of Vasunandāmrakagaṇaśrīmūlavivara; ... description of the greatness of Nisaṅgama; ... description of the greatness of Maṅkīra; ... description of the greatness of Devamāda-Gaurī.

Having heard that Kṛṣṇa had gone to the state of being cooked after bringing about the destruction of the Yādavas, Balabhadra performed a ritual immersion (*mamana*) at Prabhāsa. There, he established a *liṅga*. Then, assuming the form of a serpent (*nāga*), he went to Pātāla to receive the title from Virūḍhaka; consequently, the name of that *liṅga* was established as Nāgeśvara. [This is] the description of the greatness of the Nāgeśvara pilgrimage site.

A description of the greatness of the five Prabhāsas; therein, Śiva’s journey to the Dāruka forest for the sake of alms; a description of how the women there were inflamed with passion upon seeing the form of Śiva as he wandered in the Dāruka forest; then, by their husbands, who were filled with anger, a curse was cast upon Śiva; by that curse, his falling down right there; a description of the trembling of the earth caused by that fall; and then, through the great lamentation and so forth of the sages, the destruction of the entire host of the gods.

The departure of the terrified gods to the presence of Viṣṇu; then, at the word of Viṣṇu, the departure of the gods to Prabhāsa and the establishment of that *liṅga* in that very place. [This is followed by] the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the fivefold Prabhāsa (*prabhāsapañcaka*), the description of the majesty of Radreśvara, the description of the majesty of Karmamoṭī, the description of the majesty of Mokṣasvāmin, the description of the majesty of Ajīgartadeva, the description of the majesty of Vidavekavara, and the description of the majesty of Amareśvara.

The introduction to the narration of the greatness of Vṛddhabhārabhāsa; the departure of the sages to Prabhāsa for the purpose of beholding the Lord; the sages’ despair upon seeing the Lord covered by a crane (*baka*); the sages’ determination regarding the crane and their performance of the worship of the Sūta; the killing of the Sūta by Caṇḍabhadra, who could not tolerate his own humiliation; and then, after Caṇḍabhadra had felt remorse and was overwhelmed with grief, he heard a voice from the sky offering him counsel.

Prabhāsa approached for the purpose of making [the people] perceive their faults; having performed penance, he established a Liṅga in his own name. After Rāma had performed penance, the sages also performed penance. While they were performing penance, old age overcame them. Then, the God, being pleased, described to them the greatness of the Lord of the Liṅgas (Liṅgeśvara).

...the granting of an audience; the departure of the sages to their respective abodes after the recitation of the *Ṛgveda* and other scriptures; the establishment of a *liṅga* by Maṅki at Prabhāsa during a discourse on the greatness of Maṅkeśvara, prompted by the sages' advanced age and their desire to dispel the pride of Kuṭaja; the naming of the place "Vṛddhaprabhāsa" due to the respect shown to the aged Ṛgvids through penance; a description of the greatness of Vṛddhaprabhāsa; ... a description of the greatness of Maṅkeśvara; ...

The establishment of a Linga by Paraśurāma after performing austerities; a description of the majesty of Jalaprabhāsa; and a description of the greatness of the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean.

The description of the greatness of the Jāmadagnīśvari-gāmāhātmya; the narration of the procedure for the *śrāddha*, the description of the times for the *śrāddha*, and the description of the purification of the seven types of substances; the description of the greatness of the Prabhāsa-kṣetra on the day of the *śrāddha*;

the explanation of terms such as *pāvana* and others; the description of the Brahmins eligible for the *śrāddha*; and, within the description of the greatness of the *śrāddha*-performed Smara, first the account of the arrangement of Dakṣa’s hundred sons and the discourse on the examination of Brahmins.

Then, when the sacrifice was commenced by Dakṣa, Pārvatī, having witnessed her own insult, performed the abandonment of her body; followed by a description of the rules for the *śrāddha* rite, a praise of the rules of silence (*mauna*), and a description of those worthy of the *śrāddha*. Next, there is a determination of the months and other times suitable for the *śrāddha*. Then, Śiva, being enraged, created Vīrabhadra and, together with his armies, sent that Vīrabhadra to destroy Dakṣa’s sacrifice; this includes a description of the companions required for the *śrāddha* ritual and a detailed exposition on the various types of *śrāddha*.

The inquiry into that; the description of the greatness of the fruit of giving food such as *vakharā* and other offerings during a *śrāddha* ceremony held by the gods who had been defeated by Vīrabhadra near Viṣṇu at the Ocean of Milk; the consideration of worthy and unworthy recipients (*pātra-apātra*) in the act of giving; the departure; then the engagement in battle between Viṣṇu and Vīrabhadra; therein, the partial defeat of Vīrabhadra; the exposition of the duties of the stages of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*); the exposition of the practice of duty during times of adversity; [and the duties] on the day of the *śrāddha*.

Upon seeing Śiva arrive there while he was engaged in sexual intercourse and other acts, the gods, headed by Viṣṇu, spoke of his transgression. Then Śiva performed the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice. Following that, he conducted an investigation into the matter, expounded the rules for the Ekādaśī vow, and established the determination regarding the six funeral cakes (*ṣaṭpiṇḍa*) and so forth.

Then follows the journey to the vicinity of Tāraka, who was tormenting the gods; the arousal of desire in Śiva’s mind by Brahmā’s command; the description of the attainment of Mākaṇḍeyeśvara; the request made to Kāmadeva by the gods to perform [the task]; and the reduction to ashes of Kāma, who had been appointed as his own instrument, upon being seen by Śiva.

Description of the greatness of Puruṣṭyeśvara; then, the consolation of Rati, who was distressed by separation from her husband, through a voice from the sky; therein, the description of the greatness of Aṅgapuṣkareśvara; the establishment of [the deity]; the description of the greatness of Kṛtasmara, also known as Kāmakuṇḍa; the description of the greatness of Kratīśvara; and the description of the greatness of Kārābhara-Brahmaśāna.

The description of the supreme greatness of Kaśyapa; at one time, during the war between the Kauravas and the Pāṇḍavas, Balabhadra, having drunk liquor for the sake of his journey, [goes to] the description of the supreme greatness of Kośikeśvara; his departure for the forest; there, seeing many sages and a Sūta staying in the hermitage of Kaśyapa, he disregards them and [proceeds to] the description of the supreme greatness of Kāmāreśvara. Śaivaskā [695].

The subjects of the fifth chapter: the description of the majesty of Gautameśvara; the description of the majesty of Bhairaveśvara; the description of the majesty of Devarājeśvara; the description of the majesty of Gaṅgā; the description of the majesty of Mānavairedavara; the description of the majesty of Gaṇapati; the description of the majesty of Nīlakaṇṭheśvara situated near Mārkaṇḍeya; and the description of the majesty of Vṛṣabhadhvajeśvara-Raṅgiṇī.

The description of the majesty of Pāṇḍavakūpa; the description of the majesty of Ṛṇamocaneśvara; the description of the majesty of Pāṇḍaveśvara; the description of the majesty of Rukmavatīśvara... [and] how Bharata, having performed ten horse-sacrifices at Bhṛbhāsa, established the *Ṛgveda*; the manifestation of the Daśāśvamedha Tīrtha (which appeared there under the name Gātrotsarga because Baṅbhadra sacrificed his own limbs there); and the description of the majesty of Gātrotsargatīrtha.

The description of the greatness of Hātakya; the description of the greatness of performing śrāddha and other rites at Gātrotsarga-tīrtha; and therein, within the description of Pretatīrtha, the greatness of the triad beginning with Śaṣṭhameṣa.

The journey of Gautama to the Gātrotsarī-tīrtha; on that path, Gautama’s sighting of the Vaiṣṇava forest; a description of the majesty of the Liṅga named Durbāseśvara installed by Durbāsas; there, Gautama’s encounter with five ghosts and his expression of fear; the dialogue between Gautama and the ghosts; the appearance before Gautama of a certain Yādava who had assumed the form of a ghost and was bound by a curse; and the subsequent subduing of those ghosts by the enraged Yādava.

The narration of the history of all [the Yādavas]; the description by the *pretas* of their own actions that caused their state as *pretas*; the granting of liberation from *preta*-hood to those [Yādavas] by means of the destruction of the *kuṇapa* (corpse/impurity); then the description of the destruction of the Yādava clan by the *erakā* grass; then, having heard the cause, Gautama’s arrival at Pretatīrtha in Prabhāsa by his command and the performance of *śrāddha* for each of them; and by that, the elevation of all those *pretas* to heaven, while the one remaining Yādava named Bāja [performed the final rites].

The narration of the hymns of those [sages] beginning with Yadu; a description of the greatness of Pretatīrtha; the performance of the ritual rites, the arrival at Bhrāmaśa, and the installation of the lingas; a description of the greatness of Vrajeśvara; a description of the greatness of Indreśvara; ... [238] a description of the greatness of Anarakeśvara; the command issued by Yama to his messengers to bring the Brahmin Devakṣema, a resident of Mathurā, preceded by the hearing of the duties to be performed; and a description of the greatness of Nāgarāditya.

The instrument [of the narrative]: Then, having seen that Devadāru tree brought there, Yama issued a command that it should not be brought back; this is followed by a description of the greatness of Śrī Balarāma, Subhadrā, and Kṛṣṇa. Then, that Brahmin manifested his lack of desire to go to the earth, after which he described the greatness of Śeṣa. When questioned by the Brahmin, Yama described hell to him, including the faults such as sins that lead to the attainment of hell.

The description of the slaughter of Caṇḍa, Yuṇḍa, and others; the description of the Kāmarī Mahāṣṭamī; the description [of the pilgrimage site]; the narration of the ripening of karma (*karmavipāka*); the narration of the meritorious means for the destruction of hell; the description of the majesty of Anarakeśvara, Śraramā, Mantrābādika, and Kṣetrapāla; the description of the majesty of Vicitraśvara; the description of the majesty of Megheśvara; and the description of the majesty of Nadayeśvara.

The description of the greatness of Piṅgānadī-māhasya; the description of the greatness of Barabhadreśvara; the description of the greatness of Gukeśvara; and the description of the greatness of Caṇḍeśvara... (and so forth).

When King Daśaratha, desiring to bestow his wealth and grain upon those who were not recipients of gifts, prohibited such acceptance, the sages abandoned that wealth and grain, departed from there, and set out on a pilgrimage. Having traveled some distance, they saw lotus stalks in a pond; having gathered them and placed them on the bank, they performed their daily rites. Then, perceiving that someone had stolen those lotus stalks, they [realized] it was the truth by means of their own [divine] vision.

The construction of the Dāpatha; there, Śakra, having arrived in the form of a dog, took away their food, and knowing this, Śakra granted them boons; the establishment of a pool there under the name of Ṛṣitīrtha; a description of the greatness of Ṛṣitīrtha; the installation of Nandāditya by King Nanda, who was afflicted with leprosy, for the sake of curing his leprosy; and a description of the majesty of Nandāditya.

Pitṛyaṃpara had three sons—Saurāṣṭrasādhipatya, Ātreyakhañjañaka, and Rājasthaika—who were well-versed in the Taittirīya branch of the Veda. He installed Trita, the son of Trita, in the kingdom. Trita, having become envious, conspired with Pakata and Dvita to cast Trita into a well. Thereupon, Trita invoked the gods through mantras and satisfied them by means of those very incantations. Consequently, he caused Pakata and Dvita, who had been defeated by him, to be driven out from that place.

A description of the origin of Tanitaku; a description of the greatness of merit gained by performing *śrāddha* and other rites for the sake of one’s father; a description of the greatness of Caritadūṣatīrtha; a description of the greatness of Uvāṅeśvara; a description of the greatness of Siddheśvara; a description of the greatness of Nyumatī; a description of the greatness of Bārāhasvāmī; a description of the greatness of Chāyāṅga; a description of the greatness of Nandinīguptā; and a description of the greatness of Kanaṅanadā.

The description of the majesty of Kumbhīśvara; the description of the majesty of Gaṅgāpatha-gadāvara; the description of the majesty of Camasodbheda; and the description of the majesty of Vidurāśrama.

The great sage Maṅkaṇaka, having approached the eastern Sarasvatī, performed austerities. When he had attained perfection through those austerities, he began to dance out of wonder and amazement at the creation of the *śākarasa* (potherb juice). Thinking that the entire universe had begun to dance because Maṅkaṇaka was dancing, Śaṅkara arrived there and questioned Maṅkaṇaka regarding the cause of his dancing. Having learned the reason for Maṅkaṇaka’s dancing from him, Śaṅkara caused ashes to be sprinkled upon him with his own hand. By that [act], Maṅkaṇaka...

The cessation of activity by the astonished being; thereafter, the installation of the *liṅga* according to the word of Śaṃkara; a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Jvālī, Sarasvatī, Maṅkeśvara, and Carariṅga... (the subjects include) a description of the majesty of the three cities (*tripura*) and the three limbs (*aṅgatraya*)... a description of the majesty of Rāḍatīrtha; [the sixth... a description of the majesty of Sūryaprācī. [The seventh] a description of the majesty of Trinetreśvara... a description of the majesty of Umāpati at Devikā. & ( ( ,,.

The description of the majesty of Bhūdharayajñavarāha... [A certain other man named Śaidākha, having abandoned his own dharma, supported his family by acting as a hunter. Once, while he was engaged in the effort of killing deer along with his retinue, the sages instructed him in the proper conduct regarding that month of Vaiśākha and gave him a mantra. By the power of that mantra, his name became Vālmīki; and by that Vālmīki, through the word of the sage and the worship of the Devikā...]

Description of the praise of the Siddhibhāṣī; description of the greatness of Kāmā; description of the greatness of Mūlasthāna; description of the list of one hundred and eight names of Sūrya; and, within the section on the greatness of Cyavanāditya, description of the fruit of reciting the one hundred and eight names of Sūrya. . . .

Description of the majesty of Cyavaneśvara: the making of Aśvinīkumāras beautiful by Sukanyā; the description of how Sukanyā brought about the restoration of her husband’s handsome form and youth; then, at the word of Cyavana, the description of how he attained a beautiful form by bathing with the two Aśvins in the pool; and the description of the majesty of Cyavaneśvara.

The performance of a sacrifice by Cyavana Maharṣi for the purpose of securing the right to participate in sacrifices for his two sons, Ādānī and Kumāra, whom he had assisted; and therein, within that sacrifice, the narration of the account of the emergence of the great Asura named Madana, who was produced by Cyavana through the release of the Vajra weapon intended to obstruct the sacrificial portion of the Nāsatyas and by the power of his ascetic penance.

° The forgiveness of Śakra upon seeing this great calamity brought about by the arrows of Cyavana; then, Cyavana’s ascension to heaven after performing a rite, and his seeking forgiveness for Śakra’s transgression; a description of the boon received from Cyavana; a description of the greatness of Sukanyā and the Apsaras; a description of the greatness of the Daśaśrama-gaṅgā-ghāṭa; a description of the greatness of Ajāpāṅgeśvarī. ...

Description of the majesty of Bārāka situated to the east of Agastya’s hermitage; description of the majesty of Bhadrakāśī; description of the majesty of the Bārākā of Bhadrakarī. Description of the origin of Kumārasthāna and the majesty of Kuberamāhātmya; description of the majesty of the river Ṛṣitoyā; description of the majesty of the Bārākā situated to the north of Agastya. Narration of the conclusion of the story regarding how Vātāpi, who had assumed the form of a ram through deceit, was devoured by Agastya; [and] the account of Aṅgārapāta, Aṅgāreśvara, Viśvabhūtīśvara, and Carvaṇeśvara.

The description of the greatness of the three faces of Bhidhāṅga; the description of the origin of Kubera’s city and the greatness of Somanātha established by Kubera; the description of the greatness of Puṣyaśvara preceded by [the account of] Joganyeśvara.

The description of the greatness of Candrodaka-tīrtha, followed by the description of the greatness of Indrarāśvara; the offering of praise by all the sages; then, by the pleased Brahmā, the granting of the Sarasvatī at Devadāruvana; the performance of penance there by the sages; the description of the origin of Ṛṣitoyā; the description of the necessity of taking [the water] from Ṛṣitoyā; the description of the three pools (kuṇḍas) known as Brāhma, Vaiṣṇava, and Raudra; and the description of the necessity of performing the Gaṇabhra-yāga there. 8.
(Ten [factors]?)
...from that, [the syllable] *gaḥ* arises.

[The section on] Cābhaka: Nārada, having seen his own body covered with leprosy, gave a curse to Sāmba; Sāmba also gave the curse, "Become afflicted with old age," to Nārada. Nārada, for the removal of that old age, performed the worship of Āditya and established a *liṅga* at that very place, Trabhāsa; this is the description of the majesty of Nāradāditya. There, at Trabhāsa, Sāmba, having performed penance to dispel his own curse, established a *liṅga*, [known as] Sāṃvāditya.

The description of the majesty of Māhchhatmya; the description of the majesty of Aparanāśayana; the description of the origin and majesty of Mūlacaṇḍī; the description of the majesty of Catumukhavināyaka; the description of the majesty of Kebadeśvara; the description of the majesty of Gopārasāmihari; the description of the majesty of Bakuṭasvāmin; the description of the majesty of Uttarāka; the description of the majesty of the confluence at Ṛṣitīrtha; the description of the majesty of Marudāyodevī; and the description of the majesty of Kṣemāditya.

Description of the majesty of Mahodaya. ... Description of the majesty of Saṃgameśvara. ... Description of the majesty of Unnata-Vināyaka. ... Description of the majesty of Taṅasvāmī. [End of] section *ka*. Description of the majesty of Kālamegha.

Ka: A description of the majesty of Rakimiṇī; Dha: A description of the majesty of Rigeśvarabhadra; Śa: The defeat of the gods by the Daitya named Vaṅga, who arose from Śaṃśṛraṅga; thereafter, the Daitya’s propitiation of Lord Viṣṇu and his presentation of his own suffering; then, the battle between Viṣṇu and that [Daitya]; when their battle had commenced, Hara (Śiva) created the Taptodaka-kuṇḍa for the sake of destroying the fatigue of Viṣṇu; and by performing ablutions there in that Taptodaka-kuṇḍa...

The laughter of Viṣṇu when his throat was stepped upon by Śramaṇadita; the granting of a boon to him by Viṣṇu upon seeing that [laughter]; the establishment of the deity under the name Taṅgasvāmī according to his word; a description of the majesty of Talasvāmī; a description of the majesty of the Śaṅkhāvarta Tīrtha... In the description of the majesty of Goṣpada Tīrtha, the account of the birth of Pṛthu from King Avenara, who was like a son of the Earth (Pṛthivī), and how the earth was consumed by Pṛthu.
The description of the milking of the earth in the form of a cow for the sake of generating offspring, and the causing of the birth of subjects by Pṛthu as if by a son.

810.1 | Recalling his father’s sinful deeds again and again, Pṛthu traveled to many sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and shrines (*kṣetra*) in order to purify them. Thinking that his father’s sins might not have been washed away anywhere else, Pṛthu went to Goṣpada. By performing ablutions and other rites at Goṣpada-tīrtha, Pṛthu shook off all the sins of his father and attained liberation (*mokṣa*). This is the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Goṣpada-tīrtha.

... [The description of the greatness of the *Huṃkāra* well; the description of the destruction of Nārāyaṇagṛha; the dragging away of Āpastamba by the fishermen with water; then the fishermen, terrified of the fish, making a request to Āpastamba; the description of the greatness of the gift of a cow (*godāna*) in the dialogue between Āpastamba and King Ambarīṣa regarding the payment for Āpastamba; the description of the greatness of that very place; the establishment of the deity named Jāyeśvara; and the description of the greatness of Jāyeśvarī and Caṇḍīśvara.]

The description of the greatness of Ārdrāpūrvinarāja; the description of the greatness of the Karāṅgaṇḍa-tīrtha of Candreśvara; the description of the greatness and the procedure for the Kapi-khāṣaṣṭhī-vrata at Kapiladhārā; the description of the greatness of Jaradraveśvara; the description of the greatness of Naṭeśvara; the description of the greatness of Karkoṭakārka; the description of the greatness of Hāṭakeśvara; the description of the greatness of Nāradeśvarī; and the description of the greatness of Maṃtravibhūṣaṇā-Gaurī.

The description of the greatness of Dugakūṭagaṇapati; the description of the greatness of Kauravedavarī; the description of the greatness of Suparṇekhā; the description of the greatness of Bhaḍatīrtha; the description of the greatness of Karamāṭa; and the description of the greatness of Gaparaśvara.

The description of the greatness of Vahusuvarṇeśvara; likewise, Āpastamba’s performance of penance in the waters of the Bhavyā Sarasvatī; there, the subjects concerning the fisherman Jauḍā along with the Bharas and Malasayas; the description of the greatness of Paṇaśageśvara... the description of the greatness of Koṭīśvara; the description of the greatness of Nārāyaṇatīrtha; the description of the greatness of Śṛṅgāreśvara; the description of the greatness of Mākaṇḍereśvara.

The description of the greatness of Koṭidamaṇḍukeśvara; the description of the greatness of the eleven Rudrāṅgas; ... the description of the greatness of Hiraṇyatuṇḍapuradharyarahdakeśvara; the description of the greatness of Saṃbateśvara; and the description of the greatness of various scattered sacred sites.
Thus ends the first, most delightful section on the measurement of time within the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the second section on the majesty of Bakhrāpatha (Giranāra) within the Abhāsa-khaṇḍa.

In the *Dāmodara-māhātmya*, there is the arrival of many sages at the place known as Rajas belonging to a certain king; there, by those sages, the greatness of all the sacred sites (*tīrthas*) for the King of Elephants is recounted. Then follows the description of the origin of the name [of the elephant], the description of the *māhātmya* of Dāmodara, the etymological derivation of the word *bhava*, the description of the establishment of the deity, and the description of the *māhātmya* of Bhava.

[The text describes] the greatness of Gandhebhara, the description of the procedure for the pilgrimage to Cakratīrtha, and the sight of the twelve deer-faced children (mṛgavaktra-bālāḥ) who were performing [the rites]. Then, by means of a certain forest-guard (*vanapāṭha*), this was reported to King Bhoja. Upon hearing it, the wicked Bhoja gave much wealth to that forest-guard. Thereafter, that forest-guard went to that forest himself and [found] that deer-faced child with Bhoja.

Having taken [her], he went to his own home; then, when Ogha asked that Bāṣkali about the cause for her having attained the state of a human-eater and the crookedness of a Bhṛgu, she related it. Then, after [Ogha] had made offerings to the Brahmins, there followed a description of the events concerning Sarasvatī, whose flow of speech became clear through the consecration of the *puroḍāśa* and the *marāraṇasa* cakes, and who was traveling toward the forest. In the dialogue between Mṛgānanā and King Bhoja, there is an account of her own origin, and how, while wandering in another forest, she encountered Udākhala and Karva.

Therein is the account of the drinking of the *vīryabindu* (seminal drop) by that [hero]; then, the drinking of the *udālaka-vīryabindu* by Mṛgāvatī; then, Mṛgāvatī’s narration to Bhoja of her own birth from Udālaka through Mṛgānanā; the description of the greatness of many holy places (*tīrtha*) such as Dvāravatī and Karuṣaṣṭha; and the story of Mṛgānanā’s previous birth at Svarṇarekhā, including how she attained a divine face by offering a deer-face to Śiva, followed by her marriage to King Bhoja.

Description of the greatness of the *rekhā* in the dialogue between Sarasvatī and Bhārgava; description of the destruction of Rudra as recounted by Brahmā at the word of Viṣṇu during the dispute between Brahmā and Sadra; description of the story of Dakṣa’s sacrifice and the destruction of that sacrifice by Viṣṇu; description of the birth and marriage of Pārvatī; then, on one occasion, when Śaṅkara had vanished, Viṣṇu and the other gods set out together with Pārvatī, who was mounted upon a lion, in search of Śiva; and then, at Prabhāsa—

The journey of those [sages] to see Śaṅkara; by the command of Viṣṇu and others, the establishment of Śaṅkara as "Bhava" in his own form in the sacred field of Sthāneśvara; and the description of the origin and greatness of Bhava.

A description of the regions of the *Vasāṣatha* field by the sage Sārasvata; a description of the sequence of the pilgrimage to the *Vasāṣatha* field; a description of the greatness of days such as *gajacchāyā* for the performance of *śrāddha*; a description of the fruits of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at Bhīmeśvara, Skānda, Māreśvara, Varāyaṇya, and other holy sites; a statement on the fruit of remembering sacred fords (*tīrtha*); a description of the rules for pilgrimage; and therein, a statement on the fruit of the worship of Hari and Hara.

The description of giving seats, gifts, recitation, burnt offerings (*homa*), and the soliciting of deities and twice-born; the description of the greatness of *śrāddha* offerings and other rites. ... (In Vāmanapura, Vasiṣṭha, distressed by the loss of his son, performed austerities on the bank of the Svarṇarekhā and established a sacred site (*liṅga*) there. Then follows the description of the greatness of Somanātha installed by Vāmana, including the taking of refuge in Viṣṇu when Bali had driven away the gods; thereafter, Viṣṇu assumed the form of Vāmana for the sake of the gods' purpose...)

In the assembly of the sixty-four [sages], after making the earth tremble by lifting it with three steps, he established the quarters [of the world] following the propitiation of Somanātha; this is the description of the origin of Someśvara. Vāmana went to the Raivataka forest to take the milk of Dāmodara; having worshipped Carasi there and performed rites such as bathing and giving gifts, he subsequently went to the holy site of Vastrāpatha to see Dāmodara. Having performed a vigil (*jāgaraṇa*) there, he departed for Siddhi; this is the account of the vigil at Dāmodara-tīrtha.

Then follows the description of the greatness [of Śiva], the journey of Nārada into the dense forest for the sake of pilgrimage, and his encounter on the way with various ascetics and others; the narration of the dialogue between Śiva and Vāmana; therein, the description of the greatness of Śivarātri, including the granting of a boon to Vāmana by Śiva, and the exposition of the ritual procedure for the Śivarātri vow; and [the account of] how Nārada, having seen the Lord, spoke before Bali, knowing that the Lord would also appear in the form of the Vāmana incarnation to humble Bali.

Regarding his departure: there, Nārada, having agitated the mind of Bali by declaring that the splendor (*lakṣmī*) of Indra was even greater than his own, and having caused him to remember the deception practiced by the gods at the time of the churning of the ocean, approached Śakra himself and spoke to him in the same manner. Thus, having mutually provoked them through such disputes and the like, Nārada explained to Bali the principles of statecraft (*rājanīti*), dharma, and legal procedure (*vyavahāra*).

The granting of boons by Hara and Hara (Śiva and Viṣṇu) to Mount Kūrmada; the daily arrival of Viṣṇu to see the Lord situated in the temple of Viṣṇumandira on Mount Kūrmada, located to the south of Śabataka-parvata; the installation of Hari and Hara by the cook (Sūda) at that very Mount Kūrmada; the granting of boons to Mount Kūrmada by Hara and Hara; then, during the fifth Manvantara named Raivata, the birth of Ṛtadhvaja from Ṛtuparṇa, and the dialogue between Ṛtadhvaja and Garuḍa concerning his own son born of Revatī.

The falling of Revatī’s husband below due to the fault of his speech and the casting of his own gaze by Kaṅkaṇavat; thereafter, the digging of the Kumuda lake; the giving of Revatī to King Durdama by means of a deceptive statement; the birth of a son known as Revata through the excavation of the Revatī-pool; the description of the greatness of the Śivāruka tree worshipped by Vaiṣṇavas; and Nārada’s narration to Bali of the rules for Vaiṣṇava vows, vigils, and so forth, as well as the [consequences] of performing them without such vows.

Having performed the preparatory rites (*rādika*) with great solemnity for the purpose of the sacrifice’s commencement, he summoned the Brahmins by the command of Śukra; [the text then describes] the undertaking of the sacrifice, a description of the power of the *baliyajña*, an explanation of the methods such as the *śrāṇāyāma*, a description of the eightfold production of the primary nature (*prakṛti*), and an exposition of the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine. [It further describes] the method of meditating upon Bhava, and the arrival of Nārada before Vāmana while he was standing in the presence of Bhava; [and finally] [what was said] by Nārada to Vāmana.

The narration of the account of the subjugation of Bali; Vāmana’s rebuke of Nārada for his futile boasting; the description by Nārada of Bali’s endurance until the end of the kalpa; the narration by Nārada to Vāmana of the events concerning the slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa and others; then, at the word of Nārada, Vāmana went to the realm of Bali to restrain him, and although he was disguised as a boar, he requested three paces of land, and thereafter, through his own expansion, he occupied the entire cosmic egg.

The subduing of Bāli; the dialogue between Śakra and Svayambhū following the subjugation; Viṣṇu’s residence in the body of Bāli; and the description of the fruit of hearing the greatness of the Vakhāpatha-kṣetra—this is the second [section], the greatness of the Vakhāpatha-kṣetra, in the Śrabhā-khaṇḍa.
The chapters are the ways of the enemy.
Now, within the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, the third section is the Abuda-khaṇḍa.

The commencement of the description of the greatness of Arbuda; therein, first, the departure of Vasiṣṭha to Arbuda; having performed austerities there, his sacrificial cow, which had gone to the forest to graze on grass and other fodder, fell into a chasm; because the cow did not return in the evening, Vasiṣṭha became anxious; then Vasiṣṭha, having approached the vicinity of the chasm and heard the lowing of his own cow, meditated upon the Sarasvatī for her emergence from it; by that meditation...

Sarasvatī filled the hollow of her own garment and caused the cow to emerge; taking that cow, she went to Vasiṣṭha’s hermitage. Then, having gone to the Himavat mountain to fill it with water, Vasiṣṭha told the Himavat about the extent of the hollow and described the origin of the auspicious spring. This concludes the description of the events occurring near Vasiṣṭha’s hermitage, beginning with the account of Uttaṅka, a disciple of Gautama, who was seeking to give his preceptor’s fee.

At the request of his brother, Ruru went to the house of Saudāsa to bring back the earrings of Saudāsa’s wife, Madyantī; there, he made a vow to offer himself to Saudāsa—who had come with a tiger-like face to devour him—in exchange for the earrings. Then, from the presence of the queen, the earrings were recovered and Saudāsa was liberated from the curse. Subsequently, when the disciple of Gautama, having taken the earrings, was traveling along the road, the two earrings were dropped and seized by Takṣaka.

The abduction [of Soma]; then, out of Takṣaka’s audacity, the journey to Pātāla for the purpose of bringing him back; at that very time, the creation of a chasm there; the description of the life of Uttaṅka, the disciple of Gītamara; by the command of Vasiṣṭha and at the word of Himavat, the filling of the void with the water brought by the Nāgas, as if by a flood of clouds.

The description of the greatness of Abudāva: there, on the mountain named Divadhena, which was brought by Abuda, Vasiṣṭha performed penance; Vasiṣṭha offered a hymn of praise to Śiva; then, by the grace of Śiva, Vasiṣṭha established a Liṅga named Acaledvara; Śiva made his residence at Mandākinī; and the description of the greatness of Acaledvara. ... [End of section]. (Note: The final portion of the text provided appears to be corrupted or consists of scribal marks.)
And, do not speak thus; O Blessed One, may there be no further existence for me. What then? May there be merit. Why?

In the *Auṇḍācara*, within the description of the *Nāgatīrtha* in the dialogue between Yayāti and his son, there is a description of the bath at the *Nāgatīrtha* on the Gautamī. Therein, because her heart was agitated by a desire for a son, she conceived through a mere thought (*kevalajñāna*). Then, as she was desirous of embracing her deceased husband, she heard a voice from the sky, whereby her intent toward death was averted; followed by a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the *Nāgatīrtha*.

The description of the greatness of Vañcakhīṣṭha-āśrama; the description of the power of Acaṭeda-vara; the description of the greatness of Adrakarṇa-deva-rinetra... [and] in the description of the greatness of Gar-kadāra, Vasiṣṭha’s narration to Ajāpāla that because you attained the status of a Śūdra in previous births, you have obtained the position of kingship in this life through the worship of Kedāra-deva at Kedāra; the description of the greatness of Kedāra-deva...

A description of the duration and characteristics of the various ages; a discernment of the qualities and defects of the four yugas; a description of how all goals are attained through the power of the [Kali] age. A description of the greatness of Keṭī; the attainment of a beautiful form by the Apsaras named Capūrṇā through her bathing at Rūpatīrtha; a description of the majesty of Rūpatīrtha. In the description of the greatness of Ṛṣikiśa, King Ambarīṣa performs penance and installs an image of Hari; a description of the majesty of Dabhīkeḍa by the Siddha named Viśvāvasu.

Having propitiated Śiva, the installation of the *liṅga* by the grace of Śiva; a description of the majesty of Siddheśvarī. Seeing the Daityas defeated, the preceptor of the Daityas, Śukrācārya, reflected on how to achieve victory for the Daityas; having propitiated the Lord and obtained a boon, he brought about the victory of the Daityas and installed a *liṅga* there named Śukreśvara; a description of the greatness of the Śukreśvara *liṅga*. [The topics continue: By means of knowledge imparted by a certain woman named Maṇikikā, her...

The description of the section known as Khaṇḍakhayāti, which begins with the attainment of his true form by Maṇikarṇika; the glorification of the greatness of Lord Maṇikarṇika; the establishment of a holy ford (tīrtha) by a certain Brahmin named Guṇa who had become lame, after he had propitiated Śiva; the description of the greatness of Pagutīrtha; and the account of Citrāṅgada, a perpetrator of extreme sins, who entered the [Gaṅgā] after having cast off his lameness and established a tīrtha in his own name.

The abduction of Citrāṅgada by Vṛṣāṇa; thereafter, the casting of the sinner Citrāṅgada into hell by the messengers of Yama; the attainment of bliss by the living beings there through the casting of Citrāṅgada into that hell; then, having witnessed this marvel and observed it with his eye of knowledge, Yama reflected in his mind that because of Citrāṅgada’s performance of a bath in his sacred ford, he would attain prosperity right there and thus was not a partaker of the suffering of the hellish realm; and so, his release from that hell. Then, of him—

The departure of Vitrāṅgada to heaven in a celestial chariot surrounded by hosts of Apsarases; a description of the greatness of Yamatīrtha; a description of the greatness of Bārāhatīrtha; the bestowal of the disease of consumption upon Candra by Dakṣa, who, out of partiality toward his own daughters, cursed him for his unequal treatment; thereafter, Candra’s performance of penance and the cessation of his consumption through that penance; and the installation of a Liṅga by Candra under the name Candrabhāsa.

The description of the greatness of the Candra-prabhāsa Tīrtha. The description of the greatness of the Piṇḍodaka Tīrtha. After the Dānava named Karālī had conquered the gods, he performed propitiation of the Goddess; by the grace of the Goddess, he attained heaven. Having placed Mount Pāriyātra upon his body, the Goddess established her own residence on its peak. The gods caused the Śrīmātā [to be established] as the Goddess’s own abode. The description of the greatness of Śrīmātā. Now, the greatness of the Śūti Tīrtha: therein, [the story of] those who were thrown into the middle of the river by a washerman...

Because the Valakhilyas attained their status as lords by bathing there, that sacred ford (tīrtha) was given the name Śuddhatīrtha; this is the description of the majesty of Śuddhatīrtha. After the Daitya Niśumbha had been slain, the Goddess established her residence there, and because of this, she was installed by the gods under the name Kātyāyanī; this is the description of the majesty of Kātyāyanī. (Skanda Purāṇa, Part 69).
The six rites for the child: first, the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) for the infant; then, the naming ceremony for him by Śiva as Mahāvināyaka, [known as] Mahāvaināyakīra.
Not a bird; the narration of the nearness, the description of the greatness of Mahāvināyaka... [the description of the greatness of Kanakhala-tīrtha]. [13] || Ra ||

Description of the majesty of Cakratīrtha. ... Description of the greatness of the Pārtheda-varam [Pārtheda-vara]. Chapter 6: Description of the majesty of Manuṣyatīrtha. ... Regarding the greatness of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, while they were fighting each other in mutual rivalry, the creation of a single mediator between them; the description of the birth of the toothless [Adanta] Ṛgī; then, by means of a divine voice, causing them both to desist from their battle—[and how] Suprabhapati, who was intent on war, [beheld] her who was suckling at his breast.

Then, with an arrow, he struck Kharapra; subsequently, the king was granted a curse by the Goddess, who said, "You shall become Rudravyātra. For that very reason, the king’s [eightfold] form, extending as far as the tip of the linga, was revealed by Śiva.

The giving of false testimony by the Brahmin, the punishment of the ungrateful Ketaka, the offering of a prayer to Viṣṇu, the departure of Vyāsa, the description of the greatness of Kṛṣṇatīrtha, and [the account of] having returned to his own place, having gone to the cow-pen, having made the calf drink milk, and [telling] the news regarding the calf that had gone to the forest.

Indeed, having restrained her own companions from taking up arms against the enemy, she was prevented by them from going; yet, because she had performed propitiation when the goddess was pleased by the prayers of those oppressed by the demon Mahiṣāsura, the goddess brought about the slaying of Mahiṣāsura. In that very place, there is the description of the greatness of the Kañjavīkāśrama.

Having disregarded the tiger, he returned; seeing this, the cow was filled with wonder and recounted the events of her rescue. "O Caṇḍī, this is the fame [attained] through the command of the Lord; this is the sacred ford of the monkey, which is to be honored. Thus it was said.

Description of the greatness of Aśnitīrtha; description of the greatness of Śivarka following the arrival of Agni; how Rati caused her own lamentation because Kāma was burnt by Śiva with his arrow; hearing that lamentation of Rati, Indrasena departed for a foreign land for the purpose of destroying Indra and seizing his wealth; then, through a messenger, the account of Indrasena’s restoration to life after having first been made bodiless by Indra; the establishment of a linga by Kāma together with Rati; and the report that Indrasena had died.

Because he spoke to his wife regarding that, Indrasena was deprived of his wife; there follows the description of the greatness of the Śīghra-tīrtha and other holy sites located at Prabhāsa, and how [Indrasena] performed a penance at those various shrines, such as Somatīrtha, after having gone there. Indrasena went there.

1. The description of the origin of the Mākaṇḍeya hermitage, preceded by the illustrative narrative of the birth of Mākaṇḍi and others, along with the account of the destruction of sins through bathing at the Raktānubandha-tīrtha; 2. The description of the greatness of Udālakedavara.

Having taken the child born of Nivī-udvasenā and placed him in a basket, she set out. Because of the absence of the basket, Śikhaṇḍinī, thinking "This is a young boy," joined him with the trunk of a certain intoxicated elephant and [the child] grew. Then Rukmiṇī performed the birth rites for the infant brought from Bhogavatī by Śrī Kṛṣṇa. By Durvāsas—[this concludes the third sub-section of the Pramāru-khaṇḍa].
Thinking, "Has Rukmiṇī taken the water-jar without the bowstring? and being unable to tolerate that, he [acted] toward that Rukmiṇī.

The gift of the body. Then, having descended from the chariot with Duryodhana, he established himself upon the ground; thereafter, together with Śrī Kṛṣṇa, [he attained] the objects of the auspicious one. Now begins the fourth section on the Greatness of Dvārakā within the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa.

Oṃ! The description of the greatness of Vyāsatīrtha. When the Kali Yuga arrived, Sūta, being questioned by Śaunaka and others as to what the dwelling place of Viṣṇu would be, described the greatness of the holy ford at Gautama’s hermitage. [The description of] his abiding there; having performed his own incarnations and other deeds, the description of the greatness of the Gaṅgāsaṃtaraṇa Tīrtha, preceded by the story of King Indumati, who praised the infinite Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

When he had returned to his own place, having seen the state of the world where the Dharma was mostly in decline, and wondering what the condition of those like himself would be, he reflected upon the greatness of the Tathāgata. Having considered this, he spoke with the words of a seer; and hearing those words of the sage, [he was] oppressed by the essence of the teaching.

The description of the power of Koṭitīrtha; the departure of the sages, who were intent on employing the means for the attainment of liberation by various beings, before Brahmā; [and] Udārka and the other sages—

The description of the greatness of the Candrodbheda-tīrtha; ... — ... the offering of praise by Brahmā; then the narration by the sages who had arrived outside regarding the reason for their coming; at that time, the description by Brahmā of the majesty of the peak of Īśāna; ... — ... [Brahmā’s] giving the answer, "I do not know the dwelling place of Viṣṇu"; after hearing Brahmā’s reply, the description of the greatness of the attainment of the state of Jada upon performing the renunciation of life;
then, having set out, Brahmā went with the sages into the presence of Prahlāda; by Prahlāda, all—
Description of the majesty of Tripuṣkara. ... The performance of hospitality for the Brāhmaṇas by Prahlāda; and the narration of the reason for their arrival by the sages through the mouth of Brahmā.
Description of the greatness of Rādhāhrada. ... How the sages, through their power, brought about the presence of the Blessed One in Rādhā during the Kali Yuga. Ka ||

The description of the greatness of Gṛheśvara... [omitted] ...the description by Prahlāda of the commencement of the Kṛta Yuga in response to the sages; therein, the description of the greatness of the inseparable pair, Uddhava and Kṛṣṇa; and upon their conversation having concluded, the account of Duvasu’s return to the banks of the Gomatī after setting out on a journey—thus [ends] the description of the greatness of the Umāmaheśvara Tīrtha... [omitted] ...having heard this, Kṛṣṇa and Kṛṣṇā went there for the sake of meeting Duvasu; thereafter, by Duvasu [to] Kṛṣṇa... [omitted].

The description of the great majesty and power of Satī; the manifestation of light from the ten directions and other wonders; then, having spoken of his welfare out of fear, Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s making Durvāsas proceed to Dvārakā; Durvāsas’s arrival at his own hermitage and his inquiry regarding the greatness of the land of Gaṅgādhara; his report of that matter, yet despite it, because of Kṛṣṇa’s persistent insistence, he appoints Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī to the task of pulling the chariot.

In this forest of suffering, terrible with darkness, where the heat of afflictions is the wind and the water is impure, some praise that knowledge of the Self which regards pleasure, pain, and gold as equal. Here, it should be understood that "regarding pleasure, pain, and gold as equal" is a qualification of that knowledge. Because the reality of the Self is of the nature of pure existence (*sat*), it is devoid of differentiation; and because, in the ultimate sense, pleasure, pain, and gold are of the single form of consciousness (*cit*), pleasure, pain, and gold are equal by virtue of their non-difference from consciousness within the knowledge of the Self. Thus, the meaning is that some praise that knowledge of the Self in which pleasure, pain, and gold are equal.

§109.132. At that time, the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, this is the Dharma discourse on the Great Exposition of the Noble Truths, which has never before been taught by me. Monks, this Dharma discourse on the Great Exposition of the Noble Truths should be learned by you all, and it should be recited together in the communal recitation. §109.133. This is what the Blessed One said. Having spoken thus, the Well-Gone One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. §109.134. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, monks! “Friend! those monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, this Dharma discourse on the Great Exposition of the Noble Truths has never before been taught by the Blessed One. Friends, this Dharma discourse on the Great Exposition of the Noble Truths should be learned by you all, and it should be recited together in the communal recitation. §109.135. When this was said, the Venerable Udāyin said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Friend Ānanda, who will learn this Dharma discourse on the Great Exposition of the Noble Truths? Friend Ānanda, this Dharma discourse on the Great Exposition of the Noble Truths is difficult to understand; it is profound, deep, hard to see, and hard to realize. It is peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and comprehensible only to the wise. Friend Ānanda, the Tathāgata himself has taught it as such, and he himself has explained it as such. But friend Ānanda, when the Tathāgata himself has taught it as such, and he himself has explained it as such, who will learn this Dharma discourse on the Great Exposition of the Noble Truths? §109.136. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Udāyin: “Friend Udāyin, there are many among the monks who have heard little and are unlearned, who do not preserve what they have heard, whose minds are not cultivated, who lack wisdom, and who are not skilled in the Dharma. Friend Udāyin, these monks will not learn this Dharma discourse on the Great Exposition of the Noble Truths. Furthermore, the knowable (*vādhanya*), the thinkable (*mantavya*), the principle of egoity (*ahaṃtā*), sound (*śabda*), touch (*sparśa*), taste (*rasa*), form (*rūpa*), smell (*gandha*), speech (*vacana*), grasping (*ādāna*), movement (*visarga*), evacuation (*utsarga*), and pleasure (*ānanda*) are the thirteen great planets."

§1. The Discourse on the Great Virtue of Renunciation Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, renunciation is a great virtue; it is a noble quality, a quality of the Tathāgatas, a quality that leads to peace, a quality that leads to enlightenment, a quality that leads to Nibbāna. It is a quality that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the destruction of craving, to dispassion, to cessation, and to Nibbāna. And what, monks, is renunciation? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having completely abandoned sensual desire, dwells with a mind free from sensual desire; he purifies his mind from sensual desire. Having completely abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for all living beings; he purifies his mind from ill will and hatred. Having completely abandoned dullness and drowsiness, he dwells free from dullness and drowsiness, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind from dullness and drowsiness. Having completely abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells without agitation, with a mind inwardly peaceful; he purifies his mind from restlessness and remorse. Having completely abandoned doubt, he dwells having gone beyond doubt, unperplexed regarding wholesome qualities; he purifies his mind from doubt. This, monks, is called renunciation. This renunciation is a great virtue; it is a noble quality, a quality of the Tathāgatas, a quality that leads to peace, a quality that leads to enlightenment, a quality that leads to Nibbāna. It is a quality that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the destruction of craving, to dispassion, to cessation, and to Nibbāna. [The Blessed One spoke thus.
