(Phaṣaeālā, 30202843 . , ena oṃ vaka ka ka na viṣayā; pa0 pa° avyāyāḥ viṣayāḥ pa0 pa°) Now, in the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*, within the *Ratha-māheśvara-khaṇḍa*, this is the table of contents (*viṣayanukramaṇikā*). Satī-devī goes to her father’s presence in the vicinity of Bhūga and others; when Dakṣa asks the reason for Śaṅkara’s non-invitation, he utters insults against the gods. Unable to endure the insult to the gods and her own humiliation, Satī offers herself into the fire. Now begins the first section, the *Kedāra-khaṇḍa*, of the *Māheśvara-khaṇḍa*.

The destruction of those who had assembled there, numbering ten million, by the blows of weapons and the severing of their own limbs; the auspicious invocation beginning with the *Lokapāla* hymns; then the commencement of the *Skānda Mahāpurāṇa*; therein, the state of paralysis of the sages, headed by Śaunaka, due to fear in the Naimiṣa forest; the arrival of Vyāsa’s disciple, the great sage Ugraśravas, at the request of the gods after Śaṅkara had heard the account from Nārada and was filled with great wrath; and [the dialogue] of Śaunaka and the other sages with Lomaśa.

The striking of his own matted locks upon the summit of that mountain; thereafter, the arrival of Vīrabhadra, Kālabhairava, Bhūta, and others; the knitting of eyebrows by Rudra out of a desire to hear the majesty of Śiva; then, the emergence of the three types of fever—fever, cold, and shivering—in their respective numbers, preceded by the commencement of the Purāṇa by the great sage Romaśa; then, at the command of Śaṅkara, the description of the supreme greatness of Śiva by Vīrabhadra; therein, first, the narration of the account of the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice. In that [account]:

Dakṣa’s return to the sacrificial ground of Dakṣa-yajña with the goddesses; the notification to Śiva and his attendants by those stationed at the sacrificial ground upon seeing Rudra’s army approaching and their intent to destroy the sacrifice; the flight of Indra and the other gods out of fear of Śiva’s curse; their preparation for battle; Dakṣa’s entreaty to all the gods; and the bestowal of curses upon Dakṣa and the other Brahmins by Viṣṇu, Dharma, and Nandin.

Then follows the consolation of Nandin by Śaṅkara, the act of rebuking and censuring Dakṣa, and the burning of Dakṣa’s sacrifice by the one whose color is like a dark cloud. Then, the outbreak of a lack of peace due to Dakṣa’s reviling of Śaṅkara. 1.

The battle between Indra and the other gods and Vīrabhadra and his followers; the commencement of the sacrificial rite by Dakṣa at Kanakhala, accompanied by the thought of victory; the desire of the great sages such as Vasiṣṭha to obstruct Viṣṇu’s [portion] in that sacrifice; the arrival of Vīrabhadra into the midst of the sacrificial enclosure preceded by the defeat of the world-protectors; then the arrival of the deities led by Śiva; and there, seeing Dakṣa arrived, the great sages [addressed] Dakṣa.

The commencement of the battle between Vīrabhadra and others and the gods headed by Viṣṇu; Viṣṇu’s instruction to Śiva for the purpose of bringing him [to the sacrifice] upon seeing the defeat of the gods; the arrival of Śiva at the sacrificial ground from the southern region; Dadhīci’s departure to his own abode; [Dakṣa’s] proclamation of the destruction of the sacrifice through the improper conduct of Śiva, and his exit from the sacrificial enclosure; and Dakṣa’s undertaking of the commencement of another divine sacrifice.

After Viṣṇu had departed for his own abode, Vīrabhadra and the other attendants (gaṇas) defeated all the gods, including Śakra and the great Indra. Then, on Mount Gandhamādana, while Dakṣāyaṇī Satī was seated in her celestial chariot (vimāna), she heard through the mouth of Nandin the news of the sacrifice—how her father Dakṣa had commenced the ritual and how she had been dismembered by Dakṣa’s disciples at the sacrificial fire-pit—and accompanied by all the wives of the gods, sages, ancestors, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, she went into the presence of Śiva.

The meeting and the flight out of fear; the manifestation of Brahmā’s longing to depart for his own abode, Kailāsa, after being tormented by the words of his sons, in order to propitiate Śiva; his departure despite the instruction given by Śiva; the hymn of praise offered by Brahmā; and the request for permission from Śiva—accompanied by all the gods—for Satī to go to the sacrificial pavilion, as Śaṅkara was pleased by that praise.

The restoration of Dakṣa to life by Śiva—after he had returned following his humiliation by his father, having first joined the head of a goat with its udders to the severed body of Dakṣa; the departure of Satī after being restrained by Śiva, and her subsequent dispatching along with Nandī and others; Dakṣa’s performance of a sacrifice and the hymn of praise offered to Śiva by him; the granting of boons to Dakṣa by Śiva, who was pleased by that praise; and the description of the goddess Satī’s journey to the assembly of Śiva, Brahmā, and the other gods. ...

[The section on] traveling to Sakhavaleka; [the section on] the description of the rules for the worship of Śiva and the observance of Śiva-vows by means of a path free from hair; now begins the table of contents of the subjects contained in the *Śrī Skanda Mahāpurāṇa*.

Va Va – Ka Va 6 Vra Vaṭa Vka Ra Vada Adhyāyas: In the context of the greatness of devotion to Śiva, there is the narration of the great laughter of Indrasena, the son of Nandīśvara. Therein, although that most sinful man was being led to the world of Yama by the messengers of Yama, Yama himself paid him honor due to the power of the utterance of the Name of Śiva, under the pretext of shouting such words as "Seize him! and "Strike him! Then, saying "Wait," he placed him upon a celestial chariot and led him toward the world of Śiva.

The description of Madiganendra’s attainment of the status of a Gaṇa named Caṇḍa through the utterance of Śiva’s names; the excellence of the name of Śiva, sacred ash, rudrākṣa beads, and the Tripuṇḍra mark; the majesty of the worship of Śiva; and, in connection with that, the narration of the history of Nandin and the Kirāta. In that context, when Śiva was propitiated by Nandin with jewels, the Kirāta performed an act of devotion by offering his own head, which had been covered with a tiger-skin. Śiva, gratified by that devotion, [granted] the Kirāta the status of King of the Kirātas.

The granting of his own body as a doorkeeper to Śiva by Nandikeśvara, named Mahākāla; the majesty of devotion to Śiva; and, when a dispute arose among Uśanas, Atri, and others regarding whether to abandon the embodied form of Śaṅkara and practice the worship of the *liṅga*, the narration of the account of the practice of *liṅga*-worship by his son Lomaśa.

There, in that forest of wood, as Śaṅkara was wandering for alms with Nandī, all the wives of the sages were infatuated upon beholding his beautiful, naked form; they followed him at the instigation of Śaṅkara. Seeing their hermitages rendered empty by their departure after following him, those sages uttered a curse, causing the phallus of the Lord to fall. With that fallen liṅga, the entire cosmic egg—including all moving and non-moving beings—remained pervaded by a single form. Witnessing this, [the gods] were struck with wonder.

Upon the request of Viṣṇu and Brahmā by the gods, and at the request of the gods for the purpose of purifying the sacrificial ground, Viṣṇu descended to the earth while Brahmā went to heaven. On the summit of Mount Meru, Brahmā beheld Surabhi and the Ketakī flower. Following the false promise made by Surabhi and the Ketakī that "Brahmā saw the tip of his head," after Brahmā had returned and questioned them again, he departed once more.

In the presence of the gods, Surabhi and Ketakī first offered false testimony, stating with boastful falsehoods, "I have seen the top of the Liṅga," and they supported that claim with their own oaths. Then Viṣṇu, turning away from his fallacy, spoke the truth in the presence of all the gods, saying, "I have not seen the end of the Liṅga. Upon hearing the false words of Surabhi and Ketakī, the Lord became enraged and, through a voice from the sky, declared that Surabhi’s mouth was impure.

The non-worship of the *ketakī* flower, the non-worship of the *brāhmaṇa*, and the objects of those who approve of such acts by sharing in the consumption of *chaśa* (meat) and so forth; the giving of gifts to those who play drums and musical instruments; and likewise, the departure toward the *liṅga* of Brahmā and others who have been invited to a feast.

The praise of Śiva composed by Brahmā, the gods, and others; the command issued by Śiva—pleased by the hymns of praise offered by Brahmā and the others—to Viṣṇu, Bhṛgu, and Nārada; the hymn of praise to Viṣṇu by Brahmā and the others; the assumption of the form of the Śivaliṅga by Viṣṇu through his own manifestation as the *piṇḍī*; thereafter, the worship of the Śivaliṅga by Vīrabhadra at the behest of Śiva along with Brahmā and the others; and then, [the account] of Śaṅkara’s [manifestation] in various forms for many purposes by numerous gods and others.

The establishment of various names and lingas for the purpose of worshipping the *chiga* (liṅga) in their respective places; the establishment of the abode of Vīrabhadra, beginning with the origin of the lineage of gurus who worship the *chiga*; the attainment of the status of the first preceptor (*ācārya*) by Nandin, the bestower of the *chiga*, and the status of preceptor to the worshippers of the *chiga* by Skanda; thereafter, the succession of the lineage of gurus who worship the *chiga*; the majesty of devotion to Śiva; and therein, the supreme merit of the moth (*pataṅgī*) and the female insect (*kīṭa-paṣṭhinī*) through the cleaning of the temple of Śiva.

The narration of the life story of the daughter of the King of Kāśī; the dialogue between the daughter of the King of Kāśī and the one named Sandhyā, who was adorned with earrings; the account of how a thief, through the power of devotion to Śiva, attained the heavenly world while stealing a bell from the temple of Śiva; the description of the entire universe as being permeated by the power of Śiva; therein, the depiction of men as being composed of *ṛk* verses and women as being formed of *piṇḍī* verses; and the description of the non-difference between Ṛbhu and Viṣṇu.

A description of the worship of the Śiva-liṅga performed by Brahmā and others using jewels and other precious materials; a description of how the Daityas, such as Prahlāda, Bali, and Bāṇa, were devoted to the worship of the Śiva-liṅga; and the account of how, having attained unsurpassed power through the majesty of worshipping the Lord with devotion, they were conquered by the words of Nandin, the joy of the gods, leading them to exert themselves in the propitiation of the Śiva-liṅga. In that context, there is an incidental description by Nandin of the cause of his own monkey-like face, wherein it is told how Nandin acquired a monkey’s face due to a curse from Rāvaṇa, and how he subsequently encountered a monkey.

The granting of a curse to Rāvaṇa stating that his death shall come at the hand of someone; then, Nandin and others having gone to Veṅkaṭa accompanied by Śiva, they lowered the pedestal of the Liṅga and offered prayers to Viṣṇu; the gods’ request for an incarnation to Viṣṇu for the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa; the description of the descent of all the gods among the monkeys at the command of Viṣṇu; the incarnation of Rāma; the slaying of Rāvaṇa by Rāma; and the attainment of union with Śiva by Rāvaṇa.

The Contents of Chapter 1: The Glory of Worshipping Śiva’s Linga. The Contents of Chapter 2: The destruction of Indra’s kingdom due to the insult offered to Bṛhaspati; the description of the tumultuous battle between the gods and the Daityas led by Viṣṇu, which Indra—defeated by his enemies—joined with Brahmā and the other deities; in that battle, the encirclement of Indra’s head by the discus of Śaṅkara (Viṣṇu); Viṣṇu’s departure to the world [of Brahmā] to seek favor; and, following Viṣṇu’s instruction, Indra and the others seeking refuge at a banyan tree (*vaṭa*).

Through association with him, there is a description of the auspicious dharma (śivadharma), such as devotion to Śiva, the wearing of the five-fold marks, and the wearing of rudrākṣa beads; [an account] of the battle between the gods and the Daityas; the honoring of Śakra, who had sought refuge, at the word of Nārada; the praise of Viṣṇu when the gods were defeated by Bālin Kālanemi, who desired the jewel; and [the account of] the battle with Kālanemi—[all concerning] Viṣṇu.

Then, Indra began the churning of the ocean; thereafter, the gods and the Dānavas proceeded toward Mount Mandara for the purpose of churning the ocean. With great effort and with the assistance of Viṣṇu, they brought Mount Mandara, slew Kālanemi, and Viṣṇu vanished from sight. Then, when Indra began the slaughter of the terrified Daityas who had fallen [into the water], the gods and Dānavas commenced the churning of the ocean by fashioning it as the churning-cord.

The churning of the ocean; the prevention of that [churning] by Nārada who had arrived from the sky; thereafter, the victory of Indra upon his departure for Amarāvatī accompanied by the celestial army; the emergence [of the jewel Kaustubha]; and although Nārada said, "In times of distress, Viṣṇu should be remembered," the gods disregarded those words and proceeded with the consecration of Indra; the defeated Daityas went to Śukrācārya; and by Śukra—

The performance of penance by the Daityas, who had achieved the success of victory over the eight enclosures extending as far as Viṣṇu, following the churning of the ocean undertaken out of their own desire; ... [and] the description of the burning of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). ...

Śa: Regarding the humiliation of Bṛhaspati due to his absence, Viśvarūpa—the son of Viśvakarman and the family priest of Śakra—was appointed as the purohita. Because he was skilled in the application of various poisons and incantations, the gods were satisfied by him. However, seeing that the demons had assumed the form of the source of the world (the *jagatkāraṇa-yoni*) and were offering oblations to the gods, Śakra, with his vajra, severed the head of Viśvarūpa. This constitutes the state of hostility toward the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*). In this context, incidentally:

The narration of the origin of Heramba as requested by Śaunaka and others through Sūta Lomaharṣaṇa; the submergence of Indra in the waters due to the calamity of the sin of Brahman-slaughter committed by him; the description of the guardians of all the worlds therein; the account of the birth of Heramba from Parāśakti; the arrival of that wise Gaṇeśa before Śakti and his reporting of the incident of Indra’s Brahman-slaughter and so forth; and subsequently, by the word of Nārada, [the installation of] Nahuṣa in the place of Indra.

The performance of a hymn of praise to Śiva by Yuktaśrī; the devouring of Kālabhrūṭa by Śiva in his form as a child (chiga) who was pleased by the praise of the gods; thereafter, a consultation regarding his installation; hearing of Nahuṣa’s installation in Indra’s place, Śacī’s lamentation, and the performance of a hymn of praise to Śiva by the women of the inner apartments and all the gods; the manifestation of Śiva, who was pleased by that praise; the departure of Śiva; and the approval of all the gods for Nahuṣa’s ascension to the rank of Indra.

The consecration of Nahuṣa to the position of Indra; the instruction that one must worship Gaṇeśa at the commencement of any undertaking after eating *hākhāda*; the dispatching of Bṛhaspati to the presence of Indrāṇī by Nahuṣa out of lustful desire for her; the description of the procedure for the worship of Gaṇeśa as proclaimed by Śiva, which Indrāṇī performed; the churning of the ocean by all the gods following the marriage of Śiva; the sending of Saṃdeha to Nahuṣa to request him to come as a vehicle; and [the subsequent actions] by Nahuṣa.

The arrival of Agastya and other Brahmins as the vehicle for [the sage] Divika; then the birth of Candra, including the narration of the cause of Candra’s emergence from the ocean and the account of Garuḍa; the distance [of the journey]; then the bestowing of a curse by the compassionate Agastya that Nahuṣa shall become a python (ajagara); and thereafter, his state as a python.

From the ocean being churned, there arose the production of various jewels; the manifestation of Lakṣmī; the restoration of Nahuṣa to heaven after he had been cursed by Viṣṇu for his conduct toward her; and the subsequent installation of Yayāti in his stead. Then follows the description of his fall to the earth due to the exhaustion of his merit. While he was still young, through the depletion of his merit, he fell downward; thereafter, all the gods were seized with anxiety.

The deception of the Daityas by the goddesses in the form of the *tāṇḍava* dance; the arrival of the gods led by Indra; the departure of Bṛhaspati, who was seated at the feet of the gods and was terrified by the fear of Śacī’s curse, toward the shore of the lake for the purpose of bringing Indra; the cutting off of Rāhu’s head as indicated by the two hands of Indra during the invocation; and the wrath of the Daityas who had partaken of the nectar (*amṛta*).

While Indra was being pursued by the sin of Brahman-slaughter incurred from slaying Vṛtra, he offered his own residence to the gods; having thus purified himself, he cast the sin upon the quarters of the sky, the earth, trees, water, and women, and after granting them boons, he returned to Amarāvatī. Then followed the consecration of Indra in his office, a subject to be recited until the end of the day. Subsequently, Tvaṣṭṛ, enraged by Viśvarūpa, propitiated the Creator through ascetic penance and requested a son who would strike terror into the gods. Then...

By virtue of a boon from Brahmā, he obtained a son named Vṛtra; through that Asura Vṛtra, the Daityas attained great power and returned to their own abode. Consequently, the gods were seized with fear and held mutual consultations. At the command of Brahmā, the gods went to the hermitage of Dadhīca and requested his bones for the sake of the sacrifice. When the gods had thus petitioned him, Dadhīca, being entreated, abandoned his own body through yoga by means of Surabhī.

The creation of the *nirmāṃsaka* (fleshless) [body] by means of the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*), the tongue of the serpent (*srajihvā*), and the bone of Dadhīci; the gods' acquisition of weapons from that bone as if it were their own; the granting of the bow to the eldest of the gods by the wife of Dadhīci, named Suvarcā; Suvarcā’s command to her son Pippalāda to remain near the *aśvattha* tree, followed by her departure into *samādhi* along with her husband; the commencement of the battle between the gods and the asuras; the commencement of the battle against the asura Vṛtra; and [the preparations] for the slaying of Vṛtra.

The worship of Śiva by Indra at the command of Bṛhaspati through the performance of the Śanipradoṣavrata; the procedure for the Śanipradoṣavrata; the narration of the account of how Vṛtrāsura, who was Citraratha the Gandharva in a previous birth, incurred the curse of becoming an Asura due to the curse of Durvāsas; the procedure for the conclusion (udyāpana) of the Śanipradoṣavrata; and how, after Indra’s prowess was restored through the power of the Śanipradoṣavrata, he engaged in battle with the Daityas; and [the account] of the Daityas who fled from the battlefield.

The description of the laws of combat in the battle with Vṛtra; the description of the pleasant battle between the gods and the Dānavas; Indra’s falling into a swoon from the blow struck by Vṛtra; thereafter, Indra, having regained consciousness, performing austerities in the form of worshiping Śiva at the command of Brahmā for the sake of slaying Vṛtra; Indra, considering Vṛtra invincible by the word of Śiva, making friends with Vṛtra after a period of a thousand years and residing near him for the purpose of killing him; and the pride of Vṛtra.

On the bank of the Narmadā, Vajrapāṇi performed the worship of Oṃkāreśvara according to the Pradoṣavrata rite; however, at the time of Pradoṣa, Vṛtra neglected the worship of Śiva and, by falling asleep, suffered a loss of his ascetic power (*tapas*), which led to his misfortune and the frustration of his desires. Consequently, Indra descended from heaven and seized Vṛtra. Then, the Blessed One, being pleased by Brahmā’s prayer, instructed Brahmā regarding the Pradoṣavrata, explaining the fault of sleeping while performing the worship of the deity.

The narration of the sinful nature of the *rasa* (essence) created by the Daityas; the description of the method of worshipping Trivikrama through the association with Vasa; then, by the command of King Dāsa, the performance of the worship of Trivikrama according to the scriptures; the emergence of Indra from the belly of Vṛtra due to that power; the description of the falling of the body of Vṛtrāsura; the falling of the body into the Antarvedī between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā; and the falling of the head at Mākhva; [these are] the subjects of the chapters for six months.

The enemy of Vṛtra set out, seeking victory for Indra; thereafter, Bali—having been informed of the news of Vṛtra’s slaughter by the Daityas and acting upon the command of Śukra—obtained that chariot while performing a sacrifice. Mounting that chariot, accompanied by the army of the Daityas, Bali departed for the heavenly world to achieve victory over the gods. Hearing of his arrival, Bṛhaspati, having perceived the approach of Bali to heaven, urged Indra and all the other gods [to prepare].

Having assumed the forms of birds such as crows and others, they departed from their own abode and returned to the hermitage of Kaśyapa. There, they reported their suffering to their mother, Aditi. At the request of the gods, Aditi, out of compassion, observed the vow of the twelfth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa and performed the worship of Viṣṇu. Through Aditi’s observance of that vow, Viṣṇu appeared. Praised by the gods for his protection, the Blessed One commanded his two attendants, Sudarśana and Gadā, who were present at his side, to subdue him.

When his own lack of capability was declared, the performance of the funeral rites [was undertaken]. Then, the account of Bali’s bestowal of the entire wealth of Indra upon the Brahmins after he had been consecrated to the throne of Indra by Śukra; following that, the account of how anyone else occupying the throne of Indra—due to the absence of such giving—would attain the state of being a worm in Indra’s body immediately after the exhaustion of their merit; and, in the narration of the events of Bali’s previous birth, the story of a certain gambler who offered flowers, garlands, and other items brought for a courtesan.

Seeing it fallen on the ground due to a stumble, he resolved with the firm conviction, "May this be an offering to Śiva," whereby all his sins were destroyed. Thereafter, according to the words of Yama, after three and a half *ghaṭikās* had passed, he attained the station of Indra (Śatakratu). At that moment, he recounted to Agastya and other great sages the story of the gift of Airāvata and others. After those three and a half *ghaṭikās*, the former Indra remained in his own place and, following his rebuke of Rātri, [the narrative continues].

The humiliation of King Indra by the gambler who had made his body subject to Śacī; the king’s failure to recover the wealth previously lost; Indra’s rebuke of the gambler upon returning from Yama after seeing his own wealth, such as Airāvata and other treasures, bestowed by the gambler; the description of how that gambler was spared from hell due to the power of a gift given by Citragupta at the command of Yama; and the return of the humbled Śakra to heaven, as well as [the fate] of that gambler.

The entry [of Prahlāda] into the womb of Suruci, the wife of Virocana; Indra’s approach to Virocana—who had been deceived by him in the guise of a brahmin—and his request for alms; the description of Virocana offering his own head to Śakra, who had assumed a deceptive appearance; and the birth of Prahlāda from Suruci after the death of his father named Virocana—this is the chronological sequence following Suruci’s pregnancy.

The objects of the senses belong to Maheśvara; thereafter follows the departure toward the world of the Lord (Pati). Then, Bhārgava consecrated his father Virocana upon the throne of sovereignty. Following the defeat of Indra and the others by the boy, after their departure, Viṣṇu commanded them all to establish themselves in heaven. Then, having reflected on the reasons for desiring to remain in heaven according to the words spoken, Viṣṇu—

Together with all the Daityas and Śukra, [Bali] returned to the earth, to the banks of the Narmadā, where he performed many sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha under the guidance of Guru Bṛhaspati. At that very time of Bali’s sacrifice, the Lord, being pleased with Aditi who was fasting there, descended in the form of a dwarf (Vāmana). Subsequently, following the rites of his initiation (upanayana) and other ceremonies, He proceeded toward the sacrificial enclosure of Bali. There is a description of the honors paid to the dwarf boy by Bali; then, due to the persistence of the dwarf boy, the Lord [accepted the gift].

The request for three paces of land; when Bali had made the promise to grant him that land, Indra, in the form of a dwarf, forbade the granting of the land after first describing that banyan tree as Viṣṇu.

[The account of] Bali’s insistence on granting land to the dwarf (Vaṭu); the bestowing of the gift upon the dwarf by Śukra; the description of the Lord’s growth when the gift of land was given by Bali preceded by a solemn vow; the pervading of the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings with his two feet; Vāmana’s dispatching of Garuḍa before Bali for the purpose of requesting a third step’s worth of earth; then the arrival of Bali’s wife, Vindhyāvasī, along with Prahlāda, into the presence of the Lord Vāmana; and then by her [the offering of her own...]

The request made by Bali for the placement of three steps in the form of a dwarf upon his own head, as well as those of his son and his grandson; the command given by the Lord, pleased by that petition, for Bali to go to Sutala; the standing of Viṣṇu near Bali at the time of the step due to Bali’s prayer; and the description of the power and majesty of devotion to Śiva, exemplified by the attainment of the status of a king by a gambler in a previous birth.

In the description of the greatness of the venerable sage Raibhya, there is the narration of the account of the battle between the gods and the asura Tāraka; having heard of their defeat therein, the gods went into the presence of Brahmā, where a celestial voice commanded them to make an effort to find a wife for Śiva—who was separated from his consort—in order to bring about the slaying of the asura Tāraka by a son of Śiva, following the precedent of the killing of Andhaka. After hearing the celestial voice, they went to the Himavat mountain and made a request for the sake of producing a daughter.

The narration of the request made by Himavat to his wife Menā for the birth of a daughter; the description of the distress felt by Menā at the prospect of giving birth to a daughter. Then, considering himself to be one whose heart is bound by compassion for others, Himavat implores her; the subjects of that plea by Menā to Himavat; the bearing of the Mother of the World (Jagadambā) in her womb; and the description of the manifestation of the Mother of the World.

...the arrival of Pārvatī with Himavat to the vicinity of Maheśa for the purpose of bestowing [himself]; the joyful reception by Gaurī through her own service; the abandonment of Śiva by Gaurī; and in the meantime, the piercing of Śaṅkara with an arrow by Madana, who was incited by Devendra.

The instrument [of the plot]: the description of Śiva, pierced by the arrows of Madana, falling into a state of passion upon seeing Pārvatī; then, as Śiva reflects with discernment on the cause of his mental delusion and desires to know himself, he beholds Madana with his bow drawn and, under the sway of anger, reduces Madana to ashes with the fire from his third eye; the gods’ lamentation for the restoration of Madana’s life and their subsequent propitiation of Śiva; then the disappearance of Śiva; and [the account of] the burnt Madana.

Having observed the means of destruction employed by Rati, the wife of Madana; the astonishment of Girijā upon learning of the restoration of Madana’s life through Rati’s efforts; and then the commencement of penance by Rati at the very site where Madana was consumed by fire; meanwhile, Nārada approached Rati and engaged in conversation, after which Rati requested Nārada’s assistance; Nārada then went to the Asura Śambara and issued a command for the abduction of Rati; and finally, Śambara brought Rati to his own home by force.

The appointment [of Agni] to the office of superintendent of the kitchen following his return; then, Pārvatī’s performance of ascetic penance with the aim of attaining Śiva; the performance by Viṣṇu, together with the foremost gods such as Brahmā who were performing that penance, of the ritual with mantras for the purpose of Śiva’s taking her hand; the return of Śaṅkara—seated in meditative absorption upon a supreme yoga-throne beyond the ocean—to Brahmā and the other gods; and the hymn of praise to Mahādeva by Brahmā and the others, followed by Śaṅkara, pleased by the praise of the gods, [granting his favor].

The description of the limit for reviving Madana as he was about to be consumed by Pārvatī’s hand; the instruction to the gods regarding the renunciation of desire; thereafter, Śiva’s abiding in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and Nandin’s dismissal of his own deities; [the state] of the day.

The state of absorption (*samādhi*) in the bliss of one's own true nature; thereafter, the commencement of Pārvatī’s penance and the shaking of Śiva from his meditation through the power of that penance; Śiva’s arrival at the site of Pārvatī’s penance in the form of a young brahmin student (*baṭu*); the disparagement of the gods by the one in the form of a student for the purpose of testing Pārvatī’s mind; when Pārvatī, unable to endure this, had her friends drive away the student, Śiva’s disappearance followed by his manifestation in his own true form; the conversation between Śiva and Pārvatī; [and] Pārvatī’s...

The prayer for the hand of his daughter; then Śiva’s departure to his own world after granting a boon to Pārvatī; thereafter, following the successful completion of the penance by the daughter of the mountain named Himavat, the great undertaking of her being brought back to his own home along with Brahmā and the other gods.

Śiva’s request to Himālaya to act as a mediator for the purpose of giving Pārvatī to him; the conversation between Śiva and the Ṛṣis; after the Ṛṣis had made the decision regarding the marriage, Śiva’s return and communication of that decision; Mahādeva’s dispatching of Nārada to invite Viṣṇu and the other gods; and the arrival of Viṣṇu and the others at Śiva’s presence, where Śiva, with great preparation, performed the rites such as the worship of the Arghya.

The departure of Śiva along with all the hosts of gods toward the city of Indra; the description of Himavān’s marriage of his daughter, following the instructions previously uttered by the preceptor Garga, including the construction of an unprecedented wedding pavilion by Viśvakarman; the apprehension of all the gods upon hearing from Nārada about the artistic arrangement of divine images within the wedding pavilion built by Viśvakarman; and subsequently, the bringing of Śiva back to his own city by Himavān.

After all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, had resided in their various respective abodes, and after all the gods had been individually honored in their excellent dwellings, Manāyī performed the *nīrājana* rite for Śiva; she felt great joy upon beholding his splendor. Then, having donned her daily garments, she took a necklace in her hand for the purpose of choosing the bridegroom, meditated upon the Supreme Lord, and stood there for His inspection. With great joy, as described in the *Gaṅgā-stotra*, she proceeded toward the marriage pavilion for the taking of hands.

The bringing of Śiva through [Nandin’s] exertion; the auspicious marriage ceremony of Śiva and Pārvatī; the *nīrājana* rite for Śiva and Pārvatī performed by the holy married women (suvāsinīs), such as Arundhatī; then, during the occasion of the formal offering of the daughter by Himavat accompanied by Menā, in the context of Nārada’s inquiry regarding the proclamation of Śiva’s name and lineage, the description of Śiva’s supreme sovereignty; the performance of the gift of the daughter by Himavat; and, in the context of the secret fire-sacrifice (*guhyāgnihotra*) for Śiva and Pārvatī, [the description of] the toe-nails of Pārvatī—

The account of the birth of the sixty thousand Vātāpis from the semen of Brahmā, which was severed by the teeth of a serpent; and thereafter, the description of the marriage festival, preceded by the honoring of all the gods by the king of Himavat.

Viṣṇu, belonging to the groom’s party, performed appropriate honors for the various members of the bride’s party, such as Sadyojāta, Vindhya, Caṇḍa, and others; thereafter, the bridal procession commenced. During the procession, Śiva was questioned by Pārvatī regarding the subjects of all the gods as they returned to their respective abodes. Then, all the gods departed for their own places. Following that, Śiva and Pārvatī sported on Mount Gandhamādana. Finally, in a secluded spot, the commencement of the amorous union between Śiva and Pārvatī took place.

The gods, filled with anxiety born from that most wonderful act of love, sent Agni in secret to the presence of Śiva; then, having arrived during the time of lovemaking under the pretext of being the sacrificial fire, Agni consumed Śiva’s semen and returned to the presence of the gods; it is described how all the gods became pregnant by means of the semen discharged from Agni’s mouth; thereafter, all the gods went to Viṣṇu for refuge, and by the direction of Viṣṇu, they were [instructed] by all the gods...

The life-force of Śiva; then, by the command of the satisfied Śiva, the emission of semen from the mouths of all the gods; the description of that emitted semen as being in the form of a golden egg; then, Śiva’s issuing of the command for the semen to be poured into the womb of Agni; then, the resting of the semen within the bodies of the six wives known as the Kṛttikās—who had approached to provide fuel for the kindled fire—by means of the entry of the atoms of that semen through the channels of their own flames, thereby fulfilling the purpose of the fire.

Tormented by those clay particles due to the fear of infidelity, she released that semen into the Gaṅgā on the summit of Mount Himavat all at once. From that very moment, the six-faced boy was born from that semen. At the very time of that boy’s birth, there occurred the sudden bursting of Pārvatī’s breasts. At that same instant, Nārada returned to Śiva and related the news of the Kumāra’s birth. Then, all the gods assembled together for the purpose of seeing that Kumāra.

The return of Śiva and Pārvatī to the presence of Kumāra; the commencement of the festival celebrating Kumāra’s triumph; the attainment of joy by Śiva and Pārvatī; then, at the command of Śiva, the departure of the gods led by Kumāra for the sake of victory over the demon Tāraka; at that moment, the proclamation of the gods’ victory by a voice from the sky; in the meantime, the acceptance of the maiden named Senā, who had arrived, as his bride by Kumāra at the word of Brahmā; and thereafter, the attainment of the office of General by Kumāra.

Indeed, at that very moment, Gaṅgā, Gaurī, and Chittikā arrived and were consecrated as the mothers of Skanda by Skanda himself, who was accompanied by a host of mothers. Then Kumāra, together with all the gods, launched an assault against the demon Tāraka. Following this, the armies of the gods and the Daityas arrayed themselves; in the ensuing battle between the gods and the Asuras, when all the gods had been defeated, Viṣṇu praised Kumāra, and Kumāra then stood face-to-face with Tāraka for combat.
The destruction of Tārakāsura’s own army by Maheśvara. Chapter Two. || 2 ||

A description of the objects of the auspicious [Goddess]; the battle of that one, leaping with his own prowess, against Indra and the others; the swift defeat of the gods; the description of the hand-to-hand combat between Lord Kārttikeya and the demon Tārakāsura; the battle of Kumāra; the consolation by Kumāra of Himavat and the others who had arrived to witness the various battles; then, the destruction of Tāraka’s city by Kumāra; and then, [the state] of Kumāra following the slaying of Tāraka.

The attainment of victory by Pūṣan alone; the description of the majesty of Lord Kumāra, including the account of how even sinners become purified merely by seeing Kumāra; and how Yama, perceiving this and fearing the desolation of his own realm, approached Śiva preceded by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods, and after praising Śiva, reported that his own authority had become useless due to the attainment of heaven by people who were previously great sinners through the majesty of Kumāradroṇa; thereafter, by Śaṅkara—

The teaching on the true nature of pure dharma for the sake of turning away from *saṃsāra* and attaining purified contemplation; the description of Yama’s attainment of pure-mindedness through the instruction given by Śaṅkara; then, the offering of praise to Kumāra by all the mountains; the granting of a boon by Kumāra to the mountains that they would take the form of *śivalingas*; and, when Nandin posed a question regarding the worship of the *śivalinga*, Kumāra’s explanation of the greatness of worshipping various kinds of *ratnalingas*, *nakhalingas*, and *nādeśvaralingas*.

In this context, following the discourse on the majesty of the worship of Śiva, there is the narration of the life of the king named Śveta. While King Śveta—who had been devoted to the worship of Śiva from birth—was absorbed in meditation at the time of his death, Yama and the other guardians of the quarters were rendered powerless. Seeing them making an effort to strike him with their swords, the Supreme Lord Śiva, for the sake of protecting his devotee, reduced their forms to ashes with the fire from his third eye. Then, King Śveta arose from his meditative absorption.

Seeing Kāṭa burning before him, Vyābhri became a cloud and offered a hymn of praise; Rudra, desiring to kill him, explained that "Kāṭa was burned by me," thus recounting the cause of Kāṭa’s death. Then, at the request of King Śveta, Maheśvara restored Kāṭa to life. Kāṭa then offered a hymn of praise to the Blessed One. Following this, Kāṭa performed a eulogy of King Śveta, who was devoted to the welfare of others. Thereafter, Kāṭa, together with Yama and the other [deities], prostrated before Śiva and King Śveta.

Having praised his own state and returned, he described the greatness of the Śiva-dharma in the form of wearing the *tripuṇḍra*, matted hair, and the carrying of the *rākṣasa* [skull], and issued a command to his own messengers that the messengers of Śiva must not be led to the world of Yama. He recounted the long life of King Śvetabhūpa due to his devotion to Śiva, and introduced the story of the Kirāta regarding the Śiva-dharma: once, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha—the great festival of Śivarātri—a certain Kirāta named Caṇḍa was wandering about in the forest for as long as the day lasted.

Like a deer, he lived by killing animals; one night, while standing atop a *bilva* tree for protection, he unknowingly and effortlessly cut a *bilva* leaf, thereby performing the worship of Śiva who was situated beneath that tree. By rinsing his mouth with water, he performed the bathing of Śiva, and through the consumption of food scraps, he observed a fast without effort. Because of his lack of food, his wife also fasted, observing it out of concern for him. Then, on the following day, when she had brought food and placed it before him on the bank of the river, it was suddenly devoured by a dog that arrived there.

Great joy arose because it was thought that the gift of food to the Kirāta had been accomplished; by virtue of that, the Śiva-gaṇas brought a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) to enable the Kirāta to attain the world of Śiva—despite his having observed the Śivarātri vow out of ignorance. Then follows the Kirāta’s departure for the heavenly realm along with the Śiva-gaṇas, the description of the origin of the Śivarātri vow, and, in connection with the majesty of the Śivarātri vow, the account of how the son of a widow and a Nāmaṇī, born from a *śvapaca*, attained [liberation] in another birth through the power of the Śivarātri vow.

The description of the account of the births of Śiva and the one named Vīrabhadra; the narration of how kings such as Bharata attained perfection through the vow of Śivarātri; and the description of how, when his own side was defeated in that wager, Śiva—having lost all his possessions to Pārvatī—departed for the penance grove, leaving behind his beloved. (Dha) Now, after Śiva’s departure, Pārvatī, distressed by separation, assumed the form of a Śavarī and went into solitude to the presence of Śiva, who was absorbed in meditation; [the account] of her...

The emergence from meditative absorption upon merely seeing her; Śiva’s state of separation when Pārvatī, having been seen by Śiva, vanished; then Śiva’s request for her hand to Śabari; thereafter, Śabari’s bringing of Pārvatī to Mount Gandhamādana to petition her father for her own marriage to Śiva, who was afflicted by the god of love; and Śiva’s request for the maiden to Himālaya—in the meantime, there...

Nārada’s arrival and his exhortation to Śiva; then [the episode] of Śiva—now, once upon a time, while Śiva and Pārvatī were seated comfortably in their own abode on Mount Kailāsa, Pārvatī, having observed her own words regarding the dice game being disregarded by Śiva with cries of "ka-ka-kara-kara-kaka-viṣyāḥ," became angry and desired to depart for another forest. Then, when the gods, led by Indra and others, placed Girijā at their head and offered prayers, his anger subsided, and he returned home.

The description of the great consecration with fragrant waters upon the lion-throne of the Day-maker (the Sun); likewise, the description of the praise of the Śiva-dharma in connection with the greatness of Kedāranātha—thus ends the first section, the Kedāra-khaṇḍa, within the Māheśvara-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the second section, the Kāmarikākhaṇḍa, within the Māheśvarakhaṇḍa.

In the dialogue between Sūta and Uñjaka, at the beginning of the description of the greatness of the holy fords on the shore of the Southern Ocean, [the section on] the Greatness of the Pāñcāpsaras Tīrtha...

In the narration of the account of Smaya follows the account of Arjuna’s pilgrimage to the sacred fords (*tīrthayātrā*). Therein is described how Arjuna, having set out to bathe at the sacred fords situated on the shore of the southern ocean, was prevented from bathing by five ascetics (*tapasvin*) residing there due to fear of the crocodiles (*grāha*) in those waters. Upon seeing Arjuna’s righteous resolve (*dharmabuddhi*), the ascetics granted him the boon of long life. Then, Arjuna approached the Saubhadra-tīrtha and, having descended to bathe, proceeded to perform his ablutions when he was seized by a crocodile.

The description of how Arjuna assumed the form of a woman while lifting Bhārhadratha; the account of how he was cursed by a Brāhmaṇa who had been solicited for sexual pleasure along with his four celestial companions, resulting in the loss of his manhood; the description of his residence at five sacred sites (*tīrthas*) as directed by the words of Nārada; and then, having visited the other four sacred sites, the description of how Arjuna fulfilled the vow there and brought about the liberation of all the Apsarases.

Desiring to know the cause of Aja’s obstruction of the sacred ford, and having become suspicious, Nārada was told by the celestial nymphs, "In this matter, you must consult Śarva"; thus he set out toward the Lord.

The meeting of Aja with Nārada; after hearing from the mouth of Nārada the account of the Tāṇḍava dance, Aja’s inquiry of Nārada regarding the greatness of sacred fords (tīrthas) out of a desire to know them; then, by Nārada, the description of the events concerning Brahmā preceded by a hymn of praise, followed by the description of the dialogue between Kātyāyana and Sārasvata as told by Suśravas; therein, the exposition of the true nature of Dharma by the great sage Sārasvata to the great sage Kātyāyana, and subsequently, the description of the greatness of giving (dāna).

The account of Nārada’s travels through various lands for the purpose of acquiring wealth to bestow as gifts, his mind being intent on charity after hearing of the greatness of giving; the arrival of Nārada, who was wandering the earth, at the hermitage of Bhṛgu on the banks of the Narmadā; and, following Nārada’s description of all regions to Bhṛgu, Bhṛgu’s narration of the majesty of Stambhatīrtha located at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, under the pretext of describing the most sacred places fit for the distribution of gifts to Nārada.

Therein—the account of the tall Brahmin Devaśarman residing at Tīrthatīra; his giving of a portion of his merit to the Brahmin named Subhadra, who was situated on the bank of that very holy ford, for the purpose of performing the Daśaśrāddha for his ancestors at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; and, having heard from his brother the greatness of Stambhatīrtha located at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, Nārada’s contemplation of establishing a residence at that confluence of the Mahī and the ocean.

At the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, because the establishment of a shrine required funds, and since the acquisition of wealth was necessary according to the principle of the "autumnal grain" (*śaradadhanya*), the sages approached King Dharmavarman—who had heard of them from the words of the messenger—and requested that he grant them the six-fold foundation (*ṣaḍadhiṣṭhāna*). Having satisfied the king by explaining the meaning of one of the verses, they secured his assistance for the accomplishment of the religious gift (*dānadharma*) as previously instructed by themselves. ...

Then, having searched everywhere for the sake of obtaining a Brāhmaṇa pure in his practice of giving (*dāna-pātra*), Nārada subsequently proceeded toward the village of Kalāpa in the guise of a Brāhmaṇa. Having arrived there, he manifested a thunderbolt in his hand as a means to test the Brāhmaṇas. Among those Brāhmaṇas, a boy of only eight years of age gave the correct answer to the extremely profound questions posed by Nārada.

Then, after Nārada had manifested in his own form at the great holy site of the confluence of the Mahīsāgara and requested that he be established there by providing the livelihood for the Brāhmaṇas, the description of Daṇḍāmrāsopaniyana follows; along with that, the description of the wandering of Kacchapa-bhrama; and at the time when Nārada was washing his feet, a guest arrived, and by means of the *kapiṭamaha* [offering], eight thousand *dīnāras* were presented to him from among the Brāhmaṇas brought by him.

During the Madhuparka offering, when the Brahmin Hārīta first placed his left foot forward for washing, Nārada pronounced a curse upon all the Brahmins, saying, "You shall become fools. The Brahmins likewise returned a similar curse upon Nārada. Then follows the description of the reason for placing the left foot forward, and subsequently, the remorse of Nārada.

The recollection of the account of the Brahmin Cirakārin: therein, when Medhātithi’s son Cirakārin, at his father’s command, set out to kill his mother through an act of infidelity, he was transformed into a *viṭ* (a low-caste man) by virtue of his deliberation; immediately following this, upon the instruction of Śakra, who had arrived in the form of a Brahmin, Gautama felt remorse; as Cirakārin went toward his mother for the purpose of killing her, Gautama followed behind him; and seeing his father, Cirakārin [placed] his axe on the ground.

Having entrusted [his son] to his father, Gautama performed the funeral rites; because of his long delay, the father bestowed upon him the name "Cirakārin" (Slow-Acting). Then, the wife and son were brought back home. Nārada informed them that the curse pronounced by the Brahmins would take effect on the day of the Kaṭa festival, and thus he revealed the time of the curse. Subsequently, all the Brahmins, having been provided with gold, land, houses, wealth, and other gifts at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, were personally dismissed by Viśvakarman.

In the city of Mahīnāgapura, the account of the installation [of the deity] is described in detail by Aja; then, out of a desire to hear the majesty of the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, Nārada arrives. Nārada then begins to describe the greatness of the Mahī-sāgara-saṅgama in full detail, commencing with the narrative of Indradyumna. Having gone to the world of Brahmā, Indradyumna remains there for a long time; after he has resided there, Brahmā, for the sake of making Indradyumna manifest once again, recounts the two [deities] from Cirakāra.

Bhūka bows down; having returned from the earthly realm (bhūloka) to the vicinity of Mārkaṇḍeya—who was situated on earth after having abandoned his celestial youth—he initiates a discourse regarding his own knowledge of the wind. Upon Mārkaṇḍeya’s statement that he lacks knowledge of Indra’s news, Bhūka makes an effort to enter the fire out of grief for Indra. Then, Mārkaṇḍeya leads him even further away to the presence of Nāḍījambuka, who is longer-lived than he; by him as well, it is stated that there is no knowledge of Indra’s news.

Then, Nāḍījaṃbuka, accompanied by Indradumana and Paraśu, set out from his own hermitage to describe the cause of his long life; he led Mārkaṇḍeya and Indrayuṣṇa to the presence of an owl named Prākārakarṇa, whose lifespan was also exceedingly long. After Prākārakarṇa had explained that he was ignorant of the cause of Indrayuṣṇa’s death, Indrayuṣṇa himself described the cause of his own long life.

In this section, following the connection with the previous topic, there is a description of the greatness of Viśvadaṅkha; furthermore, the subjects include Piṣaya, Para, Bhrākārakaṇaulaṭaka, Śna, Nijavātonaminñānāṭu, Dāsīnasavana, Dvayujnasya, and Bhāṣyāyāḥ.

To demonstrate that even for one who has performed meritorious deeds (*puṇya-kṛta*), there is a necessity for the knowledge of the winds (*vāyu-vijñāna*), [the text describes] the bringing of Indradyumna, Nāḍījaṅgha, and Vakas to the presence of the long-lived vulture dwelling on Mount Gandhamādana. By that vulture, after first expressing his lack of knowledge regarding Indradyumna, the account of the cause of his own long life was told; this was because the vulture dwelling on Gandhamādana lacked knowledge of his own wind.

Gāṇḍīva, Indrayudha, Āmipraveśa, Udyoga, Dvābharā, Kāraka, Kaṇapa, Praṇaya, Yūpanābhi, and Dīrghāyu—these brothers, inhabitants of Lake Mānasa, set out toward the vicinity of Kṛṣṇa. Along with Ākaṇḍeya, Nāḍījaṅgha, Prākāra, and Kaṇī, they arrived at the shore of the lake. There, upon seeing King Indrayudha among those who had gathered on the bank, Kama paid him no respect and entered into the water. Then, Gāṇḍīva made a sign to him by means of a shadow upon the surface of the water.

While Kauravya was describing the account of Indra’s previous sacrifice, at the moment Indra’s bolt was being hurled, the gods arrived in their celestial chariot above Mount Nandana after causing a rain of flowers; there, they offered prayers to Yama so that Indra might go to the world of Brahmā. However, when Indra expressed his lack of desire to go to the world of Brahmā, Kauravya questioned him regarding the cause of his long residence there.

After Kūrma had related the account of his own previous birth and provided hospitality to Indradumna and the others, and after those six—including Indradumna—had received instruction from Lomaśa Maharṣi so that they might approach the vicinity of the Kurmas despite their very long lifespans, and following the meeting of Indradumna and the others with Lomaśa Maharṣi, when Indradumna and the rest asked the reason why Lomaśa, though possessing such an exceedingly long life, did not establish a hermitage, Lomaśa [responded] by first describing the nature of worldly existence and then [discussing] himself.

An explanation of the causes for long life; therein, a description of the greatness of worshipping the Śivaliṅga. ... Then, immediately upon hearing those words, Indra-dyumna and all the others, being solely devoted to devotion toward Śiva, approached the sage Loma-hārṣaṇa for the purpose of receiving Śiva-initiation (śivadīkṣā). The sage Loma-hārṣaṇa, having first conferred Śiva-initiation upon them all, gave instruction on the worship of the Śivaliṅga. Thereafter, Mārkaṇḍeya and the others undertook a single austerity at the commencement of their practice of Kriyā-yoga. While they were performing penance...

The arrival of Nārada in their presence; the questioning by Kapa, Śara, Ṛṣṭa, Nāḍījaṅgha, and the others, who desired to know the means for their own liberation; Nārada’s instruction to them that they must go to see the great sage Saṃvarta residing in Vārāṇasī; his description of the stratagem for testing Saṃvarta in Vārāṇasī; and the account of Nāḍījaṅgha and the others going to Vārāṇasī, discovering Saṃvarta through the stratagem spoken by Nārada, and meeting with him.

The granting of permission by Saṃvarta for [Baka] to go to the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean in order to be liberated from the curse of Nāḍījaṅgha and others; the narration of the account of the satisfaction of Mahīnada by Trasaṅga; the description of the incident of the insult to Naṅgulī which occurred because Yājñavalkya remained at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; and the detailed description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the holy ford (*tīrtha*) at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean. Having heard the majesty of the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean from Saṃvarta, Baka—

A description of how the five—Dvārakā, Gṛdhrakūṭa, Narmadā, Raivataka, and Jālandhara—attained liberation through identity with Śiva by installing Śiva-liṅgas upon reaching the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; a description of the living liberation (jīvanmukti) attained by Somaśarman and Mārkaṇḍeya; and therein, a description of the majesty of the eternal liṅga Indreśvara installed by Indradyumna.

Through the description of the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, the Śatarudriya, and so forth, as well as the praise of Īgamādāsa: *Oṃ vaṭaka va ja kakaḥ*. Now follows the description of the majesty of Kumāranātha; therein begins the account of Kumāra’s life in connection with his austerities. Therein is the birth of a son named Vajrāṅga to Diti, who was known as Dakṣakanyā. By his mother’s command, Vajrāṅga went to heaven and, having been dragged down by the foot of Devedra (Indra), was brought back to his mother's side. Then, through the mediation of Kaśyapa, there was [a reconciliation] between Vajrāṅga and Vāsava.

The release [of the thunderbolt]; then, by the command of Brahmā, Vajrāṅga’s engagement in asceticism; while Vajrāṅga was engaged in asceticism, the thorough mockery of his wife, named Varāṅgī—who was solely intent on serving him—by Śakra through various terrifying apparitions; then, having obtained a boon from Brahmā, Vajrāṅga’s withdrawal from asceticism; and, out of a desire to know the cause of his wife Varāṅgī’s terror, Vajrāṅga’s making of a search, during which Varāṅgī related what had been done by Śakra.

Having witnessed this mockery, Vajraṅga—though his demonic disposition had ceased through the power of his asceticism—performed penance once again with arrows aimed at making his beloved happy, as he resembled Mahendra’s consort. Then, Brahmā, pleased by that penance, granted Vajraṅga a boon in the form of a son who would split the jaw of Śiva and withdrew him from his austerities. Subsequently, Tārakāsura was born from Vajraṅga’s wife, and all the gods performed the coronation of Tārakāsura as king of the Daityas.

Then, desiring to conquer the gods, the Asura Tāraka went to a cave in the Pāriyātra mountain range and performed austerities. Regarding that penance, Brahmā granted him a boon consisting of invincibility by all beings except for seven days on Saturdays. Having been granted this boon by Brahmā, the Asura Tāraka seized his own kingdom.

...the consultation of the Asura Tāraka with his ministers regarding the expedition of his own army for the sake of conquering all the gods, preceded by the mobilization of the forces; then, the preparation of the entire celestial army by Indra with the approval of Bṛhaspati; the commencement of the battle between the Asura Tāraka and the Lord of the Gods; and therein, during the onset of the conflict, the description of the tumultuous battle between the armies of Tāraka and the gods, like the clash between Yama and Antaka, including the description of Yama’s defeat in that battle. ...

In battle, there was a conflict between the son of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) and the Lord of Wealth himself; while Kubera fought with Chulambha, the Lord of Wealth was defeated in that battle by the Lord of Wealth. Thereafter, Kubera emerged victorious in the engagement.

Upon his defeat, Varuṇa bound the two arms of Ijaṃbhabhuja with his noose; then, for the sake of subduing the fierce Mahiṣāsura, the Moon, with a stream of a hundred rays, caused extreme distress to all the Daityas by its intense cold. Then, observing the cessation of the cold brought about by Kālanemi through the spreading of fire, the Sun, with the arrow of Śaṃvara and the thunderbolt of Vāṇa, effected a transformation of the forms of both gods and demons. And then...

Having fallen into delusion, Kālanemi, under the impression that they were gods, slaughtered countless Daityas. Then, by Nigina, the son of Kaṭhanemi, the awakening of Kālanemi was brought about through the employment of a root-illusion (*mūlakṛtamāyā*). Upon waking, Kālanemi released his discus (*bhramāla*) to ward off the enemy. Bhaṅgāśva, mounting the great Indra-cloud (*mahendranāḍha*) and assuming a terrifying form, caused the army of the Daityas to be scattered by the spreading rays of his exceedingly hot heat. [Then] Kālanemi...

Having assumed the form of Kālamegha, the Lord of the Clouds, he caused a rain of weapons and brought about the defeat of the entire army of the gods. Then, at the prayer of the gods, the Blessed Mahāviṣṇu rose from the Ocean of Milk, mounted Garuḍa, returned to the battlefield, fought with Kālamegha, and brought about his defeat.

He indeed engaged in a fierce battle with Viṣṇu, who was desirous of slaying all the Daityas; and when the destruction of countless Daityas had been accomplished, Jambhāsura, having suffered defeat, turned his back and fled from the field of battle in a state of agitation. [Then follows: The stabilization of Viṣṇu through the hymn of praise offered by Indra as he was fleeing; the description of Indra’s preparation for battle and his engagement in a fierce combat with Jambhāsura at the command of Viṣṇu for the purpose of slaying him; and [the account] of that battle.

The slaying of the asura Jambha; following the slaying of Jambha, the flight of all the Daityas, terrified by the divine army, back to the presence of the asura Tāraka; then, having reached the battlefield together with all the Daityas, [the encounter] with the great [Tāraka].

By his prowess, he brought about the total destruction of the armies of all the gods; beholding that valor, Viṣṇu ordered all the gods to flee and himself vanished. Following Tārakāsura’s attainment of victory, he ascended with great ceremony the throne of sovereignty at Khambāyatana (Khambhat) on the shore of the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean. As Tārakāsura sat upon the throne, the goddess who is the ornament of the three worlds arrived and entered [the city]. Nārāyaṇa—

The bringing back of Tārakāsura to the presence of Indra and the other gods in the form of a fish, followed by the granting of fearlessness from Tārakāsura; then, having incurred fear from him, the departure of Indra and the other gods toward Brahmā at the command of Viṣṇu; and the assumption of authority over the positions of Indra and the other gods by the Daityas led by himself.

[The narrative proceeds as follows: Having approached the gods, beginning with Indra, they went before them and, after offering praise, reported their own suffering. Brahmā informed the gods that the Mother of the Universe would incarnate in the house of Himavat. Then, for the sake of the welfare of the gods, preceded by the performance of a hymn to the Goddess Rātri, a prayer was made for the entry of the Great Goddess, the Mother of the Universe, into his wife named Menā. At the request of Brahmā, she entered the eyes of Menā. Then, [from] Menā...

The manifestation from the presence of the Mother of the World (Jagadambā), and a description of the festival at the time of the Mother of the World’s birth. Upon the arrival of Nārada to the one named Himavat at the word of Śakra, and when Pārvatī’s auspicious hand was sought through words spoken according to the truth, Himavat became anxious; then, by describing the granting of the boon to the Lord of the Gods (Śiva) through his own cleverness, he generated great satisfaction in Pulastya. [This occurred] because Pārvatī always kept her palms turned upward.

The description of how he grants the foremost gift of fearlessness and provides protection to all living beings; the instruction given by Himavat to Pārvatī to engage her in the service of Śiva; then, Nārada’s arrival at Indra’s abode from the presence of Himavat, his reporting of the entire account, and his issuing of a command for the marriage with Hara so that she might be united with the Goddess; Indra’s command to Madana to delude Śaṅkara; and the burning of Madana while he was observing Pārvatī’s service.

Next, the piercing of Bāṇa by Śaṅkara; then, Madana being afflicted by passion, his destruction by Hara with the fire from his third eye; and finally, at the request of Rati, the restoration of Madana to life by Śaṅkara in the form of the Anekarūpa [the Many-formed].

) Furthermore, the description of Pārvatī’s performance of penance at Śivagraprastha according to the instruction of Nārada upon his return; Śiva’s arrival in the guise of a brahmin near Pārvatī while she was established in penance in order to test her steadfastness; the consolation of Pārvatī by the highly pleased Śiva following the manifestation of his own form; then, after Pārvatī had performed the selection of her husband (svayaṃvara), the invitation of all the gods; and therein, the appearance of Śrī Dakṣa in the form of a goat.

Having described their arrival, there follows the expulsion of the Daityas, such as Tāraka and others who had assembled there, by the mere sound of the syllable "Hraiṃ"; then the arrival of all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, at the site of the wedding; thereafter, the offering of the garland of choice (*varaṇamālā*) by Pārvatī at the feet of Śrī-Īśvaracarapa, in the presence of all the deities; and finally, the description of the auspicious marriage festival between Hara and Pārvatī, preceded by the approval of Brahmā and the other gods, according to the procedure prescribed in the *Śālñavidhāna*.

After the wedding, Śiva went with Pārvatī to Mount Mandara and sported in the palace of Bhavyandara. At that time, after the gods, terrified by the demon Tāraka, offered hymns of praise, Pārvatī created Gaṇapati from her own body and bestowed him upon the gods for their assistance. Gaṇapati then brought about the perpetual destruction of the Daityas for the benefit of the gods. Following that, the account of how Pārvatī adopted the Gaṇa named Vīraka as her son is narrated; and then—

While Śiva and Pārvatī were engaged in a playful exchange of jests, when Pārvatī called out Kārttikeya, she became angry; she then tormented Śiva with sharp, piercing words that struck at his vital points. Thereupon, Pārvatī emerged from the temple, and as she was departing, she commanded her attendant Gaṇa named Vīraka to block another woman from approaching Śiva. Taking Gaṇapati with her, she then departed for the Himalayas to perform penance.

Then, as Pārvatī was walking toward Śiva with her own mother’s friend Chasumāmodinī, she was instructed by another woman to announce her arrival; subsequently, she began her ascetic penance. While she was thus engaged, the Daitya named Andhaka approached Śiva in the form of Pārvatī. Recognizing that illusion through his divine power, Śiva assumed a fierce form within his own body and slew him with his trident. Immediately thereafter, by means of the wind...

In the presence of Śiva, Pārvatī uttered a loud cry of distress; hearing that, Pārvatī bestowed her bow upon the Vīrakas and Gaṇas. Then, the one whose body was wounded by those arrows departed in his true form. While Pārvatī was performing penance, Brahmā arrived in her presence and granted a boon to the Goddess. Thereafter, from the body of Goddess Pārvatī, a goddess of golden complexion emerged; she was given the name Kaurikī. Then [Pārvatī... The attainment of the state of being Gauri by Pārvatī; then Pārvatī’s journey toward Śiva; there, the doorkeeper Vīraka making a request for entry into the inner quarters; upon hearing Vīraka’s words, Pārvatī’s remorse, thinking, "I previously gave him a curse"; then Pārvatī’s granting of a boon to Vīraka—consisting of the restoration of his son Nandikeśvara and the form of a bull—after first recounting her own history.

Then, having gone near Śiva, there was a divine union with Pārvatī; thereafter followed the commencement of the amorous dalliance between Śiva and Pārvatī. In that context, at the request of the gods, Mahādeva urged Agni—who had arrived in the form of a pigeon—to consume his seed. By his command, Agni swallowed the semen. Then, seeing her husband approaching while he was desiring the wives of the sages, Svāhā assumed the forms of the six Kṛttikās, the wives of the six sages, and through the law of desire, [the seed was deposited] by Agni.

Having taken the semen by means of the six-spoked wheel (*ṣaḍāra-krama*), he deposited it in a hollow of the mountain. Then, out of grief for the loss of his wife, Agni was tormented by sorrow; he was consoled by the voice of Kāśyapa. Thereafter, on Mount Śveta, Agni protected the divine son who was staying within a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the midst of a reed-thicket. This is the account of the conduct of the six wives of the six sages. Then Viśvāmitra approached Kumāra and offered praise to Kumāra with one hundred and eight names. [The story of] Skanda by the great sage Viśvāmitra...

Following the performance of the birth rites (*jātakarma*) and other ceremonies for the Kumāra, the priestly duties were carried out; after the Kumāra had been examined by the preceptor, a name was bestowed upon him, and subsequently, the kingdom was granted to him. Then, the Kumāra was presented by Indra and the other gods. Following that, Śiva and Pārvatī approached the Kumāra and treated him with paternal affection. Thereafter, the Kumāra brought joy to all by fulfilling their desires. [Then follows] the slaying of the demon Tāraka by the Kumāra.

The description of the consecration of Kumārasvāmin into the command of the divine army at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean; Kumārasvāmin’s making of a vow to slay the demon Tāraka; his departure toward the city of Tārakāsura with his own divine forces and the subsequent battle; the dispatching of Nārada to Tārakāsura; and on that occasion, Tārakāsura’s hearing of the auspicious sounds of Kumāra’s victory being chanted by the Kinnaras while he was mounted upon Gavākṣa. Chapters. [The portion] being chanted by the Kinnaras...

Having heard the praise of Kumāra, Tāraka resolved upon the slaughter of Skanda; after deliberating with his ministers and preparing the entire host of Daityas for battle, he marched forth from his city along with the gods and the Pāramavas. Thereupon, the conflict between the gods and the Daityas commenced; in that terrible battle, Kumāra brought about the defeat of Tāraka’s vast army. Then, Lord Kumāra took his stand before Tāraka Asura for the purpose of combat.

O devotee of Śiva, although Viṣṇu instructed Kumārasvāmin [to slay him], he had no inclination to kill Tārakāsura; at that moment, Tāraka caused Indra and the other gods to flee in terror. Seeing Tāraka advancing toward Śaṅkara, a voice from the sky arose in Kumārasvāmin’s mind with the desire to slay Tārakāsura. Then, for the sake of killing Tāraka, Kumāra leaped forth from his peacock, urged Viṣṇu, and seized the power that had issued from Tāraka’s mouth.

Having observed that Tārakāsura was devoid of power, he discharged his own Śakti upon him and brought about the slaying of Tārakāsura; thereafter, at the instigation of Keśava, by means of his own Śakti, he reduced to ashes Mount Krauñca, which was filled with Bāṇa and other Daityas as well as Vyāghra and others.

Then follows the description of the marriage festival of Kumārasvāmin, which was attended by gods, gandharvas, and others, and his victory; the grieving of [the gods] due to the sin incurred by Kumārasvāmin from killing the devotees of Rudra through the slaying of the demon Tāraka; then, by the grace of Mahāviṣṇu, Kumārasvāmin, having purified himself of the taint of the sin arising from the slaughter of Rudra’s devotees, established three divine liṅgas through the medium of Viśvakarman and installed within them the two [deities] Pratiṣṭha and Acchidreśvara; thereafter, by Kumārasvāmin, [the installation] of that which was brought by Brahmādeva...

The installation of Khaṅga under the name Chumariśara; following the installation of Kumāra, the hearing of the ritual procedure for the worship of Śiva from Roka; the hymn of praise to Mahādeva Kumāreśvara by Kumārasvāmin; the granting of boons to Kumārasvāmin by Kumāreśvara; the granting of boons to Kumārasvāmin by Jagadambā, preceded by the statement that she is eternally present in the vicinity of Kumāreśvara; then the granting of boons by Kapardi-Gaṇeśvara; and [the account] of Kumārasvāmin in the presence of Kumāreśvara.

The establishment of the temple; a description of the greatness of Kumāreśvara located at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean. Then, at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, having erected a pillar of victory (*jayastambha*) at the request of the gods, the installation upon it of the third *liṅga* fashioned by Viśvakarman, known by the name Stambheśvara, as well as the construction of the Kūpa-tīrtha, and a description beginning with the greatness of Stambheśvara. Table of contents for the Mahīśvara-khaṇḍa.

The installation of tens of millions of *liṅgas* by Viṣadha, Madī, the gods headed by Sāgara at the confluence of the Jāhnavī and the Aruṇa, and others; their greatness; and a description of the narrative of the five *liṅgas*, preceded by the greatness of Siddhāmbikā, Siddhakūpa, Siddheśa, Dhavara, and others.

In connection with the majesty of the Barvarī-tīrtha, there is an account of the life of Kanyākumārī, the primordial cause known as Komārikākhaṇḍa; and in connection with that, a description of the origin of the world, the dimensions of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and the manner of the earth’s configuration. Following the discussion on the dimensions of the cosmic egg, there is a description of the structure of the celestial sphere (khagoṭa), preceded by an exposition of the arrangement of all the subterranean worlds.

Then follows a description of the arrangement of the netherworlds (*pātāla*) by way of their extent reaching to the edge of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*); a description of the various hells situated below the netherworlds; a description of the tortures experienced by the respective inhabitants of those netherworlds in those specific hells; likewise, a description of all the worlds within the cosmic egg, including the gods, the earth, and the subterranean regions; and thus, a statement regarding the supreme majesty of Maheśvara, who dwells upon the loom of the entire cosmic egg in the form of this [universe]. Then follows a description of the measurement of time (*kālaparimāṇa*). Thus...

A description of the arrangement of the entire triple-world (*traidhātuka-prapañca*); then, in the context of explaining the cause for the goat-like face of a certain young girl born among the nine children of Śatañjaya—the son of King Bharata, the offspring of Ṛṣabha—there follows a description of how she attained that compassionate goat-like face due to having compassionately deposited her own goat in the hollow of a *jālī* tree at the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, following her recollection of events from a previous birth. By her...

The establishment of Vaka by Kumāreka; the granting of a boon to Kumārī by Vakreśāna; the description of how that region became famous by the name Kaumāra-khaṇḍa due to the gift of one part of Bharata-khaṇḍa—divided into nine parts—to his daughter named Kumārī, who was born from the essence of the rays of the moon; the enumeration of the number of cities in the various regions situated within Bharata-khaṇḍa; and how that Kumārī [distributed] her own respective portions to her sons according to their order.

After first bestowing his lute, he returned to Stambhatīrtha; there, by the instruction of Radra, he accomplished the production of excellent *avānīrā* sprouts for the purpose of providing shade for Kumāra, Aśva, and Kumārī. Through the power of her asceticism, he obtained as a boon from Mahākāla—residing on the bank of the Sarasvatī—the celestial nymph Citrarekhā as his wife. [The text continues with] the description of the mountain peak of Varvarīśadhara.

The chapters [are as follows]: then, the description of the life of the Siddha named Madahākāṭhana; therein, Māṇṭi, a resident of Vārāṇasī, having observed that although the fetus of his wife named Caṭikā remained for four years by the grace of Śiva, there was no emergence of that fetus from the womb, Māṇṭi issued a command for its external delivery. Out of fear of birth and worldly existence, the fetus had no desire to emerge from the womb; then Māṇṭi [prayed] to Śiva...

The propitiation [of Śiva]; the command of his own powers (*vibhūtis*) for the sake of seating that embryo by means of Śiva; when the consolation of that [embryo] was performed through the virtues of Śiva’s powers and so forth, the birth of the prince from the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*); and the purification (*dhauti*) of that child by means of the *Kākhā*.

To Kālabhīti, who was performing penance beneath a *vilva* tree named Māpannata, the Lord approached in human form with his hand; by filling the hollows of his feet with earth, he created a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) and revealed his own true form. Then, at the request of Kālabhīti, the Lord remained there in the form of the Mahākāṭaliṅga. Through the grace of the Lord Mahākāṭa, Kālabhīti was liberated from fear of death; thus, preceded by the worship of the Mahākāṭa Liṅga, Śiva appeared in the form of Nandigaṇa through the grace of the Lord Mahākāṭa.

The description of the history of the office of the *pratīhāra* and the *prāvattānta*; then, the instruction by Mahākāla to King Karandhama regarding the nature of the Dharma, the arrangement of the four ages (*caturyugavyavasthā*), and other matters of religious duty.

Then, by Mahākālasiddha, who was purified [by the power of] Karava, there is the removal of doubts regarding the devotees of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the Goddess; a detailed exposition on the various distinctions among the different types of hands (karas); a brief description of the methods for the worship of Śākta and Śaiva deities according to their respective traditions; a description of the virtuous conduct (sadācāra) to be practiced daily; and thereafter, a description of the account of Mahākālasiddha’s attainment of the realm of Śiva.

Now follows the description of the account of the greatness of the ancient Vāsudeva as related by Nākhada; in connection with that, there is a description of the Itarāyaṇa Cāraṇa. [It tells of] a certain Itarāyaṇa named Māṇṭu, born in the lineage of Hārotā on the shore of the confluence of the Mahī and the ocean, whose son was born from the womb of his wife named Itarā.
