The liberation of Keśava from the sin of killing a Brahmin; the introduction to the pilgrimage to this sacred ford (tīrthayātrā) by Padmanābha accompanied by his son who was freed from the sin of killing a Brahmin; the journey of Aja to Suvarṇamukharī after bathing in the Gaṅgā and other waters on a holy day; the description of the Suvarṇamukharī river; the sight by Aja of the elephant Kālahasti situated on the bank of the Suvarṇamukharī and his service to its feet; and Aja’s arrival at the hermitage of Bharadvāja situated on the bank of the Suvarṇamukharī.

The sequence of Bhāradvāja’s service performed out of ignorance; the hospitable reception and honors accorded to Arjuna by Bhāradvāja; then, Arjuna’s request to Bhāradvāja out of a desire to hear about the power of Svarṇamukhī; the procedure for the marriage of Ulūpī as narrated by Bhāradvāja; and Agastya’s journey toward the southern direction of Mount Himavat in order to level the earth.

Then follows the reasoning regarding the descent of the river for the sake of the sacrifice; the great prayer of the gods to Agastya for the descent of the river Suvarṇamukharī; the performance of penance by Agastya at the source of the Suvarṇamukharī; the four-faced Brahmā’s journey to Agastya’s hermitage; the four-faced one’s exhortation to Gaṅgā at Agastya’s request; Gaṅgā’s acceptance of the descent of the river by means of a portion of herself near Agastya; and the praise of Vāyu and others regarding the Suvarṇamukharī.

The completion of the description of Suvarṇamukharī; the glorification of the greatness of the Suvarṇamukharī brought by Agastya; the majesty of Suvarṇamukharī as described by Bhāradvāja; the procedure for the gift of an image of Agastya; then the power of the sacred ford of Agastya; the determination of the source of the Suvarṇamukharī; and the subsequent chapters concerning the offering of water to the gods.
Thus ends the second [chapter] on the majesty of the sacred field of Puruṣottama (Jagannātha) in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.

(§) By means of the introduction to the dialogue between the sage Jabhi and the king, [the author] describes how even from among all the Kṣatriyas, Puṣpa was distinguished by his kingly splendor; how Viṣṇu, having been praised by the learned Mārkaṇḍeya, chose him as his own refuge; and how, on the mountain named Siddhavaṭa situated to the north of the southern peak of the Vindhya range, he declared: "I am pleased with my dwelling there; whoever goes there and beholds me marked by the royal insignia shall be cleansed of their sins. This is the description of the attainment of that auspicious place.

Description of the forest retreats; there, the arrival of the most excellent of men (Puruṣottama) was foretold. At that time, until the end of the night, they remained silent with their mouths closed; having seen this, the sages were filled with wonder—[the first] being the knowledge of the other’s power, and [the second] the majesty of the Lord. Description of the confluence of the Suvarṇamukharī; at Suvarṇamukha, the confluence of the Vyāghrapada river; description of the Śaṅkhatīrtha. ...

Then follows the description of the arrival of King Śaṅkha at the confluence of the Kāverī with the Suvarṇamukharī; the praise of Lord Madhava residing on the Vaikuṇṭhācala mountain; the description of the manifestation of the sixfold army of beings created by the Blessed One; the sequence of the earth's deliverance performed by the Boar incarnation; the account of the worship of Śeṣa-Varāha as described in the Karadatta episode; the story of King Śaṅkha; and the arrival of King Śaṅkha at Vaikuṇṭhācala by the command of the Blessed One.

The arrival of Agastya at Śrī Veṅkaṭācala for the purpose of visiting; his devotion toward the Lord upon reaching the mountain; his beholding the beautiful objects situated on Śrī Veṅkaṭācala performed by Agastya and others; the manifestation of the Blessed Lord, who was pleased by the penance of Agastya and Śaṅkha; the divine form of the Lord, gentle and pleasing, as requested by Brahmā and others; the descent of the Blessed Lord onto the golden peak at the request of Agastya; and the granting of boons, beginning with the gift of the conch-form.
The Exposition of the Greatness of Veṅkaṭācala by the Blessed One, the Sage Bharadvāja.

The manner of the penance performed by Putrārtha for the sake of a son; the praise of the gift to be made at Vaikuṇṭhācala as spoken by Vyāsa; and the section on the knowledge of Gaṅgā spoken by Vyāsa. Thus ends the first [section], the Greatness of Vaikuṇṭhācala, in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.

**Skanda Purāṇa: Chapters and Subjects** 1. **The Vision of the Lord on Mount Nīlādri:** Brahmā and the gods behold the Blessed One on Mount Nīlādri and offer praise to the Lord. 2. **The Arrival of Yama:** Yama arrives at that place. 3. **Yama’s Praise of the Blessed One:** Yama offers praise to the Blessed One. 4. **Lakṣmī’s Address to Yama:** At the command of the Blessed One, Lakṣmī speaks to Yama. 5. **Yama’s Prayer to Lakṣmī:** Upon hearing the majesty of the Śāstra, Yama makes a request to Lakṣmī. 6. **Mārkaṇḍeya’s Entry into the Boat and Wandering Everywhere:** In connection with the dialogue between Yama and Lakṣmī, Mārkaṇḍeya is taken onto a boat by Brahmā and wanders everywhere.

Having heard this account from Yama—concerning the banyan tree grove very near that place, Bābhravya’s arrival there upon hearing the news, his beholding the Blessed Lord there, Mārkaṇḍeya’s hymn of praise to the Blessed Lord, the entry of the pleased Blessed Lord into the mouth of Mārkaṇḍeya, Mārkaṇḍeya’s seeing the belly of that Blessed Lord pervading the entire universe with its thousands of cosmic eggs, and his subsequent emergence from it and remaining right there—Yama [spoke].

Under the title "Yameśvara," there is the installation of the *liṅga*, the acquisition of some wealth through various means at each sacred ford (*tīrtha*) in the context of the pilgrimage to Śrīyama, and therein, the description of the Kapālamocana Tīrtha.

It describes the greatness of that place, stating that devotion arises for all beings, from the King of the Sindhus down to the very roots of the earth, and including everything up to Brahma and the stationary world; then follows the description of the greatness of Kāmākhyā and Nṛsiṃha; the installation of the eight deities beginning with Maṅgalā in the eight directions; and the installation of the guardians of the quarters (dikpālas), such as Kapāṭhamocana, Yameśvara, Mārkaṇḍeya, Bilveśvara, Aṭerānī, Khaṇḍeśa, and Yakṣetrapāla.

The narrative of Indrayumna; thereafter, the departure of the two Brahmins toward their own abodes. Following the Lord’s assumption of a wooden body, the granting of boons to Indrayumna. The arrival there of a Brahmin and a Kshatriya named Puṇḍarīka and Ambarīṣa, who were filled with curiosity upon hearing the account of Hari possessing a wooden form and proceeded to perform a penance. Furthermore, the establishment of the Dārumaya Tīrtha by Indrayumna at that very spot, and a description of its greatness.

By the power of that sacred ford (*tīrtha*), there is a description of how Puṇḍarīka and Ambarīṣa abandoned their initial evil association; due to the abundance of their faults, there is an account of their state as hungry ghosts (*preta*); the Lord’s granting of food to them at that very spot by means of a vow consisting of not accepting food except from the Lord; their offering of praise to the Lord; and a description of their devotion through the constant chanting of the Lord’s names. ... Chapter 6.

Having heard from the Sage that these supreme objects are conducive to liberation and bestow great merit, and that a person who possesses right faith dwells there, the Jina gave this reply: "This field is adorned with groves of various trees, frequented by sages, providing merit through its sacred circumambulation, situated on the bank of the river Dadhigāminī, and possessing elevations like those of Ṛṣigiri."...

At the command of Indradyumna, the ruler of the city of Arvettī, who was eager for a pilgrimage to the sacred ford, the priest Vidyāpati set out to go to the supreme field of Puṣpapottama, which is surrounded by the Rohiṇī-ūṇḍa, Kalpavṛkṣa, and other [shrines]. On the way, he beheld Śiva and heard the excellent discourse of Vidyāpati.

Having seen Vidyāpati, who had fasted for three days, the Śabara—having ascertained his resolve that he would not take food without having performed service to the Lord—while reflecting on this, set out for the Rohiṇīkuṇḍa preceded by a journey through the forest with Vidyāpati; there he beheld the Lord and offered praise to Him; thereafter, the longing of Vidyāpati to return to his own country is described.

While he was preparing to return to his own country, at that very moment, a fierce wind arose, scattering the sand from the eyes of the gods; because of this, those gods, out of a desire to behold the Blessed One, praised the Blessed One’s splendor so that they might obtain a vision of him. [Thinking] that otherwise no one would ever see the Blessed One, they extolled the Blessed One. Then, at the end of the day, the Master of Knowledge returned, having turned back from Avanti.

A description of the placing of a garland of raw meat around the king’s neck by Vidyāpati, who was honored with gifts such as a rise in rank by the king; the performance of a hymn of praise to the Blessed One by both Vidyāpati and Indrayudha; and a description of the power of the holy sites (tīrthas) such as Puruṣottama-kṣetra, Rodinī, and Kaṇḍā, as recounted by Vidyāpati. ... ...

Then, after describing the greatness of various holy places (*tīrtha*) such as Purottama, Khetrastha, Magavat, Svarūpa, and Vaṭavrakṣāyaṇa through the power of Indra’s horse, and describing the state of the gods distressed by a fierce wind in the evening, Nārada arrived nearby. Indra honored Nārada, who then described the greatness of the Cāṇūra-vrata to Indra. [Nārada said: "Knowing that this is the Lord who has descended for the sake of divine play (*līlārtha*), I shall lead you there."
Having heard Nārada’s words, the king, causing all the citizens to rejoice together, went with his entire retinue to behold Lord Nārāyaṇa and Mādhava at Kāśī.

After Oṭūrāja’s departure, Nārada, having traveled on his way, related to Indradyumna the account of a temple of Śiva situated upon a mountain peak. There, while Śaṅkara was performing the marriage of Gaurī, he established the city of Avimukta near Vārāṇasī. Kārīrāja obtained boons from Śiva; then there was a battle between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the King of Kāśī. By means of a Sudarśana discus dispatched by Śrī Kṛṣṇa against the city of Kāśī, the head of King Kāśī was severed and the city of Kāśī was consumed by fire.

Then, Śiva, incited by [his devotee], performed the removal of the *pāśupatāstra* upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa; having defeated the Pāśupata and seeing Kāśī consumed by fire, the terrified Śaṅkara offered a hymn of praise to Viṣṇu; pleased by the hymn, Viṣṇu commanded him to establish a sacred field (*kṣetra*) named Puruṣottama after his own name; by the command of Viṣṇu, Śrī Datta established the Puruṣottama-kṣetra—thus [ends] the greatness of the establishment of that sacred field; and Śrī Vedavyāsa performed a hymn of praise to Nīlamādhava-Puruṣottama.

Then, having arrived at the field of Jyambaka known as Ekānana and worshipped Him, he offered hymns of praise to Koṭidagīśa; pleased by this, Śiva described to him how Indradyumna had become a bearer of the *vighna* (obstacle) and how he himself had become subordinate to Śiva. Thereafter, Indradyumna went with Nārada to the presence of the Lord; having paid obeisance to Viśveśa and the other deities and mounted his chariot together with Nārada, he meditated upon the Blessed One and proceeded toward the mountain of the Lord.

Śaṅkara, having assumed the guise of a pigeon and performed worship of the Lord, established the site of Kapotedā by His grace. Then, seeing the earth oppressed by the Daityas dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla), Śrī Kṛṣṇa took a bilva fruit and performed worship of the Lord in order to exterminate those demons; by the grace of Tryambaka, he conquered the Asuras and established Viśveśvara. This is followed by a description of its greatness. ...dha...

The departure toward the place where Niṭakaṇṭha was wounded, accompanied by Nārada and the king’s ministers and army; the two chapters concerning the subjects [are as follows]: Pa0 Pra—taking the fourfold army along with the sounding of kettledrums and drums, setting out from the city together with Nārada, and on the way, seeing the goddess named Cācikā stationed at the border of the Utkala country.

The description of her; the description of the welcome offered by Indradyumna upon the arrival of King Odra. Following their mutual conversation, the account of King Odra’s return to his own city at the command of Indra and Yama.

Chapter 6: Topics—Then Nārada, having gone with you to the holy site of Puruṣottama and found the Lord vanished, comforts Indradyumna by making a vow: "Having beheld the wooden body [of the Lord], I shall certainly cause you to perform the worship of the Blessed One."

Then, accompanied by Nārada, Indradyumna went to see the Lord standing upon the peak of Mount Nīla; having descended from the presence of Śiva, he beheld Narasiṃha atop the summit of the Blue Mountain and took hold of the Lord’s footstool. Then, together with Nārada, he visited the site where the Blessed One resides as Puruṣottama. Thereafter, all of them, including Indra and his retinue, offered praise to the Lord. Pleased by their hymn of praise, the Blessed One addressed Indradyumna with an unembodied voice.

The command to perform the horse sacrifice (*vājimedha*); the description of Indradyumna’s commencement of the horse sacrifice by the command of the Blessed Lord; the journey of Indradyumna to the city of Amrata at the instruction of Nārada for the purpose of installing the image of Narasiṃha; and the conversation with the son of the divine architect (Viśvakarman), who, having approached Indradyumna near the sandalwood tree, said to him: "For your sake, I shall fashion an image of Narasiṃha."

The manifestation of the deity known as Devākhya by the command of Indradyumna; then the installation of the Narasiṃha image by Nārada with his own hand; the description of the hymn of praise offered to the installed Narasiṃha image by Indradyumna; and the description of the majesty of Narasiṃha.

Having praised and addressed the gods, including Indra, for the purpose of performing the sacrifice, he undertook the great festival of the horse-sacrifice (*vājimedha-yajña*) with the assistance of the deities. By the power of that sacrifice, Indra’s splendor increased day by day; subsequently, in a dream, the Lord reclining upon Śeṣa appeared to him. When Indra related his own experience to Nārada, Nārada declared the excellent fruit of that dream. Then, having suddenly arrived at the shore of the ocean in a region near Bilveśvara—

When a certain tree appeared, its guardians were filled with wonder and reported the account of the appearance of the *vṛṣa* (bull) to the king. Thereafter, the sacrifice was completed with the ritual bath (*avabhṛthasnāna*). Nārada described the majesty of that tree, saying, "This has emerged from the body-hairs of the Blessed One. Then, the tree was installed. Later, on a certain occasion, while Indra was standing there to perform worship, he saw a worm sucking the form of Viṣṇu and asked Nārada, "Who indeed is this?"

Thinking, "I shall fashion that image," the chapters concerning the subject matter began; for that king, who was devoted to the Lord, Nārada said, "I shall fashion that image," and having spoken thus, he vanished right there upon that altar covered with cloth. [This is followed by] the description of the excellence of Nārada’s fortune.

“The king, enlightened by Nārada, performed hymns of praise to Viṣṇu; Nārada, in the form of Gaya, offered praise to Sthāṇu who was bearing the form of the Blessed One; others as well, such as Ekīṣya, described the Blessed One; Indra worshipped the Blessed One along with his retinue with various mantras, offerings, and so forth; the king gave cows there to the Brahmins for the sake of attaining that merit; and King Nanda caused the construction of a temple for the Blessed One.”

At the command of the gods, they arrived there for the purpose of consecrating the palace constructed by Viśvakarman; hearing that the worship of the Blessed One cannot be accomplished without those who have known the means through the Vedas and other scriptures, Nārada, together with King Indradyumna—who was a Brāhmaṇa reciting the Ṛgveda—proceeded toward the world of Brahmā in a celestial chariot (*puṣparatha-vimāna*). On the way, having heard from his own mouth the description of the greatness of the wooden man (*dāru-puruṣa*), Nārada instructed King Indradyumna in the worship of the Blessed One as known through the Vedas.

The manifestation of his own desire to go toward the world of Brahmā for the purpose of inviting Brahmā at the time of the sacrificial session; the manifestation of Nārada’s own desire to go toward the world of Brahmā to invite Brahmā on behalf of the king; and Nārada’s posing of a question regarding the cause of the king’s grief to the monarch whose mind was preoccupied with the affairs of state.

Having heard the queen’s reason for her distress, Nārada consoled her and dispelled her anxiety. Subsequently, Indra-yumna and Nārada went together to the world of Brahmā, which is beyond all darkness. At the gate of the palace, Indra-yumna made obeisance to Brahmā. When Brahmā asked the purpose of their arrival, Indra-yumna replied that since his palace had been destroyed by Śatī, he requested that they come so that he might re-establish the deity there. Thus he addressed Brahmā.

The command was issued for Prabhāvatī to descend to the earth along with the gods. During the installation ceremony (*pratiṣṭhā-karma*), she, together with the other gods and Padmanidhi, arrived there; having partaken of the food of the Blessed One, she worshipped the Blessed One installed in the temple with the *Puruṣasūkta*. While Indra and the others were performing the worship, various matters regarding the arrival of other kings were discussed, and then [the account] concerning Indrayudha [was told].

After Mūta related the account of his many hardships and transgressions, he offered a seat for her departure; then, by the command of Brahmā, King Indrayumna returned to the earth along with the gods, Padmanidhi, and the Brahmins. He then performed a hymn of praise to the Blessed One, after which a voice from the sky commanded him to establish the image of the Blessed One through the agency of Padmanidhi.

The construction of the chariot by Viśvakarmā at the command of Nārada, who was filled with devotion through his hearing of the *Sāhitya-saṃsmara* (the recollection of literature) by the grace of your [the Lord's] command; the fashioning of the three chariots by Viśvakarmā at the command of Nārada; the installation of that chariot by the hand of Nārada; a description of the method for the ritual of installing the chariot in connection with that [incident]; the description of the installation of the Blessed Lord within the chariot after having fashioned the marks of the *cakrin* and *mūṣin* on the chariot’s banner and having performed the invocation of Garuḍa accompanied by mantras; and thereafter, [the description of] the arrival of the Blessed Lord’s attendants.

[The description of defects such as damage caused by asking] "By which chariot part was this made? or "Whose [part] is missing?", followed by the description of the method for installing the deities of the directions around the chariot; the description of the form of the Lord Śiva; and the granting of blessings to the worlds by the Blessed One.

Oṃ. The arrival there of King Gāla together with his army; the description of how he was filled with wonder upon hearing from Indrayumna of the miseries of cyclic existence (saṃsāra) brought about by the death of Gāla’s son; then, after Gāla had become a mendicant, the narration of all the events such as his own departure for battle against Druma; and thereafter, following the mutual conversation between Gāla and Druma, Indrayumna, having recognized his own former identity as the king, [was established] upon the throne of his own kingdom by King Gāla.

The acceptance of his command following its formal installation; then, Indra’s arrival from the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) to the temple of the Lord built by Nala and others, accompanied by a shower of celestial splendors; thereafter, the construction of the chariot by Nala, who was pleased by the arrival of Brahmā; the offering of the chariot, the temple, and other gifts by Brahmā and the performance of hymns of praise to the Lord; and then, the journey of Subhadrā’s chariot (the chapters and their subjects).

The description of the praise of Subhadrā by the god Brahmā; the composition of a hymn to Balabhadra; the description of the ritual procedures and majesty of the worship of the three chariots, the great festival of Mahādevī, and the worship, bathing, and giving of gifts at Madhānadeka; [and] "I invoke you with your chariot."

The pilgrimage [begins] with the description of the establishment of the Lord’s image and the subsequent account of the destruction of his enemies; then, the sudden appearance of a terrifying form like Narasiṃha, and the description of the terror-stricken state of Viṣṇudatta and others as they behold it; the description of the fruit [of the pilgrimage] and the defeat of the enemy; the description of the great queen, Puruṣottama, Balabhadra, Sumadra, and Dadasena; the narration by Brahmā, at the word of Nārada, of the power of Narasiṃha; and [the account] of Narasiṃha by Brahmā.

The composition of hymns; the fruit of offering oblations of ghee at Madājyeṣṭhā; the majesty of lighting lamps at Sadasat; the direct manifestation and establishment of the respective deities in their own places through mantras recited at the time of the installation of deities; the description of the greatness of the lake as an ancillary of the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha) and the greatness of Vindutīrtha; the arrival of the Pitṛs and others even from Mahāveya by means of their respective forms of flight; the performance of the Brahmadaivata Indra-yajña and other rites; and thereafter—

The description of the fruits of action; the performance of propitiatory rites for Indra, Agni, Soma, Rudra, Kṣetra, Vana, Jāgaraṇa, Vīthi, Hṛṣīkeśa, and other sacred bathing sites (tīrthas); the worship of the deities of the quarters; the description of the majesty [of these]; and the description of the greatness of giving and other virtues.

The worship of Balabhadra with the *Ra-inrayanena* [mantra], of Nārāyaṇa with the twelve-syllable mantra, and of the Goddess with the *Devīsūkta*; then, the composition of a hymn by the god Brahmā for the purpose of dispelling the fear of the demons; the description of the ritual rules for the festival of the Goddess’s lying down; the granting of a boon to the Blessed One by the Lord through the merit of the four-month period (*cāturmāsya*); and the description of King Daruḍa taking up his residence at Sthānamāḍalyaka out of his own happiness.

The washing away of various kinds of sins during the Cāturmāsya; the vision of Tīrtha, Jñāna, Puruṣottama, and other deities; a description of the fruits of recitation, charity, and other acts performed with single-minded devotion;

the results [of these]; a discussion on what objects are to be accepted and what are not to be accepted during the Cāturmāsya; a narration of the rules to be observed during the Cāturmāsya; a description of the greatness of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites in the month of Jyeṣṭha; the [description of] Mārkaṇḍeya, the Banyan tree (Vaṭa), Varuṇa, Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and others; and the fruit of hearing this account of the greatness of the Cāturmāsya Uddhava-vrata.

The description of the sequence of rules regarding the auspicious times for commencing rites during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*), including the commencement of the *dakṣiṇāyana*; the description of the greatness of the sacred sites (*tīrtha-kṣetra*) such as Puruṣottama and Rāja; the fruits of various types of rituals such as hymns and worship, and the specific fruit of performing worship; the mention of the names of the deities situated in the ten directions of Puruṣottama, and the description of the manner of worshipping them. ... Śa (Sa). ... [End of fragment]

The narration of the fruits [of the rites], the worship of Nṛhari by Indradyumna after a hundred years; then, by another king, the worship of Puruṣottama and Raṅgiṇī; thereafter, the description of the greatness of bathing in the Candrayumnasaras lake, preceded by the statement regarding the attainment of great fruit through the recitation of the Nṛsiṃha mantra, as well as the hymn of praise during worship, and the granting of boons to the king by the Blessed Lord.

The majesty of beholding Puruṣottama as requested by Maśca; the majesty of the abode of Puruṣottama; the granting of a boon to King Śveta and the subsequent disappearance of the Blessed One; the description of the fruits of consuming the remnants of the Blessed One’s meal; the exposition of the manual for hymns to Puruṣottama; and the statement that through the vision of Puruṣottama, all desired fruits are obtained. 1.

The description of the fruits of wearing the remains of offerings (nimālya) from sacred fords (tīrtha), the determination regarding the *kacchikā* [head-ornament], the description of the greatness and fruits of meditating upon the Lord and visiting the Dakṣiṇāmūrti shrine during the Kali age, the description of the Jyeṣṭha-pañcaka vow, the description of the attainment of fruits by one who bathes on the Mahājyaiṣṭhī day, the description of the nature of the Lord’s compassion, kindness, and other qualities, the description of the greatness and fruits of that Puruṣottama mountain for a certain Brahmin, and the worship of the Lord after lighting five lamps.

The arrival at the sacred field of Puruṣottama; the description of its greatness, beginning with how a certain person, being possessed by a spirit, thought the food remnants of the Blessed One were [intended for him] and thus acted as a servant to the Blessed One; the account of how a fast observed on the full moon of the month of Jyeṣṭha resulted in bodily affliction for one who did not eat the food offered at the Kṛṣṇavaṭa tree; and the description of the fruits of worshipping the goddess Bhadrā of the Blessed One by other twice-born men.

The account of how Devatūṣa attained radiance by eating the remnants of offerings; the story of the twice-born man who, having abandoned the *naivedya*, was rebuked by Īśvara and subsequently attained his own daughter through the compassion born of his prayer; the description of the appearance of the *sugandhinirmālya* (fragrant remains of the garland) at the time of the destruction of the demon Damanaka; the exposition on the method of worshipping the gods with the worship of the devotees of the Lord; and the description of the fruits of eating the remnants of the grace of Nṛsiṃha along with one’s beloved, as told by Dakṣiṇāmūrti.

The description of obtaining the fruit of all pilgrimages through the performance of gifts, festivals, and vows; the description of the times for the Lord’s reclining and waking; the description of the procedure for the great festival of awakening known as Kaumudī; the description of the worship of the Lord during that time; the description of the fruit of such worship; the description of how this very worship yields the fruit of bathing at thirty million sacred sites; and the description of the festival of garments on the sixth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.

The description of the procedure and the fruits of the *prāvaraṇotsava* (the festival of the upper garment) and its vow; the description of the procedure for the day of the *puṣyasnāna* (the ritual bath under the Puṣya asterism) and its festival and vow; the description of the materials and requisites for the worship during the *puṣyasnāna* festival and vow; the description of the fruits of bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and beholding the Lord during the period of the northern solstice (*udagayana*), preceded by the rules for the transit of the sun into Capricorn (*makarasaṃkramaṇa*); the description of the procedure for the *doḍāyohaṇā* [ceremony] in the month of Phālguna; the performance of the *sāṃvatsara-vrata* on the full moon day of Phālguna; and the description of the installation of the image of Viṣṇu and the vow of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha.

Description of... (the description of the spring festival of Damana-bhañjikā; the description of the pilgrimage to Yakṣayamekṣa; the description of a hymn of praise to the Blessed One during that pilgrimage; the description of the sight of the Blessed One as a wooden statue situated atop Mount Nīla).

Following the consecration of the temple, the great sages asked what Indradyumna had done; this section concludes with the answer to their question, preceded by a description of the Lord’s true form as manifested by Indradyumna, and a summary of the majesty of Puruṣottama. It includes the hearing of the fruits of the majesty of the Purāṇas. Thus ends the second [chapter], the Majesty of Puruṣottama (Jagannātha), in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.
(-) Chapter Contents: Now, in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa, the third [section], the *Badarikāśrama-māhātmya*.

In this work, following the inquiry as to by what means liberation might be attained through the connection with the dialogue between Sūta and Lomaśa, there begins the dialogue between Śiva and Skanda. Therein, preceded by an introduction and a description of the greatness of many excellent holy sites (*tīrtha*) such as the Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Yamunā, and Narmadā, follows the description of the greatness of the sacred site known as Ayodhyā. This includes the description of the greatness of the Ayodhyā region, the description of the procedure for bathing at the Gomatī river, the fruit of the pilgrimage to the five crores of holy sites, and the fruit of bathing at the Viśrānti holy site.

The greatness of the gift of gold at Rāmatīrtha; the greatness of beholding Jagannātha preceded by a description of the fruit of bathing in the Mākaṇḍaya lake; the greatness of bathing in the Indrayumna lake; and the declaration that all desired fruits are attained by the mere chanting of the name of Badarī.

A description of the greatness of the sacred field named Badarī, preceded by its origin; the account of how Brahmā, who had united with his own daughter, had his fifth head severed by Śiva; how Śiva, taking that head in his hand, traveled to all the holy fords (*tīrthas*) to free himself from the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*); thereafter, his journey to Badarikāśrama, the lord of Girijā; how Brahmā was liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin upon reaching Badarikāśrama; and a description of the Daśāśvamedhika Tīrtha.

The journey toward the hermitage of Annarbadārikā at the command of Vyāsa; a description of the hymn of praise offered to the Blessed One; a description of the majesty of Abhitī; a description of the peaks of Nārada, Śilā, Mārkaṇḍeya, Śikhī, and Umā; a description of the majesty of the Śraiteya peak; the majesty of the Vārādī peak, where the Blessed One was praised by the gods and others; the majesty of the Nārasidī peak; a discourse on the fruit of circumambulating the Blessed One; and the vision of the Blessed One in Viśālā.

The gods, headed by Brahmā, offered praise to the Blessed One at Śīrāgha; the manifestation of the Blessed One; his disappearance after declaring that he had concealed himself out of fear that the sages might become intoxicated with pride; the installation of the Blessed One by Śiva; the fruit of the gift of the universe obtained by Badarīdaśaśena through the utterance of the name "Badarī"; and a description of the greatness of giving gifts such as the feeding of Brāhmaṇas at the sacred site of Badarī.

Description of the origin and history of the *pitṛ-tīrtha*, *kapāla-mocana-tīrtha*, and *brahma-tīrtha*; the performance of penance there by Brahmā; the offering of praise to the Blessed One by Brahmā, who was filled with joy at the sight of the Blessed One; the topics of the chapters [beginning] from the grace of the Blessed One: the characteristics of the superior, middling, and inferior times, and the longing for the Lord; the fruit of bathing in the holy ford (*tīrtha*), the characteristics of human beings, and the characteristics of the fourfold fire.

An exposition of the daily duties beginning from dawn; therein, the rules for the evacuation of urine and feces; the rules for cleaning the teeth and so forth; the performance of bathing and other rites; the determination of sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) and meat-based food (*āmiṣa*); the purification of the mouth and face, the regulation of the directions, and the attainment of authority over the six types of disciples; the Brahmin’s attainment of the right to know the meaning of all the Vedas; the attainment of the right to compose the *Saṃhitās* of the Purāṇas and other texts by Vyāsa through the power of bathing in the Sarasvatī; and the greatness of sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*) for the fulfillment of desires.

Description of the majesty of the Vasudhārā Tīrtha; the majesty of the five Dhārā Tīrthas, namely Prabhāsa, Puṣkara, Gayā, Naimiṣa, and Kurukṣetra; the departure of those [sages] for the hermitage of Badarikā in order to worship and for the cessation of their exhaustion after having bowed to the five Dhārā Tīrthas; the description of the rites following the origin of Somakuṇḍa; the majesty [of that]; and the majesty of the four Khotorvaśī Tīrthas along with the Saprapada.

The determination of the rites to be performed and those not to be performed during the month of Kārtika; at that time, the departure toward Viśāla by Indra and others, who were delighted by the Lord’s dwelling in Viśākhā.

The narrative of the Brahmin Kutsa regarding the greatness of offering lamps in the temple of Viṣṇu; in connection with the greatness of rekindling another's lamp—the establishment of Megha there at Viśākhā for the sake of providing food for the Lord, Indra, and others; the performance of hymns of praise by the gods to the Lord; the narration of the history of Indumatī’s dream; the greatness of offering sky-lamps; the narrative of the crow and the cat; and the residence of the gods in that very place by the command of the Lord.

The establishment of the *ḍokapāra* at Badarikāśrama; the description of the religious duties of the Kārttika vow through the dialogue between Candraśarman and Sunanda at that very Badarikāśrama; the majesty of the lamp (*dīpamāhātmya*); the attainment of all fruits by the donor of lamps; the description of the excellent *dharmakaṣa* tree; the description of the Daṇḍapuṣkariṇī Tīrtha... the ritual for offering the sky-lamp (*ākāśadīpa*); the account of liberation from the state of a *piśāca* through the offering of the sky-lamp; and the [offering of] lamps on the five days. Thus ends the third section, the *Badarikāśramamāhātmya*, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.

Charity; the locations for preparing Kāśika lamps; the history of Harikara and Trāhaṇi regarding the offering of lamps; the Kapṛra lamp. Now begins the fourth [section], the Greatness of the Month of Kārttika, in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.

The fruits of the recitation of the *padas* and so forth; the auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*); Śaunaka’s question to Sūta regarding the knowledge of the origin of the *Kārttika-māsavibhava*; the statement of the answer; the narration of the history of the Brahmin Harimitra and Sumedhas in connection with the description of the essential duties of Vulasī; the observation of omens (*śakunāvalokana*) at Pañcadīpa; the account of the cowherd woman Ekāṅgī and her attainment of wealth, grain, happiness, and progeny through the observance of Vatsadvādaśī; the prescription for Yama-trayodaśī; and the legend of Devalaka.

The procedure for the Naraka-Caturdaśī festival, the procedure for the Dīpāvali festival—in which the term *kaumudī* is the literal meaning—the scriptural statement regarding the Pāvaiṇa, the commencement of the Kārttika vow preceded by praise in the dialogue between Brahmā and Nārada, and the determination of performing the Kārttika vow during times of distress. ...

Brahmā spoke to Nārada regarding the duties and rules of the Kārttika vow; therein, in connection with the preeminence of service to the guru, there is the historical account and the religious duties of the disciples Medhātithi, Vṛka, and Kapila; in connection with the gift of food, the narrative of the Brahmin Savyaketu and the performance of Śrāddha and other rites; the evening worship of Mahālakṣmī, Mahākālī, and Mahāsarasvatī; the festival of Lakṣmī’s awakening and, in connection with the gift of cows, the historical account of the Brahmin Sumati; and, in connection with the remembrance of names, the narration of the Puṣkara legend.

The section [deals with] the festival of lamps (*dīpotsava*), the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*), the auspicious play of the *bakirāñya* birds, and the viewing of the *akhokana*; the narration of the history of the dull-witted Brāhmaṇa in connection with the greatness of reciting the *Gītā*; the story of the crow regarding the offering of the crest-lock (*śikhādāna*); the dismissal of the crows outside at midnight; the description of the *Sukharātri* vow; and the telling of stories by the Brāhmaṇa. Bh. Na. (Ra....)

Description of the commencement of gambling; description of the commencement of King Badali’s reign; determination of the intercalary lunar day (adhika-tithi); and a description of the nature of the vow, preceded by the determination of the requirements for the beginning and conclusion of the Kārttika vow, such as the application of cow dung in the courtyard.

The worship of *pipūjana*, the worship of Govardhana, the viewing of the combats between buffaloes and bulls at Barīvada, the ritual for bathing preceded by the determination of the time for the Māgha-pāḍī bath, the ritual for bathing that bestows progressively greater merit at wells, sacred fords (*tīrtha*), and so forth, the procedure for the worship of Varuṇa at night, the description of cattle-sports, the observation of the omen of the staff, the determination of the wood, the determination of the fruit of bathing in the Tuṅgabhadrā and Kāverī rivers, the majesty of the holy ford of the Pañcanadī river, and the procedure for the Yamadvitīyā vow. (Skanda Purāṇa, Māheśvara Khaṇḍa, Sūta Saṃhitā, Chapter 15).
There is no doubt.

The majesty of the *dhātrī* tree; the procedure for the worship of the *dhātrī*; the account of the origin of the *dhātrī* grove; a description of the deities residing in the *dhātrī*; the power of the *dhātrī*’s shade; the ancient legend (*itihāsa*) concerning that [shade]; the narration of the liberation of a mouse through hearing a story; the greatness of eating in the shade of the *dhātrī*; a description of the removal of defects by eating in the shades of the *dhātrī*; wearing a garland of *dhātrī* fruits; the offering of a row of lamps in the shade of the *dhātrī*; in the shade of the *dhātrī*...

The fruit of a meal shared by a husband and wife; the majesty of the *dhātrī* (myrobalan) fruit; the fruit of bathing with *āmalka* (myrobalan) and what is to be avoided; the fruit of offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) in the shade of a *dhātrī* tree; a description of the specific parts of the body upon which the *dhātrī* fruit should be worn; the fruit of worshipping a Brāhmaṇa in the shade of a *dhātrī* tree; the lunar days (*tithi*) for the worship of the *dhātrī*; the rules regarding eating in a forest; the majesty of the *dhātrī* tree in its native habitat; and the majesty of the *dhātrī* tree within one's home, as related in the dialogue between Satyabhāmā and Kṛṣṇa concerning Satyabhāmā’s previous birth.

A description of how Kṛṣṇa attained the state of a *brahmacārī* through the merit of his observances and vows; an explanation by Kṛṣṇa—when asked why he was the most excellent among all—regarding Satyabhāmā, concerning his defeat of the demon Śaṅkha and his status as the foremost of the Kārviyas; the sanctity of the site of Prayāga; and when the sage Parvata asked how Tulasī arose and how she became the bearer of the discus, Nārada began to recount her origin, starting with the story of Śiva being awakened by the fall of Indra’s thunderbolt.

The narration of the origin of Jalandhara through the fire of his wrath; then, the description of Jaṭādhara’s conquest of the quarters and his attainment of victory; the description of the cause for Bṛhaspati obtaining the name "Jīvana"; and Viṣṇu’s manifestation and waging of war after being praised by the gods who were defeated in battle.

In the assembly of Jaṭādhara, at the instruction of Nārada, Rāhu was dispatched by the Lord to seize the jewel among women, Pārvatī; the description of the birth of the Kīṭasūkha Gaṇas from the forehead of the enraged Śiva due to his delusion; then the description of the defeat of Rudra in the battle between the gods and the asuras; the fall of Vīrabhadra; and then the battle between Jaṭādhara and Śiva; and Viṣṇu’s consideration that the killing of Jaṭādhara would occur through the violation of Vṛndā’s chastity.
The display of Māyā; then the description of the conversation between Viṣṇu and Śiva regarding that event; and when Vṛndā had cast off her body, the mocking of Viṣṇu by the ashes thereof.

Then, Bhavānī, having slain Jalandhara in battle, remained bowed down; at the command of the Day-maker (the Sun), she was praised by the gods who were urged by Viṣṇu. Pleased by that praise, the goddesses granted three seeds (*bīja*) to the gods for the purpose of awakening Viṣṇu. From those seeds, the birth of Dhātrī, Māchatī, and Tukusī is described. Furthermore, due to Dharmadatta’s gift of merit from Kāśī, Karahā was born as a Rākṣasī; the method [of her redemption] through Kaṭahā’s words, the giving [of gifts] in the month of Kārtika, and the full description of the *ādāsa* are recounted.

The granting of boons to Daśaratha by Viṣṇu, who was pleased with his devotion, including the prophecy that he would become a king famous by the name Daśaratha in another birth through the agency of a messenger of Viṣṇu, and that the Lord Viṣṇu himself would descend as his son; the narration of the greatness of Viṣṇu’s discus; and the account of the Brahmin Viṣṇudāsa, the king of Coḍa, and his servant, concerning how the Brahmin named Viṣṇudāsa [dealt with] one who had stolen his wealth.

Seeing the Caṇḍāla from afar, Viṣṇudāsa ran after him with joy in order to offer him clarified butter; then, observing the Caṇḍāla fallen in a swoon, Viṣṇudāsa honored that Caṇḍāla with water. Thereafter, the Blessed One, assuming the form of the Caṇḍāla, bestowed his grace upon Viṣṇudāsa. By the grace of the Blessed One, a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) arrived from heaven for the Brāhmaṇa Viṣṇudāsa; while Viṣṇudāsa was ascending it and departing, [the Blessed One] remained constant.

The entry of the King of Thieves into the temple; then the Lord’s manifestation of His own form to him; the supreme devotion of the thief, the king, Viṣṇudāsa, and the Brāhmaṇa; the account of how Jayavijaya attained the state of being doorkeepers at Viṣṇu’s abode through eating the *gaṇḍakī* grass offered by a Kārtika-vow observer; the description of how Dhaneśvara attained birth in the family of a Brāhmaṇa through the merit of contact with those observing the Kārtika vow; the procedure for the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) of the Kārtika vow; the description of the fruits of merit and sin; the narrative of the devoted wife (*pativratā*); and the rules for the month-long fast (*māsopavāsa*).

The ritual for Kūṣmāṇḍanavamī; the description of the ritual for the marriage of Tuṭasī; the prescription for the Dharmīṣma-pañcaka vow; the majesty of Prabodhinī-ekādaśī; the ritual for Dvādaśī; the chapters [and their contents]: the majesty of Śravaṇa-caturdaśī; the majesty of the Tripurotsava festival; cow’s products (gavya); rājamāṣa beans; drinking and eating from a copper vessel; food prepared with curd; and eggplant (ṛntāka).

The greatness of the final three days of the Puṣkariṇī festival; the description of the fruit of the rules for listening to the Purāṇas; food defiled by them; the citron; daytime; the consumption of intoxicants; daily [observances]. Now, in connection with the weight of the greatness of the month of Kārttika, the rules that must be observed and performed by those observing the Kārttika vow are stated as follows: || 1 ||

In this regard, the rules for what must be performed are as follows: constant remembrance of Satāraka; worship of Rādhā and Dāmodara; recollection of the names of Viṣṇu, Hari, and Śiva; conquest of the senses; restraint of the mind; compassion toward all living beings; meditation on the Lord; worship of the Lord; speaking the truth; eating sacrificial food (haviṣya); the vow of eating only at night; the vow of fasting until the completion of a specific task (dhāraṇāpāraṇā-vrata); the vow of silence (mauna-vrata); the vow of celibacy (brahmacarya-vrata); association with the virtuous; worship of the *dhātrī* tree; and worship of Viṣṇu in the shade of the *dhātrī* tree.

Listening to discourses on the eternal; the gift of land; service to one's mother and father; service to one's teacher; constant beholding of the deity; singing in the temple of the deity; offering a perpetual lamp in the temple of the deity; offering a lamp at a crossroads; offering a lamp to a Brāhmaṇa; offering a lamp at the cow-pen; worship of the *tulasī* plant; worship of the *aśvattha* tree; worship of the deity, the Brāhmaṇa, and the cow; performing circumambulation of the deity; performing the circumambulation of a hundred thousand *tulasī* plants; circumambulating the *aśvattha* tree; and feeding Brāhmaṇas.

The giving of food; the giving of cows, bulls, buffaloes, and elephants; the giving of gold, minerals, and gems; and providing shelter for the destitute—one should observe these restrictive rules (*niyamas*) during the month of Kārttika. Now, the forest-like rules (*vanya-niyamas*): desire for another’s property; performing tasks for others; slandering others; following the ways of others; eating the food of others; stale food; onions; association with sinners; intimacy with other men; sexual intercourse with others; envy of others; intolerance of others’ excellence; proclaiming the faults of others; and contemplating what is undesirable for others.

Sleeping at dawn; approaching a woman who should not be approached; eating food that should not be eaten; what is declared forbidden by the scriptures; meat-based substances; false scriptures; lack of faith in the scriptures; falsehood; association with the wicked; evil conversation; meat; milk from a cow whose calf has died; food seen by a menstruating woman; cloth worn by a low-caste person; the greatness of the fruit of bathing in [impure] water mixed with molasses; the greatness of the fruit of bathing in [impure] water drunk by a dog; the consumption of intoxicants; and the sale of liquids—one should avoid these during the month of Kārttika. Thus ends the determination of what is to be done and what is to be avoided during the month of Kārttika.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Glory of Kārttikamāsa, in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the fifth [chapter], the Māgha-māhātmya, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.

Following the dialogue between Sūta and Lomahaṃsa, the Blessed One, having heard of the greatness of Māgadheśvara from Brahmādeva, describes the entire lineage of Manu, Raṃbha, and Kaṭa; he then describes the morning bath performed by the Gopīs at Māgadheśvara, the attainment of Kṛṣṇa by the Gopīs through the merit of that bath, and a detailed account of the ritual procedures for the morning bath, including the recitation of mantras such as the *Dīkṣāsukha* and others according to the rules, followed by a description of the supreme majesty of wearing the *tripuṇḍra* after the bath.

The procedure for wearing the *tripuṇḍra* mark made from clay originating from Dvāravatī, cow-dung, or earth from the feet of a virtuous person; a description of the procedure for wearing *gopīcandana* on the belly; the fruit of wearing the marks of the Lord’s incarnations upon one's own body; the statement regarding the attainment of the fruit of merit for one whose body is marked with the weapons of the Lord; the description of the eligibility for all rites for one whose body is consecrated by the eight-syllabled name of the Lord; and [the rules] for wearing the *sudarśana* discus-marked seal and the four-petaled lotus *sīmanta* garland.

Description of the *phalaka* (wooden plank); the greatness of wearing medicinal herbs, fruits, and *mātṛkā* beads; the greatness of wearing *tulasī* wood; description of the methods for installing, meditating upon, and worshipping the forms of the Lord; description of the sequential ritual procedure for the worship of the conch (*śaṅkha*) and other items accompanied by mantras; and the fruits resulting from the worship of the conch.

The description of the greatness of the *baṭa* tree; the fruit of worshipping the image of the Blessed One; the description of the efficacy of the *tulasī* plant and the merit of its worship; the subjects concerning the various classes of flowers born from the body of the Blessed One; the description of the flowers that smile at the Blessed One; the smiling of all flowers [at the Blessed One]; the greatness of offering fruits and flowers at the time of the worship of the Blessed One; and the honoring of Brahmins with gifts of food and other offerings along the path.

The majesty of the excellence of the *jāti* flower; the majesty of the ritual preparation consisting of the fruit of placing a garland adorned with a thousand *jāti* flowers upon the neck of Viṣṇu; and the majesty of remembering the names of the Blessed One by Māra.

(Description of the Greatness): Description of the meditation on the Blessed One and its greatness; description of the section concerning the instruction for hymns of praise to the Blessed One; the characteristics of the teacher and the disciple; description of the greatness of *tulasī*; the attainment of the fruit of giving all things by the gift of a *tulasī* leaf; description of the greatness of the worship of the Blessed One with *tulasī*; the hearing of the *Bhāgavata*; description of the fruit of composing and reciting the *Bhāgavata* text; description of the fruit of [recitation]; the greatness of the fruit of offering incense and lamps.

The majesty of the lamp endowed with a thousand virtues; the description of the majesty of Mathurā; the narration of the rules and procedures for the installation of the vessel, the food, and the new [images] according to the various branches of the scriptures. Thus ends the fifth section, the Majestic Glory of the Mārga-dīrgha-māsa, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.

Then follows the description of the greatness of the procedure for the offering of food (naivedya) to the Blessed One; the description of the fruits of circumambulation and other rites; the fruit of reciting the thousand names of Viṣṇu; the explanation of the reason for the Blessed One’s acquisition of the name Dāmodara; the greatness of partaking in the sacred water (tīrtha) and the prasāda; the conclusion of the ritual of worship, its formal completion (udyāpana), and the description of its fruits. This concludes the sixth section, on the Greatness of the Bhāgavata, within the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.

The narrative of King Vīrabāhu; the greatness of the single *adrīna* (*ekādrīṇa*) tree; Bharadvāja’s account of the consecration of Vajra and Parīkṣit upon the thrones of the kingdoms of Mathurā and Hastināpura during the course of a dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka; Bharadvāja’s narration of the events of Vīrabāhu’s previous birth, including the description of how Rudra, Brahmā, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and the Pāṇḍavas departed for their own abodes in a former life; and following the dialogue between Vajra Janābha and Parīkṣit—

The description of the events leading to Śāṇḍilya’s attainment of sovereignty in this life due to the merit born from his hospitality; his departure; Śāṇḍilya’s explanation of the etymological meaning of the word "Vraja" followed by a description of Kṛṣṇa’s sports there; the inquiry by Vīrabāhu regarding the cause of his attainment of the status of a *sūta* in a previous birth despite having killed a cow; and the account of how he obtained the vision of Uddhava through the acceptance of the *śrāddha* offered by the twice-born Devaśarman and his subsequent establishment of the kingdoms of Mathurā and other cities.

Having described the story of Cūta—who, despite having attained the status of a *sannyāsī*, incurred the fault of accepting the twelfth lunar day conjoined with the tenth—and having spoken thus, Śāṇḍilya returned to his own hermitage; [the text then describes] the arrival at Mathurā-maṇḍala during the sacrificial session of King Parīkṣit, the proclamation of the prohibition against the twelfth lunar day conjoined with the tenth, how [Cūta] remained in that state despite being a Brahmin due to virtuous deeds such as hospitality in a previous birth, and the establishment by King Parīkṣit and Vajra of a shrine for Govinda and Gopīlaṅkita.

The description of how the distress of the people of Mathurā was dispelled on all sides by the birth of Sanmati; the instruction that this very act constitutes the honoring of guests and so forth; the establishment of many *āma* (uncooked) ovens for the king; the unprecedented construction of wells, ponds, and other waterworks in Mathurā, as well as the installation of a *śivaliṅga*; the narration of the sequence of the concluding rites (*udyāpana*) for the Ekādaśī vow by Dvāja; and the exposition of the Akhaṇḍaikādaśī vow.

A description of the cow-pen established by Kṛṣṇa’s wife due to his absence; a description of the greatness of the vigil (jāgara) for the sake of hearing the qualities of the Lord; a description of the sequence of rituals such as giving gifts during the vigil; a description of the birth of a son on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī); and a description of the lifting of Govardhana Hill and the appearance of the Pārṣṇi, Śvitra, and others near Mount Govardhana. [This concludes] the description of the section concerning that.

The dialogue concerning Uddhava’s inquiry; the narration of the greatness of the Lord; the description of Kṛṣṇa’s childhood pastimes and so forth; the description of the greatness of the festival of the Fish incarnation (Matsyotsava), preceded by the prescription of the rules for bathing, giving gifts, worship, and other rites; the statement that by reciting the Bhāgavata text in one’s house, all desires and fruits are attained; the injunction regarding the recitation of mantras in such a house; the description of the prayers to be offered to the river at the time of bathing; [and] flowers for the Lord.

The description of the abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and so forth; the description of the attainment of liberation through hearing the Bhāgavata; the statement regarding the fruit of the worship of Śrī; and the description of the greatness of the gift of land in the form of a cow.

The results of hearing the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam* immediately; the description of the manner of worshipping the Lord—who is composed of the qualities of goodness (*sattva*), passion (*rajas*), and darkness (*tamas*)—as Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Deva (Indra), Śaṅkara (Śiva), Maheśvara, Īśvara, and others; the glorification of the instructions regarding the giving of gifts such as cows, land, gold, garments, beds, and ornaments; the description of the attainment of various states of existence resulting from these deeds; and the refutation of the notion that Śiva is characterized by the quality of darkness (*tamoguṇa*) through the acceptance of the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam*. These are the subjects of the chapters [of this work].

Parīkṣit, eager to hear the Bhāgavata, sent Uddhava as his messenger; having heard Uddhava’s words that he might hear the Bhāgavata from Śuka’s mouth, and by Uddhava’s command, Parīkṣit departed for the conquest of the quarters and to perform the horse sacrifice. The description of the singular nature of the Lord Śrīmad Bhāgavata; the glorification of listening to Śrīmad Bhāgavata; and the description of the attainment of the perfection of all goals immediately through listening to Śrīmad Bhāgavata. Thus ends the sixth [chapter], the Glorification of the Bhāgavata, in the Vaiṣṇava-khaṇḍa.

The greatness of giving rice mixed with ghee, sugar-cane juice, and the like; the items to be avoided by those observing the Vaiśākha vow; the evil consequences of performing the ritual at home; the fault of not undertaking the vow; bathing and giving gifts at the seven rivers, the Gaṅgā, natural ponds, and step-wells; the worship, offerings, and gifts dedicated to Madhusūdana; the explanation of the excellence of the month of Vaiśākha through its underlying causes; the description of the greatness of bathing in water during the month of Vaiśākha; and, regarding that subject, the story of King Hemāṅgada.

In the month of Vaiśākha, due to the gift of water, [Śrutadeva] attained birth in the womb of a lizard in the city of Mithilā; having reached that state as a lizard, he was liberated from there by Śrutadeva, his friend from Kāśī. Having heard of this wonder, the King of Mithilā was filled with astonishment and questioned him; Śrutadeva then related the greatness of the gift of water and other acts in the month of Vaiśākha, recounting therein the account of his own father. The narration of the history of Akutānaya, the sixth [incarnation]; the account of the birth of Kumāra by the Maithila sage Śrutakīrti; the praise of the Vaiśākha duties such as the giving of gifts in secret; the description of the Ayāvalya vow; the performance of the Vaiśākha duties by Jaikhānapada in the month of Vaiśākha; and the journey of Yama—distressed by the attainment of true joy by all people and the emptiness of the hells—to the presence of Brahmā.

The narration of Yama’s own suffering upon his birth; Brahmā’s consolation of Yama following an exposition on the greatness of Vaiśākha; nevertheless, Brahmā’s journey to the abode of Viṣṇu accompanied by the sorrowful Yama; Viṣṇu’s granting of boons to Yama; the praise of bathing in the *vairāja* (the confluence) for those who have transgressed the duties of the month of Vaiśākha; the praise of listening to the narrative of the greatness of Vaiśākha; and the story of the twice-born ones devoted to those rites and established in austerity.

The attainment of his own kingdom by Puru-yashas, the lord of Vaiśākha, through the practice of the Vaiśākha-dharma; then, on the third day of the bright fortnight, Viṣṇu’s creation of a son for Puru-yashas, and his attainment of the bliss of union (*sāyujya-mukti*) through the grace of Viṣṇu; and the commencement of the narration of the Vaiśākha-dharma, including the story of the twice-born named Śaṅkha in connection with the gift of sandals, wherein the twice-born named Śaṅkha narrates the Vaiśākha-dharma to a hunter.

The narration of the events concerning Dantīkhāko and Sūkta; the narration of the hunter’s previous birth; the demonstration of the equality of all beings through the example of a worm; the description of the greatness of the vital breath (prāṇa) and the exposition of the curse pronounced upon Kaṇva by the vital breath; the account of how the vital breath cursed Kaṇva, saying "Become a crow"; the explanation by the gods of the fruits of karma corresponding to the births of living beings; and the description of the hells.

The chapters and their subjects are as follows: the description of the rite for warding off evil; the description of the characteristics of a devotee of the Lord preceded by the description of the various types of dharma; the description of the religious observances (*dharma*) of the month of Vaiśākha; the liberation of a serpent through hearing the majesty of the month of Vaiśākha; the narration of that very serpent’s account from a previous birth; the dialogue between Śaṅkha and the hunter, including the narration of how the hunter attained the state of a boar in another life; the description of the greatness of the lunar days (*tithi*) occurring in the month of Vaiśākha; and the description of the *kaṅi* dharma.

The majesty of the Akṣayya-tṛtīyā; the majesty of the Vaiśākha-śukla-dvādaśī; stories of gods and brahmins residing in the Kādamīra region; a description of the majesty of the Vaiśākha-śukla-trayodaśī, caturdaśī, and the full-moon day; and a description of the fruit of hearing the majesty of Vaiśākha. ... The praise of the assembly of learned sages such as Vyāsa and others by Sūta; the description of the greatness of Ayodhyā, adorned with various trees, creepers, and lotuses, in the context of the dialogue between Sūta and Kauṇaka; the arrival of the sage Agastya at Ayodhyā; the description of the joy of Agastya upon beholding the power of Ayodhyā; the etymological derivation of the word "Ayodhyā" through the description of Ayodhyā as existing in a form beyond the three *guṇas*; and the account of Viṣṇurāma’s journey preceded by the dialogue between Agastya and Vyāsa regarding Ayodhyā.

The description of the means by which [the Lord] was brought back; the composition of a hymn to the Blessed One by Viṣṇurāma; the granting of a boon to Viṣṇuśarman by the Blessed One; at that very spot, the bringing of the flow of the river by the Blessed One with his own discus; the description of how that sacred ford became famous by the name Cakratīrtha; the installation of the Viṣṇuhari image by Viṣṇunāmapūravaika; and the description of the majesty of Viṣṇuhari.

(1) Brahmā’s arrival at Ayodhyā; (2) the performance of sacrifices after undertaking a pilgrimage and other rites; (3) the establishment of the Jahnu-khaṇḍa in his own name; (4) the description of the majesty of Brahma-khaṇḍa by the god Brahmā; (5) the majesty of the Pāpamocana-tīrtha situated on the bank of the Sarayū; (6) the description of the majesty of the Pāpamocana-tīrtha by Ṛtumañjña; (7) the majesty of the Sahasradhārā [tīrtha] by Agastya; (8) the contents of the fifty-six chapters; (9) the narration of the majesty of Svedāra-tīrtha by Agastya.

Following the completion of the sacrifice, the arrival of the sage Kautsa; the manifestation of his desire to depart for another place due to a lack of wealth after the sage Kautsa was astonished by the sacrificial materials brought for his own worship; Raghu’s departure with the intent to conquer Kubera in order to give wealth to Kautsa; the raining down of wealth by the umbrella-bearer out of fear of Raghu; and the description of Raghu giving all that wealth to Kautsa, [and] by Kautsa...

Description of the greatness of Dkītīrtha; description of the greatness of Sītākuṇḍa; when the gods were defeated by the asuras in the war between the gods and asuras, the performance of a hymn of praise to the Blessed One by the gods; the manifestation of the Blessed One upon hearing the hymn of praise to the gods; the arrival of the gods at Ayodhyā according to the words of the Blessed One; description of the fame of that sacred site under the name Gupharīti; the greatness of Gupta-harmya; the greatness of giving gifts at Cakrahariṣīṭha; and the greatness of bathing at the confluence of the Sarayū and Ghargharā rivers.

The auspicious invocation; the arrival of the Puranic sage Sūta at the assembly of the great seers, such as Śaunaka and others, who dwell in the Naibhiṣāraṇya forest; after the great seers, headed by Śaunaka, had offered him hospitality, their inquiry regarding the greatness of the sacred field and holy fords (*kṣetratīrtha-māhātmya*); Sūta’s commencement of the narration of the majesty of the sacred field of Śrī Rāmeśvara; and therein, first, the journey to the Setubandha constructed by Śrī Rāma on the southern ocean, the sight of the Setubandha, and the [vision of] Rāmasetu.

The majesty of the Narāmeśvara Liṅga; then, in connection with the account of Setubandhana, the narration of the events of the Rāmāyaṇa beginning with Śrī Rāmacandra’s departure for the Daṇḍaka forest by his father’s command, the abduction of Sītā, his alliance with Sugrīva, his journey to the seashore, and his meeting with Vibhīṣaṇa; then, following the consecration of Vibhīṣaṇa as the sovereign of all the Rākṣasas, the performance of mantras while lying upon a bed of *darbha* grass at Cakratīrtha along with the monkeys and others, in contemplation of the means to cross the great ocean.

For three nights, Rāma contemplated means to cross the ocean and waited while performing worship of the sea. Then, seeing the ocean's disregard in the form of the non-arrival of his own brother [Varuṇa] and other signs, Śrī Rāma made a vow to dry up the ocean. Terrified, the ocean sought refuge with Śrī Rāma and offered praise to him. Thereupon, Śrī Rāma, pleased by that praise, spoke for the purpose of crossing over on a bridge.

The request made by the Ocean for the construction of a bridge over himself; thereafter, the building of the bridge across the ocean by Śrī Rāma with the assistance of all the monkeys, through the monkey Nala, the son of Viśvakarman; the description of the Durbha-grass bed as being at the foundation of the bridge; and the description of the twenty-four sacred sites (tīrthas), beginning with Cakratīrtha, situated upon the bridge.

Then follows the narration of the account of the supreme siddhi at the Cakratīrtha known as Setumūga; there, on the bank of the Dharmapuṣkariṇī, the account of how the Lord Hara, pleased by the propitiation of Dharma performed by the great sage Gālava, granted a boon to Gālava and bestowed the favor of his own vehicle upon him; and further, the account of how the great sage Gālava, who was devoted to the worship of Hari, was seized by a certain Rākṣasa for devouring, but was saved by the discus Sudarśana sent forth by the Lord through the power of his hymn of praise. || 18 ||

Upon seeing the loss of his status as a Vasu caused by the curse of Vidhūma—who was tormented by the arrows of desire—Brahmā granted him a sin in the form of attaining human birth; likewise, he granted a boon to Aṭavusāyā in the form of her attaining human status. At the request of Vidhūma, Brahmā established the limit for the end of that curse. Then, on the surface of the earth, Vidhūmavasu was suddenly born as the son of King Sahasrānīka’s queen, named Sahasrānīka himself, while [the others] were born in the houses of his three attendants, who were his ministers, generals, and friends.

Having learned the circumstances regarding the end of his own curse from the words of Śakra, Sahasrānīka came to earth and married Mṛgāvatī. After the marriage to Mṛgāvatī, as Sahasrānīka was setting out for the city of Kauśāmbī, the Apsaras named Tirottamā—who had not been seen by him—delivered a curse based on her reflection upon Śakra’s words: "For fourteen years, you shall be separated from this wife of yours. While she was performing an immersion in the Kausumbha flower-lake for the fulfillment of her vow, she was carried off by a formidable bird born from the lineage of Suparṇa. There, upon the peak of Mount Udaya, Jamadagni consoled the bird-lady Śakuntalā, who was overcome with grief, and established her in his own hermitage. Then, when Śakuntalā gave birth there, Jamadagni performed the naming ceremony for her son as Udayana. Having bestowed the bracelet given by his mother, Udayana [fought] against King Rājarṣi.

Having been released, he assumed a human form and went with the *nāga* named Phina to Pātāla, where he performed his marriage with Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s daughter, Kinnarī, the sister of the *nāga* Kaṃvara, who had previously been cursed. From her, Lalitā was born; subsequently, due to a curse from Kinnarī, she became detached from worldly life. Then, having received the *tāmbūla-vīṭikā* (betel-roll) and the lute Ghoṣavatī from Kinnarī, Udayana returned to his mother at the hermitage of Jamadagni, near the hunter Śabara.

Seeing his own ring placed upon a crow, and hearing from a hunter that his father had been killed while attempting to retrieve the ring, he set out toward the hermitage of Jamadagni accompanied by his ministers and his army. Having obtained his wife Sṛgāvatī, his son Udayana, and his grandson from Jamadagni, he returned to his own city. Then, having entrusted the burden of the kingdom to his son named Udayana, he [lived] with his ministers Vasantaka, Rumaṇvat, and Yaugandharāyaṇa, as well as his sons-in-law and others.

To bring about his liberation, [the sage] went with the wife of Saragāvatī to Cakratīrtha situated on the shore of the southern ocean; there, by the mere act of bathing, his previous form was described as having been preceded by the cessation of the curse. Then, after all four of them had regained their former states, he took leave of Cakratīrtha and issued a command for his daughter to perform penance. By that command, she assumed the form of a peacock and went to the penance grove, where she performed severe austerities such as the practice of *pecābhisādhana*.

Then, by means of that asceticism, the sage Supārśva granted her boons: the attainment of sons in the forms of gods, conquerors of enemies, and humans; and having accepted those, he departed for his own abode. Subsequently, from that daughter of Diti, Mahiṣāsura was born. The bestowing of weapons produced from her own limbs; the Goddess, praised by the gods, mounting a lion and letting out a most terrifying roar for the sake of slaying the demon Mahiṣāsura; then the exceedingly fearsome battle between the gods and the armies of Mahiṣāsura; therein, the description of the Goddess’s slaughter of Mahiṣāsura’s forces in that battle; then, after the Goddess had slain the demon named Caṇḍakopa sent by Mahiṣāsura, [the encounter] with Mahiṣāsura himself who had arrived on the battlefield.

Thereafter, having returned to his own home while overcome with grief for his son, Govindasvāmin engaged in lamentation with his wife, along with his second son, named Aśokadatta.

Then, the king named Pratāpamukuṭa, being highly pleased by that gift, gave his own daughter named Madanadevī to Aśokadatta according to the marriage rites. Subsequently, having learned of Rēpēccha’s desire, Aśokadatta went to the cremation ground at night, taking with him a second anklet and human flesh; there, while he was summoning the spirits through mantras...

The arrival of the Rākṣasa woman named Vidyutkeśā, surrounded by other Rākṣasa maidens, to his presence out of a desire to consume flesh; then, the Rākṣasa woman Vidyutkeśā, highly pleased with him as her chosen suitor, gave her own daughter named Vidyutprabhā to the son of a Brahmin named Aśokadatta, preceded by the gift of one of her two jeweled anklets which remained on her foot; and furthermore, as a reward for the merit of giving his daughter to that very son-in-law, she bestowed upon him a golden tortoise.

Having taken all of that, he went into the presence of King Pratāpamukuṭa to inform him of Aśokadatta’s arrival; then Pratāpamukuṭa caused Aśokadatta to be executed. Later, on one occasion, when Aśokadatta was asked in private by Vidyutprabhā about the origin of the golden lotus she had given him, she related the account of the divine lake belonging to the Vetāla king named Kapālavisphoṭaka. Then, out of fear of Viṣṇu, she [instructed] Aśokadatta regarding the Kapālavisphoṭaka...

The journey toward the Vetāla-guarded Kāñcanaka-maṭa lake; there, having slain the bats that caused obstacles, Aśokadatta—desiring to kill the Vetāla named Kapālāsphoṭaka—was swallowed by a certain Vidyādhara named Viprakautuka who had ascended a celestial chariot. Immediately upon being swallowed by him, Aśokadatta attained the human form bestowed by the great Ṛṣi Gāṅgava.

[The syllables] Ū KA KA VA RA KA OṂ VKA [are the mantra]. Through this, there is liberation from curses, and the attainment of one's own true nature known as *sukaṇa*. Then, at the request of Vijayadatta, out of compassion for his father who had attained the state of a *vetāla*, he went with him to Cakratīrtha situated on the shore of the southern ocean and performed a ritual bath. By the mere touch of a drop of water from that holy site, the state of being a *vetāla* was removed from the *vetāla*, and he regained his status as the son of the twice-born named Vijayadatta. Then, by that Vijayadatta—

Furthermore, when [the rite] preceded by the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) has been performed, there is a description of his attainment of the status of a *vidyādhara* named Sudarśana, following the cessation of his human form; then, a description of how that sacred ford (*tīrtha*) became famous by the name Vetālakhavarada due to its connection with the state of being a *vetāla*; next, a description of the majesty of Gandhamādana situated on the southern ocean; the majesty of the Pāpavināśana-tīrtha located on Mount Gandhamādana; and therein, the narration of the account of the virtuous man named Dṛḍhamati.

Then, following the attachment to worldly objects (*sasaṅga*), there is a description of the dharma of the brave; the account of a Śūdra named Sumati, who, after performing rites such as sacrifices, animal offerings, and the construction of temples, practiced austerities while living according to the conduct of a sage; the instruction in Vedic rituals given to him by a Brahmin named Sumati; and the description of the various miserable births, beginning with hell, attained by that Brahmin Sumati due to the fault of instructing one unworthy of sacrifice; and then, after several subsequent births, his...

The Brahmin’s birth was defiled by his being seized by a *jāṅgharākṣasa*; consequently, he became excluded from Vedic rites. Then, having taken those leaves, he sought refuge with Agastya. Thereafter, by the instruction of Agastya, he was led to the *Pāpavināśana-tīrtha* situated on the shore of the Southern Ocean. Upon merely bathing there according to the prescribed ritual (*saṃkalpa*), he was liberated from the seizure of the *jāṅgharākṣasa*. Having attained all enjoyments and the fulfillment of his prior desires, he became intent upon the performance of the Vedic rites taught by him.

The account of the attainment of various births in the animal realm preceded by the terror of hell for the one named Dṛḍhamati; then, upon his gradual attainment of human birth, the drinking of the water at the holy ford (tīrtha) called Pāpavināśana located on Mount Gandhamādana in the Southern Ocean, resulting in his attainment of heaven; a description of the power of the Pāpavināśana tīrtha; then, a description of the majesty of the Sītāsaras tīrtha; and in connection with that, a narration of the story of Indra’s liberation from the sin of Brahman-slaughter while he was there with his army.

The battle between the Rākṣasa named Kapālābharaṇa and the gods headed by Śakra; the slaying of the Rākṣasa Kapālābharaṇa by Śakra in that battle; the affliction of Śakra by the sin of Brahman-murder arising from that killing; and, in the context of describing the cause for the Rākṣasa Kapālābharaṇa’s attainment of Brāhmaṇahood—how, at the command of her husband, the Nivātakavaca Rākṣasa’s wife, Suśīlā by name, produced a son through a Brāhmaṇa named Śuci, thereby resulting in Kapālābharaṇa’s [attainment of Brāhmaṇahood].

The account of the birth of Jāhmaṇavīya; then, the description of how Śakra, afflicted by the sin of killing a Brahmin, was liberated from that Brahman-slaughter through the instruction of Brahmā by means of digging a pond at Sītākuṇḍa on Mount Gandhamādana in the southern ocean, performing sacrifices, and propitiating Sadāśiva. Then follows the description of the Sītāsaras and other lakes, and subsequently, the description of the greatness of the holy site named Maṅgala.

In connection with that, there is the account of King Manojava, who was possessed of egoism. Due to the sin arising from taking the hand [in marriage] from Brahmins, he was seized by a disease called *gāra* produced by that [sin]. Following the seizure of his kingdom, he was subsequently exiled from his realm. Then, together with his wife and son, Manojava went to the forest. There, seeing his son afflicted by hunger, Manojava, overcome with grief and intense remorse, fell into a swoon.

The lamentation of his wife, named Sumitrā, and the weeping of their son; then, at that moment, the arrival of the great sage Parāśara near them; by Parāśara’s sprinkling of water purified by mantras upon the king’s head, the removal of his mental delusion; and thereafter, at the king’s request, the sage Parāśara imparting the instruction of the single-syllable Rāma-mantra, preceded by an explanation of the means for the pilgrimage to the sacred site named Maṅgala situated on the Śrīrāma-setu.

At the command of the Sage, King Manojava went with his wife and son to Maṅgalīya and performed the practice of mantra-worship for forty days. Then, before King Manojava, there appeared from the third [object] named Maṅgala a chariot equipped with a bow, two quivers, a sword, a shield, a mace, a spear, a conch, and a banner, along with its charioteer, flags, golden armor, and all royal ornaments and implements. Thereafter, Manojava offered all those objects to the sage Parāśara. Now...

The consecration of King Manojava by the sage Parāśara through mantras; the bestowal of the Brahmāstra weapon preceded by the granting of boons; then, King Manojava’s return to his own city, his destruction of King Golabha at the command of Brahmā, and his subsequent governance of his kingdom with righteousness; finally, the description of King Manojava’s attainment of the realm of Śiva after reaching the Maṅgala-tīrtha and performing austerities; and then, the description of the Kṣatriya named Ekāntarāmanātha.

Therein is the majesty of the Ārtavāpikā Tīrtha; in connection with that, the account of the younger brother of Agastya is described; the performance of penance by Agastya’s younger brother on the Himavat mountain; the offering of praise to Śiva by Agastya’s younger brother when Śiva was pleased by that penance; and then, at the word of the pleased Śiva, Agastya’s younger brother performed his ablutions in the various Tīrthas located in the secluded forest on Mount Gandhamādana in the southern ocean.

Through the practice of *samādhi*, he attained liberation; because of his immortality, that sacred site (*tīrtha*) became renowned by the name Amṛtavāpī. Then, at the time of his end, King Danumalla approached Khaṇḍa and performed penance under the guidance of his friend; thereafter follows a description of him. Next, in the context of explaining the cause for the fame of the Ekāntarāmanātha shrine, there is an account of Śrī Rāmacandra’s ascent to the realm of Vaiḍūrya (Vaikuṇṭha) due to his curse, and how his son Sucandra performed the funeral rites for his father. [The text continues with] Sucandra and others...
