A description of the events concerning the constant dwelling in solitude and the contemplation of the means for crossing the ocean; a description of the enjoyment of sovereignty by all the princes, preceded by their devotion to Rāma; and the greatness of the Hanumatkuṇḍa.

The greatness of the *ra* syllable; then the description of the greatness of Gandhamādana situated on the Southern Ocean and of the Brahma-kuṇḍa; in connection with that, the greatness of wearing the *tripuṇḍra* mark with the ashes found at Brahma-kuṇḍa; the account of the origin of Brahma-kuṇḍa; and therein, when a dispute arose between Jādyaviṣṇu and Medhyaviṣṇu regarding the matter of the *śaraṣṭhaya*, the manifestation of the Lord’s eternal *liṅga* between them, for the purpose of drying up [the area] from its source down to its end.

Brahmā and Viṣṇu set out, assuming forms of inferior size in order to find the base and the top of the Liṅga. Viṣṇu, having returned after failing to see the lower limit of the Liṅga, spoke the truth regarding its base. Brahmā, however, having returned after failing to see the upper limit, deceitfully spoke a falsehood regarding the top of the Liṅga. Then, Śaṅkara, enraged by that false speech, emerged from the middle of the Liṅga.

The bestowal of a curse upon Brahmā in the form of his becoming unworthy of worship; then, by Śaṅkara, who was pleased with that [praise], the command for Brahmā to perform a sacrifice on Mount Gandhamādana—situated to the south—for the sake of pacifying the fault of malice; by the command of Śaṅkara, Brahmā’s performance of the sacrifice on Mount Gandhamādana with the favor of Śiva; and there, by Śiva, who was well-pleased, the granting of a boon to Brahmā in the form of his being worthy of worship through the *Śrautasmārta* rites, preceded by the granting of a boon to the holy ford named Brahmakuṇḍa.

The gift [of the land], the majesty of Badmakuṇḍa, and then the description of the majesty of Hanumānchuṇḍa; in connection with that, the account of the life of the king named Dharmasakha; the incident of the scorpion sting of Sucandra, the son of King Dharmasakha; and then, by the king named Dharmasakha, who desired to have many sons, having performed the sacrificial rites according to his own words, together with his wives, his attendants, and the officiating priests.

The departure toward Mount Mūṇḍa on the Daśārṇa river, situated near the Gandhamādana mountain; bathing there and performing the *putrīyeṣṭi* sacrifice; having offered oblations and gifts such as garments and ornaments to the Brahmins; performing an ablution with his wife and returning toward his own city; there, by the power of Hanumān and Mūṇḍa, the birth of a hundred sons to that king’s hundred wives; and finally, a description of the greatness of the Agastyatīrtha.

In connection with that laughter, there is the description of the deeds of Kakṣīvān, the son of the sage Dīrghatamas. Therein, while staying at the hermitage of his teacher named Udaṅka, Kakṣīvān practiced the study of the sciences for sixty years; however, when he sought permission from the guru to return home, the guru did not grant it. Subsequently, Aruṇā described a means for his marriage. By the command of Śacī, Kakṣīvān went to the hermitage of Agastya, and having bathed in that sacred ford, he mounted a young, white, and magnificent lordly elephant that had emerged from the water, and proceeded along the path.

He went toward that city together with King Svanaya; then, at the request of King Svanaya to bestow his own daughter upon Kakṣīvat, he sent a message through the priest named Sudarśana, who was deeply distressed by that [request], and having invited him with due honors, brought him back to his own city. Thereupon, Kakṣīvat offered salutations to his father Dīrghatamas and reported the account of his studies in the sciences. Then, at that sacred ford of Agastya, by King Svanaya...

The honoring of the sage Dīrghatamas. In the meantime, a multitude of rivers arrived at that place to visit the Agastya-tīrtha; King Svanaya, through a conversation with Udaṅka and Dīrghatamas, was informed of the matter by his minister. Then, with the consent of Udaṅka, King Svanaya gave his daughter to Kakṣīvat. Subsequently, King Svanaya had the maiden brought from the city of Madhurā by his attendants and performed the giving of the bride to Kakṣīvat according to the rites of marriage.

Then follows the description of the gift of gold, cows, female slaves, villages, and other such gifts, including those for the marriage of the twice-born; the return of King Svarṇadīpta to his own hermitage in Vedāraṇya together with his son and daughter-in-law after taking leave of the sage; King Svanaya’s journey back to his own city after bathing at the Agasti-tīrtha along with the women of the inner apartments; the majesty of the Agasti-tīrtha; and then the description of the majesty of the holy site known as Rāmakuṇḍa, followed by an account of the history of the sages Sutīkṣṇa and Agastya’s disciple in connection with that.

The contents are as follows: the description of the performance of penance by Sutīkṣṇa on the bank of Rāmacandrasaras while practicing austerities; the description of the greatness of Rāmakuṇḍa through the account of the perfection of Sutīkṣṇa’s penance while he was thus performing his austerities; the description of the greatness of the Śiva-liṅga installed by Rāma on the shore of Rāmakuṇḍa; and, in connection with that, the narration of the story of Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, regarding the removal of the fault of speaking untruthfully, [including] how, in the Bhārata war, he sought to defeat Droṇa.

The spread of the false report that Aśvatthāman had been killed in battle by Bhīmasena; Droṇa’s hearing that same report from Yudhiṣṭhira and, believing it to be true, his renunciation of life through yoga; at that moment, Yudhiṣṭhira—who always speaks the truth—incurs the sin born of uttering a falsehood; and subsequently, at the time of his royal consecration following the conclusion of the war, [the occurrence of] a deceptive voice from the sky.

The statement that Yudhiṣṭhira was unfit for the royal consecration due to the sin incurred by speaking a falsehood; Yudhiṣṭhira’s subsequent expression of remorse; at that moment, the arrival of the great sage Vyāsa, who instructed Yudhiṣṭhira on the practice of bathing at Rāmatīrtha located on the shore of the southern ocean; and thereafter, Yudhiṣṭhira’s installation of his younger brother Sahadeva upon the throne, and his departure toward Rāmasetu accompanied by the preceptor Dhauṃya and his own younger brothers, Bhīma and the others.

Without mounting a vehicle, having reached Rāmatīrtha according to the prescribed ritual for pilgrimage, he performed his ablutions by the path instructed by the family priest; there, through the power of bathing at Rāmatīrtha, giving gifts, performing śrāddha rites, and observing month-long fasts, a celestial voice described Yudhiṣṭhira’s purification from the sin born of speaking untruth, followed by his fitness for ascending the throne.

The majesty of the sacred ford known as Rāmakuṇḍa; then, the description of the majesty of Lakṣmaṇatīrtha; in connection with that, the account of Balabhadra’s liberation from the sin of Brahmin-slaughter; therein, the departure of Balabhadra for the great assembly in the forest of Māhiṣmatī during his pilgrimage, as he was unwilling to witness the slaughter of the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas; and there, [the incident] of Sūta, who was seated upon the Brahmā-throne to recount the Purāṇas, being struck by a blade of *kuśa* grass unintentionally uprooted by Balabhadra’s own hand.

The attainment of the sin of killing a Brahmin from the slaughter; then, at the word of the sages, out of a desire to perform penance for the sake of the world’s welfare, he approached the sages; by the sages, for the sake of the welfare of the world, the slaying of the Rākṣasa named Bāṣkala was performed, and the description of the penance consisting of a pilgrimage to holy places (tīrtha-yātrā) up to the point of death; then the slaying of the Rākṣasa named Bāṣkala by Balabhadra; thereafter, for the duration of a year, performing pilgrimages preceded by ritual bathing in all the holy places situated on the surface of the earth; even though [the pilgrimage] had been performed...

The subjects of the chapters concerning the pilgrimage to the holy ford (tīrthayātrā) and the mission to the earth (jmadūtyā): by means of a verse, it is described how, having gone to the holy fords on Mount Gandhamādana situated by the southern ocean, through the mere act of bathing at those fords of Rāma, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin (brahmahatyā) by the grace of Rāmeśvara and Aṅgadaśona.

The glorification of the greatness of Ladamana-tīrtha; then, the description of the majesty of Jaṭā-tīrtha; in that context, as an incidental narrative, the account of the life of Uka-ācārya; and thereupon, when Śuka asked Vyāsa for a means to attain purity of mind, Vyāsa’s narration of the ancient history of Aghora-varuṇa, preceded by which is the description of the greatness of Jaṭā-tīrtha located at Rāmasetu.

Then, after Vyāsa imparted instruction to Śuka, there follows a description of the purification of the mind through mere knowledge upon reaching Jaṭātīrtha, followed by the glorification of Jaṭātīrtha. Next is the description of the majesty of Lakṣmītīrtha, and in that context, the narration of the story of Yudhiṣṭhira. While Yudhiṣṭhira was staying at Indraprastha, he posed a question to Śrī Kṛṣṇa regarding the dharma that leads to one's own abode; in response, Śrī Kṛṣṇa [expounded] to Yudhiṣṭhira by means of numerous ancient histories.

The narration of the majesty of the Lakṣmītīrtha at Gandhamādana; then, Yudhiṣṭhira, having gone to Lakṣmītīrtha and performed ritual bathing for a month according to prescribed rules, returned to his own city. Thereupon, having attained unsurpassed prosperity and sovereign power through that very [merit], he undertook with great effort and the assistance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa the performance of the Rājasūya sacrifice.

The majesty of Lakṣmītīrtha; then the description of the majesty of Abhitīrtha; and in connection with that, the narration of the account of Sītā’s purification. Therein, after Rāmacandra had slain Rāvaṇa at Laṅkā, he returned to Gandhamādana along the path of the bridge together with Indra and the other gods. Having stayed on the bank of Lakṣmītīrtha, he caused the summoning of Anala for the purpose of purifying Jānakī. Then, having arrived there, Agni declared before Rāma that Sītā was pure. Following the words of Agni, by Rāmacandra—

The acceptance of Jānakī; the establishment of the place where the food emerged as being famous by the name Ananitīrtha; and in the context of the majesty of Abhitīrtha, the narration of the life of a merchant chief named Paḍuma, wherein, after the king observed the wicked deed of his sixth son among the eight sons of Paḍumanta—named Duṣpaṇya—who had killed a village hunter, he banished him from the country; and thereafter, even though he had departed for the forest...

When Tenograśva had been killed after being submerged in the Jaṭhara [lake] by the sage Salyubharasvas, the sage offered a curse to Duṣpaṇya, saying, "The submersion of Jaṭhara shall result in your death. Then, when excessive rain occurred at the time of the monsoon, Duṣpaṇya caused the corpse of a dead elephant to enter the middle of the Jaṭhara; that elephant's body was then carried away toward the ocean by a great torrent of floodwaters.

After his death, he entered the realm of the wicked *duṣpaṇya*; immediately thereafter, he attained the state of a *piśāca*. Then, assuming the form of a *piśāca*, he approached the vicinity of Agastya’s hermitage and cried out loudly for the great sages to provide him with water for his liberation. Subsequently, for the sake of his release, the great sage Agastya commanded his disciple named Sutīkṣṇa, at his direction, to perform a ritual bath in the Abhaya-tīrtha. By Sutīkṣṇa, for the purpose of the *piśāca*’s liberation—

After bathing at Bhṛtīrtha, the merchant Piśāca, having been liberated from his state as a ghost, ascended a divine celestial chariot (*vimāna*), paid homage to the great sages, and departed for the divine realm; [this concludes] the majesty of Bhṛtīrtha. Next follows the description of the majesty of Cakratīrtha, including an account of the worship of the Sudarśana [discus] performed by a Brāhmaṇa named Ādirudra in connection with that [site], and the destruction of the Rākṣasas who were obstructing that Brāhmaṇa’s penance by means of the Sudarśana discus; [and finally] the majesty of the Tīrtha due to the presence of the Sudarśana discus.

The renown of [this place] as Cakratīrtha; by the command of Lord Brahmā, the gods performing a Māheśvara sacrifice in the vicinity of Cakratīrtha out of fear of the Rākṣasas; the narration of the account of how the god Savitṛ, whose hand was severed at the joint of the thumb during that sacrifice, attained golden hands merely by bathing in Cakratīrtha upon the word of the sage Aṣṭāvakra; the majesty of Cakratīrtha; then the description of the majesty of Svargatīrtha, along with its associated context.

The narration of the account of Kāṣṭhabherī and Bala; therein, when a dispute arose between Brahmā and Viṣṇu regarding their mutual superiority, and although the superiority of Śiva was proclaimed by means of the *praṇava*, because Brahmā and Viṣṇu persisted in their stubbornness and did not acknowledge the superiority of Śiva, Śiva manifested his own form consisting of fire and light. When Maheśvara spoke with arrogance toward Brahmā, despite Brahmā’s lack of respect for him, Maheśvara then addressed Brahmā.

The quest for the person named Kālabhairava; the slaying of Brahmā by Kālabhairava in battle, preceded by the severing of Brahmā’s fifth head; thereafter, the suturing of Brahmā’s wound by the Blessed Lord Maheśvara; the offering of praise to the Blessed Lord Śaṅkara by the god Brahmā; the granting of fearlessness to Brahmā by Śiva; and then, by the command of Śiva, Kālabhairava holding the head of Brahmā in his hand in order to purify himself of the fault of Brahman-slaughter.

By performing a pilgrimage to all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) throughout the year and gaining knowledge of the Śiva-tīrtha located at Gandhamādana on the shore of the southern ocean, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). Furthermore, because Kāraṃbhava established a skull (*kapāla*) at that very spot, that Śiva-tīrtha is designated as Kapāra-tīrtha. [The following are] the chapters and topics concerning the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the Śiva-tīrtha: now follows the description of the majesty of Śaṅkha-tīrtha; that sacred ford was established by the sage Śaṅkha after he had performed austerities (*tapas*).

The renown of Śaṅkhatīrtha arises in connection with the greatness of that sacred site; within it is the story of the Brahmin named Vatsanābha, who remained there intent on performing penance. While he was staying there, an anthill grew over him, and when he was being harassed by the falling rain which disturbed his austerities, the Lord Dharmadeva assumed the form of a great bull, stood upon the anthill, caught the torrents of rain upon his own horns, and thus protected the sage. Now, [the story continues...]

When Vatsanābha withdrew from his meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he realized that Dhruvadeva—who was standing near him in the form of a buffalo—had not been worshipped. Determining that he must once again fix his mind in *samādhi*, he made an effort to cast himself down from the peak of Mount Meru in order to abandon his life and atone for the fault of his failure to show hospitality. At that moment, Dhruvadeva abandoned his buffalo form and appeared in his own true form to prevent the Brahmin Vatsanābha from attempting to die.

The description of the performance of instruction at Śaṅkhatīrtha on the shore of the southern ocean for the purification of the mind, preceded by the removal of the fault of ingratitude; the attainment of the state of Brahman by the twice-born Vatsanābha through the instruction of Dharma following the removal of the fault of ingratitude merely by bathing at Śaṅkhatīrtha; and the majesty of Śaṅkhatīrtha.

The description of Bhārgava: Therein, while a certain blind sage—who was lame from birth and possessed of a companion—was performing intense austerities for many years on Mount Gandhamādana situated in the eastern ocean, a disease arose in his foot. Then, desiring to perform ablutions at the triad of sacred fords known as Yamunā, Gaṅgā, and Gayā, he invoked that triad of holy sites through meditation preceded by the recitation of mantras; and upon its mere invocation, the triad of holy sites named Yamunā, Gaṅgā, and Gayā appeared before him. There, by the command of the great sage, [the river]...

The three sacred fords (tīrtha) were always present there. On one occasion, at the time of midnight, while King Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa was seated near his window, certain great sages arrived in the form of swans to attend upon him. Among those sages, one sage in the form of a swan, having praised the greatness of Raikva behind Jānaśruti’s back—since the latter was unaware of it—departed for the world of Brahmā along with all the others. After they had gone, [the king...]

The departure of King Jānaśruti toward the great seers to seek the restoration of his lost wealth; then the description of the supreme majesty of the triad of sacred fords known as Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Gayā; and, in connection with that, the account of King Jānaśruti’s life. 21.

Then, by the command of King Raikva, the Piṣayas, accompanied by their wives, performed ablutions at the three sacred fords (tīrthas) known as Yamunā, Gaṅgā, and Gayā. Following the purification of their thoughts, there is a description of how they attained the state of Brahman through the grace of the knowledge imparted by King Jānaśruti. Next is the description of the majesty of Koṭitīrtha, followed by a description of the life of Śrī Rāmacandra in connection with that place, including the conduct of Śrī Rāma there and the greatness of Koṭitīrtha, as well as the removal of the sin of brahmin-slaughter incurred by the slaying of Rāvaṇa.

On the Gandhamādana mountain situated to the south, having installed the Śiva-liṅga known as Rāmanātha, [the Lord] praised the Gaṅgā for its ablution; then, piercing the earth with his own arrow-tip (Dhanuṣkoṭi), the account of how he brought the Gaṅgā from the netherworld (Rasātala) is described. Thereafter, that holy site became renowned as Koṭitīrtha. In connection with the greatness of Koṭitīrtha, the life story of Kṛṣṇa is narrated, including the departure of Vasudeva for his own city by chariot after the marriage there.

As he stood on the path, the charioteer Kasa addressed him in harsh words; however, Vasudeva, having pledged to provide protection for his sister-in-law Devakī—who was about to be slain by Kaṃsa—refrained from killing him after first offering consolation. Then, following the transfer of the unborn Ananta from Devakī, the wife of Vasudeva, into Rohiṇī by means of Yogamāyā, the birth of the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa occurred, and Vasudeva offered hymns of praise to the Lord.

By the command of the Blessed One, Vasudeva led Śrī Kṛṣṇa to Gokula and brought the daughter of Yaśodā to Mathurā. Then, while Kaṃsa was attempting to strike her against a stone slab out of fear for his own life, that primordial Māyā slipped from his hands and departed in a beautiful, divine form. Addressing Kaṃsa, the Goddess said, "Your death shall come from whomever or wherever you least expect," and she vanished. Subsequently, worship was established for her in various locations. [This concerns] those two residing in Gokula...

A description of the wrestling match between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rāma; then, having gone toward Mathurā and slain Kaṃsa, the consecration of Ugrasena to the kingdom; then, on one occasion, when Nārada and others arrived to see him, Śrī Kṛṣṇa performed an expiation (prāyaścitta) for the sake of removing the fault incurred by the killing of his mother; thereafter, following the words of Nārada and the others, Balarāma came and, merely by bathing at Koṭitīrtha, Śrī Kṛṣṇa became free from the taint arising from the killing of his mother. Now...

A description of the greatness of Sādhyārṛta-tīrtha; in connection with that, a narration of the history of King Purūravas, including his union there with the Apsaras Urvaśī; then, after a lapse of time, due to the violation of their agreement, upon their separation, the account of his meeting with Urvaśī at the confluence of the rivers at Kurukṣetra, preceded by the attainment of a son, and the resulting consolation; and thereafter, following one year, [the account] of the king at Kurukṣetra—

Furthermore, there was a reunion with Urvaśī at the lotus-lake of Tarā; the acceptance by Purūravas of his son Āyu, born from himself through the seed of Urvaśī; the depositing of the seed of Pañcacūḍā within that Urvaśī through a single night's union; then, indicated by that [sign], Purūravas’s making of a request to the Gandharvas for the continuous attainment of Urvaśī’s world; and by them, having granted him the Abhiṣṭhāṭī [dance] to that Purūravas.

For the sake of performing sacrifices, he established a fire-altar; dissatisfied with the mere enjoyment of celestial pleasures, he resolved to return to the forest. Having entrusted the fire-altar to the care of the Apsarases at the place where it was deposited, a *aśvattha* tree grew there. Then, having fashioned a lower fire-drill (*araṇi*) from four branches of that *aśvattha* tree and producing the sacred fire by friction, he performed many sacrifices and, upon reaching the world of the Gandharvas, enjoyed himself with Urvaśī. Now...

Once, during a dramatic performance before Śakra, Urvashī and Purūravas looked at each other and laughed; thereupon, the sage named Durvāsas pronounced a curse upon them, saying, "A separation from one another shall befall you both. Then Purūravas, having entreated Śakra and being told by him [how to end the curse], went to the surface of the earth with the desire to perform penance. Upon merely bathing at the holy site called Amṛta on Mount Gandhamādana situated in the southern ocean, he was released from the curse and returned again to the world of Urvashī out of love for her.

The description of sporting together; the majesty of the Sādhyāmṛta-tīrtha; then the description of the greatness of all the holy fords (tīrthas). In connection with that, the narrative of the Brahmin named Sucarita: how the Brahmin Sucarita, being afflicted by old age and rendered incapable, came to the Gandhamādana mountain in the southern region out of a desire to bathe in all the holy fords, received initiation from Śiva, and performed penance; and upon the manifestation of Śaṅkara through that penance, [the account] of the Brahmin named Sucarita.

Śrī performed the hymn of praise to Śiva. Then, in order to fulfill the virtuous conduct of Su-carita, Śrī summoned all the sacred fords (tīrthas) to the vicinity of Su-carita and, by bringing them together in one place, created a confluence of all sacred fords. Having immersed Su-carita in this single bathing-place of all the sacred fords, she issued the command for him to attain perfect knowledge. Thereupon, the sage Su-carita [attained] Śiva... [the rest of the text is illegible].

The sacred sites (*viṣaya*): the performance of bathing at *Savatī*; the account of how the Brahmin named Sucārata attained freedom from old age and regained his youth, beauty, and so forth through the performance of bathing at *Savatī*, as well as a description of the majesty of the sacred site called *Savatī*; and, in connection with the majesty of the *Dhanuṣkoṭi* sacred site, the description of how Śrī Rāmacandra, at the request of Vibhīṣaṇa, drew a line upon this [site] with his bow so that the other worlds might come to *Ṭaṅkā*, thereby describing the breaking of his own bridge at the *Dhanuṣkoṭi* sacred site. *Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrthe*.

Description of the presence of all the deities; description of the greatness of bathing at Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha during the month of Māgha and other times. [Chapter VI, Part 3] Now, in connection with the greatness of Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha, follows the description of the life of Aśvatthāman: there, having made a vow to slay the Pāṇḍavas and all the brave heroes stationed at the camp, he approached the gate of the enemy’s army at night along with Kṛtavarman and Kṛpa, and having propitiated Mahādeva, obtained from him, who was pleased, a sword of victory.

Having first entered the enemy camp where the food was being cooked by the cooks, he first slew Bhūriśravas; thereafter, he carried out the slaughter of the entire army, including all those within the camp such as Draupadī’s sons and others, and killed the troops who had emerged from the camp gates by means of Kṛtavarman and Karṇa.

Then, having emerged from the camp, Aśvatthāman and the others fled individually on chariots and with maces; subsequently, when Aśvatthāman had entered the midst of the great sages on the banks of the Narmadā, he was declared fallen by the Brahmins, whereupon he departed in shame and undertook a pilgrimage to sacred fords. Then, seeking refuge with Vyāsa residing at Badarikāśrama, he reached Rāmasetu after being instructed by Vyāsa to pacify the sin of killing a Brahmin.

The performance of service to Lord Rāmanātha Śiva at the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha preceded by bathing; then, the offering of praise to the Sun who appeared there; thereafter, the granting of boons by the gratified Mahādeva at that very spot; the majesty of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha; and then, in the course of describing the majesty of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha once more, the detailed account of King Nandana, the son of King Dharmapra, who belonged to the Lunar Dynasty (Somavaṃśa); and while he had departed for the forest to perform penance there at Nanda.

While King Amipittadharma-gupta was once engaged in a hunt and had entered the forest, he climbed a tree at night out of fear of lions and other wild beasts. There, a certain woodcutter, who had been struck by lightning, approached him seeking to protect his own life. Then follows the description of the Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha, beginning with its origin; the power of the Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha in destroying various kinds of sins; the arrival of the king near the tree where [the woodcutter] was; and thereafter their mutual conversation.

Having first established conversation and cultivated mutual trust, the king and the tiger alternately arranged their sleep and wakefulness by dividing the night into two watches. Then, while the king was asleep, the tiger said to him, "I shall set you down near the lion," but even though he said this, because of his commitment to the duty of trust, the king did not allow himself to be set down near the tiger; instead, he spoke to the tiger of the transformation that would result from betraying a friend. Thereupon, when the tiger was enraged at that, the king remained firm.

While Siṃha was present, he caused the king to fall humbly before him; at that moment, having mounted the king’s foot once more with his own claw-like foot, and having declared himself to be a sage named Dhyānakāṣṭha, he explained that he had assumed the form of a ṛṣi out of desire, and bestowed upon the king the curse, "Become insane! He then related the past account of how Gautama had attained the state of a lion through the power of a cow.

Upon hearing the words of the sage Dhyānakāṣṭha, the lion immediately ascended a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) that had assumed a form identical to his own and departed for the realm of the Yakṣas; thereafter, the sage Dhyānakāṣṭha, having assumed the form of a Ṛṣi at his own will, proceeded toward another forest by his own desire; following the departure of the sage Dhyānakāṣṭha, Dharmagupta fell into a state of madness and subsequently returned to his own city; then, seeing him thus maddened, [he... of Dharmagupta...

The bringing of that Dharmagupta, who resided at Tīranivāsa, into the presence of King Nanda; then, for the sake of ending the fault of his son’s insanity, King Nanda’s commissioning of the great sage Jaimini; thereafter, by the command of the great sage Jaimini, King Nanda took the sacred texts (dharmān) upon a leaf, went to the holy site of Dhanuṣkoṭi situated at Rāmasetu, and performed a ritual bath; and through the power of bathing at the Dhanuṣkoṭi tīrtha, the cessation of Dharmagupta’s madness.

Then follows the account of Nanda’s penance and his subsequent journey back to the penance grove; the story of Rāmanātha, protected by Dharma, returning to his own city with his ministers after performing a great worship preceded by the distribution of vast wealth; the majesty of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha; and further, in connection with the majesty of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha, the description of how Parāvasu was liberated from the sin of Brahmin-slaughter through the grace of a certain Brāhmaṇa.

In that regard, while Raibhya and the two sons of the great sage Mahāviśvāmitra—named Reva and Parāvasu—were engaged in the sacrificial rites (*adhvarakarma*), Parāvasu returned to his own hermitage at the conclusion of the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) of the sacrifice in order to inspect the performance of the domestic duties. At that time, the middle son, having donned the skin of a black antelope (*kṛṣṇājina*), was wandering about at night; he was killed by Parāvasu with a stone (*śilā*). Then, Parāvasu approached his father and said, "This is your very own [son]."

Having seen the great *roka* (meteor) struck down by himself, and having completed the funeral rites for his father, he joined the sacrificial session (*sattra*) of Sṛṣati. There, he reported to his younger brother Arvāvasu the circumstances of his father’s killing and so forth. Then, commanding his younger brother to perform the penance (*prāyaścitta*) for the removal of the sin of patricide, Parāvasu himself performed the sacrificial rites at the session of King Bṛhadasva. Subsequently, Arvāvasu remained for twelve years for the removal of the sin of Brahman-slaughter.

Having performed a vow preceded by atonement (*prāyaścitta*), when the sacrificial session (*satra*) had commenced, Parāvasu, his elder brother, falsely attributed the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) to his younger brother Arvāvasu and forcibly expelled him from the sacrificial hall of King Bṛhaduktha. Thereupon, the innocent Arvāvasu, having no other recourse, departed from the sacrifice and went to the forest to perform penance. The Sun-god (*Āditya*), pleased by that penance—

Arvāvasu’s request for a boon from the gods in the form of the restoration of his own father to life, and his request for a boon in the form of the removal of the sin of Brahmin-slaughter from his elder brother; then, having adopted the means prescribed by the gods, Arvāvasu, the younger brother, took Parāvasu, the elder brother, to the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha located on the southern ocean for the sake of removing the sin of Brahmin-slaughter from Parāvasu, and by the power of that bath, the sin of Brahmin-slaughter from Parāvasu’s father was removed. Then...

The rising of Raibhya from his seat upon the arrival of Avīci and Supārāvasu at their own home; the greatness of the power of Dhanuṣkoṭi as the destroyer of all defects such as the sin of killing a Brahmin; then, in connection with the majesty of Pundranuṣkoṭi, the description of the dialogue between a jackal and a monkey, wherein two creatures—one a jackal and the other a monkey—who both remembered their former births, recounted to one another the accounts of the deeds performed in their previous lives during their mutual conversation. This [is] their mutual...

While the bird and the monkey were conversing, the sage named Sindhudvīpa arrived nearby. Then, when the great sage Sindhudvīpa was questioned by the bird and the monkey regarding their own means of deliverance, he related the account of the salvation of a certain Brahmin named Sumati, who associated with Kirātas and drank liquor, beginning with his instruction on the Dhanuṣkoṭi pilgrimage site. In that regard, the son of the twice-born Yajñadeva, named Sumati, lived in Mahārāṣṭra; out of a lustful desire for association with Kirāta women, he sought to acquire wealth.

Through the murder of a certain Brāhmaṇa by the hand of Rābaratta for the sake of theft, he incurred the sin of *brahmahatyā* (the killing of a Brāhmaṇa). Then, having fled from that terrible *brahmahatyā*, he wandered through the entire earth and returned to his own village, seeking refuge near his father. The *brahmahatyā* forbade the protection of his father. When the *brahmahatyā* struck Sumati in the presence of his father and the others, all of them, including his father, wept in sorrow. Then—

At that very moment, Yajñadeva, having arrived there, offered prayers to Durvāsas for the removal of the fault of his son; then, by Durvāsas, he was instructed to go to the shrine of Śrī Rāma Dhanuṣkoṭi for the expiation of the sin of killing a Brahmin. Following this, in connection with the greatness of Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha, the account of the removal of the sin of violating the Guru’s wife by a Brahmin named Duvinīta is narrated. Then, [Yajñadeva spoke] to Durvāsas...

While wandering about in delusion out of a desire to know the conduct of those who are ill-behaved, there occurs the narration of the story of the twice-born named Durvinīta, who was difficult to deal with, concerning Yajñadeva. In that regard, after the death of his father—a son of a Brahmin named Īṣmavāha residing in the Pāṇḍya country—Durvinīta performed the funeral rites for his father; then, along with his widowed mother, he came to Dhokaṇa in his own country for the sake of obtaining alms and took up residence there. While living there for a long time, that man of dull intellect...

Durvinīta, due to the ripening of his past evil deeds, was suddenly tormented by the arrows of the God of Love; he forcibly dragged his own widowed mother—who cried out, "Do not come to me!"—and engaged in sexual intercourse with her. Then, after the emission of semen, Durvinīta felt intense remorse and requested a great penance for the purification of his body. Although the sages, having rebuked him as a perpetrator of a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*), expelled him, they nevertheless showed him supreme compassion.

The great sage Vyāsa gave instruction to him for the purpose of turning him away from the sin of approaching the wives of others and for the sake of his pilgrimage to Dhanuṣkoṭi. Having heard this instruction from Vyāsa, Durvinīta, together with his mother, went to the holy site of Dhanuṣkoṭi; having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), he observed a month-long fast, and at its conclusion, after breaking his fast, he returned once more to the presence of Vyāsa to request further instruction on what must be done next. Thereupon, Vyāsa gave instruction to Durvinīta regarding all the duties of a *saṃnyāsin*. Then—

After first describing the marriage of Durvinīta and his subsequent practice of the householder's life, there follows a description of liberation through the practice of *dharma*. Thus, having heard the greatness of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha as recounted by Durvāsas, the Brahmin Yajñadeva took his wife, who was afflicted by the sin of killing a Brahmin, went to the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha, and performed an ablution there with great devotion; consequently, [the sin] vanished from the sky. Now, furthermore, in connection with the greatness of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha—

The description of the Kṣīrakuṇḍa at Puṃnāga, which removes the state of being afflicted by wicked conduct; in connection with that, the narrative of the Sudrala Brahmin and others; the subject matter concerning the purification from all sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin, of the son of the Brahmin Yajñadeva named Sumala by means of the Vāṇī [river]; and having thus heard the greatness of the Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha as described by Sindhudvīpa, Hanumān and Jāmbavān went to the Dhanuṣkoṭi-tīrtha and performed their ablutions, [attaining liberation] through its power.

The description of the two horses, Sagākhvāna and Rauma, and the greatness of Dhanuṣkoṭi (111). [Section vi] Therein, a twice-born man named Durācāra, residing on the banks of the Gautamī, having been completely stripped of his Brahminhood due to association with people who were great sinners, was seized by Vātāṭha, led from the region of the Gautamī to the holy site of Dhanuṣkoṭi, and immersed in the waters of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha; by the mere act of bathing in that Tīrtha, Durācāra was liberated from the possession of the Āretāla Graha, and Śrī Dattātreya [appeared].

Having returned, he related [the account] out of a desire to know the end; and when a prayer had been made, Dattātreya first narrated the story beginning with the capture of the Vetāla by him and ending with the Vetāla’s liberation, followed by a description of the greatness of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha. In connection with that, he described how the Vetāla, in his previous birth as a Brāhmaṇa, attained the state of a Vetāla because he failed to perform the Śrāddha for his ancestors during the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada. In connection with that, he further described the fruit of performing Śrāddha on every lunar day during the Mahālaya fortnight.

The description of how, through the power of performing the *śrāddha* ceremony at Sahākhya, Queen Hariścandrā and others, as well as many ṛṣis, attained liberation from all suffering and achieved fruits such as the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) like *aṇimā*; and the greatness of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha at Śrī Dattatreya, along with the fruits of the *mahālaya-pakṣīya-śrāddha* and other rites—having heard these, the demon named Durācāra, who had abandoned his wicked ways, returned to his own home according to the path taught by Dattātreya and attained liberation through the practice of his own duties.

Description of Liberation; the glorification of the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha, which effects the cessation of one's own sins. While a sacrifice was being performed there by Mudrakha, Mahāviṣṇu appeared at that sacrifice, and he was propitiated by Mudrakha through hymns of praise. Then, in order to fulfill the desires of the sage Mudrakha, Lord Viṣṇu had Viśvakarmā excavate a vast sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in Mudrakha’s hermitage; he commanded Surabhī to fill it with milk, and when that pit was filled with an inexhaustible flow of milk by Surabhī—

The Lord, having given that sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) to Sudr̥ṣṭa for the purpose of evening and morning oblations and having bestowed upon him the name "Kṣīrasaras," granted a boon to Sudr̥ṣṭa and described the conclusion of the chapter. The subjects [discussed] are: the attainment of liberation at the end of the body for Sudr̥ṣṭa, the great sage, through the performance of his own duties such as *homa* and other rites; and, in connection with the majesty of Kṣīrasaras, the narration of the story of how Kaśyapa’s wife, Kūpā—a female crane who had been his co-wife—was freed from the sins of killing ten thousand living beings.

Description of the Great Lake Kṣīrakuṇḍa: Once, a wager was made between Vinatā and Kadrū, the sisters and co-wives, regarding the color of the horse of the Sun; when Vinatā declared the horse’s tail to be white according to its true nature, Kadrū, through deception, commanded her sons, the Nāgas, to cover the horse’s tail with the skin of their own bodies in order to make it appear black. When the Nāgas did not comply with that request, Kadrū pronounced a curse upon them.

Then the Naga named Karkotaka covered the tail of his mother Vinata with his own body and carried her. Subsequently, having come to an agreement with Kadru and Vinata regarding a wager, the dark-tailed sun-horse was presented; and because that dark-tailed horse was given, Vinata—having been defeated by Kadru and consequently distressed—accepted the state of servitude and, along with her son Garuda, carried the sons of Kadru and the Nagas. Then, Garuda asked his mother the reason for this state of servitude.

Having learned from her that she was not his mother and desiring to be freed from slavery, he went to his own mother to request food for the purpose of fetching the nectar (*sudhā*). His mother then gave the command to Garuḍa to devour the Śabaras dwelling within the ocean. Garuḍa, having devoured the Śabaras, encountered a Brahmin who had come among them along with his noble wife, a Kirātī, and sported happily with her. Then, Garuḍa, still unsatiated even after devouring the Śabaras, approached his father Kaśyapa.

To him, for the sake of removing his great hunger, he made a request for food; Kaśyapa then commanded Garuḍa to seize the elephant and the tortoise—the two brothers Vimāvasu and Supratīka—who had become such through a mutual curse, so that he might eat them. Thereupon, Garuḍa seized those two, the elephant and the tortoise, with his talons and climbed a tree named Rohiṇa standing on the bank of the holy ford called Virambā in order to stay there and eat them. As soon as he had climbed it, the branches of that tree broke.

While the great sages were clinging to that branch, Garuda, fearing they might fall, lifted the branch high up and placed it in a desolate region in the middle of the ocean, devoid of people, where elephants and tortoises were feeding. Then, when Garuda was about to set out for his own world with the nectar, there occurred portents of evil in his own world; consequently, Indra caused portents of evil to appear in the world of Bṛhaspati. (Skanda Purāṇa, Māheśvara Khaṇḍa)

The narration of the time when the Vālakhilyas incurred the curse of Indra; then, Garuḍa’s return to his own home; the description of Garuḍa’s battle with the gods; in that battle, Viṣṇu accepting Garuḍa as his own vehicle under the pretext of granting him a boon; then, Śakra’s bestowing of a boon upon him; Garuḍa bringing the nectar (sudhā) and placing it upon *kuśa* grass in the presence of the serpents (*nāgas*), thereby securing the liberation of his mother from slavery; and so forth.

When the Nāgas assembled after having acquired the knowledge [of the situation], Śakra seized the vessel of ambrosia (*sudhā-kalasa*). Having learned of this, the Nāgas arrived; mistaking it for ambrosia, they cut it with their sharp claws, but as it was not to be divided, their tongues were split, whereby they became "double-tongued" (*dvijihva*). Then, regarding his own mother, Vinatā, who had acted deceitfully, Garuḍa pronounced a curse of servitude upon her. Then, by the power of that [curse], Kaṭarā was humiliated. Then, there was the story of Vinatā, who was virtuous and possessed of good character.

Through the prayer of Kaśyapa, the pacification of the fault arising from the *kaṭara* [vow], and the command given for the purpose of bathing in the Milk Lake located at the Phumrāmāvarta on the shore of the Southern Ocean; the pacification of the fault produced by the *kaṭara* vow through the knowledge of the milk; and the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the Śrī-rasa.

Now follows the description of the greatness of Kapitīrtha: there, after the slaughter of Rāvaṇa and the other Rākṣasas, all the monkeys constructed a holy bathing place (tīrtha) and performed their ablutions; Śrī Rāmacandra granted a boon to Kapitīrtha; in connection with the majesty of Kapitīrtha, the life-story of Viśvāmitra is described; therein, while Viśvāmitra was performing austerities to attain Brahminhood, Rambhā arrived to obstruct his penance, and due to Viśvāmitra’s curse, she attained the state of a Śikhā (a crest of hair). By the sage Śatānanda...

The discharge of a *śilā* (stone) by Śiva for the purpose of driving away the Rākṣasī who had arrived to cause him distress; the striking of that Rākṣasī by that *śilā* as it fell upon a *kapittha* tree, whereby she regained her original form of Rambhā through the power of that sacred ford (*tīrtha*); and the liberation of that Rākṣasī from her curse and the attainment of the status of the Apsaras Dhṛtācī—the majesty of Kapitīrtha. ... [end of fragment]

Then follows the description of the greatness of the two holy sites (tīrtha) of Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī; in connection with that, the slaying of the lustful Brahmā by Śiva toward his own daughter; the restoration of Brahmā to life by Śiva at the request of Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī; the performance of a hymn of praise to Śiva by Brahmā; and, by Śiva’s command, the manifestation of Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī in Mandāra after the construction of their two pools (kuṇḍa), followed by the greatness of those two pools of Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī.

Ṭa: The objects [of the senses]. Now, in connection with the majesty of the *Gāyatrī-sarasvatī-khaṇḍa*, there is a description of the account of the Brahmin named Kāśyapa. Therein, while a Brahmin of the Kāśyapa lineage—who was skilled in the science of neutralizing poison—was traveling to prevent the death of Śākalya, the son of the sage Śamīka, which was to have occurred due to a portion of his future fate, that Brahmin took money from him midway and turned back; because he thus protected the life of the king, he became an object of universal resentment. Then, by the sage Śākalya himself—

Having understood the cause of the world's censure, for the purpose of removing that fault, Śākalya went to the pair of Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī Kuṇḍas situated on the chest of the Southern Ocean and performed a ritual bath. Then, Kāśyapa offered praise to Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī who had appeared at that time; they granted him boons, and by their grace, the Brahmin Kāśyapa was described as being freed from his sins. [This is] the majesty of the two Gāyatrī and Sarasvatī Kuṇḍas.

Then follows the description of the greatness of the Aghnamocana-tīrtha, Apeca-pāṇḍava-tīrtha, Devatīrtha, Suprīva-tīrtha, Nala-tīrtha, Gavāṣatī, Aṅgada-tīrtha, Gaja-gavaya-śarabhaṅga-mudgara-panasa-nirmita-tīrtha, Avibhīṣaṇa-tīrtha, and the tīrtha established by the minister of Vibhīṣaṇa, preceded by a description of the majesty of the sixty-four [tīrthas]. Next is the description of the greatness of the Sarayū river located on Gandhamādana, and of Mahādeva Rāmanātha and others; then, the description of the greatness of the Liṅga Rāmanātha installed by Śrī Rāmacandra. In that regard:

A detailed description of the greatness and praise of the worship of Śrī Rāmeśvara Mahādeva, preceded by devotion such as beholding [the deity]; a narration of the life of Śrī Rāmacandra in connection with the majesty of the Śrī Rāmeśvara Liṅga; and therein, the account of how Śrī Rāmacandra built a bridge across the ocean, slew Rāvaṇa in battle at Laṅkā, recovered Sītā, and [resided] on Mount Gandhamādana on the shore of the southern ocean.

The arrival at Prayāga; then the sages, headed by Agastya, coming there to offer their salutations to Śrī Rāma; then, following the instruction of those sages, Śrī Rāma and the sages having decided to install a *liṅga* of the illustrious Maheśvara, Bharata was commanded to go to Kailāsa to bring the Śiva-liṅga; and upon Hanumān’s return after bringing the Śiva-liṅga, seeing a *vilva* fruit, and with the consent of the sages, out of fear of the [improper] transgression of the auspicious hour (*muhūrta*).

Śrī Rāma established a Śiva-liṅga made of sand brought from the Itavālukā river and performed its worship. Thereupon, the venerable Somanātha, residing within the liṅga, emerged from the center of the liṅga and granted a boon to Śrī Rāmacandra. At the request of Rāmacandra, Nandikeśvara was installed before Lord Śrī Rāmeśvara; then, for the purpose of consecrating the Lord, he dug a well named Koṭitīrtha with the tip of his own bow and performed the ritual bathing of the liṅga. Finally, he constructed a pedestal for the back of the liṅga.

Then, after Śrī Rāma had performed the consecration of the sand-Śiva-liṅga along with his son, Hanumān brought [the original] liṅga. Upon seeing the Śiva-liṅga that Rāma had installed even before his own arrival, Hanumān described his state of being filled with grief and anger; thereafter, Śrī Raghunātha consoled Hanumān. Following that, by Rāma’s command, Hanumān installed the Hanumadīśvara [liṅga]. Thus, there is the description of the eleven Śiva-liṅgas, beginning with Rāmeśvara. Then, by Hanumān...

When Rāma, out of rashness, exerted his speed to uproot the sandbank fashioned by Sītā that he had established there, he fell down after first bowing his head to the Wind-god (Māruta) because his great effort proved fruitless; thereafter, Śrī Sītā and Rāmacandra performed acts of propitiation for the sake of Māruta’s well-being.

Śrī Rāmacandra’s causing grief for the sake of Hanumān who had fallen into a swoon; then, after the cessation of Hanumān’s swoon, Hanumān’s offering of praise to Śrī Rāma and Jānakī; Śrī Rāmacandra’s instruction to Hanumān regarding the worship of the Divine Couple (Divya-bhakty-upadeśa) and his issuing of the command for the consecration of the *Hanumatkuṇḍa*—the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) formed by the three rivers Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī arising from the spot where Hanumān fell; and Hanumān’s installation of the *liṅga* he had brought near Rāmanātha.

Now, in the context of describing the cause of the origin of the sacred footprint (tradamaha), there is an account of the birth of Rāvaṇa and others from the sage Viśravas upon Kaikasī, the daughter of the Rākṣasa Sumālī. Furthermore, because Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa were born as Brāhmaṇas, Rāmacandra incurred the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa (brahmahatyā) by slaying them; to remove that sin, Rāmacandra established the Rāmeśvara Liṅga at Setubandha. Having constructed the holy site known as Brahmahatyāvimocana near it—

Having caused the sin of Brahmin-slaughter to depart, he established it upon a stone slab; Girijā was installed on the southern side of the great Liṅga of Rāmanātha, as were the attendant deities of the quarters all around; and for the purpose of worshipping and serving the Rāmareśvara Liṅga, Rāmacandra granted villages and other means of livelihood to Brāhmaṇas.

Now, in connection with the majesty of Rāmanātha, follows the narration of the life of King Śaṅkara, the ruler of the Pāṇḍya land: how, while wandering in the forest on a hunt, Śaṅkara killed a tiger, as well as the wife of the sage Śākalya—who was dressed in tiger skin—killing her with the very same tiger-skin trap.

The killing of his own parents; [the end of] the previous chapter; the topics [of this chapter]: then the description of the manifestation of Setumādhava; the description of the account of King Puṇyanidhi through association with him; there, the weeping of the boy upon seeing [his parents]; hearing that weeping, the arrival of Śaṅkara’s disciple near him; there, having approached the boy by means of the sages, and having observed the king, the two parents weeping, and the boy, the instruction of that knowledge to the boy.

Following the act of consoling them, he carried out the funeral rites for his parents for their welfare in this world and the next by obeying their command; at the instruction of the sages, that son of the sage performed the funeral rites for his parents for their benefit in this world and the next, and at the site of Rāmeśvara, he completed the ritual procedures such as the *śrāddha* ceremony for the depositing of his parents' bones in the Hālāsya-tīrtha. Through his devotion there, the liberation of the three of them is described. Then, the Brahmins, after censuring King Dāśaratha, commanded him to enter the fire in order to expiate the sin of the slaughter of a Brahmin. Thereupon—

At the command of the Brahmins, King Śaṅkara ordered his own ministers to prepare for the consecration of his son upon his own funeral pyre; when he made an effort to leap into it, a voice from the sky prevented King Śaṅkara from falling into the fire and commanded him to worship the Liṅga of Rāmanātha in order to remove the fault of both the slaughter of a cow and the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. Then, when the Brahmins also gave their consent in that same manner, King Śaṅkara performed the service of the Śrī Rāmeśvara Liṅga for the duration of one year.

By the power of that hymn of praise, through the mouth of King Śaṅkara, there occurred, by divine command, the execution of the woman who had been universally proclaimed as guilty of both the murder of a cow and the murder of a Brahmin; and then—
The granting of boons by the Lord Śrī Rāmanātha, having manifested himself as Śaṅkara, the Purifier; the grace of Śrī Rāmanātha.

) A description of King Dācchaṅkara attaining union with Śiva. — — , Next, the hymn of praise offered to the Lord Rāmeśvara by Śrī Rāmacandra, Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā, Hanumān, and all the other monkeys, as well as by all the sages, gods, and others; and thereafter, the description of the granting of boons to Śrī Rāmacandra and the others by the pleased Lord Rāmeśvara.

Once, however, while the King of Madhurāpurī, Puṇyanidhi, was at Rāmadhuṣkoṭi, having performed meritorious acts such as the Tulāpuruṣa gift, he desired to set out for his own city. At that time, a certain woman disguised as a maiden caused him offense. That maiden spoke her intention to King Puṇyanidhi, saying, "I shall become your daughter and dwell in your house. Thereupon, Puṇyanidhi brought that charming and beautiful maiden back to his own home and gave her the name Vindhyavāsī.

In the vicinity of his own wife, he questioned her regarding the objects of meditation; then, following the inquiry into those objects of meditation, there was the search for that Lakṣmī and the arrival of Viṣṇu, who had assumed the guise of a Brahmin. There, in that garden, Lakṣmī, having assumed the form of a maiden, was forcibly [seized] while she was gathering flowers.

And there was the taking of his hand; then, having heard the weeping of the maiden, Puṇyanidhi, through his own spies, led that Viṣṇu who had assumed the form of a Brahmin to the temple of Śrī Rāmanātha and bound him with fetters. Then, in a dream, Puṇyanidhi saw that Brahmin in the form of the Lord’s abode and his own daughter in the form of Lakṣmī. From that time forward, taking his daughter and going to the place called Rāmanātha, he [saw] that Brahmin who had manifested himself as the form of the Lord.

Having seen Viṣṇu, he recognized him and offered praise followed by a request for forgiveness for his transgression; he also offered praise to that Lakṣmī who had assumed the form of his own daughter. Pleased by her entreaty, the Blessed Lord, the abode of merit, granted a boon. For that devotee, King Puṇyanidhi, the Lord established a permanent residence there under the name Setumādhava, even while maintaining His form bound in chains. [Thus it was done] by King Puṇyanidhi...

The performance of service to Lord Setumādhava; the description of the greatness of Setumādhava, wherein one attains liberation at the end of this meritorious body; (Bha) then, the description of the sequence of the procedure for the pilgrimage to Setu; having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) at one's own home to complete the pilgrimage, the detailed description of the performance of the pilgrimage, including the observance of the preliminary and daily rules; then, the description of the greatness of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha, preceded by a specific description of the Setu region.

The first section, beginning with the Setumāhātmya, within the Brahmakhaṇḍa, is as follows: [Śrī Rāmacandra] describes the account of the granting of boons at the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha; in the context of charity, while discussing the consideration of worthy recipients (*pātra*), there is the praise of the virtuous recipient in the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Dilīpa; the description of the excellence of worship, vows, and other meritorious acts performed during the specific times such as the *ardhodaya* at the bath and other rites in the Dhanuṣkoṭi Tīrtha at Rāmasetu; and the description of the greatness of reciting, hearing, and giving gifts of the Setumāhātmya, followed by the concluding summary and the final conclusion of the Setumāhātmya. Thus ends the first part, beginning with the Setumāhātmya, in the Brahmakhaṇḍa.
Now begins the second section, the Dharmāraṇya-khaṇḍa, within the first book.

The wandering of Saṅgakhā; the reception with honors by the great sages, such as Raunaka and others, of the great sage Sūta who had arrived at the Naimiṣa forest, and their making him speak out of a desire to hear discourses on the increase of Dharma; then, the commencement by the great sage Sūta to describe the majesty of Dharmāraṇya; therein, the journey of the illustrious Lord Yamadharmadeva to the assembly of Brahmā; and there, having heard the divine narrative of Dharmāraṇya being recited by the great sage Vyāsa in that assembly of Brahmā—

Yamadharmadeva’s journey toward his own city; Nārada’s arrival there before King Yamadharman; when questioned by Nārada regarding the cause of his contentment, Yamadharman relates the story of Dharmāraṇya as heard from Vyāsa in the world of Brahmā; and having heard the narrative of Dharmāraṇya from Yamadharman, Nārada’s return to the earth to see Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma.

Nārada, having been honored by Dharmarāja, spoke to Dharmarāja, who was desirous of hearing the *Āraṇyaka* narrative: "Go and bathe in the Gaṅgā during the month of Māgha; the great sage Vyāsa will arrive there, and from his mouth you shall hear the *Dharma-āraṇyaka* narrative. Having said this, Nārada vanished from that place. Then the arrival of the venerable great sage Vyāsa before Dharmarāja occurred. Then Yudhiṣṭhira, having seated Vyāsa upon the throne and worshipped him, enquired after his well-being. Thereafter, by Vyāsa...

The commencement of the narration of the *Dharmāraṇya-kathā* to Yudhiṣṭhira; then, the description of the greatness of the principal site of Dharmāraṇya, which is also known by the synonym Nidīraka; therein, the description of how that Dharmāraṇya possesses a mass of merit that surpasses all other holy forests (*tīrtha-vanāni*); then, the request made by Yudhiṣṭhira to the great Vyāsa out of a desire to know its majesty; and finally, the commencement of the *Dharmāraṇya-kathā* by Vyāsa, wherein Dharma-deva [speaks] with the desire to reveal the true nature of the Blessed Lord (*Śrī-Bhagavat*).

Having gone into the middle of the forest and meditated upon Mahādeva, [Nandī] performed a description of his ascetic penance. Then, the gods—Bhairava, Bhṛṅgiriṭi, Paraśurāma, Śiva, Nara, Vyāsa, and others—having been uplifted by that penance, went to Mount Kailāsa and offered praise to the illustrious Mahādeva. Thereafter, having understood from the words of the Lord that there was no fear for Dharma, and perceiving that all the gods were departing for their own abodes, Indra became filled with groundless suspicion; consequently, through the counsel of Bṛhaspati, he [acted] against Dharma.

The Apsaras named Urvaśī, having been won over by his ascetic power, spoke with affection; and she, having approached Dharma, caused him to listen to the objects of the senses through song and dance, while he, in turn, made her hear the duties of kingship. Then, through the intervention of the Apsaras Vardhanī, he recounted the faults inherent in the nature of her companions.

Then, there was a meeting between the Dharmarāja and the Apsaras Vaddhanyā; the Dharmarāja granted a boon to the Apsaras Vaddhanyā. Thereafter, Vaddhanyā informed Śakra of her resolve regarding Dharma, and having received permission from Śakra, she departed for her own abode. Immediately after the Apsaras’s departure, the Dharmadeva performed severe penance by sitting facing the sun. When the gods and others, their minds distressed by his fierce asceticism, went to Kailāsa and offered praise to Śiva—

Then, while Śaṅkara was performing austerities in the forest together with the gods, Dharmadeva returned; Dharmadeva offered a hymn of praise to the Blessed One, and Śaṅkara, pleased by that hymn of praise, granted a boon to the god Yama-Dharma. In the context of granting this boon, he first transformed the two-yojana forest of Yama-Dharma into a sacred grove (dharmāraṇya), and subsequently bestowed the boon upon the god Yama-Dharma. Then, he established the shrine of Dharmāraṇyeśvara there, whereupon Yama-Dharma first [established] the Blessed Viśveśvara...

The establishment of a liṅga by the Self-born One under the name Dharmeśvara; the construction of the Dharmavāpī tank; the majesty of Dharmavāpī and Dharmeśvara; a description of the majesty of Yamadharmatarpaṇa through its proximity to that [tank]; then, by Yamadharmarāja himself, preceded by a description of the glory of Dharmāraṇya, the granting of a boon of supremacy over all to the Kṣetrapāla established by himself; and then, regarding the Dharmāraṇyas.

A description of the majesty of eighteen thousand Nārāyaṇas who are the destroyers of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; in connection with that, a description of the good conduct common to all classes and stages of life, including daily obligatory rites such as morning remembrance (*prātaḥsmaraṇa*); therein, praise for the honoring of guests; then, a description of the eightfold duties of a householder, beginning with the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*); then, a description of those things to be avoided by a householder; and finally, a description of the excellence of serving the elderly, giving gifts, and so forth.

Then, [the description of] the greatness of offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍadāna*) and other rites at the Ghaṇṭākarṇa-tīrtha and the Dhmavāpī; then, in response to the inquiry of Śaunaka and others, the narration by Sūta of the conduct and duties of devoted wives (*pativratā*); in connection with the supreme excellence of the duties of devoted wives, the demonstration of the miserable consequences for women of evil conduct; the description of the rules and duties for widows; and preceded by the glorification of the gift of a conch shell at the Dharmeśvara-tīrtha, [the account of] the goddess Pārvatī hearing Indra and the other gods arrive.

Rising abruptly from his seat with the desire to depart, he did not mount his bull; instead, Skanda, wishing to know the cause of Śiva’s haste in departing, offered him a prostration. Then Śiva, preceded by an account of the Puranic narrative regarding the granting of boons such as the *khaṣṭrādi* to Skanda, described the majesty of the Dharma-forest (Dharmāraṇya) established for the sake of Sūrya and Dharmarāja, following an account of the great battle involving Brahmā, Kuvera, and others. [He then proceeded] toward Dharmāraṇya.

Eager to bring Śrī Mahāviṣṇu to Vaikuṇṭha, Śiva set out toward Vaikuṇṭha along with Skanda and the other gods, beginning with Brahmā. Having arrived there, Brahmā and the others offered praise to Viṣṇu. Upon hearing the hymn of praise from Brahmā and the rest, Viṣṇu arose. Then, when Viṣṇu questioned Brahmā and the other gods regarding the reason for his own departure from his abode, Brahmā informed him of the destruction of Dharma and the decline of the Vedas, and requested that he come there.

First, the making of the request; then, Viṣṇu, having said "So be it," mounted Garuḍa and, together with Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, and the other gods, returned to Dharmāraṇya to see Yama, the King of Dharma. Yama, the King of Dharma, offered hospitality to all the gods and composed a hymn of praise. Then, Viṣṇu made a request for boons to Yama, the King of Dharma. Thereafter, when Yama, the King of Dharma, had made a request for the construction of a great hermitage in his own Dharmāraṇya, [Viṣṇu granted it].

Viṣṇu and the other gods brought from various regions Brahmins endowed with virtuous conduct, accompanied by their disciples and retinues; having established well-provided hermitages for those sages in that Dharma Forest, they performed the rite of formal installation.

Now, among the Śāḍhyaṇas residing there in Dharmāraṇya together with their sons, grandsons, and others, there is first a detailed description of the twenty-four principal sages, including their lineages (*gotra*), ancestral clans (*pravara*), and so forth; then follows a description of the character of the Nādyaṇas born of those respective lineages; and finally, in connection with the majesty of Dharmāraṇya, a narrative concerning the Yakṣa named Jṛmbhaka.

There, at the request of all the Brahmins who were terrified by the *jṛmbhaka* yakṣas, all the gods established the Śrīmātṛs, Praśastis, Yoginīs, and Nandās—each in the form of the deity of their respective lineage (*gotra*) and ancestral branch (*pravara*)—within that Dharmāraṇya for the protection of those Brahmins; thereafter, the Brahmins who had been tormented by the *yoginīs* regained their health. Then, once upon a time, having arrived there in that Dharmāraṇya, Rudra and the other gods, in order to effect the purification of the excellent Brahmins, [approached] Viṣṇudhārā and Brahmā.

The sequence of praising the *Dharmāraṇya-kathā* in the form of a dialogue between Śiva and Skanda; therein, Śiva first asks Skanda about various subjects, after which Brahmā, desiring to benefit the foremost among the twice-born, recollects the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*) in the *Dharmāraṇya*, whereupon the wish-fulfilling cow arrives in the *Dharmāraṇya* into the presence of Brahmā.

Following the respective Brāhmaṇas, the establishment of the lineages (*gotra*) and other details for those merchants who were their attendants was performed; thereafter, all the gods offered praise to the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*). Then, by Rudra’s great favor, the Gandharva Viśvāvasu brought Gandharva maidens, and with them, the marriage of those cow-tending merchants was solemnized. Subsequently, the account of their progeny and their conduct following the Gandharva form of marriage is related.

A description of how those thirty-six thousand cowherd merchants, together with their sons, grandsons, and countless followers, dwelt in the forest of Dhama and performed services such as serving the Brahmins; the battle fought by the Rākṣasa Khara against the goddesses of the Ātreyagotra and other lineages; the slaying of the Rākṣasa Khara by Viṣṇu, who arrived there at that very moment and was impelled by [the gods], using his own discus; and thereafter, the fleeing of those [demons] out of fear of the Rākṣasa.

The re-establishment in the forest of the Brahmins and others who had been living in the Dhmīra forest after they were summoned by the gods at the command of Viṣṇu; the description of the city named Satyamandira—which was established for the welfare of the Brahmins by the Blessed One after he returned from Satyaloka, slew the Rākṣasa, and founded the city—preceded by a description of the abodes of the deities of all directions; and, in connection with the installation of Gaṇeśa there, the narration of the account of the birth of Gaṇeśa and other events from Pārvatī.

Chapter Six: The offering of prayers by the inhabitants of Dharmāraṇya for protection, preceded by the praise of Sabedeva; the acceptance of the gods' prayer by the Lord of the Gaṇas (Gaṇādhyakṣa) and his remaining there for the sake of protecting the residents of Dharmāraṇya; and the worship of Śrī Gaṇeśa by all the people of that place to ensure the successful completion of marriages and other auspicious ceremonies. Now, once upon a time in the Tretā Yuga, by a Rākṣasa named Lokajit...

When the forest of Dharma was being afflicted by calamities, then, due to the establishment of that [deity] at Satyapura, the regions of Gaṇeśa and Bhāskara were established on all sides within their own respective divisions. Then, in the forest of Dharma, to the west of Śambhu, in connection with the story of Raviketra, there is a detailed narration of the origin of the two Nāsatyas, the Aśvins. There, after Saṃjñā, the wife of Sūrya, having been scorched by the unbearable brilliance of Sūrya, was placed near the Sun; thereafter follows her practice of asceticism.

The departure; the pronouncement of a curse by Yama, who was laughing due to the partiality of his affection for his son, as he raised his foot to strike him; then, having heard the account of his mother reported by Yama, Sūrya, through meditation, learned that his wife Saṃjñā was performing penance in the form of a mare, and went to her side in the form of a horse; then, after Sūrya engaged in sexual union with the mare by inserting his phallus into her nostril, the twin Aśvins were born.

The origin of the two heated cauldrons situated at the eastern and western hoof-prints of the Sun while he was assuming the form of a horse; a description of the majesty of that heated solar cauldron (*taptaravikuṇḍa*); then, the installation of the Sun there by Brahmā and other gods under the name Bakulāditya, as well as the installation of Saṃjñā and the two Kumāras, the Aśvins; a description of the majesty of the Bakulāka [cauldron] of the solar cauldron; the reason for the fame of the name Bakulāka; and then, the account of Hayagrīva in the Dharmāraṇya forest following the conversation between Śiva and Skanda.

The account of Viṣṇu’s penance: When the gods had commenced a sacrifice on the surface of the earth, they went to Vaṅkaṇṭha to invite Viṣṇu. At that time, the Blessed One was performing austerities through the yoga of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in a secluded place, holding a bow and arrow in his hand. Then, in order to awaken him, he employed the method taught by Bṛhaspati; for that purpose, he used an ant under his control to cut the string of the bow held in the Blessed One’s hand.

The gods issued a command by means of a request for the distribution of sacrificial portions; then, as soon as [the head] was consumed by the eater, Viṣṇu’s head was severed by the blow of an axe. That head, having assumed the form of a goat, departed and remained hidden. Then, when that severed head had been purified and restored to its original state, Brahmā and the other gods were filled with joy.

Bharati conveys the command of Viṣṇu for the purpose of rejoining the head; then follows the promise by the gods to grant a share of the sacrifice to Viśvakarman. Thereafter, when the horse of the chariot that had entered the midst of the sky was brought by the gods, Viśvakarman, having severed the neck-bone of that horse, joined it to the trunk of Viṣṇu. Then the gods performed a hymn of praise to the horse-headed Mahāviṣṇu, and by Hayagrīva, who was pleased by that praise—

From Brahmā and the other gods, [the sound] "nananatatiti" arose; through that resonance, the form of the syllables *ka*, *ja*, *ka*, *ka*, *ta*, *ka*, *ga*, *ca*, and *na* was manifested. From that, the performance of the sacrifice for Brahmā and the other gods was established. Within that sacrificial ritual, there was the offering of the previously promised sacrificial portions to the Vamrīs and Viśvakarman. Having completed the sacrificial rite with Brahmā and the others, they departed for their own respective worlds.

Then, in the context of explaining the cause of Viṣṇu’s enmity, there is a description of the occurrence of the calamity in the form of the falling of Viṣṇu’s head when he was censured by Brahmā in the assembly of Brahmā; then, Viṣṇu, having assumed the form of a horse-headed being (*hayagrīva*), performed penance at the Devasaras Tīrtha in the Dharmāraṇya forest; Brahmā also stood before him and performed penance; thereafter, through the power of that Tīrtha, the horse-head of Viṣṇu became as it was before, and his body became beautiful. Then, by whom... [text ends].

The narration of how the first [wife], Sukhā, gave a curse to Viṣṇu, resulting in his fifth wife becoming like a tigress; the description of how that fifth wife’s happiness was destroyed by Hara in Dharmāraṇya; the description of Brahmā establishing Mokṣeśvara after performing the consecration of the Mokṣatīrtha; the description of the attainment of excellent fruits and the cessation of barrenness for one who bathes in the Devasaras Tīrtha; and the majesty of Mokṣeśvara.

Description of the power of the Devakhāta lake; then, the description of the installation of the lineage goddesses (gotradevīs), such as Śrīmātā, in various distinct locations to destroy the fear of *sākṣas* and other evils for the people residing in the Dharmāraṇya forest and the adjacent Paradharmāraṇya forest; the description of the specific modes of worship preceded by the description of the forms, names, and other attributes of those goddesses according to their respective locations; therein, the description of the majesty of the goddesses beginning with Śrīmātā and ending with Ānandā at Pūredirī; and now—

Following the description of the majesty of the goddesses of the heavens beginning with Śāntādevī situated in the southern direction, [this is] the description of the majesty of Śrīmātādevī. Next, following the description of the majesty of Āmāvādakīmāhātya, there is the description of the slaying of the Daitya named Kaṇāṭaka by the husband and wife residing in Yamīraṇya. Then follows the description of the events concerning the goddess Mātagī, including her silence and other matters, performed by Śrīmātādevī. [Therein is] the description of the battle of Mātagī with the Daitya Kaṇāṭaka; in that battle, having caused Mātagī to be bewildered by means of illusion, the Daitya Kaṇāṭaka [was defeated], and Śrīmātādevī returned.

The subjects [are as follows]: the refusal of her request for a svayaṃvara; then, after Śyāmākhya—the younger brother of Bhama—declared his intention to marry her, the dispatching of the demon Kāṇḍaka toward Goddess Śyāmalā; then, the slaying of the demon Kāṇḍaka by Goddess Śyāmalā in battle; then, in the context of the majesty of the Śiva-tīrtha, the description of the residence of Śrī Ḍaṅkara in the Dharmāraṇya forest; and finally, [the account] by Satu, Aiṣvika, and others.

This [section] contains: a chapter addressed to the goddess Śrīmātā for those desiring to know the specific ritual services (*viśeṣopacāra*) and the procedure for worship (*pūjāvidhi*) of the goddesses Śrīmātā, Mātaṅgī, and Ḍyāmalā; the description by the goddess Śrīmātā of the method of worshipping them; a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the goddesses Śrīmātā, Mātaṅgī, and Ḍyāmalā; and, in the context of describing the majesty of Indreśvara preceded by the majesty of Indrasaras, the narration of the account of the penance performed by Indra after he had committed the slaughter of a brahmin; the majesty of Indratīrtha and Indradhara, and [the account of] approaching their vicinity.

Thus, in the description of the episode concerning the *japa* established by Jayanta, Śiva describes to Pārvatī the seed-syllables (*bīja-varṇa*) of the deceptive mantras; through the recitation of such a mantra, the Goddess attains a state of wicked intent. Then, Śiva goes toward Dharmāraṇya and suddenly falls down; from the sweat of his body, a multitude of deceptive beings (*kūṭagaṇa*) arises. When those hosts, standing upon the deceptive wood-piles, proceed to accomplish the deceptive mantra, they achieve success and perceive him as Śiva himself.

Having heard Pārvatī’s account of her limping gait, Śiva’s command that she perform penance, her pleasing of Śiva through that penance, the renown of that place of penance by the name Dhārākṣetra, and the description of the majesty of that Dhārākṣetra; then, a detailed description of the deities Bhaṭṭārikā and Vikukṣi residing in Dharmāraṇya, as well as the lineage-deities of the Brahmins dwelling in Dharmāraṇya, such as Vaṭaṅka and others.

Nanabha, having returned from the forest of Saṃvara located in the eastern direction and so forth, performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*) for a period of a thousand years. In that sacrifice, he gratified the Brahmins by providing them with various kinds of cooked food. Then, in Dharmāraṇya, having carried out the slaughter of the Daityas who had descended due to the power of his giving, the account of his entry into heaven is described. Subsequently, once, a Rākṣasa named Udāsu returned to Dharmāraṇya and [attacked] the Brahmins and merchants residing there.

[Śiva], having become a *kādirikī* (a small, insignificant creature) because he caused excessive affliction, wandered here and there. Then, on one occasion, having been defeated by the *dānavas* in battle, he went toward the gods; subsequently, by the command of Brahmā, the *audāsureṇa* (the noble spirit), after establishing the *dharmāraṇya*, departed for his own abode. He then became one with the Lord (*īśvara*) and took up residence in Śambhugrāma, not far from Dharmāraṇya, together with his various chief merchants, such as the *daṇḍins*, *bhills*, and *caṇḍālas*.

The establishment of dwellings in the villages brought by Aṅgāmana; the explanation of the cause for those merchants' designation as "moha"; and by that very same cause, a description of the divisions among the kinsmen of the merchants residing there. Then, having heard from the mouth of Vyāsa about the fear of the Dharmāraṇya sacrifice in this manner, Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira went to Dharmāraṇya, performed the rites for purification at the holy sites, and having reached Indraprastha, he took possession of the kingdom. [End of] Dharmāraṇya.

Description of the majesty and power of Sthāṇutīrtha; then, in the context of describing the account of the Sarasvatī’s arrival at Dharmāraṇya from Satyaloka, the narrative of the conversation between the great sages and Mārkaṇḍeya; then, the description of the majesty of the sacred site of Dvārakā situated in Dharmāraṇya, along with the description of the dialogue held there; therein, the description of how Mārkaṇḍeya himself brought the Sarasvatī from Satyaloka; and finally, the description of the fruits of bestowing knowledge, performing *śrāddha*, and other rites upon the Sarasvatī. Then...

The description of the greatness of the Govatsaliṅga, preceded by the account of its origin from a calf situated in the forest of Dharma; the description of the Caṇḍāṭasthala located in front of the Govatsaliṅga; and the description of the greatness of the Gaṅgākūpaka situated near the Govatsaliṅga.

A description of the fruits of knowledge-giving, charity, *śrāddha*, and other rites at the *mokṣatīrtha* named Sarasvatī on the Iron Staff (*lohayaṣṭikā*); the striking of the staff against the chest by the gods for the sake of attaining the fruits of austerity; and a description of the battle between the gods and the Asura Loha, wherein Śaṅkara stood upon his chest as he fell face-upwards, Brahmā upon his neck, and Viṣṇu at his feet.

Then, due to the words of Brahmā, the demon Hāsa, being satisfied by the presence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and others within his own body, remained in that Dhamara forest in the very same position as he had fallen; thereafter follows the description of the granting of boons to the demon Hāsa by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
