Then follows the description of the majesty of the self-manifested Liṅga situated upon the iron pillar at Govatānnaitebhāga; then the description of the life of the demon Choda; therein, the account of the penance performed by Khohāsara on the bank of the Sarasvatī to propitiate Śiva; then, in connection with the majesty of the Dhama forest hermitage, a detailed narrative of the life of the Lord Śrī Rāmacandra, beginning from his childhood, including his marriage to Sītā, his dwelling in the forest, the battle with the Rākṣasas, the slaying of Rāvaṇa, the recovery of Sītā, his return to Ayodhyā, and his coronation.

Then, while Rāma was bathing at that most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrtha) with the desire to hear its greatness from Vasiṣṭha, and as he stood there having requested Vasiṣṭha regarding that supreme ford, the great sage Vasiṣṭha first recounted the greatness of many other tīrthas such as the Gaṅgā and the Narmadā, followed by a description of the Dhamāraṇya forest as the most excellent of all, and then a detailed exposition of its own majesty. Having heard this account of the greatness of the Dhamāraṇya field as proclaimed by Vasiṣṭha, [Rāma...]

Śrī Rāmacandra, together with his own retinue, undertook a pilgrimage to the sacred forest of Dharmāraṇya. Having gone to the city of Maḍilikapura, and then from there, at the word of Vasiṣṭha, Śatrughna abandoned the carrying of the palanquin along with the local merchants; instead, he himself proceeded on foot with his soldiers and his own attendants, performing the rites of the pilgrimage according to the prescribed rules. Having installed the two Śiva-liṅgas known as Śrī Rāmeśvara and Kāmeśvara, and having attained a sense of fulfillment, he remained composed upon the riverbank.

She was lying down with her attendants; then, at the hour of midnight, having suddenly heard the sound of her wailing, he dispatched his own messenger to her side to ascertain the cause of it. Then, that woman said, "If Śrī Rāma himself comes here, I shall relate my story. Thereupon, the messenger returned to Śrī Rāma and reported the words of that woman, whereupon Śrī Rāma went in person to the woman's side and [inquired] regarding the cause of her weeping.

When that goddess Śrīmātā, the presiding deity of Dharmāraṇya, appeared, she offered praise to Śrī Rāma and, after expressing her own suffering caused by the destruction of Dharmāraṇya by the demon Chodā, she made a prayer to Śrī Rāma for its restoration. Upon hearing Śrīmātā’s words, Śrī Rāma made a vow before the Mother of the World (Jaganmātā) to re-establish Dharmāraṇya exactly as it was, with Satyamandira as its capital city.

Having summoned his own messengers, he sent them to wherever those local *tarpaṇas* were located; having brought them forth with great honor and preceded by hymns of praise, he performed worship and hospitality for them, and bestowed upon them abundant gifts of wealth and various provisions.

Then, in the presence of those Brahmins residing in that kingdom, Śrī Rāma undertook the restoration of the sacred site of Dharmāraṇya by means of a sacrifice preceded by the distribution of gifts. Thereafter, having consulted and deliberated with the Brahmins, they described to Śrī Rāma their own duty—which consists in being averse to accepting gifts—and explained how they were devoted solely to the commands of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and the King. Then, by Śrī Rāma...

The remembrance of all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; the arrival of all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, by the mere remembrance of Śrī Rāma; the honoring of all those gods by Rāma through worship and other rites; then, the swift praise of Śrī Rāmacandra’s desire for the restoration of the holy Dharmāraṇya forest by all the gods; and thereafter, Śrī Rāmacandra, having obtained the permission of those gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, [of the holy field of] Śrī Dharmāraṇya...

Having renovated the dilapidated temples and having constructed various shrines, branches, and sanctuaries of Brahmā, he filled them all with an abundance of diverse wealth, grain, minerals, gold, jewels, and other articles, and bestowed four hundred and forty-four villages upon the Brāhmaṇas; furthermore, having presented thirty-six thousand cows, chowries, and swords to the Vāṇijas, he issued a command for them to serve the Brāhmaṇas.

At the time of his marriage and other ceremonies, he issued orders for the bearing of chowries and other royal insignia, as well as for the worship of the goddess Raṅkhdevī; furthermore, having bestowed chowries, swords, and other honors upon the Māṇḍalīkas, Maṇḍaleśvaras, and merchants of the Sapādalakṣa region, he commanded them to serve the twice-born. Then, after performing the consecration of his own family deity, he established the shrines of the goddess Śrīmātā, Jyūlya-svāmin, Harigaṇādhyakṣa, and other deities, and made arrangements for the Dugakuṇḍa tank, the Dharmavāpī, wells, and other facilities beneficial to the city.

Having inscribed an undivided edict upon a copper plate, and having bestowed it upon learned Brahmins, Śrī Rāma—having thus performed the restoration [of the land] and fulfilled his vow—worshipped and prostrated before the venerable Mother (Śrīmātā), and after making a formal request to the gods and the twice-born, described the granting of the *ṭheka* (tax-free status) for that Dhamīraṇya region, for the purpose of providing exclusive protection to the Brahmins and merchants residing therein; this is the description of the grant given by Śrī Rāmacandra on that day.

The daily service performed at the copper-plate seat (tāmrapaṭarāsana), and consequently, the constant legal proceedings of Śrī Rāmacandra against the local brāhmaṇas and merchants concerning Māruti; these are the subject matters.

Then, having received the command of the Brahmins—who had granted him the assurance of safety by promising, "Whatever you wish to request shall always be carried out for you"—Śrī Rāmacandra took leave of them and returned to the city of Ayodhyā; this is the description of his governance of the kingdom upon his arrival. Then, on one occasion during a conversation in Ayodhyā, Śrī Rāma heard from the mouth of the venerable Vasiṣṭha about the sage Dharmāraṇya, who was established among the Kṣatriyas.

Having heard the greatness of the sacred sites of Prayāga, Triveṇī, Śuti, Siddhakṣetra, Kāśī, Gaṅgādhāra, Araṇya, Suvarṇa, Harikṣetra, and others, he went with his retinue to Dharmāraṇya in order to perform another pilgrimage. Staying in Modheraka-pura, he completed the sacrificial rites together with the great sages such as Kuśika, who had been summoned by Vasiṣṭha and Atri. After performing the ritual bath at the conclusion of the sacrifice, and at the request of Sītā, he established a city named Sītāpura in front of Modheraka-pura for the sake of the learned.

The dedication to Barākaṇa; then, having gone toward Dhamaukha, the narration of the account of Śrī Rāmacandra’s gift of fifty-five *rāmas* of land—beginning from Sītāpura and extending as far as Satyamandira—preceded by the performance of the great gift (*mahādāna*) of sixteen *kalpas* to the Brahmins according to the words of Sītā and the command of his preceptor; and [the description] of the service rendered to the eighteen thousand great sages, such as Vātsyāyana, who resided in those fifty-five *rāmas*, as well as to sixty-four thousand courtesans and four times that many *candras*.

The act of bestowal; then, following a formal request by Rāma, the ordering of courtesans and Śūdras to perform service for those Brāhmaṇas; thereafter, the return of Śrī Rāmacandra to his own city; thus, the description of the account of Śrī Rāmacandra’s restoration of dilapidated temples, holy sites, and sacred locations in Dharmāraṇya; then, the description of the well-being of Dharmāraṇya due to the power of Hanumān’s protection of the Kṣetra, as told by Brahmādeva to Nārada; [and] by Yudhiṣṭhira.

The inquiry as to whether the Dharma-forest had ever suffered any decline with respect to Vyāsa; thereafter, the description by the great sage Vyāsa of the events of the Kali age; therein, the description of the history of the king named Śālivāhana, the sovereign of Kānyakubja; how that King Āma, having heard from his own preceptor the *Kaṅidhara* [text], and due to a state of mental agitation caused by the influence of Kali, became defiled in heart and accepted the Buddhist dharma instead of the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira), who is a Vaiṣṇava; and then, concerning that King Āma—

The birth of a daughter named Ratnagaṅgā to Queen Āmānāmnyā; the giving of that girl Ratnagaṅgā to King Kambhīpāla of Brahmayartā by her father because she had been captivated by the Kṣapaṇakas; at her marriage, the gift of the city of Modheraka located in Dharmāraṇya to her husband by King Āma; and thereafter, King Kambhīpāla having arrived at Dharmāraṇya and made it his own capital, the establishment of the Jaina Dharma throughout that kingdom.

[This is] the expansion. At that time, when the livelihoods of the Brahmins who held land-grant charters from Śrī Rāmacandra were being obstructed by the Jaina Dharma-practitioners, those three hundred and sixty Brahmins, having gathered together, went to King Sāvabhauma in the Kānyakubja region. They reported to him the account of the royal charters [issued by Rāma], as well as the report concerning the obstruction of their own livelihoods by the Jaina followers. Then, through those Brahmins, King Āma informed his own son-in-law of the matter.

Rāma then issued an order for the destruction of the temple; however, although there was an edict from his father-in-law, Kumārapāla—also known as Kānhapāḍā—who disregarded it and, for the sake of seizing the livelihoods of the Brāhmaṇas, spoke to them, saying, "Let proof be given by bringing Māruti here through the doctrine of atheism. Thereupon, those Brāhmaṇas, having heard that Māruti was staying at Sedabandha...

Among eighteen thousand Brahmins who had resolved to go to Śrī Rāmeśvara, fifteen thousand departed for the Lord of Rāma by way of the Kāverī river, while the remaining three thousand twice-born ones, with firm resolve, set out toward the eyes of Śrī Rāmeśvara via Māruti-bharaṇi; and as they were exhausted by great fatigue along the way, [the Lord acted] through the inspiration of Śrī Rāma near them.

When Hanumān, like the wind, arrived at the ancient site of Aṭṭana with great speed—since it was impossible to reach it by means of ordinary exertion—he first tested those ascetics (tāpasa) for many days. Then, having revealed his own form to them, he brought those ascetics back toward Setubandha-Rāmeśvara; after causing them to perform the vision of Rāmeśvara Mahādeva and other rites, he expressed his own sense of blessedness and offered praise to the Lord who dwells there, laughing aloud. Thus ends the [account of] that day.

To prevent Māra from causing harm to them by devouring them, he gave them [the hair] as a gift. Then, for the sake of providing proof to those Brahmins, having given each of them two separate small packets of hair from his own body, he presented them in succession to the King for burning.

And for the sake of reviving Śaraya once again, he gave orders for the discharge of arrows at the palace gate; then, taking two of his sandals, with very gracious and gentle words, he stayed for three nights at Śrī Rāmatīrtha near Śrī Māruti-khaṇḍa and performed the Brahma-yajña and other rites. Then, on the night of the third day, Hanumān placed those twice-born ones upon a bed of grass extending ten yojanas in width and made them sleep; while those brahmins were sleeping, he remembered the powerful wind, his own father.

Her arrival at Dharmāraṇya by means of that cart; then, when they had arrived in Dharmāraṇya along with Viśākhā and Rikhyā, those people residing in Bhāma and the sons and grandsons of those Brahmins approached them. Following the festival of their meeting and conversation with all the Brahmins residing in Bhāma, they departed for their respective homes with great ceremony. Then, on the following morning...

Immediately after the conclusion of the preliminary rites, he went to the royal assembly with them and delivered his master’s message to the king. Upon hearing that message from Māruti as it was spoken by him, while King Kumārapāla was about to disregard it, [the messenger] took one of the two hair-pouches situated on his left armpit—which contained the means for his own destruction—and cast it at the palace gate. By the mere act of throwing it, at that very moment, [the destruction of] that Kumārapāla occurred.

The King’s destruction of the entire wealth of his sons, wives, elephants, horses, and so forth; the extreme and wicked defamation of the naked mendicants (Nagna-kṣapaṇakas) and Kumārapāla by him out of excessive anger; then, at the instigation of Kumārapāla, the King’s taking of refuge in those Brāhmaṇas in their presence; and then, by those compassionate sages, the presentation to that monarch of the hair-pouch from the right armpit of Śrī Māratideva.

As soon as [the manuscript] was cast at the royal gate, the King again obtained all his wives, sons, elephants, horses, and other wealth, preceded by the restoration of his entire kingdom; then, through the realization of the power of Śrī Rāma Mārtaṇḍa, that King, having established new systems of livelihood and branches of learning for those Brahmins just as before, granted them [their lands], and from his own kingdom, he expelled all the Jainas, heretics, and others outside the Vedic fold. Then, thirty-six thousand [people of] virtuous conduct...

First, the determination of the qualifications for merchants who possess cows, goats, and various types of seeds, as well as for other traders, for the purpose of their adornment; then, the description of the authority granted by the King to the three thousand Brahmins residing at Setubandha via a royal edict concerning their livelihood; and finally, the determination that those Brahmins numbering five thousand who, upon traveling to Setubandha, violate their own vows are ineligible for the maintenance of their wandering life, while those who act with truthfulness to their vows [are eligible].

The establishment of three thousand *trayaividya* brahmins in the city of Meherakapura; and the establishment of all fifteen thousand *caturvidya* brahmins—who had violated their own vows—in the village of Meerakamrādra, in the region of Sukhavākha. Furthermore, on every full moon day of the month of Pauṣa, [the following was ordained] by all those *sataimoḍhava*, *cajaikhaividya*, and *caturvidya* brahmins.

[The section] on the description of the worship of the household deities (*kukhdevatā*) and all the ritual procedures; then, at one time, the arrival of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and other gods at Dharmāraṇya; the performance of worship and hospitable reception for them by the local Brāhmaṇas and the merchants known as Gobhijās; and the departure of those gods, such as Brahmā, back to their own abodes after having divided the residents of Dharmāraṇya into Brāhmaṇas of distinct lineages (*gotras*) and separate conduct (*vṛtti*); thereafter, [the account of] fifteen thousand [Brāhmaṇas] in fifty-five villages.

A description of the dwellings of the Cāturvidyas and the Brāhmaṇas; the fifteen names of the lineages (gotras) of the Cāturvidyas; a description of the names of the five groups of fifty villages beginning with Sītāpura; then, a detailed description of the lineages, deities, and characteristics of the Cāturvidya Brāhmaṇas residing in those five groups of fifty villages starting from Sītāpura; then, a determination of the seventeen locations beginning with Rīṭā for the Trivedi Brāhmaṇas who arrived in the vicinity of Hanumān; [and] the Caturhāti-Cāturvidyas.

A description of how long the conflict among those learned in the three Vedas (*traividyā*) lasted; then, a description of the division of castes (*jāti-bheda*) among certain Śūdras due to their adherence to the eightfold conduct (*aṣṭācāra*); then, upon the arrival of the Kali Yuga, a description of the emigration and other movements of certain Kṣatriyas among them, both due to the influence of the eightfold conduct and due to the influence of separate customs; and finally, the account of those who, having previously fled Sītāpura out of fear of King Cākīrāru and gone to dwell on the banks of the Sakhāñjamatī river, returned once more.

[This is] a description of the livelihood based on the practice of tending cows, preceded by residing in a pleasant dwelling place; and [it concerns] those youths produced through the sexual union of the four classes of Brahmins with widows and maidens by the *gopādattidhāraka* Nairdyana.

The description of the Kātyāyanas, Bhārgavas, Gokhukas, Śaineyas, and Āsneyas; then, the description of the designation "Tridaṇḍajas" for those Brāhmaṇas born of mixed unions—who were produced through marriage with Cāturvidya girls by Halumas, Matsakas, and others who had arrived [from other lands] and held the office of village headmen (grāmasthiti)—and who, due to the unavailability of brides within their own caste because of being lame, humpbacked, dwarfish, deaf, one-eyed, mute, and so forth, entered into marital relations with such girls. Of these...

First, the classification of the *jñāti* (clans) according to the divisions of the *śruti*. Now, following the description of the origin of the *jñāti* divisions of Moherakapura as previously stated, there follows a detailed account of the *gotras*, *pravaras*, *vaṭakas*, and *śākhās* of the Brāhmaṇas and others—including the Moḍhas and other groups—who, out of fear of the evils of the Kali age, established by common consent the rules for worship and other rituals based on their ancestral traditions, long-standing family customs, and local practices. [This is followed by] the account of the merchants and Śrāvakas residing in Dharmāraṇya.

Thus ends the second [chapter], the *Dharmāraṇyamāhātmya*, within the *Brahmakhaṇḍa*, which concludes the majesty of Dharmāraṇya preceded by a description of the scriptural accounts regarding the fruit of the majesty of Dharmāraṇya and the devotion of the twice-born to the *Gūḍha*.
Now, in the Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa, the third section: the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa.

Now, in the Maimiṣa forest, the great Ṛṣis headed by Śaunaka requested the Sūta, the great Ṛṣi, for the sake of generating supreme devotion to the majesty of Śrī Śaṅkara. Thereupon, the great Ṛṣi Sūta first described to the great Ṛṣis headed by Śaunaka the majesty of the five-syllabled mantra of Śrī Śaṅkara, followed by a description of the procedure for receiving that mantra from his own mouth. In the course of that discussion, he recounted the narrative of King Dāśārha, the lord of Mathurā, and therein [he told] how the king of the Dākas [married] the daughter of King Kāri.

Having married her, the king, out of a desire for pleasure and driven by the force of his vows, forcibly drew her toward himself. As soon as he touched her body, it became exceedingly heated like a red-hot iron plate. At that very instant, having been struck with fear, he asked her the reason for her body’s condition. She then explained to the king the power of the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva which she had practiced, and the king, through the grace of that holy tree, was inspired to seek out the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva.

Then, having heard those words, when the king had received the instruction on the Śrīśiva-mudrā from the preceptor Garga at a most meritorious spot on the bank of the Kālindī, his sins emerged from the pores of his body in the form of crows numbering up to one billion, and he was reduced to ashes. Thereafter, that King Dākhāha, whose body was now purified, returned to his own home with his wife—who was as cool as sandalwood through the grace of Guruḍubhāśīva—and enjoyed himself in happiness.

The administration of the kingdom; the majesty of the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva; then the description of the majesty of the Great Śivarātri on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha; therein, the majesty of fasting, the worship of the Śiva-liṅga, and the offering of *bilva* leaves; in connection with that, the narration of the history of King Amitasaḥ of the Ikṣvāku lineage; and therein, when King Mitrasena had gone out hunting and slain a certain Rākṣasa, his younger brother Chadyana assumed the guise of an ascetic.

Seeking a vulnerability and waiting for an opportunity, he approached the king in a humble guise; the king then appointed that *rākṣasa* as the superintendent of his own kitchen. Subsequently, when the king once invited his family preceptor Vasiṣṭha for a meal, the *rākṣasa*, disguised in deceptive attire, placed human flesh into his food vessel. Upon seeing that impure food, the great sage Vasiṣṭha rebuked the king.

The granting of the form of a Rākṣasa for twelve years as a consequence of a curse: Then, having heard the causeless curse, the enraged king took water in his hand to bestow it upon Vasiṣṭha; thereupon, Queen Madayantī, having seized the reins of the chariot, turned back that king who was intent on pronouncing the curse upon his preceptor; then, the water taken in the hand by that king to cast as a curse upon his guru was thrown onto his own feet, and by that [act], upon his feet...

Why did that king become famous by the name Kalmāṣapāda due to a certain transgression? After attaining the state of a *rākṣasa*, while wandering in the forest, King Kalmāṣapāda was about to devour a certain young sage (*munikumāra*). At that moment, the wife of that young sage, who was traveling with him, gave the *rākṣasa*-turned king a curse, saying, "When you come into contact with a woman, you shall become human again," and she then departed for the solar region (*sūryaloka*). Then...

After the period of the curse had elapsed, he regained his own true form and returned to his home; having heard the curse from the wife of the brahmin, his wife Madayantī, fearing her own barrenness, prevented her husband as he was entreating for sexual union. Then, when the king had departed for the forest in despair of regaining his kingdom, the sage Vasiṣṭha begot a son upon the queen Madayantī for the sake of establishing the lineage of Sūryavāṃśa. Then, toward the forest...

The pursuit by the terrible sin of Brahman-slaughter (*brahmahatyā*) from behind King Kalmāṣapāda after he had departed; the king’s, being afflicted by that Brahman-slaughter, journey to Gautama Mahārṣi in the Bhīṣmodyāna; then, the description of the conversation between the king and Gautama Mahārṣi—who had arrived with Śiva-devotees seeking to lead an old Śūdra woman named Śāṇḍālī to the world of Śiva—in the context of Gautama’s discourse on the majesty of Gokarṇeśvara for the purpose of removing the fault of the Brahman-slaughter. Therein...

Regarding the Śivadūtas, when Gautama asked them the reason for leading a Caṇḍālī woman to the world of Śiva, the Śivadūtas described the account of that Caṇḍālī’s previous birth: in her former life, she was the widow of a Brāhmaṇa who, under the sway of passion, became a Caṇḍālī. One night, having unknowingly killed a calf with her hand, she saw the calf in the light, recognized it as such, and out of remorse cried out, "Śiva, Śiva! Then, by means of her [wooden] staff...

A description of the adverse turn of fate that led her servant to attain the state of a Caṇḍālī; and [an account] of her journey toward the Gokarṇa region in order to beg for alms such as food from this Caṇḍālī, while on the way.

While she was standing on the bank of the Khatī, by the power of the chanting of the auspicious names of Śiva, Śiva remembered her; having drawn out her life-breath with his auspicious glances and joined her with divine splendor, he led her toward the realm of Śiva. Then, in connection with that, when the king asked the great sage Gautama about the nature of Śiva’s realm, the great sage Gautama described the nature of Śiva’s realm to King Mitrasaha, also known as Kalmāṣapāda, after the king had gone to the kingdom of Gokarṇa.

The description of attaining the realm of Śiva after being liberated from the torments of sins such as the slaughter of a Brahmin through the power of worshipping the Great Lord Śrī Gokarṇeśvara; then, the description of the majesty of the worship of Śrī Śiva; in that context, the description of the history of the king named Vimardana residing in the Kirāta country; how that king, despite being constantly devoted to unrighteousness, was nevertheless devoted to Śiva; and then, once in private, his wife Kuṃdarī spoke to that king most emphatically.

Although he was devoted to wicked conduct, he was intent upon devotion to Śiva; his inquiry [into the truth] arose from a desire for knowledge of the causeless [Lord]. Thereafter, the king Vimada described the events of his own previous birth: in a previous life, in the city of Paṃpā, while a great worship of Lord Śiva was being performed at the temple of Śiva on the Great Śivarātri night, he circumambulated the temple of Śiva. When that dog was about to be killed by an arrow-shot in the courtyard by people standing there, [he intervened].

A description of how she attained birth as a king through the power of the presence of Śrī Śiva; and a description of her former conduct, such as her desire for meat while in the womb of a dog, her fear, and her cruelty toward all living beings; then, by the king, a description of that noble lady’s previous life to the queen; therein, regarding her birth as a female pigeon, after she had taken a lump of meat and ascended to the peak of a mountain, she died upon being struck down by a sharp-beaked vulture seeking to seize the lump of meat, in the presence of Śrī Śaṅkara.

The description of the attainment of the status of Queen by [the protagonist] due to the absence of death; then, preceded by the narration of the account of the future seven births of both the King and the Queen as requested by the Queen, the description that the attainment of the state of Śiva will occur through the power of worshipping Śrīvidyā on Mahāśivarātri; therein, having observed King Candrasena’s constant devotion to Śiva, a celestial attendant named Maṇibhadra established friendship with him and bestowed upon that king the Cintāmaṇi jewel.

While King Candrasena was holding that funeral pyre to his neck and attempting to leap into it, other kings—unable to endure the power of that sovereign who had seized the kingdom and possessing that *cintāmaṇi* jewel—besieged him with armies. Having laid siege to the city of Avantī from all sides, at that moment, King Candrasena sought refuge in the glorious Maheśvara Mahākāla and entered the fire.

Chapter 5: The performance of the great worship (*mahāpūjā*) by Śrī Śaṅkara; on that occasion, the description of the greatness of devotion to Śiva by a five-year-old girl who had arrived at the temple of Śrī Rāma; in connection with that, the account of King Candrasena residing in Ujjayinī; and when a certain elderly cowherd woman, accompanied by her own child, had departed for her own camp after witnessing the festival of worship performed by the king, [the events involving] her five-year-old boy.

Having installed a stone *liṅga* of Śiva in a secluded, empty spot near her own camp, she took flowers as they were found and, having prepared offerings such as perfumes and parasols, performed the worship of Śiva with undistracted mind. Then, that cowherd girl arrived there and, out of anger, destroyed the Śiva-worship she had performed. Upon seeing the destruction of the worship of Śambhu, Bālakā fell into a state of unconsciousness due to extreme grief and lamentation; thereafter, what occurred?

By that Bāka, known as Kaṭha-chandasa, right there in that place, a divine golden palace made of jewels was established, containing an auspicious Śiva-liṅga. Then, being pleased, that Bāka offered an apology before Śrī Śaṅkara for the offense caused by interrupting his mother’s worship of Śiva. Then, at the arrival of evening and night, having seen from the mouth of Śrī Śiva that the entire village of cowherds had become made of divine gold, he beheld his mother there, possessing a divine form and sleeping soundly.

Having gone into the presence of his own mother and awakened her, he told her that the entire camp was made of gold. Then, having witnessed that marvel, the cowherd woman went to the king and reported the whole matter to him. Thereupon, the king, accompanied by his own charioteer and others, arrived at that camp and, seeing it to be composed of jewels and gold, he embraced that five-year-old cowherd boy. Thus, as that night passed away in joy, at dawn, [he heard] the words of the spies.

Having heard of the conduct of the son of the cowherd while staying in their own city, the kings from other lands were struck with wonder; they abandoned their state of enmity toward the king and established supreme friendship. Having entered that city and received the hospitality offered by the king, they beheld the great palace of Balarāma. Going there, they saw the celestial mansion bestowed upon the son of the cowherd as a mark of his grace. With joyful hearts, all those kings presented to the son of the cowherd garments, gold, jewels, and other gifts.

Regarding the gift of the kingdom to the cowherds stationed in that very place: at that very moment, the Lord Hanumān appeared there, accepted the worship and hospitality of all the kings, and in the midst of them all, having taken that cowherd boy under his protection, he described the greatness of the Śivarātri Pradoṣa, gave the name Śrīkara to that cowherd youth, and instructed him in the conduct of Śiva. [Then he spoke] to King Candrasena... *(Note: The source text appears to be a fragment from a Purāṇic narrative concerning the Śivarātri festival. The final sentence is incomplete, but the core meaning is as translated above.)*

[The description of how the prince named Śrokarākhya attained the world of Śiva through the power of worshipping Śiva. And now, the description of the greatness of the Pradoṣa-pūjā; in connection with that, the account of the king named Satyaratha residing in the country of Vidarbha; therein, the death of the king named Satyaratha in battle against the kings of Śālva; thereafter, his pregnant wife’s departure from the city and other places with great effort and her journey into a distant forest; and there—

When the birth of her son occurred during the delivery of that [cow], at that time, while she was drawing water from a nearby lake, she met her death by being trampled by a wild boar. On that occasion, hearing the crying of the newborn prince, a certain Brahmin woman named Mānā—a widow with one year-old calf—wandering in that region, saw the helpless infant whose umbilical cord had not yet been severed; and with a heart overcome by compassion, [she took him].

Desiring to take him back to her own home for his nourishment, she gained confidence through the words of Śaṅkara, who had assumed the form of a monk; thus, while caring for that child, she brought him back to her house. Then, while living in the city of Ekacakrā, that Brahmin woman named Umā, out of affection for her own son, provided food for the boy by collecting alms without distinction between them, and nourished him at her breast. Then, once, while that Brahmin lady was with those two...

While on his way to see a certain deity in another land accompanied by two boys, the great sage Śāṇḍilya, staying at that temple, saw those two boys; and among them, addressing the prince, he spoke of the wonderful variety of divine destinies. Upon hearing those words, when the Brahmin woman asked him out of a desire to know the lineage and other details of the boy she had brought, the venerable Śāṇḍilya [described] that boy’s...

An account of the detailed events of his various previous births is told; therein, due to the fault of interrupting the worship of Śiva during the Pradoṣa time in a previous birth, the king of the Pāṇḍyas died as a dog in a subsequent birth, and likewise, due to the fault of neglecting the worship of Śiva during the Pradoṣa time, his son also [died] in a subsequent birth.

The attainment of poverty for him and his mother due to the fault of killing their own wife out of jealousy in a previous birth; the description of their deaths in another life because of that enmity; and the description of the son of the hunchback falling into poverty in another birth because he was solely devoted to the worship of the Goddess in his previous life. Then, having explained the greatness of worshipping Śiva at twilight (*pradoṣa*), [the sage] gave instruction to both of those brothers to perform the worship of Śiva at twilight. And then...

Then, questioned by the lady named Tayomā, the venerable great sage Śāṇḍilya described, in the context of the Pradoṣa vow, the procedure for the worship of Śiva according to the scriptures, complete with its constituent parts and accompanied by musical sounds; thereafter, having performed the naming ceremony for the Brāhmaṇa youth as "Śucivrata" and for the prince as "Dharmagupta," he imparted the instruction of the Śiva-mantra to them both for the purpose of performing the worship of Śiva.

Then, having bowed to the sage Śāṇḍilya and taken leave of him, those two princes departed along with the wife of the twice-born. Subsequently, at nightfall, they stayed in the garden of the king of birds after performing worship to Śiva, in accordance with the command of their mother. Later, while the son of the twice-born was wandering on the riverbank, he discovered a treasure chest filled with gold; his mother then gave them permission to take it, provided it was divided equally between the two boys. At that time, the prince—

The Brahmin prince’s refusal to accept wealth offered by his own father, preceded by a demonstration of his lack of desire for it, and his display of contentment with what was obtained through his own good fortune; then, one day, while wandering in the forest, the sight of Gandharva maidens playing; and although he was forbidden by the Brahmin prince from going into their presence, that royal prince nevertheless went near those Gandharva maidens, [seeing] that beautiful...

Then, while the young prince was alone near him, the Gandharva princess named Draviṇa, known as Aṃhumatī, approached. As the two of them conversed with one another, both tormented by the arrows of love, the Gandharva princess offered her own pearl necklace to the prince, who was like a god upon earth, and made this vow: "I shall marry you the day after tomorrow," and then she departed with her companions.

The journey toward his father’s presence; then, having gone to his own palace with the prince Dharmagupta—the son of a Brahmin named Śucikrata—he reported to his mother, the princess Vipramāyī, the events occurring in the forest. Then, when the time for departure arrived, the prince named Dharmagupta went into that forest together with the son of the Brahmin. Having honored the two who had arrived with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, [he approached] Śarvaśaṅkara.

O King, having bestowed upon his own son-in-law, who had come for the sake of protecting the earth, the hand of his daughter according to the rites of marriage, and having granted him a vast wealth consisting of various jewels, elephants, chariots, horses, golden armor, swords, and female slaves, he himself departed by celestial chariot toward the world of the Gandharvas; there, along with that Gandharva maiden Śubhmatī, he was received with honor by the king of the Gandharvas named Dharmarāja, who was his father-in-law.

Having been granted a dowry by Śacī, and accompanied by an army of Gandharvas, he arrived at the city of Vidarbha; having slain all the enemy kings, he performed the royal consecration and ascended to the throne of his father’s ancestral kingdom. Having bestowed honors upon that Brahmin woman as if she were his own mother and honors upon that Brahmin youth as if he were his own brother, he resided in the city of Vidarbha together with that daughter of the Gandharvas, his own sister-in-law, and that prince named Dharmarupa.

A description of the exercise of sovereignty with great happiness through the power of the Pradoṣavrata and the impetuous joy of Śrī; then, a description of the greatness of the worship on the day of the Pradoṣavrata; next, a description of the greatness of the Somapradoṣavrata; and a description of the narrative of Sīmantinī, the daughter of a king, who was devoted to the vow of Damayantī. In that regard, Sīmantinī received from two Brahmins, who were skilled in the science of omens and had arrived in the presence of her father, [a prophecy of] her own future great fortune.

Then, out of fear of attaining widowhood, Bhāvivaidhanya separately sought refuge with Maitreyī, the wife of the great lord Yājñavalkya, in order to hear from her the means for the restoration of her conjugal fortune; thereafter, that Maitreyī explained to her the procedure for the worship of Śiva on Mondays; then, by that princess Sīmantinī, following the path instructed by Naitareya and others, the observance of the Monday vow (Somavāra-vrata) was commenced according to the prescribed rules; [and she was wedded] by Citrāṅgada, the son of Indrasena.

The marriage with Sīmantinī; then, while Citrāṅgada was living with his father-in-law, he once boarded a boat to cross the river Yamunā, whereupon he suddenly sank in the middle of the stream. Those on board all perished, and when it was learned that Prince Citrāṅgada had died by drowning in the boat, Ciñcā and the others were overcome with grief. Thus, Sīmantinī obtained another husband; yet, even though she had attained such a state of misfortune, [she remained steadfast].

Sīmantinī duly performed the observance of the Monday vow for three years; then, as Citrāṅgada was being submerged deeper and deeper in the waters of the Yamunā, the women of Vṛkasthala, desiring his welfare, led him to the king of the Vṛkas and informed him; Takṣaka then received Citrāṅgada with great honor and performed the rites concerning his chosen deity; and by Citrāṅgada, [the worship] of his own Lord...

The narration of Cāṇḍarīśaṅkara’s devotion; having heard his words, Takṣaka, being highly pleased, bestowed great honors upon Citrāṅgada. Hearing Citrāṅgada’s request to return to his own home, Takṣaka refreshed him with food consisting of the juice of the *tyajaskapavṛkṣa* tree and gave him much wealth, as well as a Rākṣasa and a serpent for assistance, and a horse that could travel anywhere at will and move unhindered for his vehicle.

Having bestowed the horse upon him and joined him with his various attendants, he gave the command for Citrāṅgada to return to his own abode. Then Citrāṅgada, having bowed to the king of the *takṣakas* and received his permission, mounted the horse, took up the wealth, and set out from Pātāla accompanied by those two—the Rākṣasa and the serpent—who had offered their assistance. Emerging from the waters of the Yamunā after crossing its stream, he mounted his steed on the bank of the Yamunā and began to sport. At that very moment, [he saw] her together with her friends in the Yamunā...

The giving [of the maiden] to him by Sīmantinī, who was his paternal aunt; then, having heard the news regarding Sīmantinī from the mouth of a female friend, he himself comforted Sīmantinī, saying, "We have informed your husband; he will return to you very soon. Compose your mind and do not grieve," for these are the gods of the Siddhas who move at will. Having thus consoled her, he departed for the city of his father, Citrāṅgada; there [he met] Indrasena, whose wings had been lost.

Having heard that the burden of the kingdom had been assumed by his father’s heirs, Citrāṅgada sent a message through the son of a Nāga to those heirs, requesting them to renounce the royal throne. Upon hearing Citrāṅgada’s message as reported by the Nāga’s son, all the heirs granted the kingdom to Indrasena; they informed him of the news regarding their son’s arrival and, having made a request for forgiveness, offered their propitiation. Thereafter, Citrāṅgada went to his own palace.

The failure to pay homage to his parents; the attainment of extreme joy by the parents upon receiving news of their son; King Indrasena’s dispatch of a messenger to King Citravarmā to report the auspicious news of his son's safe arrival from Pātāla; King Citravarmā’s attainment of great joy and auspiciousness upon hearing the news of the arrival of his son-in-law from the messenger; and thereafter, the king’s announcement to his daughter Sīmantinī of the joyful event along with the messenger.

Then, having summoned Citrāṅgada by means of this Śiva-mantra, and having again performed the marriage rites in full detail, Citrāṅgada bestowed his own daughter Sīmantinī upon him with great ceremony; then, after satisfying the Śvapacī woman with the ornaments and other items brought from Pātāla, he took her and returned to his own city, where he enjoyed the pleasures of sovereignty with great joy. Thus, on Mondays, the worship of Śiva and Gaurī—

A description of the attainment of all desired happiness by Śitragada and Sīmantinī through the power of that [penance]; a description of the history of the two sons of the two Brahmins named Bhītrasārasvata; therein, after Sumedhas and Sāmavat, the two sons of a Brahmin, had completed their study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (sāṅga) at Śaurikṛṣṭa, they went into the presence of the lord of Vidarbha at their father’s command to acquire wealth for their own marriage; then, the lord of Vidarbha, having observed those two sons of the twice-born as they were making their request—

"O young ones, having dressed one of you two in the guise of a woman, you shall become a Brahmin couple and approach Queen Sīmantiṇī; after receiving her hospitality, come to my hermitage, and then I will give you much wealth. When this was said, those two Brahmin youths, considering the king's command to be inviolable, dressed their friend Śaradvant in female attire and set out for the land of Niṣadha in the form of a Brahmin couple.

Then, on the Monday, between those two, the man was worshipped by Sīmantinī with the thought that he was Mahādeva, and the woman was worshipped with the thought that she was Pārvatī. At that very moment, the Brahmin’s son named Sāmavata—who had been worshipped by Sīmantinī with the thought that he was Pārvatī while wearing the guise of her female companion—truly assumed the form of a woman. Thereupon, having taken the jewels, garments, ornaments, and other gifts bestowed by Sīmantinī, Sāmavata stood between the two brothers, the sons of the Brāhmaṇa.

Upon attaining womanhood, the transformation of passion arose; consequently, Sāmavatī, having become a woman, made a request to Sumedha for the sake of amorous dalliance. Then, Sumedha, seeing his own friend—who had attained femininity—in private with her true form and in a state of sexual longing, somehow consoled her with words of discernment. Taking Sāmavatī with him, he brought her to his own home and reported the entire account to his father and her father. Then, [the two fathers], overwhelmed by grief—

Taking his two sons with him, he went toward the land of Vedabhū and spoke to that Brahmin with conciliatory words: "May you be free from the state of being a *sīlva*. At that, the king, for the sake of that Brahmin's son’s cessation of the *sīlva* state and the attainment of virtue, [approached] the sage Bharadvāja. Then, in connection with the narration of the power of the Monday vow (*somavāra-vrata*) performed by Sīmantinī, the sage Bharadvāja, through instruction on the subject matter of the *Sumedhas* and *Sāmavat*, [provided guidance] to those two.

Accompanied by the two young brahmins and Āmikāmava, he went and performed worship of the Mother of the World (Jagadambā). Appearing before him, the pleased Mother of the World declared that she could not alter what her devotee had done; she then gave her command for Sāmavatī to enjoy the pleasures of desire with Sumedhas as his wife, and granted a boon that the son of Sāmavatī’s father, the Sarasvata Brahmin, would have a son even more excellent than himself. Then, by him—

The giving away of his own daughter, named Sāmanvatī, to that Sumedhas according to the rites of marriage by means of the *Sārasvata-brāhmaṇa*; the description of their mutual enjoyment of sensual pleasures, preceded by the performance of sacrifices and the like; the description of the majesty of devotion to Śiva as established by Sumati; and how that Brāhmaṇa named Mandra, being solely intent on attachment to sense objects, came to reside constantly with a prostitute named Piñjalā; then, one day, of her—

While that righteous-souled yogi named Ṛṣabha was residing in the house of the courtesan Vardhakī, Śiva-yogin arrived. Through the performance of perfect service—beginning with washing his feet and ending with massaging them—by those two, the Brāhmaṇa Maṇḍra and the courtesan Piṅgalā, they produced in him an exceeding satisfaction until the end of the night. Then, on the second day, as he had come on the occasion of a pilgrimage, that Śiva-yogin departed; after some time, Maṇḍra the Brāhmaṇa [attained his goal].

Immediately after his death, [the child] was born to the wife of King Vañcavāha; however, at the very beginning, while she was still in the state of pregnancy, the king’s wife died due to poison administered by her co-wives through deceit. By a stroke of fate, she did not die, but rather suffered extreme agony from the burning caused by the poison. The infant born to that king’s wife also experienced intense suffering from the burning produced by the poison; thus it was for both of them.

Due to the fatal conjunction of the mother and son, the king, having observed their condition, determined by his own intellect that "even though medicine was administered by the physicians, they remain ill; surely these two have come from hell," and thus, through the mediation of his trusted ministers, he abandoned them in a desolate forest by means of a chariot. Then, while wandering in the forest with her husband Śaryāti, the queen, by the turn of fate, traveled toward the city of Vidarbha along a merchant's route found at a great distance.

This is the story of the daughter of the master of that city, [told] by a maidservant. Now, as an incidental narrative in the course of describing the majesty of Śiva, there is the account of the events concerning the temple named Mandrāha situated in the region of Avanti; therein, the sequence of the [narrative] is as follows: [the portion beginning with] "barāhmaṃ ha... [is from] the *Kavirahasya*.

The objects of the senses, having learned of that beautiful-eyed woman, brought her before her husband, Padmākara Vaidya. Then, Padmākara Vaidya, having ascertained the noble character of that queen, established her in his own home with due honor. Now, while that queen was living there in the house of the physician, by the turn of fate, her husband died from a disease such as a wound. At that time, the queen performed the funeral rites for him. Fate—

On that very day, by the power of yoga, the aforementioned Śivayogin named Ṣaibha arrived at the house of that very Vaiśya, Padmākara, on the occasion of his arrival. Having accepted the worship and hospitality offered by the Vaiśya, the Śivayogin Ṣaibha went into the presence of the queen, who was grieving for her son due to his death. Addressing her with supreme and meaningful instruction, he first made her undertake the practice of devotion to Śiva; then, having gone near her deceased son, he—

By means of ashes consecrated with the Śiva-mantra, the resuscitation of the child was performed; then, when the child had been restored to life, the queen and her kinsmen attained extreme joy. Thereafter, the yogin Ṛṣabhaśiva touched the mother and son with ashes consecrated by the Śiva-mantra; by the mere touch of those ashes, the mother and son attained divine bodies. Then, that boy was named Bhadrāyu by the yogin Ṛṣabhaśiva.

Having first described the naming ceremony and the future prosperity of both [the boy and the girl], and having heard that the child had reached the age of childhood and was residing in the house of Padmākara Vaidya, he departed for another place to undertake a pilgrimage; then follows the description of his birth in a future life as Sīmantinī, the wife of King Citrāṅgada, through the power of the worship and hospitality offered by the Śiva-yogin named Śivabhaktasabha to the courtesan Piṅgalā; and then [the account of] Bhadrāyoḥ in the house of Padmākara Vaidya.

From childhood, there was a friendship between him, the son of Padyākaraiśaya, and Sunaya, including playing together and other such activities. Then, through that very Padyākaravedaya, the two princes—the prince and the boy—were provided with the completion of their education and learning, preceded by the performance of sacraments such as the initiation (*upanayana*) via a Brahmin. Then, when Prince Bhadra reached his sixteenth year, the aforementioned master of the six-fold yoga arrived in his presence; [and] of that master of the six-fold yoga...

The meeting of Bhadrāyu with his own son and the performance of salutation; furthermore, the imparting of instruction on the true path to Bhadrāyu by the yogi Ṛṣabhaśiva, including the teaching of duties appropriate to the various stages of life (āśramas) and the ancient stories concerning the sons of kings; then, for the sake of liberation from all distress, the giving of a conch shell that grants victory and destroys all enemies to the youthful prince, which was handed over to him by the venerable Śivaseva while he was following behind.

Then, having touched his body with ashes, she gave him the strength of ten thousand elephants; having bestowed upon him a sword that brings victory by its mere sight, she instructed him in what was to be done, and having exhorted him with auspicious blessings, she received worship and hospitality from them both and departed for her desired destination. Then, the King of Magadha, the ornament of the Daśārṇa country, arrived with a vast army for battle against the King of Daśārṇa; thereafter, [the encounter] took place between the King of Magadha and the Lord of Daśārṇa.

Having fought in battle and defeated him there, he destroyed his entire army, brought the kingdom of Daśārṇa under his own control, and having bound him to his chariot, set out for his own country. Thus, while residing in the city of Vaiśyānagara, Prince Bhadrāyu heard from the mouths of people the news regarding his father’s defeat; then, with Padmākara the merchant’s son, Sunaya, as his companion, he mounted a horse and with great speed proceeded toward the kingdom of Daśārṇa, which had been devastated by his father, to the presence of the Lord of Magadha.

Seeing his army terrified by the enemy soldiers, he then swiftly entered the hostile force with an onset of fury. Blowing the victory-conch bestowed by Śiva and raising his sword of victory, he bewildered the hosts of the enemy's warriors with his arrows and struck them many times. Having bound the enemy king to his chariot, he released his father from captivity; and having liberated those wives of his own who had fallen under the enemy's power, as well as the wives and daughters of the city-dwellers, along with their cattle and wealth, he set them all free.

He sent word to his father and others in his own city; then, having entered the enemy army, he seized their wealth—women, elephants, horses, chariots, male and female slaves, and so forth—and having defeated the Lord of Magadha, he bound him along with his ministers and retinue and returned to his own city. Then, having been made to mount a chariot by Bhadrāyu, who clearly announced his own name, he performed the salutation at his father’s feet after first stating in general that he was the son of a Kṣatriya. Then...
Having come to Vedayapura together with his father’s younger brother named Sunaya, who was the son of Vedaya, Bhadrāyu established the sacred footprint there.

Then, the illustrious Śivayogin imparted the instruction on the *Śrīśivakavaca*, the hymn that provides protection from all dangers, to him; and Bhadrā, having been instructed, [remained] with him. Then, after some time had passed, his devotion to Śiva increased, and Bhadrā reported to her mother and to that noble youth named Padyākara all the accounts of the battles and other events. Then, on the second day, regarding King Citrāṅgada—who was also known by the name Candrāṅgada—he [related] that which had been previously mentioned...

The arrival of the Śiva-yogi Bhāṣyakāra before Citrāṅgada, and his issuing of commands—preceded by spiritual instruction—for the purpose of bestowing his daughter upon Prince Bhadrāyus; thereafter, at the word of the yogi Ṛṣabha, King Citrāṅgada summoned Bhadrāyus and, having bestowed his own daughter named Koṭimālinī upon him, initiated the preparations for the performance of the marriage rites; then, having dispatched a messenger to his father Vijayavāhu with due courtesy for the sake of his son’s wedding, [he awaited his return].

The invitation; the arrival of Vajrabāhu along with his retinue there in the royal capital of Niṣadha; the salutation of the father Vajrabāhu by his son Bhadrāyu upon his arrival; and when Vajrabāhu, not recognizing him and acting out of a desire to test Bhadrāyu, addressed his brother [with harsh words], the Lord of Niṣadha declared to Vajrabāhu: "This one, whom you abandoned in the forest together with your mother, is indeed your own son named Bhadrāyu"—thus was his history related.

After Vajravārāha had performed the funeral rites for his son and wife according to the prescribed rituals, he subsequently attained ultimate bliss through the recovery of his own son, Bhrātāpaṇaśaṃchi. Then, having received the honors and hospitality offered by King Citrāṅgada, he took his daughter-in-law Bhadrā and his son Bhadrāyuḥ, who was accompanied by his own daughter, and departed with a great multitude of people from the city of Vajrapura.

With great joy, he returned to his own city following the commencement of his undertaking; thereafter, Bhadrāyu, having previously performed the duties of crown prince by his father’s command, ascended to the throne and ruled over the entire circle of the earth. Following his accession to the kingdom, Bhadrāyu entered into an alliance with the minister of Hemaratha, the king of Māgadha, who had been imprisoned by his father, and secured his release from bondage. Subsequently, Bhadrāyu governed the kingdom while enjoying pleasures together with his wife, Kīrtimatī.

Thus ends the description of the merit of the worship of the Śiva-yogi performed by Bhadra in a previous birth. Now, at one time, King Bhadra, having ascended the throne of sovereignty, went to the forest with his wife and wandered there according to his own will. At that very moment, while a tiger was pursuing and harassing a certain Brahmin couple in that forest, they cried out with loud voices and offered a prayer to the king for their protection.

At that very moment, a tiger arrived and seized the Brahmin’s wife; while Bhadrāyu was attempting to rescue her, all his recitations of the Vedas became futile. When the tiger had carried off the Brahmin’s wife, the Brahmin, overcome with grief, uttered a cry of "Fie! upon the king.

Then King Bhadrāyu made various preparations for a chariot in order to console that twice-born man whose wife had been seized by a tiger; thereafter, in a secluded place, he entreated the king’s queen for the sake of his own enjoyment of desire; then Bhadrāyu, having set fire to both his wife and himself before that Brāhmaṇa and meditating upon Śiva, prepared to leap into the flames; at that very moment, for the purpose of testing his devotion, by that same [deity] who was wearing the form of a twice-born man...

The manifestation of Śrī Śaṅkara in his own form; the offering of praise by Bhadrāyus to that Śrī Śaṅkara; the granting of boons to Bhadrāyus and his wife by the Blessed Lord Śrī Śaṅkara, who was pleased by that praise; the attainment by Bhadrāyus of the enjoyment of royal happiness through the grace of Śiva; and finally, after entrusting the kingdom to his sons, the attainment of union with Śiva by Bhadrāyus, as well as [the fate] of Citrāṅgada, the father-in-law of Bhadrāyus, together with his wife Sīmantinī.

This is the description of the greatness of devotion to Śiva, beginning with the account of Dāmbhava. ... (Once, while that yogi Vāmadeva-Śiva was wandering in the forest, a Brahmarākṣasa approached to devour him and firmly squeezed his two arms; at the mere touch of his body, the yogi’s heart became filled with compassion and the rākṣasa attained the state of having all his sins destroyed. Then, by that Brahmarākṣasa, whose mind was filled with despondency through the recollection of his own past evil deeds...)

The description of how the yogi Vāmadeva Śiva, through the ripening of the evil deeds committed in his twenty-first previous birth, attained the state of a Brahma-rākṣasa and underwent the torments of hell; and then, when Vāmadeva asked, "By the mere touch of your body, the memory of my six hundred previous births has arisen, and my mind is exceedingly serene—how did you obtain such a state? the yogi Vāmadeva Śiva [applied] this ash from his own body...

By the term "prabhāva" (power), there is a description of the efficacy of the sacred ash (*bhasmasāmarthya*). In connection with that, [the text recounts] how, when the foot of the wicked Vāsiṣṭha Brāhmaṇa residing in the Draviḍa country was placed upon the head of a dog, by the mere touch of the ash from the foot of Atrikṣetraprabha, that Brāhmaṇa was instantly struck by a tumor on his inner organ as declared by Śiva. Thus, what was spoken by Vāmadeva is not [contradicted]; now follows the description of the majesty of the sacred ash (*bhasmamāhātmyavarṇana*).

The description of the account of the divine yogi named Vāmadeva through the attachment to *tadghama* (the ash); the greatness of the ash (*bhasmamāhātmya*); having heard the greatness of the ash, Brahmarākṣasa’s making a request to Vāmadeva to hear the greatness of the ash again in detail; the attainment of a divine celestial vehicle (*vimāna*); ascending that vehicle, their departure for the world of Śiva (*śivaloka*) with the Śabara couple, and the husband’s attainment of *sārūpya-mukti* (liberation in the form of Śiva). Thus.

The description of the greatness of the majesty of Śraddhā; then the description of the greatness of the vow of Māmadahēśvara, which bestows the accomplishment of all goals; thereafter, while Vāmadeva begins to describe in detail the greatness of the sacred ash (bhasma) to the sages residing in that region, Indra arrives slowly, followed by the arrival of all the gods, including Śakra and others, before the Blessed Lord Mahēśa during that great festival as He stands upon the mountain peak.

The offering of praise preceded by the worship of Maheśvara; thereafter, in the context of a dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Mahīdhara regarding the path taught by Vadaśvakhara, a detailed description of the greatness of the triple-ash mark (*tripuṇḍra*) and its application; and then, in connection with the discourse on the greatness of the ash, a narration of the account of the Śabara.

In that place, once while Prince Siṃhaketu, the son of King Pāṃsukūṭa, was wandering in the forest for the purpose of hunting, a certain Śabara follower who had gone along to assist him saw a Śiva-liṅga with its pedestal broken atop a certain stone slab in the woods. Taking it, he went into the presence of the prince and questioned him out of a desire to know the ritual procedure for the worship of the Śiva-liṅga. Then, that prince, in jest toward him, [said] constantly...

The performance of the worship of Śiva according to the prescribed ritual using funeral ashes (*citābhasma*), and by that Śabara, having taken those ashes to his own home, performing the daily worship of the illustrious Lord Śaṅkara with offerings according to the path taught by the prince and with a spirit of devotion; then, on one occasion, while that Śabara was distressed with anxiety because he had no funeral ashes for the worship of Śiva, [the prince], taking pity upon him, [provided] his own body for cremation; thereafter, by that Śabara, [the worship continued].

In the very vicinity of his own burnt house, having performed the complete ritual worship of Śrī Raṅkara with the ashes from the funeral pyre produced by the burning of his own wife, at the conclusion of the worship, when he made the daily invocation of his wife Śabarī for the sake of obtaining the grace of the Lord, at that very moment, the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) appeared before Śabarī.

His daily arrival and stay were as they had been before, and the condition of that house remained as it was previously. Then, while he was conversing with his wife in a state of alarm, he asked a question out of a desire to know the procedure for performing the *śrāddha* rite. Upon hearing that question, the venerable Śarudradeva consoled his wife, the Śabarī, set fire to his own house, and in its midst, he himself narrated the account of the conduct of the daughter of the sage, named Śāradā.

There, when the husband of that Śāradā, the Brahmin Padmanābha, died while traveling abroad, and she had returned home after his passing, Śāradā once went to the presence of the blind sage named Naidhruva who had arrived at her father’s house. When she offered salutations to that venerable blind sage, the sage bestowed upon her a blessing, saying, "May you be endowed with beauty and possessed of sons. Then...

Having learned of her situation from others, the sage Naidhruva gave her detailed instruction on the procedure for the worship of Maheśvara so that she might attain good fortune; then Śāradā undertook the vow of the Lord of Umā as told by the sage. Subsequently, her father, mother, and others, along with Śāradā, made a solemn agreement to ensure her residence until the completion of that vow according to its full requirements, in order to destroy the misery of her widowhood. Then, by that [agreement]...

I remained right there until the conclusion of the *naidhruva* vow performed by the great sage Śāradā. Then, for the duration of one year, Śāradā stayed in the presence of that venerable sage and performed the practice of the Maheśvara vow according to the prescribed rules. At the end of that year, she performed the concluding ceremony (*udyāpana*) of that vow; on the night of the day of the concluding ceremony, she engaged with the great sage Naidhruva in recitation, meditation, and austerity.

The manifestation of Śrī Jagadambā through the power of the devotion of those two at that moment; immediately thereafter, by the grace of Śrī Jagadambā, that blind man attained the status of the lord of Naidhruva-mahar-loka; then, when a hymn of praise was offered to Jagadambā by Śāradā together with the lord of Naidhruva-mahar-loka, the highly pleased Jagadambā, following the request of the lord of Naidhruva-mahar-loka, [proceeded] with a description of Śāradā’s previous birth.

“‘This girl shall obtain the bliss of love with her husband in a dream,’ [said Śiva]. Having granted this boon to Śāradā, he gave her this command: ‘When you see in a dream the person who has enjoyed both yourself and another, then give him [your son] born from your own womb. Then, being well-pleased, Śāradā, the daughter, performed worship and honors for her father, the sage Naidhruva. Then, [she did the same] for the sage Naidhruva and the parents of Śāradā.”

Having secretly informed everyone of the granting of boons by the Mother of the World (Jagadambā) and other matters, she departed for another land of her own accord; then, through the grace of Śāradā, the illustrious Jagadambā, she began to wear a pregnancy-belt due to engaging in sexual union with her husband. Subsequently, hearing that Śāradā was pregnant despite being a widow, all the people, led by Dhakāraka, gathered together in one place and performed a ritual incantation (*mantra*) to bring about her death. Thus...

When an investigation was conducted regarding Tejaneṭu, the truth of Śāradā’s innocence was established through truthful testimony. Upon hearing this, the men and women of Supāraṇanagara, having learned the true account from Śāradā herself in private, joyfully offered her their blessings and returned to their respective homes. Subsequently, Śāradā gave birth to a son; when the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) had been performed for that son of Śāradā, named Śāradeya, by his preceptor—

Immediately following her initiation into the truths, she was described as having reached the further shore of complete mastery over the knowledge of all four Vedas, along with their limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*upāṅga*), by means of those very four [Vedas]. Then, once upon a time, during a great festival of Śiva at the sacred site of Rukarṇeśvara Mahādeva, while they were staying there at Prayāga for that purpose, that Śāradā also went there together with her son and all the people residing in her village. There, in a dream, she beheld [the Lord] who bestows delight upon his abode.

The husband of that Brahmin born in Pūā was [named] Dīna; he, too, daily beheld Śāradā—who granted him pleasure in his dreams—and his son, who was dear to him and born from himself. Then, his mind overcome with wonder, he approached her and questioned Śāradā out of a desire to know her history. Thereupon, Śāradā related the entire account of her life to him. Then, by him...

Then, by the command of Śāradā’s parents, the Brahmin took the boy and Śāradā and departed for his own home. Subsequently, after that Brahmin had died in the course of time, Śāradā followed her husband onto the funeral pyre. Thereafter, both husband and wife went to their divine abode. Thus ends the description of the power of the Umā-Maheśvara vow.

[This is] the sixth chapter concerning both princes, namely Bhadrasakhasuta, known as Sudharama, and Tarakalya, the son of a royal minister. Now follows the description of the majesty of the *radarākṣa* (the auspicious eye-mark). In that context, within the narrative of the merit of wearing the *sadrākṣa*, [it describes] how the two sons of the ministers, from their very birth, lived in a state of supreme friendship with the sovereign of the Kadamira region; and how both of them, having always renounced ornaments made of gold and jewels—

Once, when King Madrasena, filled with great wonder upon seeing his son's extreme devotion to wearing *rudrākṣa* beads, had returned home from a journey, he honored the sage Parāśara according to the prescribed rites of worship. Then, desiring to know the reason for their mutual fondness for wearing *rudrākṣas*, he questioned him. Thereupon, that great sage Parāśara recounted the history of their previous births as the prince and the minister’s son. In that account, there was a woman living in the village of Nandi who possessed great opulence...

In the house of a certain dark-complexioned woman named Mahānandā, who was constantly devoted to the worship of Sadāśiva, there lived a cock and a crow. Having placed Rudrākṣa beads upon their ears, arms, and crests, they attained proficiency through daily instruction in that Vedic chant. Every day, at the time of twilight, they would perform a dance before Śiva during her recitation of the Veda. Then, one day, a certain Śiva-yogin observing the Śiva-vow arrived at her abode, and his hand—

Desiring to see his divine jeweled bracelet, that physician, though she was a courtesan, made a request for three days to remain under his control, saying, "Having accepted what you have brought, I shall serve you according to the duty of a wife. Then, having heard her words, that physician, who was devoted to the vow of Śiva, said, "So be it," and [brought] her the stone linga of Hara which he worshipped daily, along with a jeweled divine linga of Dveta.

Saying, "If it perishes, my life will perish," she gave orders for the protection of that *liṅga* through great effort. That prostitute, honoring the merchant's command, took the *liṅga* he had given her, placed it upon the pillar of the portico, and entered her own house. During the night, while walking along the road, she met that merchant happily and went to sleep with him. Then, at the time of dawn, when a fire suddenly broke out, [the *liṅga* was destroyed] by that prostitute.

The burning of the entire theater; the immediate arrival there by that awakened Vidyādharī and the swift release from their bonds of the cock and the monkey who had been tied up by the king and the Vidyādhara; the fleeing far away out of fear of the fire by the released cock and monkey from that site of the theater; and when the entire theater was in flames, [the sight of] a pillar standing in the theater [rising] above it.

Furthermore, there was the burning of the phallus made of trembling gold that had been deposited, resulting in the destruction of the *kavaka* fungus; then, upon seeing the fragments of that linga, the physician resolved to die and gave orders for the construction of a funeral pyre to enter into a state of great bliss (*mahānanda*).

Then, having bound the physician firmly with ropes, that courtesan Mahānandī had him placed upon a pyre outside the city. When that pyre was set ablaze, that devotee of Śiva entered it. Seeing the physician enter the pyre, the deeply distressed courtesan Mahānandī, honoring the vow of chastity for three nights and following the dharma of a faithful wife, gave away all her possessions to the devotees of Śiva.

Having circumambulated him three times and meditated upon Śiva, she prepared herself to enter that boat in order to follow her husband in death; at that moment, the Lord Śaṅkara himself appeared there and, having restrained her, told her how he had come in the form of a fisherman for the sake of testing her devotion, and then led Mahānandā, his devoted wife, along with all her attendants to the world of Śiva. At that time, while the rest of her family members remained behind, the house was set on fire.

Having released them from their bonds and driven them far apart, when the cock and the monkey both died by being crushed under their respective weights, it was revealed through another narrative that the monkey had now attained the status of a prince and the cock the status of a minister’s son; this was the account of the past lives of the prince and the minister’s son related by means of a parable. Furthermore, after Parāśara Muni had cast a shadow [of his vision], he prophesied that for that excellent minister’s son, a fever would arise on the seventh day from the onset of the illness.

Having learned of that and having consoled the sorrowful Bhadrasena with words of awakening, he instructed him on the performance of the recitation of the *Rudrādhyāya* for the sake of averting the death of that prince named Suṣarman. Then, at the king's request, while that supreme sage performed the daily consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the prince along with Brahmins endowed with vows, penance, and good conduct, preceded by the chanting of the *Rudrādhyāya*, on the seventh day, suddenly, in an instant, [the prince]— (Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated. The translation above reflects the available portion.)

Having attained awakening immediately thereafter, the prince then recounted how, while in the state of unconsciousness, he had previously encountered Śiva’s messengers and suffered defeat at their hands; subsequently, the sages Parāśara and others bestowed blessings upon that royal prince and proclaimed safety for the king; then, after all the Brahmins had been honored by the king, King Bhadrasena [acted] toward that royal prince.

Regarding his future fortune, King Bhadraśena honored the sage Parāśara by offering him food and other hospitality. Then, while the king was seated comfortably with his son and the great ṛṣis headed by Parāśara, the great yogin Nārada arrived there. After King Bhadraśena had performed the rites of worship for Nārada, the latter addressed the king, saying: "Yama has come here to take away your son."

The narration of how Vīrabhadra, dispatched by Śaṃkara, carried out the command of Yama; the description of Yama offering salutations and composing a hymn of praise to Vīrabhadra, followed by the account of Vīrabhadra’s release of Yama; and the departure of Nārada after bestowing his blessing—saying that through the power of the consecration following the recitation of this chapter, the fear of death has been averted for your son, he shall attain a lifespan of ten thousand years along with all happiness, and he shall be free from fear.

The bestowing of blessings upon the king and his sons by the great seers such as Parāśara and others, their respective departures for their own hermitages, and thus the description of the conclusion of the Radrādhyāya.

—In the context of describing the greatness of listening to the Purāṇas, there is an account of the story of a base Brāhmaṇa named Vidura and his wife named Bindulā. Therein, a certain day, that base Brāhmaṇa named Vidura, who was devoted to a paramour and constantly associated with him, saw his own wife—who had been consorting with that paramour—engrossed in sexual pleasure with him. Having seen her, he reproached her, saying: "Having given sexual pleasure to those men, you should take wealth from them [and give it to me]."

"Give me wealth for my livelihood so that I may enjoy myself with a courtesan; you, however, enjoy yourself with a paramour. Having said this, both of those base individuals engaged daily in wicked conduct. In this manner, after some time had passed following the death of that merchant-beggar, Vidūṣaka—whose youth was somewhat advanced—went one day on a festival to the Gokarṇa shrine for a pleasure pilgrimage, accompanied by his paramour’s son and his own kinsmen.

Having gone there to a certain place while an ancient sage was reciting a Purāṇa, Vidulā heard from the mouth of that reciter, at the time of hearing the Purāṇa, the account of Yama’s torments: "Upon the temples of passion of women devoted to paramours, the servants of Yama cast a mass of blazing sprouts. Her heart burning with the memory of the evil deeds she had constantly committed with her lover, Vidulā went in secret to that foolish reciter and initiated this discourse out of a desire to know the means for the pacification of the consequences of her own misdeeds; then he [spoke].

By the instruction of the Paurāṇika, Vindumatī—having been reminded of her own terrible sin of infidelity merely by hearing the Purāṇa, and being terrified of the most intense torments of hell—was first consoled and then instructed to listen to the Purāṇic narratives that establish devotion to Śiva, preceded by the chanting of the mantra of Śiva’s names along with devotion to Śiva. Thereafter, Vindumatī herself, from that very same Paurāṇika who was devoted to Śiva, heard the Purāṇic narratives centered on devotion to Śiva. The Purāṇa...

Through the power of hearing [the teachings] of that Bindulakhācārya, as the afflictions of *rajas* and *tamas* were gradually destroyed within her heart, Śrī Śaṅkara entered it. Thereupon, she daily performed devotion to Śrī Śaṅkara according to the path instructed by him. By the power of her devotion to Śrī Śiva, she completely severed the bonds of all karma and, at the end, departed for the world of Śiva. There, in the world of Śiva, she was received with honor at the feet of Śrī Pārvatī, the Mother of the Universe, who had arrived there.

Then, having heard from the mouth of the Pārvatī that her husband had attained the state of a Piśāca, she made a request to the Gandharva named Tumburu—who was staying on Mount Vindhya—to recite the Purāṇas for her husband. At her request, Tumburu went to the Vindhya mountains and, upon reciting the stories of the Lord of Śrī Gaurī to that Piśāca, he brought about the liberation of that lord of the Vidulas from his Piśāca birth.

The description of the departure for the world of Śiva after ascending a celestial chariot; the description of how those two children attained liberation in the form of Kaivalya through the singing of the venerable Ādivarāha; and the conclusion of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Brahma-purāṇa, purified by the hearing of the meritorious narrative that brings about the realization of the venerable Śiva. Thus ends the third section, the Bāhya-uttara-khaṇḍa, within the Brahma-khaṇḍa.
Thus ends the third section, the Jāhnavī-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. || 3 ||
Now begins the fourth section, the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, in the great Purāṇa known as the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. Chapter [number].
Or else, here follows the first chapter of the Kāśī-khaṇḍa.
(-) || [End of section] ||

The auspicious invocation; the Sūta’s commencement of the narrative of the Kādī-khaṇḍa of Vyāsa; Nārada’s bathing in the waters of the Narmadā, his worship of Oṃkāra, and his sight of the Vindhya mountain before him; a description of the Vindhya range as an incidental digression; and the description of how the sun’s path was obstructed by the growth of the Vindhya, after hearing the words of the sage Nārada that Bheru was acting with arrogance—this being on one hand, while on the other there is no connection with Bharadvāja.

The description of the world’s instability due to the fierce heat of the sun; the praise of Brahmā by the gods; the prior pacification of the gods by Brahmā through describing the meritorious conduct of the men who come to Satyaloka in order to demonstrate the absence of fear there; at Brahmā’s word, the description of the departure of the immortals, eager for the festival of the *Śrīkāśī-Dākāśīdarī* to go to the presence of the sage Agastya at Śrṛṅgaverapura in order to dispel the distress caused by the world’s singleness; and a brief description of Kāñcī.

[The narrative continues: Having performed a pilgrimage to the sacred field of Kāśī, including visits to Maṇikarṇikā, Viśveśvara, and other sites, the gods went to the hermitage of Agastya. There, in that hermitage, the gods beheld Agastya in the form of Upamanyu. Incidentally, there is a description of Upamanyu; and in connection with this, the conduct of chaste women is described. Then, at the request of Bṛhaspati, who was praying for the prevention of the growth of Mount Vindhya which was obstructing the path of the sun, Agastya offered consolation to the immortals. [The account of] the gods...

Having accepted the request of the gods for his departure to his own celestial realm, Agastya Muni set out with his wife toward Kāśī to effect the subduing of the Vindhya mountain. While the sage was traveling, grieving at the separation from Kāśī, he lamented fervently before the deities such as Īśāna, Nātha, and Kāra. Upon seeing the sage Agastya approaching, the Vindhya mountain consented to its diminution, promising that it would remain so low until the sage’s return. Thus, the sage spoke before the mountain, saying, "It shall not grow again until my arrival."
