The performance of the *Mahālakṣmī-stotra* by the sage Agastya; the granting of boons to Agastya by Mahālakṣmī; the departure of Agastya for the south; the description of the greatness of sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha-māhātmya*) and, in that context, the narration of the excellence of the Kāśī-kṣetra; and the illumination of the Kārīṣmatī [river], which brings all sacred sites into the Kāśī-kṣetra.

The arrival of the earth [in the form of a cow] within the body of the Brāhmaṇa named Śivaśarman, a resident of the city of Mathurā; the intense anxiety of that twice-born man regarding the pilgrimage to the seven cities; his departure from home for the purpose of visiting those seven cities; his completion of the pilgrimage to Ayodhyā and subsequent arrival at Prayāga; the description of the greatness of Prayāga by a group of sages; the account of the Brāhmaṇa’s journey to Kāśī; his departure for Mahākālavana; the description of the great majesty of Mahākāla through his association with it; and the account of the pilgrimage to the holy site of Māyāpurī—[this is] the [account] of the Brāhmaṇa.
Having ascended a golden celestial chariot attended by the Vaiṣṇava hosts named Puṇyaśīkha and Suśīkha, Māyāpuyī reached the end of his life and ascended the path of the sky as a twice-born man.

In the *Māyāpurī* section of the *Yuktikalpataru*, there is a narrative concerning how the liberation of a deceased twice-born man named Śivarāmaṇa was not attained. To demonstrate that direct *sāyujya* (union) is not found in the six cities beginning with Māyā, the dialogue between Śiva and his attendant Viṣṇu begins. Following the account of the twice-born man, there is a description of the conduct of virtuous men residing in the worlds of the Piśācas, Guhyakas, and Gandharvas. Then, for the purpose of honoring the deceased twice-born Śivarāmaṇa who has arrived in the realm of Yama, [the attendant] performs a respectful worship.

The arrival of Dharmarāja; the question of the twice-born, "How is this? upon hearing the gentle words and gentle forms of Dharmarāja; the description of the world of Yama in brief by way of explaining Yamadeva’s two forms; the description of the world of the Apsarases; the description of the world of the Sun; the determination of the greatness of the Gāyatrī mantra in connection with the description of the worship of the Sun; and the determination of the procedure for offering the *argha* oblation.

—The description of the excellent city of Sahasrākṣapura; the description of the city of Vītihotra known as Aryiṣmatī; the narration of the origin of Kaśānu, along with the account of the sage named Viśvānara residing in the city of Jyotiṣmatī; the description of Guciṣmatī, followed by the account of the sage going to the sacred field of Kāśī and performing penance near the Vīreśvara Śiva-liṅga; the month of Trayodaśa (the thirteenth day of the lunar fortnight) for those devoted to helping others; and the greatness of Kāśī, which surpasses all other holy places such as Śrīraukasikhara and others.

The manifestation of Śiva’s face upon the Liṅga at Bāṭaspeṇa; the narration of the Abhiṣāṭaka hymn; the departure of the sage, who was satisfied by the splendor of Śiva’s mountain, to heaven; and later, the birth of Vaiśvānara from Śuciṣmatī; the birth of a son named Śubhahūta; the description of the purificatory rites such as the *jātakarma*; and the parents’ falling into grief upon hearing from Nārada that the boy named Vaiśvānara possessed the marks of a "Gaṇḍa" on his hand according to the science of palmistry (*sāmudrika*); and the departure of the sage’s son to Kāśī for the sake of practicing penance.

The performance of religious observances after establishing a weary man [in his place]; the words addressed by the sage’s son to Kuñjara, who had come for alms, saying, "I cannot bear to take anything from you"; Indra’s attempt to strike down the mountain peak upon hearing those words; the fainting of the sage’s son; the arrival of Śiva there; the description of the monkey’s attainment of lordship over the quarters and other honors through Śiva’s boon; and the description of various other worlds.

In the Vindhya forest, for the sake of saving the life of a caravan leader named Śigākṣa who desired to travel toward the city of Viśvanātha, there was the attainment of joy through the gift of his own life; then the description of the Varuṇa-śāka tree; the carrying away of Śuciṣmat, the son of the patriarch Kardama, by a crocodile while he was playing in a lake; and having heard of his son’s death in the lake, the sage’s departure to the abode of the gods after disregarding the excessive devotion shown during worship, and the bringing of Sauīrumāra, the son of Vākaka.
Having established an image of Śiva at Kārohaṇa, the pure-minded young sage performed austerities and, through the grace of Śiva, attained the world of Aruṇa.

A description of the city of Gāndhavatī belonging to Pavana, the life-breath of the world; the performance of penance by the pure-souled Kāśyapa after establishing the image of Śrīkāntā; the emergence of that [image] from beneath the door-panel of Śivā’s palace; a description of the city of Alakāvatī belonging to Guhyakeśvara; and the account of how in the city of Kāmpilya, a son named Guṇanidhi—who was devoted to the ocean of virtues—was born to a Brāhmaṇa named Yajñadatta, yet became addicted to vice despite his name, and how he was restrained for a long time by his mother.

The description of the father’s banishment of Suta from his own home due to his misconduct, and the subsequent offering of lamps; the account of how he, having been raised by a Chandala and having his head shorn on the night of Śivarātri because of his theft of food, attained the status of a prince of the Kaliṅga kingdom; and the description of how, through his offerings of lamps at the temples of Śiva there, he attained in another birth the state of being the son of Viśvāvasu, and how, by performing unbearable austerities, he became a friend of Śiva and attained lordship over the Yakṣas and others. Om Vara Om.

Oṃ Oṃ! Among the sixty daughters of Dakṣa Prajāpati, Rohiṇī and the other twenty-seven maidens shared a single husband. When the Danava lords, Andhaka, and his soldiers were slain by the gods in battle, their blood fell upon the sacred ground of Śrī Śiva. From that place, the fire of their sin was extinguished. He [the Moon], whose face is like the eye of Arundhatī, beheld this from the world of the Moon (Candraloka). Having established the lineage of Soma, who was born from the mind of Brahmā, in Vārāṇasī, he then departed for his own abode.

The performance of great austerities and the account of his attainment of great sovereignty through the grace of Śiva;—having established [himself] in this direction, a brief description of the realm of the stars (*nakṣatraloka*) accomplished by Soma after he obtained his wife and performed penance in Vārāṇasī according to the boon of Śiva; the abduction of the preceptor’s wife by Soma, the son of Atri; the account of the battle between Sūrya and Candra; and the restoration of Tārā to Bṛhaspati by Candra at the word of Brahmā, which brought the battle to an end.

In that [chapter], the birth of Budha; the worship of Śiva performed by Budha; and the description of the boons granted by Śiva to Budha, including his sovereignty over the Kapālas and the attainment of his own natural complexion... [and] the restoration of Śukra to life by Bhārgava through the Saṃjīvanī mantra; at the request of the gods, Nandikeśvara brought Śukra by means of a divine [power] and deposited him within his own mouth; the description of the battle between Andhaka and his army against the Pramathas; and the emergence of Śukra from the mouth of Śiva.

A description of Śukra’s performance of penance in Vārāṇasī and his attainment of boons such as lordship over the world through the grace of Śiva; the account of Datta’s lordship over the world and so forth; the performance of penance by Āṅgirasa in Vārāṇasī for the sake of Śiva’s grace; the attainment of lordship over the world and the status of preceptor of the gods by Diva through the favor of a boon; the account of the birth of Śanaiścara from the shadow (Chāyā) which was a likeness of Māṇḍātṛ’s wife; and [his] becoming the chief among the planets through the performance of penance in Vārāṇasī.

And there is no description of your own attainment; rather, [the story begins] with Dhruva, who, having been insulted by his stepmother while seated on his father’s lap, went to the forest for the sake of penance at his mother’s word, and [there] met you, O Lord. Then, having beheld you, he attained the highest state, as well as the worlds of the gods. Chapters and Subjects: Chapter: Description of the city of Īśānī inhabited by the devotees of Śiva. Subjects: Description of the greatness of the Īśānīgama established by the host of Rudras beginning with Ajaikapāda. Subjects: [The account] of [Dhruva] residing in Madhuvana on the bank of the Yamunā.

A description and examination of Dhruva’s penance; and the direct vision of the Blessed Lord by Dhruva. [The Lord says: "O Dhruva, I shall grant you the station of the pole-star (Uttarāyaṇa), which is the support of the universe; nevertheless, go with me to Kāśī and perform the worship of the Liṅga there, so that you may attain fulfillment. Having thus instructed him, the departure for the city of Kāśī with the Blessed Lord; and there, having attained fulfillment through the installation of the Liṅga by Dhruva, his return to his own home.

1. The conversations of the inhabitants of Mahārjanatapokhō who had gathered in Satyaloka with Brahmā, and the description of the creation of Kādi by Brahmā preceded by the propitiation of the twice-born.

The description of the measurement in *yojanas* from the world of the elements (*bhūloka*) up to the world of Śiva; the narration of how Viṣṇu, through worship here, grants the state of self-identity (*ātmasātmya*) to the devotee; the account of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of Viṣṇu by Śiva; and the description of how the twice-born [devotee], upon dying in Māyāpura, attains residence in the abode of Viṣṇu for twelve thousand years and enjoys various pleasures. Then, when his merit is exhausted, he attains the status of a king in the village of Nandivardhana and, while protecting his subjects, hears the story of Kāḍī, whereby joy arises within him as he recalls his own past life.

Having performed the ritual installation of the Śivaliṅga named Baddhakāṭeśvara at Viśavasa-varā-tupa-ra-hāttra, King Divodāsa was performing austerities before it. Śiva, having arrived for the purpose of testing him, and after the test was concluded, made a friend of the king; the description of the duration of the king’s stay follows the account of the divine day as explained by the attendants of Viṣṇu.

[The account of] the venerable Giri, having circumambulated Agastya Muni together with his wife; the *Skandavana* and the *Kumāradalana*; the hymn to Skanda composed by Agastya; the sages’ discourse to Skanda regarding the greatness of Kāśī; the description of the fruits of residing in Kāśī as established by Skanda; the narration of the origin of Avimukta; the description of Viṣṇu’s penance on the banks of the Ṛkṣakariṇī; [the account of] Maṇikaṇikā; the description of the identity of Gaṅgā; and the recitation of the *Daśaharā-stotra*.

—“Because of the weight of Śiva’s presence in Kāśī, there is no mention of great or minor sins for those who die in Gaṅgā; however, in another region, a certain twice-born man named Vādahīka, a husband of a *vṛṣalī*, was killed by a tiger in the forest. As a vulture carrying his bones and flesh was departing, it fought with another vulture. By the falling of those bones into the Gaṅgā at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Jāhnavī, he attained liberation from the various types of sins that had caused him to fall into hells such as *Avīcī*.”

Beholding that Vāhīka attain happiness even though he had been cast away by others, it caused wonder to all; finally, having ascended a celestial chariot (*vimāna*), the Vāhīka departed for the heavenly realm (*svargaloka*). There follows the narration of the majesty of the Gaṅgā, including the statement that those who are incapable [of pilgrimage] obtain a fruit equal to that of the knowers [who have traveled]; the *Sahasranāma-stotra* of the illustrious Gaṅgā which wards off great sins; the description of the superior majesty of the sacred field (*tīrtha*) at the confluence of the Gaṅgā brought down by Bhagīratha at Maṇikarṇikā; and the description of the location of the auspicious *Śivaraṇa* situated to the south and north.

The appointment of Dedaṭīvināyaka to inflict punishment upon those who commit suicide within [the city] without Śiva’s command; the narration of the history of Dhanañjaya the merchant; and in the etymological explanation of the name Vārāṇasī, the origin of King Kāṭa from Śiva after he had severed the head of Brahmā; the departure of King Kāṭa from Prayāga in the guise of a Kāpālika due to the fear of the sin of killing a Brahmin arising from the severing of Brahmā’s head; and the arrival there of Kāṭabhairava, who was pursued by the sin of Brahmin-slaughter in the form of a six-faced phantom.

The journey to Pātāṭa; therein, a description of the stationing of Kāla and Maira at the Kapālamocana Tīrtha for the washing away of all sins. Then follows the account of the birth of the son named Harikeśa to the wife of the Yakṣa named Pūrṇabhadra, who was called Kuṇḍalā, through her divine worship. From his childhood, Harikeśa was devoted to Śiva; out of fear of being beaten by his father, he departed for the Kādambarī forest. There, he described to Pārvatī the celestial Ānandakānana as ordained by the gods. Āna...

...the account of how Maheśvara, pleased by the penance of Harikeśa at Nandakānana, granted him the status of Daṇḍapāṇi, followed by the description of the eight Daṇḍapāṇis. ... Then follows the description of the origin of the place named Jñānavāpī and the glorification of its greatness; the abduction of the daughter of Darisvāmin, a resident of Kārī, who was worshipping at Jñānavāpī, by a Vidyādhara enamored of her beauty; and while that Vidyādhara was being slain, the battle between the Rākṣasa and the King, as well as the mutual [conflict] between the King and the Vidyādhara.

The narration of the abandonment of the body by the daughter of Harisvāmika, who, believing herself to be a Vidyādharī, feared death at the hands of Rāhu; the marriage of the two after they had both attained royal bodies and witnessed the painted scroll there; their journey to Kāśī with Mālyaketu and Kalāvatī; the performance of the Kāśī pilgrimage there, and the account of both of them ascending the Adhiśma mountain and departing for heaven according to the instruction of Śiva at the confluence of the Jñānavāpī; and the description of the majesty of the Jñānavāpī.

In the context of describing the noble conduct (*sadācāra*) of Brāhmaṇas who attain Kāśī, there is a detailed exposition of the duties to be performed daily (*nityakarvyadharma*). Following the description of the noble conduct of Brāhmaṇas, there is an exposition of the duties regarding the twice-born (*dvija*) and others. Since the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*) cannot be established without a woman of auspicious characteristics, there is a detailed exposition of the characteristics of women (*strīlakṣaṇa*), followed by a description of the eight types of marriage (*vivāha*). Furthermore, there is an extensive narration of the auspicious conduct that leads the twice-born and others to the attainment of Kāśī.

... [This section contains] an account of the conversation between Divodāsa and Pehāsa; an explanation of the origin of the name Avimukta at Avimukta; a description of the nature of forbidden conduct, such as traveling to Kārikā-kṣetra and the prohibited practices of certain Brahmins; and a definition of the prescribed conduct for those in the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśramin*).

[The section contains] a detailed exposition of the duties of forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and ascetics (*yati*), followed by the narrative of Yoga; an account of the signs preceding death for those who are near its end; and a description of the means [to liberation] interspersed with the majesty of the holy site of Kāśī. While King Divodāsa was residing in Kāśī and ruling the earth, all the gods, beginning with Viśveśvara, abandoned that city and departed for Mandarācala. A description of the happiness of the subjects under King Divodāsa’s reign follows, as well as how even the gods, having abandoned heaven, went to the earth; and having witnessed that—

[The description of the suffering caused by separation from Kārttikeya as the King’s own power was proclaimed; the account of how the host of Yoginīs crushed King Divodāsa with a stone in order to force him to abandon the sacred field of Kāśī; the narration of how the sixty-four Yoginīs, by Śiva’s command, created obstacles for King Divodāsa in the city of Kāśī; and the enumeration of their names...]

Then, having brought about the discovery of Divodāsa’s hidden treasure, there is the arrival of Śiva as directed by others for the purpose of expelling him from Kāśī; the description of how Ravi, intent on seeking a vulnerability while Divodāsa was engaged in various efforts against his kingdom, divided himself into eight forms and established his residence in Kāśī itself; the description of the location of Roṭāraka; the narration of the procedure and majesty of the pilgrimage to that holy site; and the definition of Uttarākaṅkuṇḍa, including the account of the daughter of a twice-born man who remained there after the death of her parents.

The performance of penance in the vicinity of Rākā; Gaurī’s bestowing of boons upon him in the form of her own companionship; the description of the majesty of Uttarārka Kuṇḍa; the account of how Sāmba, the son of Kṛṣṇa, contracted the disease of leprosy due to the curse of Kṛṣṇa arising from his insult of Nārada; the cessation of that disease through his performing penance after constructing a pool in Kāśī under his own name for its remedy; and the narration of the majesty of Sābāditya along with the majesty of the Kuṇḍa, occurring in connection with the forest exile of the Pāṇḍavas.

The journey to Kāśī; there, the propitiation of the Sun by Draupadī; the granting of a boon to her by the Sun; the determination of the location for the residence of the Sun worshipped by Draupadī; the description of the majesty of the Māyāditya; the narration of the dispute between Kaṭa and Vinatā regarding the color of Uccaiḥśravas; therein, the defeat of Vinatā by Kāpavya (Uśanas) and the resulting imposition of slavery upon her; the description of Garuḍa’s fetching of the nectar (*sudhā*) to remove his mother’s servitude; and [the events] of Vinatā and Garuḍa at Kāśī.

The first part of the Śrī Kāśī-khaṇḍa consists of the account of the performance of penance preceded by the installation of the Śiva-liṅga, and the description of the majesty of the Khakholka-sūrya shrine preceded by the granting of boons to those two.
Now, from the Kāśīkhaṇḍa, that very [account] is as follows:

Description of the majesty of Aruṇāditya; narration of the cause of Vinatā’s servitude; description of the majesty of Vṛddhāditya worshipped by Vṛddhahārīta; the performance of penance by Suyeṣṭha after installing Śiva-liṅgas at Kāśī at the command of Viṣṇu; description of the majesty of that [deity] preceded by the name Kerāvāditya; a brief description of the Ādityas of Vimalagaṅgā; and the arrival of Caturañjana, sent by his enemy to dig up the treasure buried by Divodāsa, into Kāśī in the guise of a Brahmin.

The account of how the site was made auspicious by the performance of ten horse-sacrifices (*daśāśvamedha*) and the description of the greatness of that sacred ford (*tīrtha*); the description of the departure of Śaṅkuṇa and others at the command of Śiva, in order to ascertain the situation of the Yoginīs sent by Śiva—who had established their own bodies there and remained in that very place—and to expel Diti’s son; and the description of the battle.

In the context of describing how the Aroṣaṇa [liṅga] was installed by a multitude of Kapardis who were exceedingly devoted to Śambhu, there is the narration of the laughter of the twice-born named Vāsmitika; the description of the liberation of the Piśāca created by him; and the account of the greatness of the pilgrimage to the Tīrtha that grants release from sin.

The description of the majesty of the Śiva-liṅga installed by the Gaṇa Piga; and how those Gaṇas and others who were sent by Śiva during the day to observe the state of Kāśī, having witnessed their own non-return [to the world], entered Kāśī at the command of Śiva, as described in the section on the entry of the Lord of Gaṇas.

Assuming the guise of an astrologer from the Gaṇeśa temple, the description of Gaṇeśa’s appearance on Kāyāvarohaṇa; the deluding of many people residing in the city through his own *māyā*, and the description of Gaṇeśa’s conversations with the king’s wives in the inner apartments; at the assembly of King Divodāsa, the description of the king followed by Gaṇeśa’s narration of future events in the form of instructions given to the Brahmins upon their arrival; the description of the locations of Gaṇeśa such as Agnīdhra, Darśa, Candra, and others; and then—

While Śiva was overcome with anxiety due to the loud lamentation, Gaṇeśa also described the manifestation of Viṣṇu for the purpose of uprooting King Divodāsa; he described the various locations of Viṣṇu in Kāśī, and described the manner in which Viṣṇu, Lakṣmī, Garuḍa, the Buddhist mendicant, and the disciple established the Buddha-dharma. Having made the subjects inclined toward unrighteousness, according to the words of Gaṇeśa, Viṣṇu, in the form of a twice-born, gave instruction to the king regarding the installation of the image of Śiva; [the king] then worshipped the phallic emblem of Śiva.

Having ascended the celestial chariot of King Divodāsa, [the sage] proceeded toward the city of Kaiḍāsa. Then, in connection with the hymn of praise to Gaṇeśa composed by Dibi, there follows a description; the naming of Gaṇeśa as Daṇḍirāja; the account of how a daughter was born from the power of his own penance; her performance of austerities at the command of her father; the granting of a boon to her by Brahmā; and how, upon seeing her, Dharma’s passion was kindled, leading to their mutual union on the banks of the Ganges and Yamunā, where their sins were washed away by the rays of the sun, resulting in the birth of Vedaśiras from the sage.

The narration of how the daughter of Śimapsaras, named Dhūtapāpā, attained purification and liberation; a description of the majesty [of that place]; a brief description of Vaiṣṇava sites such as Ādikeśava, Avatārakṣetra, and Keśava; a description of the various holy places established by Vidumādhava, including the distribution of food and other offerings; and a description of how the sage Viduma, through the account of Vidumādhava, obtained the fruit of his desires and the attainment of the discus-bearing Lord.

When Viṣṇu and the others had entered Kairāsapura by means of the essence of Viṣṇu’s discourse with Divodāsa, they went to the abode of Hara to bring him there by day. There follows the description of the Kapiratīrtha established by Śiva, the account of the manifestation of the Bull-bannered Lord at Kapiratīrtha, and the description of the penance of the sage Jaigīṣavya. Then comes the account of the attainment of the supreme state by Śiva, the description of the extraordinary nature of the mountain, and the arrival of those who had come from various regions to see Śiva along with his attendants and Ambā on Mount Mandara.

The glorification of Śiva for the twice-born and the narration of the *Ṣattraiṃśacchata* (one hundred and thirty-six); the description of the majesty of various Śiva-liṅgas such as Parāśareśvara, Māṇḍavyeśvara, Jābāḷeśvara, Kandukeśvara, and others; the determination of the locations of the Śiva-liṅgas situated in Kāśī beginning with Śaileśvara; and the account of how, through the grace of Śiva, a certain courtesan attained another body after performing dances, songs, and vigils near Raleśvara as directed by Śiva.

The description of the appearance of the daughter of the Gandharva king named Vasubhūti; the account of her marriage and other life events with Ralaśvaravaryīchaga-pramāva, the son of Ralaśvaravaryī, who was born from the supreme sacrificial fire; the narration of the majesty of Dākṣāyaṇīśvara; and the account of the greatness of Kṛttivāseśvara, by whom Śiva granted the boon that Gajāsura—the son of the demon Madiṣa—who was otherwise incapable of being slain according to the rules of ritual, would be killed by him. Chapter 7. [End of] Part A (Ka).

(28d) [The account of the origin of Kṛttivāseśvara]; the description of the assembly of the sixty-eight *āyatanas* known as Śubhada, situated in various locations; the description of the stationing of nine crores of Caṇḍas, accompanied by their retinues such as Vetālas, in various places for the purpose of guarding the city; and [the account of] the Goddess Kālarātri going to the presence of Nārāyaṇa to subdue the demon Durgāsura, the son of Nara, who was unconquerable by men and had usurped the sovereignty of the three worlds.

The arrival of the army of the demon Durgāsura at the presence of the Blessed Lady upon the command of Kātharaśiva; the description of the emergence of Śakti from the body of the Goddess upon seeing the wicked army engaged in battle; the account of the combat between the demon Durgāsura and the Blessed Lady;

the enumeration of the names of the weapons issued from the body of the Blessed Lady; the description of the battle between the Daitya and the Goddess; the narration of the hymn of praise offered by the Goddess Durgā, who was satisfied by the slaying of the demon Durgāsura; and the exposition of the fruits of worshipping Durgā and Bhairava.

The enumeration of the four syllables beginning with *Oṃ* as described by Śiva to Pārvatī; the narration of the origin of *Oṃkāra* in the context of describing its manifestation; the account of the hymn to *Oṃkāra* composed by Brahmā; and the description of the greatness of the *Oṃkāra-Śaligrama*. Furthermore, the story of Damana, the son of Bharadvāja, who became detached after studying the sciences of the Pādma-kalpa; his meeting with the sage named Garga on the banks of the Narmadā; the description of the majesty of *Oṃkāra* as expounded by the sage Garga; and the power of this mantra to ward off the sins accumulated over many births for the sake of a Kṣatriya.

...and the description of his various manifestations, as well as the determination of his essential identity. ... Ka. ... A description of the greatness of the Śivayogin named Trikhecanā, preceded by an account of the history of the Pāṇava dynasty residing in the palace built of jewels, rubies, and pearls. Dha. ...

In this section, as an incidental discussion following the description of the Kedāra-mahātmya, there is the narration of the story of Ujjini and Nīritha; the glorification of the greatness of Śiva through the account of Yama, Dharmarāja, and Dharmeśvara; the description of the various forms of Śiva witnessed by those who perform dharma and austerity; and the narration of the granting of boons by Śiva to the bird-children, as well as the account of the destruction of the demon Dharma-druhā. (Skanda Purāṇa)

Six chapters describe in detail the Manoratha-tṛtīyā-vrata, known as the Viśvamukha, dedicated to the deities Gaurī and Vināyaka; it was ordained by Śiva for Bikhyā Pukhomajā, beginning from the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra and ending on the third day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna.

[The narrative continues with] the removal of the fear and distress of Indra by the slayer of *Chata* (the demon); the performance of penance by the one called Dharmeśa at Kāśī, in the northern quarter, in the presence of the Liṅga known as Kṣivāṅga; the account of how he obtained his previous birth after being cursed for the sin of killing a Brahmin and for performing the work of others; the description of the conduct of Mitrajit during the manifestation of the terrifying Vīreśvara; and how King Mahiṣṇava, having slain the demon Kaṅkāla with his trident, [rescued] the daughter of a Vidyādhara named Aṅyagandhinī, who had been killed by the demon Kaṅkāṭa.

The wedding by the *gāndharva* rite and the arrival [of the prince] with her in Kāśī; the king’s response to the queen regarding the desired third-day vow (*abhīṣṭatṛtīyāvrata*). Based on the essence of the *Śataprabhālu*, the description of the vow for the goddess Gaurī—the "third day of the beloved" (*abhīṣṭatṛtīyā*)—as prescribed by the queen for the bright third day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa. Through the performance of the vow, the queen’s attainment of a son; and the sending of that newborn, who had been placed before the goddess Vikaṭādevī by his mother, near the Mothers headed by Māheśvarī by the command of the goddess Riddhadevī. His mother—

The state of Śivārka becoming a *liṅga* through the performance of penance near the goddess Pañcamudrā in Bālaktyānandakānana by the renowned Vikhuṣṭa; the acquisition of the name Vīreśvara for this very *liṅga* and the description of its great majesty; and the granting of various boons by Vareśvara Śiva to him, along with a sequential description of the holy places situated at the confluence of the Asi and Gaṅgā rivers that were mentioned.

[The narration of the glorious Ādikeśava and other holy sites (tīrthas) established by King Bīreśvara for his friend, the son of the king; the description of how, despite performing extensive austerities after installing a linga of Śiva in the Bhānandakānana forest, Durvāsas remained without fruit and consequently cursed Śiva; the manifestation of Śiva’s linga and so forth; and the naming of that linga Kāmeśvara due to the fulfillment of Durvāsas’s desire, along with a detailed account of its greatness...]

A description of the majesty of Viśvakarmaśvara in Kāśī, preceded by an account of how he was fashioned by Viśvakarman and his subsequent designation; and a description of the commencement of a sacrifice by the Prajāpati Dakṣa—who was an enemy of Śiva—without Śiva and Umā, following an incidental account of the origin of Dakṣeśvara.

Ka: Having heard from the mouth of Nārada the account of the sacrificial rite, Satī, as if disregarding the words of heaven, set out toward Dakṣa’s sacrifice. There, having heard this news regarding her father from the mouth of Śiva, she became extremely enraged and performed the abandonment of her body. A detailed description follows of the great festival of the arrival of the venerable Viśveśvara at Suktimaṇḍapa in Kāśī. Then, the destruction of the sacrifice and the severing of Dakṣa’s head by Vīrabhadra, a gaṇa of Śiva; and finally, the restoration of the head by Vīrabhadra at the command of Śiva.

The attainment of liberation through the form of the Ram-faced [Lord], the establishment of the Śiva-liṅga at Kāśī and the performance of penance while beholding it, the narration of the origin of Daśāśvamedha, the installation of the Pārvatīśa-Śiva-liṅga by Pārvatī, the description of its greatness, and the glorification of Gaṅgeśvara—the Gaṅgā-liṅga established by Gaṅgā at Viśvanātha-Śivalgaon.

The account of Brahmā receiving a boon from Śiva that his form would be equal to that of Sākara, his installation of a Śiva-liṅga in Kāśī, and his performance of penance on the Revā; the description of the greatness of that Tīrtha preceded by the narration of the granting of boons to Nīlakaṇṭha and the Revā; the description of the greatness of the Satīśvara-liṅga installed by Satī in Kāśī for the purpose of ascending to heaven; and the description of the greatness of the Śiva-liṅgas known as Asateśvara, Karuṇeśvara, and Jyotīrūpeśvara.

25. At Kāśī as well, having made the *mujamūṇvī* (the staff of silence) his own, Hari heard the Kālāgama statement that "Śiva alone is to be served" (*śevyo reḥ sevyaḥ*). There follows a description of the paralysis of Vyāsa’s speech brought about by Śauṇḍa and others. Then, by the instruction of Viṣṇu, Vyāsa, through contact with Viṣṇu’s throat, ceased from his paralysis and performed a hymn of praise to Śiva. This is followed by the account of the release from Vyāsa’s curse, a description of the true nature of the *chṛccharā* and other [mantras], and the narration of the incident of Vyāsa being expelled outside the Kārī [temple].

The description of all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) situated within the consecrated site (*dīkṣitra*) that removes all sins; and the exposition of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the supreme deity of Kāśī-kṣetra named Śrī Viśveśvara, as told by the venerable Śambhu to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods.

...the description of the sequence of the pilgrimage sites ending with the Kāśīkhaṇḍa, the description of the pilgrimage beginning with Paśupatinātha, and the description of the hearing, reciting, and writing of the Kāśīkhaṇḍa; this is the latter portion of the Kāśīkhaṇḍa.
Thus ends the fourth section, the Kāśī-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. || 4 ||
In the Śrī Bhaviṣya Mahāpurāṇa, the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa.

Ka.
Now, in the section on Avanti, first is the majesty of the sacred field of Avanti.

Now, first of all, there is the hymn to the illustrious Mahākāla-deva by the performer of the supreme auspicious rite; the glorification of the Mahākāla forest; the arrival of Vyāsa near Sanatkumāra; the commencement of the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Vyāsa; therein, the description of the origin of Khaṣṭu at the beginning of the Kalpa; the description of the penance performed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; the description of the praise of Devaṅgateśvara; and the account of how Brahmā was addressed as "Kapāṭin" by the gods.

Following the detailed description of the staff-bearing messenger who had arrived at the head of the Gaṅgā, [the narrative describes] his departure before Śiva by the command of Brahmā for the purpose of destroying Śiva; Śiva’s journey to the hermitage of Viṣṇu; Viṣṇu’s offering of a gift to Śiva; the battle between the man born from the side of Viṣṇu and the man born from the mouth of Brahmā; and the prescription of penance by Brahmā for the fault of having unleashed the missile that caused the destruction of Śiva.

In the context of the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Nārada, there is a description of the origin of Vaiśvānara; the departure of Nara and Nārāyaṇa toward the Badaryāśrama; the granting of boons beginning with the status of being the feet by Śaṅkara, who was pleased upon seeing their penance for the welfare of the world; their installation there; the worship of Nara and Nārāyaṇa; the abiding of Śiva in that very place at the word of Pāda; and the arrival of the gods, led by Brahmā, there for the purpose of beholding Śiva.

Then follows the performance of penance for a thousand years; at the conclusion of that penance, the vision of Śiva; the granting of boons to the gods by Śiva; the installation of Agastya at the command of Śiva; a description of the greatness of the Kapālamokṣaṇa Tīrtha; a description of the rules for residing in the Mahākālavana forest; and a description of the majesty of Mahākāla, preceded by an account of the fruits obtained by men who dwell in that residence in the Mahākālavana forest.

In this section, there is a description of the greatness of giving (*dāna-māhātmya*) within the context of the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Lyaṣa in the Mahākālavana; a description of the origin of Kalahaṇḍeśvara when a quarrel arose between Śiva and Gaurī; a description of the origin of Kalahanāśanaṇḍa; a description of the greatness of giving in Kaṭanāganaṇḍa; a description of the origin and greatness of the Apsaras-tīrtha; a description of the greatness of bathing, giving, and other rites at the Apsaras-tīrtha; and a description of the greatness of the Apsarakuṇḍa.

The description of the battle with the Rākṣasa named Hākhāda, who assumed the form of a buffalo and was born from the Mahiṣakuṇḍa; the account of Śiva’s defeat of the Rākṣasa and the installation of a Liṅga at that very spot; and the glorification of Mahiṣakuṇḍarudra and Kauṭumbikeśvara.

Taking a garland of *parijāta* flowers, the lord of the Vidyādharas went to the enemy of Indra (Vishnu). There, he gave that garland to the goddess Bhadrakālī, who was performing her service. Seeing that the goddess had been adorned with that garland, Indra, fearing the destruction of his own [position], cast a curse upon the Vidyādhara. By the command of Indra, the lord of the Vidyādharas arrived at Avantī. There, through the knowledge [attained] at the sacred site (*tīrtha*), the lord of the Vidyādharas returned to his own abode. [This concludes] the majesty of the Vidyādhara-tīrtha.

Description. Ka: Description of the majesty of Makaṭeśvara; description of the majesty of Rītaṅga-tīrtha... Ka: The majesty of Rājantha-tīrtha situated on the western side in the midst of the four oceans; there, the narration by the sage Agastya, who had swallowed the four oceans, concerning the attainment of the fruit of a son for King Sucandra through his wife Khadaśnā; at the word of that [sage], Sudurjaya’s departure for Gandhamādana to propitiate Śiva; [and] by the word of Śiva, [the arrival] upon the mountain...

Therein is the journey; the offering of the four oceans by means of the four oceans as a substance; the granting of boons to the king by the four fires; the location of the sacred site (*tīrthasthāna*) at that very place; and the description of the fruits of merit for those who dwell in the chapters concerning the four oceans.

[The description of the greatness [of the site], including the illustration of the attainment of the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) by [the sage] Dhaṭṭa; the description of the greatness of Keśvara-tīrtha at Suvarṇajāṭa; the description of the greatness of Yameśvara; the description of the greatness of Sadrasasama; the description of the greatness of Śaṅkara-vāpī-tīrtha; the establishment of his own *liṅga* by Diva after performing worship of Sūrya, and the description of the greatness of Śakarāditya; the description of the greatness of Nīḍagandhavībhrama, and [the merit gained] by performing *śrāddha* and other rites there.]

In the context of the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Vyāsa concerning the greatness of various sacred fords (*tīrtha-māhātmya*) beginning with Sāna-dāna, Manu and others describe the birth of the goddess Ekānaṃśā from Jñāna; they describe how Brahmā, oppressed by the Rākṣasa Tārakāsura, called to mind the goddess Niśā; how she, for the sake of destroying Tāraka, explained the means to Brahmā; how Brahmā established her right there; and the description of the greatness of the path of the goddess Ekānaṃśā, wherein she remained during the battle between the gods and the demons.
The arrival of the Daityas Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa and their defeat; the naming of Pārvatī by Śaṅkara as "Harasiddhi"; a description of the majesty of Hara; and a detailed description of the Śvara Tīrtha.

The description of the majesty of Mahāmāyā; the description of the majesty of Kapāṭeśvara; the description of the majesty of the pilgrimage to the Kharvaṭī Tīrtha; the description of the majesty of Hanumatkeśvara; the description of the coronation of Rāma and the others in the kingdom of Ayodhyā after the slaying of Rāvaṇa; [the account of] Hanumān going to Laṅkā to request the Linga, taking it, and returning to Avantī; the installation of the Linga on the bank of the lake and Hanumān’s performance of his ablutions; and upon seeing the Linga move at the conclusion of the bath, [his realization that it was] by the command of Śiva through her [Mahāmāyā].

The installation of that *liṅga*; the description of the *daluma* and *pāvaityā* at the command of Vibhīṣaṇa; the description of the greatness of the *chigaṃta-napṛśaṣyā* and the *śavaṭayakciṇī* pilgrimage site; the description of the greatness of the *piṅkācaka-tīrtha*; the description of the greatness of the *diṣarāoeśa-caratīrtha*; the description of the greatness of *agasyeśvara* and others; the description of the greatness of *duṇḍeśvara*; the description of the greatness of *umarukeśvara*; and the description of the greatness of *anādikasyeśvara*. These are the subjects.

The description of the great festival procession at Bhaṭukapamena, the glorification of the majesty of the pilgrimage, and the abandonment of his studies by Prince Aniruddha, who was born in the city of Rājapura.

The description [of the situation], the description of the sixfold association formed by those who had committed the offense through their supernormal powers, the making of a plan for his slaughter upon seeing the Naga [Nirgrantha] who was intent on giving instruction, and the sharing of the sin by going to the cave at his word.
The act of humbling one's own retinue; therein, [it refers to] the experience of the fruits of evil by those staying at home, such as fathers and others.

Having committed the act, he felt remorse and, having sought refuge with the great sages, offered his prayers; then, through the practice of the mantra bestowed by Viśvāmitra, the destruction of his sin was described; thereafter, because he was born from a clump of reeds (*kāṇḍa*), the great sages gave him the name Vālmīki; by that [name], Vālmīki... Kuśa—

Having gone to Sthī and propitiated Śiva, the establishment of a *liṅga* under his own name; a description of the majesty of Vāsmīkī and others; a description of the greatness of Ḍakeśvara, Abhimukha-varśavara-kamiśava-sanaḍāmaṇeśvara, Caṇḍeśvara, and other divine [shrines]; a description of the beauty and the purifying majesty of Kāṭavana; and [the description] of those situated in all directions all around Kāṭavana.

[Description of the greatness of the deities beginning with Pigakheda; description of the seven karṣas and the Himavat; the greatness of the pilgrimage to Pañceśānī; the greatness of Akareracara; description of the greatness of Brahmakuṇḍa; description of the greatness of the Mandākinī-tīrtha. (Oṃ... Description of the greatness of the place named Aṅkapadā; exposition of the deeds of the sages Vaṭarāma and Kṛṣṇa; regarding the removal of sins...]

The giving of the preceptor’s fee by those two, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, who were engaged in their duties; the slaying of the demon Śaṅkha while staying with his mother; their journey to the abode of Yama; the defeat of Yama there; the recovery of Sāndīpani’s son; their arrival at the shore of the ocean; the description of the worship of the Liṅga situated in Avanti at the place called Ardhanārīśvara and the taking of the five-headed [serpent] Mūrdhapañcaka.

The majesty of Candrāditya; the majesty of Karabheśvara; the majesty of Gaṇeśa; a description of the majesty of Kusumeśvara and Jyeṣṭheśvara; a description of the majesty of Divadvāra; a description of the majesty of Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara; [the majesty of] Brahma—||
[Blank]

The greatness of Śvaramādātavya; the greatness of Bhyāṇīkuṇḍa; the greatness of Yajñavāpī; the description of Paḍupati, Drapura, Rūpaṅka, Kedāruṇḍaka, Riṇḍā, Jāgaṃva, Cakravīya, and others; the chapters on the Lord of Semavatī and the Lord of Khgisa; the description of the greatness of Agastyeśvara; the description of the holy sites (tīrtha) preceded by the enumeration of the names of various individual liṅgas situated at every step; the description of the greatness of Oṃkāreśvara during the time of the battle with the demon Andhaka; and the greatness of Abhayeśvara.

The description of the performance of a hymn of praise to Śiva by the Asura Andhaka, who was unable to endure the defeat inflicted upon him by the goddess Caṇḍī on the occasion of the Aṅgārakī Caturthī vow; the description by Śiva of the great majesty of the Anaraka Tīrtha therein; in that context, the description of hell and the description of the torments of hell; the statement regarding the means for avoiding hell; the greatness of offering lamps at the Anaraka Tīrtha; and the description of the procedure for the ritual worship and the fruit obtained through the offering of lamps.

The description of the greatness of Jañjādi-vṛddhiprātya and other sites; the description of the greatness of Kedāreśvara-tīrtha; the description of the greatness of Jaṭātīrtha, Indratīrtha, Candraśekhara, Kuṇḍeśvara, Gopātīrtha, Vipātīrtha, Nadeśvara, Rāmeśvara, and other holy places; therein, the performance of the *śrāddha* rite for his father Daśaratha by Rāma; and [the descriptions of] Saubhāgyatīrtha, Ghṛtatīrtha, Yogeśvara, Devīraṅkhāvatī, Sudhodaka, and Suyeśvara.

The description of the greatness of the holy sites (tīrtha) such as Punatīrtha, Pattaneśvara, Dudharpa, Sthavira, Banāyaka, Kāmodaka, and others; the installation of Kedārārka by Arjuna at the command of Śakra; the stopping of the sun by Arjuna at the word of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; the granting of boons to him by the sun-god Sūrya when he was appeased; the offering of praise by Arjuna; the installation of the Sun-god there itself under the name Narāditya by the command of Sūrya for the sake of men; the description of the greatness of Narāditya; and the offering of praise by Śrī Kṛṣṇa to him.

The description of the greatness of Keravāditya; the narration of the birth story of Skanda, including the emission of semen by Kāma at the command of Raukara, the swallowing of Śiva’s seed by Agni, the discharge of that seed into the Gaṅgā, the entry of that seed into the wombs of the six Kṛttikās who had come there to bathe, and the subsequent birth of Skanda; and the description of the greatness of Raktamedatīrtha. ...

The contents [of this section] are as follows: a description of the majesty of Naradīpatīrtha established by Ṣaṣṭha; the installation of the Mothers, beginning with Cājuṇḍā, on the bank of the Baṅkṣu; a description of the ritual procedure for the worship of the Māṭhikās; an account of how Andhaka attained the status of a Śiva-gaṇa; a description of the majesty of Pama-mākāravana; and within the dialogue between Śiva and Brahmā, a description of the city named Kanakaśṛṅgā; and a description of the majesty of Uśastharī.

A description of the greatness of the city named Avanti; the performance of penance by the demon Tripura, invoking Brahmā, in Ujjayinī; the granting of a boon to him by the Lord; the approach of Indra and the other gods, who were oppressed by Tripura, before Śiva; the granting of fearlessness to them by Śiva; the installation of Cāmuṇḍā for worship in Avanti by Indra and the others; the defeat of the Daityas by Śiva at the word of Cāmuṇḍā; and because the Dānava Tripura was conquered there, it was named Ujjayinī.

A description of the fame of the city; a description of the majesty of Ujjayinī. Having performed the churning of the ocean to produce jewels due to the absence of gems, and then, for the sake of seizing the nectar (*pīyūṣa*) that emerged from it, during the battle between the two [the gods and the demons], the Blessed One (*bhagavat*), assuming the form of Mohinī, acted to distribute the nectar; therein, while Rāhu was standing among the ranks of the gods under a disguise, he severed his head. Therein also is the establishment of a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) for the purpose of removing the affliction caused by Rāhu and Ketu.

A description of the greatness of Rāhutīrtha; a description of the greatness of bathing in the Ratnakuṇḍa; a description of the history of the city named Padmāvatī; a description of the splendor of the city of Kumudvatī; a description of the majesty and origin of Kumudvatī; within the description of the Mahākālavana, a description of the Nandana forest; a description of the Kāmadhenu; a description of the history of the city named Amarāvatī; ... [fragmentary] ... a description of the majesty of the city known as Vidākhā.

A description of the regulation of the measurement of time, beginning from the *nimeṣa* and ending with eighty-four *kalpas*; the journey of Śiva, who wears the crescent moon, to the three worlds for alms; at the time of giving the alms, when Śiva struck Viṣṇu’s finger with his trident, the emergence of a stream of blood from Viṣṇu’s finger; the account of how that very stream transformed into a river and became famous by the name Śiprā; the description of the battle between Bāṇāsura and Kṛṣṇa; and therein, the mutual combat between Śiva and Viṣṇu.

The dispatching of the messenger; the defeat of the Śauvaṃcara in the region of Meṣyā during the two fevers, Raudra and Aiṣṇava; the description of the regions of Bhavyā; the description of its famous place by the name Varannī; the description of the majesty of the Uvaraghna-tīrtha; in connection with the description of the Pāpanāśinī-tīrtha, the king’s departure for the forest on a hunt; having tied his horse to a banyan tree, the king falling asleep right there. Then—

The crow flew down upon the king’s head; while the king was tormented by its pecking, the messengers of Yama arrived there. Then, as the king had gone to the realm of Yama at the time of his suffering from Yama's torments, the flesh of his body, being devoured by the crow, fell into the *riprā* (the sacrificial pit). By that merit, the king went to the world of Śiva. Amidst the assembly of Yama and the messengers of Yama, the majesty of the *śiṅgrāma* (the village) is described. [The crow], having become a beggar (*bhikṣu*), went to the world of the Nāgas; because of the absence of alms-food (*bhikṣākhādya*) there, he remained in a single pool of twenty-one serpents located there.

The serpents, terrified by the consumption of their own kin, offered praise to Vāsuki; then, accompanied by all the snakes, they went to Śiva and performed his worship. Pleased by this, he established the Kaṇḍa there, known as the Amṛtodbhava, and the description of the great festival [of that] was told. Then, having gone to the world of Brahmā, Indra, oppressed by Hiraṇyākṣa and others, related the entire account to him. Lord Brahmā explained to the gods the reason for the enmity between Jaya and Vijaya.

The narration of the sequence of births of Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu; the description of the descent as a boar for the slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa; the description of the origin of the river Riprā from the body of the boar; the description of the beauty of the river Riprā; the description of the majesty of Dibhrāma; the description of the majesty of the holy site named Sundara in Mahākālavana; the description of the majesty of the Piśācamocana Tīrtha; and therein, the narration of the story of the twice-born Devakhāta. ... [End of section].

Description of the majesty of the Nīkhagaṅgā: Agastya’s performance of penance on the Vindhya mountains for the purpose of uplifting the land submerged in the waters of the Revā; the departure of Vindhyavāsinī, who recognized his penance, to Ujjayinī; description of the majesty of the Vindhyavāsinī-vimukhada Tīrtha; description of the majesty of the Māndhātṛ-kṣetra-sadrasa Tīrtha; description of the Kṣātā-saṅgama Tīrtha; and the majesty of the Kṣātā-saṅgama Tīrtha as it was given to Śiva by Sūrya and Anasūyā following their dispute.

The description of the majesty of Gayātīrtha; therein, within the praise of Gayātīrtha, the departure of all the gods, who were oppressed by the Rākṣasa Daṇḍa, to the abode of Brahmā; the performance of the hymn of Viṣṇu by Brahmā and the others after going to the world of Viṣṇu; the journey of everyone to Gayātīrtha by the command of Viṣṇu; the description of the majesty of the Śrāddha rite performed according to the prescribed rules at Gayātīrtha; the description of the majesty of the Phalgu river situated in the sacred field of Gayā; [and the description of] Ādigayā, Buddhagayā, Viṣṇupadī, Gayākāṣṭha, and Gadā...

The merit of bathing and giving gifts at sacred fords (tīrthas) such as Icchāvatī, Aśvatthavāyara, Pratasuktikarī, Ilā, and Acchodā; therein, within the dialogue between Nārada and the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis), the description of the greatness of the vow of the Seven Sages by Nārada; in the description of the majesty of Puruṣottama, the description of the greatness of the month of Māgha in the context of the dialogue between Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa; the narration of various injunctions regarding vows and observances in the intercalary month (adhimāsa); and the description of the greatness of bathing and giving gifts during the month of Māgha in the intercalary month.

The majesty of dwelling in the Mahākāla forest; the majesty of the sequence of worship of Puruṣottama; the majesty of the knowledge of the excellent river Jaṭācarī; the majesty of the Bhāgīrathī-Rāmā-tīrtha; the majesty of the Kārikī river; the description of the majesty of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites during the intercalary month (adhimāsa); the majesty of Gomatī-kuṇḍa; the majesty of Kāṭā; and the description of the attainment of the fruits of merit from bathing and other rites at Gomatī-kuṇḍa.

A description of the supreme *mūrti* of Vāmana at Kaṇṭheśvara, including the lion and the heroic Lord; therein, the account of Bali being oppressed by the Daityas and going to the world of Brahmā to report the events concerning all the offerings; the narration by Brahmā of the means for the propitiation of Viṣṇu; therein, within the context of the dialogue between Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods, the recitation of the thousand names of Viṣṇu; the description of the fruit of those thousand names; and the narration of the greatness of the establishment of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) and the sequence of events regarding the incarnation of Vāmana.

The description of the Vīreśvara, Kāla, and Airāvata tīrthas; therein, the narration of the eight Mairavas; the story of King Janamejaya and the Āstika in the context of the sacrifice named after the Nāgas; the description of the greatness of the nine pools (navakuṇḍa) and the teeth of Śeṣa; and the majesty of the Ramāsaras tīrtha.

The topics include: the description of the greatness of Daśahatīrtha preceded by the account of the birth of Ucihaja; the description of the majesty of Kuṭumbeśvara followed by the description of the penance of Dṛścamahādeva and others; the description of the greatness of Devaprabhāga-tīrtha; the greatness of Ānandabhairava-tīrtha; and within the description of Akhaṇḍaśvara-tīrtha, the account of how even the great sinner Brahmadatta attained the world of the gods upon dying there; and the dialogue between Nārada and Brahmā.

... a description of the greatness of the Akhaṇḍasara Tīrtha as an incidental topic; the greatness of the Karkarāja Tīrtha; a description of the Vidhūmrāci Tīrtha; a description of the fruits of the Cāturmāsya vow; the greatness of the Bindusara and Ramyasara Tīrthas; the sequential enumeration of names preceded by a calculation of the number of Tīrthas; and a statement regarding the sequence of the pilgrimage to all the Tīrthas culminating in the Devayātrā.

Description of the fruits of hearing the majesty of the Avanti-kṣetra; description of the conclusion of the work. Thus ends the first [section], the Majestic Glory of Avanti, in the Āvantya-khaṇḍa. || 6 ||
Now, in the section on Avanti, the second [chapter] concerning the greatness of the eighty-four *liṅgas* situated in Avanti is declared.

Now begins the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara concerning the greatness of the eighty-four *liṅgas*. In this regard, first is the description of the greatness of the Īśvara-liṅga; in connection with that, the narration of a former history. Therein, for the sake of the gods' happiness, Kaṃbhayoni slew the Daityas; subsequently, fearing the sin of slaughter due to his remorse, he performed worship of Īśvara and, by Śiva’s command, established a *liṅga* of his own name. Then follows the description of the greatness of that Agastyēśvara-liṅga. Now...

A description of the majesty of the Guheśvara Liṅga: there, after Maṅkaṇaka had performed penance, at a certain time he attained a miracle by swallowing a ladleful of vegetable juice from his hand and began to dance; because of that, all mobile and immobile beings began to dance, and the gods immediately departed for the world of Śiva; Indra then brought about the removal of Maṅkaṇaka’s poverty, and by the command of Śiva, the installation of the Liṅga at Mahākālavana was performed; and a description of the supreme state attained through Maṅkaṇaka’s speech.

The description of the majesty of Gadeśvara; then, the description of the majesty of Duṇḍeśvara: therein, the journey of the Gaṇa named Duṇḍha to the assembly of Indra; there, seeing Rambhā being tormented, Indra bestows a curse upon Duṇḍha who was inflamed by desire; thereafter, having attained human birth through that [curse], Duṇḍha propitiates Śiva in the Mahākālavana forest and establishes a Liṅga in his own name; the description of the majesty of the Duṇḍeśvara Tīrtha, including its origin and other details.

Now follows the description of the supreme majesty of the *ḍamaruka* drum: therein, the defeat of the descendants of Raghu along with Indra and the other gods in battle against the Daitya Vajra, son of Ruru; their departure for the world of Brahmā; the description of the battle between Vajra and the maiden Kanyakā who emerged from the body of Brahmā; and the description of the defeat of the *kṛtyā* created by Vajradhara.

The performance of worship to Īśvara through rites (*kṛtya*) and other means; the description of the battle between Umā and Īśvara; the destruction of the army by the sound of the *ḍamaru* drum sounded by Īśvara; thereafter, the installation of the *liṅga* named Ḍamarukeśvara there; the description of the greatness of the Ḍamarukeśvara-liṅga; then, the description of the origin of Svarṇajaṭeśvara; therein, the casting of Śaṃkara’s semen—produced while he was sporting with Pārvatī—into the Gaṅgā by Agni, who was distressed by that heat.

Then Vahni gave Kāñcana a chariot drawn by horses, by means of which he attained renown everywhere; having seen this, Vahni presented Kāñcana as a son to Śaṅkara; at the command of Śaṅkara, Kāñcana went to the great forest; and after Kāñcana had performed austerities, by the word of Īśvara, he established a Liṅga in his own name.

Then follows the description of the great beauty of Svarṇajaṅgharaṅga; next, the description of the greatness of Triviṣṭapeśvara, including Nārada’s speech regarding the establishment of Triviṣṭapa in Mahākāṭhavana, and the description of the greatness of Triviṣṭapeśvara.

(Now begins the description of the greatness of the pilgrimage to Kapāleśvara: therein, during a great horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha-yajña*), Śaṅkara arrived while holding a skull in his hand; upon seeing Śaṅkara’s appearance, the Brahmins showed him contempt; then Śiva placed that skull within the sacrificial enclosure and departed; unable to endure it, they threw the skull away; thereupon, the earth sank down under the weight of the thousand-fold skull; seeing that miracle, the Brahmins were struck with wonder.)

The performance of the hymn of praise to Śiva, the installation of the limbs [of the deity] under the name Kapāleśvara, and the description of the greatness of Kapāleśvara which removes great sins such as the killing of a Brahmin—[from the Skanda Purāṇa].

Chapters and Subjects: Now begins the description of the seventh chapter, the "Opening of the Gate to Heaven" (*svargadvāra*). Therein is the description of the battle between Vīrabhadra and the other attendants of Śiva, incensed by the insult committed by Dakṣa at Dakṣa’s sacrifice, on one side, and Viṣṇu and the other gods on the other; therein follows the defeat of Viṣṇu and the other gods, and the closing of the gate to heaven by the attendants of Śiva. Then, observing that they were unable to enter heaven, the gods, by the command of Viṣṇu, depart for the Mahākālavana forest to perform worship of Śiva.

Therein: the establishment of the *digasthāpana* (the fixing of the directions) at the Svargadvāra [tīrtha]; the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Svargadvāra; then, the description of the majesty of Karkoṭakeśvara, including the performance of penance by the Nāga Karkoṭaka in the Mahākālavana forest for the sake of destroying Mada; the granting of a boon to him by the Lord Śiva, pleased by that penance; the establishment of a shrine named after himself by Śibi; the description of the majesty of Karkoṭakeśvara; then, the description of the majesty of Siddheśvara, wherein—

For the sake of attaining spiritual perfection (*siddhi*), Vātarirāka performed austerities in the Devadāru forest; his journey to Mahākālavana, where he established the *Siddhiśvara* Liṅga after performing penance there, and a description of the greatness of the Siddhiśvara Liṅga, follows. Next is the description of the greatness of the Lokapāda-vara Liṅga: how, by the command of Viṣṇu, the world-protectors (Lokapālas), having been defeated by Hiraṇyakaśipu, went to Mahākālavana to perform austerities, and through the power of that penance, they were freed from their demonic state.

The departure to their respective abodes; the installation of the *liṅga* in Mahākālavana under the name Lokapāla; a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the deity Lokapāla; then, a description of the majesty of Kāmeśvara. Therein, Brahmā, having generated Kāma for the purpose of bringing about creation, dispatched him with instructions regarding twelve locations and twelve forms. By means of a fire, he reduced to ashes the *kanda* (root) of his body which was causing agitation. Having learned of her husband’s fate, Rati broke into lamentation. Then—

By the command of Śiva, Kāma, having become bodiless, went to the Mahākālavana forest; there, having performed penance, he established his own form (Aṅga). Then follows the description of the greatness of Kāmeśvara and the directions, and subsequently the description of the greatness of Ḍuṭambakeśvara. There, having drunk the *kāṣṭhadaṇḍa* that emerged during the churning of the Ocean of Milk, [he experienced] that which arose from it.

Unable to endure the burning sensation, Śaṃkara gave the *kālakūṭa* poison to the Brāhmaṇas; taking it, they went to the Mahākālavana forest on the banks of the Śiprā. Chapter [Number]: Topics—The depositing of that *kālakūṭa* poison upon the ground near the feet of Kāmeśvara by the Brāhmaṇas; the description of how the Brāhmaṇas who had arrived there seeking refuge were restored to life by Śiva after being smeared with the *kālakūṭa* poison; and the arrival of Śiva at that place.

The naming of Kuṭumbakeśvara, and the greatness of the pilgrimage site (liṅga-māhātmya) of Kuṭumbakeśvara. ... Now follows the greatness of the pilgrimage site of Indraneśvara: there, due to the loss of his merit, Indra fell from heaven; subsequently, out of remorse, in order to achieve imperishable fame, he took refuge with Mārkaṇḍeya in the Himavat mountains and, by his command, went to the Mahākālavana forest and performed the worship of Śiva. By that means, having attained imperishable fame, he established a liṅga in his own name.

Description of the Greatness of Indreśvara Liṅga; then, description of the Greatness of Īśāneśvara Liṅga: there, having been defeated by Tuṇḍa, the son of Muṇḍa, the gods went at the command of Diva to the Mahākāru forest and performed the worship of the Śiva-liṅga; Daśvareṇa Bhrasana named that liṅga after himself as Īśāneśvara; the gods offered hymns of praise to Īśāneśvara; and the description of the Greatness of Īśāneśvara Liṅga.

Now follows the description of the greatness of the Apsarasesvara Liṅga. There, while Rambhā was dancing in the assembly of Śakra, she was distracted by the Gandharvas; having witnessed her ruined dance, Śakra angrily bestowed a curse upon Rambhā. To counteract that curse, at the word of Nārada, she established her own name as a Liṅga in the Mahākālavana forest. By worshipping it constantly and pleasing Śiva, she obtained a boon from him and returned to her own abode. This concludes the description of the greatness of the Apsarasesvara Liṅga. Now:

A description of the majesty of Kalaṭhkaṭedavaraṅiga; therein, when the three worlds were shaken by the dispute concerning Umāmadeśvara, the quarters became filled with the sound "kakhakaṭhe" arising from all sides, and consequently, that *liṅga* was given the name Karukara; a description of the majesty of Kaṭarakaṭeśavaraṅiga.

Now follows the description of the greatness of the *liṅga* of Nāgacaṇḍeśvara; therein, the arrival of the gods at the *liṅga* established by Nāgacaṇḍa; when the fault of consuming meat and blood (*nimāṃsaraṃghana*) arose during its worship, the establishment of another *liṅga* near that *liṅga* of Nāgacaṇḍeśvara; by that means, the cessation of the gods' fault of consuming meat and blood; and the description of the greatness of the *liṅga* of Nāgacaṇḍeśvara. (End of section).

Then follows the description of the greatness of the *pratīdarśa-liṅga* of Īśvara. Therein is described how Nandin, the gatekeeper stationed at the entrance, did not allow Umā and Maheśvara—who were sporting there—to enter the inner apartments because he was unaware of them; how Śiva, becoming enraged by this, pronounced a curse upon Nandin; and how, as a result of that curse, Nandin went to Mahākālavana on earth and established a divine image under the name Pratihāreśvara, and through its grace, returned once more to the world of Śiva.

The return [to the hermitage]; the description of the greatness of Pratihāreśvara; then the description of the greatness of Kukkuṭeśvara: therein, due to the constant consumption of cocks in a previous birth, King named Kaurika was cursed by Tāracūḍa to become a cock; for the removal of that curse, he performed the worship of the Liṅga known as Pakṣiyonivimocana in the Mahākālavana forest; by that, his state of being a cock came to an end, and he installed the Kukkuṭeśvara Liṅga.

The description of the greatness of Kukkuṭeśvara; then, the description of the greatness of Karkaṭeśvara. In that regard, while King Dharmamūrti was desiring to know the cause of his attainment of the state of a crab, he questioned Vasiṣṭha; and by Vasiṣṭha, in response to that inquiry, it was explained that his attainment of the state of a crab was due to a sin committed by him in a previous birth.

The narration of the account: how Karakaṭa, having seized a body by means of some *rāyasa* (magical power), caused a *śivāpra* to fall; then, at the end of time, through the power of Śiva’s grace, the attainment of a supreme state in this very [place]; the description of the greatness of Karakaṭeśvara; then the description of the greatness of Meṣanādeśvara; therein, how due to the non-performance of sacrificial rites such as the *daujanya* by a king named Madāndha, there was a lack of rain on earth, and consequently the gods departed for the world of Brahmā; thereafter, by the command of Brahmā...

The journey of the gods to Mahākālavana; the praise of the Liṅga installed there by the gods during a drought; the description of how rain was obtained through the worship of that Liṅga; consequently, the naming of that Liṅga installed by the clouds as Meghanādeśvara; the description of the greatness of Meghanādeśvara; then, the description of the greatness of Mahāṭyeśvara Liṅga; then, the description of the greatness of Sukteśvara Liṅga; therein, [the account of] the thirteenth year spent at Sukti-tīrtha located near Mahākāla.

The arrival of a certain hunter at the mango tree of the Brahmin named Sukti while he was meditating upon Nārāyaṇa; the description of how the hunter attained excellence after his wickedness was removed through the sight and touch of the sage; the description of the hunter’s practice of penance while staying in the water and his liberation through the recitation of the eight-syllable mantra; the description of the liberation of a certain tiger who had come to that same place by hearing that mantra; and the account of the tiger’s previous birth as told by the tiger himself.

The narration of his own curse preceded by an account of the battle; the departure of the tiger and the virtuous Brahmin to the Bhṛgukaccha forest; the installation of a Liṅga there; and a description of the greatness of Suktīśvara. 1. Ma.

Now follows the description of the majesty of Someśvara: there, having seen the moon’s partiality toward Rohiṇī while neglecting the other wives, Dakṣa, out of anger, pronounced a curse upon Soma. Consequently, Soma departed for Satyaloka; from there, he went to Vaikuṇṭha along with Brahmā and offered hymns of praise to Viṣṇu. By the command of Viṣṇu, Soma proceeded to the Mahākālavana forest, where he installed a *liṅga*. This account describes how Soma’s disease of consumption (*yakṣmaroga*) was pacified by that act, as well as the description of the majesty of Someśvara.

Now follows the description of the greatness of Anarakeśvara. In that regard, preceded by a description of the sequence of torments in hell, Nimi—despite possessing a great abundance of merit—went to the abode of Yama due to a certain sin. Then, through the sight of Anarakeśvara, all his sins were destroyed; he ascended a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) and went to the world of Indra. To Nimi, who was distressed by the suffering of living beings undergoing the torments of Yama, [the Lord] granted eternal peace. This concludes the description of the greatness of the pilgrimage to Anarakeśvara.

Then follows the description of the majesty of Jaleśvara; therein, preceded by the narration of the story of King Vīradhanvan, is the description of the majesty of Jaleśvara, including the account of the installation of the image of Jaleśvara and other details.

Now follows the description of the greatness of Rāmeśvara: how twenty-one times the earth was rendered devoid of Kṣatriyas by him; how, for the sake of removing the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa, he visited various holy places on the banks of rivers but did not perceive the absence of that sin; and how, upon the instruction of Nārada, he went to the great forest of Madana near Jaṭeśvara; having performed penance there, he established a Liṅga in his own name to destroy the sin; and the description of the greatness of the Rāmeśvara Liṅga. ...

Now follows the description of the majesty of the Cyavaneśvara Liṅga: therein, after the sage named Cyavana had married the daughter of King Śaryāti, he performed penance in Mahākālavana and established a Liṅga in his own name; this is the description of the majesty of the Cyavaneśvara Liṅga.

Oṃ. The glorification of the greatness of Akrūraśvara-Ṛṣi; then the glorification of the greatness of Kuṇḍeśvara-Ṛṣi. Therein, when Śiva had vanished due to some cause while Pārvatī was mounted upon his lap, Pārvatī, distressed by the separation from her beloved, performed a rite of pregnancy (antarvat-kāraṇa) [and thus] gave birth to one named Kuṇḍa. Hereafter, the glorification of the greatness of Khaṇḍadava-Ṛṣi; therein, concerning the son of Priyavrata, King Madrāśva...

[The section] on the departure for Mahākāṭavana due to the words of Kubhayoni; there, the installation of a *liṅga* for the sake of fulfilling broken vows, and the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Khaṇḍeśvara-liṅga. [End of Pa. Now, the description of the majesty of Pattaneśvara-liṅga. [End of Dha. Now, the description of the majesty of Ānandeśvara-liṅga: how Ānanda, the son of Anamitra, having gone to Mahākāṭavana for a certain reason, installed a *liṅga* under his own name; and the description of the majesty of Ānandeśvara-liṅga. [End of Ka.]

Now follows the description of the greatness of Kanthaḍeśvarī; therein, the account of how a Brahmin named Pāṇḍava performed penance on account of a rag (*kanthā*) and established a shrine named Kanthānāma, as well as the description of the greatness of Kanthaḍeśvarī.

The description of the great majesty of the Ayonija-Īśvara Liṅga: When the son of Brahmā, Kuśadhvaja, fell from heaven, Brahmā became enraged and cast him down to earth with his matted locks; from this, the Asura Vṛtra was born. Then followed the battle between Vṛtra and Indra, in which Indra was defeated. At the command of Bṛhaspati, Śakra went to the Mahākālavana forest to conquer Vṛtra. By the power of his penance, he slew the Asura Vṛtra, and for the sake of removing the sin of that slaughter, he established the four directions (Dikpālas) there.

The description of the majesty of Indreśvara. Next, the description of the majesty of Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara, including therein the account of Mārkaṇḍeya’s birth and the installation of a *liṅga* by Mārkaṇḍeya under his own name in Mahākālavana; the description of the majesty of the *liṅga* of Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara. ... Next, the description of the majesty of the *liṅga* of Hṛṣīkeśvara; therein, the narrative of Ripusūdana and the description of the majesty of Śiveśvara.

Now follows the description of the greatness of the *Kusumeśvara* Liṅga; therein, the name *Kusumeśvara* was given because it is a place for the sport of flowers, followed by the description of the greatness of the *Kusumeśvara* Liṅga.

Now follows the description of the greatness of Dasyeśvara Liṅga: therein, Śrī Aṅgiras, having established a Liṅga in the Mahākālavana forest for the destruction of his own cruel disposition, performed its worship, whereby that cruel tendency ceased; the description of the subjects of its chapters and the granting of a curse against Kagaṇa; the establishment of a Liṅga named Sakhanātha by Kuṇḍa in the Mahākālavana forest for the sake of removing that curse; and the description of the greatness of Kuṇḍeśvara Liṅga. Now follows the description of the greatness of Dasyeśvara Liṅga.

In that regard, after the slaughter of the Sāma-gāthā Brāhmaṇa, King Caṇḍaparāja was afflicted by the curse uttered by that Brāhmaṇa. Following the instruction of Nārada, he went to the Mahākālavana forest. There, for the sake of curing his leprosy, he established an image of Aṅga. Then follows the description of the majesty of the Lord Ṭaṅbeśvara, who is known by the name Saikateśvara; and the description of the majesty of the Gaṅkheśvara Liṅga, where the Gaṅgā descended from the matted locks of Śiva onto the earth, which is why it is called Gaṅkhaśavara.

The description of the greatness of the pilgrimage site of Ṛgīśvara established by Mārkaṇḍeya, including the procedure for the worship of Gaṅgeśvara and other rites. Next, the description of the greatness of the day of Aṅgārakeśvara; the description of the greatness of Aṅgārakeśvara.

Then, the description of the greatness of Uttareśvara: therein, the departure of Indra and the other gods, who were afflicted by the nine planets, to Śiprā at the command of Śiva; the establishment of the Linga by Uttaramegha; the description of the greatness of Uttareśvara. Next, the description of the greatness of Nirkocaneśvara.

Now follows the description of the majesty of the Vīreśvara Liṅga; then the description of the majesty of the Abhayeśvara Liṅga; therein, the account of the birth of the son Gāraka from a portion of Śiva’s body; then the description of the majesty of the Parathukeśvara Liṅga; then the description of the majesty of the Sthāvareśvara Liṅga; then the description of the majesty of the Śaṭeśvara Liṅga, wherein the Goddess [slew] the demon Andhaka with her trident.

Having performed the installation of the Śanānanā-liṅga, there is a description of the greatness of the Śaṭheśvara-liṅga. Next, there is a description of the greatness of the Ukāreśvara-liṅga; therein is described the greatness of the Ukāreśvara-liṅga installed by the syllable *ukāra* issued from the mouth of Śiva, according to the word of Śiva. [End of Chapter]. Chapter 106.

Now follows the description of the majesty of Viśveśvaraṅga: how King Vidūratha, having taken birth as a wicked man for twelve lifetimes due to the fault committed during his previous life, attained the state of a Caṇḍāla in the thirteenth birth; and how, through constant devotion in the presence of Śiva, he was born again as a king by the name Viśveśa. Furthermore, it describes how, remembering his former birth, he established a *liṅga* there in the Mahākālavana forest, followed by the description of the majesty of Viśveśvaraṅga.

(dha) Now follows the description of the majesty of Kaṇṭeśvara Liṅga. Therein: the arrival of a certain king, who had been defeated by his enemies, at the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha; at his word, the king’s journey to Mahākālavana and the performance of worship after the installation of a Liṅga; the renown of that Liṅga under the name Kaṇṭeśvara, as he became free from thorns [enemies] and devoted to his brothers; and the description of the majesty of the Kaṇṭeśvara Liṅga. ...

Now follows the description of the majesty of Siṃheśvara. Therein is the arrival of Brahmā when Gaurī was performing penance for the sake of attaining Śiva; by the word of Brahmā, the birth of a lion from the mouth of the goddess while she was holding her hand [in prayer], and the description of milk flowing from the goddess’s breasts for the sake of nourishing it; the departure of the lion to the Mahākāṭa forest by the command of Pārvatī; the description of how he attained the status of being Gaurī’s vehicle; and the establishment of a *liṅga* by that lion under his own name—[this is] the Siṃheśvara-liṅga. Now...

The description of the greatness of the Revateśvara Liṅga: how the gods, having been invited there by Revata Sūpatra, went to Kailāsa; how, at the word of Śiva, they came to the Mahākālavana forest and established a Śiva-liṅga there under his own name; and the description of the greatness of the Revateśvara Liṅga.

[This is] the description of the greatness of the Ghaṇṭeśvara Liṅga. Therein: the departure of the Gaṇa Vaṃṭa, who had abandoned Śiva, to the world of the gods in order to see the celestial singers; Nārada’s seeing him there and reporting it to Śiva; the granting of a curse by the enraged and incensed [Śiva] to the Gaṇa named Veṭa; and for the sake of removing that curse, his going to Mahākālavana at the command of Nārada and the installation of the image of Śivī; and the description of the greatness of the Ghaṇṭeśvara Liṅga. [...]

Now follows the description of the greatness of the Prayāgeśvara Liṅga: therein, in the dialogue between Priyavrata and Nārada, Nārada’s distress caused by Sāvitrī; Nārada’s attainment of knowledge through the vision of Sāvitrī; upon seeing that, Sāvitrī being questioned by the Noble One (Priyavrata) and her narration of all that occurred; the attainment of steadfastness through going to Prayāga; Priyavrata’s request for a boon; the chapters and topics; Nārada’s departure with him to Prayāga; having gone there, the installation and worship of the Liṅga.

Description of the majesty of Prayāgeśvara-Kiṅgi... [Section *ba*]: Description of the majesty of Siddheśvara-liṅga; therein, the meeting of King Aśvaśiras with the great sages Jaigīṣavya and Kapila; his taking refuge in the Lord’s true nature through wonder at the illusory power (*māyā*) displayed by those two; and by their command, that king’s journey to Mahākālavana and his worship of the liṅga to attain perfection (*siddhi*); description of the majesty of Siddheśvara-siddha-liṅga.

Now follows the description of the greatness of the Matangeśvara Liṅga.
