Therein is the account of the installation and worship of the Liṅga by Sugatividrapattra, and the description of the greatness of the Matangeśvara Liṅga. Next follows the description of the greatness of the Saubhāgyeśvara Liṅga: there, a certain king’s wife, named Samatī, being deeply afflicted by separation from her husband, worshipped the Liṅga with the desire to recover her husband; then, through the grace of that [Liṅga], her husband returned, and she attained the state of supreme auspiciousness.

The glorification of the greatness of Saubhāgyeśvara Liṅga; then the description of the greatness of Rūpeśvara Liṅga. Therein, the tasting of the *Padyarāja* at the hermitage of Kaṇva; there, having seen the daughter of the sage Kaṇva, he, impelled by lust, committed adultery with her; that was perceived by Kaṇva through his eye of knowledge, and he pronounced a curse upon them both, whereby they were transformed into the forms of trees; thereafter, by the command of Kaṇva, the two of them went to the Mahākāla forest, where [they attained liberation] through the worship of the Liṅga.

The description of the attainment of one's true form; then the description beginning from the sight of the Lord’s form; next, the description of the greatness of the Dhalusāhaleśvara mountain, wherein the daughter of King Vidūratha was abducted by the demon Kusuṃbha; thereafter, the battle of that [demon] with the two sons of Vidūratha; and thereupon, King Vidūratha, having learned of the defeat and captivity of his two sons, went to the Mahākāla forest with the permission of the sages for the sake of their victory.

The worship of the bow; by the power of that worship, the acquisition of the bow, sword, shield, and quiver by him; the defeat of the Daitya through the aid of that bow; the description of how that king, together with his wife, daughter, and others, attained liberation at the conclusion of the *Śuklapāpī* festival; the description of the greatness of the *Dhanuḥsāhasreśvara* Liṅga; then the description of the greatness of the *Paśupatīśvara* Liṅga; therein, the installation of the Liṅga by King Paśupālaka and its worship.

The description of the greatness of Bhadrali, the lord of Paḍupati. Then follows the description of the greatness of Brahmadavaraṅga: therein, the departure of the Daitya Puṣkoma to the Ocean of Milk with his own army in order to conquer Viṣṇu; upon seeing him, Brahmā’s departure to the mountain Sahya in order to seek victory over the Daitya; the description of how Śiva, being pleased by his penance performed there, brought about the defeat of the Daitya; the installation of a Liṅga by Brahmā under his own name; and the description of the greatness of the Brahmavaraliṅga.

[Then] follows the description of the majesty of Jalyeśvara: therein, the account of King Jalpa, who, having established his five sons in the kingdom, departed for the forest; thereafter, having learned of those five sons through mutual discord among their kinsmen, the aged king, distressed by their separation, went to the Mahyakā forest at the command of Vasiṣṭha; the establishment of a *liṅga* there under his own name; and the description of the majesty of that Jalyeśvara-linga. Then follows the description of the majesty of the Kedāreśvara-linga; therein—

The departure of the gods, including Brahmā, who were afflicted by the cold, to Kailāsa; their journey toward that direction after meditating upon Śiva there; the description of the cessation of the suffering from the cold through the power of that merit; and the detailed glorification of the Kedāreśvara Liṅga.

Now follows the description of the greatness of the Piśāceśvara Tīrtha: the description of the wicked conduct and the attainment of [divine] power by one named Soma; therein, the dialogue between the Piśāca and the Brāhmaṇa Śākaṭāyana; the departure from the state of being a Piśāca due to the words of Śākaṭāyana and the journey to the Mahākālavana forest for the sake of liberation; the worship of the Lord there and the attainment of liberation by that Piśāca; the description of the greatness of the Piśāceśvara Tīrtha; and then the description of the greatness of the Saṅgameśvara Tīrtha, wherein—

At the request of Subāhu, the narration of the account of his previous birth; thereafter, the description of how he attained liberation by casting off the form of a king through the grace of the boon of Saṅgameśvara; and the glorification of the greatness of the Saṅgameśvara-boon.

° Then follows the description of the lineage of Duṣyanta; the departure of King Duṣyanta for the hunt in the forest; there, the story of the sage named Kaṭa who was deluded by a *kaṇṭhā* (tattered garment), and his failure to act [properly]; the loss of the kingdom; the chapters on the objects of desire (*viṣaya*) and the smoke of worldly existence; the chapters on meditation (*dhyai*); the attainment of the kingdom by him through the worship of Śiva in the Mahākāra forest; liberation at the end after the enjoyment of all pleasures; the description of the majesty of the lineage of Duṣyanta; and the attainment of the Supreme (*parāpatti*). Duṣyanta.

Now follows the description of the greatness of Prayāgeśvara. Therein is the account of Gaṅgā, who was chosen by Manu, obtaining eight sons; the liberation from human birth through Gaṅgā as intended by Nārada’s words; the departure to Īśāneśvara; and the removal of sins through the worship of that [liṅga].

The description of the greatness of Prayāgeśvaraṅga; the account of his journey by the command of Viṣṇu to Mahākālavana, where, having performed the worship of Śiva, a light emerged from the Śivaliṅga, and by means of that light, the supreme victory over Śambara was achieved; and the description of the greatness of the Candrādityeśvara Liṅga.

Now begins the description of the majesty of Karabheśvara: the pursuit of the camel by King Vīraketu while he was traveling to Gayā; the disappearance of the camel in a great forest; thereafter, the account of how, with the permission of Kaśyapa, the king attained the state of Kailāsa through the worship of Karabheśvara in the Mahākāṭavana forest; and the description of the majesty of Karabheśvara’s physical form.

Now begins the description of the greatness of Rājasthaleśvara. Therein is described how Brahmā, having performed the work of creation and seeing that it was without a king, granted kingship for the sake of conquering enemies; how King Ripuñjaya, by means of his son Vasuprajādhāṭana, dispelled the fear caused by drought, excessive rain, and other calamities; how he went to the great Kāṣṭhavana forest, worshipped Śiva, and by His grace brought about the establishment of happiness for the subjects; and finally, the description of the greatness of Rājasthaleśvara. Now.

The section on the glorification of the greatness of Vaḍaṭavarāha: therein, Maṇibhadra, known by the name Vaḍaṭa, goes to the forest with his wife to sport; there, a battle occurs between Vaḍaṭa and the Rākṣasas led by Kiraṇavat, resulting in the defeat of the Rākṣasas; then, Maṇibhadra the Yakṣa, enraged by the conduct of his own son, pronounces a curse upon his son Vaḍaṭa; for the sake of removing that curse, Vaḍaṭa goes to the Mahākālavana forest, where [he attains liberation] through the worship of Śiva.

Description of the greatness of Mośpra; description of the boon received by Vaḍaledeva. — Then follows the description of the majesty of Araṇedevvara, wherein is related how Aruṇa, the son of Vinatā born of Kaśyapa, went to Mahākālavana upon the instruction of Nārada and, through the worship of Śiva, attained the office of the Sun’s charioteer; description of the greatness of Gama. [00tha];

[Then follows the description of the supreme majesty of Candrādityeśa; therein, after the gods were defeated by Śambara, the account of how Candra and Sūrya [worshipped him]. Next follows the description of the supreme majesty of the boon-granting Puṣpadanteśvara; therein, when the Brahmin named Śini performed the propitiation of the boon-granting lord for the sake of obtaining a son, the description of how he obtained a son named Puṣpadanta through his grace; the establishment of a Liṅga of Śiva by Puṣpadanta in the Mahākāra forest; and the description of the supreme majesty of Puṣpadanteśvara.]

The arrival at the sacred site of Avimukta at the request of the maiden Vidyā, daughter of King Citrasena; the description of his attainment of liberation through the worship of Śivakīrti there; the description of the majesty of Avimukteśvara; then, the description of the majesty of the Hanumatkedāra Liṅga, including the account of Hanumān’s leap across the ocean preceded by the description of the Rākṣasīs, and how Hanumān attained the state of a *balī* (offering) through the worship of the Lord; and finally, the description of Hanumān as he appeared before Rāma after the slaying of Rāvaṇa and the consecration of Rāma’s kingdom.

When a certain Brahmin had uttered an insult against Hanumān, Hanumān went to Mahākālavana and performed the worship of Śiva; [this section contains] the glorification of the *Hanumatkeśvara* Liṅga. Next, the description of the majesty of the *Svapneśvara* Liṅga; therein, the description of the narrative of Kalmāṣapāda, followed by the description of the story of the *Duḥsvapnanāśaka* Liṅga named Satyakeśvara; [and finally] the description of the majesty of the *Svapneśvara* Liṅga.

...—Now follows the description of the greatness of Vigaleśvara; therein is the description of the four birds situated in the four directions. There, the daughter of Piṅgala named Vigalā, having remembered the evil deeds of her previous birth along with her father and mother, went to the great forest of Mahākāṭa by the command of Dharma. Having gone there, she established [the deity] in the directions under her own name; this is the description of the greatness of the god Vigaleśvara.

Now follows the description of the greatness of the Kāyāvarohaṇeśvara Liṅga: therein, at the time of the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, Dakṣa and the others, having been defeated by Vīrabhadra, Aṭṭahāsī, Kālī, and the rest, went to Mahākālavana; there, through the worship of the Liṅga, all their bodies descended [from their state of affliction], whereby the name Kāyāvarohaṇeśvara was established for it; and [finally] the description of the greatness of the Kāyāvarohaṇeśvara Liṅga.

Now follows the description of the majesty of the Biveśvara-liṅga. Therein is the account of how Kapila propitiated Śiva and obtained the boons of invincibility and the power to assume any form at will; likewise, how Viṣṇu was propitiated by the sage Bisa with the request for a boon, saying, "Act in such a way that Kapila shall say to me, 'I am afraid of you,'" and how Viṣṇu granted the boon, saying, "So be it," and subsequently made Kapila's prayer true by manifesting himself before him. [End of Chapter 1].

The objects [of the narrative] are not without purpose: the description of Kṛṣṇa’s battle with the monkey Kapiṣṭha, who was insulting his own words; then the defeat of Kṛṣṇa; thereafter, at the word of Śakra, the propitiation of Lord Viśveśvara by the monkey, through whom the binding of a verbal agreement was made—namely, "I am afraid of you"—and the description of the majesty of Viśveśvara; then the description of the majesty of Uttareśvara; therein, the journey of the king of Ayodhyā named Parīkṣit to the forest for the sake of hunting; and there...

He engaged in conversation with a certain maiden through a continuous flow of words; taking her with him, while the king was away, he entered a pond and went to the underworld (*pātāla*). There, Parīkṣit composed a verse. At the command of Parīkṣit, the chief ministers and others carried out the killing of the frogs. Then, one frog, having related the account of his own previous births, spoke of the sin of being a frog due to a severe curse. When the frog had thus informed the maiden of the matter, [she departed].

The handing over of the maiden who had arrived following her recollection to that [deity] after she had been examined; the cessation of Gālavadatta’s curse through the worship of Uttareśvara; the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Uttareśvara; and the description of the hearing of the fruit of the narrative concerning the majesty of the eighty-four *liṅgas* situated in Avantī, followed by the concluding description of the majesty of the eighty-four *liṅgas* located in the Avanti-khaṇḍa. Thus ends the second [section], the majesty of the eighty-four *liṅgas*, in the Avanti-khaṇḍa.
Now begins the third section, the Revā-khaṇḍa, within the Avanti-khaṇḍa.

The auspicious invocation; the description of the Revā; the description of the preeminence of the Purāṇas, Dharmaśāstras, and Ātmavidyā in the context of the dialogue between Sūta and Dvaipāyana; the enumeration and naming of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas and Upapurāṇas; and the description of the fruits of listening to the Purāṇas. ... ,..

In the context of the dialogue between Janamejaya and Vaiśampāyana, during the time of their departure for exile in the forest, the journey of the Pāṇḍavas toward the Vindhya mountains is described. Therein is recounted the arrival at the Vindhya forest and the meeting with Mārkaṇḍeya; the description by Dharmarāja (Yudhiṣṭhira) of the greatness of various holy places (*tīrtha*) and other matters concerning Mārkaṇḍeya, who was staying there and was performing his meditations; the description by Mārkaṇḍeya of the majesty of the Gaṅgā and other sacred sites (*satīrtha*); and subsequently, the even greater majesty of the Revā.

In the narration of his own history by Mārkaṇḍeya, there is the description of the state of the world at the end of the eon; while he was standing on the shore, a certain woman arrived there taking a boat; Mārkaṇḍeya’s boarding of the boat with Manu; the description of Mārkaṇḍeya’s hymn of praise to the Blessed Lord; Mārkaṇḍeya’s vision of Mahādeva situated on the peak of Mount Śrīkūṭa; and in the account of the woman’s history, the origin of the Narmadā and the description of the inexhaustibility of the Narmadā through the grace of Śaṅkara.

In this section, titled "The Dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Mārkaṇḍeya Concerning the Narmadā," there is a description of the seven [sins] through the context of the conversation; the location of the Narmadā extending as far as Saprakṣa; then, the description of its origin by Yudhiṣṭhira to Mārkaṇḍeya out of a desire to know the majesty of the Narmadā; the narration of the majesty of the Narmadā by Mārkaṇḍeya; therein, first, the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of the name Narmadā; and the ancient account of the dialogue between Mahādeva in the form of a peacock and the Narmadā during the Mayūra-kalpa.

A description of the imperishability and other attributes of the Narmadā; a description of the origin of the Narmadā and the Godāvarī from a cleft in the peak of Mount Trikūṭa; a description of the origin of the seven principal mountain ranges from the third peak of Trikūṭa, which had become split apart; and a description of the majesty of the Narmadā’s name along with its underlying causes. ... ||

Description of the emergence of rivers and other features at the time of the Kūrma-kalpa... Description of the gift of a crane (*baka*) by Mārkaṇḍeya to someone at the end of the kalpa; the description of the answer given by the crane, questioned by Mārkaṇḍeya, regarding how the stability of the world, its dissolution, and so forth occur; Mārkaṇḍeya hearing a certain sound; the gift of a girl residing in the *dvīpas* (islands); then the sight of the temple of Maheśvara; the gift of a girl who was performing the worship of the divine linga; and by her—

The narration of her own name, Narmadā; the description of her origin from the *bakaka* (crane-cotton) plant; seeing the Lord reclining at the time of the cotton [season], and likewise seeing a certain maiden and observing Śaṅkara, the performance of a hymn of praise by Indradyumna together with Kāṇḍeya; the description of the dialogue between Śaṅkara and Narmadā; the account of the fruit of knowing the origin of Narmadā, and so forth; the description of the presence of Narmadā throughout all the kalpas; and the fruits and merits of bathing in the Narmadā.

The fruit of studying and reciting the Vedas on the banks of the Narmadā; the fruit of bathing, giving gifts, chanting, offering oblations, and performing sacrifices in the Narmadā; the fruit of the merit arising from the sight of the Narmadā; the description of how all desires, such as the attainment of supernatural powers (*siddhis*), are fulfilled by dwelling together with the Narmadā; the description of the various rites, such as the application of sacred ash (*bhasma*), to be performed on the banks of the Narmadā; the description of the supreme majesty and form of the Narmadā, which is greater than even the eternal [Goddess]; and the composition of a hymn to the Narmadā by the sages who had assembled on her banks at dawn.

A description of the names of the twenty-one *kalpas* in their respective order; a description of the abodes of the gods within those *kalpas*; a description of the commencement of the dissolution (*saṃhāra*) at the end of the *kalpa*; a description of the scattering of the winds, heat, and bodies during the time of the *saṃvarta*; a description of the *kalpa* by Brahmā; and a description of Brahmā’s performance of praise for the Lord.

The description of the twelve suns of the *saṃvartaka* age scorching [the world]; the description of the agitation of the five elements; the description of the dissolution of the universe; the description of the gods, including Brahmā, sitting together with Viṣṇu, who had assumed the form of a child at the end of the night of the dissolution; the description of the merging of the four Vedas into one; the description of the rain falling in torrents like the downpour from a massed cloud; and the description of Mārkaṇḍeya performing a hymn of praise to the Lord out of fear while all fourteen worlds were gathered together in a single place.

In this [section], the *Mārkaṇḍeya Parva*, there is the granting of a boon by the Blessed One to Mārkaṇḍeya through the Narmadā assuming a certain form; the praise of the Narmadā by Mārkaṇḍeya; the narration of the events of the Śrī-Vārāha Kalpa; the description of the signs and characteristics of the dissolution of all beings; the performance of a hymn of praise by Mārkaṇḍeya, who was alone and terrified, to the Lord reclining upon Śeṣa; the appearance of a certain goddess; and finally, the disappearance of the goddess Earth, who acted upon the instruction of Mārkaṇḍeya.

At the commencement of the description of the majesty of the sacred fords (tīrthas) situated on the banks of the Narmadā, there is first of all the narration of the origin of the river Kapilā. Then follows the performance of penance directed toward Lord Īśvara in order to obtain Gaṅgā and the other sixteen rivers as wives; the granting of boons to Āpnuvat by Śaṅkara, who was pleased by that penance; and the narration of the origin of the Vidarbhā.

The description of how Duryodhana, having been approached by Agni who had assumed the form of a Brahmin to beg for alms, offered him various objects; the prohibition of those offerings; then, the sight of Agni in his true form to the grieving king; the description of King Duryodhana’s performance of the sacrifice and the greatness of the assembly of sacrificial priests; and the description of the bestowal of boons.

The two [sages] were filled with wonder at the abundance of fire in the sacrificial pit; having understood the cause of that, [the narrative proceeds to] the description of the greatness of the confluence of the Niṣkagaṅgā with the Yamunā. ... . Bha.

The performance of the marriage; the description of the greatness of the account of the origin of Jāleśvara; when the gods, including Indra, were oppressed by the asuras such as Bāṇāsura, [the narrative] describes how they performed the worship of the Sun with a certain mantra at the bank of the Narmadā and installed a linga, as well as their seeking refuge in Viṣṇu at Ravitīrtha; thereafter, the greatness of the bestowal of knowledge upon all the gods, including Brahmā and Viṣṇu, on Mount Kailāsa.

The arrival [of Nārada]; there, the praise of Maheśvara by the celestial sages; at the command of Śiva, Nārada’s description of the marriages of Bāṇāsura and Mandodarī with Rāvaṇa, preceded by an account of their sporting and pastimes in a celestial chariot; the arrival of Rāvaṇa’s son nearby; at the word of Bāṇāsura, Nārada’s desire to see the wives of Bāṇa in the inner apartments; Meghanāda’s installation of a Liṅga of Śiva under his own name after performing worship of Śiva; and the knowledge of the Meghanāda Tīrtha.

O brothers, [this is] the greatness of the bestowal of the fruits of the Madhūkadhvaja pilgrimage, bathing, giving gifts, and so forth, as requested by Bāṇa and narrated by Nārada concerning her. [Section] Ka: The narration of the greatness; Na: ... the establishment of the image by Dārukākhya, the friend of Dakra, through the grace of Śiva; the description of the greatness of knowledge and other virtues at the Dāru-tīrtha; and, in connection with King [Kārtavīrya’s] service to Nārada, the description of the agitation of Tripura. — [Section]: The description of the greatness.

The performance of hospitality by Śiva; the arrival of Śaṅkara with Pārvatī in a celestial chariot at Dāruvana, sent by Śiva for the purpose of slaying Tripura; the reduction of the enemies to ashes by Bāṇa, the lord of Dāruvana, following the dialogue between Kaṅkara and Pāravatī; the description of the greatness of Bāṇa’s offering of a garland of Śiva upon his head and his subsequent hymn of praise to Śiva; and the description of the greatness of the Narmadeśvara Tīrtha.

...the granting of boons to the demon Bāṇāsura by Daśśvara; the hymn of praise offered by Brahmā to Kapilā, who had emerged from the Avālā lake at the Jvāleśvara Tīrtha; the description of the origin and greatness of Kapilā at the command of Brahmā; and the description of the majesty of the Amareśvara Tīrtha. ...

“*To himself:* The arrival of the mortal world; the description of the installation of various deities in the different limbs of the river Kapilā; the description of the greatness of the merit of bathing and giving gifts at the confluence of the Kāverī in the context of the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Mārkaṇḍeya; therein, the description of the greatness of the knowledge and other [virtues] at the banks of the Kapilā...

[In the *Verīsaṃgama-jñāna*,] Kubera performed various austerities and observances, such as the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow; then, having worshipped the Lord of Gods with a leaf of the *dāru* tree named *karañja*, by His grace he established a shrine of Śiva in his own name and returned home. [This section contains] Kubera’s hymn of praise to the Lord, the narration by Vasiṣṭha of the greatness of bathing at that sacred ford (*tīrtha*), the greatness of bathing at the *Karañjeśvara-tīrtha*, and then the greatness of the *Dāru-tīrtha*.

A description of the majesty of Kuṇḍaleśvara Tīrtha, established by Kuṇḍala, the son of Viśravas; the majesty of Brahmāvarta Tīrtha... [omitted]; the arrival there of the sister of Yājñavalkya while she was searching for her brother; the majesty of Putraśvara; the majesty of Śakaraśvara; Ga... [omitted].

In a dream, Yājñavalkya vomited and discharged his semen; while Rātarvaṅkrama was searching for it here and there, the greatness of Abhitīya was manifested; there, the daughter of a certain king named Duryodhana, who had been previously betrothed to him, came into the presence of Yājñavalkya along with his sister.

The narration of the entire account following the sister’s affectionate words; how, when Yājñavalkya’s sister Mūtabhadrakaṭakā became pregnant due to contact with his seminal fluid, she went to the Aśvattha tree on Mount Ṛkṣamūla and described her arrival there; and how, at the foot of a Pippala tree, Nārada—the sage known as Pippalāda—observed the affliction caused by the planet Saturn to himself and [saw] Saturn traveling through the sky.

The casting down [of Baka] by the mere utterance of his own ṛṣi-name; the insistence that Śaneśvara will not cause affliction for Baka until he reaches sixteen years of age; the creation of a *kṛtyā* by reviving it through the *ameyī-dhāraṇā*; the dispatching of that *kṛtyā* against Yājñavalkya, his father; the departure of Yājñavalkya, terrified by the *kṛtyā*, to the worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Kuvera for his own protection; and the naming of that *kṛtyā* "Yogīśvarī" by Śaṅkara.

A description of Piṣpalāda’s performance of austerities; the establishment of the shrine named Piṣpalādeśvara by Piṣpalāda after his own name; a description of its majesty and the greatness of the Śūlabheda Varatīrtha. A description praising Śūlabheda; a description of the origin of the Śūlabheda Tīrtha, including an account of the granting of boons to the Asura Andhaka; and within that description of the origin of the Śūlabheda Tīrtha, an account of how the Asura Andhaka, having conquered the gods, abducted Śacī.

The gods' journey to the world of Brahmā; the gods, having offered praise to Brahmā, explain the reason for their arrival; the gods' journey with Lord Brahmā to the world of Viṣṇu; the gods, led by Brahmā, offering hymns of praise to Viṣṇu; Viṣṇu granting a promise of safety to the gods; the subduing of Andhaka, who was difficult to conquer in battle, by the Blessed One; Andhaka's offering of hymns of praise to the Blessed One; and, by the command of Viṣṇu, the commencement of a battle between Śakra and Kaṭa.

The shaking of Mount Kailāsa by Andhaka as he entered; the great battle between Andhaka and the enraged Diva (Śiva); the arrival of Durgā there for the sake of Śaṅkara’s cause; Andhaka’s defeat through Durgā’s assistance; Andhaka’s performance of a hymn of praise to Śiva; and during the conflict between Uttānapāda and Śaṅkara, the description of the battle between Andhaka and Viṣṇu; and therein, having slain the Asura Andhaka with his own weapon, Śaṅkara’s departure together with Umā.

The journey to Kailāsa; the offering of praise to Śaṅkara by the supreme and subordinate deities on Kailāsa; thereafter, the establishment of the Śūlabheda Tīrtha at the site of the battle with the Asura Andhaka; the description of the majesty of the Śūlabheda Tīrtha, including the rules regarding the examination of worthy and unworthy recipients for gifts and other regulations; the description of the greatness of the practice of giving and dharma in the waters of Śūlabheda; the narration of the account of Dīrghatapasvin; and the description of the story of Ṛṣabhaṅga’s ascent to heaven.

The narration of the account of Dīrghatapas’s ascent to heaven along with his attendants; the description of the greatness of Śūlabheda and the account of King Kārīra’s journey there; the descent of the Gaṅgā to the earth, the description of the greatness of bathing and other rites on the banks of the Gaṅgā; the description of the greatness of Devarilā; and the arrival of the maiden named Bhānumatī, the daughter of Vacedinātha, at the bank of the Revā after she had gone to Vainya.

The description of Bhānumatī’s journey to Oṃkāreśvara, Amarakaṇṭaka, Cakratīrtha, Śūlabheda, and other holy sites; then, the description of the majesty of Devakhāta; in connection with that, the departure of a Śabara hunter into the forest with his wife for the purpose of hunting; the Śabara’s journey to the edge of the lake and his gathering of lotuses upon hearing the voice of his wife and her words; and the Śabara’s performance of worship to Śiva with those lotuses after going to the holy sites such as Śūlabheda.

The dialogue between Bhānumatī and the excellent Śiva; the performance of all rites for holy fords (*tīrtha*) and ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*) by the Śabara; the description of the majesty of the fruits of visiting holy fords, offering water, giving gifts, and so forth; Bhānumatī’s journey to the Mārkaṇḍeya-hrada on the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*) and her performance of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites; the hunter’s departure to heaven; the account of Bhānumatī performing penance at the Śvala-hrada in the context of the conversation between Uttānapāda and Śiva; the description of Bhānumatī’s residence in heaven; and the description of her journey [to that realm].

The description of the greatness of Śūrabheda; the description of the greatness of the Puṣkariṇī-tīrtha; the greatness of the Āditya-tīrtha; and, in the context of the dialogue between Uttānapāda and Īśvara, the description of how the gods attained success through the worship of Śiva, the descent of the Gaṅgā from heaven, and the attainment of liberation through the Maṇināga and other excellent tīrthas; the composition of hymns for the Naimiṣāraṇya by those who had reached the state of fearlessness; and the description of the Sun-god (Ādityeśvara) situated on the bank of the Śeṣa.

The description of the greatness of the *Māhātmya-caraṇa*, including the account of how those Brahmins afflicted by sins such as eating forbidden food were purified through knowledge of the sacred field (*kṣetra*) and other means, and became solely intent on the contemplation of the Supreme. Following the description of the *Indravatāpa* penance, there is the description of the greatness of the *Śakreśvara-tīrtha*. Then follows the description of the greatness of the *Dhāpidika-cmareśvara-tīrtha*, the description of the greatness of the *Agastyeśvara-tīrtha*, and the description of the greatness of the *Ānandeśvara-tīrtha*.

— [This is] the description of the greatness of the Mārutī-tīrtha. In the course of describing the greatness of the Laṅkaśavara-sīmā, there is a description of the performance of penance by the Dānava Kālaṭha; the granting of a boon to him by Śiva; the bull Nandin’s desire to bring about the defeat of the Dānava in battle; the sight of the approaching Dānava and the Lord’s departure for Kaiḍāsa together with Umā, mounted upon the bull; and the pursuit of the fleeing Dānava by the arrow discharged from the bow by Indra, Brahmā, and the other gods.

The opening narrative; the narration by Nārada to Viṣṇu concerning the affliction caused by the Dānavas and other events; Viṣṇu’s assumption of the form of a maiden near the Nyagrodha tree through his illusory power (*māyā*) for the purpose of deluding the Dānava; the Dānava, infatuated upon seeing the maiden, placing his hand upon his own head until it turned to ashes; thereafter, Viṣṇu’s departure to his own abode; the installation of Ṭaṅkeśvara; and the description of the greatness of bathing at the Ṭaṅkeśvara Tīrtha.

— Description of the greatness of Dhanada-tīrtha. ... Description of the greatness of Maṅgaleśvara, preceded by the account of the forest of Megheśvara established at Saṅgaṭa. ... Description of the greatness of Bhaṭṭavinirmita-tīrtha. ... Description of the greatness of Kāmeśvara-tīrtha. Mutual recognition; the effort made by the two [sages] who had previously been friends according to their own mutual agreement; therein, the subjects concerning the path of the Kadru serpent from the mountains.

When the curse was pronounced, Maṇināga performed austerities to ward off that curse and established a Śiva-liṅga; [this is followed by] a description of the greatness of the gift of knowledge and other such acts, and a description of the majesty of the Gopāreśvara Tīrtha, which emerged from the earth during the performance of penance by Kāmadhenu.

The description of the greatness of the Gautameśvara-liṅga established by Gautama and the Gautamī-tīrtha; the description of the greatness of the Mīneśvara-vīrya; the performance of penance by Nārada on the northern bank of the Revā; the granting of boons to Nārada by Śiva, who was pleased by that penance; the establishment of the Śivaraṭa by Nārada at the command of Śiva’s word; the description of the greatness of the fruits of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at the Nāradeśvara-tīrtha; and the description of the greatness of the offering of curd and honey at the two tīrthas of Ṛddhiskanda and Madhuskanda.

The glorification of the Dadhiskanda and Madhuskanda tīrthas; the establishment of a liṅga by Nandin—who had come from various other holy sites after performing austerities there—to pull out the bank of the Dadhiskanda-Madhuskanda [river] and deposit it in another cave; the description of the greatness of the Nedikeyvara tīrtha; and the description of the greatness of the Varuṇeśvara tīrtha.

Following a description of the *vahitīrtha*, there is a description of the greatness of the *dadhiskanda* and other sacred sites; then, in the description of the greatness of *Hanumatīśvara*, it is told how Rāma went to the Kāśī region for the purpose of worshipping Śiva after having brought about the destruction of Rāvaṇa and the others. After the destruction of the Rākṣasas, Hanumān performed the *stambhana* (paralysis) of Nandana by obstructing the flow of the Brahmahatyā sin. For the sake of removing that Brahmahatyā, Hanumān came to the Narmadā river. Then, Lord Śiva was pleased with Hanumān due to his penance performed at *Hanumatchatā*.

The installation of the *liṅga* by Hanumān at the command of the Lord’s word; the wandering of the prince named Itarāhu, son of King Supāva; the subjects regarding Hanumān’s pillar; the arrival of the Piṅgalākṣa Brahmin who had come there for the sake of the bones; his meeting with the prince; and the description of the greatness of the nearby Kedāra-tīrtha. [...]

Dha, Dha: And from the *Satrādśca*: a description of the greatness of the Nārāyaṇa deity installed by Nara and Nārāyaṇa at Śikhaṇḍirājatantra, concerning the King who was about to perform the rite of throwing bones [into the fire], preceded by the narrative of the dialogue between a Brahmin and a maiden; and a description of the greatness of the Lord of Hanumanteśvara, including a certain account of Pūru.

The description of the greatness of Koṭīśvara-tīrtha; the greatness of Ṛmitīrtha; the description of the supreme fruits of granting knowledge and other gifts at the tīrthas of Rameśvara, Lakṣaṇeśvara, and Kumbheśvara; how the Moon, having given twenty-one daughters to Daśarṇa, chose Rohiṇī and felt displeasure toward the others, and out of affection for his own daughters, gave them the form of stars to the Moon; the offering of praise by Bhīma to Koṭīśvara; thereafter, by the command of Īśāna, the installation of the Liṅga known as Somanātheśvara. Somanātheśvara—

The description of the story concerning Kaṇva, who was freed from ten thousand sins of Brahman-slaughter by the power of Kiṅkaprabhāvakarī; and the description of the greatness of the Somanātha temple on Mount Raṅga.

(And the description of the greatness of the Piṅgaladāra Tīrtha; the description of the greatness of the Ṛṇatrayamocana Tīrtha; the description of the excellent Kapiñjeśvara Vīrtha; the description of the greatness of the Pūtikeśvara Tīrtha; and the description of the greatness of Cakratīrtha established by Viṣṇu. Then, seeing the gods defeated by the Dānava Vālameṣa, Brahmā went into the presence of Viṣṇu. Having heard the benediction uttered by the gods, the Blessed One granted a promise of fearlessness to the deities. Thereafter, a mutual battle took place between Viṣṇu and Vālameṣa.)

The impelling of Śaśarākha; then, by means of his own discus, the Lord’s severing of his head; seeing that severed head floating in the waters of the Narmadā, the establishment of a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) there; the renown of that *tīrtha* under the name Cakratīrtha—also known as Jalaśāyin; and therein, the description of the greatness and the performance of specific rites such as bathing and giving gifts; the description of the greatness of Caṇḍāditya-tīrtha; the description of the greatness of Yamahāsya-tīrtha; and the description of the greatness of Kaṭadoḍī-tīrtha.

In the context of describing the birth of Vyāsatīrtha, there is an account of the life and ascetic practices of the sage Parāśara; the giving of a certain fisherman’s daughter by the sage Parāśara at the conclusion of his penance; his addressing her as "O princess" and recounting the story of her previous existence; then, following their union with that woman of celestial fragrance, the description of the birth of Vyāsa from the power of the sage Parāśara; and [the subsequent events] by Vyāsa...

The performance of penance by Dātaṭa; the granting of boons by the Lord Śiva, who was pleased by that penance; Vyāsa’s composition of the hymn to Narmadā and his installation of the image of Śiva on the bank of the Narmadā. The description of the fruits of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at Vyāsatīrtha; the glorification of the greatness of Prabhāsatīrtha; the description of the greatness of Nāgeśvaratīrtha; the description of the greatness of Mārkaṇḍeyeśa established by Mārkaṇḍeya; the description of the greatness of Saṃkarṣaṇatīrtha; and the description of the greatness of Manmathedvara.

A description of the majesty of the confluence of the Eraṇḍī; there, Anasūyā and Atri, being childless, experience great sorrow; then, out of a desire for penance, Anasūyā goes to the confluence of the Eraṇḍī situated on the bank of the Aluñcayā; at the conclusion of her penance, the arrival of the three deities beginning with Brahmā; the granting of boons by the gods to Anasūyā for the sake of obtaining sons; then, a description of the account of the three sons named Durvāsas, Datta, and Soma given to Anasūyā; and finally, a description of the majesty of that sacred site (tīrtha).

The narration of the story of the farmer Govinda, who was tormented by attachment and grief for his son; the description of how he attained the state of a worm while lying upon that very ground; then his journey with his wife to the confluence of the Eraṇḍī river to seek refuge; their liberation from suffering through the gift of cows, land, gold, and other offerings; the description of the fruits of hearing the *Govindāṣṭaka*; the glorification of the majesty of the Eraṇḍī confluence; and the glorification of the majesty of the Añjirasa-tīrtha (also known as the Aṅgāraka-tīrtha).
—The description of the greatness of Pāṇḍutīrtha. ||| Ta ||| (||)

— Description of the greatness of Trilocana-tīrtha; the battle between the gods and the demons; Indra’s performance of penance on the banks of the Narmadā after being overcome by the sin of Brahman-slaughter upon killing Vṛtra; the arrival of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara at the conclusion of his penance; the establishment of Śiva-liṅgas there by their command; description of the greatness of Indratīrtha; and the description of the greatness of Kaṇḍoḍī-tīrtha.

The journey of the Dānava named Kambu to the bank of the Narmadā for the sake of penance; Śaṅkara, being pleased by that penance, granting him a boon; the establishment of a Liṅga of Śiva by Kambu; the greatness of the Kaivarta and Devatīrtha; the establishment of a Śivaliṅga by Soma after he had performed penance at that Tīrtha which destroys sins; a description of the majesty of Somatīrtha and Candrahāsa-tīrtha; and in the description of the majesty of Kohanasvatīrtha, a description of the eye created by Brahmā.

The description of the establishment of the four-fold caste system; the terrifying of Yama mounted upon his buffalo out of fear after hearing the words "Slay! from the Brahmin who had consumed the remnants of the *sat-cāra* offering; the vision of the Lord through the recitation of the *Śata-rudriya* hymn; the description of the defeat of Yama; the installation of the Kodaṇḍasvāmī [liṅga]; the description of the greatness of the Kodaṇḍasvāmī Tīrtha; the description of the greatness of the Kamedeśvara Tīrtha; and the description of the greatness of the Nedeśvara Tīrtha.

The narration of the causes for obtaining the two names Rerā and Ādityabhāskara; the description of the asceticism of Ravija; the installation of the Śivaliṅga by Ravi; the description of the majesty of Ravitīrtha; the description of the majesty of the Ayoniprabhava-tīrtha; and the description of the majesty of Abhnitīrtha.

Then follows the description of the greatness of Śarakuṭeśvara-tīrtha; the description of the greatness of Brahma-tīrtha; the description of the greatness of Deva-tīrtha; the narration of the origin of Nāga-tīrtha, including the account of Vinatā’s anger; the description of the greatness of Nāgadeva-tīrtha; the description of the greatness of Ādivārāha-tīrtha; the narration of how the four world-protectors (lokapālas) performed the worship of Īśvara and obtained boons from the Lord; and by those same four world-protectors, the establishment of the Śivaliṅgas.

Description of the greatness of the four shrines beginning with Kuberādi; description of the greatness of Rāmeśvara Tīrtha. — — Description of the greatness of Siddheśvara; the granting of a curse by Gautama to Indra for his union with Aditi; the burning of Indra by the power of Aditi’s penance. || 45 ||

In this section concerning the glorification of Rukmiṇī-tīrtha, the subjects of the chapter are as follows: the description of the slaying of Śiśupāla by Kṛṣṇa; the liberation from the curse of Aditi who had been struck with her foot by Balarāma; the establishment of a Liṅga named after herself by Mahilā; the description of the seventh day of Ādityeśvara; and the description of the majesty of Karkaṭeśvara.

The description of Śakra performing penance after being struck by the curse given by Gautama; the narration of the greatness of Śakreśvara Tīrtha; the narration of the greatness of Soma Tīrtha; the narration of the greatness of Antāpeśvara Tīrtha; the description of the battle involving Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Caidya, Māgadha, and others; the description of the destruction of Rukmiṇa performed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa; the description of the marriage ceremony between Rukmiṇī and Kṛṣṇa; [and] the [shrine] established by Rukmiṇī.

A detailed description of the great majesty of Raṅkrimiṇī-tīrtha; a description of the majesty of Yojanaika-tīrtha; ... a description of the majesty of Dvādaśī-tīrtha; ... and a description of the majesty of Kitna-tīrtha. A detailed description of the majesty of the various rites—such as bathing, giving gifts, recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), and the pouring out of water—at this Āsmāhaka-tīrtha; ... and a description of the majesty of Sineśca-tīrtha; ... [and so forth].

Chapter 28: Description of the greatness of Maṅgalavastīrtha; ...; description of the greatness of Chiṅgavāyada-tīrtha; when Kāmadeva was reduced to ashes, the gods' performance of various rites for his restoration; the penance performed by Aṅga after he had been cursed by Śiva, and the removal of that curse; the greatness of the Liṅga of Āṅgu-meśvara; in the description of the greatness of the Liṅga of Aṅkārakeśvara, the account of the birth of Śvetaja; and the sequence of the births of the three beginning with Rāvaṇa—thus ends the [number of] chapters.

The description of the greatness of Viṣayāpūrvavāra; the description of the greatness of Bhāgaṅeḍavara; the description of the greatness of Ādityeśvara Tīrtha; the description of the greatness of Karkaṭeśvara Tīrtha; within the description of the origin of Śuklatīrtha, the narrative of Cāṇakya being bitten by two crows; the description of Cāṇakya’s transformation into Kauṭilya; the account of the attainment of success by Cāṇakya; and the description of the greatness of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at Śuklatīrtha.

A description of the majesty of the Haṃkārasvāmin Tīrtha; a description of the majesty of the excellent Saṃgama Tīrtha; a description of the majesty of the Anaraṅkeśvara Tīrtha; a description of the ripening of karma (karmavipāka); a description of the Gabhastila Tīrtha; a description of the majesty of the fruits of great gifts (mahādāna) such as the Dhruvavrata and others; the majesty of the gift of lamps and other offerings to Yama on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina; and a description of the majesty of the Anaraṅkeśvara Tīrtha.

A description of the majesty of Mokṣatīrtha; a description of the majesty of Sarpetīrtha; a description of the majesty of Gopaśvaratīrtha; a description of the majesty of Kanāgatīrtha; a description of the majesty of Sāvairīśvaratīrtha; and a description of the majesty of Siddheśvaratīrtha.

A description of the greatness of Siddheśvarī-tīrtha; the installation of Śiva by Mārkaṇḍeya after performing penance with the permission of Śiva; a description of the greatness of the granting of boons to Mārkaṇḍeya; Rāvaṇa and others performing penance and receiving boons from Śiva; the installation of the excellent Liṅga by Kera; and a description of the greatness of Amareśvara.

—In the context of the story of Māṇḍavya’s impalement on a stake, there is the account of King Devapaṇa, who had obtained a daughter through the grace of the Lord; the abduction of his daughter, named Kāmaparamodinī, by a Śabara disguised as a hawk; the description of the lamentation performed by her companions upon the abduction of the princess known as Kāmaparamodinī; and the dispatching of ministers and others by King Devapaṇa, having heard of that event from his spies, for the purpose of investigating it at the hermitage of Māṇḍavya.

Having seen the ornaments on Nyagrodha’s body, he reported that matter to the king; then, by the king's command, the arrival of the Ṛṣis at the place where Māṇḍavya was impaled on a stake; the description of how they proceeded to cast a curse upon the king; then the description of the ripening of karma (*karmavipāka*) as told by the great Ṛṣi Māṇḍavya to the other Ṛṣis; the departure of the Ṛṣis for their own hermitage at Māṇḍavya’s command; and there, the arrival of Śāṇḍilya carrying a sick man on his shoulder.

The description of the conversation between Śāṇḍilī’s wife and Māṇḍavya—who was trembling as the staff shook due to the impact of the blow when she, unaware, had struck his feet with her own foot out of fear of her husband; the mutual pronouncing of curses upon one another by them both; the return of the celestial sages (*devarṣis*) to Māṇḍavya’s hermitage and their discourse there; and the bringing of the maiden by the Śabara before King Devāpi due to Māṇḍavya’s curse.

The liberation from bondage of Sūrya, who had been obstructed by that Brahmin’s wife through her own practice of *pātivratya* (devotion to her husband); the description of Śāṇḍilya bestowing life once again; the description of the greatness of bathing, giving gifts, and other rites at Māṇḍavyatīrtha; ... the description of the greatness of Śuddheśvara Tīrtha; and the description of the greatness of Gopiśvara Tīrtha.
Description of the greatness of Kapiḷeśvaratīrtha, established by Kapila on the banks of the Narmadā for the sake of redeeming the sons of Sagara; description of the greatness of Gaṅgābahukatīrtha.

Description of the majesty of the Gautameśvara Tīrtha;—in the introduction to the majesty of the Duṇḍhāśvamedhika Tīrtha, within the dialogue between Śaṅkara and Pārvatī, the narration of the majesty of the Śarara Tīrtha by a certain Brahmin who performed penance; the departure of a bull toward the gods after it beheld its protector; the offering of praise to Śiva; the granting of boons to the bull by Īśvara; the establishment of the Liṅga; and the origin of Śukaccha and the Śararākaccha Tīrtha.

A description of the greatness of the gift of knowledge and other virtues; a description of the greatness of the Kedāreśvara Tīrtha... [the establishment of the holy site named Dhautapāpa by Śaṃyu, who was afflicted by the sin of Brahman-slaughter resulting from the severing of the fifth head of Brahmā]; a description of the greatness of the Dhautapāpa Tīrtha; [a description of the greatness of the Eraṇḍī Tīrtha]...

— [The description of] Garuḍa’s composition of a hymn to Cāmuṇḍā; by the grace of Cāmuṇḍā, Garuḍa’s installation of the image of Kanakhaḍeśvara; the description of the majesty of the Kāṅābhirudra Tīrtha, preceded by the description of the origin of Varāḍa, followed by the description of the majesty of Udīṇevarāitīya; the description of the majesty of Candrabhāsa, also known by the name Candrahāsya; the description of the majesty of Dvādaśāditya Tīrtha; and the dispatching of Apsarases and others by Indra for the purpose of disturbing the penance of Nara and Nārāyaṇa. — 103. — 104. — 105. — 106. — 107. — 108. — 109. — 110. — 111. — 112. — 113. — 114. — 115. — 116. — 117. — 118. — 119. — 120. — 121. — 122. — 123. — 124. — 125. — 126. — 127. — 128. — 129. — 130. — 131. — 132. — 133. — 134. — 135. — 136. — 137. — 138. — 139. — 140. — 141. — 142. — 143. — 144. — 145. — 146. — 147. — 148. — 149. — 150. — 151. — 152. — 153. — 154. — 155. — 156. — 157. — 158. — 159. — 160. — 161. — 162. — 163. — 164. — 165. — 166. — 167. — 168. — 169. — 170. — 171. — 172. — 173. — 174. — 175. — 176. — 177. — 178. — 179. — 180. — 181. — 182. — 183. — 184. — 185. — 186. — 187. — 188. — 189. — 190. — 191. — 192. — 193. — 194. — 195. — 196. — 197. — 198. — 199. — 200. — 201. — 202. — 203. — 204. — 205. — 206. — 207. — 208. — 209. — 210. — 211. — 212. — 213. — 214. — 215. — 216. — 217. — 218. — 219. — 220. — 221. — 222. — 223. — 224. — 225. — 226. — 227. — 228. — 229. — 230. — 231. — 232. — 233. — 234. — 235. — 236. — 237. — 238. — 23

The objects of Bhavyā’s sight (Paṭala); the objects of Bhavyā’s sight (Paṭala). The offering of the Gaṇas and other entities residing within the cosmic egg; the description of the greatness of the Viṣṇumocana Tīrtha by the Apsarases, who were filled with wonder at its partial manifestation;

the composition of a hymn to Nara-Nārāyaṇa in the form of a Rāhu; the return of the Apsarases and others to their own celestial realm; the description of the greatness of the Puṣkaratīrtha for Indra; the narration of the account of Viṣṇuśarmā during the introduction to the description of the Bhārabhūtī Tīrtha; and the description of the greatness of Śrīpati.

The arrival of Śiva disguised as a young brahmin student (*baṭu*); the description of the fulfillment of the promise made by the student, and the fruits of knowledge regarding one's own *śrīpatikṣetra* and the gift of cows and other offerings.

The bathing of the wicked who had violated their vows in the waters of the Narmadā; the restoration to life of Lakṣmī—who, having heard from the mouth of Indra of Nārāyaṇa’s power, desired that Nārāyaṇa, was then reduced to ashes by Śiva, and subsequently revived—by means of the command of Śiva; the establishment of a *liṅga* there, whereby that sacred site became famous by the name Bhārabhūti; his performance of penance at the edge of the ocean; the marriage with Lakṣmī performed by the gratified Nārāyaṇa; and his attainment of the status of Śrīpati.
The description of the greatness of the Bhārabhūti Tīrtha; the description of the commencement of the marriage of the treacherous Vaiśya named Sukeśin; and the narration of the story.

Description of the majesty of Śrīpati; ... description of the majesty of Pukhikha-tīrtha; description of the majesty of Daṃsa-tīrtha; ... description of the majesty of Yuṇḍita-tīrtha; description of the majesty of Mūṭasthāna-tīrtha; description of the majesty of Ekaśāra-Ḍiṇḍimeśvara-tīrtha. The King’s removal of Māṇḍavya, who had been impaled upon a stake, from that stake; the arrival of Kaṅkara there; and description of the majesty of Āmaṅeśvara-tīrtha.

Dha: Māṇḍavya’s narration of ancient accounts, such as the story of Śaukarābhra and Dākṣāyaṇī; Māṇḍavya’s description of the majesty of the holy site of Śrīkapāka-tīrtha; ... [the] composition of hymns to the Goddess; descriptions of the Goddess’s various forms and her diverse names; the description of the majesty of the holy site of Śaḍeśvaragiri; ... [the] installation of the Śivaliṅga by Nāga; the description of the majesty of that Śaḍeśvaragi[ri]; ...
the description of the majesty of Āṣāḍhī-tīrtha.
Description of the greatness of Āścinī-tīrtha; ... description of the greatness of Eraṇḍī-tīrtha.

A description of the greatness of Sāvitrītīrtha; a description of the greatness of the Saṃdevatīrtha after the destruction of King Jaina—who had committed an offense against his father Jamadagni—was accomplished twenty-one times; and after the slaughter of the Kṣatriyas was performed, the establishment of Jāmadagnyeśvara by Paraśurāma for the sake of purifying that sin, followed by a description of the greatness of Jāmadagnyatīrtha and a description of the ritual for the worship of Jāmadagnyeśvara.

The description of the majesty of Koṭitīrtha. ... The description of the majesty of Koṭitīrtha. The description of the majesty of Dha-peṭāmahatīrtha. ... The description of the majesty of Loṭaṇeśvaratīrtha. The description of the majesty of Na-karītīrtha. ... The description of the majesty of Haseśvara preceded by the dialogue between Bṛhaspati and Indra. ... — " " " The description of the majesty of Dakṣakanyātīrtha. ...

Description of the majesty of the Tīrtha of Tiodeśvara; description of the majesty of the Dadadeba-yuvaṇauvadutīrtha; description of the majesty of the Vāseśvara-tīrtha; description of the majesty of the Koṭīśvara-tīrtha; the falling [of the deity]; the offering of praise to Śiva by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others; and the worship of the Liṅga by Śaṃkara, who was pleased thereby.

The establishment of a Śiva-liṅga by the one named Alakhikā through the power of her own name; the description of the greatness of Acakīśvara-tīrtha and the narration of its ritual procedure; thereafter, the gods having gone to the excellent holy site of Hīṭakeśvara, the installation of that very liṅga there; [the description of its majesty]; and the description of the greatness of worshipping the liṅga. ... Chapter 6.

The account of how Bhānu, together with his wife Śāntā, performed austerities for the sake of curing Bhānumatī of leprosy; how, by uprooting the quarters of the world, he caused the Gaṅgā to descend from the netherworld (pātāla); how, by the command of Śiva, he attained the state of being marked by three tusks (Tridaśāṅka) and established the Śivaliṅga named Vimaleśvara; and the description of the greatness of the Vimalatheśvara Tīrtha, including the narrative of how Triśāṅku, at the request of Vasiṣṭha, made preparations for his own ascent to heaven. ...

When Vasiṣṭha declared that this was impossible, [the king] harbored a wicked resolve in his mind to seek another preceptor. [The text then contains] a description of the procedure for pilgrimage to all the sacred sites (tīrthas) located on the banks of the Narmadā in their proper order, specifically regarding those tīrthas. Disregarding the words of Vasiṣṭha, out of wickedness or according to his own will, he prepared to go toward Triroka; [this section includes] a description of the majesty of the son of Vasiṣṭha. ...

[The passage describes] the pronouncing of the curse, "Become a Caṇḍāla! By that curse, Khadyota attained the state of a Caṇḍāla; subsequently, through remorse, [the narrative includes] the account of his undertaking a pilgrimage to holy sites (*tīrthayātrā*), his majesty, and his merit. Then, by the command of the suffering Triśaṅku, Hariścandra—the son of Viśvāmitra and the grandson of Triśaṅku—was consecrated in the kingdom by the ministers.

A description of the hearing of the Revākhaṇḍa, the recitation [of it], and the proclamation of the fruits of giving and other such acts; the departure of Trishanku along with him on foot into the great forest; and the enumeration of the various holy fords (*tīrtha*) and confluences (*saṅgama*), as well as a description of the excellence of those holy fords.

The journey of Caṇḍāla as he travels through the forest; his arrival at the hermitage of Triraśaṅku; then, by Vidurāmitra, a description of the sequence of the pilgrimage preceded by a calculation of the number of holy sites (tīrthas) and an account of the ruined state of all those sites. Having heard this account, [the king] made a vow, saying, "I shall lead you to heaven in this very body. Following the conclusion of the Revākhaṇḍa, there is a description of the fruit of giving the manuscript of the Revākhaṇḍa.

And by that Caṇḍāṭha, for the sake of dispelling his sins, there was wandering together through many holy places and sacred fields; while they were thus enjoying themselves, [the third section, the Revākhaṇḍa, within the Āvantyakhaṇḍa, concludes].
Thus ends the fifth section, the Āvantya-khaṇḍa, in the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. || 9 ||

Even though Brahmā had not granted permission for such an act, Viśvāmitra, through the power of his own asceticism, caused Triśaṅku to attain heaven with his physical body by means of an extraordinary sacrificial session (*āṣika-sattra*) performed through a Brāhmaṇa; then, at the conclusion, having performed the ritual bath (*avabhṛtha-snāna*) and other rites, he attained the status of a friend to the sacrifice (*yajñasakha*). Indeed.
Now, in the Skanda Mahāpurāṇa, the sixth section, the Nāgara-khaṇḍa.

The auspicious invocation following the praise of Viṣṇu by Śiśupāla, who, due to the absence of his attainment of heaven, was challenging Vidura; the commencement of the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka; therein, having heard the question of Śaunaka and composed a hymn to Nṛsiṃha to provide an answer to him, [Sūta] departed for heaven with his physical body.

In the context of describing the origin of Tīrthas, the charioteer describes Śiva’s journey to the hermitage of the sages while separated from his consort; the gods, having witnessed the mutual dispute between the creation of Viśvāmitra and that of Brahmā, approach Brahmā there; seeing a naked ascetic (digaṃbara) like a bull, they pronounce a curse upon him; by that curse, Śiva departs from that very place; thereafter, for the sake of the stability of the world, Brahmā and the others go into the presence of Viśvāmitra. Viśvāmitra...

The departure of Triśaṅku to heaven at his own word because he had no other recourse; the voluntary return of Vidūratha, the enemy of Indra, at his own will; and the conclusion of the narrative of Triśaṅku.

The fame of Hāṭakeśvara spread among all people, and they heard of the journey there; even Vidūrimitra abandoned his own land and took up residence right there. Thinking that this sacred field (*kṣetra*) was one where liberation is attained even without performing sacrifices and other rites, he established the image of Lord Hāṭakeśvara by the command of the deity. Because of that, the Nāgas also traveled everywhere with him. Regarding the greatness of Hāṭakeśvara, [it is told how] Ramānāmnī, the daughter of Diraṇyakaśipu, directed Viṣṇu for the sake of obtaining offspring.

The performance of penance; then, by the grace of Viṣṇu, the birth of the demon Vṛtra; the departure of Dadhīci to the land of Dadhīca for the purpose of producing marrow, at the request of Viṣṇu made by Indra and the others for the sake of slaying Vṛtra; the defeat of Vṛtra by the thunderbolt fashioned from Dadhīci’s bones; Śakra’s journey to Hāṭakeśvara to dispel the sin of Brahmin-slaughter resulting therefrom; the removal of that sin through the worship of Hāṭakeśvara; his return to his own abode; and the description of the greatness of Hāṭakeśvara by Śakra.

The dispatching of Saṃvarta, son of Niruṣa, to Nāgabali; the departure of Saṃvarta, son of Niruṣa, to the realm of the Nāgas by the command of Śakra; the return of Saṃvarta, son of Niruṣa, to the city of Śakra, being terrified by the curse arising from the destruction of the sacrificial post (chiga); then, at the command of Vṛṣapati, Śakra’s journey to the presence of Himākhya to dispatch his sons Viḍapūika and others; and [the account] of those known as Bhaināka, Nadivardhana, and Raktabhūṅga, who, though commanded for Śakra’s business by Himākhya, did not accept the command.

Having observed the displeasure of his three sons, Śakra bestowed a curse upon them. Out of fear of that curse, he went to the mountain named Raktaśṛṅga in order to purify the Naga-cave; there, by means of the Devanadī river, he established many holy bathing sites (tīrthas) that bring happiness to Raktaśṛṅga. [This concludes] the description of the purification of Raktaśṛṅga and Rikharotsāha performed by Ikṣvāku.

In the description of the greatness of the Iṅkha-tīrtha: the king’s hunting expedition to the Camatkāra-nagara; there, the killing of a deer by the king through a miracle while it was suckling its fawn; the contraction of leprosy upon the Lord of Camatkāra due to a curse uttered by a doe; and the [subsequent] state of that leprosy.

The removal of the curse; King Camatkāra’s journey to the holy site of Śaṅkhatīrtha in the land of Hāṭakeśvara; the description of the eradication of King Camatkāra’s leprosy through bathing at Śaṅkhatīrtha; and the glorification of the majesty of Śaṅkhatīrtha. Chapter 19: In the dialogue between King Camatkāra and the sages, within the account of the origin of Śaṅkhatīrtha, [the story of] Likhita, who—having been accused of theft by Chitraratha for stealing a calf from the sacrificial cow of the sage Vṛṣaṇa—was subsequently released by Chitraratha.

Then follows the cutting off of Śaṅkha’s hand; thereafter, Śaṅkha’s performance of penance at Hāṭakeśvara; the granting of a boon to Śaṅkha by the god, pleased by that penance; the description of how he regained his hand through the merit of the *ūrvaiva* sacrifice; the founding of a temple after his own name there by him; the description of the greatness of Śaṅkha-tīrtha preceded by the origin of Śaṅkha-tīrtha; and the giving of the city to the Brāhmaṇas by King Camatkāra, following the command of the Brāhmaṇas.

While residing in the city, he gave instructions to his son; having inscribed the blessings of Brahmadatta and his own kingdom upon leaves, he departed for Daṇḍakeśvara at Camatkārapura in order to practice asceticism. There, having propitiated Śiva, by the grace of Śiva he established a *liṅga* under the name Acaṇḍeśvara.

From the *Aceśvaramāhātmya*: "In the city of Camatkārapura, one cow from a certain cowherd’s herd went into the forest out of greed for grass; her owner, the cowherd, also went into the forest after her. Then, after some time, the description of how both attained the state of being birds is given. Following that, the description of their births is told: the cowherd was born into the womb of a lord of thieves (*dāṇodhipati*), while the cow was born into the womb of a minister (*mantrin*). Then, having remembered the events of their previous lives, [the two... "

The attainment of liberation through the path of Śemānika by performing circumambulation of Camatkārapura; a description of the greatness of the circumambulation of Camatkārapura; a description of the excellence of the greatness of the circumambulation of Camatkārapura, preceded by a description of the power of Mount Raktāṅga; a description of the supreme fruit of serving Lord Raktaśaṅkara while staying at the confluence of the Raktā; a description of the holy sites situated in the four quarters of Camatkārapura; therein, first, in the context of describing the greatness of Gayāśiras.

The departure of Vidūratha on a hunt into the forest; there, as Vidūratha was pursuing birds and deer, his horse, exhausted by wandering from forest to forest, fell upon the ground. Then, leaving the horse right there, Vidūratha proceeded on foot in pursuit of the birds. After traveling a great distance along the path, he beheld three hunters, Māṃsāda and the others.

Upon hearing the words of Māṃsāda and the others, Vidūratha entered the hermitage of Ṛśyaśṛṅga and engaged in a conversation with the sages, followed by a description of the performance of the evening rites.

On the following day, [there was] the departure of Vidūratha to the Khaner [region]. At the Pitr-tirtha well of Gayāri, Vidūratha related to Māṃsāda and the others the story of his own and others' liberation. Māṃsāda and the others offered the Śrāddha to the ancestors. Then, I went with Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā to the Pitṛkūpikā-tīrtha. By performing the Śrāddha there, Rāma and the others attained direct vision of their ancestors. Then, as he was contemplating treachery in order to kill Rāma and Sītā within his mind... [the text continues].

Khakmaṇa’s journey to the Vāramaṇḍana-tīrtha; the removal of his defects through the knowledge of that sacred site; thereafter, the departure for the southern mountain, the Yāmyadri; and a description of the Bāṭamaṇḍana-tīrtha, beginning with its origin... [and so forth].

In the description of the origin of the twelve Tīrthas: first, the account of Mārkaṇḍeya, the son of Sṛkaṇḍa; how he attained long life through penance and established a Liṅga at Hāṭakeśvara; the majesty of the Bāṣkalamukha Tīrtha; and within the majesty of the Bārmaṇḍana Tīrtha, the description of the birth of the forty-nine Maruts from Kaśyapa and Diti, the entry of Śakra into Diti’s womb, the cutting of the fetus by Śakra, and the subsequent pacification of the grief caused by that [act].

Śakra’s acquisition of knowledge at the Vāṭamaṇḍana Tīrtha; the cessation of Śakra’s faults through that knowledge of the Tīrtha; a description of the greatness of the Vāṭamaṇḍana Tīrtha; in the description of the Gṛdhratīrtha, the arrival of hunters there after seeing birds perched in the shade of a certain sage; the flight of the birds from there out of fear of the hunters; the pursuit of the birds by the hunters; the birds’ immediate attainment of human form upon entering a lake; and the subsequent events.

The bathing rite at that lake even by those who had attained [liberation] through the *Sṛgañayukhā* vow; the manifestation of beauty even for those who were previously emaciated by hunger; the description of attaining liberation from suffering; the glorification of the Sakhagati-tīrtha; the account of how Vāmana, having pervaded the worlds with two steps at the time of Bali’s sacrifice, placed his third step upon the region above the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) when it was split open, and thereafter the descent of the Gaṅgā; and the majesty of the Viṣṇupada-tīrtha preceded by its origin.

In the description of the majesty of the Gaṅgā flowing from Viṣṇu’s foot, there is an account of how a certain Brāhmaṇa, who was performing a sacrifice, was freed from the sin of killing a cow through the grace of that [river]; a description of the majesty of the Gaṅgā flowing from Viṣṇu’s foot; a description of the twelve hells by Yama under the pretext of visiting Gokarṇa; a description of which specific sin leads to which particular hell; and an account of Gokarṇa’s journey to Camatkārapura with Yama’s permission, where his liberation through bathing at the holy site is described.

Description of the greatness of the Gokaṇa Tīrtha. ... Enumeration of the time periods from the Aṇu-manvantara to the end of the Caturyuga; exposition of the fourfold duties (cātuṛṇya-karma); description of the origin of the Caṇḍālas, beginning with the washermen; and specifically, the description of the greatness of Kaṇikāla. ... page.

In the dialogue between Bṛhaspati and Indra, there is a description of taking refuge in all sacred fords (*tīrtha*). Then, at the command of his father Sūta, Vatsa performed the service (*śuśrūṣā*) of the great sage. When the great sage saw that his own disciple Devarāta was becoming lustful toward his daughter-in-law, he discharged his semen. From that semen, a goat was born; at the end of ten months, a girl was born from the goat. Devarāta gave the girl to Vatsa as a wife. After a long time had passed, the woman died due to a snakebite, and Vatsa [remained] alone.

The departure into the forest; despite the sages offering him various consolations, his commencement of a curse out of anger; while he was pronouncing that curse, the description of a conversation with one serpent who had assumed human form; and as that being transformed into human shape recounted a previous injury to Vatsa, it was told how in a former birth, when a swarm of bees had settled upon a cluster of lotuses in a lake belonging to Hāṭakeśvara, the sage had cast a curse.

The narration of the origin of his birth as a serpent; by that serpent in human form, the giving of instruction to the calf; therein, through attachment, the description of the common characteristics of swans and other such beings; and thereafter—

The determination in Vatsa’s own mind to perform a great worship of the Lord out of remorse for the slaying of the serpent; the description of how Vatsa attained perfection through the worship of Siddheśvara; the account of the origin of Siddheśvara; how, by the command of Bṛhaspati, Vatsa established an image for the sake of obtaining a son and performed worship, whereby he gained a son; the description of the majesty of Siddheśvara; and, in the context of describing the majesty of Nāgahrada, the account of how the nine Nāgas [were established] by the command of Brahmā.

The journey to the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara; the establishment of a linga there under his own name; King Indrasena’s death from the bite of a serpent; thereafter, Indrasena’s arrival in a dream before his son to inform him of his attainment of the state of a preta; the son’s journey to Nāgatīrtha by his father’s command; the description of his father’s liberation through the performance of *piṇḍa* offerings and the worship of the linga there; the glorification of the majesty of Nāgatīrtha; and the description of Saghṛṣitīrtha.

The description of the seven modes of worship; the account of the origin of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣi) as a sacred ford (tīrtha); during a twelve-year drought when the land was parched with hunger, the wandering of the Seven Sages everywhere; their arrival in the kingdom of King Ṛṣādarbha; seeing a young boy there, they made an effort to see him along with their attendants; meanwhile, King Ṛṣādarbha arrived there and held a conversation with them; then, [the account] of the Seven Sages desiring to eat the flesh of the young boy...

The journey to Camatkārapura, the construction [of the temple], and the installation of the Liṅga. During the description of Agastya’s hermitage: while a conflict was arising between the Vindhya and Meru mountains, the sun, his path being obstructed, went to Agastya’s hermitage; at the sun’s request, Agastya turned the Vindhya mountain face-downward and proceeded to Hāṭakeśvara in the southern direction. Having gone there with his wife Upamudrā, he installed the Liṅga. This is followed by the description of the greatness of Agastya’s hermitage.

In the first [chapter], describing the cause of Agastya’s drinking of the ocean, there is a description of the defeat of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the others in their battle with the Daityas; then, having determined that the defeat of the gods would not occur without the destruction of Dharma, Śaṅkara, through his power, brought about the ruin of the Daityas who were intent on knowledge, sacrifices, and rituals; and by his command, the regions of the Daityas dwelling in Jambūdvīpa were destroyed for the sake of slaying them.

The performance of Agastya’s *parārdhana* (final oblation); Agastya’s churning of the ocean for the sake of the gods’ mission; the destruction of the Daityas by the gods; the naming of the seat established by Agastya as "Citraśilāvarapīṭha" by the gods because they made it their own body; ... the description of the majesty of Citraśilāvarapīṭha; the description of the origin of the temple named Duḥśīla; ... the description of the majesty of the Dhundhumāradevaramaṅga.

The description of the greatness of Yayātīśvara-Ṛṅga; the establishment of the Śiṣṭas there by Brahmā; then, by the command of Brahmā, the arrival of Sarasvatī at that place to establish the Ṛṅgas; thereafter, the great sage Maṅkaṇaka performed penance there and established the Ṛṅgas; the description of the greatness of Citraśilā and the group of Maṅkaṇaka-liṅgas; the performance of penance at Hāṭakeśvara by Indra and the other gods, who were oppressed by Vāṣkali, at the command of Viṣṇu; and then, on the day of the Cūḍā-cayana sacrifice, according to the word of Bṛhaspati.

The satisfaction of the Blessed One through worship; the engagement in battle with Bāṣkali at the command of the Blessed One; the defeat of the Daitya Bāṣkali by the Blessed One and Śakra’s return to his own abode; the Blessed One’s residence there and the establishment of a Liṅga; the description of the birth of Jaratkāru; the account of the origin of Viśvāmitra’s sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa); and therein, the description of the arrival of Menakā at Vidarbhāmitra’s hermitage and the teaching of the duties of women by Vidarbhāmitra to Menakā.

When Menakā, having disregarded the rules of chastity (*pātivratya*) as described by Viśvāmitra, was questioned as to her origin and destination, and when she became agitated by Viśvāmitra’s words, Viśvāmitra censured her union with a friend. When their meeting was thus rejected by Viśvāmitra, Menakā, tormented by great sorrow, pronounced upon Viśvāmitra and Viśvāmitra upon Menakā a mutual curse in the form of old age. Thereafter, [the story continues] with the King of Mithilā... [text truncated].

The release from the curse; Viśvāmitra’s establishment of a *ṭhiga* there; the description of the greatness of the Tripuṣkara Tīrtha at Viśvāmitrakunda; the description of the greatness of the Sarasvatī Tīrtha; the arrival of the sage Ambuvīci, son of Balabhadra, at the Sarasvatī Tīrtha with his son—the mute Puṣya—in order to remove the son’s muteness; the removal of the son’s muteness through bathing and the offering of oblations there; and Ambuvīci’s hymn of praise to the Sarasvatī.

Description of the Greatness of the Sarasvatī Tīrtha: In the description of the greatness of Mahākālavana, King Radrāsena, accompanied by his wife, travels to Hāṭakeśvara. Having worshipped the Lord there and given many gifts to the Brahmins, the king recounts his own previous birth to the assembly of Brahmins. Then, that merchant-born man, who had fasted due to the lack of food and was accompanied by his wife, goes to the great Mahākālavana forest. There he beholds the Lord.

The performance of worship by King Amararada; his birth in the royal garden through the power of that merit; a description of the greatness of Mahākālavana; in the section on the greatness of Umāmaheśvara, the propitiation of Umāmaheśvara by Hariścandra for the sake of obtaining a son; the granting of a boon for a son by Umāmaheśvara, who were pleased by his penance; Hariścandra’s departure to his own palace after receiving that boon; and thereafter, [his journey] to the holy site of Hāṭakeśvara for the sake of worshipping Umāmaheśvara.

The establishment of the Chiga shrine; a description of the greatness of Umā-Maheśvara; a description of the greatness of Kalaśeśvara; the arrival of Durvāsas at the house of King Kaṭaśarūpa; and the king’s offering of hospitality, honors, and a complete meal to Durvāsas, who had come there to break his four-month fast. While eating from that vessel, [Durvāsas] cursed Kaṭaśarūpa with the words, "Become a tiger," by means of a well-prepared dish of meat. Thus, through the curse of the sage Durvāsas, [the king was transformed].

The description of attaining the state of a tiger: In the dialogue between Nandinī and the tiger, Nandinī makes an oath in the presence of the tiger; at the tiger’s word, Nandinī returns to her own place and causes her calf to become a tiger; Savārīṣṭhā and Nandinī go to the tiger’s death; having seen her truthfulness through that, the tiger, filled with remorse, asks her a question in order to test her logic; and [the story of] the tiger who attained his true state due to a curse, by worshipping the *arciṣmat* [fire] established by the arrow shot from Nandinī’s eye.

Having uttered curses that would deprive him of his sovereignty, he regained his kingship as before; thereafter, having performed the propitiation of Hari, he established a Liṅga in his own name and departed for the world of Śiva; [this concludes] the description of the greatness of Kaṭhaśaivaraṅaga.

The description of the greatness of Rādrakoṭi; the narration of how King Mitrasaha attained the state of a rākṣasa due to a curse from Vasiṣṭha; how that king, following the conduct of rākṣasas, even killed brahmins and others; how, for the removal of the sin of brahmin-murder, he undertook a pilgrimage to holy places at the instruction of Vasiṣṭha after the pronouncement of the curse; and how, by bathing in the holy sites on the Bhāruṇatī, he was liberated from the sin of brahmin-murder and resumed his reign as before.

A description of the greatness of Śramaṇā regarding the journey to the world of Śiva after the end of one’s reign; a description of the greatness of Naṅgesthāpivacarmamuṇḍā, preceded by the narrative of Nakhā; a description of the greatness of Naledara, established by Nakhā under his own name, which wards off diseases and other undesirable evils; and within the Sāṃbāditya-māhātmya, the account of how Gākhva, having received a boon through the grace of Āditya, obtained a son by worshipping Sāṃbāditya due to his lack of offspring, followed by a description of the greatness of Sāṃbāditya.

A description of the narrative of the pilgrimage to Gāṅgeya; a description of the establishment of the four Liṅgas by Gāṅgeya; a description of the greatness of Śivagaṅgā-Mādhāla. ... [Omission] ... Vidura performing penance for the sake of obtaining a son and establishing a Liṅga in his own name; a description of the majesty of Vidureśvara; a description of the account of the temple built by Vidura. [Omission] ... Māhittha, the son of Bhṛgu and Varuṇa, establishing the deity named Narādivyeśvara; a description of the majesty of Narādivyeśvara.

In the *Śrīmiṣṭhātīrthamāhātmya*, there is a description of the origin of the Poison-Maiden (*viṣakanyā*), and an account of how the sage who refused to abandon her met his death. Having heard the public scandal concerning her, the Poison-Maiden departed for the forest to perform penance. On the way, Pārvatī approached her in the guise of Indrāṇī; seeing the Poison-Maiden distressed by the recollection of her previous birth and performing severe penance such as standing upon heated stones, Pārvatī appeared. After she had received a boon from Indrāṇī, she once again engaged in austerities.

While Pārvatī was performing her penance, Śiva became enamored of her; Viṣakaṇyā’s praise of Pārvatī; Pārvatī’s departure with Viṣakaṇyā to Mount Kailāsa; the description of the marriage festival; the worship of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) by Soma at the temple of Comilla after he had been freed from the curse of his father-in-law through the deception of Romaka Mahārṣi; the removal of Soma’s curse by the power of that [Lord]; and the installation of a Liṅga under his own name at Somanātha.

...the description of the greatness of the goddess Camatkāraprasthāpitacamatkāridurgā; ... the description of the greatness of Ānaṅgaśekeśvara and Sādareśvara, and the narration of their origin; in the context of the description of Rāmahada, the journey of Jamadagni with his army; and upon seeing the power of Kāmadhenu there, when Jamadagni was asked for her by Haihaya—who was filled with agitation and accompanied by his hosts—and refused to give her, [Haihaya] became enraged.
