The slaying of Jamadagni; having heard of his father’s murder, Paraśurāma performed the funeral rites for his father and made a vow to rid the earth of the Kṣatriyas, after which he killed Sahasrārjuna in battle.

After killing the Kṣatriyas twenty-one times, Paraśurāma went to Hāṭakeśvara and performed the Śrāddha for his ancestors with their blood. Having offered the entire earth to the Brāhmaṇas, he caused the ocean to recede to create space for his own dwelling. He then forcibly gave that earth back to the Kṣatriyas; however, when they became arrogant, Rāma slaughtered them. Thus, having cleared the earth of Kṣatriyas twenty-one times, he finally restored it to the Brāhmaṇas.

The establishment of the Galotīrtha by Ākībova at the word of an old Brahmin; the description of the special fruit obtained through the Śrāddha for those killed by weapons at Rāmahada; a general description of the majesty of Rāmahada; the account of the slaughter of the Pāṇḍavas, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and others during the episode of the killing of Tārakañjura; thereafter, the departure of the Kauravas for Dvāravatī; the description of the marriage of Duryodhana with Bhālumatī; and then the subsequent chapters.

Furthermore, the journey of the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas together with Yudhiṣṭhira to Hāṭakeśvara; the narration of the events concerning the installation of the Bhāsa-liṅgas and other matters performed by Dhṛtarāṣṭra; the installation of one hundred and one liṅgas there at Hāṭakeśvara by Dhṛtarāṣṭra and others; the installation of separate liṅgas by Droṇa and the others, as well as by the Pāṇḍavas, Yudhiṣṭhira, and the rest, each according to their own names; the description of the consecration of the liṅgas performed by the Kauravas, Pāṇḍavas, and Yadus; and the glorification of the majesty of the sacrificial ground.

A description of the eradication of leprosy through bathing in the three Tīrthas at the site of the roots of *muṇḍīra*, *kārañja*, and *priyaṅgu*, based on the account of a certain man afflicted with leprosy; a description of the greatness of the site of the roots of *muṇḍīra*, *kārañja*, and *priyaṅgu*; and an account of how, at the time of the marriage of Hiraṇyakaśipu and Vṛtra, Brahmā’s semen was spilled by Pārvatī, and how that sinful Brahmā, having propitiated the head of Rudra, brought about the removal of his fault.

The description of the greatness of Harāśrayavedikā; the description of the greatness of Rudraśīrṣa, including the narration of how the sin of a certain unchaste Brāhmaṇa woman was destroyed by the sight of Rudraśīrṣa, as well as the description of the liberation from sin of Queen Vidūrathā through the sight of Rudraśīrṣa; the description of the greatness of Rudraśīrṣa (Jāgeśvara); the description of the greatness of Vāṅkhilyāśrama, including the account of the wrath displayed toward Śakra by the Vālakhilyas; and the description of the greatness of Suparṇa, known as Bākhkhilyā.

Having received the jar of nectar consecrated by the Vāruṇis, Atharvaṇikas, and Bhaṭṭas, Kaśyapa gave it to his wife for the sake of drinking; through the consumption of the jar of nectar, the birth of the bird Garuḍa occurred from Kaśyapa, and the daughter of the Brahmin was given as a bride to Garuḍa. Then, Garuḍa departed along with the two Brahmin maidens. Subsequently, Nārada was burned; then, having been granted a boon by Viṣṇu, all of them—Nārada, Garuḍa, and the others—went to Hāṭakeśvara. Having gone there, by Nārada and Garuḍa...

The episode of Viṣṇu’s manifestation: Having seized Viṣṇu while he was eating in the city of Bhogavatī, Garuḍa brought him before Viṣṇu; when Satyabhāmā arrived, she likewise cursed Rādhā, saying, "Become a crane," and gave a curse to the maiden that she would become a crane. By the command of Viṣṇu, the sage Nārada, along with his son, was sent away; and having given the food of Śāṇḍilī—which was as powerful as poison—to Garuḍa, who was seated before Viṣṇu, Śāṇḍilī mentally uttered a curse.

The reduction of Garuḍa to ashes. Having seen his own son bitten by a serpent, Viṣṇu-Garuḍa went to the excellent mountain Hāṭaka; there, having bowed to Rudra, Śīrṣaka, Kālarudra, Nīlarudra, and the others, he described how Garuḍa’s golden wings had again been reduced to ashes. Then, for the sake of removing leprosy, King Veṇu went toward the excellent mountain Suparṇa, and through the worship of the Lord, he offered praise to Śāṇḍilya. [This concerns] a Brahmin girl who was bitten and cursed by the sages, and [the story of] Viṣṇu’s curse.

In the *Iṣṇāvatāra* [chapter], the description of the sin of being the sister of Niṣṇu (Viṣṇu), which was the cause of the curse bestowed by Sumada; the seeking out of Brahmā for the sake of removing that curse; the granting of a boon to him while he remained in his own abode; the naming of that deity by Brahmā as "Gajavakrā-Mahālakṣmī"; her performance of penance; and the description of the majesty of Bhagavatī Mahālakṣmī, preceded by the removal of the curse by Brahmā.

Chapter 155: [Ḍa] For the purpose of increasing the joy of King Ḍaṅkaṣa through the marriage with twenty-seven maidens, and for the sake of the moon’s worship of Hāṭakeśvara, there is the establishment of the twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) under their respective names. [The section on] the greatness of the Nakhoma temple concludes here. In this chapter, titled "The Increase," regarding the city of Eraṇya, for the sake of the city's prosperity, the following subjects are treated: the making of a formal request by Viṣṇu for the hand of a Brahmin maiden; the marriage of Viṣṇu... [text fragment].

The bringing of the Brahmin; the bestowing of a curse upon that maiden by Viṣṇu, saying "Become one whose mouth is poison"; the battle; the manifestation from a single sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) of deities such as Revanta, Kaśyapa, and Yama; or else, for the purpose of warding off the danger arising from that [battle], the establishment of an arrangement for those two aged women regarding the objects fit to be seen by them; then, the installation of the Liṅga named Hāṭakeśvara by his own name; and the narration of the majesty (māhātmya) of Ambā and Vṛddhā.

At the command of his father, Ambāvuddha, [the sage] established his own sandals (*pādukā*) for the purpose of severing the lineage of those deities who cause the destruction of children; by the wearing of these sandals, the suffering of people was brought to an end. He described the sins of those who do not honor the sandals. While Śaṅkara was engaged in meditation, a maiden was born from his third eye; at the word of Śaṅkara, she attained her own supernatural power (*siddhi*) through the worship of the sandals, having surpassed even her elder brothers.

The youngest brother, Śaṅkhalu, considering the performance of sacrifices for the sake of wealth to be the lowest practice, described how he brought about a drought through his power; because of that, while wandering in the forest, the learned Vidvāmitra went to the house of Caṇḍāṭha and performed the five great sacrifices there with dog-meat obtained from another.

For that reason, when Agni became angry, he concealed his own self. When the gods, desiring to perform the *abhicāra* rite, mentioned their own names—such as "elephant" (*gaja*) and so forth—the Fire-god, enraged, pronounced a curse upon those elephants and others. Then, when Brahmā asked the reason for Agni’s concealment of his own self as he was carrying away the marrow (*majjan*), Agni replied: "Because Indra caused a rain of dust, and because I offered the hindquarters of a goat (*ajaghani*) consecrated by the *abhimantrya* rite, I concealed my own self. Thus it is told.

The causing of rain by his own command; thereafter, the granting of boons to Brahmābhraya; the naming of that lake as Abhitīrtha; the greatness of the continuous stream of clarified butter (*ghṛta-vaso-dhārā*) poured into the fire there; the restoration of the elephants and other creatures afflicted by the Brahmins through the granting of boons by the gods beginning with Brahmā; then the departure of the deities to their respective abodes; and the description of the origin of Abhitīrtha.

In this section, the bathing performed by a certain Śūdra at the Gomukha-tīrtha is described; following the account of the origin of the Gomukha-vīra, there is a description of the majesty of the Gomukha-tīrtha. Therein is the narration of how King Ambarīṣa performed austerities for the sake of curing the leprosy of his son who had been afflicted by it, and how the Blessed One, being pleased, revealed the fault committed by that son in a previous birth. Furthermore, there is the description of how, by the command of the Blessed One, the son’s leprosy was eradicated through bathing at the Gomukha-tīrtha.

Description of the majesty of the Gomukha-tīrtha: ... [the account of] Paraśurāma, out of envy, cutting down the *rohayaṣṭi* (prosperity-stick) with his axe and establishing the Khohayaṣṭi-tīrtha; the description of the arrival of the *rohayaṣṭi*; the description of the origin of the goddess Ajāpāla-nirbhataka-mātaḥ; the departure of Ajāpāla for the island of Hāṭakeśvara at the word of Vasiṣṭha; the granting of a boon to him by the goddess, who was pleased after he had propitiated her there; and the establishment of Ajāpāla in the kingdom through the acceptance of that boon.

Seeing that the virtuous people remained [safe] while the wicked went to hell, and observing the lack of refuge for sinners, Adaca departed for the world of Brahma. While staying there, Śiva heard of this; he assumed the form of a tiger and went into the presence of the king. Enraged by the tiger’s devouring of the goats, the king dispatched Caṇḍidatta and his men, who were themselves devoured by Śaṅkara in the form of the tiger. Subsequently, due to the absence of other goats, the tiger conversed with the king, saying, "Ha! You fool! and so forth. Then—

Having abandoned his tiger-form, Śiva granted him the vision of his true self; Ajāpāṅga’s description of Śiva; the king’s journey to Pātāla at Śiva’s command and his installation of a *liṅga* under his own name; the installation of Caṇḍī by Ajāpāṅgadevarī under her own name; and the description of the greatness of Ajāpāṅgadevarī. King Daśaratha, having heard from Jyotiṣmat the future events concerning the piercing of the Krauñca mountain by Rāma and others, set out slowly toward Laṅkā for battle in order to prevent them. Of him—

Then, being pleased by that courage, Śanaiścara made a promise and granted him assurance, saying, "I shall not pierce Rohiṇī. Regarding the fruit of the dialogue between Śanaiścara and Daśaratha, after Śanaiścara had first made the vow, "I shall not break the cart of Rohiṇī," and subsequently bestowed his blessing, Indra described his own form and caused the sky to resound with laughter. Then, having learned from Daśaratha’s words that there is no happiness for one who is childless, [the king] acted for the sake of obtaining a son.

The sixth chapter concerns the undertaking of a collective effort for the purpose of performing penance. Having gone to the holy site of Hāṭakeśvara, Daśaratha performed penance; Viṣṇu, gratified by that penance, granted a boon to Daśaratha, saying, "I shall incarnate as his four sons. Viṣṇu, worshipped by him at the place where Daśaratha had performed penance, took the name Rājasvāmī after himself, and named the pond constructed by Daśaratha the "Rājavāpī" (the King’s Pond).

Nam: A description of the greatness of Rājasvāmī and Rājavāpī; on the occasion of the pilgrimage to Rāmeśvara, after Rāma had abandoned Sītā and fashioned a golden Sītā, he began a sacrifice, at which point Durvāsas arrived; a description of the dialogue between Durvāsas and Rāma.

Lakṣmaṇa’s departure from the city by the command of Rāma due to his violation of Rāma’s order; the description of Lakṣmaṇa’s purification of his fault through bathing in the Sarayū; then, Lakṣmaṇa’s departure of the life-breath through the practice of yoga; Rāma’s grieving upon seeing Lakṣmaṇa ascended to the celestial realm; the consolation of Rāma by the ministers; and the utterance of a voice from the sky forbidding the cremation of Lakṣmaṇa’s body when Rāma was about to offer it—saying, "The funeral rites shall not be performed for one who has renounced."

Then, after the performance of the funeral rites for Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma’s arrival at Kiṣkindhā by means of the Puṣpaka chariot is described, along with the honors and hospitality offered there by Sugrīva. Following that, having mounted the Puṣpaka, he went together with the monkeys to the hermitage of Rāma; there, Vibhīṣaṇa paid homage to Rāmacandra. Then, Śrī Rāma, accompanied by all of them, arrived at the holy site of Hāṭakeśvara and established the deity Rāmeśvara there.

A description of the majesty of Rāmeśvara; a description of the consecration of the five temples of Lakṣmaṇa; the arrival of Rāma at the Ānarta-baḍāga lake together with the Rākṣasas; therein, within the dialogue between Rāma and a Brahmin, a description of the greatness of that lake in the narrative account of the previous birth of Andhaviri, who was traveling toward heaven seated in a celestial chariot (vimāna) accompanied by Apsarases; and a description of the greatness of the Ānarta-maitīṅka-pika.

(Then, after Śrī Rāmacandra had departed for his own realm, the Rākṣasas who had arrived at the holy site of Hāṭakeśvara to worship Śiva saw the Brāhmaṇas who had been brought there; having devoured them, they tormented the remaining Brāhmaṇas. Upon seeing this, the son of Śrī Rāma, filled with wrath, brought about the defeat of the Rākṣasas. The Rākṣasas then cast many corpses into that lake. Having sent a message to Vibhīṣaṇa through an envoy...)

The prevention of the Rākṣasas from entering Jambūdvīpa; the description of the installation of the six lords and the lord of the earth (Kṣitīśvara). When the sun had set, Vibhīṣaṇa, by means of a Vyaṃtara spell, caused the Rākṣasa army led by Daityeśvara to vanish at dawn, and the filling of the four-faced lingas established by the Rākṣasas with earth. There, in that auspicious region situated to the east of the Bhrāṣṭrakhaṇḍa mountain, King Bṛhadaśva arrived; there, upon the appearance of a divine omen, the king performed a circumambulation. Then...

At the time of digging the earth—description of the fourfold *ekaṅgada* mountain; description of the king’s minister digging up the land made level by the Caturāśras; description of the account of covering the mouth of the Rākṣasa; ... description of the majesty of the *lapatīrthas*; ... [and] the origin and majesty of the sixty-eight *tīrthas*, by the Brahmin named Vatsānvayacambhūta, [concerning] Hāṭakeśvara situated in Pātāla.

The subjects of the chapters are as follows: the performance of the worship of Śiva by one who was eager to bring the Lord to the Śvaramabha region; the establishment of the *liṅga* through the grace of Śiva; then, at the command of that [Lord], the construction of a temple for the sixty-eight *liṅgas* arising from the *gonoddhava*, and after worshipping Śiva, the establishment of those sixty-eight *liṅgas* named after the [sages] through His grace; and finally, the narration of the account of the establishment of the *liṅgas* performed by Āḍaṇaiśivaramaṇ. In the description of the sixty-eight holy sites (*tīrtha*) within the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī: Nārada, Vyāsa, and others, having worshipped Śivagaṇa at Camatkāra-kṣetra after attaining knowledge and other virtues, offer praise to the holy site; followed by a description of the sixty-eight holy sites of Vārāṇasī. [This includes] a detailed account of the names of the various rivers located along the banks of the Śarayu, as well as a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the sixty-eight holy sites.

"At one time, Queen Damayantī, the consort of King Nala, traveled to the sacred site of Hāṭakeśvara. There, on the day of Hari-bodhinī (the eleventh lunar day), she perceived a holy ford (*tīrtha*). Seeing Damayantī meditating upon the Lord, another Brāhmaṇa woman spoke this description of Damayantī. After her meditation, Damayantī gave her own personal ornaments to all the Brāhmaṇa women, with the exception of those ascetic women (*tāpasī*); then, together with all the other Brāhmaṇa women, excluding the ascetic women, [she proceeded] to the theft and the striking [of the thief]."

There was no laughter; likewise, every day the queen gave ornaments to them, yet on the fifth day, when those four queens of the king’s brother-in-law did not accept the ornaments, she took the ornaments from them and went to the presence of the King to cast a curse upon him. She went to the house of the Brahmins who had brought water, accompanied by many other twice-born men. Then, having gone to the earth, she traveled to Hāṭakeśvara every month, the lord of Ānarta; having gratified the Brahmins, she departed after performing rites for peace.

By those [arrows] with which the rejection and removal of the ornaments given by Damayantī was performed; by those whose husbands were made to travel through the path of the sky to their own hermitage by the power of their own merit, while they themselves rejected the ornaments given by Damayantī out of pride; by those husbands who fell right there [upon rejecting them]; and by those four archers who had arrived via the path of the sky—having shot at that cause—they bestowed the boon upon Damayantī, saying, "Be as you wish."

Then, having reached the state of being a stone there, Damayantī fell; having heard that account, the King of Vidarbha arrived there to propitiate the twice-born. Seeing his wife turned into stone, the king described how that land became barren through the casting of a handful of dust. Having established the origin, greatness, and other qualities of that barren spot, he returned to his own city. By the word of the sage, someone must perform a sacrifice every month for her sake.

Realizing that the suffering of the Brahmins was even greater because they would not accept gifts of wealth and other offerings made under the pretext of Prahlāda by the lowest of Brahmins, and after everyone had offered prayers there, they described their own purity—excluding one Brahmin—by means of performing a ritual bath at that sacred site (*tīrtha*). Then, that distressed Brahmin, being impure, made prayers on behalf of all the Brahmins, and an altar for the sacrificial fire (*agni*) was established at that sacred site.

The description of the greatness of the *abhniṅṇḍa* for the purification of the three-fold origin (*trijātaka*). A certain wicked twice-born man, having gone to the forest, performed austerities; Śiva, pleased by those austerities, granted him a boon. While Devarāta, the king of Camatkārapura, was residing there, his son named Kratha went to Nāgatīrtha. There, Kratha killed the son of the lord of the Nāgas, named Radrāmāra, with an arrow from his bow. Upon learning of the killing of his son, the father [Devarāta], along with the Mothers (*mātṛs*) and others, [was filled with grief].

Causing grief, he then became enraged and, having summoned the people standing before him along with the noble ones, first had Kratha, together with his family and brothers, fed upon by dogs; thereafter—

He requested permission for his departure; having seen his own city, he resolved to dispel the suffering of his son. He approached a *tri-jāta* Brahmin among his own people and related that sorrow. Upon hearing it, the *tri-jāta* performed propitiations to Śiva and, to remove the fear of poison, obtained a boon from Śiva. For the sake of rendering the snakes residing there venomless, he bestowed upon them the great mantra "Na garaṃ na garam" (Neither poison, nor poison), which causes the removal of snake venom.

Through the victory of that great mantra, by causing the serpents to become city-dwellers (*nagara-tvakaraṇa*), he bestowed upon that city the name [of the mantra]; he gave the name "Nāgara" to the Brahmins residing there; the serpents, rendered poisonless, fled from that place; and [the text contains] a description of the account of the origin of the city.

The description of the lineage and other details of the birth of Rajashiraha Brahmana; the narration by Trijata of his own experiences while serving as a servant to the Brahmanas; and the description of the arrangement of the sacrificial rites performed by Bhadrayajna and the conduct of the Munis.

(The biting by Bhadraṭṭikā, the sister of a Brahmin, who was incited by the female ascetic Revatī; the female ascetic Revatī’s taking of Bhadraṭṭikā’s curse and her subsequent birth in human form; the propitiation of the Goddess performed by Revatī; the establishment of a sacred ford (tīrtha) under her own name at the word of the Goddess; the Goddess’s bestowing of many names upon her, such as Ambā and Durgā; and the description of the origin and greatness of the Ambārevatī Tīrtha.)... .

In the narrative of Ādiśeṇa, Takṣaka, having become enraged, cast Bhadrīkā into the underworld (pātāla); then Bhadrīkā uttered a curse upon Takṣaka, saying, "Become ashes. Upon his subsequent supplication with prostrations, she withdrew the curse. Takṣaka then transported Bhadrīkā to a wooden palanquin; there, in order to test her own purity and chastity, Bhadrīkā asked him to kindle a fire, and when that fire was ignited, by means of her power, she rendered the fire cold and caused a rain of flowers to fall.

The composition of the hymn for the sixty verses of Verabadṛkatabha; Bhaddikā’s arrival at her own home after escaping death through the words of a divine messenger; by her, the establishment of a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) right there under her own name; the narration of the origin and greatness of the Bhaddikā-tīrtha; the description of the account of the birth on earth of Maṇuṣya, who had fallen from heaven due to his wickedness, in the form of Raivata-nūpa; the description of the king Raivata’s conquest of the earth; and [the account of] Kṣemaṅkarā, having installed her son in the kingdom.

The departure of Rāka with Bhāryā to the forest of Raivata; then their journey to the holy site of Hāṭakeśvara and the installation of the image of Śivā; [these are the subjects of the first chapter]. In the second chapter: the description of the manifestation of Kātyāyanī for the sake of slaying the Daityas, beginning with Mahiṣāsura; the granting of a curse by Durvāsas to King Dīrghabāhu, saying "Become a buffalo"; then, having attained the state of a buffalo, his worship of Śiva at Hāṭakeśvara by the command of Umā; and [the assurance] that his death shall not occur without her [Śivā].

The granting of the boon of invincibility to others after speaking; the description of the greatness of Mahiṣa-tīrtha; the description of the battle between the gods and the demons at Mahiṣapura; the causing of the defeat of the Daitya army by the gods; the holding of a consultation by all the gods together with Indra; and for the sake of increasing their own splendor, Kātyāyanī’s mounting of a lion and going to the Vindhya mountains to perform penance; and [the account of] Mahiṣāsura, who was overcome by desire upon seeing her in her form of radiant energy, along with his army.

Having arrived there, she made a request for her to become his wife; when the Goddess rejected Mahiṣa’s words, the great battle between the Goddess and the enraged Mahiṣāsura is described. Then, as Kātyāyanī began the effort to bind the hair of the Daitya Mahiṣa and proceed toward his destruction, Ahalyā offered a hymn of praise to the Goddess. Thereupon, out of compassion, the Goddess granted life to Mahiṣāsura; thus [ends] the account of Kātyāyanī following the defeat of Mahiṣa.

The subduing and establishment [of the Goddess] by treading upon the demon Mahiṣāsura; a description of the majesty of Kātyāyanī; and, having been propitiated by the praises of the gods who were terrified by Hiraṇyākṣa, the Lord assumed the form of a buffalo and, because he asked "Where shall I tear [him apart]? (*kva dārayāmi*), the mountain peak situated there was named Kedāra; a description of the majesty of Kedāra.

While the washerman named Śuddhaka was describing the greatness of Śūrpāraka, he unknowingly dropped some fine garments into the middle of the washing vat. Upon hearing this, the washerman’s daughter informed her friend, the fisherman’s daughter, of what had happened regarding her father’s work. Having learned of it, the fisherman’s daughter recalled a body of water that caused black cloth to turn white, and she informed the washerman’s daughter of this means. Then, the washerman’s daughter also told her father, Śuddhaka, of the method described by her friend.

The Introduction: therein, the washing of those garments by Baka with the resulting illusion of their extreme whiteness compared to before; the washerman’s narration of the circumstances of the garments to the Brāhmaṇas; the attainment of fame for that pool as Śuklatīrtha; a description of the greatness of Śuklatīrtha; and the birth of Vālmīki, also known as Valmīkajaṅgha. Following this, the description of the origin of Sukhārati-tīrtha and the narration of the account of the birth of Vālmīki, whose other name was Chohajaṅgha; and a description of the majesty (māhātmya) of Sukhārati.

The description of the birth of the maiden named Karṇotpala to King Satyasandha through the grace of the Karṇola-tīrtha; the departure of King Satyasandha, accompanied by his daughter, to the world of Brahmā when asked by Śakra, "To whom shall this Karṇotpala be given?"; the daughter’s petition to her father, who was about to remain there in the world of Brahmā at the word of Brahmā; the king’s return to his own country at the daughter’s request; and the performance of an *āśvarya* (miraculous rite) upon seeing the calamities in the land, as witnessed by those residing there.

The mutual conversation between them and their narration of their respective life stories; the description of Satyasandha’s performance of penance right there near the pit along with his daughter; the establishment of a shrine by King Satyasandha after he had performed penance; and the description of the greatness of the boon granted to Satyasandha.

The performance of penance by Karṇotpalā, the daughter of Satyasandha, for the sake of obtaining a husband, directed toward the Goddess; and upon her performing a bath at a sacred ford after being sent there by the Goddess following the occasion of that penance, a description of her attainment of youth; and when Kāmadeva, having beheld her beauty, made a prayer with lustful intent, Satyasandha, having learned his daughter's intention, [bestowed] his daughter upon that Kāma according to the marriage rites.

The performance of the gift; the establishment of the Karaṇotpatti by [the king] himself in the presence of the goddess Karṇotpā; the description of the greatness of the holy site (tīrtha) of Karṇotpā. ... Having entered a kingdom devoid of a ruler, by the word of Satyasaṃdha, the birth of sons named Aṣṭaka and others occurs in the Suputra Kuṇḍa through the power of the Lord of Ānata; the description of the greatness of that excellent lake. ...

Yājñavalkya, enraged by the fact that Śākalya’s teacher had disregarded his own command, reported to his own guru the knowledge he had learned from that teacher; in order to acquire that same knowledge, he performed worship of the Sun. Thereupon, the Sun bestowed upon Yājñavalkya the *khila* (supplementary) Vedic knowledge. Having become a bird (*uḍu*), Yājñavalkya took refuge in the right ear of the Sun and studied the Vedas as they emerged from the mouth of the Sun. After completing the acquisition of all branches of knowledge, Yājñavalkya—

The contents of this chapter include: the establishment of the *Nirvāṇakaraṇa* Upaniṣad, which conveys the meaning of the Vedas; the founding of a sacred site (*tīrtha*) named after himself at Hāṭakeśvara; and a description of the greatness of the *Yājñavalkyāśrama-tīrtha*. In this chapter, having observed Yājñavalkya’s particular affection for his wife Maitreyī, he desired to cultivate a similar affection in her toward himself. To achieve this, he went into the presence of Śāṇḍilī, his second wife named Kātyāyanī. Śāṇḍilī—

The narration of Kātyāyanī’s own account of her circumstances; the performance of the worship of Gaurī by Kātyāyanī for a period of one year at the word of Śāṇḍilī; the description of the origin of the five-piṇḍa Gaurī; the description of the greatness of Sānī, the greatness of the five-piṇḍikā Gaurī, and the greatness of Gaṇapati installed by Vara; and the description of the origin and greatness of Ajāgraha as established by Ajāpāla.

The departure of Hārīta’s wife to a reservoir for the sake of bathing; the arrival of Kāmadeva at that very place due to his latent passion for pleasure; Hārīta’s bestowing of a curse upon both Kāma and his own wife after learning of all this; the description of how Hārīta’s wife attained the state of a stone there by the power of Pārvatī’s bow; and the description of how Kāma, having become a stone, was freed from his curse through the worship of Khaṇḍaśikhā according to the words of a Brahmin—this concludes the description of the origin of the pond, wherein [the story of] Vīraśarman the Brahmin and his daughter [is told].

The performance of vows such as the *Cāndrāyaṇa* for the sake of removing the two defects; the performance of a vow by the maiden as well; her grasping the hand of a leper-like Brāhmaṇa at the word of Indra; her journey to sixty-eight holy places (*tīrthas*) in accordance with her husband's command; the giving of a bow by those two to Māṇḍavya, who was impaled on a stake; her causing the obstruction of the sun; and the rising of the sun at the word of the gods, "We shall restore your husband to life. [The restoration] of the leper-like Brāhmaṇa.

His death; his restoration to life by the gods; the granting of a boon to that chaste Dīrghā by the gods. ... Māṇḍavya’s pronouncement of a curse upon Yama for causing him to enter a Śūdra womb; the description of the origin and majesty of the Dīdhikā pit. The narration of the cause of Māṇḍavya’s acquisition of the *cūla* (tuft of hair). ... [E]—The performance of penance by Dharmarāja to destroy the curse given by Māṇḍavya; the description of the origin of Dharmarājeśvara. ...

A description of the grief resulting from the death of the son of a Brahmin named Upādhyāya, born of the Kayapavaṃśa lineage, who was five years old; then, out of anger, the Brahmin’s pronouncement of a curse upon Yama; Yama’s journey to the abode of Brahmā after being cursed; Yama’s departure for Hāṭakeśvara at the word of Brahmā in order to terminate the curse; thereafter, Yama assuming the form of a twice-born man, approaching the Brahmin’s house, and returning that son to the Brahmin; and finally, the installation of a Śivaliṅga by Dharmarāja.

The description of the narration of the majesty of King Dharma; the description of the narration of the story of King Dharma’s son; and, within the description of the greatness of the giver of sweet food, the account of how King Vasusena, despite making many gifts, went to his own abode and attained the state of hunger because he had not offered food [to the deity]; and when Vasusena was thus afflicted and questioned by Nārada, the arrival of Nārada at that very moment and his telling of the entire account to him. Vasusena’s...

Nārada, for the sake of others, delivered his father’s command and message to Satyasena, the son of Vasuṣeṇa, instructing him to perform daily acts such as the distribution of food at ancestral *śrāddha* ceremonies and other rites. Having heard his father’s message from Nārada, Satyasena gave alms-food to his own father. Due to a lack of food caused by drought, Satyasena performed the worship of Śiva; being dissatisfied with the meager offerings, Śiva granted him whatever desired food and other provisions he wished. Thereafter, Satyasena [became known] by the name Miṣṭānnadeśvara.

The establishment of the Niṅga [temple], the narration of the majesty of Miṣṭāndeśvara, the creation of obstacles for Jābāchi’s penance, and the arrival of Rambhā there; then, having agitated the mind of Jābāchi through Rambhā, his dalliance with her in the form of a celestial nymph (chatrīmabhāva); Jābāchi seeing Rambhā’s daughter and taking care of her; when she had reached youth, Citrasena, the Gandharva, approached Kaumāravatī, the daughter of Jābāchi, and took that daughter of Jābāchi away.

The Gandharva’s departure for Devamandira; then, while searching for his daughter, Jāvāli found that Gandharva fleeing with his own daughter from Devamandira, and having seized them both, he beat his daughter and pronounced a curse upon the Gandharva. The Gandharva, having performed austerities to remove the curse, established a linga after the curse could not be revoked. Furthermore, Jāvāli’s daughter, named Phaḍavatī, also performed austerities to counteract the curse, and through those austerities, she attained divinity.

While a dialogue was taking place between that maiden and the sage Jābāli in the form of a counter-argument, the maiden rendered her father Jābāli speechless. Then follows the description of the greatness of the triple Yoginīs—Jābālīśvarī, Citāgnesvarī, and Phalavatī. In the description of the greatness of Āmareśvara, having heard of the defeat of the gods by the Daityas, [the sage] performed the propitiation of Ādityeśvara; and through the grace of the Lord, the defeat of the Daityas at the hands of the gods in the battle between gods and Daityas is described, as well as his attainment of immortality.

The naming of the single shrine as Amareśvara; a description of the greatness of the Amareśvara shrine; a description of the splendor of Amareśvara; a description of the names of Āditya, Vasu, Rudra, and others; a description of the greatness of the Amareśvara Kuṇḍa and the birth of Śuka; then a description of the dialogue between Vyāsa and Śuka.

Due to the separation from his teacher Śuka, Vaṭikā—the mother of the second son, whose other name is Pigā—worships Śiva out of grief and receives boons; Vaṭikā establishes a shrine in her own name; and a description of the greatness of Vaṭikeśvara.

In the description of the origin of the pit of sport (Kelīśvabhra), the birth of the Asura Andhaka from Hiraṇyakaśipu is told, followed by the account of his acquisition of the kingdom. Then, after performing penance for sixty thousand years, Andhaka obtained a boon from Brahmā. Intoxicated by that boon granted by Brahmā, Andhaka conquered the gods including Indra, and having even defeated Śambhu, he waged war against the Lord of Kuṇḍaja, Śambhunīra, together with the Goddess Amitābhnī.

The description of the origin of Keṭīśī when the chariot was driven by Śuka, who had been requested by Andhaka after his defeat in battle with his own Daityas—just as Śambhu [did for Skanda]—and thereafter, Andhaka’s receiving a boon from that Goddess and performing a hymn of praise to Keṭīśvarī; the description of the majesty of Keṭīśvarī and the departure following the description of the majesty of Cakrapāṇi; and then the pilgrimage undertaken by Āluna, who, having liberated the cows, performed a sacrifice at the holy site.

The journey to Hāṭakeśvara and the installation of Cakrapāṇi; the description of the majesty of Cakrapāṇi; the description of the majesty of Rūpatīrtha; the description of the birth of Tilottamā; the departure of Tilottamā for Kailāsa with Brahmā; and as Tilottamā was bowing to heaven and performing circumambulation, Pārvatī, observing the purity of Śiva’s mind, uttered a curse upon Tilottamā, saying, "Become ugly. Then, taking that Tilottamā, Pārvatī went to Hāṭakeśvara.

The journey to Rūpatīrtha; by means of that, Pārvatī’s granting of a boon to Tilottamā, who was previously established there; the origin and greatness of the Apsaraḥkuṇḍa; and the description of the majesty of Īśvarīṣīṭha. — Chapter [X].

In Hāṭakeśvara, there is a description of the worship of the twelve Ādityas, the eight Vasus, and the eleven Rudras; a description of the greatness of [offering] flowers and other items; and therein, the giving of advice by the father of a maiden—a Kṣatriya—to his own wife regarding the bestowing of the girl upon Maṇibhadra.

After the marriage of Maṇibhadra, Maṇibhadrabhedara mocked the Brāhmaṇa named Puṣpa; the city-dwellers, having offered consolation to that Brāhmaṇa, invited him for a meal. Then, in order to satisfy public opinion, Puṣpaka went to Camatkārapura, and from there, he departed with his ministers.

Having performed the fire sacrifice (*homa*) with his own flesh according to the ritual manual (*sāṅga*), including the offerings to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt and others, he returned to his own abode. Then the Sun, possessing the power to assume various forms such as the jewel-bearing mountain for the sake of the one named Puṣpa, bestowed two *rātikās* upon him. Subsequently, the Brāhmaṇa Puṣpaka, having bathed, established the deity Puṣpāditya; this is followed by a description of the majesty of Puṣpāditya.

By the power of the *sūryadatta-gāṭikā* (the medicinal pill of Sūryadatta), having assumed a form resembling Maṇibhadra with a fourfold [splendor], he went to the house of Maṇibhadra. Having gone to the house of that true Maṇibhadra, he gratified the eunuch standing at the door with garments and other gifts, and gratified his wife with clothes, ornaments, and so forth. Having enjoyed himself comfortably with her, he engaged in sexual union. Then, at the word of that false Maṇibhadra, the eunuch at the door of the true Maṇibhadra was rebuked. False...

The description of the dispute between the real Maṇibhadra and the artificial Maṇibhadra at the royal palace; then, upon the king’s command, the refusal of the artificial Maṇibhadra’s wife to accept him as her husband; and finally, by the king’s order, the execution of the artificial Maṇibhadra through a tree-felling axe by means of a royal messenger. Ya.

[The contents of] the chapters on the subject matter: Having summoned Āptavān, [the king]—by means of that artificial flower-form Maṇibhadra, through the power of the *māhikā* spell, and by assuming the body of Puṣpaka—brought about the happiness of Māhikā with that flower-offering. Then, having given wealth to his own sons with that flower, he went to the sacred field of Hāṭakeśvara for the sake of expiating the committed sin, performing the *puṣkaraṇa* rites and so forth.

The performance of the invitation for the *trāhmaṇa* (the Brahmin), the description of the temple of Puṣpāditya and the greatness of the origin of the serpent from the beginning, ... [in the narration of the vow of Śrīśaila and the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and the weeping horse], the description of the procedure for worship with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) including the preliminary rite (*nyāsa*), when the purification of Puṣpa’s sin was achieved through the method of atonement (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed by a certain Brāhmaṇa named Puṣpacandra after he had thoroughly examined the scriptures.

The humiliation of Puṣpacandra and Caṇḍaśarman by the world; thereafter, the performance of penance by that Brāhmaṇa Caṇḍaśarman; while Puṣpacandra was circumambulating [the deity] and Caṇḍaśarman was performing an oblation of his own flesh into the fire, the manifestation of Bhairava, Īśvara, Sūrya, and Nārāyaṇa, and their granting of their own teeth; the description of the purification of the sins of Puṣpacandra and Caṇḍaśarman through the attainment of their desired forms; the narration of the origin of the Brahmanagara; and then, once again, [the account of] Puṣpacandra and Caṇḍaśarman on the banks of the Sarasvatī.

Having gone there, Caṇḍaśarman, who had performed worship preceded by the construction of a temple, established the deity Nāgareśvara; his wife Śākambharī also established the goddess Śākambharī; and Caṇḍaśarman established Nāgarāditya on the bank of the Sarasvatī. [This is] the description of the greatness of Nāgareśvara, Nāgarāditya, and Śākambharī.

The topics [covered] are: the narration of the birth of Viśvāmitra; Gadhi’s journey for the purpose of requesting the daughter of Gādhi; then, having heard the king’s reply that he would give the girl upon receiving a thousand dark-colored horses with one black ear, Ṛcīka performed austerities on the banks of the Sarasvatī to obtain those dark-colored horses; thereafter, by the power of his mantras, Ṛcīka went into the presence of Gadhi while appearing as a dark-colored horse; the description of the origin of Aśvatīrtha; and the granting of the gift.

A description of the worship of the Śaṅku-paricāra and the excellence of its commencement; a description of the removal of the curse of Oduṃbarī; the arrival of those deities along with Tatreśvara; and a description of the account of Sāvitrī’s pronouncement of a curse upon the group of Mothers when they departed from her presence, desiring to return to their respective abodes. Also, a description of the account of the birth of Oduṃbara, which preceded that [curse].

At the conclusion of the sacrifice, Brahmā summoned all the inhabitants of the city and recounted to them the entire account of what had occurred, including the origin of the sacred ford (tīrtha). Then, for the sake of the Avabhṛtha bath, the sages departed from the presence of Brahmā to Puṣkara. [The text continues with] the granting of boons by Brahmā to Indra and the other gods, the granting of a boon at that time by Brahmā to Yakṣman who had arrived there, and the description of the origin of the Yakṣmatīrtha.

A description of the ill omens and portents arising at the time of Sāvitrī’s return to the sacrificial pavilion; the arrival there of the Apsarases, including Dhṛtācī; and a description of their singing, instrumental music, laughter, and other such activities.

Nārada’s narration of the account of Gāyatrī’s marriage and other events to Sāvitrī; Sāvitrī’s distress upon hearing that account told by Nārada; her departure for the sacrificial pavilion with her mind untroubled, having placed no faith in Nārada’s words due to Gaurī’s speech; Sāvitrī’s censure of Brahmā and the pronouncing of a curse upon him; Sāvitrī’s pronouncing of curses upon Indra, Agni, the Nāgas, the Brāhmaṇas, the officiating priests (ṛtvij), and others; and thereafter, Sāvitrī’s departure from there on foot alone.

The journey after ascending the mountain; the description of the greatness of Sāvitrī. When Sāvitrī had departed, Gāyatrī remained there and, for the sake of neutralizing the curses bestowed upon all by Sāvitrī, granted boons. ... [There follows] the performance of the three daily libations (savanas) by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; the description of the equality of their ages; the description of the divisions of time from a *nimeṣa* up to the end of a *kalpa*; and the description of the majesty of the sandals (*pādukā*) situated at the sacred site of Chamarikātīrtha for the sake of attaining knowledge of Brahman.

In the description of the two Kumārikā Tīrthas, the Brāhmaṇa recounted how, having resolved in their minds that their separation would occur at the conclusion of the marriage between the daughter of the Brāhmaṇa Chāndogyabrāhmaṇaka and the daughter of Ralnavatī, the queen of the lord of Ānarta, they devised a stratagem; then the Brāhmaṇa returned to the city of Vadraka, the lord of Daśārṇa, who was the ruler of Ānarta.

On one occasion, while a certain son of Viśvāvasu named Parāvasu—a Brahmin learned in the Vedas—who had gone to the house of a Veda-reciter, was overcome by sleep at night, he committed an act of incest out of thirst, affliction, and ignorance. Thereafter, filled with remorse, he went in the morning to Śaṅkhatīrtha, shaved his head and so forth, and like an outcaste, remained from afar in the house of a low-caste person, performing intense penance along with fellow ascetics. Then, those fellow ascetics, having declared their approval of him, said: "O Rātravatī..."

The instruction on the expiation was that his sin would be removed by the sucking of the breast and the tasting of the lips of Ratnāvatī; then Viśvāvasu, at the command of his preceptor, related the entire account. Thereupon, the Brahmin learned in the Dharmaśāstras prescribed the expiation consisting of the drinking of the jar of clarified butter as declared by the sages. Seeing Viśvāvasu thus afflicted, his parents uttered cries of lamentation. Then, through the eating of food and the sucking of the breast and tasting of the lips of Ratnāvatī, the purification from the sin of drinking liquor was accomplished. Thus it is said.

Having heard the expiation prescribed by the learned Brahmins, all those sages returned to the king and made a request for the sake of restoring the Brahmin’s life. When the king replied that his own daughter should be granted as a favor for the Brahmin’s expiation, she, out of love for her son, gave her command to the Brahmin to perform the expiation by wearing her garment and tasting the nectar of her lower lip. Thereupon, the Brahmin, out of affection for his mother, did exactly as he was told.

The description of the flow of milk from the breasts of the Brahmin woman Ratnāvatī while she was present; the account of how the Lord of the Dṛśāṇas became enamored of her; Ratnāvatī’s insistence on marrying him alone; her insistence that her friend, the Brahmin woman, should not marry as well; and how those two, Vatastoka and Ratnāvatī, went to the Maiyajña hermitage to perform penance, where, by the command of Bhavaiyajña, they entered a reservoir of water.

The performance of austerities; then, when the grace of the Lord has been obtained, the installation of the two [images] by those two; a description of the majesty of the pair of holy places at Śrījāhyaṇī; ... —[followed by] a description of the majesty of various [sites], preceded by accounts of their origins, including the three forests, the three cities, the three groves, the three wandering [places], the three ascetic seats, the three mountain peaks, and the great rivers such as the Narmadā.

In the dialogue between Viśvāmitra and Bharata regarding the sacrifice (*bhavayajña*), when Viśvāmitra had committed an error concerning the purification of the city for Bharata’s sacrifice, Śrī Rāma—by touching the dust of the feet of Aditi, who was present in the form of a cow—liberated him from the curse and granted permission for the sacrifice to proceed. Then, through the grace of Bharata-yajña, who possessed knowledge born of humility and offered a pedestal (*pīṭikā*) and other gifts there, [the sage] praised him with the *Śrīsūkta*. At the word of Rāma, having arrived at Dhāṭakeśvara along with Āditya, Datta, Nanda, and Gautama...

He was purified by the recitation of hymns such as the *Pāvamānī* from the *Sasvanāmabhiśagasthā*, by the reading of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, and by the worship of the *Ratha-āditya* and other local deities; he described the majesty of *Gautameśvara*, *Ahilyeśvara*, and *Katānandeśvara*, and performed the *Parana-nirṇaya*.

In the description of the majesty of Śaṅkhatīrtha, when the lord of Ānarta had become afflicted by leprosy, Nārada asked, "O Lord of Ānarta, by whom must this [disease] be cured? When the Nāgaras replied, "By no one," King Bhaṭṭayajña gave them the answer: "By those very Nāgaras. Then followed the description of his deeds in a previous birth; and Nārada declared that because the speech of those Nāgaras—who perform the bathing and other rites at Śaṅkhatīrtha—is true for the purpose of removing sins such as leprosy, it is by those very Nāgaras that the three-fold [cure] must be provided.

The discourse beginning with "it should be given," the description of the Bharvayajña, therein the description of the origin of Śaṅkhatīrtha, the description of the account of the installation of Śaṅkhāditya, the description of the definitive statements regarding Śaṅkha... the description of the majesty of the holy site of Śaṅkhāditya. 1.

A description of the various regions situated one after another, including the account of Nāgaraviddhi; ... in the context of explaining the causes of the defects of the *nāgabahnī*, Nārada’s narration to Ānarta of the churning of the ocean by the one named Siddhasena; in the dialogue between Viśvāmitra and Ānarta, the description of the battle between Hiraṇyākṣa and Indra; therein, upon seeing his own defeat, the description of the emergence of the fourteen jewels beginning with the Kaustubha from the ocean; and therein, at the time of consuming the nectar (*amṛta*), the encounter of Rāhu—who was joined by a trick—with Viṣṇu; and thereafter—

In the dialogue between Śakra and Viṣṇu, [there is] the description by Śrī Viṣṇu of how the heads of those slain in battle might become *prata* (liberated) through the severing of their heads with the Sudarśana discus; and how, when the skull of Airāvata was split open and a stream of blood flowed forth, Viṣṇu, being pleased, explained the *prata-śrāddha* to Śakra. The translation above interprets the core narrative elements: the conversation between Indra and Viṣṇu regarding the liberation (*pratattva*) of warriors killed in war, the role of the Sudarśana discus in decapitation, the flow of blood from Airāvata's skull, and the subsequent teaching on the *prata-śrāddha* ritual.)

The conclusion: because she is the tethering post for the elephant [of the senses], she is given the name Nāgavahvī. In the dialogue between Śakra and Viṣṇu known as the Vāṇīvatsaraka, there is an account of the greatness of the fruit of performing *śrāddha* at Gayā. By worshipping Śakra, the king ascends a celestial chariot bestowed by Śakra and goes there constantly. Om.

Having placed his trust in the words of Viṣṇu, Śakra mounted Airāvata and went to your presence. There, having consumed betel leaf from Śakradanta belonging to those residing in Camatkārapura, he returned to his own abode. By that same messenger, Vāṇī, who was delighted, he saw [the sage] in his own garden; then, honored by the trees standing in that hermitage, Śakra offered them greetings such as inquiries after their welfare. For the purpose of establishing the fame of the *nāgavallī* (betel vine) upon the earth, he was urged by Indra, and the *nāgavallī* was brought forth. This is the origin of the betel leaf.

(Performing the *śrāddha* and other rites at Gayākūpa; the arrival of Brahmā there; the glorification of the greatness of eating *dāruka* fruit everywhere except in the case of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite; [the statement] "The worship of the Viśvedevas must be performed, but not the *ekoddiṣṭa*"; the narration by Brahmā of the release from the curse of Indra upon the Viśvedevas through bathing at Śaṅkhatīrtha for Ānartaudhipati; and [the account of] Śaṅkha, preceded by his loss of kingdom and his subsequent suffering.)
The establishment of the system; the description of the origin and names of the Kūṣmāṇḍa and other [deities]; the description of the greatness of the Bāṭamaṇḍanaka Tīrtha...

the description. In the description of the greatness of the Viśvāmitrīya Tīrtha, there is the description of Viśvāmitra together with Savarṇā; in the description of the great festival of Indra at the Bhāskara Tīrtha, following the occasion of a sexual encounter with Aditi, Gautama bestows a curse upon Indra; the description of the greatness of the Vāpī [tank]; and [the account] of the Kārpaṭika’s role for the purpose of destroying the thumb of Ratnākṣa, the ruler of Ayodhyā.

Then, at the request of his brother Bṛhaspati, Gautama went to Nāḍhāṭakeśvara and bestowed the beauty born of his eyes upon the place where the wound was located on Indra’s body. By bathing at the Bhāskara-tīrtha and worshipping the Sun-god on the seventh lunar day, the removal of the defect [was achieved]; furthermore, within five nights, there was the granting of land and the attainment of worship. There follows a description of the greatness of the festival of Indra’s pride after five nights, the establishment of a holy site named Ratnāditya, and a description of the majesty of the Ratnāditya-tīrtha.

[The description of the establishment of the Lord known as Indradyumnavāsa by Śiva, who, having heard from his own father the curse that he would be the cause of Adityā’s widowhood, resolved upon death; the causing of great suffering to Sāmba, the son of Kṛṣṇa, by Śatānanda as he was traveling along the royal highway for that purpose; then, Gautama’s consolation of Śatānanda; and the arrival of all the city women at the windows and doors, abandoning their respective duties. Sāmba—

By that act, some of them fell due to the loss of consciousness caused by their agitation; then, having learned of all that misconduct from Nandinī—who had arrived in the guise of her own wife and was sporting with Kṛṣṇa’s calf out of ignorance—she entered the fire in remorse. She then related the entire account as it had occurred and, following the procedure prescribed in the Dharmaśāstras and the Brāhmaṇas, she was instructed on the means for purification by her sister. Subsequently, [the story continues] of how he was purified through the six-fold penance.

By the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Sāmba departed today; the account of his journey, the description of the cessation of the disease of that Sāmba, the hearing of the establishment of holy places by Sāndanānna, and the narration of the divine greatness of Sāmba and others residing in Kūra.

1. The account of the birth of Gaṇanātha; the granting of a boon to Dānātha by Gaṇanātha through his grace; Viśvāmitra’s departure upon hearing of the slaughter of his horse by the son of Rohitāśva; Viśvāmitra’s defeat at the hands of Vasiṣṭha when he sought to seize the wish-granting cow (Kāmadhenu) after learning of its power; thereafter, Viśvāmitra’s performance of penance to acquire Brahmanical luster; and the prevention of his attainment of Brahmanical status by Śiva.

The narration of the greatness of the procedure for the worship of Gaṇapati by Viśvāmitra; the attainment of Brahminhood by Viśvāmitra through the worship of Gaṇapati. Then, in the context of the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka, the narration by Viśvāmitra of the Śrāddha-kalpa concerning the lordship of Bhartṛyajña to Rodraśva; therein, the description of the causes of the eligibility for Śrāddha, such as for whom the Śrāddha should be performed, and so forth; and the determination of the rules for performing the Śrāddha.

The description of the fruits resulting from performing the *śrāddha* on the *vyatīpāta* and other such occasions; the departure at a certain time of the ancestors who have received the *amāśrāddha*, *vyatīpāta-śrāddha*, and others to the world of Brahmā; their narration of their own experiences; the consolation of the ancestors by Brahmā; the performance of the benefit for all through the prescription of the *amāśrāddha*, *gayāśrāddha*, and so forth; the description of the origin and history of the *śrāddha*; the description of the greatness of the *kutapa* and other specific times for the *śrāddha*; and the description of the characteristics of the vessels and other implements used in the *śrāddha*.

The characteristics of the *śrāddha* sacrifice, worship, and mantras; a description of the procedure for the *śrāddha*; the wicked persons who must be excluded from the *śrāddha*; the description of the nine classes of ancestors, such as the Abhiṣvātta-gaṇa, by the satisfied Indra after he had conquered the six enemies—women, dice, hunting, drinking, sleep, and idle wandering; the statement of the faults incurred upon hearing the words of the wicked and others; a description of the various times suitable for the *śrāddha*; the enumeration of the guests worthy of the *śrāddha*; and the determination of the Brahmins eligible for the *śrāddha*.

The abandonment of faith; the description of the six types of Śrāddhas performed during the "elephant's shadow" (*gajacchāyā*); the praise of giving food to the ancestors with meat such as that of the rhinoceros and others during the Śrāddha; the description of the fault incurred by failing to perform the Śrāddha out of negligence;

the description of which month presides over which specific month and so forth; and the description of the various substances suitable for the Śrāddha, such as rice mixed with sesame, black gram, and the like.

The description of the destination and the manner of performing the *śrāddha* for those who have died after consuming poison, those who have died from snakebites, those who have been burned by fire, those who have perished in water, those who have been killed by weapons, and those who have died by hanging or other such means; the determination of the *śrāddha* for those who have died in a forest fire; and the praise of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) as the destroyer of obstacles in the performance of the *śrāddha*.

(The description of the rules for the Śrāddha rite ending with the Mantrapūta; the description of the Ekoddiṣṭa rite; the description of the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha; the description of the rules for determining the Navaśrāddha; the description of the rules for determining the Sapindīkaraṇa Śrāddha; the explanation of the causes for the generation of progeny; then, in the context of the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Bhīṣma, the description of the various hells; and the description of the arrangement of merit, sin, and dharma in the world of Yama, [including] by which sin one goes to which hell.)

The description of Rāpi and others; the description of the means for dispelling the torments of hell through various supreme transgressions; the description of liberation from the torments of hell by casting one's body and bones into holy bathing places such as Yaṅga; the narration of the means for removing the torments of hell by falling from the banks of the Rāyacitta river, as well as by other means; the statement that sins are not destroyed by worshipping Jalaṅgaya during the Cāturmāsya period; and the description of the gift of water and food at Vidra, along with the story of Hiraṇyakaliṣu and Putrabharaha.

The acceptance of the kingdom by Andhaka, the youngest brother, after [the elder brothers] had renounced it; the defeat of the gods by Andhaka after he had propitiated Brahmā and obtained a boon; the propitiation of Śaṅkara by Śakra, who was defeated by him; and by Śaṅkara, pleased by that propitiation, for the sake of awakening Andhaka, [the granting of] the Gaṇeśa Vīrabhadra, and the gifts of food, water, jewels, gems, garments, gold, cows, and land.

The discourse on recitation; the discourse on the fruit of reciting the Vedas; the dispatching of the twelve [deities] and others; the rejection of the words of Gaṇeśa, Vīrabhadra, and others; the discourse on the fruit of the *cāturmāsya* and other oblations performed by one who is arrogant due to having received a boon from Brahmā; the description of the majesty of the offering of clarified butter (*ājya*), the offering of vajras, and the offering of ghee; the description of King Roka’s contempt for the Asura Andhaka; the discourse on the fruit of offering buttermilk (*takra*); the discourse on the attainment of worlds such as Somaloka through the offering of sesame seeds and so forth; and [the account of what happened] when he was enraged by the one who performed the *cāturmāsya*.

Śaṅkara, having mounted his bull, engaged in battle with the demon Andhaka; [the account of] Kaṭhu’s arrival in Amarāvatī and a description of the greatness of giving. ... There, having fought with the demon Andhaka, by the request of that demon Andhaka, Śaṅkaridīti determined what was to be abandoned and what was to be accepted regarding food and vessels during the Cāturmāsya; he established those items—both those to be abandoned and those not to be abandoned, including animals, grains, and goods—within the enumeration of the Śaiva hosts; and [there is] a description of the origin of Śaṅkaridīti. Dhā.

Description of the wandering mendicant (cāraphaṭa), the fruit of abandoning false speech, and the description of the fruit of renouncing desired objects; having learned of the condition of his father Andhaka, Caraka performed penance there at Hāṭakeśvara; through that penance, he established the determination of what is permitted, prohibited, and mandatory in the presence of Viṣṇu; following the discourse on the fruits of giving land and other gifts, Brahmā granted him a boon consisting of freedom from old age and death; thereafter, by the word of Śukra, Senānī—

The narration; the description of the greatness of the Brahmācāryavrata among the Viṣṇuvratas; how, during the Cāturmāsya, [Viṣṇu] conquered the gods by means of the Vidyādevīs, established the Daityas in their respective positions of authority over the gods, and himself, through Vṛka, determined the rules for the destruction of the enemies of Indra; and how, having established himself in those positions of authority, he ruled over the three worlds.

The description of the fruits of worshipping Viṣṇu during the Cāturmāsya; the description of the fruits of performing the three-fold worship of Viṣṇu; the description of the supreme sin-destroying power of the *Sāṅkṛti* [mantra]; then, the narration of the fruit for one who performs only the milk-oblation by means of the *Vaka* mantra, which had been granted as a boon by Brahmā; and the [narration] of the penance.

The granting of boons by Mota after having approached [the deity]; the description of the origin of Khaṣṭadha and others during the performance of the discernment of the sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) in the worship of Viṣṇu; Indra’s narration of the entire account to Bṛhaspati out of fear that the demon Bṛkāsur would come to the Cāturmāsya festivals; the departure of the gods to the Milk Ocean at the command of Bṛhaspati, who was possessed by Piṣayu; and Indra’s description of the fruit of reciting the *Puruṣasūkta* sixteen times.

The section beginning with the syllable *ukāra*: having performed austerities there at the Ocean of Milk, [the text] describes the sequence of worship through the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), such as the invocation, using the mantra from the *Ratyekapuruṣasūkta*. It describes the eligibility of the gods, beginning with Śakra, for the removal of their suffering; then, preceded by a description of the Lord reclining upon Śeṣa at Hāṭakeśvara, it describes the greatness of the sixteen-fold worship (*ṣoḍaśopacārapūjā*) and the majesty of offering lamps.

The journey; having gone there, the description of devotion beginning with the slight offering of food and ending with the contemplation of union (*sāyujya*) by that *jaṭhaśāthin* through making his bed upon a tiger skin; the description of the attainment of the bliss of unbroken sovereignty; and the description of the greatness of the vow of the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārtika. [Chapter] 4: [The procedure for] the worship of the Blessed One with offerings (*upacāra*) during the Cāturmāsya.

An exposition on the fruits of the observances, vows, burnt offerings, recitations, and gifts performed during the Cāturmāsya rites when engaged in the practice of the *sat-chāyā* (the shadow of the virtuous); the analysis and explanation of the terms *sat* and *chāyā*; the description of the *sat-chāyā* within the section on austerity (*tapas*); a description of the greatness of bathing at dawn in the *Cāturmāsya-māhātmya* from the dialogue between Bhāradvāja and Nārada; furthermore, the enumeration of the names of the eighteen *prakṛtis* (constituent elements) preceded by the description of their respective duties; and therein, the account of the origin of Brahmā.

The description of the fruits of bathing; Viṣṇu’s creation of the month of Māgha for the sake of increasing the prosperity of the world; the hearing of the celestial voice; the description of the fruits of performing penance thereafter; the description of the fruits of performing Japa, Homa, and other rites; the performance of Govinda-pūjā; the description of the Cāturmāsya vows; the description of the eligibility of those [classes] for the rites; the fruit of remembering the names ending with Śūdra; and the description of the rules for the necessary observances during the Cāturmāsya.

The chapters contain the following subjects: an exposition of various classifications; a discernment of their respective qualities; a description of the majesty of devotion to Viṣṇu; the account of the Śūdra caste; the narrative of the purification of Vejavana; the arrival of Gālava at the house of Paijavana; a description of the great hospitality and honors shown to Gālava by Paijavana; Gālava’s discourse on the majesty of Tuṅgasīmañjaya and others; a description of the majesty of worshipping the deity established at Iṣaligrāma; and the Lord’s [teachings] in the dialogue between Gālava and Paijavana.

A description of the ritual procedure for the worship of the single form [of Śiva] preceded by the twenty-four distinct names beginning with Kerāva; a description of the various divisions of the village of Śāḍhiprāma; a description of the origin of the deity at the crest of the Śāḍhimarāma mountain; a description of the ancient account of the origin of the village of Śākhigrāma on the Gaṇḍakī river, including the narrative of Dakṣāyaṇī’s departure from her husband Himavat; a description of the marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī; a description of the hymn of praise offered to Śiva by Kāma; and [the arrival of] Indra and the other gods, who were oppressed by the demons led by Tārakāsura, before Brahmā.

The departure of Mandarācala for Śivaddīnātha; ... during the time of amorous play at the festival of Śiva, the arrival of the fire sent by the gods there; having consumed the semen bestowed by Śiva, Brahmā went to Pātālā; having perceived her own exhaustion from the exertion of sexual intercourse, she became a flame (śikhā), and the bestowing of a curse upon all the inhabitants of heaven; on a certain occasion, the departure of the gods, who had been defeated by the Daityas, to the world of Brahmā.

Then, in consultation with Brahmā and Indra, Rudra, together with the attendants of Viṣṇu, assumed the forms of Hari, Hara, and others in order to establish the oneness of his own [manifestations]. Therein, within a single body, he bestowed the emblems of Viṣṇu such as Garuḍa and others, as well as the emblems of Śiva such as the bull and others. By this singular vow of Viṣṇu and Śiva, heretics were caused to be struck with wonder. Furthermore, he established the sin-destroying image of the Great Goddess (Mahādevī) joined with Viṣṇu, and [established] the deities headed by Agni in the temple.

The description of Pārvatī residing in the *vilva* tree, of Vṛndā on a donkey, and of Ṭhakmī on a camel; the narration of the curse of all those [deities]; and the description of the first *aśvattha* tree, beginning with the miraculous appearance of the *aśvattha* tree directed toward the gods by a voice from the sky.

The description of the greatness of the *namovāṇī* (the mantra of salutation); therein, the installation of deities such as Brahmā and others within each leaf; the description of the planting of *tulasī*; the description of the fruit resulting from consuming *tulasī* leaves; the description of the installation of deities upon the leaves of the *tulasī*, which is superior even to the midday [merit]; the greatness of carrying dry *tulasī* wood; the description of how one attains the fruit by making *tulasī* dwell in Indra’s abode; and the description of the greatness of *tulasī*.

In the dialogue between Jayā and Pārvatī, concerning the origin of the universe, there is an account of the fruits resulting from the service and worship of the Viśvavṛkṣa (the Universal Tree). It includes a description of the installation of various deities upon the different limbs of the Viśvavṛkṣa, a description of the deities residing within its thorns, and an account of the origin of the universe.

When the celestial voice had ceased, [the Lord] spoke to Viśvāśvattha, Paṭāratu, Rasyākhyacata, and Kvāṇa regarding the performance of worship by the gods, including Indra, during the Cāturmāsya. Then, having been addressed by Hari as the Supreme Lord, he commanded the gods to return to their respective abodes. Thereupon, remembering the curse bestowed upon him by Devī, for the sake of neutralizing that curse, the gods performed the worship of Māheśvarī and offered hymns of praise to Māheśvarī at the very confluence of the Gaṇḍakī river, where there was a stone known by the name Śāligrāma.

A description of the attainment of one's own nature; a description of the greatness of the Śāligrāma stone. A description of the greatness of offering sesame seeds during the Cāturmāsya period; the installation of deities in the four months. The installation of the gods—Śakra, Varuṇa, Yama, Kubera, and others—in their respective order within various specific trees; a description of the greatness of the tree. A description of the conciliation of Pārvatī performed by Śaṅkara.

At Mount Mandara, during the Cāturmāsya festival, while Hara was intent upon the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the gods departed for their respective abodes after he had said, "Therefore, you must come to assist me so that Pārvatī may be gratified by Hara. Then, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, Hara performed a penance (*yatya*) to please Bhavānī; and in connection with that ritual at Mandara, [the assembly of] the gods headed by Brahmā, as well as the celestial sages (*devarṣi*) such as Nārada and Vyāsa, [gathered].

The arrival of the great sages (maharṣis); at that time, the arrival there of the Śrīrāga and other musical modes (rāgas) conceived by Hara; while Hara’s dance was proceeding there, the rendering of assistance by Nārada and others, as well as by the Vidyādharas and others; the composition of hymns to Hara by Pārvatī, who was delighted by Hara’s dancing; a description of Hara’s tāṇḍava dance; and a description of the pride of Śaṅkara and Nārāyaṇa. 8. Table of Contents.

In the dialogue between Nāgarakhaśin and Pārvatī regarding the Cāturmāsya, there is a description of the twelve-syllable mantra of Viṣṇu (*oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya*) and the two-syllable mantra of Rāma (*rāma*) as taught by Śiva to Pārvatī in their conversation. Following Śiva’s command, Pārvatī went to perform penance on Mount Arbuda; meanwhile, Śiva, afflicted by desire, went to the Yamunā to bathe. There, due to his lack of knowledge of Śiva, the water became black from the soot of Hara’s body, and the Yamunā became distressed.

The establishment of Divasthana through the prayer of Yamunā; the founding of Haratīrtha by Hara; Śiva’s departure for Kailāsa after receiving a curse due to some other cause; the composition of a hymn to the Goddess by Śiva; the gods’ approach to Hara, distressed by the curse of Hara; the subsequent establishment of Amarakaṇṭakatīrtha and the description of its majesty; and the installation of Nīlakaṇṭha there by the gods, followed by the composition of a hymn to Nīlakaṇṭha.

The summary of the essential narrative of the Cāturmāsya; the account of the birth of Kārtikeyasvāmin; [the story of] Ṣaḍānana bowing to the lord of the rivers and crossing the ocean with his wife; thereafter, Śibi’s journey across the islands and oceans such as Viṣṇudvīpa and Nāthadvīpa, whereupon he beholds Viṣṇu and offers a hymn of praise to Viṣṇu; and, in connection therewith, a description of the yoga of meditation.

Śābeya, having attained the yoga of meditation, requested the yoga of knowledge; when his prayer was made to Śiva, Śiva explained the attainment of the yoga of knowledge through the twelve-syllable mantra. [The text contains] a description of the seed-syllables (*bīja-varṇa*) of each syllable of the twelve-syllable mantra, a description of the nature of Viṣṇu, a description of the nature of the Lord Virāṭ, and an exposition of the yoga of knowledge.

The description of the battle between Kārttikeya and the demon Tāraka, preceded by the consecration of Kārttikeya as the commander-in-chief of the celestial army at the request of the gods oppressed by the Asura Vāraka; therein, the account of the slaying of the demon Tāraka, and the composition of a hymn to Kārttikeya by the gods.

The chapters include: a description of the greatness of the Bhīṣmapañcaka; a presentation of the procedure for the worship of the Lord who is visible to mortals; therein, a description of the Lord’s lying down; a description of the greatness of the Añjalyaśayana-vrata; a description of the greatness of the Maṅkaṇeśvara-tīrtha; and [the account of] a certain thief who, having gone to steal the wealth of men and women who had arrived at the temple of the God for the sake of a vigil on Śivarātri, climbed up and took his position upon a Kaṇikāra tree standing nearby. Of him—

While a thief was sleeping beneath a *kāṇikāra* tree on a mountain slope, a jackal perched above him. Out of ignorance, the thief playfully plucked and threw down the leaves of the *kāṇikāra* tree. That night, though he intended to steal the wealth of others, he remained awake effortlessly. Through this act of worship—which occurred even without his conscious knowledge—there arose for that thief a separation from his thieving nature and the attainment of a state of pure sattvic being. Thereafter, with a purified mind, he performed a single act of worship to Śiva.

...the description of the procedure for the worship of Śiva through the attachment to the [Śiva] thread; the narration of the greatness of worship, keeping vigil, and other rites performed during the day and night; then, the birth of the deceased thief, the lord of Daśārṇa, into the family of [a king], by the power of his merit; the description of his attainment of the kingdom; the arrival of great sages such as Śāṇḍilya and Pucchasti at the palace of the lord of Daśārṇa; the bestowing of auspicious blessings and other gifts upon the king by the sages; and the description of the greatness of Śivarātri. ... ga.

The description of the greatness of the Siddha-Śavara; the determination of the procedure for the Tulāpuruṣa gift; the description of the ritual for the Tulāpuruṣa gift; the description of the greatness of the Tulāpuruṣa gift; [the letter] *dha*; the exposition of the means for attaining the status of a Cakravartin; therein, the description of the ritual for the gift of golden land accompanied by mantras; the description of the fruit and greatness of the gift of land; the description of the greatness of Gotameśvara; the description of the greatness of Kapāleśvara established by Indra; therein—

The *Trāsura*: after attaining the kingdom, Śakra, afflicted by the sin of *brahmahatyā* (the killing of a Brahmin) due to the slaughter of the Asura Vṛtra, travels to sixty-eight sacred fords (*tīrthas*) at the word of Brahmā in order to remove the fault of that *brahmahatyā*. By the falling of his head into the lake of Viśvāmitra, the removal of the *brahmahatyā* is described, as well as the installation of a *liṅga* in that very place, its glorification, and the [account of] Vāta... there.

And by describing the greatness of the previous birth of Vātakeśvara, who was established by Chanarādyaṇa. Then, in response to the question of King Aṅguta—“How can there be liberation from sin for people?”—there is the description of the fruit resulting from the gift of the *pāpapiṇḍa* (sin-ball) performed through the *Bhareyajña* sacrifice; therein, the description of constructing the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and other structures, the installation of the deities such as Earth (*Pṛthivī*) and others on all sides, the description of the ritual procedure for worship with their respective mantras, the description of the water-offering accompanying the gift of the *pāpapiṇḍa*, and the *brahmahoma*.

After residing there for a long time as a benefactor to Indradyumna, Brahmā sent Indradyumna back to the earthly realm so that his fame might once again become unmanifest on earth. Upon returning to the earthly world with joy, Indradyumna encountered Mārkaṇḍeya, who was living there; however, when Indradyumna asked him to relate news concerning the city of Rocaka in order to recognize his own fame, Mārkaṇḍeya was unable to do so. Seeing this, he [Indradyumna]... [text truncated]

At the request of Indradyumna from Kāmpilyapura, [Indradyumna] went with Mārkaṇḍeya to the vicinity of Nāḍījaṃbūka. There, after Indradyumna and Mārkaṇḍeya had explained the purpose of their arrival to Nāḍījaṃbuka, Nāḍījaṃbuka related his own history, recounting how in a previous birth he attained the status of a Rākṣasa and so forth. He further described how, at the time of the transit of the sun into Capricorn (makara-saṃkramaṇa), Śiva was pleased by the offering of a covering of ghee upon the linga and granted him a boon.

The description of the gift; then, because Indradyumna was free from disease, Māṭhara led him, who possessed a longer life even than that of Nāḍijaṅgha due to his knowledge of the vital breaths (vāta), into the presence of Uddālaka, named Prācīnayogya.

After Prākārakarṇa, who was like the sun, had related his knowledge of the news regarding Indradyumna, he explained the reason for his own long life. Then, because Indradyumna—who remained indifferent due to his lack of knowledge regarding his own wind—was distressed, Prākārakarṇa demonstrated the uselessness of the knowledge of the news concerning Indradyumna held by Nāḍījaṅgha and Indradyumna; and so, Prākārakarṇa himself brought Pradyumna, Mākaṇḍeya, Nāḍījaṅgha, and Baka to the presence of that long-lived one residing on Mount Gandhamādana. By him...

Garuḍa related the news of Indradyumna, preceded by a description of his extraordinary knowledge; he recounted the story of how Indradyumna, though indifferent due to his ignorance of his own former births, had undertaken the effort to offer oblations to the fire; and how, at the request of the vulture who sought to save his own long life, Garuḍa brought the crane dwelling in Lake Mānasa—along with Nāḍījaṅgha and Prākārakarṇa—to the presence of Indradyumna. Then, those who had arrived there at the shore of the lake...

Having seen Indrayumna in the middle [of the water], the tortoise entered the water itself. (In the context of describing the greatness of Indrayumna, there follows an account of how Indrayumna went to heaven by the grace of Viṣṇu; this constitutes the latter part of the chapter. Then, when the vulture asked him the reason for his appearance in the water, that tortoise related the entire previous history of Indrayumna; and when Indrayumna’s deliverance from the battle with the Kīta was accomplished, [the story] concluded regarding Indrayumna.)

The gods caused a rain of flowers; then, at that very moment, a divine messenger brought a celestial chariot and made a request to Indrayumna to go to the world of Brahmā. Indrayumna, having declared his own lack of desire to go to the world of Brahmā, questioned Kūma with the wish to understand the cause of that very long life.
