The narration by Kūrma of his own previous history and the protection of Indradyumna and others; thereafter, having met with the great sage Lomaśa for six hundred years and learned from him the cause of Lomaśa’s eternal youth, all of them established seven sacrificial fires (saptarigasthāpana) according to their respective names; then follows the description of the origin of the seven fires, the description of the measure of lifespan beginning from a *nimeṣa* up to the duration of the four ages starting with Kṛta, and [the description of] the *agniṣṭoma* and other sacrifices.

Through these [verses], there is a description of the attainment of the worlds of the gods, such as the world of Brahmā and others; a description of the conditions, laws, and so forth of the worlds throughout the four yugas; following that, a specific determination of the Kali age; a description of the measure of the lifespans of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other deities; a description of the measures of the lunar and solar months; and, in the context of the story of Durvāsas, a statement of the authority regarding the conduct of a certain monastery head named Nivāṇucana, who was situated before [him].

The description of the measurement of a *yuga*: A certain thief, wishing to seize a *nirvaśuc* (one who has renounced worldly ties), feigned the status of a disciple in order to gain his confidence. After some time had passed, while the *nirvaśuc* was traveling with the disciple toward the city of *Suraṅgā*, the disciple placed his own bundle in the *nirvaśuc*'s hand. Then, having gone a great distance and performed such acts as voiding urine and excrement, when the *nirvaśuc* departed, the thief took that bundle from the disciple of the *nirvaśuc*.

The monastery superintendent named Nikaśyucāka, having learned of this, felt grief; then Duḥśīla and Chandhaka, with that wealth as their support, engaged in trade. After taking a wife, Duḥśīla’s son was born, and for the sake of obtaining another son, he went with his wife to Camatkārapura. There, having met with Duvasas and reported to him all the deceitful actions he had committed against his brother, by the word of Duvasas, Duḥśīla... [text ends]... performed [the rite].

The description of the regions of Prabhaṭyā, the establishment of the *liṅga* under its own name through the singular act of giving, and the account of the end of the suffering caused by the obstacle known as Duḥśīleśvara; and the description of the delusion of both Duḥśīleśvara and Durvāsaseśvara. ...

Duḥśīla established a *liṅga* named Niveśvara at Udera; then Duḥśīla’s wife, Śākambharī, established a *liṅga* named Śākambharī-durga. Then, when Duḥśīla had passed away, Duḥśīla’s wife, Śākambharī, performed the funeral rites for that Duḥśīla in the fire. [This is] the description of Daḥrīḍeśvara, Niveśvara, and Śākambhu. By visiting eleven *tīrthas*, one reaches the field of Dāṭakeśvara.

The arrival of the eleven Rudras with a spirit of mutual emulation to see [the Lord]; then, for the sake of all of them simultaneously obtaining a vision [of Him], the assumption of eleven forms; the offering of praise by the sages upon beholding that eleven-fold form of Śiva; the establishment of the shrines of those eleven Rudras in that very place; the description of the greatness of the manifestation of the eleven Rudras; the enumeration of the names of the eleven Rudras; the description of the greatness of giving gifts in the presence of the eleven Rudras; and, in the context of describing the twelve Ādityas—

While he was intent on performing external sacrifices, Indra, disguised as the wife of Brahmā, caused a cowherd’s daughter to be brought out from the cow-pen; after the marriage of Gāyatrī and Brahmā, Sāvitrī arrived; due to the curse given by Pitāmaha (Brahmā), Śunaḥśepa took birth in the house of Cārāyaṇa—the great-grandson of Bharata—as Yājñavalkya; and when that Yājñavalkya was seen by his great-grandfather Cārāyaṇa, who was distressed by his own wickedness for having been a paramour of another's wife, [the narrative continues].

The expulsion of Yājñavalkya from his own hermitage; thereafter, having become a disciple of Śākalya, he resided in his house; then, on one occasion, while proceeding in the order of disciples to the royal palace to offer blessings preceded by rites of peace, he was treated with contempt by the king; subsequently, when the repentant king made a request for him to be sent back to the royal residence, [the narrative concerns] his departure for the royal palace.

Yājñavalkya’s obedience to his teacher; having disregarded that command of the teacher, Yājñavalkya’s prohibition against going to the house of that king; then, due to the extreme indignation of that angry teacher toward him, Yājñavalkya’s vomiting out the knowledge he had studied and reporting that knowledge back to the teacher; thereafter, the performance of propitiation to the Sun for the sake of obtaining knowledge; and then, having received the knowledge from the Sun and honored the Sun, [the teaching of] five hundred chapters.

The discourse by Parāśara on the *Skānda-mahāpurāṇa-āgama*; therein, the description of the conclusion of the *Nāgara-khaṇḍa*. Regarding the topics: having made a promise to Yājñavalkya regarding the instruction of the *Sūrya-vidyā*, Yājñavalkya’s arrival near his teacher Śākalya to offer the preceptor’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*); then, having related the knowledge obtained from the Sun as the preceptor’s fee to Śākalya, Yājñavalkya’s departure with his disciples to the presence of the twelve Ādityas along with Śākalya; the origin of the twelve Ādityas and the origin of the Aruṇa Āditya.

The description of the account of Yājñavalkya preceded by the description of the greatness of Tīrtha-māhātmya; the description of the majesty of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa; the narration of the efficacy (*phala-śruti*) of the Nāgara-khaṇḍa; the description of the qualification of Rāru’s disciples; and the description of the qualification for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Purāṇas.
Thus ends the sixth section, the Nāgara-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa. 6.
Now begins the seventh section, the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa.
Chaka!
Now, in the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, first is the majesty of the sacred site of Prabhāsa.

The auspicious opening invocation; a description of the occasion for Sūta’s attendance upon Śaunaka and others; a description of those who are qualified and unqualified to hear the narrative; the offering of salutations by Śaunaka and others toward Sūta; a description of the characteristics of a narrative and the examination of its merits and defects; a description of the examination of the marks of Vedic (Āgama) and human-authored (Pauruṣeya) poetry; a description of the names and sequence of the eighteen Purāṇas; a description of the names and sequence of the Upapurāṇas; and a description of the number of verses contained within the Mahāpurāṇas.

The description of the greatness and the procedure for the gift of the manuscript of the eighteen great Purāṇas; the description of Mount Kailāsa; therein, the description of Śiva’s assembly hall and the preceding description of Śiva’s throne; then, the hymn of praise to Śiva by the Goddess (Pārvatī); the dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī; thereafter, the description by the illustrious Śiva of the Yoga of Vibhūti (divine manifestation) to Pārvatī; then, the description of the greatness of sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas); therein, specifically, the description of the greatness of the Bhramāsaka-kṣetra; and [the account] out of a desire to hear the greatness of the sacred sites situated within the Bhramāsaka-kṣetra.

The topics include: Pārvatī’s offering of a garland to Śaṅkara; the description of the majesty of Someśvara; the description of the form of Someśvara marked by the five faces and other signs; the hymn of praise to Soma; further, in the narration of the majesty of Someśa, the explanation by Śiva himself of the reason for his wearing a garland of skulls; the statement by Śaṅkara, addressed by Pārvatī, regarding the boundaries and the great extent of the sacred field of Prabhāsa-kṣetra; and the description of the sequence of the pilgrimage to Prabhāsa-kṣetra.

The description of the journey through the threefold non-duality known as Madiśvasaṣṇavatra; therein, the description of the manifestations of the heart; the description of the fruits of reciting the *mṛlayuja* and other mantras; the description of how even great sinners dwelling in the sacred field of Prabhāsa attain liberation; and the description of the greatness of the hosts of *caiva-gaṇas* who protect the sacred field of Prabhāsa. (Section VI)

A description of the great sages such as Śarīri, the gods, the celestial beings (*devardha*), the holy fords (*tīrtha*), and sacred rivers such as the Gaṅgā, all residing in the sacred precinct of Prabhāsa; a brief description of the praise for the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍadāna*) at Prabhāsa; a description of the majesty of various kinds of gifts in the field of Prabhāsa; a description of the hosts of deities residing in that field; and a description of the true nature of the Lord Śambhu as distinct from the eight forms such as Parāhādi, which are of a partial nature; and a description of the majesty of Somanātha.

In the seventh chapter, while the description of the attainment of Somanātha is being told, there occurs a description of the Lord (Śiva) manifested as Somanātha, following the words of Pārvatī; this includes a sequential enumeration by name of all the Brahman-Prajāpatis of that time, as well as the mention of the names of Someśa in connection with the various *kalpas*, preceded by Śaṅkara’s description of his incarnations corresponding to each respective *kalpa* for the sake of Pārvatī.

The narration of the names of Pārvatī and the gods; then, in the seventh Brahmā-cycle known as Śatānanda, the account of how Candra propitiated Śiva and, having obtained a boon from the Lord, established the shrine of Someśvara under his own name; a detailed description of the extent of that sacred site (Prabhāsa-sthala), including a description of the locations of Devikā, Umā, the Pīṭhas, Garbha-gṛha, Gosukha, Aśvamedha, Meṣaka, and others; and finally, a description of the greatness of all the holy fords (tīrthas) surrounding Someda.

Description of the account of the manifestation of Somanātha; description of the origin of the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*) such as *ṛddhi* attained by Soma and others, as well as the science of mantras such as the *Gāruḍa*; the sequential narration of Ruṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and others who attained liberation through the worship of this Someśa; description of the sovereignty of Someśvara; and the hymn of praise to Śiva by the Goddess, who was struck with wonder upon hearing the words of Śiva—who appeared like ten million Suns—after the passing of a day during the conflict between Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others.

The instrument [of the narrative]; then, by the pleased Diva (Śiva), the granting of a boon to Pārvatī, stating, "I shall describe the majesty of the shrines (*chigas*) situated in the sacred field (*śrāmasaketa*)," and the making of a request concerning the ten incarnations (*avatāras*) of Viṣṇu; then, by Śaṅkara, the description of the dwelling places of Brahmā and others at Prabhāsa, the description of Hari’s (Viṣṇu’s) presence, and the account of his birth as told by Diva; the making of a permanent residence in Kṣatra, and [the placement] of the five deities within the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*).

A description of the sacred sites; a sequential description of the Viṣṇudeva located at the Prabhāsa-kṣetra in Chāgadaṇḍa and other places, as well as the Tākeśvara and Ṛṅgītīrtha within the Jambūdvīpa region; and a description of the greatness of the Ṛṅgītīrtha situated at the Prabhāsa site.

A description of the land of Prabhāsa as the most excellent of all sacred fields; a description of the eight surrounding mountain ranges of Kuru; a description explaining the extent, boundaries, and distinctions of Jambūdvīpa; therein, a description of Bhāratavarṣa as a land of meritorious action and virtue; a description of the arrangement of the constellations above Bhārata, which stands in the form of a tortoise; and [the description] of the ninth part of Bhārata, known as Parāśamikā, measuring two hundred yojanas.

The description of the abode of Śiva; the description of the field of illusion (bhramāsakṣetra) and the wise ones dwelling therein; the account of the manifestation of the field of illusion and the creation of the Lord’s chariot by Paraśurāma; the explanation of the reason for naming that place Prabhāsa; the description of the majesty of Āriṣṭa-kṣetra and other sites; and the description of the birth of the Sun-god from the eye of Brahmā through the splendor of the Lord while Svāyaṃbhuva Manu was presiding over the earth, followed by the account of his birth from the union with Sūryabhūmi. Then...

The production of crops, followed by the production of human beings and others; the generation of medicinal herbs by Svāhā, Svadhā, and Karīṣi; the description of the origin of the Ādityas beginning with Sūrya, and the birth of the Daityas beginning with Hiraṇyakaśipu; the birth of Śaṅkhaśāpa from Hiraṇyakaśipu; the description of the birth of the maiden named Purañjanā from Viśvakarman to the sister of Virocana, the son of Śiva; and [the account of] Saṃjñā, unable to endure the splendor of the Sun, [sending] Chāyā to the presence of the Sun.

After her installation, there was her asceticism and then her departure; when Saramā wiped away the tears from the eyes of the Sun-god with her hand, the Sun-god, out of anger, gave a curse for the destruction of her offspring. Then Saramā went to the house of her father; thereafter, after explaining the reason for her arrival, she went again to the vicinity of the Sun by her father’s command. Following that is the description of the domains of Yama, Yamunā, and Śanaiścara, and the origin of the Pitṛs (Ancestors). Due to some other cause, [the Sun] was about to curse his own mare...

The arrival of Sūrya at the house of Viśvakarman; Viśvakarman performing the hospitable rites for Sūrya with joy and offering him consolation; then, while Viśvakarman began to diminish Sūrya’s supreme splendor by means of a lathe, the Seven Ṛṣis offered hymns of praise to Sūrya; Viśvakarman also offered a hymn of praise to Sūrya; Hāhā, Hūhū, Nārada, Tumburu, and others sang songs; and the Apsarases, headed by Menakā, offered praise to Sūrya in the form of songs.

The commencement of singing; the playing of various kinds of musical instruments; the description of the birth of the horse-maned [Sūrya] from the mare-form of Saṃjñā when she had gone to the forest for penance; the origin of Rājamatara; the description of the birth of Yama; the departure of Yama, who had attained the state of a beast due to a curse from his mother, to the holy site of Prabhāsa; and there, having propitiated Śiva and cast off his beastly nature by the grace of Śiva, [his remaining] at that place by the command of Śiva.

The establishment of the regions, and the description of the greatness of Yama’s direction; following the carving of the Sun-god, who was seated upon the *rami* tree in Śākadvīpa, by Viśvakarman, his descent to the earth under the name Hiraṇyagarbha; his subsequent renown in the Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages by the names Sūrya, Savitṛ, Bhāskara, and Arkastha; the prohibition against eating the leaves of the *arka* tree in connection with the description of the greatness of the Sun; and the description of the merit of giving gifts such as buffaloes at the holy ford of Arkastha.

The narration of the origin of the site named Prabhāsa-pavitra; the description of the time for worship and other details preceding the recitation of the mantra for the worship of Sthāṇu; the account of the greatness of Siddheśvara and Jaigīṣavyeśvara, including Jaigīṣavya’s performance of penance at Prabhāsa; and the granting of the supreme boon of the yoga of knowledge by Sthāṇu, who was pleased by his long austerity as he performed the Nirāhāra, Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such vows.
The establishment of Jaigīṣavyeśvara and Siddheśvara by Jaigīṣavya; a description of the majesty of Jaigīṣavyeśvara and Siddheśvara; and a description of the origin and majesty of Pāpanāśana.

Having observed that the triple world was eclipsed by the splendor of the Rākṣasas stationed in Pātāla, and having performed meditation upon the Blessed One, Prabhākara beheld with his wrathful gaze the falling of the Rākṣasas from the sky onto the earth; then their descent into Pātāla, and subsequently their establishment at the entrance of the Pātāla cave. There follows the description of the greatness of the fruit of bestowing knowledge at Trisaṅgama, and its subsequent renown by the name Śrīmukhadvāra.

A description of the birth of Sunanda and other attendants from the cavities of Pātāla; a statement of the greatness and the ritual procedure for the worship of Sunanda and others; then, a description of the ritual procedure for the worship of Āditya, wherein the nature of Āditya as consisting of the three Vedas is described. First, regarding the cleaning of the teeth, there is a determination of the types of tooth-sticks (kāṣṭha) such as the Āyāga; a description of the method of cleaning the teeth; a description of the excellence of the purification of the mouth and the heart through the use of water from the Arka plant; a description of the rules for bathing and other rites while standing upon an Arka branch; and the greatness of the Sun.

The description of the recitation of the *phaṭ* mantra preceded by the narration of the *ntra*; the description of the ritual worship (*upasthāna*) with the hymn beginning with *ud u tyam*; the description of the procedure for worshipping the Sun with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) using mantras such as *ari dūtam ā* and *kṛṣṇena*; the description of the worship of the deities of the *śṛṅgaṣīṭa* and others on all sides; the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) preceded by the praise of Akaisthala; and, in the context of describing the anecdote regarding the moon’s origin as an ornament upon Śiva’s head, the narration of the events of the Vārāha Kalpa.

In that regard, there is the description of the origin of the moon from the ocean when it was being churned for the sake of producing the fourteen jewels; furthermore, there is the account of Śiva bearing that moon upon his head, and how, because of bearing the moon on his crest, Śiva became renowned by the name "Śaśibhūṣaṇa" (the Moon-Adorned).

(1) A description of the sixteen digits (*kalā*) of the moon according to the sequence of the sixteen lunar days (*tithi*); (2) a description of the *āṅacakra* extending from the letters *ca*, *ṭa*, *tha*, etc., up to the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*); (3) a brief description of the life stories of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśāna during the first *parārdha* of Brahmā; (4) then, in the second *parārdha*, a description of the birth of Dakṣa and others, followed by an account of the origin of the seven sages (*saptarṣi*) and so forth, as well as the accounts of the incarnations of Candradatta, Tātreya, and others; (5) a description of the various incarnations of Viṣṇu according to their respective ages (*yuga*), beginning with the Kṛtayuga—

The description of the incarnations of Gāraṃbha, Kucaka, Kucubha, Śakuna, and Vaṇana; the description of the incarnations of Vyāsa and others; the sequential account of the incarnations of the Daityas, including Hiraṇyakaśipu’s performance of penance while remaining in a pit to conquer the worlds of Indra and the other gods, and his subsequent attainment of sovereignty over the three worlds; then, after narrating the birth and other details of Bali, the description of Bali’s power; the description of the birth and life-story of Prahlāda; and the description of the birth and characteristics of Kāleyīya, [followed by] the account of Viśravas. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.1.59)

The origin of the Bḍakadra Viṣayas; the account of the birth of Kumbhakarṇa, Rāvaṇa, and others; the narration of the destruction of Rāvaṇa by Śrī Rāma; the account of the birth of Śibi-pāṭha; the description of the names of the nine Pautrastyas; the description of the lineage of Puṣkara-dhanuṣka and others; herein the narration of the wives of Bhadrāśva—namely Ghṛtācī and the ten Apsarases beginning with Bhadrā—and the Bhāskarapallīs; and the description of the production of the Soma juice by Atri from the wife of Pramācara (Bhadrā). Then, by Atri...

Having drunk that Soma juice while performing austerities, [the moon was created] from the flow of the essence of the Soma that had issued from his eyes; the description of the origin of the Soma consisting of that Soma; having taken that Soma which was divided into eight portions, the description of the production of herbs through its cooling nature; the account of the production of grains such as *kulattha* and *śyāmāka*; the description of the origin of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*s); the narrative of how the Moon was granted lordship over the lunar mansions, herbs, and so forth; and by the Moon—

Beginning with the Rājasūya sacrifice, having appointed Viṣṇu, Sanatkumāra, and others as the *brahmā*, the *sadasyas*, and the various ṛtviks in their respective positions, he commenced the sacrifice. Upon its completion, having gratified the ṛtviks and others with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and other gifts, [the narrative proceeds] to the account of the birth of Diti; by his command, Dakṣa procreated sixty daughters, among whom Candra gave those daughters in marriage to Dharma and the others, as well as the seven daughters of Kaśyapa.

The offering to Soma; the description of the names of the ten wives of Kaśyapa; the description of the names and lineages of the twenty-seven wives of Kaśyapa who were the wives of Soma, as well as the two wives of Bharadvāja, the two wives of Kṛśāśva, and the two wives of Atri and Aṅgiras; and the narration of the entire account by those other wives of Indra to Indrāṇī, following the fact that Candra had caused the other wives—excluding Rohiṇī—to suffer distress.

Having given Dakṣa his daughter Sati, and having observed the Moon’s partiality toward other daughters, Dakṣa, out of anger, bestowed upon the Moon the curse of the disease of consumption (*yakṣma*) as a sinful affliction. Then, at Dakṣa’s word, once the Moon was cured of the disease of consumption and leprosy, he went to the vicinity of the southern ocean in order to perform the worship of Śiva.

—Not by fear, but by the grace of Śiva alone, having seen that mountain named Smaraṇa, he took up the staff of those sages such as Marīci who were performing various fasts and other penances on that very mountain; having performed seven circumambulations around them, and then, through the propitiation of Śiva, having caused Śiva to appear, he offered praise to the manifested Śiva. Then, having heard the hymn of praise from Candramauli, Śiva, with a gracious mind, [bestowed] upon Candra... [the fruits] of the three daily prayers (*sandhyā*). (Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment of a Sanskrit narrative concerning a devotee’s journey to Mount Smaraṇa, his encounter with sages, and his subsequent worship of Śiva, culminating in a boon granted to the Moon-god, Candramauli.)

The granting of boons preceded by the establishment of the rules for Daśadatta’s curse; Śiva’s description of the power of gods and brahmins; and the narration of extraordinary matters. Then, having taken the sacrificial ground given by Divadatta, Candramas gave orders for the installation of the Liṅga at Viśvakarmeṇa. Thereafter, having returned to his own world, he commanded the minister Hemagarbha to bring the materials for the sacrifice to Prabhāsa. At the word of Candramas, the minister Hemagarbha procured the sacrificial materials and went to Prabhāsa.

As for "going": Viśvakarman fashioned the sacrificial enclosure, the wives of the gods, and the *śāḍhā* constellations; then, having constructed the sacrificial pits along with Brahmā and the others, and having established the twenty-four *bhūtas*, the *maruts*, the *sādhyas*, the *viśvedevas*, the *vasus*, and so forth in their respective places, when the sacrificial rite was commenced, he ensured that no deficiency existed in any of the materials and performed the work for all. Having stationed the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others, and having caused the moon together with Rohiṇī to stand firm, [he acted] with Brahmā accompanied by Sāvitrī.

Having performed the *sarvimbaraṇa* rite, he assigned the office of *hotṛ* to Bṛhaspati, the office of *adhvaryu* to Vasiṣṭha, the office of *udgātṛ* to the Marīcis, and the office of *brahman* to Nārada; having thus appointed them and performed the worship of all, he gave sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and commenced the sacrifice. Having completed the sacrifice with the *avaśratha* and other rites, he established the image of Someśvara. In the tenth *manvantara* of Śvārociṣa, during the Tretā Yuga, [the sage] propitiated Śiva through the lineage of Rodinī, and having made Śaṅkara his witness, he offered hymns of praise.

Then, by that divine Śiva, who bestows the attainment of all desired goals, there was the narration of the measurement of the directions for Somaśvara; the description of the sequence for the worship of Someśvara; the narration of the fruits of the pilgrimage to Someśvara; the description of the departure of the Moon from his affliction; the mention of the flowers dear to Someśvara; and Pārvatī’s discourse with Saṅkara regarding the granting of boons to wicked people and the departure of the Candranadī and other rivers to their respective places by the command of the Lord of the World.

The description of the sacrifice performed by Śaṅkara for the sake of those devoted to the King of Satis (Śiva) when he was nourished; the statement on the non-difference between Hara and Hāri (Viṣṇu); the description of the incarnations of the Lord as Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana, and others; the description of the various types of liberation, such as *sārūpya*; the description of the rules for the propitiation of Śambhu, including the *setu* fast and other observances; and the description of the greatness of the Monday vow (*somavāra-vrata*), wherein, after a long time had passed while residing at Svayaṃprabha-nagara with his wife Sudīlā, the Gandharva named Ghana begot a daughter named Senā.

In order to perform the marriage ceremony for Gandharvasenā, the leader of the Dikhaṇḍi Gaṇas named Ghana, acting through his servant, sent a proposal for the bridegroom; having heard the words of the Gandharva maiden named Gandharvasenā—such as "While the leader of the Dikhaṇḍi Gaṇas travels through the sky, there is no one at all who possesses a form equal to mine"—the leader of the Dikhaṇḍi Gaṇas, upon seeing the Gandharva maiden who was proud of her beauty, granted her a boon that would bring about her desire.

The Gandharva army, having made a request on behalf of the group of Śikhaṇḍins, received a curse; at the word of Śikhaṇḍin, he went with the Gandharva army to the hermitage of Gośṛṅgin on the mountain named Himavat for the purpose of removing [the king's] leprosy; there, the Gandharva named Ghana told the entire account of his daughter to that sage Gośṛṅgin; and Gośṛṅgin, having heard it from him, explained the means for effecting the removal of the leprosy, as did the Gandharva named Ghana and Gandharvasenā.

The journey to Gośṛṅga, the peak of Śiva; there, having performed the worship of Śiva through the Monday-vow (*somavāravratādi*), the Gandharva Senānī received the grace of Śiva and, after destroying the demon Chuṣaṭha, obtained boons from Śiva; the disappearance of Śiva right there; the departure of the Gandharva named Ghana and the Gandharva Senānī to their own abodes; and finally, the conclusion of the description of the greatness of the Monday-vow (*somavāravratamāhātmya*) by Dakṣa for the purpose of establishing the glory of the Monday-vow.

An account of how Soma, having become afflicted with leprosy, was freed from his disease through the grace of Śiva and the performance of the Soma-vrata and other rites; thereafter, by that same sage, an exposition for a certain Gandharva named Candra on the practice of the Monday vow (soma-vāra-vrata), preceded by the description of the ritual procedure beginning with the cleansing of the face and ending with the bath; followed by the description of the materials for the worship of Īśvara and the ritual procedure for the worship of Śiva accompanied by mantras; and finally, the description of the ritual for performing the concluding rite (udyāpana) on the ninth Monday.

The description of the giving of gifts, beginning with clothing and ending with food, for the satisfaction of the twice-born, the Rurus, the gods, and others; then, having completed the Monday vow (*somavāravrata*) according to the procedure taught by Gośṛṅga, Śiva, being pleased, brought about the removal of the leprosy of Gandharvasenā; and to the north of Someśvara, the Gaṇa named Ghanavāhana established a Liṅga under the name Gandharveśvara. [End of] Gandharva...

The installation of the Linga by Gandharvasenā, the daughter of Ghanavāha and the leader of the Gandharvas, performed under the name Vinānna; a description of the majesty of Gandhaveśvara; and a description of the majesty of Seneśvarī. ... na.

Dha: The Gandharva Vananāśaka’s inquiry regarding the performance of the vow for the sake of fully understanding the procedure for the Somavāra-vrata; thereafter, the description of the procedures for the vision of Somanātha by those who have arrived; the narration of the rules for the pilgrimage to Somanātha; the determination of the eligibility (*adhikāra*) for the fruit of the pilgrimage; the exposition on what things, such as those to be avoided or not avoided, should be considered and described by a person intent on performing a pilgrimage to a sacred site (*tīrthayātrā*); and [the rules] regarding the performance of great gifts (*mahādāna*).

The glorification of the merits of Prabhāsa-kṣetra; a description of its superiority over all other sacred sites; an exposition on the various rules regarding the lunar days (tithis); a detailed account of the fruits of giving sixteen specific gifts on each of the sixteen lunar days; a description of the results of death occurring within the Prabhāsa-kṣetra and the qualification for proceeding to the world of Śiva; the recitation of mantras for bathing at the holy ford (tīrtha); and, in the section concerning the procedure for pilgrimage and the majesty of the various holy sites, first, the knowledge of the Jñānavāpī-tīrtha.

The description of performing the shaving of the head and other rites, followed by the statement that bathing again yields twice the fruit even compared to bathing at the Someśvara Tīrtha; the description of the prohibition against women shaving their heads entirely; the description of women removing all their hair except for leaving two tufts on both sides of the head; the description of the seven locations where shaving and other rites are prescribed; the description of the prohibition against women boarding a great ocean vessel without having undergone shaving; and therein, the description of the procedure for offering oblations and other rites following the mantra-accompanied bath.

The description of the greatness and the fruit of the gift of bulls and other animals; the narration of the incident regarding the ocean’s fault of being unapproachable caused by the granting of a boon to the twice-born; when the sacrifice (*sattra*) of the gods was commenced there, those [sages], fearing the violation of the twice-born’s command, considered the ocean to be their refuge and hid their respective bodies within that sea; when the obstruction of their arrival at the sacrifice occurred due to the fault of consuming meat—because the ocean had provided food to them with meat and such—the Brahmins rendered it undrinkable.

The narration of the pronouncement of the curse upon the ocean; the ocean’s offering of prayers to the Brahmin; the account of the establishment of the holy ford (tīrtha) known as Vaḍavānala; the worship of Gaṇapati for one day and the journey to Someśvara; and there, the sixteen-fold ritual worship (ṣoḍaśopacāra-pūjā) of Someśvara.

The description of the ritual injunctions; the description of the majesty of the worship of Someśvara; when the war between the gods and the asuras was set in motion on account of Soma, the departure of the gods, defeated by the Daityas, for the hermitage of Dadhīci; then, the description of the offering of their respective heads to the great sage Dadhīci by all the gods; the description of the procedure for the pilgrimage to Aśvatīrtha; and therein, after performing the bath and other rites, having performed the libations (tarpaṇa) as part of the bathing ritual, [the gods] drank the essence of the bones established there by Kapardin along with Jaḍa, and [received] the boon from Dadhīci.

He went there together with his wife named Subhadrā; then, while staying at that hermitage, Dadhīci put on Bala’s semen-saturated garment and went to the river where Subhadrā had reached her season. There, as Subhadrā was bathing in the river, the semen entered her womb through her bathing, resulting in conception. Then, out of fear, he stood at the foot of an *aśvattha* tree and abandoned the embryo, saying: "By which wicked one—whether knowingly or unknowingly—has the depositing of an embryo been made in the womb of me, a devoted wife?"

"He shall die"—thus was the curse pronounced. Thereupon, the gods arrived there, desiring to extract the horse-sacrifice [the sacrificial horse] from him. Knowing that Dadhīci had performed the act of offering his own body as food for the horse, the gods made an effort to take his bones. Then, for the purpose of fashioning the thunderbolt and other weapons, Dadhīci relinquished his body. Following that—

The gods, led by Indra, took the bones of Dadhīci and fashioned from them their respective weapons, such as the thunderbolt, staff, and noose. Then, because of Dadhīci’s death, the gods consoled Subhadrā, who was overwhelmed with grief. Upon hearing that Dadhīci’s son was Utaṅga, Subhadrā was filled with joy. Subhadrā performed the funeral rites and other ceremonies for Dadhīci. There follows a description of the origin of the four classes of beings: the viviparous, the oviparous, the sweat-born, and the soil-born. Finally, Subhadrā gave her son the name Pippalāda.

Having performed the rites of consecration as prescribed in the Vedas, Pippalāda then made a vow to devour the gods who were chewing betel nut; he then departed for the Himālayas to perform intense worship. For the purpose of creating a *kṛtyā*, Pippalāda produced a mare by churning a fire-pit with a horse. From that mare and stallion, the birth and growth of Vaḍavānala (the submarine fire) occurred. To devour the gods, at the word of Pippalāda, Vaḍavānala went to the city of the gods (*svar*). Then, the gods—

A description of the events concerning the horse Vāḍava, which was praised by Mahāviṣṇu... [including] Viṣṇu’s issuing of a command to the goddess Sarasvatī to restrain the Vāḍava fire toward the ocean, and then Sarasvatī’s taking up the Vāḍava fire and going to the ocean after being pacified by Brahmā.

The crossing of the Sarasvatī by the Vaḍavānala (Submarine Fire); the offering of praise to both the Sarasvatī and the Vaḍavānala by the ocean; when the water of the ocean was being consumed by the Vaḍavānala, the aquatic creatures sought refuge with Kṛṣṇa; Kṛṣṇa’s granting of a promise of safety to them; thereafter, having stood upon the ocean filled with inexhaustible waters, the performance of worship to the gods and Viṣṇu; the description of the descent of the Sarasvatī at Prabhāsa-kṣetra and its greatness; [the location of] the Sarasvatī at the foot of the Pippala tree.

Departing toward the northern direction at night, he then proceeds to the description of the greatness of Siddheśvara and Prācīsarasvatī; there, the Pāṇḍavas circumambulate [the site] facing eastward, and subsequently turn to face westward. Following this is the description of various holy bathing places (tīrthas) situated on the banks of the Sarasvatī, the description of the five streams beginning with Hāriṇī, and the description of the greatness of the Nighnāgama-kani-vīthī along the Sarasvatī.

After the destruction of the Kauravas, Yudhiṣṭhira’s journey to Hastināpura with Kṛṣṇa is described; then, at the time of Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīma, Añjanā, and Ghaṭotkaca’s departure for Gajapura, Yudhiṣṭhira tells the gatekeepers that Nara and Nārāyaṇa must be barred from entry. When Añjanā asks a question out of a desire to know why they should be barred from the gates, they reply to him: "They are to be barred because they are vessels of fault for having caused the death of Bhīṣma and others, as well as the slaughter and burning of Duryodhana and his kin. Thus it is told by Añjanā.

The inquiry made by Aṅga regarding the means for the removal of evil and the performance of expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) directed toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa; thereafter, Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s explanation of the cessation of sin through bathing at the Prācīsarasvatī Tīrtha; subsequently, the journey of Aṅga with Śrī Kṛṣṇa toward the Prācīsarasvatī, where he brought about the removal of his own sins through observances such as fasting for three nights and bathing for three nights; and [the account] of Dharmabhīma, Nakula, Sahadeva, and others, who likewise [acted] after learning of the power of the Prācīsarasvatī.

In that [chapter], there is the arrival [of the sages]; the destruction of the sins of those [sinners] through their bathing and so forth; and a description of the majesty of the Prācī-Sarasvatī. When Śiva was asked by Pārvatī what purpose the throwing of a bracelet into the water serves during the time of bathing, he related the story of Indumatī. In that context, the great sage Kaṇva arrived at the hermitage of Bṛhadratha; after Bṛhadratha had performed hospitality and other rites for Kaṇva, they engaged in a mutual discourse on matters of dharma. Then, [the cause of] Indumatī’s attainment of sovereignty—

Out of a desire to know [the truth], she offered it to Kaṇva; Kaṇva then related the account of Indumatī’s life in her previous birth. In that previous birth, he described how she was a great elephant and how, at the time of her ritual bath at the Someśvara Tīrtha, a bracelet fell from her hand. He explained that by the power of that bracelet’s falling into the holy water, she was born as a princess in another life. Upon hearing those words of Kaṇva, Indumatī—

Having bowed with her face cast downwards, she went silently to her home; then Kaṇva departed for his own abode. Subsequently, Vahadratha, together with Nandumatī, went to Prativai on the banks of the Sarasvatī and performed the casting of the bracelets. By that act, the divine nature of both Vahadratha and Indumatī was described, as well as the glorification of the majesty of casting the bracelets.

The description of the greatness of Kapardīśvara, the destruction of the Daityas by the gods, and Pārvatī’s composition of a hymn; then, following the words of the Goddess, the gods go to holy sites such as Someśvara, perform rites such as bathing, and through the worship of Kapardīśvara, restore their kingdom; the description of the majesty of Kapardivināyaka; in the account of the pilgrimage to Prabhāsa, the journey to the Kedāreśvara Tīrtha after visiting the shrine of Kapardīśvara; and the worship of the two Liṅgas in the vicinity of Bhīmeśvara.

In the description of the great majesty of Kedāreśvara: Śibi’s journey together with his wife; their arrival at Kedāreśvara; there, the king’s performance of the *jāgara* vigil and other rites for the sake of Raibhya and the groups of sages; thereafter, the inquiry made by Raibhya and the others to learn of Śibi’s past-life history and to understand the reason for his departure from Someśvara to come to Kedāreśvara; and finally, the narration by the king of the events of his own previous birth.

The description of his birth as a Śūdra who was unfit for the performance of sacrifices and service to Brahmins; then, the account of himself and his wife traveling to the holy site of Prabhāsa when they were afflicted by hunger and thirst during a time of drought; and there—

Having bathed in all the holy waters (tīrthas) and performed various rites of limb-worship and the like, he then went to Rāmasaras. Every day, he would gather the lotuses found in Rāmasaras, sell them, and sustain himself with that very income. Then, at a certain time, while staying in a palace with his wife on a certain floor, he suddenly heard the sound of a cry for help. Realizing that someone in a certain place was calling for assistance during the night vigil, he [went] there with his wife to sell lotuses.

The journey together; there, [the story] of Vṛddhiṅgin, also known as Kedāreśvara; to the south of the altar of Anaṅgavatī; by that Śūdra, who was the sixth person among those keeping the vigil, the description of the fruits of the Śivarātri vigil to him; then, the description of the attainment of birth in a royal family in another life due to that Śūdra’s performance of the Śivarātri vigil, fasting, and other rites along with his wife; [the story of] Kedāreśvara (Rudreśvara).

Description of the majesty of Digamātā. In the description of the majesty of Bhīmeśvara: Śvetaketu, having performed penance at Prabhāsa, established a linga named Śvetaketavīśvara; subsequently, Bhīmasena, desiring to perform a pilgrimage, worshipped that linga and gave it the name Bhīmeśvara—description of the majesty of Bhīmeśvara. Topics: Description of the majesty of Devamātā-Bhaikheśvara; and of Caṇḍīśa, who was propitiated by the host of Caṇḍas established by Caṇḍa.

A description of the greatness [of the deity] preceded by the exposition of the rules for worship; a description of the greatness of Ādityeśvara; a description of the greatness of Someśvara; a description of the account of the origin of Aṅgāraka from the falling of a tear upon the earth from the eye of Śiva, who was desirous of burning Tripura; a description of the greatness of Aṅgārakeśvara; a description of the greatness of Budheśvara established by Budha; and a description of the greatness of Vṛhaspatīśvara established by Guru.

Having propitiated Rudra with *śukra*, and having obtained the *sajīvanī* mantra through the grace of Rudra, Śukra attained the status of a preceptor (*prahatva*) and established a shrine in his own name; this is the description of the greatness of Śukreśvara in Aṅga.

In this account of the greatness of the Śānaiśvara Liṅga, it is described how Śanaiścara performed the worship of Śiva in order to attain swiftness on his slow day (Mandavāra); thereafter, by the permission of Śiva, Śanaiścara established the Liṅga; and the fruits resulting from the worship of Saurīśvara, such as the removal of afflictions caused by Saturn, are recounted. Furthermore, at one time, having heard from the mouth of Vasiṣṭha that "when Saturn goes piercing the circle of Rohiṇī, there shall be a twelve-year famine," Daśaratha [acted].

In order to dispel that distress, he mounted his chariot, traveled through the path of the sky near the vicinity of Rāśanaiścara, and engaged in battle. When Śanaiścara saw Daśaratha’s chariot and perceived the destruction of all beings unleashed by the weapon of the Eye of Time (*kāladṛṣṭi*), out of fear he said, "Choose a boon. Thereupon, Daśaratha accepted the boon of a prohibition against the breaking of the cart of Rohiṇī by Śanaiścara. After that, Daśaratha performed a hymn of praise (*stotra*) to Śanaiścara, and [the planet] was pleased by the recitation of that hymn.

The discourse on the non-inflicting of pain; the description of the majesty of Raneśvareśvara. The description of the majesty of Rāhīśvara installed by Rāhu. For the sake of attaining lordship over the planets, Ketu propitiated Śiva and, by his command, installed Ketavīśvara to the north of Rāhīśvara; the description of the majesty of Ketavīśvara. [The account of] Soma, who possesses the eightfold supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*, together with his sixty-four companions, for the sake of Soma’s own gratification.

The installation of a *chiga* after propitiating Semiśvara at Prabhāsa near Someśvara; the description of his own sufferings, beginning with the birth of Khathojāta and ending with [the ordeal] by Pārvatī, following the *barārodaśvaraliṅga*; the flight in the ten directions; the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Ajādevī—this constitutes the triad of Rudra’s powers (*rudraśāktitraya*). [Folio 16 recto: The description of the majesty of Jādlīmegakhadevī. . .

The description of the greatness of Tainavīruṅitaumāvīkṣākhākṣī; the description of the greatness of Raudrī, her own goddess; ... Chapter [number]: the description of the greatness of Airaveśvara; the description of the greatness of Lakṣmīśvara; Chapter [number]: the description of the greatness of the Bāḍaveśvara Liṅga; ... [Chapter number]:

the description of the greatness of the Vāḍavānara-dhāriṇī Goddess Sarasvatī, who, having come to the sacred site of Prabhāsa, performed the ritual bathing in the ocean, offered worship, and established the Liṅga; the description of the greatness of Arśvara-liṅga; ... the description of the greatness of Kāmeśvara.

(The description of Pārvatī performing penance in the great forest of Krodhana out of anger toward Śiva; then, the granting of boons by Śiva, who was pleased, to Pārvatī; the description of the greatness of that penance grove and the statement that it yields the fruit of all spiritual perfections; the installation of the *liṅga* there; the description of the majesty of Gaurī’s penance grove; the description of the majesty of the excellent *vara-liṅga* installed by Varaṇa;
the description of the majesty of Īśvara installed by the wife [Pārvatī] who was deeply afflicted by the suffering caused by her husband; and the description of the majesty of Jaḍhavāsa Gaṇapati.)

Having propitiated Śiva in his entirety, the royal sage Śākalya established a liṅga; the names of the sages who performed that rite were Jaireśvara, Sābikesvara, Gākhveśvara, and Śākalyeśvara. [Chapter 15] Contents: A description of the excellent Thakulīramaḍa situated near Kaṭaṭhakaleśvara; how Viṣṇu, having struck down the Daitya Meghavāhana with a kick of his foot, [established a shrine] there under the name Ādinārāyaṇa.

A description of the beautiful temple of Uttankeśvara at Untanka; the construction of a dwelling there; the account of a certain parrot who, having built a nest in a tree together with his wife, describes the events occurring near the river named Saṃnihitā; therein, the residence of Viṣṇu along with his retinue due to fear of Jarāsaṃdha; thereafter, the parrot’s dalliance with his wife within that nest; the departure at dawn from Mathurā; and finally, their arrival on the seashore where Viṣṇu and the others were desirous of hunting.

The description of the attainment of the fruit of merit by performing a ritual bath when the Saṃnihitī [river]—which was brought there effortlessly by Kṛṣṇa through the power of his meditation alone in a previous birth—has arrived nearby; the description of the excellence of Sudrā’s birth as a result of her vow to Agastya; the description of the power of making gifts and other offerings there by Agastya, who remembered his previous birth; and the glorification of the majesty of Saṃnihitī.

The description of Kriṇāphaṭha; the narration of the majesty of Caiśvānareśvara; at the time when [the site] was unknown to the Pāṇḍavas, the arrival of Śambhu and the installation of the Liṅgas by each of the five [Pāṇḍavas] under their respective names; the description of the majesty of Pañcālikeśvara; the description of the majesty of the Liṅga; the description of the majesty of the Gautameśvara Liṅga; the enumeration of the names of the eleven Rudras; therein, the first: the description of the majesty of Bhūteśarudra.

In the description of the glorious Daityasūdana [temple], first is the description of the seven kalpas beginning with Vāmana and ending with Aditisūdana; then follows the description of the majesty of Nīṭaradra. Therein, in the hymn to Viṣṇu by the conqueror of the Daityas, there is an account of the various incarnations of Viṣṇu; thereafter, the description of Viṣṇu along with his discus, and the imperishable description of Kapālīśvara Rudra.

(The defeat of the Daityas with his assistance, the establishment of the Blessed One by the slayer of the enemies of the Daityas; the description of the names of Vṛṣabheśvara occurring in every Kalpa; the description of the majesty of the Liṅga named Vṛṣabheśvara established by the Bull; ... [the description of the majesty]; the description of the fruits of worship such as fasting and other rites performed at Kāśī following the description of its majesty; the narrative of the origin of Cakratīrtha and the description of its majesty.)

The description of the names and designations of the *Ayambakeśvara-māhātmya* throughout the various ages; the bathing, giving of gifts, and other rites at *Udyabakeśvara*; the unification of the gods to create a woman for the purpose of slaying Mahiṣāsura—who had become intoxicated by the boon granted by Brahmā—and the description of the fruit [of those acts];

the description of the *Urayavakeśvara-māhātmya*; Nārada’s acceptance of that woman as his wife and his issuing of a command to Mahiṣāsura; the description of the *Avoreśvara-māhātmya*; and [the account of] Mahiṣāsura, together with his army, having heard [that command] from her mouth.

The departure with her attendants; the description of the manifestation of Mahākāleśvarī; the account of the attainment of supernatural powers (siddhi) by one named Citrāṅgada in the Kṛtayuga at that excellent site; the creation of a female form from her own body by the Goddess after observing the intention of Citrāṅgada; thereafter, the Goddess became famous by the very name Mahākāleśvarī; the description of the greatness of Mahākāleśvarī; the destruction of the demon Mahiṣāsura; and the offering of praise to that Goddess by the gods. Then...

The description of the greatness of Bhairavacrama by the gods; the establishment of that very place therein; the exposition of the ritual for the worship of the Goddess and the recitation of the true mantras; the description of the greatness of the goddess Dugodā; the description of the greatness of Tigrakāra; the description of the greatness of Yogīśvarī; and the description of the greatness of Kāneśvara-liṅga.

The sages, oppressed by the demon named Meṣavāhana, perform a hymn of praise to Viṣṇu; having heard that hymn, [the Lord], out of compassion, describes the majesty of the Yogeśvara Liṅga. The Earth, tormented by the burden of the Daityas, goes to Mount Bhṛbhāsa; there, having established a goat and propitiated Rudra, she receives a boon through the grace of Rudra. [This section concludes with] the description of the majesty of Prathvīśvara (Candreśvara).

While residing in Vārāṇasī, Pauṇḍraka, who bore the insignia of Vāsudeva, boasted of his own greatness by comparing himself to Daṇḍapāṇi and Cakradhara; he challenged Vāsudeva to battle, and there, Pauṇḍraka was slain by Vāsudeva.

Poṇḍu’s son commissioned a *kṛtyā* (magical female spirit) for the purpose of destroying Vāsudeva. Vāsudeva defeated that *kṛtyā* with his Sudarśana discus. Having been vanquished, that *kṛtyā* sought refuge with Śiva. Then, in order to protect the *kṛtyā*, Śaṅkara struck Viṣṇu—who had arrived with his discus—with his own arrows. Seeing Sudarśana returning without having accomplished the task requested by Ikṣvāku, the Lord, filled with wrath, seized the discus—which had been repelled by Śiva’s shafts—in his hand.

The departure of Kṛṣṇa to Kāśī for the purpose of destroying the *kṛtyā* created by Kaṭhabhairava; the residence of Kṛṣṇa there under the name Cakradhara at the request of the hosts of Daṇḍapāṇis stationed there for the protection of the body [of Śiva]; a description of the majesty of Daṇḍapāṇi and Cakradhara; and a description of the majesty of Sāṃbādityeśvara. Therein, Sāṃba—who was born to Kṛṣṇa and Jāmbavatī and was proud of his beauty—insulted Durvāsas; thereafter, the enraged Durvāsas [cursed] Sāṃba.

“Why have you become a leper?”—this was the pronouncement of the curse. While Nārada had come to Dvārakā to take Kṛṣṇa’s discus, Sāmba insulted him out of pride in his own beauty; having settled that enmity, at a certain time when Kṛṣṇa had begun playing in the water with the women, Sāmba suddenly went there upon hearing Nārada’s words. Seeing Sāmba arrive, the wives felt mental agitation toward him, and Śrī Kṛṣṇa, perceiving their state, spoke to them.

“You two shall become oxen in the hands of thieves”—thus was the curse bestowed. Then follows the account of the removal of the evil sin upon Sāmba. Thereafter, remembering the curse previously given by the sage Durvāsas, Sāmba, being deeply distressed, went to the sacred field of Prabhāsa and performed the propitiation of the Sun-god (Āditya). Sāmba offered hymns of praise to the Sun; at the conclusion of the hymn, the Sun-god, being pleased, granted the desired boon to Sāmba and brought about the removal of the evil. [This section contains] the enumeration of the names of the twelve Ādityas, in that very place.

Chapter [X]: The installation of the image of Sāmba by his own son; the description of the majesty of Sāṃvādityeśvara. Chapter [XI]: The description of the majesty of the goddess Kaṇṭakaśodhinī situated near Sāṃvādityeśvara. Chapter [XII]: The arrival of Śaṅkara at Dakṣa’s sacrifice wearing the guise of a mendicant while holding a skull-bowl (*kapāla*); the casting of the skull-bowl into the center of the sacrificial pavilion; the utterance of cries of "Hā! upon seeing the skull-bowl cast there; and then, by Maheśvara [responding] to the praise of the sage Mada.

The manifestation of his own true nature; the installation of the *liṅga* there under the name Kapāṭeśvara; a description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Kapāṭeśvara; how ten million (*koṭi*) Brahmins, having performed penance at Kapāṭeśvara, established a *liṅga*, thereby causing it to become famous by the name Koṭīśvara; a description of the majesty of Koṭīśvara; a description of the majesty of Brahmā; a description of the majesty of Pitāmaha (the Grandfather) in his forms as Bālarūpin and Vṛddharūpin; and thereafter, a calculation of the duration of Brahmā’s lifespan up to two *parārddhas*.

The individual naming of the fourteen Indras over twenty-seven kalpas; the narration of the reasons for Brahmā’s performance of penance at Prabhāsa and the establishment of the *liṅga* there, followed by a description of the installation of the *Brahmayasvara-liṅga*; a description of the greatness of Hiraṇya during the midday pilgrimage; and, in the context of describing the procedure for the worship of Brahmā, a detailed account of the honor and venerability of the Brāhmaṇa due to his distinguished nature, along with the [names of] the fourteen Indras.

A description of the infliction of punishment by Yama upon those who revile Brāhmaṇas; an account of the fruits of protecting the twice-born; a description of the various livelihoods of Brāhmaṇas, such as the Prājāpatya and others; a description of the rules for the performance of vows such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa according to the duties of the four castes; and a description of the disparagement of Brāhmaṇas.

A description of the various kinds of devotion through the offering of betel-leaves (*tāmbūla-pūjā*); an exposition on the procedure for the five offerings (*pañcagaṇya-vidhi*); an exposition on the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *Gāyatrī*; a description of the procedure for worship with the sixteen services accompanied by mantras (*ṣoḍaśopacāra-samantraka-pūjā-vidhi*); a description of the pilgrimage of Brahmā (*brahmayātrā*); the specification of the dwelling places of Brahmā; a description of the greatness of Brahmā in the form of Bālakṛṣṇa; and within the description of the greatness of the *Pryeśvara-liṅga*, [an account] of Viśvānarī, one of the sixty daughters given by Dakṣa to Dharma.

The birth of a son named Vasu, counted as the eighth among the Vasus, from the maiden; the installation of a *liṅga* by that Vasu named Pratyūṣa at Pramāsakṣetra under his own name, followed by a description of the greatness of Pratyūṣeśvara; a description of the greatness of Anireśvara installed by Anira; [110] the installation of a *liṅga* by the eighth Vasu named Prabhāsa, and a description of the greatness of Prabhāseśvara. Oṃ Oṃ Va Ṭū Daraka. Table of Contents.

The *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*: Subjects. Regarding the subjects [of this section]: having propitiated the Lord at Prabhāsa, the four [sages] beginning with Pāśupata attained perfection; the establishment of the *liṅga*; the description of the greatness (*māhātmya*) of the Citrapathā river; the description of the greatness of Citreśvara, who, while still in his physical body, had his eyes plucked out by Yama; and the description of the greatness of Pāḍupateśvara. ...

The account of how the sister named Citrā remained in the form of a river to search for her brother; the description of the origin of the Cicrapathā river; the praise of Śiva by Uttānapāda’s son, Śruva, after propitiating Nārāyaṇa at Prabhāsa; the installation of a Liṅga named Dhevaśvara; the description of the greatness of the Dhuvedavara Liṅga; and the description of the greatness of the Kapardaracintāmaṇi Liṅga.

The description of the various sacred seats (*pīṭha*) and locations within the identity of the Vaiṣṇava power named Siddhalakṣmī; therein, the description of the majesty of Vicitreśvara; the description of the majesty of the Siddhalakṣmī-pīṭha situated in the sacred field of Prabhāsa; the description of the majesty of Vicitreśvara; the description of the majesty of the Mahākālī-pīṭha; and the description of the majesty of Puṣkaraṇḍa.

While the sacrifice of Soma was being performed, Brahmā went to Prabhāsa together with the gods; there follows a description of the greatness of Gajakumbhodra for the purpose of establishing Somanātha. Then, Candra performed the consecration of Brahmā, and subsequently, when the time for the installation of the Liṅga arrived, Pitāmaha [acted] by means of the Chāyā-śāpa.

The establishment of a shrine by Dharmarāja after performing austerities at Prabhāsa; the greatness of the Yameśvara shrine; the mental recollection of Puṣkara during the festival; the arrival of the Puṣkaras there due to that recollection; the naming of that holy ford (tīrtha) as Puṣkarāvarta because of the occurrence of whirlpools (āvarta) therein; the description of the greatness of the river Puṣkarāvartikā; and the description of the greatness of the Brahma-kuṇḍa created by Brahmā.
Regarding the greatness of the form of Kuṇḍalaka, King Sudakṣiṇa, having married Sunandā, the daughter of the King of Gāndhāra, [lived] with his wife Sunandā—

The description of the greatness of the cool speech that brings an end to suffering; ... and not [so], § Dha. Taking joy, she performed vows such as the fast of Śivarātri together with him; therein, the description of the greatness of Lomareśvara established by Māṭhama on that Śivarātri. ... Va, through the description of the greatness of that [place], the merchant's son named Dhana performed the fast of Śivarātri; the description of the greatness of Kaṅkālabhairava and Kṣetrapāla regarding her vow of Śivarātri. ... i.

While the merchant named Dhana was searching for his wife, he encountered the merchant Tṛṇabindu, who had cut off his finger as a sign of penance. Tṛṇabindu had performed austerities for a thousand years, drinking only a drop of water from the tip of his finger every month. He then severed the ear of Dhana’s wife and made her wear a garment of bark; having appointed her as his guardian, he established her in the direction [of the north].

Having heard the news of the cutting off of Karṇa’s earlobes and the resulting clamor, he cut off the skull of Kuṇḍalin. When his father, the scribe named Sapa-mitra, had passed away, Citra, his son, went to Prabhāsa and, having performed worship to the Sun, proceeded to the Anīka-sudarśana [lake] to see that skull. Sudarśana and Sunetra went there to Prabhāsa, and after praising the Sun in various ways, they obtained their desired boons. Then, while he was immersing himself in the lakes for a bath—

The account of the Kuṇḍaṅinakapāṭha; the description of the construction of the Kuṇḍakūpa; the narration of the majesty of the Kuṇḍakūpa. By the command of Yama, the messengers of Yama led Citra with affection to the world of Yama; therein, the description of the supreme majesty of Yama as the lord of living beings. Regarding the ritual of Caritraḍelaka, the establishment of the name Citrarūparetī; the name "Bhramasi Citreśvara"; the installation of the Liṅga; the description of the majesty of Citrāditya. The description of the majesty of Sāvitrīśvara installed by Sāvitrī.

At one time, while Prabhāsa was playing his lute, two drops of saliva fell upon the ground. When Nārada, seeing this, asked Brahmā, "What is this? at Brahmā’s command, Nārada performed severe penance as a supreme expiation for the sin incurred by destroying the sacrificial Brahmins. By the grace of Śiva, he established Bhairava at that spot, and the majesty of Nāradaśvara-Bhairava is thus described. ...

When the sacrifice was commenced by Brahmā, he perceived that the completion of the sacrifice would not be possible due to the absence of materials; therefore, he resolved to perform the propitiation of Śiva in order to obtain the necessary substances. Then, by the command of Śiva, Sarasvatī began to flow in the form of material wealth. Having gathered vast riches consisting of golden lotuses produced from that Sarasvatī, Brahmā brought the sacrifice to completion. It was at that very spot that the deity known as Hiraṇyeśvara was installed. This is the description of the greatness of Hiraṇyeśvara.

Description of the greatness of the *Gāyatrī-hrada* established by Gāyatrī. Description of the establishment of the *Ratnakuṇḍa* by Viṣṇu after performing penance. Description of the greatness of Ratneśvara. Description of the greatness of Garḍeśvara. Description of the greatness of Satyabhāmeśvara. Description of the greatness of Anaṅgadeva established by Anaṅga. Description of the greatness of Ratnakuṇḍa. Description of the greatness of Aśvineśvara. ...

In the first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of Sāvitrī," Śaṅkara describes the origin of the Vedas and other matters; then Brahmā makes preparations to perform a sacrificial rite (*yajña-karma*); thereafter, Nārada arrives at the Puṣkara pilgrimage site and prepares the sacrificial ground; and although the Adhvaryu priest sends an invitation to Sāvitrī for the sacrifice, Sāvitrī issues a command to him, saying, "I will not go alone. Regarding the subsequent matters concerning Ambā: [the text continues].

[She] became engrossed in the duties of her own household; then, because of that delay, [she] said to Brahmā, "Sāvitrī does not come! Thereupon, overcome with anger, Brahmā issued a command to Śakra to bring another wife. Then Śakra took a certain cowherd girl and brought her into the presence of Brahmā. Subsequently, Brahmā married that cowherd girl and commenced the sacrifice. Then Sāvitrī, surrounded by celestial women, went there to that sacrifice.

Savitri, having become angry because her husband had begun a sacrifice after marrying another woman, cursed Brahma for his failure to prevent it despite hearing her words; she then cursed Indra for appointing an Abhira woman to prevent the river from overflowing, resulting in Indra’s defeat by his enemies in battle; and likewise, Savitri [cursed] Vishnu.

The bestowing of a curse by Sāvitrī that causes separation from her husband; likewise, the bestowing of a curse upon other gods by Sāvitrī; Viṣṇu’s offering of praise to Sāvitrī; Gāyatrī’s granting of boons to all [the gods] for the sake of removing the curse imposed by Sāvitrī; the description of the various methods for the recitation (*japa*) of Gāyatrī; Sāvitrī’s journey to Prabhāsa; and the description of the majesty (*māhātmya*) of Sāvitrī residing in the sacred field (*kṣetra*) of Prabhāsa. ... (Ṭha).

Now follows the description of the greatness of the Vata-Savitri-vrata. Thereupon, King Ashvapati performed the worship and propitiation of Savitri in order to remove his childlessness. By the boon granted by the pleased Savitri, a daughter named Savitri was born to King Ashvapati. Through her own merit, that Savitri chose Satyavan alone as her husband.

"Vyāmīti" means making a firm resolve. In this regard, Nārada related to Avanti the entire account of Satyavat’s virtuous conduct; then followed the description of the marriage between Sāvitrī and Satyavat. Subsequently, at a certain time, Satyavat went to the forest with Sāvitrī to gather sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, and other items. While he was splitting wood, a headache arose; thereupon, Satyavat left the wood right where it was, approached Sāvitrī, and fell asleep. Then Yama arrived.

Description of the dialogue between Yama and Sāvitrī: Yama extracts the life-force (jīva) from Satyavat’s body and departs; Sāvitrī follows Yama; and although Yama employs various means to dissuade Sāvitrī from following him, she persists.

The granting of a boon to Sāvitrī upon seeing her firm resolve; the liberation of her husband from Yama through his grace; the description of the three nights, the regions, and the attainment of tranquility at the banks of the Travaṭa river; Sāvitrī’s departure with her husband to her own hermitage; the description of the great power of Sāvitrī’s vow, rituals, worship, charity, and so forth; the narration of the concluding rites (*udyāpana*) for Sāvitrī’s vow; and the description of the greatness of Bhūtamātṛkā, including the account of Pārvatī’s birth on Mount Daśāpāda during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara.

The description of the birth of one daughter from Pārvatī’s *rajas* while Pārvatī and Śaṅkara were sporting for a thousand divine years after their marriage; the description of that daughter’s physical form; the description of the names of her other female companions; and likewise, the description of the birth of one male being from Śiva’s seed.

The command given by Śaṅkara to those two sons of Śiva to go to Prabhāsa; the granting of a place for their residence; a description of the festival occurring on the first lunar day; a description of the emergence of five crores of innumerable monkeys from the body of that Bhūtamātā; and a description of the greatness of Bhūtamātākāmā. (Chapter 80)
The description of the majesty of the Śaivasvateśvara Liṅga. ... [End] ||

After Daśaratha performed austerities, he established the lineage of the ten lords of the chariots (Daśaratheśvara). Regarding the greatness of Daśaratha’s boon, Bharata, the son of Āgnīdhra, divided the island into nine parts and assigned them as principalities for his nine sons. Among those, in the ninth part at Prabhāsa, which was formerly known as Kaumārika, Bharata established Bharateśvara; this is followed by a description of the greatness of Bharateśvara.

Description of the majesty of Karākeśvara, Gargaśava, Puṣkareśvara, Satrayeśvara, and others; description of the majesty of Kuntīdvāra as spoken by Kuntī at the time of the arrival of the Pāṇḍavas accompanied by Draupadī at Prabhāsa; description of the majesty of Arakasthara; description of the majesty of Siddheśvara; description of the majesty of Veśvara; [page numbers]; topics of the Bhavyā chapter; description of the majesty of Māṇḍavyeśvara and others. “` (.

The description of the greatness of Puṣpadanteśvaraga; the description of the greatness of Śetrapāḍedavara; and the description of the greatness of the opening of the venerable mouth of the host of Mothers at Vamunandā.

The description of the greatness of Nisaṅgama; the description of the greatness of Mekīdavara; the description of the greatness of Devamādanaurī;—having heard that Kṛṣṇa had met his end after performing the destruction of the Yādavas, Balabhadra’s journey to Prabhāsa, where he installed a Liṅga; then, having assumed the form of a serpent, Balabhadra’s departure to Pātāla through Vidavāra, whereby that Liṅga was given the name Nagivara; and the description of the greatness of the Nagivara Liṅga.

A description of the greatness of Prabhāsa-pakva; therein, Śiva’s journey to Dārakavana for the sake of instruction; a description of how the sight of Śiva’s form as he wandered in Dārakavana kindled the passion of the women there; then, by their husbands who were filled with anger, a curse was cast upon Śiva; by that curse, his fall occurred right there; a description of the trembling of the earth caused by that fall; and the destruction of all the inhabitants, including the great Bhava and the others.

The departure of Moticandra toward Viṣṇu; then, by the word of Viṣṇu, his journey to Prabhāsa and the establishment of that [liṅga] in that very place; and the description of the greatness of the Amareśvara door after visiting the Prabhāsa-pañcaka.

The section describing the greatness of Vṛddhaprabhāsa: the sages’ journey to Prabhāsa for the purpose of seeing the gods; their performance of penance there at Vajreśvara; the removal of the sages’ old age through that penance; the granting of a vision of the gods to them by the satisfied deity; the departure of the sages to their respective abodes after beholding the gods; the naming of the place Vṛddhaprabhāsa because the sages were burned away by their penance due to their advanced age; and the description of the majesty of the confluence at Vṛddhaprabhāsa.

The establishment of the Paraśurāmeśvara Liṅga by Paraśurāma after performing austerities; a description of the majesty of the Jaṭhaprabhāsa Liṅga; and a description of the majesty of the Jamadagnīśvara Liṅga.

(Description of the Greatness of Pañcaprabhāsa-kṣetra: In the description of the greatness of Śrītasmara, first is the account of Dakṣa’s arrangement of his hundred sons; then, when Dakṣa commenced a sacrifice, Pārvatī, perceiving her own insult, performed the abandonment of her body; thereafter, Śiva, having become enraged, manifested Vīrabhadra and dispatched him along with his armies for the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice; and when the battle had commenced there—)

The gods, defeated by Vīrabhadra, went to the Ocean of Milk near Viṣṇu; thereupon Viṣṇu engaged in battle with Vīrabhadra. Seeing Vīrabhadra somewhat defeated there, the enraged Śiva arrived at that place. Upon seeing that Śiva had arrived, Viṣṇu and the other gods fled. Then Śiva brought about the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.

Then follows the journey to the vicinity of the Lord of the Gods, who was oppressed by Tāraka; the kindling of desire in Śiva’s mind by Brahmā’s command; the dispatching of the god of love (Kāmadeva) by the gods; the reduction of Kāma to ashes by Śiva upon seeing him as his own adversary; the consolation of Rati, who was overwhelmed with grief at the separation from her husband, by a celestial voice; the establishment of a linga there; the description of the greatness of Smaradahana, also known as Kāmakuṇḍa; and the description of the greatness of Kāmāraṇya at a certain time.

When the war between the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas had commenced, Balabhadra, having drunk liquor for the purpose of setting out on his journey, went to the forest. There, having seen many sages and a *sūta* residing in a hermitage, he disregarded them; then, seeing the Lord [Viṣṇu] concealed, the sages were filled with grief. The sages made a determination regarding the pilgrimage to Hṛṣīkeśa, followed by a description of the majesty of Śabarādri and a description of the majesty of Maṅkīśvara, as well as a description of the majesty of the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean.

—The description of the performance of the *śrāddha* rite; the description of the proper time for the *śrāddha*; the description of the examination of Brahmins; the description of the extraction of the seven types of poison; the description of the days suitable for the *śrāddha*; the exposition of the *pārvaṇa* and other rites; the description of Brahmins worthy of being invited to the *śrāddha*; the slaying of Sūta by Balabhadra, who could not endure the insult offered to him when the worship of Sūta was performed during the *śrāddha*; and thereafter, the verse uttered by Balabhadra out of remorse, as a voice from the sky spoke.

Having heard that instruction, he went to Prabhāsa and, having performed austerities for the sake of removing his faults, established a Liṅga in his own name; in the section describing the greatness of Maṅkīśvara at Rāma, it is told how Maṅki established a Liṅga at Prabhāsa to dispel his state of being a Kuṭaja tree; in the description of the rules for Śrāddha, there is an account of the praise of the rule of silence; then follows the description of the food used in Śrāddha, and the detailed determination of the censure of specific months and times for Śrāddha.

The description of the necessity of companionship in the rite of *śrāddha*; the description of the various types of *śrāddha*; the description of the fruit and majesty of giving food, water, and other offerings on the day of *śrāddha*; the consideration of worthy and unworthy recipients in the act of giving; the explanation of duties for those of mixed castes (*varṇasaṅkara*); the explanation of the performance of religious duties during times of distress and illness; the description of the faults incurred by engaging in sexual intercourse and other acts on the day of *śrāddha*; the consideration of gifts to be given under such circumstances; the description of the rules for the vow of *Ekādaśī*; and the performance of the offering of the six *piṇḍas* and other rites.

Description of the majesty of Mākaiṇḍeyeśvara; description of the majesty of Pukhustyeśvara; description of the majesty of Puheśvara; description of the majesty of Kratīśvara; description of the majesty of Kadyapeśvara; description of the majesty of Kaurikeśvara; description of the majesty of Kumāreśvara; [from] the Skanda Purāṇa; topics of the Bhaviṣya [Purāṇa]; description of the majesty of Gautameśvara.

The description of the greatness of Devarāja-īśvara; the description of the greatness of Māntrada-vara; the description of the greatness of Nīlakaṇṭha-īśvara located near Mārkaṇḍeya; and the description of the greatness of Vṛṣabhadhvaja-īśvara-liṅga.

The description of the majesty of Ṛṇamocaneśvara; the description of the majesty of Rakmavatīśvara; the manifestation [of the deity] there under the name Gātrotsarga due to Balabhadra’s casting off of his own limbs; the description of the majesty of Gātrotsarga; the description of the majesty of performing *śrāddha* and other rites at the holy site of Gātrotsarga; therein, within the description of Pretatīrtha, Gautama’s journey to the Gātrotsarga-tīrtha; and on that path, Gautama’s making of a well for the thirsty. Therein...

The terrifying encounter with five ghosts in the forest by Gautama; the dialogue between Gautama and the ghosts; the ghosts’ narration of their own history and the cause of their state as ghosts to Gautama; Gautama’s arrival at the Pretatīrtha in Prabhāsa by their command after hearing the reason for their condition and performing the *śrāddha* rites for each of them; the description of how those ghosts attained liberation through that act; and the glorification of the greatness of the Pretatīrtha.

Description of the majesty of Indreśvara; in the description of the majesty of Anarakeśvara: Yama’s command to his own messengers to bring Devaśarman, the Brāhmaṇa residing in Madhurā; then, after having brought that Devaśarman, Yama’s repeated command to his messengers not to bring him back; the manifestation by that Brāhmaṇa of his lack of desire to go to the earth; and then, upon being questioned by that Brāhmaṇa, Yama’s description of hell to the Brāhmaṇa.

The description of the faults such as sins that lead to hell; the narration of the ripening of karma (*karmavipāka*); the narration of the means of merit for liberation from hell; the description of the majesty of Anarakeśvara, Megheśvara, and Balabhadreśvara. Chapter 228: The description of the majesty of Mairaveśvara; the description of the majesty of Gaṅgā; the description of the majesty of Gaṇapati; the description of the majesty of the Jāmbavatī river; the description of the majesty of Pāṇḍavakuṇḍa; the description of the majesty of Pāṇḍaveśvara.

The establishment of the *Ṛgveda* by Bharata after performing ten horse-sacrifices; the greatness of the Daśāśvamedha Tīrtha; the description of the greatness of the Durbāseśvara Liṅga installed by Durbāsas; the performance of a sacrifice by the Yādavas who had assumed their true forms at the word of a single Ṛṣi; the pronouncing of a curse upon the Yādavas and Andhakas by the sages overcome with anger, which brought about their destruction; and finally, the description of the destruction of the Yādava host by means of *erakā* grass.

Then, after the destruction of all the Yādavas, the one known as Vajra—the survivor among those Yādavas—performed the funeral rites for them; having gone to Prabhāsa, he established an image [of Kṛṣṇa]. [The text then contains] a description of the greatness of the Vajreśvara Liṅga, a description of the greatness of the Hiraṇyā River, a description of the greatness of Nāgarāditya preceded by the account of the Syamantaka jewel, a description of the greatness of Varabhadra, Subhadrā, and Kṛṣṇa, and a description of the greatness of Śeṣa...

Nor [does it contain] a description of the slaying of Caṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and others; nor a description of the most delightful greatness of the Goddess preceded by such descriptions; nor a description of the greatness of the Mantras, the Bahiṣpārṣadas, and the Pārṣadas; nor a description of the greatness of Nandīśvara; nor a description of the greatness of the Piṅgā River. Chapter One.

And furthermore: Regarding the objects of the *abhvā* [the non-existent], there is the description of the churning of the ocean by the gods and demons; having churned the ocean and set aside the moon, after all the gods had consumed the nectar (*amṛta*), the remaining portion was seized by Rāhu. Upon seeing that the moon was swallowed by the demon, and after the attainment of immortality, the making of the moon [into the emblem] is described. Then follows the description of the greatness of the Lord of the Mountain (*Girīśvara*) at the confluence of the rivers. *Bh.* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa).

The drinking of water from the *Abhitavaṭāka* well situated at Sṛtamakharva by the gods; the arrival of Akhaṇḍapāśupatācārya at that very spot while he was traveling on horseback; the digging of a well in that same location and its naming as the *Śarāpāna-kūpa*; 2. A description of the majesty of the Śarāpāna [well]; 1|259. A description of the majesty of Parṇāditya; 1|260. A description of the majesty of Siddheśvara; a description of the majesty of Nyaṅkuvatī.
