Description of the majesty of Nedinīguā. ... Description of the majesty of Kanakanandā. ... Having ascertained [the truth], the women took an oath of truth; there, Śuka arrived in the form of a dog, and the description of the arrival of the excellent lord of the Imbhis. The description of the arrival of the excellent son of Yaṅga. The taking of the blue garment and the gift of a cow to them by Koṇa. Thereupon, the arrival of the noble Kāriīrya and the description of the giving of the *camasa* vessel. The establishment of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). The description of the arrival of the noble Ṛṣitīra. ...

The Description of the Greatness of Vidūratha’s Son. By means of this [son], who was struck by a disease, the construction of a stone chariot was undertaken. Having approached the Sarasvatī river from the west with his army, when his father had passed away, he established Niṣṇātra, the son of Trita, in the kingdom. Trita, having harbored resentment toward him, caused a conflict between Ekata and Dvita; however, Trita, having invoked the Bhāradvāja gods there, brought satisfaction to them through the very power of Manu’s wrath. By that—

The extraction of Sāraṇa from the well by Bahiṣmān; the description of the origin of Tritakūpa; the description of the greatness of merit through performing funeral rites (*śrāddha*) and other ceremonies at Trita; the description of the greatness of Vikapa-tīrtha; and how, thinking that [the dance] had begun while he was dancing, Śaṅkara arrived there and, having understood Maṅkaṇaka’s reason for dancing, caused ashes to fall upon him from his own hand; and how Maṅkaṇaka, filled with wonder, ceased his dancing. Then—

Description of the greatness of Ripuraṅga; narration of how Agastya consumed Vātāpi, who had assumed the form of a ram through deceit; description of the greatness of Āgastya-bhāsa; description of the greatness of Iauḍa-tīrtha; description of the greatness of Baśrama-gaṇeśvara; description of the greatness of Sūraya-prācī; description of the greatness of Bākhārka situated to the north of Agastyeśvara; and description of the greatness of Trinetreśvara.
Description of the majesty of Ajāpāṭeśvarī; ... [description of] Devikā; ... description of the majesty of Vālārka situated at Agastyāśrama; ... description of the majesty of Bhūdharayajñavarāha. ...

A description of the greatness of the three *liṅgas* named Pātāka-Gaṅgeśvara, Viśvāmitreśvara, and Bāḍheśvara; the account of how a certain Brahmin named Vaiśākha, having lost his own wealth, maintained his family by practicing the duty of a hunter; a description of the majesty of Somanātha established at Chaveranagara by that same Vaiśākha; how he once, when his enemies were arrogant, performed the worship of the Lord; and thereafter, how the sages instructed him regarding Vaiśākha, followed by a description of the greatness of Nītibhadrakāṭī.

Having instructed him, he imparted the mantra to him; by the power of that mantra, his name was changed from Vāsmṛki to Bhadrakāṭya, and he came under the influence of the greatness of Bālāka. ... ra ||
The description of his attainment of perfection by that Vālmīki, O Goddess—||

The description of the greatness of Kuyarasthānotpattikuyera; the description of the greatness of Kāmādātmayavarbha; the description of the greatness of Mūḍhalsthānanāhātya; the description of the greatness of Puṣyeśavara; the description of the greatness of Paravakramajogandheśvara; the description of the list of one hundred and eight names of Sūrya; the fruit of reciting the one hundred and eight names of Sūrya within the greatness of Cyavanāditya; the description of the greatness of Canadarodakatī; the description of the greatness of Pūmkinnera; and the description of the greatness of the river Ṛṣitoyā.

The story of Sukanyā’s marriage to Aṣṭāvakra and Ādavibhyām; how, when her husband’s beauty and youth had faded, she caused them to be restored through the grace of Śiva; the search for Sarasvatī by the two of them in the Devadāru forest at the command of Brahmā; the performance of penance by Cyavana together with Aṣṭāvakra and Ādavi in a pool according to their word; the description of the drinking of the waters of the Ṛṣitoyā; the description of the attainment of a beautiful form; and the description of the boon granted by Cyavana.

Description of the three sections known as Jāyava, Vaiṣṇava, and Raudra; description of the greatness of Gupraprayāga; and the description of the majesty of Śayobhāva by the great sage Cyavana for the purpose of establishing the authority of the two celestial youths who had rendered him assistance. Chapter 66.

The performance of a sacrifice by Tiddhāra; therein, in that sacrifice, the description of the greatness of the *saṅgārada* jewel, which was released by Cyavana to obstruct the Nāsatyas from receiving their share of the sacrifice; the account of the emergence of the great asura named Kātyoddhavamadana for the destruction of Taraka; and the description of the greatness of Siddheśvara.

Seeing that the great Daitya had arrived at his own hermitage, Śakra made a request to Cyavana; thereafter, Cyavana described the greatness of the boon granted by the Lord of the Gandharvas. Having surrounded the sky, he sought forgiveness for Śakra’s transgression. [This is followed by] the description of the glory of Uttareśvara and the description of the glory of Sukanyāsaras.

The topics of the subsequent chapters [beginning] from the description of the greatness of the Gaṅgā located near Sammārtha: the giving of a curse by Sāmba upon seeing his own self as devoid of power; the bestowing of a curse by Sāmba upon Nārada, saying "Become one who is subject to old age"; the worship of the Sun performed by Nārada after learning about old age; the description of the greatness of Unnata-svāmin; the installation of a Liṅga at that very place in Śrabhāsa; and the description of the greatness of Nāradāditya.

Description of the majesty of Makṣakaṭha; therein, the establishment of a Liṅga by Soma after performing penance to remove his own curse; the description of Sāṃvāditya...; the description of the majesty of Da... Saṃgameśvara; the description of the majesty of Aparanārāyaṇa; (f. . the description of the majesty of Unnata-Vināyaka; (f. . d) the description of the majesty of the origin of Mūla-Caṇḍīśa; da ... the description of the majesty of Talasvāmī. ha i .
The description of the greatness of Catuḥkhavināyaka; ... the description of Kālameṣa-māhātmya; the description of the greatness of Kevaḍeśvara. (||)

...the description of the greatness of Vaḍha-Hātaṃya; the description of the greatness of Maṅkiṣṭhayāsata; the description of the greatness of Uttarāka; then the battle between Viṣṇu and Smatala; the description of the greatness of the confluence of those two with the Ṛṣitīrtha; ... (and then) the construction of the temple of Vāṅmaṇḍanī; the description of the greatness of the goddess Pithamardāyī; ... .

The granting of a boon by Viṣṇu to Nana-pa-tadūṭa; the establishment [of the deity] there under the name Taṭa-caṇāttaṅasvāmī; a description of the majesty of that Svāmī; a description of the majesty of Kaṇṭakaśoṣaṇī; and a description of the majesty of the Śaṅkhāvarta Tīrtha.

The description of the greatness of Brahmaśavara; the description of the greatness of Goṣpada-tīrtha; the description of the birth of Pṛthu from the son of the god [Dharma]; the description of the greatness of the place where the seed was sown by Pṛthu; the description of the milking of the Earth in the form of a cow for the sake of producing that [seed] by Pṛthu; the shattering of the mountain by Pṛthu, who acted like a father toward his son; and the description of the greatness of Chigaṃdvatha.

Pṛthu, repeatedly recollecting his father’s sins, wandered through many sacred fords and holy sites (*tīrtha-kṣetra*) in order to purify them. Thinking that his father’s sins might not have been washed away anywhere else, he went to the Goṣpada ford. Therein lies the description of the greatness of Durgā. By performing ablutions and other rites at the Goṣpada Tīrtha, Pṛthu shook off all the sins of his father and attained liberation (*mokṣa*).

The description of the greatness of the Goṣpada-tīrtha; the performance of penance by the sage Āpastamba in the waters of the Sarasvatī; the description of the greatness of Nārāyaṇaguhā; the dragging away of Āpastamba by Jāḍa, Nāpa, and Vahni; then, the performance of the Prāyaścitta (expiatory rite) by Āpastamba when he was censured by Dhīva, Aimeya, and Mīta; the description of the greatness of the gift of a cow (*godāna*) in the dialogue between Āpastamba and King Ambarīṣa regarding the payment of the price for Āpastamba; in that same place, the description of the greatness of Jāleśvara; and the installation of a *liṅga* under the name Jāleśvara.

The description of the greatness of the *Hṛkārakūpa*. The description of the greatness of *Caṇḍīśvara*. The description of the greatness of *Āpūravinnarāja*. The description of the greatness of the *Candareśvara-karāṇḍa-tīrtha*. The description of the greatness of the procedure for the sixth vow (*ṣaṣṭha-vrata*) at *Kapiladhārā* and *Kapiṭeśvara-Kapiṅga*. The description of the greatness of *Jaradraveśvara*. The description of the greatness of *Naledavara*. Herein is the description of the greatness of *Karkoṭakārka*, and the description of the greatness of *Hāṭakeśvara*.

— Description of the Greatness of Nāradeśvarī. Description of the Greatness of Mantravibhūṣaṇā-Gaurī. Description of the Greatness of Durgakūṭa-Gaṇapati. ... — Description of the Greatness of Kauraveśvarī. Description of the Greatness of Suparṇeśa. Description of the Greatness of Mahātīrtha. ... — Description of the Greatness of Karamāṭha. ... — Description of the Greatness of Rāparaścara. ... — Description of the Greatness of Bahusuvarṇeśvara.
Now, in the Bhaviṣya-khaṇḍa, the second [section]: the Greatness of Vakhāpatha (Giranāra).

In this section on the majesty of Dāmodra, many sages arrived at the house of a certain king named Rajasāṃhañjaka; there, the king questioned the sages regarding the greatness of various sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and fields (*kṣetra*), and [the text describes] the majesty of their names.
Thus ends the first section, the delightful Prabhāsa-kṣetra-māhātmya, within the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa.

[Then follows] the description of the discovery of the treasure during the third hunt. A certain forester reported to King Bhoja that he had seen a cow, a goat, and gold. Upon hearing this, King Bhoja gave much wealth to that forester. Then, having gone to that forest with the forester, Bhoja took that crooked young girl and went to his own home. Thereafter, Bhoja questioned that young girl regarding the cause of her human body being so crooked and deformed.

In that *Akūyana* sacrifice performed by Bhoja, there was the offering of the *prabhakaraṇa*. Then follows the description of the account of both previous births, clearly related by Sarasvatī while she was eating the *puroḍāśa* consecrated by the *Sārasvata* bull; this occurs during the conversation between Sarasvatī and King Bhoja, in the context of her describing her own origin. Therein is the departure for another forest by Udāravarmā, who was filled with passion for her; there, his [Bhoja’s] seed fell into a drop of water. There, by a certain woman, that drop of Udāravarmā’s seed was consumed. Then...

The narration by Mṛgānanā to Bhoja regarding her own birth from Udālaka; the description of the greatness of various holy sites such as Dvārakā, Cakratīrtha, and others; and the account of how Mṛgānanā attained a divine form in Suvarṇadvīpa through the offering of a boar’s head in her previous birth, followed by her marriage to King Bhoja, along with the glorification of Suvarṇadvīpa.

In the dialogue between Rāma and Sārasvata regarding the dispute over the elder brother, there is a description of the destruction of Jarāsandha at the word of Viṣṇu; then, in the narration of the story of the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha) by Viṣṇu, there is a description of the destruction of that sacrifice; followed by a description of the birth and marriage of Pārvatī. Then, on one occasion, having seen Śaṅkara disappear, Viṣṇu and the other gods set out with Pārvatī—who was mounted upon a lion—to search for Śiva. Thereafter, they [arrived] at Prabhāsa, in the sacred field of Bakāpatha.

The vision of Śaṅkara; the establishment of his own form at the Vakhāpatha-kṣetra by Roka under the command of Viṣṇu and others, with the name Bhava; a description of the greatness of the origin of Bhava; a description of the instructions given by the sage Sārasvata to King Bhoja, who was desirous of making a pilgrimage to the Vakhāpatha-kṣetra; a description of the sequence of the pilgrimage to the Jañjāyathaka-kṣetra... [and] the statement of the fruits [to be gained] at Bhīmiśvara, Skāndrāmeśvara, and other holy sites, as well as a description of the rules for pilgrimage.

[The text describes] the description of the fruits of bathing, giving, recitation, fire-offerings, and honoring the gods and brahmins there; the arrival of Vasiṣṭha at the city of Vāmana after performing austerities on the Golden Line (Svarṇarekhā) for the sake of his son’s grief, and his subsequent departure from that very place by the grace of Śiva to the banks of the Sarasvatī; and thereafter, how Viṣṇu, assuming the form of a dwarf (Vāmana) at the request of the gods, caused the sinking of Bali by taking three strides of land in the assembly of Bali.

Having propitiated Somanātha, [the Lord] established the quarters; on the day of the moon (the new moon), Vāmana went to the Ravatka forest to receive the gift from Dāmodara. There, having worshipped him together with [Dāmodara] and performed the rites of bathing, giving, and so forth, he then traveled northward to the Vasnapatha region to reach the abode of Dāmodara. Having performed a vigil there, he proceeded toward Siddha. [The text then contains] a description of the greatness of the vigil observed for Dāmodara.

Then follows the journey of Manu into the dense forest; his travel along the path, which includes visiting various sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and shrines (*kṣetra*); the vision of Śiva; the description of the dialogue between Śiva and Vāmana; the narration by the divine Vāmana of the excellence of Indreśvara; the description of the greatness of Śivarātri; the exposition of the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) for the Śivarātri vow; and the departure of Nārada for Brahmaloka. There, having been told by Nārada that the splendor of Devendra is even greater than his own, Indra’s mind was [filled with wonder].

Having agitated the ocean at the time of its churning, and having caused even Bali—the one deceived by the gods—to be reminded [of his duty], Nārada approached Śakra in the celestial realm and spoke to him in the same manner. Having mutually provoked each other with harsh words and the like, Nārada explained the conduct of royal policy, such as the use of spies and stratagems. Then, by means of a description of the Śataśṛṅga mountain, he led [Śakra] to the mountain Kamadudaka situated to the south of Bharata, where the Lord resides in the temple of Viṣṇu; there, [Śakra] beheld the Lord.

Having seen this, the Lord, knowing that he would effect the subjugation of Bali through the form of the Vāmana incarnation, observed the daily arrival of Hari; by his power, he established the two deities Hara and Hari right there on Mount Kūṭaśṛṅga, and granted boons to Hara and Hari for that mountain. Then, during the Vaivasvata Manvantara, when the son of Raivata named Revata was born, the sage Ṛtadhvaja, having been deceived by a fool, engaged in a dialogue with Garuḍa regarding the fault of the foolishness of his own son, who was born of Revatī.

The dragging down of Revatī’s husband by the sage Kacha through the casting of his own gaze; thereafter, the birth of a son known as Revata from the digging of the earth; Nārada’s narration of the procedure for Vaiṣṇava vows, vigils, and so forth; likewise, having performed the Vaiṣṇava vows and vigils without [proper initiation], Bali, in order to cause the destruction of the wicked, summoned the Jāṅgamas with the permission of Śukra and undertook the commencement of a sacrifice; a description of the power of Bali’s sacrifice; and an exposition on the methods of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and other practices.

An eightfold description of the origin of *prakṛti*; an exposition of the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*) according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine; a narration of the methods of meditating upon Bhava; the arrival of Nārada before Vāmana while he was staying at the abode of Bhava; Nārada’s recounting to Vāmana of the entire history of Bali’s sacrifice and other events; Vāmana’s rebuke of Nārada for his habit of instigating futile quarrels; and Nārada’s description to Vāmana of the state of existence at the end of the kalpa.

The narration of the deeds concerning the slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa and others; then, at the word of Nārada, Vāmana, having arrived at the city of Bali, requested from Bali—though he was disguised as a dwarf—three paces of land, and thereafter, by binding himself, pervaded the entire cosmic egg with his own self and performed the subjugation of Bali; in the dialogue between Sarasvatī and Bhoja, following the subjugation of Bali, Viṣṇu’s abiding within Bali’s heart; and the greatness of the Vastrāpatha Kṣetra—thus ends the second section on the greatness of the Vastrāpatha Kṣetra in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata-khaṇḍa.
Now, within the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa, the section concerning the Ṭhṛlīya-ma-vuda.

The commencement of the description of the greatness of the Abudācaṅku; therein, first, Vasiṣṭha’s journey to Abudācaṅku; having performed austerities there, his sacrificial cow, having gone to the forest to graze on grass and such, falls into a chasm; because the cow does not return in the evening, Vasiṣṭha becomes anxious; then Vasiṣṭha, approaching the vicinity of the chasm and hearing the lowing of his own cow, performs meditation upon the Sarasvatī for her emergence; by that meditation, the Sarasvatī...

Having filled the hole with his own blood, he caused the cow to emerge; taking that cow, he went to Vasiṣṭha’s hermitage. Then, having gone to the Himavat mountain to fill that hole for Vasiṣṭha, he related the extent of the cave to Himavat, and by the command of Himavat, the account of the origin of the Śarabha was told. This is the description beginning with the story of the opening located near Vasiṣṭha’s cave, concerning Uttaṅka, a disciple of Gautama, who sought to give the preceptor’s fee to his teacher’s wife.

At the request of his brother, Kaṇḍarīka set out for the house of Saudāsa to bring back the earrings of Saudāsa’s wife, Madayantī. There, seeing Saudāsa—who had assumed the form of a tiger to devour his own body—he made a vow to give himself over to him. Subsequently, he obtained the earrings from the queen; however, due to Saudāsa’s curse, he lost his memory. Then, as the disciple of Gautama was returning with the earrings, he placed them in the middle of the road, where they were seized by Takṣaka.

The abduction [of the children]; then, Takṣaka’s journey to Pātāla for the sake of bringing them back; at that very time, the filling of the void by the mountain brought from Himavat at the command of Vasiṣṭha, as if by a divine wind; and thereupon, the performance of penance by Vasiṣṭha on the mountain named Ābaddha for the purpose of establishing a dwelling for Śiva; and then, by Vasiṣṭha, through the grace of Śiva, the mountain was established under the name Aṭṭahāsa.

The description of the greatness of Nāgatīrtha in the dialogue between Yayāti and Śukra; the description of Gautamī’s journey to Nāgatīrtha with her husband; how, because her heart was agitated by the desire for a son as she set out to find one there, she conceived a child in secret; then, when she was about to enter the funeral pyre out of grief, she was dissuaded from death upon hearing a voice from the sky; and the description of the greatness of Nāgatīrtha and the greatness of the Vaṃśiṣṭha-āśrama.

[Description of the nature of Kedāreśvara... Description of the greatness of Aṭṭahāsa, Karṇahradatīrtha, and Netramāhātmya; in the description of the greatness of Kedāra, Vasiṣṭha’s narration to Ajāpāla regarding his previous births as a Śūdra and how he attained the status of kingship in this life through the worship of Lord Kedāra; description of the greatness of Kedāreśvara; description of the measurements of the bull [Nandin] and other matters; examination of the duties of the four ages; and the power of all holy places due to the influence of the Kali age.]

Description of the journey; description of the identity of Keṣṭī with Caramā; the attainment of a beautiful form by the Apsaras named Capū through bathing at Sūpatīrtha; and a description of the greatness of Rūpatīrtha.

In the description of the greatness of Harṣakiṃśa: the royal sage Ambarīṣa, having performed austerities, installed an image of Hari; a description of the grace bestowed by Daśīkeśa; a Siddha named Viśvāvasu, having propitiated Śiva, installed Kiṅga through Śiva’s grace; and a description of the greatness of Siddheśvara-kiṅga. [Furthermore,] seeing the Daityas defeated by the gods, the preceptor of the Daityas, Śukrācārya, being overcome with anxiety regarding the victory of the Daityas, propitiated Kara and obtained his hand, thereby effecting the victory of the Daityas at that very place under the name Rukeśvara-Ṛṣi.

The installation of the Liṅga; the description of the great beauty of Śukeśvara-kṣetra—these constitute four chapters. The subjects include: the attainment of her true form by a certain woman named Maṇikarṇikā through the practice of knowledge, and the extensive narration of the section (khaṇḍa) known as Maṇikarṇikā; the description of the majesty of Maṇikarṇikeśvara; and the description of the majesty of Paṅgutīrtha—the establishment of a holy site (tīrtha) by the name of a certain Brahmin named Kenavirtava, who had become lame, after he propitiated Śiva and was cured of his lameness.

The water entered the mouth of Citrāṅgada, who had committed an exceedingly great offense; thereupon, the messengers of Yama seized the sinner Citrāṅgada and cast him into hell. By the casting of Citrāṅgada into hell, the living beings there experienced a surge of happiness. Then, having seen this immediately and observed it with his power of knowledge, Yama reflected in his mind: "By performing a bath in my sacred ford (tīrtha), he shall experience the cessation of the sufferings of that hell right here."

His liberation from hell; then the departure of Citrāṅgada to heaven by means of a celestial chariot surrounded by hosts of Apsarases; a description of the greatness of Yama-tīrtha; a description of the greatness of Vārāha-tīrtha; the granting of the Yakṣma-disease-inducing curse by Dakṣa to Candra because of his partiality toward his own daughters; then the performance of penance by Candra; the cessation of his Yakṣma disease through that penance; and the installation of a Liṅga by Candra under the name Candrabhāsa.

Description of the greatness of Candrabhārabhāsītīsa; description of the greatness of Piṇḍodaka-tīrtha; how the Dānava named Karika, having conquered the gods, performed propitiation and attained heaven through the grace of the Goddess; placing a mountain peak upon his body, the Goddess made her abode on its summit; the gods’ establishment of Śrīmātā as the Goddess; and the description of the greatness of Śrīmātā.

Next is the majesty of Śuklatīrtha: there, because the clothes thrown into the middle of the river by a washerman attained whiteness (*śuklatva*), that sacred ford was given the name Śuklatīrtha; then follows the description of the majesty of Śuklatīrtha. After the goddess had slain the demon Niśumbha, she remained there on the Avadācala mountain, whereupon she was established by the gods under the name Kātyāyanī; then follows the description of the majesty of Kātyāyanī. (Skanda Purāṇa, Māheśvarakhaṇḍa). [The topics of the Puja-bhavyā and Para-bhavyā].

The description of the greatness of Piṇḍāraka-tīrtha; the naming of it by Śiva as Mahāvināyaka; the description of the greatness of the Mahāvināyaka-kanakhala-tīrtha; the narration of its proximity; the description of the majesty of Mahāvināyaka; the glorification of Cakratīrtha; the description of the greatness of Pārtheda-vara; and the description of the splendor of Manuṣyatīrtha.

While Brahmā and Viṣṇu, who were vying with one another and fighting, were engaged in combat, the king Suprabha, intent on hunting, pierced with an arrow the doe that was suckling her fawn in their midst; thereafter, the origin of the Liṅga from that tooth is described; then, by means of a voice from the sky, they were made to desist from their battle, and [the deer] was restored to the king.

The pronouncement of a curse, saying, "You shall become a hunter"; the statement of a wager that whoever sees the end of the king's life-span shall be great; the acquisition of false knowledge by Brahmā in the presence of Śiva; in that very forest, the narration of the story of a certain cow named Kapilā who had lost her calf, and Śiva’s bestowal of a curse of unworthiness upon Brahmā because of that; likewise, the description of the conversation between the tiger and the monkey.

Then, near the tiger, Kapikhyā [the female monkey] was about to give a portion of the Brahmin’s food; at that moment, someone gave him a curse. Then Viṣṇu, having entrusted [her] to his own place, went to the cow, made her drink milk, and told the calf the news of what had happened in the forest regarding the granting of the boon by Śaṅkara. Thereafter, the greatness of Kṛṣṇatīrtha was described. Having summoned [the calf], he saw the calf-grazing in the forest; then, having restrained the calf, he [spoke to] his friends.

The description of the account of the birth of Māsuhaṭā. ... Having arrived and related everything to her friends in the presence of the tiger, she was prevented from departing by them; nevertheless, when the Goddess was pleased by the propitiation performed with the teeth of Mahiṣāsura which had been brought by her friend, she carried out the slaying of Mahiṣāsura. Disregarding even that place, she returned to the vicinity of the tiger. Seeing the cow’s state of being truthful and eloquent, the gods, their eyes wide with wonder, [named the place] Caṇḍikāśrama.

A description of the account of the installation [of the deity]; a description of the majesty of Caṇḍikāśrama; the granting of life to Gave by means of that very ritual action; the liberation from a curse for him alone; the renown of that very place by the names Kapittha and Nava; the origin and majesty of the Śivagaṅgā pool; a description of the majesty of Annitīrtha; and, preceded by a description of the majesty of Śivariṅgamahedavara, a description of the majesty of the gift of barley-meal (saktu).

For the sake of destroying Indrasena’s night and seizing his wealth, he wandered in a foreign land; then, through a messenger, Indrasena’s wife Rati caused him grief by burning the God of Love (Kāma). Having heard that grief born of separation from Rati, the messenger spoke words of salutation and reported that the king was well; thus, the destruction of Indrasena’s wife [was described]. Then follows the account of how Kāma, desiring to avoid the sin of killing a woman, restored himself to life by becoming bodiless (anaṅga); and how he established a residence on Mount Kailāsa together with that Rati.

The destruction of Kāma by means of the Somatīrtha and other holy sites located at Prabhāsa; the account of Indrasena going there and describing the greatness of the *Ivara* (Lord Śiva); the description of how, due to the absence of the removal of sin, one becomes bound by sin only through bathing at the Raktānubandha Tīrtha; the narration of the story of Mārkaṇḍeya’s birth and so forth, preceded by an illustration of the origin of the hermitage of Mārkaṇḍeya; the description of its greatness; and the description of the greatness of Uddālakerava. The [account of] Udvanaja.

The seizing of Pārvatī by the demon Ḍepa and his attempt to make her a child’s plaything; the description of the greatness of Siddheśvara due to Pārvatī’s absence from that place; Rohiṇī’s perception that this was a child and her placing him upon the shoulder of a certain intoxicated elephant; the description of the power of Gajatīrtha; and the description of the origin and greatness of Śrī Devakhāta.

... Description of the majesty of Vyāsatīrtha; description of the majesty of the Gautamāśrama-tīrtha; description of the majesty of the Kuṅasaṃtāraṇa-tīrtha, preceded by the narrative of King Indumatyaprastuta; description of the majesty of Parañyurāma-tīrtha; ... description of the majesty of Koṭitīra; description of the majesty of Candrodbheda-tīrtha; ...
description of the majesty of Īśānīśikhara; description of the majesty of the origin of Brahmapada; description of the majesty of Radrhada; description of the majesty of Aviyuktakṣetra.

When Sūta was questioned by Śaunaka and others as to where Viṣṇu’s place of residence would be in the Kali Yuga, he described the condition of the world during that age. Having performed his incarnations and other deeds there, when the infinite Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa had returned to His own abode, [Sūta] observed that the Dharma had become almost extinct; reflecting in his mind on how those like himself would survive, he spoke these words to the sages. Upon hearing those words of lamentation, [he explained] the means for people oppressed by the limbs of the Kali age to attain liberation.

The departure of the sages who were desirous of joining Brahmā; the performance of a hymn of praise by the sage Uddālaka Āruṇi; then, the narration by the sages of the reason for their arrival as asked by Brahmā; at that time, Brahmā’s reply, "I do not know the abode of Viṣṇu"; having heard Brahmā’s reply, the sages’ attempt to give up their lives; then, Brahmā going with the sages into the presence of Prahlāda; and Prahlāda’s reception of all the sages and Brahmā as guests.

The sages, out of a desire for the happiness of Brahman, explain to Prahlāda the reason for their arrival; the sages express their anxiety to Prahlāda regarding the activities of the Lord in the Kali age; Prahlāda provides an answer to the sages by describing the commencement and duration of the Kṛta age; having heard that Uddhava had departed on a journey to the bank of the Gomatī after the conversation between him and Kṛṣṇa had concluded, and that Duvasas was returning there, the sages set out to see Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā and to meet Duvasas. The manifestation of the power of the Lord to Durvāsas by Kṛṣṇa; then, after exchanging mutual inquiries regarding their welfare, Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s earnest entreaty for Durvāsas to visit Dvārakā; Durvāsas’s disclosure of his own disposition to Kṛṣṇa, who was requesting his arrival; nevertheless, due to Kṛṣṇa’s extreme persistence, the description of Durvāsas setting out for Dvārakā after appointing Rukmiṇī and Kṛṣṇa to the task of driving the chariot; and in the midst of the journey, Śrī Kṛṣṇa [comforting] Rukmiṇī when she became thirsty.

By treading upon the surface of the earth with his foot, he pierced the underworld; from Bhogavatī, he brought forth [the hair-tuft] that was dear to him. Then Rukmiṇī consumed the hair-tuft brought by Śrī Kṛṣṇa from Bhogavatī. Duryodhana, thinking, "Did Rukmiṇī take the hair-tuft without my command? and being unable to endure it, cast a curse upon her.

Then Durvāsas was made to descend from his chariot and stand upon the ground by Varada; thereafter, Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī consoled Durvāsas. Then, having led Durvāsas to his own home, [Kṛṣṇa] offered him the water used for washing the feet of that sage and performed the offering of *arghya*. There follows a description of the procedure for the offering (*ānava-vidhi*), a description of the greatness of the ritual bath (*snāna*) preceded by the worship of the Viśvedevas, and how one’s own body is rendered fulfilled through that washing.

Description of the greatness of bathing at the confluence of the Gomatī; description of the majesty of the Lord residing on the banks of the Gomatī. Having heard the curse uttered by Durvāsas against Rukmiṇī, she was filled with great sorrow; Nārada’s arrival at that place; description of the greatness of Rukmiṇī-tīrtha. After Nārada had enlightened Rukmiṇī in many ways, [he stayed] with Rukmiṇī at Rukmiṇīśa-tīrtha.

In the description of the greatness of the Chṛkaṭāsī Tīrtha, it is told how King Geṇa, having performed sacrifices and other rites, ceased those activities permanently and went to the Bhāgīrathī Tīrtha for the sake of liberation; there, in the Rukmiṇī-vana situated on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī, a detailed account is given of how he joyfully performed thousands of gifts of cows. Then, having heard the story of Jaimini—a sage dwelling in a certain forest—and of Rukmiṇī, the king reflected, "How could the word of a dog be false? and with a steady mind, he performed the gift of cows.

Then, having gone from her house to the assembly of the Naga kings, Durvāsas made a gift of the cow to Bhāgīrathī, to Rukmiṇī, and to the other trees standing in the forest; subsequently, Nṛga caused that very cow to be given to another Brāhmaṇa. As he was departing taking that cow, Rukmiṇī made a firm resolve to die. Knowing Rukmiṇī to be intent on death with a rope around her neck, Garuḍa carried Śrī Kṛṣṇa there. Then—

Durvāsas also, having felt remorse within himself, thinking "What have I done?", approached Rukmiṇī; [the narrative describes] the departure of Śrī Rukmiṇī and Kṛṣṇa to the forest grove of Raivataka, then the bestowing of a curse upon the King by the two of them saying "Become a lizard," the pacification of that curse through forgiveness, the liberation of Rukmiṇī from the sorrow of the curse, and so forth.

The lifting by Śrī Kṛṣṇa with his own hand of King Śṛga, who had fallen into the state of a hog due to his enmity toward Vena; the mutual granting of boons by Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Duvasu on the banks of the Gomatī for the sake of benefiting the people through their respective sixteen clans; the granting of a boon to King Cagara; the departure of Śṛga to heaven by means of a celestial chariot through the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; the construction of a temple there; and therein, a description of the greatness of the Gomatī bank, along with a brief account of Dvārakā and Mathurā.

Description of the Greatness of the Nṛgatīrtha, also known as Chṛkalāsa. — Description of its greatness; therein, within the dialogue between Bṛhaspati and Indra, the occasion for describing the greatness of Kaṭhikāla; therein, the description of the greatness of Viṣṇupada-tīrtha; [and] by means of various gifts such as water, food, and clothing at Kaṭhikāla, [there is the removal of] obstacles such as madness and fever caused by spirits.

In the description of the greatness of the Gopracāra-vīrtha, it is told how the Gopīs spoke to Uddhava, the husband of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of inquiring after his own welfare; Bṛhaspati’s conciliation of the gods at the Senāndra sacrifice; the procedure for the pilgrimage to Dvārakā; and the sending of Uddhava to the cowherd settlement (goṣṭha) for the purpose of instructing the Gopīs. Then, seeing that Uddhava had arrived, the Gopīs offered him hospitality, including a seat and other honors, and questioned him regarding the reason for his coming.

In the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Sanatkumāra, following the description of the Lord’s pastimes at Dvārakā through the power of Sanatkumāra’s asceticism, there is the crossing of the Gomatī River; then Uddhava, having explained the reason for his arrival and the welfare of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the others, describes the greatness of the cowherd women’s grief. ... ha nama ...

The act of consoling; the description of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s dark complexion by the gopīs individually out of fear of breaking their affectionate anger; the description of the procedure for the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; and the description of the greatness of bathing, giving gifts, and feeding brāhmaṇas. ... The subjects of the chapters are as follows: the arrival of Śrī Kṛṣṇa at the lake where the grief of the gopīs had been allayed; the description of the greatness of the Candra-tīrtha situated on the bank of the Gomati river; the manifestation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s form to the gopīs; the bathing, giving of gifts, and worship performed by the gopīs in that lake during their conversation with Śrī Kṛṣṇa; the description of the greatness of the Moon (Soma) temple at Mayanibheta; and the exposition of the mantras for the ritual procedures of the *cakra* and other rites.

Right there, by the command of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, other lakes were constructed by the cowherds. Then, the Daitya Rañca arrived at that place; seeing that Daitya who had arrived, Śrī Kṛṣṇa established his own residence right there at the Gopī-saras for the sake of that Daitya’s subjugation, according to his own pleasure. By Śrī Kṛṣṇa, through his own bliss...

The severing of the head by the circle of teeth of the foremost of cowherd women; the description of the battle with other demons after seeing that Daitya slain by Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma; then the description of the battle between the demon Śarāda and Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa; therein, the description of the majesty of Brahma-saras, the description of the majesty of Indra-saras, and the description of the majesty of the Pañcanada-tīrtha.

The description of how Śrī Kṛṣṇa captured the Rākṣasa Chuśura, placed him upon his back, and established a divine image (diviriga) over him; the description of the greatness of Ṛṣitīrtha and Siddheśvara. The worship of Rukmiṇī; a description of the excellent [sacred] sites; a description of the greatness of the holy places situated on the banks of the river rising from that [site]; a description of the hearing of the fruits of the story of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; a description of the fruits of beholding Śrī Kṛṣṇa in Dvārakā; a description of the sequence of the ritual for the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī; a description of the attendants of the Lord, preceded by an account of the group of servants such as Sudāmā and others; a description of the fruits of remembering the departure for Dvāravatī; [and] the desire to go there oneself.

A description of the greatness of the city of Dvārakā as it were a ladder, followed by a narrative concerning the moonstone (*candrakānta*); therein, a description of how even the merit of sacrifices, gifts, breath-control, and recitation of the Vedas is surpassed by the sight of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; and upon seeing the futility of various vows while traveling through the city of Dvārakā, his parents came to him in a dream and [spoke] to him.

A brief description of the events concerning the subduing of Vaṅin during the narration of the Kṣmatīrtha; the imparting of instructions by Cakra at the confluence of the Gomatī; the arrival of Durvāsas at the holy site while wandering among many other tīrthas after the Brāhmaṇa Candradharman had gone to Dvārakā upon hearing the instructions of his ancestors; the description of the deliverance of the ancestors from hell as soon as Durvāsas became aware of it; the statement of the fruits of taking refuge in Dvārakā; and the departure for Dvārakā.

The account of Durvāsas being struck with a shoe by Bali; then, the description of the greatness and the power of wearing *tulasī* for Durvāsas who was distressed by that shoe-stroke; [the account of] Bali going to Pātāla to inform his father of his own wretched state; the description of the pride and majesty of the city of Dvārakā through the acceptance of the boon granted by Kṛṣṇa upon the arrival of the children; and the narration of the events concerning himself as they occurred at Cakratīrtha to Vāmana.

...in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Durvāsas, [it is said]: having heard the words of Durvāsas, Vāmana—due to being dependent on another, thinking "I have no independence at all"—consoled Durvāsas by saying: "O Brahmin, I am not independent; I am subject to the will of others. Thus he spoke to Durvāsas.

Having spoken thus, and having delighted [Bali] by saying, "If there be the command of King Bali, then I shall come for the sake of destroying the Daityas," [the sage] described the means for uprooting the fourfold sins born of anger and other vices, and gave a description of the characteristics of a devotee of the Lord. Then, Durvāsas bowed down to receive the command of King Bali; thereafter, Bali did not accept Durvāsas's request for alms, but instead took hold of the feet of the Lord. Then, the Lord, after increasing His own form, [bestowed it upon] Durvāsas.

The journey to Cakratīrtha together with Balabhadra; and there, at Cakratīrtha, following the arrival of Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma, and Durvāsas, a description of the performance of the hospitable rites (*sānāhika-vidhi*) for Durvāsas.

The results of keeping a vigil (jāgara); the results of giving gifts such as cows, land, sesame seeds, and clothing; the results of daily recitation of the *Bhāgavatam*, the life stories of the Gopīs, the *Gītās*, the *Nāmasahasra*, and the *Svarakādi*; the greatness of the vigil on the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī-jāgara*), including the description of its supreme excellence even over other forms of worship; the chapters and topics; the description of all the gods, holy fords (*tīrthas*), and sacred sites (*kṣetras*) coming to the place of the vigil on the twelfth lunar day dedicated to Viṣṇu; and the greatness of the vigil on the twelfth lunar day.

The inquiry made by Gautamī, who had fallen into impurity through contact with sinful people, to the sages headed by Nārada regarding the means to dispel her own impurity; the distress of Gautamī upon finding those sages, beginning with Nārada, unable to provide an answer to her question; the divine voice speaking to Gautamī, telling her to go to Dvārakā for the sake of removing Gautamī’s suffering; and then, preceded by an eagerness to travel to Dvārakā, the description of the Gomatī river.

The description of the festival procession for the arrival of the great sages Nārada and Gautama toward Dvārakā; the description of the arrival of all the holy places (*tīrthas*) there; the manifestation of Dvārakā in embodied form; the performance of circumambulation by Nārada and other perfected ones out of joy upon their arrival at Dvārakā; and the performance of circumambulation in Dvārakā by Śaṅkara and other deities, as well as by sages such as Gautama who had reached the banks of the Gautamī and other sacred sites.

The undertaking of the praise of the Blessed One; a description of the dwellings established at various sacred fords (*tīrtha*) such as Kārīṣagaṇya, Prayāga, and others on all sides around Dvārakā; a description of the greatness of the pilgrimage to Dvārakā preceded by the account of the ascetic who was liberated from the mass of sins committed in his body merely by the sight of a wretched traveler from Dvārakā; a description of the greatness of the moving and non-moving entities situated in Dvārakā; the greatness of the Dvārakā region;
the greatness of the Blessed One’s presence in Dvārakā; and a description of the greatness of the name "Dvārakā."
Thus ends the table of contents regarding the subject matter contained within the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa.

Chapter 1: Description of the procedure for bathing at the Gomatī river in Dvārakā. Chapter 2: Description of the marks of the discus on the face of Sudaśana residing in the city of Dvārakā, the knowledge of the Gomatī, and the description of the worship of Kṛṣṇa, devotion to ascetics, charity, *śrāddha* rites, and other such practices. Chapter 3: Description of the fruits of performing rites such as the *vṛṣotsarga* (the ritual release of a bull) and hearing the greatness (*māhātmya*) of Dvārakā. Thus ends the fourth section, the Dvārakā-māhātmya, within the Śrī Paramasaṃhitā.
Thus ends the seventh section, the Prabhāsakhaṇḍa, of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa.

Since the reality of the Self (*ātmavastu*) is of the nature of pure existence (*sat-tva-rūpa*), it is devoid of distinctions; and because the clod of earth (*loṣṭa*), stone (*aśman*), and gold (*kāñcana*) are essentially of the nature of pure consciousness (*cid-ekarūpa*) within the Supreme Reality, they are equal through their identity with consciousness. Thus, the meaning is that some praise that ignorance in which the clod, stone, and gold are equal—namely, that ignorance wherein the clod, stone, and gold are regarded as identical.
